```
  256x128x64_1x2_h       732.9 - 747.5   spread 2.0%   ~747 TF
```

**`rs2` run alone is perfectly stable at ~746 TF.** The bimodal 734/666 only appeared when it ran *third*, after two other configs in the same process. So it isn't allocation alignment or cluster placement — it's **state carried between configs inside one process**.

That matters far beyond this one config:

```
                        sweep (254 cfgs, one process)   isolated    error
256x128x64_1x2_h              757 TF                     747 TF     -1.3%
256x128x64_1x2_h_rs2          751 TF                     746 TF     -0.7%
128x256x64_1x2_v              672 TF                     728 TF     +8.3%   <- badly under-measured
```

**The entire 3,905-run sweep was taken with 254 configs running back-to-back in one process** — and it under-measured at least one config by 8%. The 15 tier-1 rows we pinned yesterday were selected from that data.

This is the same class of trap already recorded in `project_test2_measurement_traps` — the leaked split-K arena that degraded cuBLAS and made a config look 288% better than it was.

And the real numbers are *better* than we thought. On `down-fwd`, our best is **93.4% of cuBLAS** (747 vs 800), not the 86–89% the sweep implied.

Let me find what state is leaking, because if it lives in our library it affects production too, not just the benchmark:
> tool `Bash`: Look for persistent state that could leak between configs

No leaking state in our library — every `static` hit there is a `constexpr` helper. So the contamination is in the harness, not in BluBLAS. Good news for production.

But this **invalidates the premise the whole campaign was built on.** Recomputing `down-fwd` with isolated measurements:

```
                         sweep said    isolated (real)
our best (256x128_1x2_h)   757 TF        747 TF
cuBLAS                     809 TF        800 TF
                        -> 93.6%      -> 93.4%
```

We are **6.6% behind on this shape**, not the 30% I've been quoting. The "69.6% same-variant gap" came from `128x256x64_2x1_v` measuring 566 TF in a contaminated sweep — it's ~682 even in the noisy multi-config run and we haven't yet measured it clean.

Let me get the honest same-variant number:

```bash
# SERVER — isolated, 5 samples each, the configs that matter for down-fwd
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=7
for cfg in 128x256x64_2x1_v 256x128x64_1x2_h 256x128x64_1x2_h_rs2 128x256x64_1x2_v 192x192x64_1x2_h; do
  printf "%-24s" "$cfg"
  for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
    ./build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --shape=16384x2048x5632 --layout=nn --cfg=$cfg 2>&1 \
      | awk '/^(128|192|256)x/{printf "%s ", $6}'
  done
  echo ""
done 2>&1 | tee h27z_test2/t1_isolated.log
```

The first line is the one that matters — `128x256x64_2x1_v` is cuBLAS's variant in our coordinates. Against cuBLAS's 800 TF it gives the true same-variant gap for target #1.

## What this means for the plan

**The sweep is a shortlist tool, not a selector.** It runs 254 configs in one process and mis-measures by up to 8–10%, unevenly. It won't promote a genuinely bad config into the top 10, so it's fine for narrowing 254 → 10. It is not fine for choosing the winner among close candidates — which is exactly what we used it for.

**The 15 tier-1 rows were chosen from that data.** Not necessarily wrong (on this shape the sweep's rank-1 and rank-2 are the isolated top two, just 6 TF apart), but not trustworthy either. Re-deriving them properly is ~150 isolated runs — top 10 candidates × 15 shapes, roughly 25 minutes — and that's cheap for removing a systematic error from the thing we ship.

**And the gap may be much smaller than we thought.** If 6.6% on `down-fwd` is representative, then a campaign framed around "we're 15–30% behind on identical variants" was chasing a measurement artifact. I want the isolated numbers for a couple more shapes before saying that's general — but it's the direction the evidence points, and I'd rather say so now than after we spend a week on ncu.

on the strategy , i changed the approach from adding new variants to first making our existing ones stronger , the reason is that we already own 5 of the 6 variants cublas uses on this model , and when i measured our kernel running cublas's own config it was slower than our own tuned pick on every one of the 21 call sites , so the gap is not about missing variants , it is about our implementation of the same variant being slower , so the plan is to make it apples to apples first , build the identical configuration cublas uses , find where we lose , fix it , and only then run the cross comparison tests again to pick the best variants , i also decided not to touch the dispatcher during this work , it stays at yesterday's measured 96.4 percent and all the experiments run standalone

first finding is that our comparison table was wrong , cublas is called with swapped operands everywhere , in our test harness and in blutrain both , so cublas's M is our N , which means the tile it reports as 256x128 is actually 128x256 in our terms , and the cluster and rasterization flip the same way , after correcting this the number of call sites where we run the same tile as cublas drops from 13 out of 21 to 4 out of 21 , and on 11 sites cublas is running the exact transpose of our tile , that is 43 percent of our gemm time where we were never running their tile at all

second finding is two things that stop us matching cublas exactly today , the pipeline depth parameter in our kernel is dead code , it is declared in the template and mentioned in a comment and used nowhere else , so the depth is always derived from shared memory no matter what is passed , and we cannot reach cublas's 4 stages on the 128x256 and 256x128 tiles because our epilogue keeps the whole output tile in shared memory which eats the space , cublas keeps only a small slice , the other thing is split-k which is registered only on the 64x64 tile , the machinery itself is tile independent so it is only a registration gap , both of these are fixable and are part of the plan , not separate work

third finding is the important one , the benchmark harness was mis-measuring , the gpu clocks were not locked so the first configs in a run got boost clocks and later ones did not , and worse , when several configs run inside one process the earlier ones affect the later ones , our main config measured 746 tflops when run alone and swung between 666 and 735 when it ran third , after locking clocks at 1620 mhz and running one config per process everything became stable within 1 percent , this matters because the 3905 run sweep we used to pick the 15 tier-1 rows ran 254 configs back to back in one process , so it has up to 8 to 10 percent error and it under measured one config by 8 percent

what this changes is the size of the problem , on the first target shape our best config measures 93.3 percent of cublas when measured properly , not the 86 percent the sweep said , and cublas's own variant running in our kernel measures 86.1 percent , not the 69.6 percent i had been working from , so the gap on identical variants is about 14 percent and our overall gap on this shape is under 7 percent , i had been about to spend days profiling a 30 percent gap that was mostly a measurement artifact , the good part is our pinned config for this shape turned out to be within 0.15 percent of the best one anyway , so yesterday's dispatcher table is not wrong here

next is to re-measure the top candidates for all 15 shapes properly with locked clocks and one config per process , that is about 150 runs and 25 minutes , the sweep is still useful for narrowing 254 configs down to 10 but it cannot be trusted to pick the winner between close ones , after that i will know the real gap per shape and can start the actual kernel work on whichever one is genuinely behind , everything is documented in sections 57 , 58 and 59 with the rollback point recorded so we can always get back to today's state

```bash
The 3905-run sweep that selected the 15 tier-1 rows ran 254 configs back-to-back inside one process, and that mis-measures. 128x256x64_1x2_v reads 672 TF in the sweep and 728 TF run alone, an 8.3% under-read, while 256x128x64_1x2_h_rs2 reads 751 against 746 - so the error is not a constant offset and it is large enough to reorder close candidates, which is exactly what the sweep was used for.

Two separate causes. Clocks were unlocked, so the first config in a process ran on boost and later ones settled. And state carries between configs within a process: 256x128x64_1x2_h_rs2 holds a stable 746 TF when it is the only config in the process and swings between 666 and 735 when it runs third. ### CLAUDE [2026-08-10 11:14 IST]
```

Good question — let me be precise, because it's partly a knob and partly not.
> tool `Bash`: Read the epilogue store-buffer write path

Straight answer: **it is not a portable knob like the other features.** Here's exactly how it works.

## Why it's different from cluster/raster/swizzle

Those are real template parameters that reach the kernel:

```cpp
_CLUSTER_M, _CLUSTER_N   -> Config::CLUSTER_M/N   -> used
_RASTER, _RASTER_SWIZZLE -> Config::RASTER...     -> used
_SWIZZLE_BYTES, _C_BOX_N -> Config::..._OVERRIDE  -> used
_SPLIT_K                 -> Config::SPLIT_K       -> used
```

`_LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH` is **dead code** — declared, documented, referenced nowhere. Depth is always computed from shared memory:

```cpp
LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH = (231424 - STORE_BUF_BYTES) / STAGE_BYTES
```

So there's nothing to "port". Depth is an *output* of the smem layout, not an input.

## The actual blocker is the shared-memory layout

```
today:   [ stage0 ][ stage1 ][ stage2 ][ c_buf = full BM x BN tile ]
           49152     49152     49152     65536                        = 212,992

needed:  [ stage0 ][ stage1 ][ stage2 ][ stage3 ][ small c_buf ]
           49152     49152     49152     49152     <=34,816           <= 231,424
```

The epilogue buffer `c_buf` sits **after** the pipeline stages at `smem + LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH*copy_size`, and is laid out `[BN/C_BOX_N][BM][C_BOX_N]` — every chunk resident at once, both warpgroups sharing it and owning disjoint chunk ranges.

To get the 4th stage, `c_buf` must hold **2 chunks instead of all of them**:

```
256x128 with C_BOX_N=32, double-buffered:  2 x 256 x 32 x 2 = 32,768  -> depth 4
128x256 with C_BOX_N=64, double-buffered:  2 x 128 x 64 x 2 = 32,768  -> depth 4
```

## So the work is a kernel change, in four places

1. `STORE_BUF_BYTES` becomes a function of `C_BOX_N` and buffer count, not `BM*BN`
2. `c_buf` indexing changes from `[NCHUNK][BM][C_BOX_N]` to `[2][BM][C_BOX_N]`
3. the epilogue loop restructures from *write-all-chunks → store-all → wait-once* to *write chunk → store → wait-before-reuse*
4. the two warpgroups currently share one buffer with disjoint chunk ranges — with only 2 slots they now contend, so that needs a barrier or per-warpgroup slots

## But — and this is the important part — it's **one** change, not per-kernel

`LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH` is derived, so the moment `STORE_BUF_BYTES` shrinks, **every tile gets a deeper pipeline automatically**. `128x256` and `256x128` go 3→4, `128x128` goes 6→7, `128x176` 4→5. No per-variant work, and it unlocks targets #1, #2 and #6 together — 16 sites, 27,440 launches, 58.8% of our GEMM.

## Two real risks

**Correctness.** Reusing a chunk slot before its TMA store retires is silent corruption — right answers most of the time, wrong under timing pressure. Needs strict `tma_store_wait<1>()` discipline, and validation that doesn't fall into the zeroed-C trap from §H27z.48 (a harness that memsets C can't see unwritten tiles).

**It may not help.** §H27z.57 records the evidence: on the two 192x192 sites where our stage count *already equals* cuBLAS's, we're still at 73–92%. Equal depth, same gap.

## So I'd do it in two steps, and the first is an hour

**Step A — make `_LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH` real** (fix the dead parameter, ~20 lines). Then force depth **2** on `128x256` — which fits today (`2×49152 + 65536 = 163,840`) — and compare against the natural 3.

- 2 ≈ 3 → depth is saturated, the 4th stage buys nothing, and we skip Step B entirely
- 2 clearly worse than 3 → depth is on the critical path, Step B is justified

**Step B — the epilogue restructure** (the four changes above, plus validation).

Step A isn't a detour from your plan — it's the cheapest way to know whether Step B is worth days of risky epilogue surgery, and it also fixes a parameter that currently lies about what it does. Shall I write Step A?

Agreed — that's the right way round. Let me find out what we already have to work with.
> tool `Bash`: Inventory the reference sources we already have

All three references are here. Let me research the actual question: how does CUTLASS avoid paying for the epilogue buffer out of the pipeline budget?
> tool `Bash`: Check how CUTLASS lays out mainloop vs epilogue shared memory

CUTLASS uses a **struct**, not a union — so it also adds epilogue + mainloop. Which means the trick must be in how big its epilogue tile is:
> tool `Bash`: Read CUTLASS SM90 epilogue shared storage sizing

That's the answer, and it's a first-class template parameter in CUTLASS:

```cpp
class EpilogueTile_,                        // (EPI_TILE_M, EPI_TILE_N) — a SUB-tile of the CTA tile
static_assert(CTA_M % EPI_TILE_M == 0);
static_assert(CTA_N % EPI_TILE_N == 0);

make_shape(EPI_TILE_M, EPI_TILE_N, StagesC)   // C smem
make_shape(EPI_TILE_M, EPI_TILE_N, StagesD)   // D smem
```

Epilogue smem = **EpilogueTile × Stages**, not `BM×BN`. Plus a `ReuseSmemC` flag that aliases D onto C. Let me get the default sizes CUTLASS actually picks:
> tool `Bash`: Find CUTLASS default EpilogueTile and stage counts for SM90

**Found it, and it cross-validates against cuBLAS's measured smem.** CUTLASS's `EpilogueTileAuto` for a cooperative schedule:

```cpp
tile_m = min(128, CTA_M)
tile_n = gcd(min(32, CTA_N), CTA_N)
StagesD = min(EpiTiles, 2)          // double-buffered
```

So for a **256x128** CTA tile: `EPI_TILE = 128 × 32`, 2 stages →

```
128 * 32 * 2 bytes * 2 stages = 16,384 bytes
```

And we **measured cuBLAS's 256x128 kernel** at 213,188 total with 4 stages → `213188 − 4×49152 = 16,580` left for epilogue + barriers.

**16,384 predicted vs 16,580 measured.** CUTLASS's formula reproduces cuBLAS's shared-memory layout to within 200 bytes. That's not a guess any more — we know exactly what cuBLAS is doing.

## What it gives us

Our epilogue buffer is `BM×BN×2` = **65,536** for 256x128. CUTLASS's is **16,384** — 4× smaller. Substituting:

| tile | our store today | CUTLASS-style | our depth today | new depth | cuBLAS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 256x128 | 65,536 | 16,384 | 3 | **4** | 4 ✅ |
| 128x256 | 65,536 | 16,384 | 3 | **4** | 4 ✅ |
| 128x128 | 32,768 | 16,384 | 6 | **6** | 6 ✅ |
| 192x192 | 73,728 | 16,384 | 3 | **4** | 3 (we'd exceed) |

`(231424 − 16384) / 49152 = 4.37 → 4`. **Exactly cuBLAS's stage counts**, and one *more* than cuBLAS on 192x192.

## The design this dictates

Two things I had wrong in my sketch:

1. **Chunk along M as well as N.** I proposed `[2][BM][C_BOX_N]` — full BM rows. CUTLASS uses `EPI_TILE_M = 128`, so for BM=256 it walks M in 2 chunks too. Our tile is `[2][128][32]`, not `[2][256][32]`.
2. **128 aligns with our warpgroups.** On M-split tiles each consumer warpgroup already owns BM/2 = 128 rows — so `EPI_TILE_M=128` maps exactly onto one warpgroup's row range, which removes the buffer-contention problem I flagged earlier. That's a real simplification.

So the target is: **epilogue tile 128×32, double-buffered, one slot per warpgroup**, replacing the full-tile buffer.

Two more things worth pulling before we write code, since you asked for absolute understanding:

Design documented as **§H27z.61**. Summary of what the research established:

## The answer to "if cuBLAS can, why can't we"

**We can. Our epilogue buffer is 4× bigger than it needs to be, and that's the whole 4th stage.**

Three independent sources agree on the mechanism:

| source | epilogue smem for a 256x128 tile |
|---|---|
| **CUTLASS** `EpilogueTileAuto` | `min(128,CTA_M) × gcd(32,CTA_N)` × 2 stages = **16,384 B** |
| **DeepGEMM** `SMEM_CD_SIZE` | `STORE_BLOCK_M × (swizzle/dtype)` × stages — same structure |
| **cuBLAS, measured** | `213,188 − 4×49,152` = **16,580 B** |

**CUTLASS's formula predicts cuBLAS's measured shared memory to within 200 bytes.** That's not inference any more.

Ours is `BM×BN×2` = **65,536 B** — the entire output tile, resident at once. The code says why:

> *"Single-buffered epilogue store tile (no double buffer in v1 — correctness first)"*

A v1 shortcut nobody revisited. It costs 28.3% of the whole smem budget.

## Two corrections to what I proposed earlier

1. **Chunk along M as well as N.** I said `[2][BM][C_BOX_N]` — full BM rows. CUTLASS uses `EPI_TILE_M=128`, so BM=256 walks M in 2 chunks too.
2. **That removes the contention problem I flagged.** `EPI_TILE_M=128` is exactly our per-warpgroup row range on M-split tiles (`WG_M = BM/2 = 128`), so each warpgroup gets its own slots instead of sharing one buffer.

Target design: **128×64 epilogue tile, double-buffered = 32,768 B**, using DeepGEMM's swizzle-atom rule for N — which is already our `sw_atom_elems(SW128) = 64`. Gives depth **4** on 256x128 and 128x256, matching cuBLAS exactly, and 6 on 128x128.

## On the silent-corruption point

You're right that corruption would mean we implemented it wrong, not that it can't be done. But it's worth naming precisely *where* the risk lives so we review it properly: it's one thing — **`tma_store_wait<EPI_STAGES-1>()` must be placed so a slot is never rewritten before its store retires.** That single placement is the entire correctness argument. Everything else is mechanical.

And validation has to avoid the trap from §H27z.48 — a harness that memsets C to zero cannot see unwritten output regions, which is exactly how the grouped-raster bug survived every test we had. So: NaN-prefilled C with beta=0, plus residue shapes, plus the full 250-config matrix.

## What I'd do first, and it's an hour

`_LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH` is currently dead code. Making it real is ~20 lines and gives us two things: depth becomes verifiable rather than inferred, and we can force **depth 2** on 128x256 (which fits today) to test 2-vs-3 before committing to the restructure.

If 2 ≈ 3, depth isn't the constraint and the epilogue work won't pay — §H27z.57 already shows equal-depth 192x192 sites still 8–27% behind. If 2 is clearly worse, the restructure is justified and we build it knowing why.

## But I won't extrapolate 3→4 from two points

Tempting to fit `t = a + b/D` — with two points and two parameters it fits exactly and predicts ~914 TF at depth 4, which would be *above* cuBLAS. That's a model with zero degrees of freedom. Not evidence.

We can measure the curve instead. **`128x128` derives depth 6**, so we can force 3, 4 and 5 on it and see where the knee actually is:

That's the entire question, because it decides whether the rewrite is worth days.

## Two ways forward

**Option A — measure the curve first (~30 min).** `128x128` derives depth 6, so 3, 4, 5, 6 are all buildable *today* with no epilogue change. Measuring those four gives us the shape of the curve:

- if it's still climbing at 5→6 → depth dominates everywhere → **build it, and expect more**

Agreed. Let me work through each vertical properly. There are five things we must understand exactly, and I'll do them one at a time.

**Vertical 1 — our own accumulator→(row,col) mapping**, since everything else keys off it:
> tool `Bash`: Read our wgmma fragment row/col mapping

**Vertical 1 solved, and it makes the implementation far simpler than I feared.**

Our fragment layout, derived from `cute::SM90::GMMA::CLayout_64xN`:

```
row = t1 + 8*v1 + 16*t2     t1=(lane>>2)&7,  t2=lane>>5,  v1=(reg>>1)&1
col = 2*t0 + v0 + 8*v2      t0=lane&3,       v0=reg&1,    v2=reg>>2
```

The critical term is `col = 2*t0 + v0 + 8*v2`. Since `2*t0 + v0 ≤ 7`, every lane's column stays inside the 8-wide group selected by **`v2 = reg_idx >> 2`**.

So for any `EPI_TILE_N` that's a multiple of 8:

```
chunk = col / EPI_TILE_N = (8*v2) / EPI_TILE_N = (reg_idx >> 2) / (EPI_TILE_N/8)
```

**Chunk membership is a function of the register index alone — not the lane.** It's compile-time known inside the unrolled loop.

That kills the thing I was worried about. There's no lane-dependent predicate, no wasted iterations, no divergence. The restructure is just splitting the existing `r` loop into contiguous compile-time ranges:

```
EPI_TILE_N=32, WGMMA_N=128 -> 4 chunks, r ranges [0,16) [16,32) [32,48) [48,64)
```

and each chunk becomes: write → fence → store → commit, with `tma_store_wait<EPI_STAGES-1>()` before reusing a slot.

## Two constraints this exposes

**`EPI_TILE_N` must divide `WGMMA_N`, not just `BN`** — the chunk index is `(nchunk0+nc)*(WGMMA_N/EPI_TILE_N) + v2/(EPI_TILE_N/8)`, which only stays integral if it divides the wgmma width. My current `static_assert` checks `BN % EPI_TILE_N` — that's too weak and I'll tighten it.

**`C_BOX_N` must equal `EPI_TILE_N`.** `C_BOX_N` is the TMA descriptor's box width and is currently derived independently. If the staged chunk is 32 wide but the descriptor boxes 128, the store reads 96 columns of garbage. They have to be locked together.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-10 12:50 IST]

Sorry — I went too deep. Let me lay it out plainly.

## The problem, in plain terms

Our GEMM runs at ~86% of cuBLAS in the real training run. We found out **why**, and it's one piece of code: the **epilogue** — the part of the kernel that takes the computed results and writes them back to memory.

It has **two faults**, both measured:

**Fault 1 — it hogs shared memory.**
The epilogue parks the *entire* output tile in shared memory before writing it out: 65,536 bytes on a 256x128 tile, which is 28% of everything the chip gives us. cuBLAS parks only a small slice: 16,580 bytes.

That memory has to come from somewhere, and it comes out of the **pipeline stages** — the buffers that let the kernel load the next chunk of data while computing the current one. cuBLAS affords **4** stages. We only fit **3**.

And we proved stages matter: forcing our kernel down to 2 stages made it **29% slower**. Then we measured where the benefit stops — it's at 4. So we're one stage short of the sweet spot, purely because the epilogue is eating the space.

**Fault 2 — it writes to shared memory the slow way.**
We use plain stores; cuBLAS uses a special instruction (`stmatrix`). Measured on the identical tile: **224,990 memory bank conflicts for us vs 5 for cuBLAS**, and we execute **2.1× as many instructions**.

**The proof these are the cause:** epilogue cost matters more when K is small (less maths per write). Our results line up exactly with that — shapes with K=2048 run at 84–86%, K=5632 at 92.6%, K≥11264 at 95–99%. Perfectly ordered by K.

## What we're doing about it

Fixing **Fault 1** first: instead of parking the whole output tile, park **two small slices** and write them out one at a time as they're filled. That frees the memory, which gives us the 4th stage.

Fault 2 (`stmatrix`) is a separate, harder job for after.

## Where we actually are right now

**Done:** I added the switch for the new small-buffer mode. It's **turned off**, so nothing has changed in the shipped code yet — that's deliberate, so we can't break what already works.

**Just figured out the hard part.** My worry was: when we write results in small slices, how does each thread know which slice its values belong to? If that answer depended on the thread, the code would be messy and slow.

It doesn't. I traced our own formula and each thread's values always sit in a fixed 8-column group determined by a **counter the compiler already knows**. So splitting the write loop into slices is a clean, simple change — not the messy one I expected.

## What's left before writing the code

Three checks, all small:

1. The memory-write instruction has a "width" setting that must match the new slice width — confirm they line up.
2. Confirm exactly where the "wait for the previous slice to finish sending" goes, so we never overwrite a slice still in flight.
3. Confirm odd-sized matrices (where the tile doesn't divide evenly) still behave.

Then: write it, test it hard, measure it.

**Why I'm being careful rather than just typing it out:** if we get the "wait" wrong, the kernel gives *correct answers most of the time* and wrong ones occasionally. That's the same failure mode as the tile bug from a few days ago that passed every test we had. So it gets checked properly before it goes in.

More importantly: **the descriptor is built once per launch with `boxDim = C_BOX_N`, and the store loop already issues one TMA per `C_BOX_N` chunk.** So the *store* side already does exactly what we want. The only thing wrong is that the *buffer* holds every chunk instead of two.

That reduces the change to: set `C_BOX_N = EPI_TILE_N`, shrink the buffer, change one index from `ch_global*BM` to `(ch_global % EPI_STAGES)*BM`, and interleave write/store.

**Vertical 4 — the synchronisation, which is the part that must be exactly right:**
> tool `Bash`: Read the TMA store synchronisation primitives and nesting

**Vertical 4 answered.** The current structure is:

```
write ALL chunks into c_buf
barrier_sync(g, 128)              // all 128 threads done writing
tma_store_fence()                 // fence.proxy.async.shared::cta
if (lane_in_wg == 0) {            // ONE thread issues every store
    for a: for cc: tma_3d_smem2gmem(...)
    tma_store_commit()            // cp.async.bulk.commit_group
    tma_store_wait<0>()           // cp.async.bulk.wait_group.READ 0
}
```

The crucial detail: our `tma_store_wait` is `cp.async.bulk.wait_group.**read** N` — it waits until the **smem source has been read**, which is exactly the guarantee needed to reuse a slot (and cheaper than waiting for the destination write to land).

So the correctness rule for double-buffering is precise:

```
before writing slot s again:
    if (lane_in_wg == 0) tma_store_wait<EPI_STAGES-1>();   // issuer waits
    barrier_sync(g, 128);                                   // propagate to other 127 threads
```

The barrier is **not optional** — lane 0 issues and waits, but the other 127 threads do the writing, so without it they'd race ahead and overwrite a slot still being read. That single barrier is the whole correctness argument.

Complete design documented as **§H27z.63** — all five unknowns closed. Where we stand:

## What we now know for certain

**The hard part turned out to be easy.** Which output chunk a thread's value belongs to depends only on the **register index**, not the thread — `col = 2*t0 + v0 + 8*v2` and `2*t0+v0 ≤ 7`, so every lane stays inside the 8-column group picked by `v2 = reg>>2`. The write loop splits into compile-time register ranges. No divergence, no predicate, no waste.

**The store side needs no work at all.** `C_BOX_N` is already a knob, the descriptor is already built once per launch with `boxDim = C_BOX_N`, and the loop already issues one TMA per chunk. We only pin `C_BOX_N = EPI_TILE_N` and change one index.

**The whole correctness risk is one line.** `tma_store_wait` is `wait_group.**read**`, so it retires when the smem source has been read — the right guarantee for slot reuse. But lane 0 issues and waits while all 128 threads write, so a `barrier_sync` must follow the wait. Without it the other 127 threads overwrite a slot the TMA engine is still reading: correct output most of the time, corrupt under load. Same signature as the grouped-raster bug that passed every test we had.

**Residue and batching need nothing new** — bounds come from the rank-3 descriptor's real extents, and chunking doesn't change the coordinates handed to it.

```
          depth 3 -> 4                 == cuBLAS
affects   16 call sites, 58.8% of our GEMM time
```

### CLAUDE [2026-08-10 14:05 IST]

Good question, and the answer has three separate parts.

Let me check our actual code rather than answer from theory:
> tool `Bash`: Check for atomics in split-K and in BluTrain kernels
> tool `Bash`: Compare final losses across runs with identical and differing kernels

Perfect natural experiment sitting in our own data. `nsys_train_blublas` and `nsys_train_blublas_after` had **byte-identical kernel mixes** — I verified earlier that not a single launch moved. Same code, same data, same seed:

```
run 1 (blublas)        train 9.817209   val 9.872180
run 2 (blublas_after)  train 9.795377   val 9.853102
                       differ by 0.0218        0.0191
```

**That is pure run-to-run non-determinism, measured.**

## Is matmul deterministic? Three separate answers

**1. Our GEMM kernel: YES, deterministic.** Each output element is owned by one fixed thread, the K-loop runs in a fixed order, and there are no atomics anywhere in the SM90 path. Run it twice, get bit-identical output.

**2. Our split-K: also deterministic.** No `atomicAdd` in `src/level3/splitk/` — it writes fp32 partials to a workspace and a separate reduce kernel sums them in a fixed order. (That's why it doesn't appear in the grep at all.) And in the 1.7B run `SPLIT_K=1` on all 34,720 launches, so split-K isn't even used.

**3. But different kernels give different answers — legitimately.** Float addition isn't associative, so `(a+b)+c ≠ a+(b+c)`. A 256x128 tile and a 192x192 tile sum the same K products in a different order and land on slightly different values. Both correct. That's why our validation uses a tolerance against cuBLAS rather than bit-exactness.

**The training run is non-deterministic — but not because of matmul.** It's `atomicAdd` in BluTrain's own kernels: `GQA_bwd_sm90.cu` (attention backward, our single largest kernel at 4.4 s), `EmbeddingKernels.cu`, `GradNormKernels.cu` and five others. Atomics complete in whatever order blocks happen to finish, and that order changes every run.

## Does it matter at scale?

**For training quality: almost certainly not.** 0.0218 out of 9.8 is **0.22%**. Both runs are equally valid training runs — they just take slightly different paths. Training contracts toward a minimum rather than amplifying perturbations, so this doesn't blow up. I should be honest that this is the standard understanding rather than something we've measured — we only have 10-step data, no long-run evidence.

**For our benchmarking: it's fatal, and worth internalising.**

```
run-to-run noise, identical kernels     0.0218
blublas vs cuBLAS (before)              0.0255
blublas vs cuBLAS (after2)              0.0123   <- SMALLER than the noise
```

The noise is the **same size as** the backend difference, and **bigger** than the after-fix difference. So when I noted a few days ago that "losses moved toward cuBLAS after the table change" — that was over-reading it. That shift is inside the noise floor and I shouldn't have offered it as supporting evidence.

**Practical rule: never use training loss to compare backends.** Correctness gets validated at the kernel level, where our GEMM *is* deterministic and we can demand bit-exactness or a tight tolerance against cuBLAS on a single call. Loss curves are only good for "did it diverge / NaN", not for "is backend A better than B".

### CLAUDE [2026-08-10 14:31 IST]

Neither — there's a better third option, and it's the one that's actually robust.

## The problem with doing it in one go

Edit 4 changes two things at once: **how the loop is structured** (write/store interleaved instead of write-all-then-store-all) and **how big the buffer is** (whole tile → two small slices). If it comes back wrong, we won't know which one broke it.

## Split it so each half is independently provable

**Stage 1 — restructure only, same memory.** Set `EPI_TILE_N = BN` and `EPI_STAGES = 1`. That's *one* chunk covering the whole tile in *one* slot — byte-for-byte the same shared memory as today, running through the *new* code path. Result must be **bit-identical** to the off path.

This proves the rewrite is correct while changing nothing about memory. If it fails, the bug is purely in my restructure.

**Stage 2 — shrink it.** `EPI_TILE_N = 32`, `EPI_STAGES = 2`. Now the buffer drops to 32,768 and depth goes 3 → 4. If Stage 1 passed and Stage 2 fails, the bug is in the chunking or the `tma_store_wait`/barrier — a much smaller place to look.

That's the correct and efficient answer: same total work, but a failure tells you *where* it is instead of leaving you bisecting a 115-line diff.

One thing it needs — my assert currently forbids `EPI_STAGES=1`:
> tool `Bash`: Allow single-slot mode for the identity check

So the answer to your question: **staged, not one-shot.** Same work, but a failure points at one specific thing instead of leaving us bisecting a 115-line diff in the function where mistakes are silent.

## The plan, concretely

| stage | setting | buffer | what it proves |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | `EPI_TILE_N=BN, EPI_STAGES=1` | 65,536 B (same as today) | the **restructure** is correct — result must be bit-identical |
| **2** | `EPI_TILE_N=32, EPI_STAGES=2` | 32,768 B | the **shrink + slot recycling** works → depth 3→4 |

Stage 1 changes zero memory and runs the new code path. If it's not bit-identical, the bug is purely my loop rewrite. If Stage 1 passes and Stage 2 fails, the bug is in the chunking or the `tma_store_wait` + barrier — a handful of lines, not a hundred.

## The gap: edits 2 and 3 have never been compiled

They're inert *by construction* — `USE_CHUNKED_EPILOGUE` is false, so no runtime path changes. But I've written `static_assert`s and a new `C_BOX_N` expression and **not once run the compiler over them**. That's not proven, it's assumed.

And there's a specific risk in what I wrote:

```cpp
!Config::USE_CHUNKED_EPILOGUE || (WGMMA_N % Config::EPI_TILE_N == 0)
```

When the flag is off, `EPI_TILE_N` is **0** — so that's `% 0`. Short-circuit evaluation should stop it ever being computed, but "should" isn't good enough for a modulo-by-zero in a constant expression. Let me remove the doubt entirely:
> tool `Bash`: Make the divisibility assert safe when the flag is off

So: **yes, a test is needed** — a build. Everything measured is solid, but three edits have never been through the compiler, and a `static_assert` that doesn't compile blocks everything downstream.

```bash
# LOCAL — push edits 2 and 3
cd /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/BLUBLAS/BLUBLAS_kota/BluBridge-BLAS
git add src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM90/
git commit -m "pin the C TMA box to the epilogue chunk, tighten the asserts, allow single-slot bring-up

When the epilogue stages a chunk instead of the whole tile, that chunk is what the TMA store reads, so the descriptor's box has to be the chunk width. Disagreeing does not fail: the store transfers whatever the rest of the buffer holds, so the output is wrong with nothing reporting it. EPI_TILE_N therefore overrides every other C_BOX_N derivation while chunking is on.

The divisibility rule moves to the work grid because that is the only place WGMMA_N exists. The chunk index is nc*(WGMMA_N/EPI_TILE_N) + (reg>>2)/(EPI_TILE_N/8), so EPI_TILE_N has to divide the WGMMA width rather than merely BN, and getting it wrong would route some lanes into a neighbouring chunk. The divisor is written as a guarded ternary because EPI_TILE_N is 0 when chunking is off and leaning on || short-circuiting to keep a modulo by zero out of a constant expression is not worth the doubt.

EPI_STAGES may now be 1. It is useless in production but it is what lets the restructure be proved on its own: EPI_TILE_N equal to BN with one slot runs the chunk loop once over the whole tile with the same memory and store pattern as today, so the result must come back bit-identical, separating an error in the loop rewrite from an error in slot recycling."
```

## One thing the derivation gave us that's worth writing down

Working out 4b's predicate, the compile-time property holds all the way through. With `C_BOX_N = EPI_TILE_N` and `wg_ch_start = nchunk0 × R` (where `R = WGMMA_N/EPI_TILE_N`):

```

```

Both `nc` and `v2` are unrolled loop indices, so `if (ch != wg_ch_start + epi_ch) continue;` is **fully compile-time** — the compiler deletes the non-matching iterations outright. No runtime predicate, no divergence, no wasted work. That's the simplest correct way to write it and it costs nothing.

- **4b** — chunking with `tma_store_wait<0>()` kept after every chunk. Fully serialised, definitely correct, no recycling risk. Proves the *chunk split* alone.
- **4c** — relax to `tma_store_wait<EPI_STAGES-1>()` + the barrier. That's the only line where slot recycling can go wrong, tested by itself.

So the dangerous part ends up isolated to a single change, which is exactly what we wanted.

## What the analysis established

**The predicate is compile-time — now verified against the real code**, not just the layout formula. With `wg_ch_start = (nchunk0 × WGMMA_N) / C_BOX_N`:

```
ch - wg_ch_start = nc*R + v2/(EPI_TILE_N/8)
```

Both are unrolled loop indices, so `if (ch != wg_ch_start + epi_ch) continue;` compiles away entirely. No divergence, no cost.

**The pre-epilogue barrier is correctly outside my loop** — it means "accumulators final", which is once per tile, not per chunk.

**`EPI_NCHUNK` must be `C_NCHUNK0`, not `my_c_nchunks`** — the latter is a *runtime* value under an asymmetric split and can't bound an unrolled loop. Same pattern the existing store loop already uses.

## The new finding

**Split-K never touches `c_buf` at all** — it writes fp32 partials straight to global and `continue`s. So:

1. **Chunking × split-K must be forbidden.** Wrapping that path in a chunk loop would repeat the workspace stores `EPI_NCHUNK` times — same values, still correct, but N× the global traffic and completely silent. `static_assert` it off.

2. **And split-K has been carrying a buffer it never uses.** `STORE_BUF_BYTES` is allocated and subtracted from the pipeline budget regardless:

```
64x64   sk*   depth 13 -> 14 if dropped
128x128 sk*   depth  6 ->  7
256x128 sk*   depth  3 ->  4      a whole stage, for a one-line change
```

That's a free win with no epilogue rewrite — `STORE_BUF_BYTES = USE_SPLIT_K ? 0 : ...`. It doesn't help the 1.7B model (`SPLIT_K=1` on all 34,720 launches), so it's not a priority. But it means our split-K configs measuring **28–37% of cuBLAS** were partly handicapped by dead memory, and any future split-K measurement should drop it first or the numbers understate what split-K can actually do. Worth remembering given `kv-wgrad` is the one shape where cuBLAS beats us with split-K.

## 4b is now fully specified

```
EPI_NCHUNK = USE_CHUNKED ? C_NCHUNK0 : 1
static_assert(!(USE_CHUNKED && USE_SPLIT_K))
per chunk:  skip if epi_ch >= my_c_nchunks
            write: if (ch != wg_ch_start + epi_ch) continue
            buffer index: chunking ? (epi_ch % EPI_STAGES) : ch
            store: cc restricted to epi_ch
            tma_store_wait<0>() KEPT — serialised, no recycling yet
```

Every unknown is closed. 4c then relaxes that one wait line to `<EPI_STAGES-1>` plus the barrier — the single place recycling can break, isolated by itself.

**Assumed, and I have NOT checked it:** what `WGMMA_N` actually *is* for our tiles. My whole plan needs `EPI_TILE_N` to divide it — and Stage 1 wants `EPI_TILE_N = BN = 128`. If `WGMMA_N` is smaller than 128 on `256x128`, **Stage 1 won't even compile**, and my ladder falls over at the first rung.

That's a real hole. Let me close it:
> tool `Bash`: Find how WGMMA_N is actually derived

The chain is `N_GRAIN = B_IS_MN ? sw_atom_elems(B_SWIZZLE) : 1`, `SPLIT_M = (MATOMS % 2 == 0)`, then `wgmma_n_pick_free(BN, N_GRAIN, SPLIT_M)`. Let me read the rest and evaluate it rather than guess.
> tool `Bash`: Read the remaining constexpr helpers to evaluate WGMMA_N
> tool `Bash`: Evaluate WGMMA_N for the tiles we plan to test

**That found a real error in my plan.** Here are the actual values:

```
tile      layout  B_SWZ  N_GRAIN  SPLIT_M  WGMMA_N    EPI_TILE_N=BN?   =32?
256x128     all     128       64    True       128        YES           YES
128x256     all     128       64    True       256        YES           YES
128x128     all     128       64    True       128        YES           YES
192x192     all      64       32   False        96        NO            YES
```

**`192x192` has `WGMMA_N = 96`, but `BN = 192`.** So `96 % 192 ≠ 0` — my Stage 1 setting of `EPI_TILE_N = BN` **would not compile on 192x192**. The assert I added in edit 2 would have caught it at build time rather than producing wrong results, but the ladder would have stalled at the first rung and I'd have been debugging why.

The cause: `MATOMS = 192/64 = 3`, so `SPLIT_M = (3 % 2 == 0)` is **false** — 192x192 splits along N instead of M, giving `WGMMA_N = 96` with each warpgroup owning one 96-wide chunk.

**The correct Stage-1 rule is `EPI_TILE_N = WG_N_WIDTH0`, not `BN`** — that's what makes `C_NCHUNK0 = 1` (one chunk, the identity case). It happens to equal `BN` when `SPLIT_M` is true, which is why it looked right for `256x128`, but it's `WGMMA_N` when the split is along N.

```
256x128   Stage 1: EPI_TILE_N = 128   (= BN, SPLIT_M true)
128x256   Stage 1: EPI_TILE_N = 256   (= BN)
128x128   Stage 1: EPI_TILE_N = 128   (= BN)
192x192   Stage 1: EPI_TILE_N =  96   (= WGMMA_N, N-split)
```

`EPI_TILE_N = 32` divides all of them (`96 % 32 == 0`), so **Stage 3 is safe on every tile** — only the identity stage needed correcting.
> tool `Bash`: Record the Stage-1 correction

Corrected and documented as **§H27z.64b**.

## What the check was worth

I had written "Stage 1: `EPI_TILE_N = BN`" in the design and it reads as obviously correct. It isn't. On `192x192` the warpgroups split along **N**, not M (`MATOMS = 3`, so `SPLIT_M` is false), giving `WGMMA_N = 96` — and 192 doesn't divide 96. The build would have failed at edit 2's assert, and I'd have been debugging the ladder instead of the kernel.

The general rule is `EPI_TILE_N = WG_N_WIDTH0` (whatever makes `C_NCHUNK0 = 1`), which equals `BN` only when `SPLIT_M` is true.

## Verified state of the 4b plan

**Read from the code, not assumed:**
- `wg_ch_start = (nchunk0*WGMMA_N)/C_BOX_N`, `ch = tile_col/C_BOX_N`, `tile_col = (nchunk0+nc)*WGMMA_N + col`
- `col = 2*t0 + v0 + 8*v2`, and `2*t0+v0 ≤ 7` proven arithmetically → a lane never crosses an 8-column group
- split-K writes to global and never touches `c_buf`
- `my_c_nchunks` is runtime, so the loop must be bounded by `C_NCHUNK0`
- the pre-epilogue barrier sits outside the chunk loop

**Evaluated from the real constexpr chain:**
- `WGMMA_N` = 128 / 256 / 128 / 96 for our four tiles
- `EPI_TILE_N = 32` is legal on all four
- identity-stage values: 128, 256, 128, **96**

**Still assumed:** nothing I'm aware of in 4b. The one thing I'd flag is that `WG_N_WIDTH0` is a `Sm90WorkGrid` value while `EPI_TILE_N` is a `Config` parameter, so the test aliases have to hardcode the right number per tile — there's no way for the config to derive it. That's fine for deliberate probes, but it means a wrong value is a build error rather than something the type system prevents.

## Corrected ladder

```
Stage 1   EPI_TILE_N = WG_N_WIDTH0, EPI_STAGES=1   one chunk, one slot   -> BIT-IDENTICAL
          (256x128 -> 128,  192x192 -> 96)
Stage 2   EPI_TILE_N = half of that, EPI_STAGES=2  memory unchanged      -> recycling alone
Stage 3   EPI_TILE_N = 32,           EPI_STAGES=2  memory drops          -> depth 3 -> 4
```

Ready to write 4b. Everything in it is now traced to a line of code or an evaluated expression rather than an expectation.

## Where we are

```
Stage 0   flag off                     PASS   inert across 103 configs
Stage 1   1 chunk,  1 slot, 65,536 B   PASS   bit-identical, zero cost isolated
Stage 2   2 chunks, 2 slots, 65,536 B  PASS   bit-identical, chunk split correct
Stage 3   4 chunks, 2 slots, 32,768 B  next   memory drops, depth 3 -> 4
```

Two things still untested, and they're the two that matter:

**Slot recycling isn't live yet.** 4b keeps `tma_store_wait<0>()` after every chunk, so each slot is fully drained before it's rewritten. Stage 2 has two slots but never actually reuses one under pressure. That's edit **4c** — relaxing the wait to `<EPI_STAGES-1>` plus the barrier, which is the single line where recycling can go wrong.

**Memory hasn't dropped.** Everything so far has been at 65,536 bytes with depth 3, deliberately. Stage 3 is `EPI_TILE_N=32, EPI_STAGES=2` → 32,768 bytes → **depth 4**.

Order matters here. If I do Stage 3 before 4c, the depth change and the still-serialised wait land together and a slowdown would be ambiguous. But 4c on its own (2 chunks, unchanged memory, relaxed wait) is a clean isolation of the recycling.

So: **4c next, then Stage 3.**

One thing I want to verify before writing 4c, rather than assume: whether `tma_store_wait<N>` is legal with `N > 0` given only lane 0 issues the stores, and what `cp.async.bulk.wait_group.read N` guarantees when the commits came from a single thread. Getting that wrong is exactly the silent-corruption case, so I'll read it out of the PTX semantics and our own usage before touching it.

Right — let's settle it from the sources rather than reason about it.
> tool `Bash`: Check how CUTLASS and DeepGEMM use a nonzero TMA store wait
> tool `Bash`: Read the wait semantics and DeepGEMM's slot-reuse gate

**Doubt cleared, from two independent sources.**

**CUTLASS's own definition** — same instruction as ours, with the semantics spelled out:

```cpp
// Wait until at most Count committed TMA_STOREs are pending and all prior commits are complete
template <int Count>
tma_store_wait() { asm volatile("cp.async.bulk.wait_group.read %0;" ...); }
```

**DeepGEMM's shipping store loop** uses exactly the pattern I planned:

```
39:   tma_stage_idx = (tma_stage_idx + 1) % kNumTMAStoreStages;
54:   cute::tma_store_wait<kNumTMAStoreStages - 1>();
118:  cute::tma_store_fence();
120:  if (epilogue_warp_idx == 0 and cute::elect_one_sync()) { ...store... }
132:  __syncwarp();
```

So `wait<N-1>` with N slots is the standard, and issuing from a single elected thread is what they do too.

Three things this settles that I'd been unsure about:

1. **`N > 0` is legal and normal** — not an edge case.
2. **The `ch >= EPI_STAGES` guard I planned is unnecessary.** `wait<N-1>` returns immediately when fewer than N groups are pending, so it's a no-op on the first chunks. DeepGEMM calls it unconditionally. Simpler and less to get wrong.
3. **Our sync must differ from theirs.** DeepGEMM ends with `__syncwarp()` because its store is warp-scoped. Ours has **128 threads writing** and lane 0 issuing, so it needs `barrier_sync(g, 128)` — a warp-level sync would leave 96 threads free to overwrite a slot still being read. That's the one place we cannot copy them.

The .read form retires when the shared-memory source has been consumed, which is exactly the condition for overwriting a slot and is weaker and cheaper than waiting for the global write to land. DeepGEMM's shipping epilogue uses the same wait<stages-1> against a modulo slot index, so the pattern is standard rather than invented here.

```bash
No guard on the first chunks: with fewer than EPI_STAGES groups outstanding the wait retires immediately and is already a no-op.

The barrier after it is not optional and is the one place DeepGEMM cannot be copied. Their store is warp-scoped so they follow with __syncwarp. Ours is issued by lane 0 of a 128-thread warpgroup while all 128 threads write, so a warp-level sync would leave 96 threads free to overwrite a slot the TMA engine is still reading - correct whenever the store happens to win the race, corrupt under load, and passing tests either way.
```

I verified that `N > 0` is legal and that DeepGEMM uses `wait<stages-1>`. I did **not** verify the actual question I raised: **the thread scoping** — what the wait guarantees when only lane 0 issued the commits. I asserted it and moved on.

Let me actually read it.
> tool `Bash`: Read DeepGEMM's exact wait/store thread scoping

**Now it's genuinely cleared** — and DeepGEMM's code answers the exact question:

```cpp
// Wait shared memory to be released
if (epilogue_warp_idx == 0)
    cute::tma_store_wait<kNumTMAStoreStages - 1>();
cutlass::arch::NamedBarrier::sync(kNumUMMAStoreThreads, 0);
```

**The wait is guarded to a single warp, then immediately followed by a barrier across all the storing threads.** That is exactly the structure I wrote — `if (lane_in_wg == 0) tma_store_wait<EPI_STAGES-1>();` then `barrier_sync(g, 128)`. Confirmed by a shipping implementation rather than inferred, and their comment ("wait shared memory to be released") confirms the `.read` reading too.

So: the commits are per-thread, only the issuing thread has groups to wait on, and the barrier is what makes its wait mean anything to the other 127. My 4c matches.

## But reading it surfaced something else

DeepGEMM's store side orders things differently from ours:

```
DeepGEMM:   tma_store_fence()  ->  barrier  ->  single thread issues
ours:       barrier            ->  tma_store_fence()  ->  lane 0 issues
```

Theirs guarantees **every** thread has fenced its own writes before the issuer proceeds. Ours has lane 0 fence and then immediately store — another thread's fence may not have retired at that point. Whether that matters depends on whether `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta` orders the whole CTA's prior writes or only the calling thread's, and I don't know that for certain.

Two things about it:

- **It's pre-existing.** That ordering is in the shipped kernel, not something 4c introduced, and it's been validated across the full matrix for months. So it's not a regression and it doesn't block this work.
- **It's worth resolving separately.** If the fence is per-thread rather than CTA-scoped, our ordering is technically weak and would fail in the same silent way — just rarely enough that nothing has caught it. Both reference implementations put the fence first, which is at minimum a reason to match them.

I'll note it as an open item rather than change it mid-series — swapping two lines in the store path while we're validating a different change would confound the ablation.

Being honest about what 13 clean runs do and don't prove:

**What they show:** the two-chunk recycling path produced bit-identical output 13 times, including 5 with a second process on the GPU.

**What they don't:**

1. **13 is 13 samples.** A race with a narrow window could fail 1 in 10,000. Passing repeatedly lowers the probability; it doesn't establish absence.
2. **The contention was weak.** Your `nvidia-smi` showed **0% util, 140 W** — the background loader spends most of its life in process startup and allocation, not on the GPU. So the store engine was rarely actually behind, which is the condition that exposes premature reuse.
3. **The NaN-prefill test wasn't run.** With C zeroed, a region we fail to write reads 0 — and while that *should* show as a large error against the reference, our own notes say this harness can't see unwritten output, and I'm not going to hand-wave past a trap we've already been bitten by.
4. **Coverage is one config on 15 shapes.** Not the 250-config matrix with chunking on, not `batch > 1`, not residue shapes beyond what those 15 happen to include, not other tiles or cluster shapes.
5. **The fence-ordering question is still open** — we order `barrier → fence → store` where both CUTLASS and DeepGEMM do `fence → barrier → store`. I called it pre-existing, which it is, but it interacts with exactly this code path.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-10 17:05 IST]

You're right. Repeating a run proves nothing about a race — it just samples the timing distribution. We need **structural** proof. Here's what actually settles it.

## A — Does the hazard exist at all? (detects it whether or not it manifests)

`compute-sanitizer --tool racecheck` instruments every shared-memory access and reports WAR/WAW/RAW hazards **even when the timing happens to work out**. That's the difference between "it didn't break this time" and "there is no race".

```bash
# SERVER — racecheck. Small shape: it's 10-100x slow.
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=3
which compute-sanitizer || ls /usr/local/cuda/bin/compute-sanitizer

compute-sanitizer --tool racecheck --racecheck-report all \
  ./build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --shape=512x256x256 --layout=nn \
  --cfg=256x128x64_1x2_h_ep64s2 2>&1 | tail -30
```

```bash
# SERVER — synccheck: illegal or divergent barrier usage
compute-sanitizer --tool synccheck \
  ./build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --shape=512x256x256 --layout=nn \
  --cfg=256x128x64_1x2_h_ep64s2 2>&1 | tail -20

# initcheck: reading smem/gmem that was never written -> catches an unstored chunk
compute-sanitizer --tool initcheck \
  ./build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --shape=512x256x256 --layout=nn \
  --cfg=256x128x64_1x2_h_ep64s2 2>&1 | tail -20
```

Run the **unchunked** config through the same three first, as a control — if racecheck already reports hazards on the shipping kernel, its output on ours means nothing without that baseline.

## B — Did the compiler actually emit the sync, in order?

The wait and barrier are only correct if they survive optimisation and stay ordered. That's checkable in the SASS, not inferable:

```bash
# SERVER — is the wait+barrier actually in the generated code, before the stores?
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
cuobjdump -sass build/libmyblas.so \
  | awk '/ep32s2|ep64s2/{f=1} f&&/^\s*$/{exit} f' \
  | grep -nE "BAR\.SYNC|BSSY|BSYNC|UBLKCP|ASYNC|LDSM|STS" | head -40
```

Want to see, per chunk: the bulk-wait, then `BAR.SYNC`, then the shared stores, then the copy issue. If the barrier isn't between them, the ordering we reasoned about isn't what runs.

## C — Coverage that isn't timing-dependent

```bash
# every output element written? (NaN-prefilled C, beta=0 -- the §H27z.48 test)
./build/test_bgemm_sm90_beta 2>&1 | tail -20
# residue: nothing divides evenly
./build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --shape=4095x2047x1023 --layout=nn \
  --cfg=256x128x64_1x2_h,256x128x64_1x2_h_ep64s2 2>&1 | tail -5
# batch>1 -> the rank-3 descriptor path
./build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --shape=2048x2048x2048x4 --layout=nn \
  --cfg=256x128x64_1x2_h,256x128x64_1x2_h_ep64s2 2>&1 | tail -5
```

## What I can and can't promise

`racecheck` clean + `synccheck` clean + the barrier visible in SASS + NaN/residue/batch coverage is **structural** evidence — it says the hazard isn't there, not that we got lucky. That's a genuinely different class of proof from 13 passing runs.

The one caveat I won't paper over: racecheck models thread-to-thread shared-memory hazards. Whether it also models the **async proxy** (the TMA engine reading smem) I don't know for certain — if it doesn't, it can't see the specific hazard we care about, and the SASS check plus the DeepGEMM/CUTLASS precedent carries more weight. I'll find out from its output rather than assume, and tell you which it turned out to be.

Start with `racecheck` on the unchunked control, then the chunked one.

**Chunked is clean too: 0 hazards, matching the control.**

But I want to be straight about what that does and doesn't cover, because there are two limits here:

**1. The async proxy.** racecheck tracks thread-to-thread shared-memory hazards. The SASS is the one I trust most here. racecheck tells us threads aren't racing each other; it may not model the copy engine at all. But if the machine code shows `bulk-wait → BAR.SYNC → STS`, the ordering the correctness argument depends on is guaranteed by hardware semantics — no tool modelling required.

If the barrier isn't there, or sits in the wrong place, then all thirteen clean runs were luck and we found it the right way.

**Identical — to the error.**

**Chunking introduced exactly zero hazards.** The same count on all three, on a shape with real pipeline pressure, is a clean negative result for our change.

And the fact that it's *exactly* 296,020 across three configs with different epilogue structures tells you what those hazards are: **racecheck doesn't model mbarrier or TMA synchronisation.** Our kernel is warp-specialised — producers and consumers coordinate through `mbarrier.try_wait` and async copies, none of which racecheck understands, so it flags every producer-write/consumer-read pair as an unsynchronised hazard. A genuine timing-dependent race would produce *different* counts under different epilogue structures, not the same number three times.

That also explains the small shape reading 0 — fewer stage rotations, fewer flagged pairs.

Worth recording that the shipping kernel reports 296,020 racecheck hazards so nobody panics at it later, but it's not a defect and it's not ours.

Your SASS symbol is there now — the mangled name ends `...Li0ELi1ELi32ELi2EE` (RASTER_SWIZZLE 0, SPLIT_K 1, **EPI_TILE_N 32, EPI_STAGES 2**), three of them, one per layout. So now the check racecheck *can't* do:

```bash

  f&&index($0,"Function : "){exit}
  f' /tmp/sass.txt | grep -nE "BAR\.SYNC|DEPBAR|BULK|ASYNC|STS|LDS" | tail -50
```

I want to see, per chunk: the bulk-store wait, then `BAR.SYNC`, then the `STS` writes, then the copy issue. If the barrier is present and ordered, the guarantee comes from hardware semantics and doesn't depend on racecheck modelling the copy engine at all.

If the compiler hoisted or dropped it, that's the real defect and this is where it shows.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-10 18:13 IST]

**The ordering is confirmed in machine code.** Reading the sequence at `0x6ef0`–`0x77e0`:

```
STS  [R*+0x30030] ...        <- chunk N writes slot 0
BAR.SYNC R2, 0x80            <- warpgroup barrier (128 threads)
FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S           <- tma_store_fence (async proxy)
   [gap 0x72b0 -> 0x7480]    <- TMA store issue lives here
DEPBAR.LE SB0, 0x1           <- tma_store_wait<1>   (EPI_STAGES-1 = 1)  ***
BAR.SYNC R2, 0x80            <- barrier BEFORE any reuse               ***
STS  [R5+0x34000] ...        <- chunk N+1 writes slot 1
```

Four things fall out of this, and none of them were assumptions:

**1. The wait count is right.** `DEPBAR.LE SB0, 0x1` = "block until at most 1 outstanding" — that is `cp.async.bulk.wait_group.read 1`, exactly `tma_store_wait<EPI_STAGES-1>` with `EPI_STAGES=2`. The template arithmetic survived into SASS.

**2. The barrier was not hoisted or dropped.** `BAR.SYNC` sits between the `DEPBAR` and the first `STS` of the next chunk, at consecutive addresses with nothing in between. This was the actual risk — the compiler cannot see that the copy engine reads that buffer, so if it had reordered here we'd have a silent corruption that no amount of running would reliably catch. It didn't.

**3. The two-slot layout is literally in the addresses.** Slot 0 at `0x30000`, slot 1 at `0x34000`. The difference is `0x4000` = 16,384 = `BM × EPI_TILE_N × 2` = 256×32×2. That is the slot stride, byte-for-byte. Within a slot, `0x35000` is `0x1000` = 4096 = 64 rows × 64 B, which is the `row0 + a*64` term. The buffer is laid out exactly as designed.

**4. The final drain is there.** `DEPBAR.LE SB0, 0x0` at `0x9340` — `tma_store_wait<0>()`, the full drain before the kernel releases the buffer, followed by the CTA-wide `BAR.SYNC 0x0`.

One thing my grep missed: the TMA store instruction itself. On Hopper the mnemonic is `UBLKCP`, which doesn't contain the string `BULK`, so it fell in that `0x72b0`–`0x7480` gap unseen. Closing it:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
FN=_Z17bgemm_sm90_kernelI18Sm90WarpspecConfigILi256ELi128ELi64ELi1ELi2ELi0ELb1ELb1ELi1ELi0ELi0ELi0ELi40ELi232ELi0ELi1ELi32ELi2EEL10Sm90Layout0EE
awk -v fn="$FN" '
  index($0,"Function : ")&&index($0,fn){f=1;next}
  f&&index($0,"Function : "){exit}
  f' /tmp/sass.txt > /tmp/ep32s2.sass

echo "--- opcode census ---"
grep -oE "^\s+/\*[0-9a-f]+\*/\s+@?!?P?[0-9]?\s*[A-Z][A-Z0-9._]+" /tmp/ep32s2.sass \
  | grep -oE "[A-Z][A-Z0-9._]+$" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn \
  | grep -E "BLK|DEPBAR|BAR\.SYNC|FENCE|STS|ELECT" 

echo "--- the gap: 0x72b0 - 0x74b0 ---"
awk '/\/\*72[b-f]0\*\//,/\/\*74b0\*\//' /tmp/ep32s2.sass | grep -vE "^\s*$"
```

I want the `UBLKCP` count to be **4** (one per chunk, unrolled) and each one to sit after its `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S`. If those line up, the epilogue is structurally proven — not "it passed N runs", but "the machine code cannot do otherwise."

To be explicit about the racecheck number, since it's the thing that looked alarming: all three configs report **296,020 errors, identical**. Racecheck models `__syncthreads`, not `mbarrier` or the async proxy, so in a warp-specialised kernel it flags every producer-write/consumer-read pair in the mainloop as unsynchronised. A real race would move that number when the epilogue structure changes — it didn't move at all across unchunked, 2-chunk, and 4-chunk. It's a tool limitation on the shipping kernel, worth writing down so it doesn't scare anyone later, but it is not a defect and it is not ours.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-10 18:15 IST]

**Proven. The full sequence is in the machine code:**

```
0x72b0  FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S           tma_store_fence
0x72c0  @P0 BRA 0x7490               non-electing threads skip
0x7330  VIADD R10, R8, 0x30000       slot 0 address
0x73b0  UTMASTG.3D [UR12],[UR18]     TMA store, rows 0-63
0x73e0  VIADD R8,  R8, 0x31000       + 0x1000 = row 64
0x7450  UTMASTG.3D [UR12],[UR18]     TMA store, rows 64-127
0x7470  UTMACMDFLUSH                 cp.async.bulk.commit_group
0x7480  DEPBAR.LE SB0, 0x1           wait: at most 1 outstanding
0x7490  BSYNC B0                     warp reconverge
0x74a0  BAR.SYNC.DEFER_BLOCKING R2, 0x80    <- all 128 threads wait
        ... next chunk's STS ...
```

The one thing I couldn't have known without looking at SASS is visible at `0x72c0` / `0x7490`: **the `DEPBAR` is inside the predicated region.** Only the electing thread executes the wait — that's `if (lane_in_wg == 0) tma_store_wait<...>()` compiled literally. The other 127 threads branch straight past it to `BSYNC`. On its own that would be a bug: 127 threads would sail into the next chunk and overwrite a buffer the copy engine is still reading, and it would corrupt only under timing pressure, which is precisely the failure that survives casual testing.

`BAR.SYNC` at `0x74a0` is what makes it safe, and it is there, one instruction after reconvergence, before any `STS`. One thread waits; the barrier propagates that wait to the whole warpgroup.

The count arithmetic closes it. `DEPBAR.LE SB0, 0x1` = at most 1 pending. After committing chunk N there are ≤2 in flight (N−1 and N), so the wait retires **N−1**. The next `STS` targets slot `(N+1) % 2` = the slot **N−1** used. The buffer being overwritten is exactly the one whose store just finished — no slack, no overlap, correct by construction rather than by luck.

The census command died on shell quoting, not on anything real. Cheap to redo, and I want it only to confirm all four chunks got the same treatment rather than just the one I read:

```bash
  printf '%-14s %s\n' "$op" "$(grep -cF "$op" /tmp/ep32s2.sass)"
done
```

Expect `UTMASTG` = 8 (4 chunks × 2 row-halves) and `DEPBAR` = 5 (4 chunk waits + the final `<0>` drain).

`UTMASTG` **8** and `UTMACMDFLUSH` **4** are exactly the predicted values — 4 chunks, 2 row-halves each, one commit per chunk. The chunk loop is fully there.

Three counts came in above what I predicted, and I'd rather place them than wave at them:

| op | predicted | actual | |
|---|---|---|---|
| UTMASTG | 8 | **8** | ✓ |
| UTMACMDFLUSH | 4 | **4** | ✓ |
| DEPBAR | 5 | **6** | +1 |
| FENCE.VIEW | 4 | **5** | +1 |
| STS | 64 | **128** | 2× |

The `STS` factor of two has an arithmetic explanation. Each consumer warpgroup owns 128 rows × 128 cols = 16,384 elements over 128 threads = 128 fp32 accumulators per thread = **64** packed `bf16x2` stores. Getting 128 means two static copies of the write path. The instruction at `0x74b0` in the earlier dump — `FSETP.NEU.FTZ.AND P1, PT, RZ, UR16, PT`, a float compare against zero — is almost certainly the `beta` test, giving a beta==0 fast path and a beta!=0 read-modify-write path. That fits the other counts: the two paths would double the `STS` but converge before the store, which is why `UTMASTG` stayed at 8 rather than 16.

That's a hypothesis with supporting evidence, not a fact yet. Placing all three by address settles it:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
echo "=== DEPBAR ==="       ; grep -nF "DEPBAR"     /tmp/ep32s2.sass | cut -c1-95
echo "=== FENCE.VIEW ==="   ; grep -nF "FENCE.VIEW" /tmp/ep32s2.sass | cut -c1-95
echo "=== UTMASTG ==="      ; grep -nF "UTMASTG"    /tmp/ep32s2.sass | cut -c1-95
echo "=== STS target offsets ==="
grep -oE "STS \[R[0-9]+\+0x[0-9a-f]+\]" /tmp/ep32s2.sass \
  | grep -oE "0x[0-9a-f]+" | cut -c1-5 | sort | uniq -c
```

If the STS offsets cluster into two identical sets over the same `0x30000`/`0x34000` slot bases, the beta-path reading is confirmed and the 2× is inert duplication.

One thing worth saying plainly about the direction of the surprise: an **extra** `DEPBAR` and an **extra** `FENCE` are both conservative. More waiting and more ordering cannot create a race — only fewer can. So these two overshoots don't put Stage 3's correctness back in question; the proof from the last dump stands. They're a cost question, not a safety question, and if the 5th fence turns out to be redundant that's a small win to collect later rather than a defect.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-10 18:20 IST]

Everything is placed. Both overshoots dissolve, and the prediction was right in each case:

**`DEPBAR` — 5 TMA waits, not 6.** Line 684 is `WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE gsb0, 0x0`, which is `wgmma.wait_group` — the accumulator wait, a different instruction my substring grep swept up. The real TMA-store waits are exactly the predicted five.

**`FENCE.VIEW` — 4 in the loop, plus the prologue.** `0x0150` is the mbarrier-init fence at kernel entry. The chunk fences are the other four.

Laying the addresses end to end gives the complete pipeline, every instruction accounted for:

```
DEPBAR SB0,1  0x1740    chunk0 wait (nothing in flight yet - vacuous, correct)
  STS -> slot0 (0x30000)
  FENCE 0x3570  ->  UTMASTG 0x3670, 0x3710  ->  UTMACMDFLUSH
DEPBAR SB0,1  0x3740    retires chunk0
  STS -> slot1 (0x34000)
  FENCE 0x5430  ->  UTMASTG 0x5530, 0x55d0  ->  UTMACMDFLUSH
DEPBAR SB0,1  0x5600    retires chunk1
  STS -> slot0
  FENCE 0x72b0  ->  UTMASTG 0x73b0, 0x7450  ->  UTMACMDFLUSH
DEPBAR SB0,1  0x7480    retires chunk2
  STS -> slot1
  FENCE 0x9170  ->  UTMASTG 0x9270, 0x9310  ->  UTMACMDFLUSH
DEPBAR SB0,0  0x9340    drains chunk3
```

Four chunks, two slots, strict alternation, every reuse of a slot preceded by the wait that retires its previous store. That is the design, compiled literally.

The `STS` 2× resolves too, and the way it resolves is itself the proof. 64 per slot base (`0x300xx`/`0x302xx`/`0x310xx`/`0x312xx` = 64, same again on `0x34xxx`). Per thread per chunk is 16 packed stores; 4 chunks = 64 per path; two paths = 128, splitting 32+32 into each slot. Consistent with a `beta==0` / `beta!=0` pair, which is what the `FSETP.NEU ... RZ` at `0x74b0` was testing.

The decisive part: **the sync instructions are not doubled.** 5 DEPBAR, 4 fences, 4 commits, 8 UTMASTG — all exactly the 4-chunk count. If both `STS` sets were live in a single execution, there would have to be 8 store pairs to move them. There are 4. So the two sets are mutually exclusive branches through one pipeline, not two sets of live writes. No further check needed to close correctness; the counts do it.

Stage 3 is proven on structure. The buffer overwritten at each step is the one whose store just retired, and that holds because the machine code cannot do otherwise — not because thirteen runs happened to pass.

Line 573 is the answer, and it says my test shapes were invalid:

```
[BluBridge SM90] cuTensorMapEncodeTiled: invalid argument (1)
```

`cuTensorMapEncodeTiled` requires the **global stride to be a multiple of 16 bytes**. I picked `4095x2047x1023` and `511x257x129` — every dimension odd. At bf16, 2047×2 = 4094 bytes, 1023×2 = 2046, 4095×2 = 8190; none divides 16. Whichever dim lands on the leading axis, the descriptor is unrepresentable. Those shapes cannot be expressed in TMA at all, which is why **all 267 configs** failed identically with `MaxRelErr` exactly 1.0 — output all zeros, kernel never ran. I conflated "tile residue" with "odd dimensions"; they're different things and only the first is what we needed to test. My error in choosing them.

**But the run found a real bug anyway, and it's a bad one:**

```
[BluBridge SM90] cuTensorMapEncodeTiled: invalid argument (1)
exit=0
```

The encode fails, we print a message, and then **return success with a zero-filled output buffer**. No error propagates. No non-zero exit. A caller that doesn't scrape stdout — BluTrain, for instance — silently trains on zeros. That's exactly the failure class that survives every test suite, because `grep -c FAIL` reads clean and the process looks healthy. It also explains the four vanished `nt` cases: no PASS/FAIL line was ever printed.

That's a genuine defect, independent of the epilogue work, and it needs a real fix — the encode result must propagate as an error, and unaligned leading dimensions should be rejected up front with a clear message rather than producing zeros. I'm flagging it rather than fixing it now, so Stage 3 doesn't get tangled with an unrelated change.

Redoing the validation with shapes that are actually tile-residue and TMA-legal — every dim a multiple of 8 elements (16 B), none a multiple of its tile:

3. **match cuBLAS's 6 variants** across the 21 call sites, optimize each to parity
4. **cross-comparison tests** to pick the winner per call site

Plus Fault 2 inside step 3: the `stmatrix` write path, 224,990 bank conflicts against cuBLAS's 5.

## Where we actually are

**Item 1 is done and proven.** Chunked epilogue, 4th stage real (215,040 → 231,424 B), +7–8%, 83.5% → 90% of cuBLAS on the K=2048 shapes, bit-exact everywhere, 820/820 regression clean.

**Items 2, 3, 4 have not been started.** Fault 2 not started.

So: one of four items, in a day.

## The part that should bother you more than the test count

**Today's work currently delivers zero to the trainer.** `ep32s2` is a probe config. It isn't in the dispatcher. And the 1.7B run pins `256x128x64_1x2_h_**rs2**` on 10 of 13 call sites — I benchmarked against plain `_h`, which is not what ships. Until `rs2 + ep32s2` exists and is pinned, we have a proven kernel improvement and a 96.39% trainer, unchanged.

That's not a detour I was proposing for fun. It's the last mile of item 1. One build, one run.

## Was I diverted?

**On substance, no** — Fault 1 was item 1, and the proof depth was what you asked for after the "lucky runs" concern.

**On process, yes, and that's the real cost.** Two specific things:

- I picked `4095x2047x1023` as a residue shape. All-odd dimensions are illegal for TMA — every one of 267 configs failed, and that round trip taught us nothing about chunking. My error.
- Worse: I ran **six separate round trips** today, each a 1–2 minute GPU job with you pasting output in between. The GPU was idle almost the entire day. That should have been *one* script — build, ablate, validate, regress, report — run once.

That's the answer to "why are you optimizing these long paths": I was serialising through you instead of batching through the machine.

## What happens next, as one job

```bash

make -j$(nproc) 2>&1 | tail -5
nvidia-smi -i 3 -lgc 1620
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=3 bash tools/h27z65_bank_fault1.sh 2>&1 | tee test_reports/h27z65.md
```

That script — which I'll write now — does: validate `rs2_ep32s2` correctness, measure it against `rs2` on all 13 call sites, and print the pin/no-pin verdict per site. One run, one report, no round trips.

Then Fault 2 (`stmatrix`) as the next single unit of work, same structure — implement, one script, one report.

Split-K I'd put **last** of the four, and I want to flag why rather than silently reorder: split-K fixes wave quantization on low-K shapes, and this model's GEMMs are K=2048–50304. It's needed for completeness, but it will not move the 1.7B number the way Fault 2 will.

Want me to write that script and the `rs2_ep32s2` registry row now?

**Added 4 shippable configs** ([Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh:1258](src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM90/Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh#L1258)) — chunking combined with the baselines the trainer actually pins, not with plain `_h`:

|---|---|

13 of 15 covered. `kv-dgrad` (128x176) and `kv-wgrad` (64x128) can't take `EPI_TILE_N=32` — 176 isn't divisible by 32, and 64x128's store buffer is only 16 KB so shrinking it frees nothing. The script prints them as SKIP rather than dropping them silently.

**One script** ([tools/h27z65_bank_fault1.sh](tools/h27z65_bank_fault1.sh)) that does everything in a single run: refuses to start on unlocked clocks, checks every candidate is bit-exact *before* quoting any timing, then measures base vs chunked on all 15 sites, 3 reps, one process each, interleaved so drift hits both arms equally, and prints a per-site PIN / KEEP verdict.

```bash

cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && git pull
make -j$(nproc) 2>&1 | tail -5
nvidia-smi -i 3 -pm 1 && nvidia-smi -i 3 -lgc 1620
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=3 bash tools/h27z65_bank_fault1.sh 2>&1 | tee test_reports/h27z65.md
```

This answers the only question that matters for item 1: **does chunking still pay against `rs2`, per call site.** If it does, those rows go into the dispatch table and the trainer moves off 96.39%. If `rs2` and chunking turn out to be fighting over the same L2 effect, the verdict column says KEEP base and we know that instead of assuming it.

One thing for when we then run the trainer: BluTrain compiles from its own vendored `BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/BluBridge-BLAS/src/`, not the repo root. That bit us before — a validator passing 15/15 while the trainer ran unchanged code. It'll need the sync before the end-to-end number means anything.

Everything checks out. What the deep pass actually found:

**The 192x192 bug, root-caused in code rather than guessed.** `c_buf` is a *single buffer shared by both warpgroups* ([template.cuh:3383](src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM90/Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh#L3383)). The unchunked path indexes it by the **global** chunk index `ch`, and the two warpgroups own disjoint global chunks — so they never collide. The chunked path replaced that with `epi_slot`, which is **warpgroup-local**. Under `SPLIT_M` that's still safe because the warpgroups are separated by row (`row0 = g*WG_MATOMS*64`). Under an N-split, `row0 == 0` for *both* — they share every row and differ only in column, so collapsing to local slots puts them on identical addresses.

The pass/fail split is exactly `SPLIT_M = (BM/64) % 2 == 0`:

| variant | BM/64 | SPLIT_M | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 256x128 rs2 / v | 4 | even → M-split | PASS |
| 128x256 v | 2 | even → M-split | PASS |
| 192x192 v | **3** | **odd → N-split** | **FAIL** |

Not a plausible story — a complete correlation with a mechanism.

**Fix**: `EPI_WG_SLOTSETS` gives each warpgroup its own slot set when the split is on N, and is `1` (no change) under `SPLIT_M`. A `static_assert` pins `Config::EPI_SPLIT_M == WGrid::SPLIT_M` so the sizing and the indexing can never drift apart again.

**Proof of no regression**: compiled HEAD and the fix locally, dumped SASS for the already-validated `256x128 ep32s2` kernel — **3,072 instructions, byte-identical**. The 820/820, 24/24 and 18/18 results don't need re-running.

**And a second thing the arithmetic caught**: carrying `EPI_TILE_N=32` over to 192x192 would have shipped a variant that buys nothing. With the fix, `2·2·192·32·2 = 49152` leaves `(231424−49152)/49152 = 3.71 → 3` stages — the same 3 the unchunked path already had. `EPI_TILE_N=16` gives 24576 → **4 stages**. So I registered `192x192x64_1x2_v_ep16s2` as well, and the script now measures both so the run separates "overlap only" from "overlap + 4th stage" on that tile instead of assuming the 256x128 answer transfers.

Worth recording separately: the C-store loop carries a comment arguing no cross-warpgroup barrier is needed *because the ranges are disjoint by construction*. Chunking silently invalidated that premise. The bug wasn't a missing barrier — it was an invariant a comment depended on being quietly removed elsewhere.

-what i thought to do

today i planned to finish the depth-4 item, which is the first of the four things on our list, and to do it the way we agreed - build it in three stages, test and ablate after every single edit so each piece is separately known, and prove it structurally instead of running it a few times and calling it correct, then measure it against the configs the trainer actually pins and put the winners into the dispatch table
