i built the three stages and ablated each one on its own, and the ladder did what it was meant to do - it split the gain instead of just reporting it, stage one costs exactly nothing so the chunk loop itself is free, stage two gives about one and a half percent from the store overlapping the next chunk, and stage three gives another five point seven on top which is the fourth pipeline stage appearing, shared memory goes from 215040 to 231424 which is the same stage count cublas uses, then instead of trusting the runs i pulled the sass out of the shipped library and checked the actual machine code - four chunks, two slots, eight tma stores, four commits, five waits, and the barrier sitting between the wait and the next write where it has to be, the slot addresses are exactly 16384 apart which is the slot stride byte for byte, so the recycling is correct because the instructions cannot do otherwise, on top of that residue passed 24 of 24 including the case where the leftover is only 8 columns and three of the four chunks have nothing valid in them, batch passed 18 of 18, and the whole config matrix passed 820 of 820 which is what says my shared-code edits did not disturb the other 266 configs

then i found a real mistake of mine, all of that was measured against 256x128_1x2_h and the trainer does not run that config, it pins the rs2 version on nine of the fifteen call sites, and raster swizzle changes the tile ordering which changes l2 behaviour in the epilogue which is the exact thing i was modifying, so the plus seven percent i had was never a prediction of what pinning it would buy, i should have caught this at the start because the pinned configs were in my own call-site table from earlier in the session, i rebuilt the measurement against the real baselines and the first numbers say two useful things - chunking and raster swizzle do compose, the shallow-k site gains six point eight percent on top of rs2, but chunking actually loses four point six percent on lm_head-wgrad where k is 16384, which fits everything else we have seen because epilogue cost scales as one over k so on the deep shapes the extra waits are pure overhead, that means the answer is per call site and not one global switch

while doing that a genuine kernel bug came out, the 192x192 variant returned garbage with error in the tens of thousands while every other chunked variant was bit exact, i read the epilogue code instead of guessing and the cause is that the store buffer is shared by both warpgroups, on tiles where the split is by row the two warpgroups write different rows so one buffer is fine, but 192x192 splits by column instead and then both warpgroups write every row and only the column index separates them - which is exactly the index my chunking replaced with a per-warpgroup slot number, so they were overwriting each other, the pass fail pattern matches that split perfectly across all four variants, i fixed it by giving each warpgroup its own slots only when the split is by column, and i proved the fix cannot disturb the working tiles by compiling before and after locally and diffing the sass of the already validated kernel, 3072 instructions both sides, identical, so the earlier validation still stands without rerunning it, i also worked out that 32 wide chunks do not free a stage on 192x192 at all and 16 does, so i registered that variant too rather than assume the 256x128 answer carries over

i also wasted your time twice with bugs in my own test script, one where the shape column is sixteen characters wide so my pattern silently dropped the six biggest call sites and reported them as failures when they had passed, and one where a single broken variant aborted the whole run, both are fixed and i now dry run the script against a fake binary before sending it, everything is documented, tomorrow is the measurement run and then pinning, after that fault 2 which is the stmatrix write path, then the variant matching, then split-k last

The gains track K exactly as the epilogue theory predicts: K=2048 sites get +6.8 to +9.6%, K=5632 gets +3.6%, K≥11264 gets +0.5 to +1.7%. Biggest win is `gate_up-fwd` at **+9.58%, 84.0% → 92.0% of cuBLAS** — which is also the largest forward GEMM by FLOPs.

Two things I had wrong, both now corrected by measurement:

**My `ep16s2` prediction failed.** I argued 16-wide chunks would free the 4th stage on 192x192 and therefore pay. The arithmetic was right — it does free the stage — but it still loses (−6.14% vs ep32s2's −7.07%). Freeing the stage helps by about a point and doesn't come close to covering the cost. The likely reason is that chunking narrows the TMA store box (96 → 32 → 16 columns, i.e. 64 → 32 bytes per row), and N-split tiles also pay *double* the buffer because each warpgroup needs its own slot set — so they get less stage benefit for the same overhead. Worth registering the variant to find that out, but the prediction was wrong.

**Yesterday's −4.6% on `lm_head-wgrad` was noise.** Median-of-3 gives **+0.56%**. Those were n=1 numbers taken from correctness runs, which is why I flagged them as directional only — that caution was warranted.

So the two runs are different jobs. Let me check how the 96.39% baseline was actually taken:

Now the protocol is pinned down. **These are two different jobs** and the 10 steps you're thinking of is the nsys one:

| purpose | config | steps | what you read |
|---|---|---|---|
| **kernel identity** — is the right variant running | `bluscript_config_profile.yaml` | 10 | kernel names, never throughput |
| **throughput** — the 96.39% number | `bluscript_config.yaml` | run to ~step 10, then Ctrl+C | tok/s from steady steps 2–8 |

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/BluTrain
grep -oE "bgemm_sm90_kernel<Sm90WarpspecConfig<[^>]*>" profiling_reports/nsys_train_blublas/cuda_gpu_kern_gb_sum.txt \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
echo "=== chunked kernels (EPI_TILE_N=32, EPI_STAGES=2) ==="
```

The chunked configs end their template argument list with `..., (int)32, (int)2>`. Non-zero there means the trainer is genuinely running the chunked epilogue. Zero means the dispatcher isn't reaching it in the real workload — and that would be the same class of trap as the stale vendored copy, caught before we spend time on a throughput number.

> tool `Bash`: Scan output.md for step throughput lines

Nothing's wrong — those two numbers are from **different configs**, so they were never comparable.

| run | config | grad_accum | dt/step | tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| earlier plain run | `bluscript_config.yaml` | 128 | ~78,000 ms | 26.8K |
| this nsys run | `bluscript_config_profile.yaml` | **4** | ~2,572 ms | 25.4K |

The profile config does an optimizer step every **65,536** tokens instead of every **2,097,152** — 32× more often. All the per-step fixed cost (optimizer, grad-norm, LR update, logging) gets amortised over 32× fewer tokens, so tok/s drops. That's the config, not the kernels. nsys overhead adds a bit on top.

This is exactly what that config's header warns about: *"DO NOT READ THROUGHPUT OFF A RUN WITH THIS CONFIG."*

It doesn't matter for what we're doing, because we read the **ratio** of ours vs cuBLAS on the *same* config with the *same* profiling. And the profile run is actually the better instrument here — look at the stability:

```
step 2   25479.56
step 3   25479.80
step 4   25478.82
```

0.004% spread, versus the full-config run still ramping through 18.4K → 24.7K → 26.8K at the same step numbers.

Run the cuBLAS arm so we have the pair:

```bash

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 make nsys-train MODE=production WITH_BLUBLAS=0 NP=1 2>&1 \
  | tee ~/gautam_k/blublas/test_reports/h27z69_nsys_cublas.log | tail -40
```

### CLAUDE [2026-08-11 11:54 IST]

Good question, and it's not wrong — it's arithmetic, and it checks out exactly.

A "step" is `grad_accum` micro-batches of forward+backward, then **one** optimizer update over all 1.73B parameters. The optimizer cost is **fixed per step** — it doesn't care how many tokens fed into it.

```
tok/s = (ga × 16384) / (ga × T_micro + T_opt)
```

So the fixed `T_opt` gets spread over 32× fewer tokens at ga=4 than at ga=128. Solving with your two measured points:

```
ga=4    →  4×T_micro + T_opt =  2,572 ms
ga=128  → 128×T_micro + T_opt = 78,178 ms
─────────────────────────────────────────
124 × T_micro = 75,606      →  T_micro ≈ 609.7 ms
                                T_opt   ≈ 133.2 ms
```

Check it back: `128 × 609.7 + 133.2 = 78,175 ms` against 78,178 measured. And the optimizer share:

- ga=4 → 133/2572 = **5.2%** of step time
- ga=128 → 133/78178 = **0.17%**

Predicted throughput difference: **5.2%**. Observed: 26,828 → 25,481 = **5.3%**. It lands on the nose.

So the drop is entirely the optimizer being amortised over fewer tokens. Expected, correct, and it happens identically on both backends — which is why the ratio is unaffected.

There's a bonus in that arithmetic worth noticing: the grad_accum effect alone accounts for **all** of the gap, leaving essentially nothing for nsys overhead. With 610 ms micro-batches and large kernels, nsys's per-launch cost is negligible here. That means the profiled ratio we're about to compute is trustworthy, not just internally consistent.

Run the cuBLAS arm and we have the pair:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/BluTrain
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 make nsys-train MODE=production WITH_BLUBLAS=0 NP=1 2>&1 \
  | tee ~/gautam_k/blublas/test_reports/h27z69_nsys_cublas.log | tail -40
```

### CLAUDE [2026-08-11 11:57 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Read the cuBLAS run section of output.md

Both arms, same box, same config, same profiling. Steps 2–8 steady state:

| backend | mean dt/step | mean tok/s |
|---|---|---|
| cuBLAS | 2511.78 ms | 26,091 |
| blublas | 2573.55 ms | 25,465 |

**97.60% of cuBLAS end to end.** Both ways of computing it agree exactly (tok/s ratio 0.97600, dt ratio 0.97600), and per-step spread is 0.17% on both arms — a much cleaner instrument than the full-config run.

Three things about this, in order of importance.

**1. I cannot yet claim "+1.2 points from chunking."** The 96.39% baseline was on a *different box* with a *different config* (ga=128). Comparing 97.60% to it crosses two changes at once. The clean claim today is only: **97.60% on this box**. To attribute the gain to chunking I need the pre-chunking dispatcher measured *here*, and I don't have it. That's a gap in the experiment, and it's the same class of error as measuring against `_h` instead of `_rs2` yesterday.

For what it's worth, the ga=4 config *flatters* us slightly — the backend-independent optimizer step is 5.2% of step time at ga=4 versus 0.17% at ga=128, which dilutes the GEMM gap. Correcting for that puts the ga=128 equivalent at roughly 97.5%, so the direction holds, but that's arithmetic, not a measurement.

**2. The loss divergence is one-sided and growing, and that needs checking.**

```
step   ours      cuBLAS    ours − cuBLAS
  2   12.372823  12.371309   +0.0015
  3   12.138550  12.128131   +0.0104
  4   10.695275  10.678774   +0.0165
  6   10.351429  10.326351   +0.0251
  8    9.891715   9.854586   +0.0371
  9    9.831535   9.790644   +0.0409   (val: 9.884 vs 9.849)
```

Monotonic, always positive, ours always the worse loss. The frozen baseline recorded agreement to ≤8.1e-4; this is 50× that. It may still be pure chaotic drift from reduction-order — but a *consistent sign over eight steps* is not what random drift usually looks like, and I'm not willing to call it noise without a control.

The control is cheap and decisive: **run blublas twice.** If two identical blublas runs diverge from each other by a similar monotone amount, it's chaos and this is fine. If they track each other tightly, the backend difference is real and needs investigating before anything ships.

**3. Kernel identity is still unverified** — that's free, the captures already exist:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/BluTrain
echo "=== chunked kernels actually launched? ==="
grep -c "(int)32, (int)2>" profiling_reports/nsys_train_blublas/cuda_gpu_kern_gb_sum.txt
echo "=== our GEMM kernels by time ==="
grep -E "bgemm_sm90_kernel" profiling_reports/nsys_train_blublas/cuda_gpu_kern_gb_sum.txt | head -12
echo "=== cuBLAS GEMM kernels by time ==="
grep -E "nvjet" profiling_reports/nsys_train_cublas/cuda_gpu_kern_gb_sum.txt | head -12
echo "=== top-10 overall, both ==="
head -15 profiling_reports/nsys_train_blublas/cuda_gpu_kern_gb_sum.txt
head -15 profiling_reports/nsys_train_cublas/cuda_gpu_kern_gb_sum.txt
```

Then the determinism control:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/BluTrain
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 make nsys-train MODE=production WITH_BLUBLAS=1 NP=1 \
  NSYS_OUT=nsys_train_blublas_run2 2>&1 \
  | tee ~/gautam_k/blublas/test_reports/h27z69_nsys_blublas_run2.log | tail -25
```

If run2's losses match run1 digit-for-digit, our path is deterministic and that +0.041 is a genuine backend difference to explain. If run2 differs from run1 by a comparable amount, it's drift and we move on.

Two things fall straight out of that, and the second is the important one.

**Non-GEMM time matches to 1 ms out of 20.8 seconds.** That's as clean a validation of the experiment as you could ask for — the two runs are byte-for-byte the same workload apart from the BLAS, so nothing is confounding the comparison.

**The entire GPU-time deficit is GEMM.** We lose 1.400 s on GEMM; total GPU deficit is 1.399 s. There is nothing else. That means every point we claw back in GEMM converts directly into end-to-end — no dilution from anything else on the GPU. It also sets the ceiling: closing GEMM to 100% would take total GPU time from 33.903 s to 32.504 s, and nothing beyond that is available from BLAS work.

GEMM at 89.3% against the §H27z.56 baseline of 86.1% is the right direction, though that baseline was a different box and config, so I'd treat +3.2 points as indicative rather than measured until we run the pre-chunking arm here.

Where the remaining 1.4 s sits needs per-call-site pairing — the aggregate rows lump several shapes into one kernel (the 17,280-call entry has a 359 µs standard deviation, so it's clearly serving many shapes). ### CLAUDE [2026-08-11 12:08 IST]

Straight answer: I said it, it wasn't fabricated, and **it does not survive contact with the real workload.** In the trainer, nothing beats cuBLAS.

Here's the comparison that matters, same two shapes:

| shape | our TF (harness) | our TF (trainer) | cuBLAS TF (harness) | cuBLAS TF (trainer) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| lm_head-dgrad 16384x2048x50304 nt | 805.7 | 792 | **741.4** | **840** |
| lm_head-wgrad 2048x50304x16384 tn | 765.6 | 727 | **753.2** | **850** |

**Our numbers agree between the two (805→792, 765→727). cuBLAS's don't — it runs ~13% faster inside BluTrain than inside our benchmark harness.** So the "108.7%" and "101.6%" were us beating a handicapped cuBLAS, not the cuBLAS the model actually runs.

That's a real problem beyond these two rows: **every "% of cuBLAS" figure produced by our standalone harness is optimistic.** Config *selection* isn't affected — that's ours-vs-ours — but the whole 423-case table's reported %cuB, and the 88.2%/92.9% style numbers, are measured against a weaker reference than reality. The trainer pairing is the truth; the harness is not.

Most likely cause, and it's checkable: BluTrain calls cuBLAS with **swapped operands** — `(opB, opA, N, M, K)` — and our harness almost certainly calls it straight. Same math, different memory layout, different heuristic pick. The split-K evidence supports it: in the trainer cuBLAS chooses `128x128_64x6_1x2_h_splitK_NTT` for wK/wV-wgrad, which needs a workspace it may not have in our harness.

**Now, the pairing itself — where the 1,400 ms actually goes:**

| rank | site | ours% | lost | our tile | cuBLAS tile |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | gate_up-fwd | 91.8% | 256 ms (18.3%) | 256x128 1x2_h | **192x192** 1x2_h coopB |
| 2 | gate_up-wgrad | 84.9% | 242 ms (17.3%) | 192x192 1x2_**v** | 192x192 **2x1_v** coopB |
| 3 | wQ-dgrad | 49.1% | 157 ms (11.2%) | 256x128 1x2_h | 256x128 1x2_h coopA |
| 4–5 | down-dgrad, down-fwd | 90–94% | 157 ms | 256x128 | 192x192 / 256x128 |
| — | wK-wgrad + wV-wgrad | 59.4/60.7% | 91 ms (6.4%) | 64x128 | **splitK** |

Three things I'd flag before anyone acts on this:

**wQ-dgrad's 49.1% is probably not real.** `attnOut-dgrad` is the *identical* shape (16384x2048x2048 nt) with the *identical* config and reads 89.9% at 207.6 µs, versus wQ-dgrad's 372.0 µs. Same shape, same kernel, 79% apart. The pairing script's own docstring notes BluTrain's `WITH_MYBLAS` backward path runs wgrad on a **secondary stream** — so these kernels overlap and per-kernel wall duration inflates. That row needs checking before it's chased; it's likely 157 ms of contention, not deficit.

**Tile choice, not epilogue, is now the top item.** On gate_up-fwd and down-dgrad cuBLAS picks **192x192** where we pick 256x128; on gate_up-wgrad we both pick 192x192 but it uses the **2x1_v** orientation against our 1x2_v. That's your step-3 (match cuBLAS's variants) showing up as the biggest measured lever — 500 ms of the 1,400 ms.

**Split-K has a concrete price tag now:** 91 ms, 6.4%, on the two shapes where cuBLAS uses it and we don't.

Overall: **ours 690 TFLOPS (69.8% peak) vs cuBLAS 773 (78.1% peak), 89.3%.**

**Did it buy anything — honest answer: yes, and I can quantify it, but from an estimate rather than a direct A/B on this box.**

I have today's per-site base-vs-chunked measurements (h27z65) and today's per-site call counts and times (the pairing). Multiplying them out:

| site | our GEMM time | measured gain | saved |
|---|---|---|---|
| gate_up-fwd | 3.116 s | +9.58% | 298 ms |
| wQ/wO-fwd (×2 sites) | 1.188 s | +6.82% | 81 ms |
| wQ/wO-dgrad (×2) | 0.835 s | +6.98% | 58 ms |

| others (5 sites) | — | +0.5–1.7% | 17 ms |
| **total** | | | **≈ 615 ms** |

So without chunking our GEMM would be **13.73 s** instead of 13.11 s:

| | without chunking | with chunking |
|---|---|---|
| GEMM vs cuBLAS | **85.3%** | **89.3%** |
| total GPU vs cuBLAS | 94.2% | 95.9% |
| end-to-end (est.) | ~96.6% | **97.60%** |

**≈ +4 points of GEMM, ≈ +1 point end-to-end.** That's consistent with the old baseline's 96.39%, which is reassuring but not the basis of the claim — the claim comes from measurements taken today on this box.

Two caveats I won't paper over:

The +4 points is **computed, not measured**. Each input is a real measurement from today, but I combined them arithmetically rather than running the pre-chunking dispatcher here. Given yesterday's lesson about wrong baselines, that distinction matters.

And note the wall-clock gain is smaller than the GPU-time gain — 1,400 ms of GPU GEMM deficit maps to only ~62 ms/step of wall deficit, because the backward pass overlaps wgrad on a secondary stream. Roughly half the GEMM time we lose is already hidden behind other work. That caps what any GEMM optimisation returns end-to-end, and it's worth knowing before spending days on fault-2.

```
ours   : 144 x STS, ZERO STSM, 224,990 bank conflicts
```

Before touching code, I worked through the layout question that decides whether this is even implementable — and it resolves well:

**Our wgmma accumulator layout already matches stmatrix's source layout.** From `CLayout_64xN`, decomposing the warpgroup thread id as `t = t0 + 4·t1 + 32·t2`:

```
row = t1 + 8·v1 + 16·t2
col = 2·t0 + v0 + 8·v2
```

Fix `v1, v2`. Within a warp, thread `t = t0 + 4·t1` holds **row `t1`, columns `2·t0` and `2·t0+1`** — an 8×8 block where thread `t` owns row `t/4`, cols `2·(t%4)`, `2·(t%4)+1`. That is *exactly* the `m8n8.b16` fragment layout. And `v0` ∈ {0,1} are the two adjacent columns that pack into one `bf16x2` register. So no register shuffle is needed — the pairs we already build are in the right registers.

**But there's something the §H27y.10 write-up didn't work out, and it changes the plan.** Our store buffer is linear:

```
c_buf + slot·(BM·C_BOX_N) + brow·C_BOX_N + cic
```

With `C_BOX_N = 32` bf16 = 64 B row stride, 32 lanes writing consecutive rows hit banks `(row·16) % 32` = only banks 0 and 16 → **16-way conflict**. Unchunked at `C_BOX_N = 128` the stride is 256 B → `(row·64) % 32 = 0` → **32-way conflict, every lane on one bank**. That is the 225k.

So the conflicts are a **layout** problem, not an instruction problem. `stmatrix` on a linear layout would still conflict — CUTLASS gets conflict-free stores because STSM is paired with an **XOR-swizzled** smem layout, and the TMA descriptor is created with a matching swizzle mode so the copy engine reads it back correctly.

That means fault-2 is potentially two independent changes, and the cheaper one may carry most of the win:

- **swizzle the C store buffer + set the matching swizzle on the C TMA descriptor** — kills the conflicts
- **`stmatrix`** — cuts the instruction count (2.11×), needs the swizzle to be worth much

C descriptor confirmed: `CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_NONE` — the store buffer is **linear and unswizzled**. That's the bank-conflict source.

Now the authoritative `stmatrix` spec:
> tool `Bash`: Locate the stmatrix section in PTX ISA 9.3
> tool `Bash`: Read the full stmatrix specification

Spec read. Here's what's now **verified** versus what's still **open** — I'll keep these separate because the difference matters.

## Verified from PTX ISA 9.3 §9.7.15.5.16

**Addressing (`.x4`):** threads 0–7 supply `addr0–addr7` = the eight **row start addresses** of matrix 0; threads 8–15 → matrix 1; 16–23 → matrix 2; 24–31 → matrix 3.

**Data:** *"A group of four threads stores an entire row of the matrix"*, and for `.x4` *"elements of the third and fourth matrices are stored from the subsequent source registers"*. So register `r_m` of **every** thread carries matrix `m`, and thread `t` holds **row `t/4`, columns `2·(t%4)` and `2·(t%4)+1`**.

Note those are two *different* groupings of the same 32 threads — thread `t` supplies an address for matrix `t/8`, but data for all four matrices via `r0..r3`. That's the part I wasn't sure of; the spec settles it.

**Alignment:** *"a group of four consecutive threads stores 16 bytes. The matrix addresses must be naturally aligned accordingly."* → every row address must be 16-byte aligned.

## The key result: our accumulator layout already matches

From `CLayout_64xN` with `t = t0 + 4·t1 + 32·t2`:

```
row = t1 + 8·v1 + 16·t2      col = 2·t0 + v0 + 8·v2
```

Within a warp, thread `t = t0 + 4·t1` holds **row `t/4`, cols `2·(t%4)` and `2·(t%4)+1`** — identical to what stmatrix wants. The `v0 ∈ {0,1}` pair is exactly the `bf16x2` we already pack. **No register shuffle needed.** The four matrices map onto `(v1,v2) ∈ {(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)}` = a 16×16 block, giving `r0..r3` directly.

Alignment holds too: with `C_BOX_N=32`, row addresses are `(brow·32 + c0)·2` bytes and `c0 ∈ {0,8,16,24}`, so every one is 16-byte aligned.

Instruction count: 32 packed values per thread per atom → **8 `stmatrix.x4` replacing 64 `STS`**. That's the 2.11× instruction gap.

## The correction to §H27y.10's framing

§H27y.10 treats this as "we don't use STSM". The bank math says it's really a **layout** problem:

| layout | row stride | banks hit | conflict |
|---|---|---|---|
| unchunked, `C_BOX_N=128` | 256 B | `(row·64)%32 = 0` — all one bank | **32-way** |
| chunked, `C_BOX_N=32` | 64 B | `(row·16)%32` ∈ {0,16} | **16-way** |
| + stmatrix, still linear | 64 B | 16 B per row instead of 4 | **4-way** |
| + XOR swizzle | — | — | **0** |

So `stmatrix` alone gets us 16-way → 4-way, not to cuBLAS's 5 conflicts. CUTLASS is conflict-free because STSM is paired with a **swizzled** smem layout — and our C descriptor is `CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_NONE`, so the buffer must currently stay linear for TMA to read it back correctly.

One promising accident: `C_BOX_N=32` is **exactly 64 bytes**, which is the natural width for `CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_64B`. Fault-1 may have set fault-2 up.

## What I still need before writing code

1. **TMA swizzle rules** — does `SWIZZLE_64B` accept `boxDim[0] = 32` bf16, and what XOR pattern does the copy engine apply, so our store addresses match it? (cuda.h / driver docs)
2. **Does cuBLAS swizzle its C buffer?** We have their SASS — the address arithmetic before `STSM` will show an XOR if it does.
3. **Empirical proof of the thread→element mapping.** Figure 107 is an image, so the text alone doesn't fully pin it. A ~40-line standalone kernel that writes known values via `stmatrix` and reads smem back is *absolute* proof rather than spec inference — and it's the cheapest way to be certain.

I'd do (3) first since it's self-contained and settles the foundation. Want me to write that probe kernel?

```cpp
if      (BLK_K0 % size<1>(Layout_K_SW128_Atom) == 0) return SW128;   // 128 B row

```

**Found it. This is the answer, straight out of cuBLAS's SASS.**

```
LOP3.LUT R21,  R21, 0x1f, RZ, 0xc0    ; R21 = lane & 31
LOP3.LUT R169, R21, 0x7,  RZ, 0xc0    ; r = lane % 8        <- row in the matrix
SHF.R.U32.HI R23, RZ, 0x3, R21        ; m = lane >> 3       <- matrix index 0..3
IMAD     R168, R169, 0x9, RZ          ; r * 9
LOP3.LUT R23,  R168, R23, RZ, 0x3c    ; (r*9) XOR m         <- 0x3c IS XOR
IMAD.SHL R23,  R23, 0x10, RZ          ; * 16 bytes
STSM.16.M88.4 [R23+UR32], R24
```

`LOP3` immLut `0x3c` = `a ^ b` (0xF0 ^ 0xCC). **cuBLAS swizzles.** Decoding it:

`r*9 = r*8 + r`, and since `r < 8` the two terms occupy disjoint bit fields, so `r*9 = (r*8) | r`. Therefore:

```
granule = row*8 + (row XOR m)        , granule = 16 bytes
```

**8 granules per row = a 128-byte row, with the granule position XOR-ed by the row index.** That is exactly `Swizzle<3,3,3>` / SW128 — and it is conflict-free, which is where their 5 comes from and our 192.

Two more things fall out of the same block:

**Their epilogue buffer is tiny and per-warp.** `UIMAD.U32 UR32, UR26, 0x400, UR32` with `UR26 = tid>>5` — each warp gets **0x400 = 1024 bytes = 8 rows × 128 B**. Warpgroups step by `0x2000`. So cuBLAS stages **8 rows at a time per warp**, not the whole tile.

**The second STSM confirms the width.** `R170 = (lane & 0x18) | 0x20`, `R169 = R170>>3` = `m + 4` — so matrices 4–7, columns 64–127. Eight 8-wide matrices = **64 bf16 columns = 128 bytes** per row.

## So the answer to "how come cuBLAS does it"

| | ours | cuBLAS |
|---|---|---|
| row width | 32 bf16 = **64 B** | 64 bf16 = **128 B** |
| swizzle | **none** | XOR by row (SW128) |
| buffer shape | `BM` rows × 64 B | **8 rows** × 128 B, per warp |
| buffer size | 32,768 B (chunked) | ~16 KB total |
| conflicts | 192 | 5 |

It isn't stmatrix — my probe already proved stmatrix alone changes nothing (B == A, 192 both). It's **128-byte swizzled rows plus a small 8-row staging buffer**.

And that resolves the tension I was worried about: cuBLAS gets a *wider* row **and** a *smaller* buffer than us, because they stage 8 rows per warp instead of all `BM` rows. So going to 128-byte rows does **not** have to cost us the 4th pipeline stage — 8 rows × 128 B × 4 warps × 2 warpgroups × 2 slots ≈ 16 KB, which is *less* than our current 32,768.

Before I design against this I want to confirm the 8-row staging and the buffer total from their SASS rather than from one address expression — that's the next check, and then fault-2 has a concrete, proven target shape.

| | ours (192x192) | cuBLAS (192x192) |
|---|---|---|
| epilogue row | 32 bf16 = 64 B | **64 bf16 = 128 B** |
| swizzle | none | **XOR by row** |
| buffer shape | `BM`=192 rows | **8 rows per warp** |
| epilogue smem | 73,728 B | **16,384 B** |
| mainloop stages | 3 | **4** |
| conflicts | 192 | 5 |

**They get a wider row *and* a smaller buffer, because they stage 8 rows per warp instead of all `BM` rows.** Our buffer is 4.5× larger and half as wide.

```
192x192: 4 stages = 196,608 ; budget 231,424 → 34,816 left for the store buffer
cuBLAS-shaped epilogue = 8 rows × 128 B × 4 warps × 2 wg × 2 slots = 16,384   ✓ fits with room
256x128: same STAGE_BYTES (49,152) → same 34,816 available                    ✓ fits
```

So adopting cuBLAS's epilogue **shape** gives us the 4th pipeline stage *and* conflict-free stores *and* uses less shared memory than we use today — on both tile families. row 7 → 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0   = g^7

`CU_TENSOR_MAP_SWIZZLE_128B` **is** `granule = row*8 + (row XOR g)` — bit-for-bit the permutation decoded from cuBLAS's SASS. And part 2 proves we can drive it: write smem through that formula, TMA out, every one of 512 elements lands correctly.

**One correction to something I stated too confidently earlier.** I said "8 consecutive accumulator registers → one `stmatrix.x4`". That's true for the **16 rows × 16 cols** arrangement I used in probe 1. cuBLAS uses **8 rows × 32 cols** — its four matrices are column blocks `m = 0..3` all at rows 0–7 (`granule = row*8 + (row^m)`, so `m` is a column index, not a row/col pair). Under that arrangement `v2 = m`, so the four registers are:

```
r0..r3 = acc[2·v1 + 16j + {0, 4, 8, 12}]  (each paired with +1 for v0)
```

**stride 4, not consecutive.** Still no shuffle — every register is still a `v0` pair owned by the same thread — but the indexing differs, and if we adopt cuBLAS's tile shape we must use cuBLAS's grouping. Worth catching now rather than in a wrong kernel.

## What's proven

| link | evidence |
|---|---|
| stmatrix semantics (address by `t/8`, data by `t/4`) | PTX 9.3 spec **+** hardware probe, 0/256 mismatches |
| our accumulator already matches — no shuffle | probe **+** `wgmma_frag_rowcol` source |
| **stmatrix alone buys nothing** | measured: 192 vs 192 conflicts, 3.230 vs 3.217 ms |
| the swizzle is the mechanism | measured: 64 conflicts, 1.97× |
| 64-byte rows can never be conflict-free | 4 granules vs 8 rows — structural |
| cuBLAS uses `row*8 + (row XOR g)`, 128 B rows, 8 rows/warp, 16 KB | decoded from their SASS, 3 cross-checks |
| `SWIZZLE_128B` **is** that permutation | measured, 0/512 both directions |

**§H27y.10's framing was wrong.** "We use STS, cuBLAS uses STSM" is not the gap — I proved stmatrix on our current buffer changes literally nothing. The gap is that cuBLAS's C buffer is **128 bytes wide and XOR-swizzled**, and ours is 64 bytes and linear.

## The design it points to

```
                    ours today        cuBLAS        proposed
row width           64 B              128 B         128 B
swizzle             none              XOR by row    XOR by row (SWIZZLE_128B)
staging             BM rows           8 rows/warp   8 rows/warp
epilogue smem       32,768 B          16,384 B      16,384 B
mainloop stages     4 (256x128)       4             4
conflicts           192               5             ~5
```

The budget closes with room: 4 stages × 49,152 = 196,608 of a 231,424 budget leaves 34,816, and the new epilogue needs 16,384. So this gets the 4th stage **and** conflict-free stores **and** uses *half* the shared memory we use now — on both the 256x128 and 192x192 families. It supersedes fault-1's `EPI_TILE_N=32`, which reached the 4th stage by narrowing the row, i.e. by making the conflicts worse.

## One thing I will not assume

The probe used an **8-row** box. The XOR is over 3 bits, so a taller box *probably* repeats with period 8 — `granule = row*8 + ((row%8) XOR g)` — which would let one TMA store cover 16 or 64 rows instead of 8 and cut the store count substantially. **Not tested, so not assumed.**

It's a two-line change to the probe (`R = 8` → `16`, prediction → `(row%8)`). Worth settling before coding, because it decides whether the epilogue issues one TMA per 8 rows or per 64 — and that's the difference between cuBLAS's 276 `UTMASTG` and our current 3.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-11 13:10 IST]

Everything is now settled, and **three results differ from what I predicted** — which is exactly why we tested.

## Confirmed

**TEST 1 — SW128 period is 8 rows, at every box height.** `granule = row*8 + (g ^ (row%8))`, identical at R = 8/16/32/64. One TMA store can cover 64 rows.

**TEST 7 — rank-3 works identically.** Our C descriptor has a batch axis; swizzle is unaffected.

**TEST 9 — residue works.** A 64×8 box clipped to a 40×5 matrix swizzles identically, 0/200 wrong.

**TEST 8 — the whole path is correct end to end.** STSM → swizzled smem → TMA → gmem: **0/512 wrong**. That link had never been tested.

## Three corrections to what I claimed

**1. "stmatrix alone buys nothing" was too broad.** Test 8 timing:

```
STS  through swizzle : 0.570 ms
STSM through swizzle : 0.295 ms   1.93x
```

On the *linear* layout STSM was worthless (192 vs 192 conflicts, 3.230 vs 3.217 ms). On the *swizzled* layout it's **1.93× faster**. Once the swizzle removes the conflicts, the bottleneck moves to instruction issue — and STSM issues 4× fewer stores. So the correct statement is: **swizzle first, and only then does stmatrix pay.** Both changes are needed, in that order.

**2. My SW64 and SW32 formulas were wrong.** Measured:

```
SW64,  box 32x8:  rows 0,1 → g^0 ; rows 2,3 → g^1 ; rows 4,5 → g^2 ; rows 6,7 → g^3
SW32,  box 16x8:  rows 0-3 → g^0 ; rows 4-7 → g^1
```

So `SW64: g ^ ((row>>1)&3)` and `SW32: g ^ ((row>>2)&1)` — not `row % SPAN`. That reconciles with CUTLASS's `Swizzle<B,M,S>`: with M=3, S=3 the hardware XORs the B bits at offset-bit 6 into the B bits at offset-bit 3, and the row's bit position shifts with the row width. Unified rule, now matching all three modes:

```
granule ^= (row >> (3 - log2(SPAN))) & (SPAN - 1)
```

**3. TEST 6's FAIL is my harness, not hardware.** `SWIZZLE_NONE` is linear as expected; I compared it against the swizzled prediction. 64 of 512 "matched" — exactly row 0, where `g^0 = g`. Cosmetic. Same for the garbage numbers in tests 2/3 grids — my print loop walks the full 8-granule span while those boxes are only 4 and 2 granules wide; the *checks* only cover real columns and both pass.

## One useful constraint discovered

A narrow box under SW128 works, but **the smem row stays 128 bytes**. A 32-column box occupies a 128 B row using only 4 of 8 granules — half the shared memory wasted. That matters for 192x192 (`WGMMA_N=96`): it would need SW64 or padding, not SW128.

## The implementation, as a ladder

Same structure that worked for fault-1 — each stage separately built, ablated and validated, so we always know which piece did what:

**Stage A — swizzle only.** Store buffer becomes `granule = row*SPAN + (g ^ (row>>(3-log2 SPAN)))`, C descriptor becomes `SWIZZLE_128B`, writes stay plain STS. Expected: conflicts 192 → 0, and that alone was 1.97× on the store microbenchmark.

**Stage B — stmatrix on top.** Swap STS for `stmatrix.x4` in cuBLAS's 8×32 arrangement, registers `acc[2·v1 + 16j + {0,4,8,12}]`. Expected: a further 1.93× on the store path.

Both as validated template knobs per your standing rule — `EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES` and `EPI_USE_STSM`, defaulting off so every existing config is bit-identical until explicitly opted in.

**One design constraint the probes surfaced:** SW128 needs a 128-byte row, i.e. `WGMMA_N` a multiple of 64. `256x128` has `WGMMA_N=128` ✓. `192x192` has **96** ✗ — it needs SW64 (`(row>>1)&3`), which the probe also pinned down. So the knob has to select the mode per tile, not hardcode 128B.

Budget check for 256x128: 4 stages × 49,152 = 196,608, epilogue 8 rows × 128 B × 4 warps × 2 wg × 2 slots = 16,384 → **212,992 of 231,424**. Fits, keeps the 4th stage, and uses *less* smem than today's 32,768-byte chunked buffer.

**72/72 PASS, all four configs, zero failures** — including the swizzled ones on `4088x2056x1016`, the 8-valid-column residue case I was most worried about. The swizzle is bit-exact.

Now the two measurements that decide whether Stage A worked:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
for C in 256x128x64_1x2_h_rs2_ep32s2 256x128x64_1x2_h_rs2_ep64s1 \
         256x128x64_1x2_h_rs2_swz128s1 256x128x64_1x2_h_rs2_swz128s2; do
  echo "===== $C"
  CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 ncu \
    --metrics launch__shared_mem_per_block_dynamic,l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu_mem_shared_op_st.sum \
    -k regex:bgemm_sm90_kernel --launch-count 1 \
    ./build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --shape=4096x2048x2048 --layout=nn --cfg=$C 2>&1 \
    | grep -E "shared_mem_per_block_dynamic|bank_conflicts"
done
```

What each number means:

**Shared memory** tells us the pipeline depth landed where the budget predicted — `swz128s1` ≈ **231,424** (4 stages, `STORE_BUF` 32,768) and `swz128s2` ≈ **215,040** (3 stages, 65,536). `ep32s2` should also read 231,424, and `ep64s1` 231,424. If s1 doesn't reach 231,424 the sizing is wrong and the speed number would be meaningless.

**Bank conflicts** is Stage A's entire claim. `ep32s2` and `ep64s1` are unswizzled and should show a large count; `swz128s1`/`s2` should collapse. The microbenchmark said 192 → 0, but that was one warp on one tile with nothing else touching shared memory — the real kernel has the mainloop's traffic in the same counter, so I expect a floor rather than a literal zero. What matters is the **delta between swizzled and unswizzled at identical geometry**, which `ep64s1` vs `swz128s1` isolates exactly: same 64-wide chunk, same single slot, same stage count, differing *only* in the swizzle.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-11 14:01 IST]

**Stage A works, and the numbers are decisive.**

| config | layout | bank conflicts | smem (B) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ep32s2` (currently pinned) | 32-wide, linear | **396,769** | 229,376 |
| `ep64s1` (control) | 64-wide, linear | **918,310** | 229,376 |
| **`swz128s1`** | 64-wide, **swizzled** | **1,413** | 229,376 |
| `swz128s2` | 64-wide, swizzled, 2 slots | 2,435 | 212,992 |

**The isolated comparison is `ep64s1` vs `swz128s1`** — identical chunk width, identical slot count, identical stage count, differing *only* in the swizzle: **918,310 → 1,413, a 650× reduction.** Against the config we actually ship today it's **396,769 → 1,413, 281×**.

And the shared-memory figures confirm the depth landed exactly where the budget said (ncu's Kbyte = 1000 here):

```
swz128s1 : 229,376 = 4 x 49,152 + 32,768   -> 4 STAGES  ✓
swz128s2 : 212,992 = 3 x 49,152 + 65,536   -> 3 stages
ep32s2   : 229,376 = 4 x 49,152 + 32,768   -> 4 stages
```

So **`swz128s1` uses the same shared memory and keeps the same 4 pipeline stages as the config we currently pin, while removing 99.6% of the bank conflicts.** That's the design target hit exactly — and it also confirms the `ep64s1` control was worth building, because a 64-wide *linear* buffer is actually **2.3× worse** than the 32-wide one (918k vs 397k), exactly as the bank arithmetic predicted. Widening without swizzling would have been a regression.

Now the number that decides whether it ships:

```bash
done
```

Four configs × 4 shapes × 3 reps, one process each, clocks locked. `rs2` is the pre-chunking baseline, `ep32s2` is what ships today, and the two `swz` variants are Stage A.

§H27z.63 measured the epilogue overlap at +1.5% and the 4th stage at +5.7% — but both on a conflicted buffer. With conflicts down 281× the balance between `s1` (4 stages, no overlap) and `s2` (3 stages, with overlap) is genuinely unknown, which is why both are in the run.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-11 14:08 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Read the Stage A speed results

Honest result: **Stage A does not beat the config we already ship.** Medians of 3:

| shape | rs2 | **ep32s2** (shipping) | swz128s1 | swz128s2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16384x2048x2048 nn | 633.61 | **674.43** | 664.38 | 648.33 |
| 16384x11264x2048 nn | 645.84 | **701.28** | 694.10 | 663.51 |
| 16384x2048x2048 nt | 628.22 | **675.82** | 666.81 | 647.97 |
| 16384x5632x2048 nt | 631.41 | **674.22** | 668.17 | 650.15 |

`swz128s1` is **0.9–1.5% slower** than `ep32s2`, despite having **281× fewer bank conflicts**.

**The most important thing this tells us: bank conflicts are not the bottleneck at these shapes.** Removing 99.6% of them bought nothing. That matches §H27y.10's own caveat — *"at these shapes we are tensor-core bound, which is why 225k bank conflicts and 2x instructions still only cost ~3%"* — but I had been treating the 224,990 number as the headline problem. It isn't.

**Why `swz128s1` loses is structural, not a bug.** To afford a 128-byte swizzled row it had to drop to `EPI_STAGES=1`, giving up the epilogue's double-buffered overlap. §H27z.63 measured that overlap at +1.5%, and the gap here is 0.9–1.5%. The swizzle gains and the lost overlap cancel almost exactly.

And `swz128s2`, which keeps the overlap, is worse still — because 2 slots × 64-wide rows = 65,536 B costs the 4th pipeline stage (212,992 vs 229,376 smem). The 4th stage is worth more than the overlap, as §H27z.63 also found.

**So the current buffer shape forces a three-way trade — swizzle, overlap, 4th stage — and we can only have two.** That's not a fundamental limit, it's a consequence of me keeping the `[slot][BM][C_BOX_N]` structure. cuBLAS doesn't have this problem because it stages **8 rows per warp**, not all `BM`:

```
per-warp 8-row staging: 2 slots x 8 rows x 64 cols x 2 B x 4 warps x 2 wg = 16,384 B
depth = (231,424 - 16,384) / 49,152 = 4.37 -> 4 stages
```

**All three at once**, in a quarter of the shared memory we use today. That's the design §H27z.73 documented and that Stage A did *not* implement.

One measurement missing before deciding: **`ep64s1`'s speed**. It has the identical geometry to `swz128s1` (64-wide, 1 slot, 4 stages) and differs only by the swizzle, so it isolates what the swizzle is actually worth:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
for SL in "16384x2048x2048 nn" "16384x11264x2048 nn"; do
  set -- $SL; echo "===== $1 $2"
  for C in 256x128x64_1x2_h_rs2_ep64s1 256x128x64_1x2_h_rs2_swz128s1; do
    for i in 1 2 3; do
      CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 ./build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --shape=$1 --layout=$2 --cfg=$C 2>&1 \
        | awk -v c=$C '$4=="PASS"{print c, $6, $7, $8}'
    done
  done
done
```

If `swz128s1` ≫ `ep64s1`, the swizzle is genuinely valuable and the per-warp restructure is worth building. If they're close, then even 918k conflicts cost little here, and fault-2's remaining value is mostly the `stmatrix` instruction count rather than the conflicts — which would change what we do next.

You're right on both counts, and the data you just produced proves the first one against me.

**The controlled pair — identical geometry, only the swizzle differs:**

| | ep64s1 | swz128s1 | |
|---|---|---|---|
| conflicts | 3,672,805 | **3,028** | 1213× |
| duration | 239.33 µs | **229.31 µs** | −4.2% |
| tensor active | 78.11% | **81.57%** | |
| 16384x2048x2048 nn | 640.98 | **665.12** | **+3.8%** |
| 16384x11264x2048 nn | 661.59 | **693.19** | **+4.8%** |

**So my claim that "bank conflicts are not the bottleneck" was wrong.** The swizzle is worth 3.8–4.8% at fixed geometry, and the ncu duration confirms it independently (−4.2%). I said it before running the control. That was the error.

**And yes — I deviated.** §H27z.73 decoded cuBLAS's structure from their SASS and I documented it: **8 rows per warp, 128-byte rows, ~16 KB total.** Then I implemented the swizzle on **our** `[slot][BM][C_BOX_N]` buffer instead. That's why `swz128s1` had to drop to `EPI_STAGES=1` — our shape makes a 128 B row cost 65,536 B, so the swizzle and the overlap can't coexist. **cuBLAS doesn't face that trade because it doesn't stage the whole tile.** I had the answer written down and built something else.

The measurements now decompose cleanly, and both effects are real and roughly additive:

```
ep64s1   640.98   64-wide, linear,   1 slot
swz128s1 665.12   64-wide, SWIZZLED, 1 slot    swizzle  = +3.8%
ep32s2   674.43   32-wide, linear,   2 slots   overlap  = +5.2% over ep64s1
```

We have never had both. The reason is purely how much we stage:

```
today   [slot][BM=256][64]  x2 slots = 65,536  -> swizzle OR overlap, not both
cuBLAS  8 rows per warp                = 16,384  -> both, comfortably
```

**The correct fix, taken from cuBLAS's structure rather than invented:** stage one **64-row atom** at a time per warpgroup instead of all `BM` rows —

```
[slot][warpgroup][64 rows][64 cols] = 2 x 2 x 64 x 64 x 2 = 32,768 B
depth = (231,424 - 32,768) / 49,152 = 4.04 -> 4 stages
```

**Swizzle + overlap + 4th stage, simultaneously**, in the same 32,768 B `ep32s2` already uses. Predicted ≈ 674 × 1.038 ≈ **700 TFLOPS on nn 2048**, ~93% of cuBLAS, versus 674 today.

The change is contained: the buffer is indexed by `(slot, warpgroup, row-within-atom, col)` instead of `(slot, global brow, col)`, and the existing chunk loop generalises from *chunk* to *(atom × chunk)* — the atom loop becomes part of the pipeline instead of sitting outside it. cuBLAS's 8-row granularity is finer than that, but 64 rows already fits the budget, so I'd take the smaller step first and only go to 8 if the measurement asks for it.

## Where we are

**Step 1, Fault-1: DONE and shipped.** Chunked epilogue, 11 call sites pinned, dispatcher validated 15/15, trainer measured **97.60% of cuBLAS** end to end (GEMM 89.3%), and confirmed running in the real workload — 27,440 chunked launches.

**Step 1, Fault-2: research finished and proven; first implementation attempt is not shippable.**

The research is complete and nothing in it is assumed:
- stmatrix semantics — spec + hardware probe
- our accumulator already matches, no shuffle needed
- cuBLAS's layout decoded from their SASS: `granule = row*8 + (row XOR g)`, 8 rows/warp, 128 B rows, 16 KB
- `SWIZZLE_128B` **is** that permutation — 0/512 both directions
- period, narrow box, SW64/SW32, rank-3, residue, STSM→TMA — all measured

Stage A built the swizzle and it's **correct** (72/72 bit-exact) and **effective** (conflicts 3,672,805 → 3,028, +3.8–4.8% at fixed geometry). But it's **1.4% slower than what we already ship**, because I put it on our existing buffer shape instead of cuBLAS's, and that shape forces a three-way trade:

```
swizzle   +3.8%   (measured, ep64s1 vs swz128s1)
overlap   +5.2%   (measured, ep64s1 vs ep32s2)
4th stage +5.7%   (measured, §H27z.63)
```

`ep32s2` (shipping) has overlap + 4th stage. `swz128s1` has swizzle + 4th stage. **Nothing has all three**, because a 128 B row across all 256 `BM` rows costs 65,536 B and there's only 34,816 B of headroom.

## What's next

**Immediate — the fix, from cuBLAS's own structure.** Stage one **64-row atom** per warpgroup instead of the whole tile:

```
[slot][warpgroup][64 rows][64 cols] = 32,768 B   (same as ep32s2 uses today)
depth = (231,424 - 32,768) / 49,152 = 4 stages
```

All three at once. Predicted ≈ **700 TFLOPS** on nn 2048 against 674 today, ~93% of cuBLAS.

**Then Stage B — `stmatrix`.** The probe measured it at **1.93× on the store path**, but *only once swizzled* (on a linear buffer it was worth literally 0%). So it goes second, on top of the restructure.

**Then the remaining plan:** step 2 split-k, step 3 match cuBLAS's variants across the 21 sites, step 4 cross-comparison for the dispatcher.

And your point about references is the right standing rule: cuBLAS is the target, everything else is corroboration. When CUTLASS and cuBLAS disagreed here — CUTLASS's cooperative epilogue picks a 32-wide tile, cuBLAS uses 64 — following CUTLASS would have led us to exactly the narrow row that can't be conflict-free. The SASS is the source of truth; I should have built to it the first time instead of half-adopting it.

Starting the restructure now.

The 64-wide linear layout has 2.3× the conflicts of the 32-wide one (3.68M vs 1.59M), which is exactly why `ep64s2r64` sits 4.2% *below* `ep32s2`. The swizzle pays that back and adds a little on top.

The honest arithmetic: `ep32s2`'s 1.59M conflicts cost about **0.4%** of runtime. That's what removing 106× of them buys, and the duration agrees (227.81 → 226.88 = −0.41%).

They differed only in **time** (0.570 vs 0.295 ms, 1.93×), because with conflicts already gone the bottleneck moves to instruction issue and `STSM` issues 4× fewer stores. So the split is clean:

- **swizzle → kills conflicts** (Stage A, done)
- **stmatrix → kills instruction count** (Stage B, ~1.93× on the store path)

That also matches §H27y.10's two separate observations: 224,990 conflicts *and* 2.11× the instructions. Those are two different problems with two different fixes, and I had been treating them as one.

**On the residual 14,950 — I don't know where it comes from, and I won't guess.** The bank arithmetic says the epilogue write should be exactly zero: for a fixed granule `g`, rows 0–7 land at bank group `4·(g^r)`, and as `r` sweeps 0–7 the XOR makes `g^r` take all eight values, so all 32 banks are hit once. That predicts 0, and the microbenchmark measured 0. Something else in the real kernel is contributing the remaining 0.94%.

Finding it is a source-level attribution, if we want it:

```bash

  --cfg=256x128x64_1x2_h_rs2_swz128r64 2>&1 | grep -B3 -A3 "STS" | head -40
```

Worth noting it's 0.94% of what we started with and the config is already the fastest we have, so I'd treat it as a curiosity rather than a blocker — but it should be *known* rather than assumed, and right now it isn't.

**Part 1 — the epilogue work is not tile-specific, so it isn't wasted.** `EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES` / `EPI_ROWS` are template knobs on `Sm90WarpspecConfig`. If step-3 moves a site to `128x256_2x1_v`, adopting the swizzle there is *one registry line*, not a rewrite. **Part 2 — but you're right that we're likely optimising a tile we won't keep.** From the nsys pairing, at almost every site where we currently pin `256x128_1x2_h_rs2`, cuBLAS picks something else:

| our site | we use | cuBLAS uses (our coords) |
|---|---|---|
| wQ/wV/wK-fwd, attnOut-fwd, down-fwd | 256x128 c1x2 rh | **128x256 c2x1 rv** coopA |
| wQ/attnOut/gate_up/lm_head-dgrad | 256x128 c1x2 rh | **128x256 c2x1 rv** coopA |
| gate_up-fwd | 256x128 c1x2 rh | **192x192 c2x1 rv** coopB |
| down-dgrad | 256x128 c1x2 rh | **192x192 c1x2 rh** coopB |

So the tile we just tuned is one cuBLAS uses at **zero** of those sites.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-11 15:15 IST]

Yes — that's the right frame, and it makes the work land in the right place. Let me lay out the 6 against what we have.

## cuBLAS's 6 distinct variants, translated into our coordinates

(their `BMxBN` is our `BNxBM`, their `CXxCY` is our `CYxCX`, their raster flips — verified from `cublasGemmEx(handle, opB, opA, N, M, K)`)

| # | cuBLAS kernel | in our coords | stages | our tile exists? | what's missing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `192x192_64x3_1x2_h_coopB` | 192x192 c2x1 rv | 3 | ✅ | — |
| 2 | `256x128_64x4_1x2_h_coopA` | **128x256 c2x1 rv** | **4** | ✅ | **4th stage** |
| 3 | `128x256_64x4_2x1_v_coopA` | **256x128 c1x2 rh** | **4** | ✅ | — (Fault-1 gave it) |
| 4 | `192x192_64x3_2x1_v_coopB` | 192x192 c1x2 rh | 3 | ✅ | — |
| 5 | `192x192_64x4_2x1_v_coopB` | **192x192 c1x2 rh** | **4** | ✅ | **4th stage** |
| 6 | `128x128_64x6_1x2_h_splitK` | 128x128 c2x1 rv | 6 | ✅ | **split-K** |

**We have all six tiles/clusters/rasters.** Three things are missing, and they're specific:

- **#2 — `128x256` needs a 4th stage.** Today: `(231,424 − 65,536)/49,152 = 3.37 → 3 stages`. cuBLAS runs 4.
- **#5 — `192x192` needs a 4-stage variant.** Today: `(231,424 − 73,728)/49,152 = 3.21 → 3`. cuBLAS has both a 3-stage and a 4-stage 192x192.
- **#6 — `128x128` needs split-K.** We only have split-K on `64x64x64`. Depth is already 6 there, so that part matches.

**And `coopA`/`coopB` is not a missing feature.** §H27z established from an 18-kernel opcode census that they're labels for whether blocks-per-warpgroup is even or odd, with *no instruction difference* — and we derive that automatically through `WGMMA_N`. So nothing to build.

## Why today's work is exactly the mechanism for two of the three

The `EPI_ROWS` atom staging I just built is precisely what buys those missing 4th stages:

```
128x256, atom-staged + chunked : 2 wg x 2 slots x 64 x 32 x 2 = 16,384
                                 (231,424 - 16,384)/49,152 = 4.37 -> 4 stages
192x192, atom-staged + chunked : same 16,384 -> 4 stages
```

So the epilogue knobs aren't a detour from the apples-to-apples path — they're the **only** way we reach cuBLAS's stage counts on #2 and #5. I just applied them to the wrong tile first.

**Correction to something I said earlier:** I claimed `192x192` "isn't behind" on depth because it runs 3 against cuBLAS's 3. That's only true for variants #1 and #4 — cuBLAS *also* ships a 4-stage 192x192 (#5), used at `down-dgrad`, and there we are a stage short.

## What I'd do next

Build the missing three on the variants that will actually be used:

1. `128x256_2x1_v` + chunk/atom-stage → 4 stages (variant #2)
2. `192x192_1x2_h` + atom-stage → 4 stages (variant #5)
3. `128x128_2x1_v` + split-K → variant #6 (this is your step-2, and it now has a concrete target)

Then measure all six against cuBLAS per call site — genuinely apples-to-apples, same tile, same cluster, same raster, same depth.

One caveat I won't paper over: the depth numbers above are **derived from the budget formula, not measured**. Every previous time I trusted that arithmetic it held, but it should be confirmed by ncu on each new config before we read anything into the speed. Shall I start with #2 and #5, since the knobs already exist and are proven?

### CLAUDE [2026-08-11 15:29 IST]

Found it, and it's a real bug in my code — not something to guess at.

**My stmatrix block runs *before* the chunk filter.** The original loop order is:

```cpp
float v0 = acc[...] * alpha;          <- I inserted HERE
...
const int ch  = tile_col / C_BOX_N;
if (USE_CHUNKED && ch != wg_ch_start + epi_ch) continue;   <- filter is AFTER
```

With `EPI_TILE_N=64` and `WGMMA_N=128` there are **2 chunks per `nc`**, so my block fires for *both* chunks on every pipeline unit — chunk 1's data gets written into the slot during chunk 0's unit and shipped as chunk 0. That's exactly the magnitude of error we see.

The scalar path was correct because its filter sits between the pack and the store. Mine skipped it entirely.
> tool `Bash`: Add the missing chunk filter to the stmatrix path
> tool `Bash`: Recompile from the repo root after the fix

You're right — I fixed one bug by reasoning, and that's not the same as knowing the path is correct. Let me verify against the sources before running anything.

(Note: `STSM` count went 32 → 16 with the fix, consistent with it no longer firing on both chunks.)
> tool `Bash`: Find how CUTLASS drives its STSM epilogue copy

Line 887 is important — `copy(tiled_r2r, tRR_rD_src, tRR_rD_dst)`. There's a **register-to-register** step before the R2S copy. That's exactly the "does CUTLASS shuffle before stmatrix" question:
> tool `Bash`: Inspect CUTLASS's register-to-register step before STSM

**`using CopyOpR2R = void;`** at both sites that select `SM90_U32x4_STSM_N` (336 and 799). Confirming that means no shuffle:
> tool `Bash`: Confirm no-shuffle and check the other two references

`IsUseR2R = !is_void_v<CopyOpR2R>` with `CopyOpR2R = void` → **false → no register shuffle.** CUTLASS goes accumulator → convert → STSM directly, matching my probe and matching cuBLAS's SASS (their `F2FP.BF16.F32.PACK_AB` feeds `STSM` registers with nothing in between).

DeepGEMM has an SM90 path — that's the closest independent implementation:
> tool `Bash`: Read DeepGEMM's SM90 stmatrix usage

DeepGEMM uses `"l"` (64-bit) for the address where I use `"r"` (32-bit) — both are legal (the PTX examples show `.b64`, CUTLASS uses 32-bit, and my probe validated `"r"` at 0/256). Let me see how they compute the address and group registers, which is the part that corroborates my arithmetic:
> tool `Bash`: Find DeepGEMM's stmatrix call sites
> tool `Bash`: Read DeepGEMM's SM90 bf16 epilogue stmatrix call site

Three independent sources now agree, and my arithmetic checks out against all of them.

**CUTLASS** — `IsUseR2R = !is_void_v<CopyOpR2R>` and `CopyOpR2R = void` at both STSM sites → **no register shuffle**. Accumulator → convert → STSM directly.

**DeepGEMM** — `sm90_bf16_gemm.cuh:322`:

```cpp
col ^= row % (kSwizzleDMode / 16);
```

`kSwizzleDMode/16` is granules per row; at 128 B that's `col ^= row % 8` — **identical to our formula**, and their pointer arithmetic uses `row * (16*8) + col * 16`, i.e. a 128-byte row stride. That's a third confirmation of `granule = row*8 + (row XOR g)` alongside cuBLAS's SASS and our hardware probe.

**DeepGEMM also settles a design question.** They use `.x2` with matrices = the two **row halves** of one column block (`accum[i*4+0..1]` → v1=0, `accum[i*4+2..3]` → v1=1, same v2). cuBLAS uses `.x4` with matrices = four **column blocks** at the same 8 rows. Both are valid — the arrangement is chosen entirely by the addresses you supply — which confirms my reading of the spec rather than contradicting it. I followed cuBLAS's.

**Re-deriving my grouping against that:** for cuBLAS's arrangement, register `q` is matrix `q` = column block `4gj+q`, so `v2 = 4gj+q`, and the accumulator index `v0 + 2·v1 + 4·v2 = (2·v1 + 16·gj) + 4q = r + 4q`. Data row is `t1 = (lane>>2)&7`; address row is `lane&7` of matrix `lane>>3`. That is what the code does.

**So the design was right and the failure was an integration error, not a design error** — my block sat above the chunk filter, so it fired on both chunks per unit. No amount of reading CUTLASS would have caught that; only diffing my insertion against the surrounding loop did, which is what found it.

The fix is in and compiles (`STSM` 32 → 16, consistent with no longer firing twice). Push and re-test:

*(the 310.16 reading on `ep32s2 nt` is a contended run — I used the other two)*

And the counters say why, in the opposite direction to what I predicted:

| | duration | conflicts | **instructions** | tensor |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ep32s2 | 227.52 µs | 1,586,613 | 39,963,856 | 82.61% |
| swz128r64 | **226.75 µs** | **15,034** | 43,309,688 | **83.00%** |
| stsm | 232.45 µs | 28,963 | **45,927,364** | 81.39% |

**`stmatrix` *increased* the instruction count** — 43.3M → 45.9M. It was supposed to cut it. Each `stmatrix.x4` does replace four `STS`, but the address it needs is far more expensive: every lane must compute a *different* address (row `lane&7` of matrix `lane>>3`), including the column-block position and the swizzle XOR, whereas the scalar path reuses `t0`/`t1` it already has. The address arithmetic costs more than the four stores saved.

**And conflicts went 15,034 → 28,963, which I cannot explain.** The probe measured STSM-through-swizzle at exactly **0**, with the same addressing formula. Something about the kernel context differs and I don't know what. I'm not going to guess at it.

**The probe over-stated stmatrix's value.** Its 1.93× compared STS vs STSM in a tight loop where the address was nearly free. In a real epilogue the address computation dominates, and the store is a small share of a kernel running 83% tensor-active. That's a lesson about the microbenchmark, not about the hardware.

## Where fault-2 actually lands

- **Stage A (`swz128r64`) is a genuine, if small, win**: +0.2–0.5% over what we ship, 106× fewer conflicts, same memory, same 4 stages, 36/36 bit-exact. Worth pinning.
- **Stage B (`stmatrix`) is a measured loss** at −1.9% to −2.6%. The knob stays, defaulted off, with the numbers recorded so nobody retries it blind.
- §H27y.10's framing — "224,990 conflicts and 2.11× instructions, fix with STSM" — turns out to be **wrong on both counts**: the conflicts were a layout problem (fixed by the swizzle, worth +0.4%), and stmatrix makes the instruction count *worse*, not better, once you pay for its addressing.

Total from the whole fault-2 line: **+0.4%**. Against that, the nsys pairing attributes **~570 ms of the 1,400 ms** GEMM deficit to tile and variant mismatch — the 128x256 and 192x192 variants cuBLAS actually uses, which is your step-3.

I'd pin `swz128r64`, document all of this, and move there.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-11 15:59 IST]

You're right — I concluded "stmatrix doesn't pay" when the real question is *why cuBLAS's stmatrix is cheap and mine isn't*. Their SASS answers it, and I already had the evidence in front of me without reading it properly:

```
LOP3.LUT R169, R21, 0x7,  RZ, 0xc0    ; rr = lane % 8
SHF.R.U32.HI R23, RZ, 0x3, R21        ; m  = lane >> 3
IMAD     R168, R169, 0x9, RZ          ; rr * 9
LOP3.LUT R23,  R168, R23, RZ, 0x3c    ; (rr*9) XOR m
IMAD.SHL R23,  R23, 0x10, RZ          ; * 16
STSM.16.M88.4 [R23+UR32], R24
...
LOP3.LUT R168, R169, R168, RZ, 0x3c   ; (rr*9) XOR (m+4)
IMAD.SHL R168, R168, 0x10
STSM.16.M88.4 [R168+UR32], R32
```

**cuBLAS's per-lane address offset depends only on the lane.** `R23` and `R168` are computed **once**, and every subsequent store is `[R23 + UR32]` — the only thing that changes is `UR32`, a *uniform* register. Zero per-store address arithmetic.

Mine recomputes `atc`, `acic`, `arow`, and the full `epi_swz_index` (a multiply, a shift, a mask, an XOR) **inside** the loop for every stmatrix. That's the +2.6M instructions.

And the algebra says it's hoistable — with `arow = band + rr` where `band` is a multiple of 8:

```
epi_swz_index = arow*8 + ((arow%8) ^ g)
              = band*8 + [ rr*8 + (rr ^ g) ]
              = band*8 + [ (rr*9) ^ g ]        <- exactly cuBLAS's R23
```

The bracket is **pure lane** (plus the unrolled `gj`), so it can be precomputed once per warp — two values, for the two column-block groups — exactly as cuBLAS keeps `R23` and `R168`.

Let me confirm this structurally against their full epilogue rather than from one fragment:
> tool `Bash`: Classify instructions in one cuBLAS epilogue region

**There it is.** One cuBLAS epilogue store region, classified:

```
16  F2FP           (the fp32 -> bf16 packs)
 2  STSM
 1  UTMASTG
 1  UTMACMDFLUSH
 1  FENCE
```

**Zero integer instructions.** No `IMAD`, no `LOP3`, no `SHF` anywhere in the store region — every bit of address arithmetic is hoisted out, leaving only convert + store. Mine recomputes the whole index per store, which is exactly the +2.6M instructions and the −2% .

And the algebra makes it hoistable, which is what `IMAD R168, R169, 0x9` in their prologue *is*:

```
addr_elems = slot_base + band*64 + ((rr*9) ^ g) * 8
             \_______/   \______/   \____________/
              per unit    unrolled    PURE LANE  <- hoist, 2 values (g = 4*gjl + am)
```

Fixing it the way cuBLAS does:
> tool `Bash`: Hoist the stmatrix address the way cuBLAS does

Compiles. Now the structural check — does our store region look like cuBLAS's (convert + store, no integer math)?
> tool `Bash`: Classify our stmatrix store region against cuBLAS's

Only 2 STSM back-to-back in that window — let me measure the thing that matters directly, static instruction count, and compare against both the STS version and my pre-hoist attempt:
> tool `Bash`: Compare static instruction mix: STS vs STSM before and after hoisting

Pattern bug — double `E`. Redoing:
> tool `Bash`: Compare instruction mix with the corrected mangled pattern

Static counts tell a clearer story than I expected:

| | total | STSM | STS | IMAD | F2FP |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| STS `swz128r64` | 3080 | 0 | 128 | 646 | 128 |
| STSM pre-hoist | 2032 | 16 | 0 | 342 | 64 |
| **STSM hoisted** | **2016** | 16 | 0 | **333** | 64 |

Statically STSM is **35% smaller** (2016 vs 3080) — so the instruction *code* is much leaner, yet the **dynamic** count was *higher* (45.9M vs 43.3M). Fewer static instructions executing more work means the difference is in what actually runs, not what's emitted — most likely the beta handling: the STS path compiles to two separate branches (128 STS = 2×64, one taken), while my STSM path is one predicated body (64 F2FP).

The hoist itself only saved 16 static instructions, so ptxas was already doing most of it — my diagnosis was right in principle but the compiler had beaten me to it.

I verified the hoisted address is algebraically identical before trusting it:

```
old = (arow*8 + (rr ^ g))*8 ,  arow = 16*wp + 8*v1 + rr
    = (16*wp + 8*v1)*64 + (rr*8 + (rr^g))*8
    = (16*wp + 8*v1)*64 + ((rr*9) ^ g)*8          = new   ✓
```

### CLAUDE [2026-08-11 16:11 IST]

12/12 PASS after the hoist, so the algebra held. But the hoist only recovered part of it:

| | duration | conflicts | dynamic inst |
|---|---|---|---|
| `swz128r64` (STS) | **227.55 µs** | **14,820** | **43,303,956** |
| `swz128r64stsm` pre-hoist | 232.45 µs | 28,963 | 45,927,364 |
| `swz128r64stsm` hoisted | 229.18 µs | 30,401 | 45,777,472 |

The hoist bought 1.4% (232.45 → 229.18) but **STSM is still 0.7% slower**, with 2× the conflicts and 5.7% more dynamic instructions.

**Two things now contradict each other and I can't resolve them from what I have:**

1. **Static code is 35% *smaller* (2016 vs 3080) while dynamic instructions are 5.7% *higher*.** Fewer instructions emitted, more executed. Something in the STSM path runs far more often than the static count suggests — most likely the beta handling, which ptxas compiles as two separate branches for STS (128 STS = 2×64, one taken) but as one predicated body for STSM (64 F2FP).

2. **STSM shows 2× the conflicts of STS on the identical swizzled layout** — 30,401 vs 14,820 — when the probe measured **both at exactly 0**. One plausible mechanism is that `STSM.16.M88.4` moves 512 B per instruction against STS's 128 B, so it necessarily takes ≥4 shared-memory cycles and ncu may bill the extra cycles as conflicts. That's a *hypothesis*, not something I've shown.

I'm flagging both as unresolved rather than papering over them.

**Where this leaves the epilogue work, honestly:**

- **Stage A (`swz128r64`) is a real win** — +0.2–0.5% over what ships, 106× fewer conflicts, same memory, same 4 stages, bit-exact everywhere. **Pin it.**
- **Stage B (`stmatrix`) is a measured loss** even after being implemented the way cuBLAS does it. Keep the knob off, keep the numbers recorded.
- §H27y.10's diagnosis was wrong in both halves: the 224,990 conflicts were a *layout* problem worth ~0.4%, and stmatrix does not reduce the executed instruction count in our epilogue.

**And the sizing argument hasn't changed.** Everything in fault-2 lives in a ±2% band, because we're 83% tensor-active and the epilogue is mostly hidden. The nsys pairing put **~570 ms of the 1,400 ms** GEMM deficit on tile and variant mismatch — `128x256_2x1_v` and `192x192`, the variants cuBLAS actually runs and we don't.

My recommendation: pin `swz128r64`, document everything including the two unresolved items, and go to step-3. Chasing the remaining epilogue mystery is real engineering but it's bounded at a fraction of a percent, and there's a 40% gap sitting untouched.

Right. The single most informative next action serves both step-2 and step-3, and it's already written and dry-run verified: the apples-to-apples run.

For the split-K sites specifically it's exactly the isolation we need — at `kv-wgrad` (2048x512x16384 tn) cuBLAS uses `128x128_64x6_1x2_h_**splitK**`, which in our coords is `128x128 c2x1 rv`. The script runs **our `128x128_2x1_v` without split-K** against our current `64x128x64` pin. So it splits that site's 34 µs deficit into:

- **how much is the wrong tile** (fixable by re-pinning, today)
- **how much is genuinely split-K** (the step-2 build)

Right now we'd be guessing which, and we already have split-K on `64x64x64` — so it's possible we need a re-pin, not a new kernel.

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
nvidia-smi -i 1 -pm 1 && nvidia-smi -i 1 -lgc 1620
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 bash tools/h27z70_apples.sh 2>&1 | tee test_reports/h27z70.md
```

~10 minutes, 15 sites, medians of 3, one config per process, correctness checked before any timing is quoted. It prints a per-site verdict: **cuB-CFG BETTER / our pin better / tie**.

What each outcome means for where we go next:

- **cuBLAS's config wins on a site** → we're choosing wrong and can re-pin immediately, no new kernel
- **our pin wins** → our config choice is already better than cuBLAS's for that shape, and the deficit there is implementation, not selection
- **cuBLAS's config loses badly** → that tile is weak in our library and needs the Fault-1 knobs applied (which is where `swz128r64` and the `EPI_ROWS` work get reused on the tiles that survive)

That last case is the one that connects today's epilogue work to step-3 properly — `128x256` and `192x192` are the two tiles cuBLAS actually uses, and both are currently a pipeline stage short of it. We now have the exact mechanism to fix that; we just applied it to the wrong tile first.

Both questions answered by the data — and it's a clean, coherent story.

## Why our existing split-K doesn't help here

```
kv-wgrad 2048x512x16384 tn
  64x128x64  (our pin)  456.3   <- best
  64x64x64              240.6
  64x64x64_sk2          227.8
  64x64x64_sk4          221.3
  64x64x64_sk8          205.7
  64x64x64_sk16         179.7
  64x64x64_sk32         135.1   <- monotonically WORSE
  128x128x64_2x1_v      350.6
```

Split-K makes it **monotonically worse**, and that's correct behaviour, not a bug. With 64x64 tiles this shape gives `32 × 8 = 256` tiles on 132 SMs — about two full waves. **There is no idle machine to fill**, so split-K only adds workspace traffic and a reduce pass. Every extra slice is pure overhead.

**But look at what cuBLAS is doing.** With `128x128` there are only `16 × 4 = 64` tiles — *half* the machine idle. Bare, that costs us: our `128x128_2x1_v` reads **350.6**. cuBLAS runs the *same* tile with split-K and gets **648**. So their strategy is: take the **larger, more efficient tile** and use split-K to fill the machine, rather than shrinking the tile to manufacture tiles.

That's the missing capability, now with numbers behind it: `128x128` bare 350 → cuBLAS's `128x128+splitK` 648. Our best alternative is 456. **Split-K on a wider tile is worth roughly +40% at this site**, and `kv-dgrad` needs nothing (our `128x176x64` at 89.7% is already best; K=512 is far too small to split).

## Your questions about our split-K, answered from the source

Reading `Splitk_reduce.cuh` rather than from memory:

**Strategy: (A), a separate deterministic reduce pass** — and we did **not** copy cuBLAS's kernel. We confirmed cuBLAS uses the same *strategy* two independent ways (§H27z.8): its own config API reports `REDUCTION_SCHEME = COMPUTE_TYPE` (fp32 workspace, not INPLACE/atomic), and its ncu SASS shows **0 `ATOM`/`RED` instructions** with 48 LDG/STG. CUTLASS's `reduce_split_k.h` is the same shape — a plain fixed-order loop.

**Deterministic: yes.** Accumulation is a fixed `for s` loop in slice order, identical every run, **no `atomicAdd` anywhere**. The file cites CUTLASS's own warning that their atomic path "cannot guarantee deterministic numeric behavior… rounding error will depend on the order of accumulation" — disqualifying for reproducible training.

**Precision: equal or better than non-split.** Summing K as S groups then combining is a 2-level tree, whose error bound is *tighter* than one flat sequential accumulation. Partials are fp32, the accumulator is fp32, and there is exactly **one** narrowing — the final store — same as the non-split epilogue. The old "6–626% cancellation" scare was a relative-error-on-near-zero artifact (§H27z.9).

**alpha/beta applied exactly once, in the reduce.** Per-slice would raise alpha to the S-th power and add the C term S times.

One thing I have *not* verified and won't claim: the file says strategies **(B) CUTLASS turnstile** and **(C) BluTrain map-reduce** "come after and get measured against this" — future tense. Whether that comparison was ever run, I don't know yet.

Let me verify the split-K path actually supports this tile rather than assuming it's generic.
> tool `Bash`: Map every split-K touchpoint in the template
> tool `Bash`: Read split-K constraints and the launcher side

The infrastructure is genuinely tile-agnostic and carefully done — `splitk_begin/end` cover any K and any S with no divisibility precondition, workspace is `S × batch × M × N` fp32, `gridDim.z = SPLIT_K`. But **one thing worries me** and it's exactly the kind of thing that would make `sk2` do nothing:

`gridDim.z = SPLIT_K` multiplies a **persistent** grid. If `grid` is sized to the machine (132), then `S=2` launches 264 CTAs at ~229 KB smem each — 1 CTA/SM — so the two slices land in **two sequential waves** rather than side by side, and split-K buys nothing. For it to fill the idle half, `grid × S` must be ≤ the resident capacity.
> tool `Bash`: Find how the persistent grid is sized under split-K
> tool `Bash`: Read the grid sizing decision

**`num_clusters = min(total_tiles, max_clusters)`** — the grid is capped at the tile count, not blindly at the machine. That's the right shape. But it depends on whether `total_tiles` counts *clusters* or *CTAs*, which decides whether `grid × S` fits:
> tool `Bash`: Check whether total_tiles accounts for the cluster

Verified end to end, and the arithmetic now predicts the outcome precisely.

`total_tiles` counts **clusters**, and `grid = total_tiles × CLUSTER_SIZE`. For `kv-wgrad` 2048x512x16384 tn on `128x128_2x1_v`:

```
grid_m = 2048/128 = 16 ,  grid_n = 512/128 = 4
mega_grid = 16/2 x 4/1  = 8 x 4 = 32 clusters
grid = 32 x CLUSTER_SIZE(2) = 64 CTAs        on 132 SMs -> HALF IDLE
```

That is exactly why the bare tile reads 350 TF — confirmed by construction, not inferred. And:

```
smem = 6 x 32,768 + 32,768 = 229,376  ->  1 CTA/SM  ->  132 resident
S=2 : 64 x 2 = 128 CTAs   <= 132   both slices CO-RESIDENT   <- should ~2x
S=4 : 64 x 4 = 256 CTAs    > 132   two waves            <- expected to fall off
S=8 : 512 CTAs                     four waves           <- worse still
```

So `sk2` is the one that should work, `sk4`/`sk8` should regress, and that's a falsifiable prediction rather than a hope.

Other checks that passed:
- `static_assert(!(_EPI_TILE_N > 0 && _SPLIT_K > 1))` — our configs have `EPI_TILE_N=0`, no conflict
- workspace `2 × 1 × 2048 × 512 × 4` = **8 MB**, trivially fine
- `splitk_begin/end` give exact K coverage for any K and any S — no divisibility precondition, and the same constexpr is used host-side for sizing and device-side for each CTA's range, so they cannot disagree
- reduce is deterministic fixed-order fp32, alpha/beta applied exactly once, one final rounding

Because `0.00000` only happens when our K-accumulation **order** matches cuBLAS's exactly — and cuBLAS changes its order per shape, so no single config can be exact everywhere:

| shape | cuBLAS does | our config that matches | result |
|---|---|---|---|

| 2048x2048x16384 | **no split** | non-split | **0.00000** |
| 2048x2048x16384 | " | `sk2`, `sk4` | 0.683, 0.733 |

Two GEMMs that both compute the right answer but sum K in a different order **will** differ in the last bits. That's not error, it's arithmetic — and `maxRelErr` divides those last bits by the output value, so a tiny absolute difference on a small output prints as a big relative number.

**But I want to be straight with you about how far that's proven.** I can show the *pattern* is reduction order (the exact-match cases prove our arithmetic is right whenever orders align). What I have **not** shown is that the non-zero cases are only small-magnitude elements. The harness's pass rule is `|a−b| ≤ 0.05·|b| + 0.5`, and that **+0.5 absolute floor is loose** — an element with `|b|=0.7` and `|a−b|=0.5` would pass while printing a large relative error, and I can't distinguish that from a genuine problem with the numbers I have.

Working it back from the reported values: the worst element satisfies `0.73·|b| ≤ 0.05·|b| + 0.5`, so `|b| ≤ 0.735` and `|a−b| ≤ 0.54`. That bounds it to small outputs, but it doesn't tell us the *typical* output magnitude, so I can't yet call 0.54 negligible.

**Split-K works.** Medians of 3 at `kv-wgrad`:

| config | TF | %cuB | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `64x128x64` (current pin) | 455.48 | 70.3% | |
| `128x128x64_2x1_v` bare | 350.81 | 54.0% | half the machine idle |
| `128x128x64_2x1_v_sk2` | 572.56 | 88.5% | +63% over bare |
| `128x128x64_2x1_v_sk4` | 508.89 | 78.5% | |
| `128x128x64_2x1_v_sk8` | 415.43 | 63.9% | |
| **`128x128x64_sk2`** (no cluster) | **607.63** | **93.6%** | ← best |
| `128x128x64_sk4` | 542.93 | 83.6% | |

**Our worst site goes 70.3% → 93.6% of cuBLAS. +33% at that shape.**

Three things the data confirms:

**The CTA arithmetic predicted the S curve exactly.** `sk2` wins, `sk4` and `sk8` fall off monotonically — because at 229 KB smem it's 1 CTA/SM, so `64 × 2 = 128 ≤ 132` is co-resident while `sk4` (256 CTAs) and `sk8` (512) run in 2 and 4 waves. That's the `S = largest pow2 ≤ floor(132/64) = 2` rule from §H27z.12, landing on the nose.

**The cluster is a liability here.** No-cluster `sk2` beats `2x1_v` `sk2` by 6.1% (607.63 vs 572.56) — the multicast machinery costs more than it earns at this shape. Worth having built both.

**My 2× prediction was optimistic.** Bare 350.81 × 2 = 701; we got 607.63, i.e. **1.73×**. The missing 0.27× is the reduce pass and the fp32 workspace traffic — real costs I hadn't priced in. Honest correction rather than rounding it up.

**Impact on the trainer:** this shape is `wK-wgrad` + `wV-wgrad`, 2 of 21 call sites, which the nsys pairing put at 48.2 + 42.6 = **90.8 ms of the 1,400 ms** GEMM deficit. At a 0.75× time ratio that recovers **~58 ms**, roughly **4% of the whole GEMM gap** — from one re-pin.

And it's only this shape: every other wgrad site has plenty of tiles (`2048x2048` → 256 tiles, `2048x11264` → far more), so they're not occupancy-limited and split-K would only add overhead. That's exactly why cuBLAS uses split-K at this one site and nowhere else — which we've now independently reproduced from both the numerics and the timing.

That settles it, and the proof needs no more code — look at which rows share the value:

```
2048x512x16384   64x128x64        (non-split, SHIPPING)  rel=0.466  abs=1.000000
2048x512x16384   128x128x64_2x1_v (non-split, SHIPPING)  rel=0.466  abs=1.000000
2048x2048x16384  128x128x64_sk2   (split-K)              rel=0.683  abs=1.000000
2048x2048x16384  sk4              (split-K)              rel=0.733  abs=1.000000
```

**`maxAbsErr` is exactly `1.000000` in every disagreeing case — split-K and non-split alike.** Our ordinary non-split kernels, the ones that passed 820/820 and ship today, disagree with cuBLAS by *precisely the same absolute amount* when their K-order differs. Split-K introduces **nothing new**.

And the value being exactly `1.000000` twelve times over, across two shapes and three configs, is itself the signature: a real numerical fault would produce varying magnitudes. A value quantised to exactly 1.0 is **one bf16 representable step** at the output magnitude — the two accumulation orders produce fp32 results that round to adjacent bf16 values. bf16 has 8 bits of mantissa, so ULP is 1.0 for outputs in [128, 256), which is the right ballpark for a K=16384 dot product.

So the split-K correctness story is now closed with no assumptions left:

| | |
|---|---|
| wrong answers? | **no** — disagreement is 1 bf16 ULP, identical to our shipping non-split kernels |
| deterministic (ours)? | **yes** — 5/5 bit-identical, fixed-order reduce, no atomics |
| deterministic (cuBLAS)? | **yes** — 5/5 identical, 0 ATOM/RED in its SASS |
| bit-exact vs cuBLAS? | **yes**, when the K-order matches (`sk2` at the shape cuBLAS splits) |
| precision loss? | **none** — fp32 partials, fp32 accumulate, one final rounding |
| speed | **455 → 607.6 TF, 70.3% → 93.6%** of cuBLAS |

`rel` was never the right lens: it divides a 1-ULP difference by a small output. That's exactly the artifact §H27z.9 identified, now measured rather than argued.
