## Your questions

**Are conflicts bad?** Yes. Shared memory has 32 banks of 4 bytes; if lanes in a warp hit different addresses in the *same* bank, the access **serialises** — one instruction takes several cycles. Wasted time, always.

**How much do they actually cost us?** Measured at fixed geometry (`ep64s1` vs `swz128s1`, identical tile/slots/stages, only the swizzle differing): **3,672,805 → 3,028 conflicts, 239.33 → 229.31 µs = −4.2%**. So real, but modest — because at 83% tensor-pipe utilisation the store is largely hidden behind the math.

**Can we reach zero?** In isolation, yes — the microbenchmark measured **exactly 0** for both STS and STSM through a correct swizzle. In the real kernel we keep a residual (18,966 here, 14,820 on 256x128). **I don't know where that residual comes from** and I've flagged it as unresolved rather than guessed. It's 0.05% of what we started with.

**Does cuBLAS have zero?** §H27y.10 measured cuBLAS at **4–5** — but on a *different shape and harness*, so it isn't comparable to these numbers. That's answerable properly, since the matrix test runs cuBLAS as its own reference:

The 4th stage *hurts* here, and the swizzle hurts more. The mechanism is clear from the geometry: 192x192 is **N-split** with `WGMMA_N=96`, so atom staging gives `3 atoms × 3 chunks = 9 pipeline units`, each paying a wait + barrier + TMA store, and each store is only **32 columns = 64 bytes wide**. > tool `Bash`: Find a SASS dump of the exact lm_head-fwd kernel

The exact one isn't dumped, but `192x192_64x4_2x1_v_bz_coopB_TNN` is the same tile, cluster and raster — the scheduler prologue will be the same family. Extracting how it decodes tiles from `CTAID`:
> tool `Bash`: Extract cuBLAS's tile-index decode from CTAID

This is their tile scheduler, and it's readable. The repeated pattern is unmistakable:

```
UIMAD.WIDE.U32 UR16, UR5, UR15, URZ    ; 64-bit multiply
USHF.R.U32     UR11, UR17, UR15, URZ   ; take the HIGH word, shift
UIMAD.U32      UR14, UR11, UR15, UR5   ; n - q*d  (negated divisor)
```

That's **magic-number division** — integer `div`/`mod` by a *runtime* divisor, done without a divide instruction. And it appears **four times in sequence**, each feeding the next.

A four-level `div`/`mod` decomposition of `CTAID.Y` is precisely a **grouped rasterization** scheduler: linear tile id → (group, row-in-group, col-in-group, …). So cuBLAS is doing exactly the thing our `RASTER_SWIZZLE` knob was built for — that's now evidence, not my guess.

The critical detail is *where the divisors come from*:
> tool `Bash`: Check whether the scheduler divisors come from kernel params

**Proven.** Every divisor is a **kernel parameter** loaded from constant memory:

```
ULDC UR15, c[0x0][0x340] / [0x344] / [0x348] / [0x34c]
ULDC UR15, c[0x0][0x218] / [0x21c] / [0x220] / [0x224]
ULDC UR16, c[0x0][0x228] / [0x22c] / [0x230] / [0x234]
ULDC UR16, c[0x0][0x238] / [0x23c]
```

Each `div`/`mod` stage consumes a **`{divisor, magic, shift}` triple** — the standard reciprocal-division trio — and there are at least four such stages chained together.

So, as fact rather than inference:

1. **cuBLAS decomposes its linear CTA index through ≥4 levels of `div`/`mod`** before touching memory. That is a grouped/swizzled rasterization, which confirms the mechanism our `RASTER_SWIZZLE` targets.
2. **The group sizes are host-computed per launch**, not baked into the kernel — they arrive as parameters. cuBLAS retunes the traversal order for every `(M,N,K)`.
3. **Ours is compile-time and single-level** — one `log2(group)` constant per config, `0` (off) on the 192x192 pin.

That's the structural difference behind 66% vs 87% L2, and it's the first explanation today that came from their code rather than from my reasoning.

Our discretised equivalent is exactly what I registered — `rs2/rs4/rs8/rs16` chosen per shape by the dispatch table, which is per-shape tuning at coarser granularity. Now motivated by evidence.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-11 18:57 IST]

Good question — let me check both the source and what it actually compiles to.
> tool `Bash`: Read our tile-decode function

**We use naive runtime `/` and `%`. cuBLAS uses precomputed magic numbers.**

```cpp
// SW == 0
mega_row = mega_tile % mega_grid_m;      // runtime divisor
mega_col = mega_tile / mega_grid_m;

// SW > 0  -- THREE divisions, and gsize is DATA-DEPENDENT
const int group = mega_tile / per_grp;
int gsize = slow_ex - group * S;  if (gsize > S) gsize = S;  if (gsize < 1) gsize = 1;
const int slow  = group * S + (idx % gsize);
const int fast  = idx / gsize;
```

`gsize` is clamped per group, so **the divisor changes every loop iteration** — the compiler can't hoist a reciprocal for it even in principle. Checking what it actually emits:
> tool `Bash`: Check what our tile decode compiles to

**Answer: we use naive runtime division. And the SASS proves it.**

```
                            I2F  F2I  MUFU
192x192_1x2_v    (SW=0)      5    5    5
192x192_1x2_v_rs2 (SW=1)     6    6    6
```

`I2F → MUFU.RCP → F2I` is the **float-reciprocal integer division** sequence nvcc emits when the divisor is a runtime value — roughly 15–20 instructions each. We do **5–6 of them per tile**, inside the persistent tile loop.

cuBLAS does **zero**. Their sequence is:

```
UIMAD.WIDE.U32 UR16, UR5, UR15, URZ   ; multiply by host-supplied magic
USHF.R.U32     UR11, UR17, UR15, URZ  ; take high word, shift
UIMAD.U32      UR14, UR11, UR15, UR5  ; n - q*d
```

≈3 instructions per div/mod, with the `{divisor, magic, shift}` triples arriving as kernel parameters from `c[0x0][0x218…0x34c]`.

And our swizzled path is worse than the plain one in a way I hadn't noticed:

```cpp
int gsize = slow_ex - group * S;  if (gsize > S) gsize = S;  if (gsize < 1) gsize = 1;
const int slow = group * S + (idx % gsize);
const int fast = idx / gsize;
```

`gsize` is **data-dependent** — clamped per group — so its divisor changes every iteration. Magic numbers can't be precomputed for it even in principle, which is why `rs2` emits *six* divisions instead of five. Our grouped rasterization is currently paying more per tile than the ungrouped path, before it delivers any L2 benefit.

**So there are two separate defects in the same function, both now proven rather than inferred:**

1. **Traversal order** → L2 66% vs 87% → 2.43× the DRAM traffic
2. **Naive runtime division** → part of the 2.18× instruction count

And the fix for both is the same shape as cuBLAS's: compute the traversal parameters **host-side per launch** and pass `{divisor, magic, shift}` triples in, so the device does multiply-high + shift. That also removes the data-dependent `gsize`, because the host can pick a group size that divides evenly instead of clamping at runtime.

Before I write any of that, the `rs` measurement still needs to run — it tells us whether grouping helps *at all* at our granularity. If `rs4` moves L2 from 66% toward 87%, the magic-number work is worth doing properly; if the L2 rate doesn't budge for any group size, then traversal grouping isn't the lever here and the magic numbers would only address the instruction count.

That run is the one I'd do next, and it's already staged.

GPU 3 is a colleague's job (`./_runner_`, PID 1486433, 125 GB, 100% util). The ~130 MiB on 0/1/2 with **no process listed** is worth identifying — especially GPU 1, which is ours.

```bash

fuser -v /dev/nvidia0 /dev/nvidia1 /dev/nvidia2 2>&1 | head -20
lsof /dev/nvidia1 2>/dev/null | head
# any of our binaries still alive?

# nvidia-smi's own view, including graphics contexts not just compute

nvidia-smi -q -i 1 -d MEMORY | head -20
```

Two likely explanations, and they need different responses:

**Benign** — ~130 MiB is roughly what the driver reserves per GPU once a context has ever been created, and **persistence mode keeps that reservation alive** after the process exits. Note GPU 1 shows `Persistence-M: On` — we enabled that ourselves with `nvidia-smi -i 1 -pm 1`. GPUs 0 and 2 show `Off` yet still hold 130 MiB, so it isn't only persistence, but driver-reserved memory is the usual answer and it costs us nothing out of 143 GB.

**Not benign** — a leaked context from one of our runs. That matters because we now allocate a **split-K workspace** (`acquire_workspace`, 8 MB at `kv-wgrad`), and if a process is lingering it would both hold memory and skew timing. `fuser` will show it immediately if so.

If `fuser`/`ps` come back empty, it's driver reservation and we ignore it. If a stale `test_bgemm_*` or `ncu` is still running, that would also explain any odd timing in the last few measurements, and I'd want to re-run the `rs` diagnostic clean rather than trust it.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-11 19:11 IST]

**Grouped rasterization works — and beats cuBLAS on memory. And it buys essentially nothing in time.**

| config | L2 hit | DRAM | duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | 67.18% | 9.91 GB | 5.24 ms |
| rs2 | 77.59% | 6.52 GB | 5.21 ms |
| rs4 | 83.36% | 4.47 GB | 5.23 ms |
| **rs8** | **88.24%** | **3.96 GB** | **5.21 ms** |
| rs16 | 84.50% | 5.25 GB | 5.23 ms |
| **cuBLAS** | 87.37% | 4.16 GB | **4.64 ms** |

`rs8` **exceeds cuBLAS on both memory metrics** — higher L2 hit rate, lower DRAM traffic — and the kernel is **0.6% faster**. Nothing.

The curve is real (rs2 < rs4 < rs8 > rs16, with 16 over-grouping), so the mechanism works exactly as intended. It just wasn't the bottleneck.

**And my bandwidth reasoning was wrong.** I said 10.12 GB was "~3.4 ms of a 5.24 ms kernel", assuming ~3 TB/s and no overlap. H200 is ~4.8 TB/s, and 9.91 GB / 5.24 ms = **1.89 TB/s = 39% of peak**. We were never bandwidth-bound. After rs8 we're at 0.76 TB/s = 16%.

## What the bottleneck actually is

Four hypotheses tested and eliminated, each on measurement:

| hypothesis | verdict |
|---|---|
| epilogue / chunking | −18.7% to +0.4% |
| bank conflicts | cuBLAS has **129× more** and wins |
| DRAM traffic / L2 reuse | **beat cuBLAS**, 0.6% gain |
| — | |
| **instruction issue** | **1.057 B vs 486 M, tensor 81.64% vs 91.87%** |

And the arithmetic closes exactly:

```
5.24 ms x (81.64 / 91.87) = 4.66 ms      cuBLAS measured: 4.64 ms
```

**The entire remaining gap at `lm_head-fwd` is that we execute 2.18× the instructions, and those extra instructions steal issue slots from the tensor pipe.** Recover the tensor-pipe occupancy and the time lands on cuBLAS's, to within 0.4%.

So the magic-number division is now the *right* target — but for the right reason. It's an **issue-slot** fix, not the memory fix I framed it as an hour ago. The 5–6 `I2F/MUFU.RCP/F2I` sequences per tile are ~100 instructions of pure overhead in the persistent loop, and cuBLAS pays ~3 per div/mod.

**On pinning `rs8`:** standalone it's a wash (0.6%, within noise), but it cuts DRAM traffic 2.5× for free, which can only help when the trainer has other kernels competing for bandwidth. I'd pin it, while being clear the isolated gain is ~0.

Next I'd find where the other ~470M instructions go, since division alone won't be all of it:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
for K in bgemm_sm90_kernel nvjet; do
  echo "===== $K"
  CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 ncu --metrics \
smsp__inst_executed.sum,\
smsp__sass_thread_inst_executed_op_integer_pred_on.sum,\
smsp__inst_executed_op_shared_st.sum,\
smsp__inst_executed_op_shared_ld.sum,\
sm__inst_executed_pipe_tensor.sum,\
smsp__average_warps_issue_stalled_no_instruction_per_issue_active.ratio \
    -k regex:$K --launch-count 1 \
    ./build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --shape=16384x50304x2048 --layout=nn --cfg=192x192x64_1x2_v_rs8 2>&1 \
    | grep -E "inst_executed|integer|shared_st|shared_ld|stalled"
done
```

The integer-op count against cuBLAS's is the one that tells us how much of the 571M is index arithmetic versus something else.

> tool `Bash`: Opcode census of cuBLAS's 192x192 kernel

Direct answer to your question, and the census just gave me the mechanism — it's bigger than instruction count.

Look at cuBLAS's mix: `UIADD3` 3197, `UMOV` 2001, `ULDC` 1771, `UIMAD` 1702, `UISETP` 1150, `USHF` 575, `UPRMT` 483 = **10,879 of 29,072 = 37.4% on the UNIFORM datapath**.

Hopper has a separate uniform register file (`URx`) and uniform datapath for warp-scalar work. It runs **in parallel with the vector datapath** and doesn't compete with the tensor pipe for the same issue slots. cuBLAS puts essentially its entire scheduler there.

§H27y.10 already recorded this and I'd forgotten it: *"40.6% vs 5.9% uniform-datapath ratio"*.

Let me confirm ours:
> tool `Bash`: Compare our uniform-datapath usage against cuBLAS's
> tool `Bash`: Confirm the division signature and vector-vs-uniform integer split

**Proof complete.**

```
                MUFU   I2F   F2I        IMAD(vector)  UIMAD(uniform)   uniform share
ours              6      6     6            388            63             17.6%
cuBLAS            0      0     0            414          1702             37.9%
```

**cuBLAS has literally zero runtime divisions.** And the integer work inverts: cuBLAS does **4× more** integer multiply-adds than us in absolute terms (2116 vs 451) — but **80% of theirs run on the uniform datapath**, while **86% of ours run on the vector datapath**.

## Direct answer: yes, and the mechanism is bigger than instruction count

The causal chain, every link measured:

1. `decode_mega_tile` divides by runtime values
2. nvcc emits `I2F → MUFU.RCP → F2I`, and **`MUFU` has no uniform-datapath equivalent**
3. So the tile index is computed on the **vector** datapath — and everything derived from it (addresses, predicates) stays vector. Our 113 `R2UR` instructions are the compiler shuttling those vector results *back* to uniform registers afterwards.
4. Vector instructions compete with `HGMMA` for issue slots
5. → **tensor active 81.64% vs cuBLAS's 91.87%**
6. → `5.24 × (81.64/91.87) = 4.66 ms` against cuBLAS's measured **4.64 ms**

cuBLAS's `UIMAD.WIDE + USHF` magic-number division is uniform-datapath, so their entire scheduler runs **in parallel with** the tensor pipe instead of stealing from it.

So it isn't "fewer instructions" — it's **moving the scheduler off the datapath that feeds the tensor cores.** That's why they can afford 4× more integer work than us and still hit 91.87%.

This also retroactively explains §H27y.10's recorded "40.6% vs 5.9% uniform-datapath ratio", which was measured a month ago and never acted on.

## How I'd validate it, in order

The leading indicators come *before* timing, so we know whether the change did what it's supposed to before arguing about wall clock:

```
1.  grep -c MUFU        must go 6 -> 0
2.  uniform share       must rise 17.6% -> ~35%+
3.  tensor active       must rise 81.64% -> toward 91.87%
4.  only then: duration
```

If (1) succeeds but (2) doesn't, the divisions were only part of what pins us to the vector path and there's more to find. If (2) succeeds but (3) doesn't, the uniform-datapath theory is wrong and I'll say so.

The implementation is the cuBLAS shape: host computes `{divisor, magic, shift}` per launch, passes them as kernel parameters, device does `UIMAD.WIDE` + `USHF`. It's one shared function (`decode_mega_tile`) plus the launcher, so it lands on every variant at once.

## what changed

One function, `decode_mega_tile`, plus one launcher line — so it lands on every SM90 variant at once.

There were exactly **three** runtime divisors, each reached from two sites (producer + consumer warpgroup), and nvcc folds each `/`+`%` pair into one reciprocal:

| divisor | used for | reciprocals |
|---|---|---|
| `mega_grid_m * mega_grid_n` | `task_id` → (batch, mega_tile) | 2 |
| `S * fast_ex` | → group | 2 |
| `gsize` | → slow/fast | 2 |

That's **6 — exactly the MUFU count ncu measured**, which is the first independent confirmation the diagnosis pointed at the right instructions. Every other `/` and `%` in the loop divides by a compile-time constant and never produced MUFU.

Two of the three divisors disappear outright rather than becoming magic numbers: `mega_tile/(S*fast_ex)` is `(mega_tile/fast_ex) >> SW` since `S` is a compile-time power of two, and `gsize == S` (every group but the last) collapses to a mask and a shift. Only `mn`, `fast` and `tail` remain, all built **host-side** — CUTLASS's `find_divisor` verbatim. I deliberately did *not* compute them on device: the magic number needs a 64-bit divide, which nvcc lowers to a long software routine. Host-side is also what cuBLAS's `ULDC` instructions imply — those are param-bank loads, i.e. constants their host already computed.

## proofs, both local — no H200 needed

**1. Exhaustive equivalence, old decode vs new** — 128,690,120 combinations across raster × swizzle × cluster × grid × tile: **0 mismatches**, task_id split included. Two things the patch relies on were audited rather than assumed: the tail path is genuinely exercised (7.9M tiles) and always equalled `md.tail`; and the old `gsize < 1` clamp **never fired once**, confirming it was dead code before I removed it.

**2. SASS diff, sm_90a, Makefile flags, whole NN TU (292 kernels):**

```
MUFU    1298 →     0      I2F  1298 → 0      F2I 1298 → 0
ULDC    3423 →  6241  (+2818, magic numbers from the param bank)
IMAD   75851 → 67853      R2UR 20083 → 17609
total 601952 → 575064  (-26,888, -4.5%)
```

Per-kernel MUFU went from {4:170, 5:106, 6:10, 7:4} to **0 for all 292** — the 6-MUFU group is the `rs8` class ncu measured. The two `splitk_reduce` kernels are **byte-identical** (3016 lines), which is the control: they don't decode tiles, so they prove no collateral change. TN, NT and dispatcher also build clean at 0 MUFU.

I built the "before" side in a scratch copy of the tree, so your working file was never reverted at any point.

**Two things I want to flag rather than let you find later:**
- **SM103 still has the naive pattern** — 39 sites across 4 Blackwell files, in a separate template with a different shape (`mn_tile % grid_n`). I did *not* touch it: it needs B300 validation and this campaign is H200. Recorded as an open item, not silently skipped.
- **Nothing about speed is proven yet.** Static counts prove the division is gone; they do not prove the datapath actually moved. Uniform share, tensor active and duration all still need the H200, in that order.

```bash
  END{ printf "sm90 gemm kernels : %d\nMUFU in them      : %d   <- must be 0\nMUFU elsewhere    : %d   (fp32 sm89/sm86, expected non-zero)\n", k, sm90+0, other+0 }'
```

**step 2 — correctness, before any timing.** Note I am deliberately *not* passing `--skip-2d` here: this change is in the tile decode, and 2D clusters are exactly the shapes that exercise different `mega_grid_m/n` paths, so they are the ones that most need checking.

**step 3 — the mechanism, per-kernel not aggregate:**

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 ncu --kernel-name-base mangled -k regex:bgemm_sm90_kernel \
```

`128x112x64_1x2_v` is a size-2 cluster that passed on all four previous shapes in this very run. Every one of these passed repeatedly before failing.

That is §H27y.18's signature verbatim: *"Which raster failed varied between runs (`4x2_h` once, `4x2_v` the next), so raster was never the discriminator."* Adding each config to the skip list just hands the failure to the next config in line — which is exactly what happened across runs B→C→D. I burned three runs doing that. My error in approach.

And run D landed on **`520x1032x264b`** — that is *the* §H27y.18 bisection shape (`520x1024x264x3`): M=520 gives an M residue of 8, batch>1. The producer-tail fix took it from 7/8 FAIL to 0/8 back when the matrix was 337 configs × 6 shapes; we're now at 889 × 18, and the section explicitly declined to call it closed.

## the actual lever

**All four failures say "in timing"** — none in the correctness check. The benchmark loop hammers many iterations, which is what widens the exit skew until the race fires. Correctness doesn't need that loop.

```bash
cd /root/gautam_k/blublas

# only the 4 genuinely silently-wrong configs (§H27z.44 C2) — no more chasing
SKIP="--skip=128x112x64_2x2_h --skip=128x112x64_2x2_v --skip=128x112x64_1x4_h --skip=128x112x64_1x4_v"

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 ./build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --no-bench $SKIP \
  --resume=test_reports/h27z83_resume.tsv 2>&1 | tee test_reports/h27z83_correctness.md

grep -E "PASS,|UNTESTED|ABORTED_ON" test_reports/h27z83_correctness.md | tail -3
```

`--no-bench` also drops the 128x112 cluster skips back to just the four real ones, so we get genuine coverage of the rest. It'll be much faster without timing loops.

**Also: `--resume` is not persisting.** Every run has printed `resume : 0 results already present`, so each one redoes everything from scratch — that's why we keep re-running the same 856-case shapes. Worth a `ls -l test_reports/h27z83_resume.tsv` to see if it's even being written.

## what's already settled for my change

4,128 PASS, **every non-split-K one bit-exact at 0.00000**, across four complete shapes including a batched one. The decode change is correct. The intermittent batched/M-residue LAUNCHERR is a real pre-existing defect — the §H27y.18 residual — and it belongs on open items as a genuine bug affecting batched workloads, not as a footnote. It is not something the tile decode touches, and no amount of skip-listing will fix it.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-11 21:12 IST]

Let me show you the actual mechanism rather than describe it:
> tool `Bash`: Read the dispatch table lookup

`lookup()` at [Bgemm_sm90_dispatch_table.h:922](src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM90/Bgemm_sm90_dispatch_table.h#L922) is a binary search keyed on (M, N, K). Binary search **only works if the array is sorted** — it throws away half the array at every step based on that assumption.

Let me demonstrate what appending actually does:
> tool `Bash`: Demonstrate the silent lookup failure

"Unfindable" means: **the row is physically in the file, but the search can never reach it.**

Look at the appended case above. The row `(4096,4096,4096)` sits at index 5. Binary search compared three rows — `(4096,2048)`, `(16384,50304)`, `(8192,4096)` — and never once looked at index 5, because it had already decided that half of the array couldn't contain the key. It returns `0xFFFF`, "not found".

The mechanism: binary search discards half the remaining array at every step, and that's only valid if the array is sorted. Put a small key at the end and the search throws away the half it's actually sitting in. You can open the header, see your row right there, and the lookup still says not found.

Let me confirm what happens next:
> tool `Bash`: Check the fallback path on lookup miss

Confirmed at [Bgemm_sm90_dispatcher.cu:168](src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM90/Bgemm_sm90_dispatcher.cu#L168):

```cpp
unsigned short cfg = lookup(kTable_nt, kTableSize_nt, M, N, K);
if (cfg == 0xFFFF) cfg = tree_nt(M, N, K);   // miss -> fitted tree fallback
```

So on a miss it quietly falls through to the decision-tree fallback and runs **a different config**. No error, no warning, no crash — and the GEMM still produces **numerically correct results**.

That's what makes it dangerous. It isn't a correctness bug, it's a **measurement-poisoning** bug. The symptom of a bad append is:

> "i pinned the winning config at that site, rebuilt, re-ran the trainer... and the number didn't move"

and the natural conclusion is *"the chunked epilogue doesn't help there"* — when in fact the pin was never used and the old config ran the whole time. You'd throw away a real win based on a measurement of something you never actually measured.

That's why the doc flags it as §H27z.55b and why I re-sorted the 11 rows instead of appending them. The table is `static const` and sorted by (M,N,K); every insert has to go in its sorted position, not at the end.

A cheap guard, if you want it — a `static_assert`-style sortedness check so a bad insert fails at build time instead of silently degrading:

```cpp
for (int i = 1; i < kTableSize_nn; ++i)
    assert(key(kTable_nn[i-1]) < key(kTable_nn[i]));   // in a debug/test path
```

Worth adding at some point, since the whole 225-entry table depends on an invariant nothing currently enforces.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-11 21:19 IST]

MUFU = **Multi-Function Unit** instruction — the SASS op that runs on the SFU (special function unit), the hardware block for transcendentals and reciprocals: `MUFU.RCP`, `.SQRT`, `.RSQ`, `.SIN`, `.EX2`, `.LG2`.

The reason it showed up in our *integer* tile math: **NVIDIA GPUs have no integer divide instruction.** There is no `IDIV` in SASS. So nvcc lowers a runtime `a / b` into a float-reciprocal sequence. Let me show you the real thing from today's pre-change dump:
> tool `Bash`: Show the real MUFU divide sequence from the SASS

There it is: `MUFU.RCP R4, R4`.

**Why an integer divide produces a float reciprocal:** there's no integer-divide instruction in the ISA, so nvcc computes `a / b` as `a × (1/b)` — convert to float (`I2F`), take the reciprocal on the SFU (`MUFU.RCP`), convert back (`F2I`), then a Newton-Raphson refinement and fixups to make the result exact for integers. About 15–20 instructions for one `/`. That's why our three divisors produced 6 `MUFU` and exactly 6 `I2F` and 6 `F2I` — they come as a set.

**Two costs, and the second is the one that mattered:**

1. The SFU is a narrow, high-latency unit — roughly a quarter of the ALU's lanes. Bad, but survivable.

2. **There is no uniform-datapath version of MUFU.** Look at the register names in the two dumps:

```
BEFORE:  MUFU.RCP        R4,  R4              <- R  = vector registers
AFTER:   UIMAD.WIDE.U32  UR4, UR4, UR5, URZ   <- UR = uniform registers
         USHF.L.U64.HI   UR7, UR6, 0x2, UR7
```

Hopper has a **second, separate datapath** — the uniform datapath, with its own `UR` register file and its own instructions (`UIMAD`, `USHF`, `UIADD3`, `ULDC`). It runs *in parallel* with the vector datapath and exists precisely for warp-uniform scalar work — loop counters, addresses, tile indices. Every thread in the warp computes the same tile index, so that math *belongs* on the uniform path.

But `MUFU` only exists in vector form. So the instant the tile index touches a runtime divide, that value — and everything derived from it — is stuck on the vector datapath, competing with `HGMMA` (the tensor-core instruction) for issue slots. That was the whole theory: cuBLAS runs 80% of its integer work uniform, we ran 86% vector.

The magic-number fix replaces `x / d` with `(x × magic) >> shift` — plain integer multiply and shift, which *can* run uniform. That's why `ULDC` jumped +2,818 (the magic constants arriving from the parameter bank) and `R2UR` dropped 2,474 (fewer vector→uniform shuttles).

And the honest ending: the mechanism is exactly as described and it did move tensor occupancy cleanly — just by 0.9 points, not the 10 I expected. Real, understood, and not the bottleneck.

| candidate | verdict |
|---|---|
| DRAM bandwidth | we're **ahead** of cuBLAS |
| L2 hit rate | we're **ahead** (88.24%, 3.96 GB with `rs8`) |
| bank conflicts | cuBLAS has 2.4M and is faster; we have 18.8k |
| tile shape | matching cuBLAS's tiles lost on **15/15** sites |

## what it does

**Groups the 15 shapes by which cuBLAS variant they get**, then for each group runs *our* matching tile+cluster against cuBLAS on those exact shapes:

| group | cuBLAS variant | our tile+cluster | shapes |
|---|---|---|---|
| g1 | `192x192_64x3_1x2_h_coopB` | 192x192 c1x2 | 1 |
| g2 | `192x192_64x3/4_2x1_v_coopB` | 192x192 c2x1 | 3 |
| g3 | `256x128_64x4_1x2_h_coopA` | **128x256** c1x2 | 7 |
| g4 | `128x256_64x4_2x1_v_coopA` | **256x128** c2x1 | 3 |
| g5 | `128x128_64x6_1x2_h_splitK` | 128x128 + splitK | 1 |

The tile flips because of the operand swap — that's the production-verified mapping, not a guess: the 223-case nsys run matched launch counts 7/7 exactly (cuBLAS `320x128_1x2_h` ↔ our `128x320_c1x2`, cuBLAS `128x256_2x1_v` ↔ our `256x128_c2x1`).

I sweep by `--tile`/`--cluster` instead of pinning one config, so it automatically covers **both rasters** (the h/v mapping is the one part that was never proven) **and** every epilogue variant including the 4-stage chunked ones. Then it prints the best matching variant per shape with cuBLAS measured in the same run, and nsys confirms which kernel each side actually issued.

Two bugs I caught before handing it over, rather than after: the field map (`maxAbsErr` shifted `ourTF` from `$6` to `$7`, so the old map in `h27z65_bank_fault1.sh` is stale and would have printed garbage), and `sort` shuffling the header into the middle of the table.

Output lands in `test_reports/h27z85/ALL.md`. Once it's done we take the worst rows into ncu + SASS, which is the actual step-3 work.

## the finding

It is **not** a general kernel problem — it's specifically **192x192**:

```
our 192x192          n=4   mean 83.1%   (81.6 - 84.8)
our 256x128/128x256  n=10  mean 88.5%   (75.4 - 95.2)
our 128x128          n=1   mean 89.2%
```

On the tiles we're good at we reach **95.2%**. Every one of the four 192x192 variants sits at 81–85% and nothing else does. And the two sites that dominate the deficit — lm_head-fwd (V4, 81.8%) and gate_up-fwd (V3, 84.8%) — are both 192x192. So the six eliminations weren't wrong, they were just aimed at the wrong level: the problem is our **192x192 implementation**, not the kernel design in general.

Two side facts worth keeping: raster is **per-shape, not a rule** (V3 wants `_h`, V4/V5/V6 want `_v`), and the single worst row is V8 at K=512 (75.4%) — a narrow-K problem, separate from 192x192.

Good — let me think through what can actually prove each, because they need different instruments.

## the layout mapping — provable directly, and it's easy

This one is **not** circular, because we control the *input* (the layout we ask cuBLAS for) and observe the *output* (the kernel name it picks). We're not choosing cuBLAS's side.

Call cuBLAS at the same M,N,K under `nn`, then `nt`, then `tn`, and read the nvjet suffix each time. If `nn` always yields `NN*`, `nt` yields `TN*`, `tn` yields `NT*`, the mapping is proven by construction *of the input only*. This is exactly the method that settled `bz` = beta-zero in H8 (`bz_probe.cu`: same shape, beta=0 vs beta=1, one token changed).

## the raster — harder, and here's why

Raster is the CTA→tile walk order. It is **not** in the launch record and **not** readable from SASS (the divisors arrive via `ULDC` from the param bank, so the assembly shows the load, not the value).

But it *does* leave a physical fingerprint. Our own source defines it:

```
RASTER 0 = v : M-fastest, walk down M, reusing B
RASTER 1 = h : N-fastest, walk across N, reusing A
```

Different walk order ⇒ different operand reuse ⇒ **different DRAM read volume and L2 hit rate**, and the gap is large on an asymmetric shape. So: measure cuBLAS's `dram__bytes_read` + `lts__t_sector_hit_rate` on a shape where M≫N, then measure *our* same-tile config in **both** rasters, and see which one matches. Non-circular, because cuBLAS's side is measured, not chosen.

There's also a deductive argument worth stating: their frame is our transpose (proven). Their `h` = "walk across *their* N" = "walk across *our* M" = our `v`. That follows from the proven tile transpose — **provided** their `h` means N-fastest, which is an assumption about their naming. The fingerprint test is what removes that assumption.

## what each instrument can and cannot do

| question | nsys | ncu | SASS |
|---|---|---|---|
| layout mapping | **yes** — kernel name per requested layout | no | no |
| raster | no | **yes** — DRAM/L2 fingerprint | no (divisors are runtime params) |
| cluster | done — `clusterX/Y/Z` | — | — |
| tile | done — clamp-free grids | — | — |

**Our `1x2` and our `2x1` both launch `(2,1,1)` too.** `clusterDim.x = CLUSTER_SIZE`, y=z=1 — `CLUSTER_M`/`CLUSTER_N` are applied *internally* via `cluster_rank % CLUSTER_M`. So the launch record can't distinguish our 1x2 from our 2x1 any more than it distinguishes cuBLAS's.

What the launch data actually proved:
- cuBLAS clusters are 1-D of size S — **true**
- cuBLAS's name pair `1x2` vs `2x1` is a *logical label*, not the launch dims — **true**

What it did **not** prove: that cuBLAS's `1x2` is our `2x1` rather than our `1x2`. That's internal on both sides, exactly like raster — so it needs the same fingerprint treatment.

## the completing test — 2 more runs

We tested `2x1_v` vs `2x1_h`. The full grid is `{1x2, 2x1} × {v, h}`, and all four exist for 128x256:

```bash

for c in 128x256x64_1x2_v 128x256x64_1x2_h; do
  CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 ncu --kernel-name-base mangled -k regex:"bgemm_sm90_kernel|nvjet" \
    --metrics dram__bytes_read.sum,lts__t_sector_hit_rate.pct,gpu__time_duration.sum \
    -o test_reports/h27z87/fix_$c --force-overwrite \
    ./build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --cfg=$c --shape=16384x2048x4096 --layout=nn --bench > /dev/null 2>&1
  echo "done $c"
done
```

Then rerun the same python with all four configs and whichever of the four sits on cuBLAS's fingerprint is the counterpart — cluster **and** raster settled together, by measurement, with nothing assumed.

If `2x1_h` still wins against all three others, then cuBLAS `1x2_h` = our `2x1_h`: cluster label transposes, raster letter doesn't. Odd-looking but perfectly coherent — the tile is a *logical* (M,N) thing so it transposes, while the raster is a *physical* grid-walk order so it doesn't.

## the method

An M-fastest walk fixes `n` and sweeps every `m`, so it traverses **all of A once per n-column**. If A exceeds L2 it cannot be cached between columns, therefore:

```
DRAM reads  >=  grid_n x sizeof(A)        hard lower bound
```

Symmetrically for N-fastest with B > L2. A measurement **below** a bound doesn't make that walk unlikely — it makes it **impossible**. On the 6 shapes where both A and B exceed L2 the bounds are two-sided, so exactly one walk survives.

The single-shape version already showed the strength of this: cuBLAS measured 264 MB against an M-fastest minimum of 1,074 MB — **4.1× below**. And our own `_v` measured 1080 MB against that same 1,074 MB bound (ratio 1.006), which validates the model, since our source independently defines `v` = M-fastest.

## and it tests cluster too

I was wrong to call cluster proven from launch dims. **Our `1x2` and our `2x1` both launch `(2,1,1)`** — `CLUSTER_M`/`CLUSTER_N` are applied internally via `cluster_rank % CLUSTER_M`. So the launch record can't separate them either. Cluster and raster are now tested together: `{1x2, 2x1} × {v, h}` on the same tile and shape.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-12 15:57 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Locate the h27z88 reports locally
> tool `Bash`: Compare all configs against theoretical minimum traffic

The test **disproved its own premise** — and in doing so found something much more important.

## the raster question is malformed, and the answer is: undetermined

6 of 14 shapes came back `CONTRADICTION` — cuBLAS measured **below both bounds**. If the walk were pure M-fastest it needs ≥ `grid_n × A`; pure N-fastest needs ≥ `grid_m × B`. cuBLAS is under both. Arithmetically, **cuBLAS does neither pure walk.**

Look at how efficient it is:

```
shape                    min(A+B)   cuBLAS   x min
2048x512x16384    tn         84       84     1.00     <- perfect reuse
2048x2048x16384   tn        134      134     1.00
16384x512x2048    nn         69       71     1.02
16384x2048x2048   nn         75       79     1.05
```

1.00× the theoretical minimum is impossible for any pure 1-D walk on these grids. cuBLAS uses **grouped/swizzled rasterization** — a tiles-of-tiles walk that keeps a window of *both* operands in L2. So "is cuBLAS's `h` our `v` or our `h`" has no answer: their raster field isn't a pure walk direction.

The closest-config tally agrees — `1x2_v`:3, `1x2_h`:3, `2x1_v`:2, `2x1_h`:6. Nothing wins everywhere, so by the rule the script holds itself to: **undetermined, and I'm not picking one.**

## the finding that actually matters

Same data, different column — our best config vs cuBLAS, as a multiple of minimum traffic:

```
shape                       cuBLAS    ours best    we move
16384x11264x2048  nn  gate_up-fwd    4.75x       15.89x     3.3x MORE
16384x50304x2048  nn  lm_head-fwd    8.41x       25.04x     3.0x MORE
```

**On the two sites that dominate the entire deficit, we read 3× more data from DRAM than cuBLAS.** gate_up-fwd is the 930 ms loss; lm_head-fwd is the one we've been chasing for two days. Both are 192x192 `nn`.

And on most other shapes we're fine — even slightly *better* than cuBLAS (1.60 vs 1.93, 1.81 vs 1.86). It's specifically these two.

This also reframes §H27z.82's "DRAM is not the bottleneck." That was measured with `rs8` — a **grouped** raster. With pure rasters we're 3× worse. Which says grouped rasterization isn't a minor tuning knob here; it's the mechanism cuBLAS uses to get near-minimum traffic, and it's worth a great deal on exactly these two shapes.

## next

We already have `192x192x64_1x2_v_rs2/rs4/rs8/rs16`. None were in this sweep — I only tested pure rasters. The obvious test is those four on the two bad shapes, against cuBLAS:

```bash

for s in 16384x11264x2048 16384x50304x2048; do

    ./build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --cfg=$c --shape=$s --layout=nn --bench > /dev/null 2>&1
  echo "done $s $c"
done; done
```

If `rsN` closes the 3× gap, that's the lm_head-fwd answer — and it's a knob we already have, not something to build.

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
python3 - <<'PY'
import csv,io,subprocess,glob,os,re,collections,statistics as st
U={'byte':1,'Kbyte':1e3,'Mbyte':1e6,'Gbyte':1e9,'%':1,'us':1,'ns':1e-3,'ms':1e3}
def load(p):
    out=subprocess.run(['ncu','-i',p,'--csv'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout
    a=collections.defaultdict(lambda: collections.defaultdict(list))
    for r in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(out)):
        k=r['Kernel Name']; w='cuBLAS' if 'nvjet' in k else ('OURS' if 'bgemm_sm90_kernel' in k else None)
        if not w: continue
        try: a[w][r['Metric Name']].append(float(r['Metric Value'].replace(',',''))*U.get(r['Metric Unit'],1))
        except: pass
    return a
D=collections.defaultdict(dict); CB=collections.defaultdict(list)
for p in sorted(glob.glob('test_reports/h27z89/*.ncu-rep')):
    m=re.match(r'(\d+)x(\d+)x(\d+)_(192x192x64_1x2_v(?:_rs\d+)?)\.ncu-rep$', os.path.basename(p))
    if not m: continue
    key=(int(m.group(1)),int(m.group(2)),int(m.group(3))); cfg=m.group(4).replace('192x192x64_1x2_v','plain').replace('plain_','')
    a=load(p)
    D[key][cfg]=(st.mean(a['OURS']['dram__bytes_read.sum']),
                 st.mean(a['OURS']['lts__t_sector_hit_rate.pct']),
                 st.mean(a['OURS']['gpu__time_duration.sum']))
    CB[key].append((st.mean(a['cuBLAS']['dram__bytes_read.sum']),
                    st.mean(a['cuBLAS']['lts__t_sector_hit_rate.pct']),
                    st.mean(a['cuBLAS']['gpu__time_duration.sum'])))
order=['plain','rs2','rs4','rs8','rs16']
for key in sorted(D):
    M,N,K=key; mn=(M*K*2+K*N*2)/1e6
    cb=tuple(st.mean(x) for x in zip(*CB[key]))
    print(f"\n### {M}x{N}x{K} nn    theoretical min A+B = {mn:,.0f} MB")
    print(f"{'config':<10}{'DRAM MB':>10}{'x min':>8}{'L2 hit%':>9}{'us':>9}{'  vs cuBLAS DRAM':>18}")
    print(f"{'cuBLAS':<10}{cb[0]/1e6:>10,.0f}{cb[0]/1e6/mn:>8.2f}{cb[1]:>9.1f}{cb[2]:>9.0f}{'--':>18}")
    for c in order:
        if c not in D[key]: continue
        d,l,t=D[key][c]
        print(f"{c:<10}{d/1e6:>10,.0f}{d/1e6/mn:>8.2f}{l:>9.1f}{t:>9.0f}{d/cb[0]:>17.2f}x")
PY
```

If `rsN` moves DRAM but *not* duration, then the traffic was never what was costing us there, and I'll say so rather than claim the win.

Exactly what you wanted — and no GPU needed, because the decode is deterministic arithmetic. Here is our raster, drawn:

```
RASTER = v (0)                        RASTER = h (1)
      N0   N1   N2   N3               N0   N1   N2   N3
M0     0    8   16   24          M0    0    1    2    3
M1     1    9   17   25          M1    6    7    8    9

    VERTICAL: walks down M          HORIZONTAL: walks across N
```

That's direct observation, not inference — `v` is vertical (M-fastest), `h` is horizontal (N-fastest). It confirms the 12/12 DRAM result exactly.

## and it shows what `rsN` actually is

```
RASTER = v + rs4                      RASTER = v + rs8   (grid has only 6 N-columns)
      N0  N1  N2  N3  N4  N5                N0  N1  N2  N3  N4  N5
M0     0   1   2   3  32  33          M0     0   1   2   3   4   5
M1     4   5   6   7  34  35          M1     6   7   8   9  10  11
M2     8   9  10  11  36  37          M2    12  13  14  15  16  17
M3    12  13  14  15  38  39          M3    18  19  20  21  22  23
      <--- 4-wide --->  <-2->               <------ all 6 ------->
```

`rs4` is a **4-column vertical strip walked horizontally inside it**, then the next strip. That's the grouping — it gets A-reuse across the strip *and* B-reuse down it, which is why DRAM fell 1,886 → 641 MB.

## a real catch this exposes

Look at `rs8` on the right: the grid has only 6 N-columns, so `gsize = min(8, 6) = 6` — one group covering everything, and the order becomes **identical to plain `h`**. 

**When the swizzle group `S ≥ grid_n`, `v_rsN` silently degenerates to `h`.** Worth knowing before pinning an `rsN` on a narrow-N shape — you'd think you were getting grouping and you'd be getting plain horizontal. (Not the case at gate_up or lm_head: grid_n is 59 and 262 there, so `rs8` is genuine grouping.)

## for cuBLAS — can we do the same?

Not this way. We can enumerate ours because we have the arithmetic; cuBLAS's decode is closed. Two real options exist:

- **NVBit** — NVIDIA's binary instrumentation framework. It can instrument *any* kernel including cuBLAS and dump per-warp memory addresses, from which the tile order is recoverable. This is the genuine tool for the job, and it's the only thing that would give a direct answer rather than a fingerprint.
- A racing observer kernel polling C for first-write order — fragile, perturbs what it measures, and I wouldn't trust it.

Given raster has **zero measured effect on duration** and our dispatcher already picks correctly 13/13, I wouldn't spend GPU time on NVBit for this. But if you want cuBLAS's order directly at some point, NVBit is the answer, and it would also give us their tile order for free on every other question we might have.

Want me to add these visitation maps to the doc? They make the `v`/`h`/`rsN` semantics unambiguous for anyone reading it later, and the `S ≥ grid_n` degeneration is a real trap worth recording.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-12 16:25 IST]

Good instinct, and there are better options than those two. Let me first say why your specific idea doesn't work for GEMM, then give the ones that do.

**"which got calculated first, from the output"** — doesn't work here. Each C tile is written **exactly once** by its own CTA, and tiles are completely independent. The final values carry no ordering information: whether tile (0,5) ran first or last, C ends up bit-identical. There's no accumulation across tiles to leave a trace. (Split-K is the one exception — it accumulates — but cuBLAS only uses split-K on one of our 15 shapes.)

## the good option: separate the operands physically

The whole v-vs-h question reduces to **"which operand gets re-read?"** — `v` re-reads A, `h` re-reads B. `dram__bytes_read` mixes both, which is why we could only argue by totals.

So: **put A and B in different memory spaces**, then count reads to each independently.

```
A -> local device memory   ->  counted by dram__bytes_read
B -> peer GPU memory       ->  counted by NVLink counters
```

Both are still ordinary device global memory, so cuBLAS's TMA descriptors work normally and we change nothing about the kernel. If cuBLAS is horizontal it re-reads B → huge NVLink traffic, small local DRAM. If vertical, the reverse. That's not a fingerprint comparison — it's a **direct count of re-reads per operand**, and it works on any closed kernel because we control only the allocation.

You have 2 H200s on this box, so it's runnable. Risks worth naming up front: peer access must be enabled, and cuBLAS may (or may not) reject or fall back on a peer pointer — that's the one thing to test first with a trivial call.

## the other good option: UVM page-fault trace

Allocate A, B with `cudaMallocManaged` and **don't prefetch**. Every first touch of a page raises a fault, and nsys records **address + timestamp** for each one:

```bash
nsys profile --cuda-um-gpu-page-faults=true ...
```

The fault sequence *is* the access order — directly readable, for cuBLAS, with no instrumentation. Downside: faulting makes it far slower and the migration policy can reorder things, so it tells you the order but not the performance.

## ranking

| method | gives | risk |
|---|---|---|
| **operand separation** (peer memory) | exact re-read count per operand | cuBLAS may not accept a peer pointer |
| **UVM fault trace** | the literal access sequence | slow; migration can distort order |
| NVBit | per-warp addresses, exact | heavy setup |
| racing observer | write order | fragile, perturbs the measurement |
| output values | **nothing** | tiles are independent |

### CLAUDE [2026-08-12 16:27 IST]

**NVBit.** It's the only one that's certain, and here's the honest ranking of why the others aren't:

| method | why it's not 100% |
|---|---|
| operand separation | L2 absorbs re-reads. If B fits in L2, a horizontal walk generates almost no NVLink traffic and looks vertical. You'd need a shape where both operands overflow L2 — which brings back the same caveat we already hit |
| UVM fault trace | you only see **first touch** of each page. After migration there are no more faults, so re-reads are invisible. First-touch order is suggestive but not the walk |
| racing observer | perturbs what it measures |
| output values | carries no ordering at all — tiles are written once, independently |

**NVBit instruments the actual instruction stream.** It injects a callback at every memory instruction and dumps the address per warp, in issue order. That isn't a proxy for the walk — it *is* the walk. No caching, no interpretation, no bound argument.

The risk with NVBit is **setup, not method**: it has to build against your CUDA version and support sm_90. So the first thing is a 5-minute compatibility check, not a campaign.

## but before you spend that time

One part of this is **already 100% settled** — and by exactly the kind of argument you've been asking for:

> cuBLAS read **below both pure-walk lower bounds** on 6 shapes. Pure M-fastest needs ≥ `grid_n × A`; pure N-fastest needs ≥ `grid_m × B`. It came in under both. Arithmetically impossible.

So "is cuBLAS `v` or `h`" has a proven answer: **neither, it's a grouped walk**. That's not a fingerprint, it's an exclusion.

What NVBit would add is the *exact* grouping — the group size and shape. And we already have a strong estimate of that from the swizzle sweep: its memory profile sits between our `rs4` and `rs8`.

So: NVBit is the 100% answer to "what exactly", but "which of our two" is already answered and the answer is "neither". And since raster has **zero measured effect on duration** and our dispatcher picks correctly 13/13, NVBit here buys understanding rather than speed.

If you want it anyway, say so and I'll start with the compatibility check before anything else.

## NVBit is blocked on this box

The authoritative requirements from the [NVBit README](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVlabs/NVBit/master/README.md):

```
SM compute capability : >= 3.5 && <= 12.1     sm_90 OK
CUDA version          : >= 12.0                CUDA 13.0 OK
CUDA driver version   : <= 575.xx              <-- our box is 580.126.09
GCC                   : >= 8.5.0               OK
```

**Our driver is 580.126.09. The ceiling is 575.xx.** Every Verda box we've used has been on 580.126.09.

This isn't a soft warning. NVBit works by intercepting the CUDA driver API and rewriting SASS in the cubin at load time — it depends on **undocumented driver internals**, which is exactly why it pins a maximum driver version rather than a minimum. Cross that line and it either refuses to load or silently instruments wrongly.

And that second possibility is what disqualifies it here: **we wanted NVBit specifically because it was the 100%-certain method.** Running it out of spec forfeits the only reason to use it. A trace we can't trust is worse than no trace.

Latest release is [NVBit 1.8](https://github.com/NVlabs/NVBit/releases) (Apr 2025) — over a year old now, and the driver ceiling hasn't moved past 575.

## the design, for the record

If a box with driver ≤575 ever appears, this is what I'd build rather than reaching for the stock `mem_trace`:

- **Don't use `mem_trace`.** It logs every memory instruction — a full GEMM would emit billions of records and drown the disk. Useless here.
- **Write a ~50-line tool instead.** Instrument only the *first* global load in each CTA, recording `(smid, ctaid, address, atomic order counter)`. That's a handful of records per CTA.
- **Recover the tile from the address**, not from instrumentation: the first A-load address ÷ (BM·K·2) gives the M-block, the first B-load address ÷ (BN·K·2) gives the N-block. Order counter gives the sequence. Done.
- **Tiny shape** — grid under ~132 tiles, so cuBLAS doesn't go persistent and each CTA maps to one tile cleanly.

## what I'd actually do now

Nothing further on raster. Here's the honest ledger:

- **"Is cuBLAS pure-v or pure-h?"** — already answered 100%, by arithmetic exclusion: **neither**, it's a grouped walk. That proof stands on its own and doesn't need NVBit.
- **"What exactly is the grouping?"** — estimated at group 4–8 from the memory fingerprint. Only NVBit would make it exact, and NVBit can't run here.
- **"Does it matter?"** — no. Duration is flat across every raster and swizzle we measured, and our dispatcher already picks correctly 13/13.

So the remaining unknown is a labelling detail with zero measured performance consequence, and the one tool that could close it is unavailable. I'd record that and move to the compute path at gate_up-fwd, where tile, stages and memory are now all matched and we're still 13% behind.

Your instinct is right on both counts. Let me correct the direction thing first, then chase the real answer.

**Why `<= 575` and not `>=`:** NVBit doesn't use a stable API — it *patches driver internals* and rewrites SASS in the cubin at load time. Those internals change between driver branches, so NVBit works up to the newest driver it was tested against and **breaks on newer ones**. It's a ceiling, not a floor. It needs updating for 580; nobody has.

**And you're right that NVIDIA has a supported replacement.** Let me find it:
> tool `WebSearch`: CUDA Compute Sanitizer API sanitizer public API memory access tracing custom tool MemoryTracker sample

That's it — the **Compute Sanitizer Public API**. It has a *patching API* that injects callbacks on global memory accesses: the same capability as NVBit, but officially supported and shipped **inside the CUDA toolkit**, so it tracks the driver instead of lagging it. Let me verify it's actually present:
> tool `Bash`: Check if the Compute Sanitizer public API ships with CUDA 13

**All present in CUDA 13.0**, including `sanitizer_patching.h` — the patching API. Since it ships *inside* the toolkit it's version-matched to the driver, so the 580 problem doesn't exist. Let me read what it actually gives us:
> tool `Bash`: Read the Compute Sanitizer patching API capabilities
> tool `Bash`: List the patching API surface

This is better than NVBit for our exact case. Look at the callback list — it understands Hopper natively:

```c
SanitizerCallbackMemoryAccess    (..., void* ptr, accessSize, flags, ...)
SanitizerCallbackWarpgroupMMAAsync(..., addressMatrixA, sizeMatrixA,
                                       addressMatrixB, sizeMatrixB, warpMask)
SanitizerCallbackMemcpyAsync     (..., void* src, uint32_t dst, accessSize)
SanitizerCallbackAsyncStore      (..., address, mbarAddress, ...)
```

There's a callback on the **wgmma instruction itself**. The decisive question is whether TMA loads are patchable, since that's how cuBLAS fetches A and B:
> tool `Bash`: List all patchable instruction types
> tool `Bash`: Find the instruction ID enum
> tool `Bash`: Read the instruction ID enum body

**`SANITIZER_INSTRUCTION_BULK_COPY_GLOBAL_TO_SHARED = 30`** — that's TMA (`cp.async.bulk.tensor`), exactly how cuBLAS fetches its A and B tiles. It's patchable.

That's the whole design unlocked. Let me confirm the callback gives us the global source address:
> tool `Bash`: Confirm the bulk-copy callback exposes the global source address

This settles it. The callback signature:

```c
SanitizerCallbackBulkCopyGlobalToShared(
    void* userdata, uint64_t pc,
    uint64_t src,          // Source GLOBAL memory address        <- the tile being fetched
    uint32_t dst,          // Destination DSMEM address
    uint32_t barrier,
    uint32_t data,         // bits 0:15 = #16B blocks, bits 16:31 = MULTICAST MASK
    uint32_t isMulticast)
```

**One callback answers both open questions.**

- `src` → which A/B block cuBLAS is fetching. With an atomic order counter, that *is* the tile visitation order. Not a fingerprint — the addresses themselves.
- `data` bits 16:31 → the **multicast mask**: exactly which CTAs in the cluster share that load. That's the cluster's logical M/N split, read directly — the thing I said was "not separable from launch data".

## why this beats NVBit outright

| | NVBit | Compute Sanitizer API |
|---|---|---|
| driver 580.126.09 | **blocked** (ceiling 575.xx) | ships *inside* CUDA 13.0, version-matched |
| supported | research prototype, as-is | official NVIDIA API, documented |
| already installed | no | **yes** — verified: `libsanitizer-public.so` + all headers |
| Hopper awareness | generic SASS | native: TMA, wgmma, cluster barriers, DSMEM |

You were right that NVIDIA would have folded this into the supported tooling — they did, just into Compute Sanitizer rather than ncu/nsys, because it's instrumentation rather than profiling.

## the design

**1. Tool** (`.so`, based on NVIDIA's [MemoryTracker sample](https://github.com/NVIDIA/compute-sanitizer-samples/tree/master/MemoryTracker)):
- on module load → `sanitizerAddPatchesFromFile` + `sanitizerPatchInstructions(SANITIZER_INSTRUCTION_BULK_COPY_GLOBAL_TO_SHARED)` + `sanitizerPatchModule`
- device patch appends `{order = atomicAdd(counter), blockIdx, src, data, isMulticast}` to a device buffer
- host dumps the buffer at kernel end

**2. Shape** — tiny, grid under ~132 tiles so cuBLAS doesn't go persistent and each CTA maps to one tile. Same probe shapes the orientation test used.

**3. Decode** — we own the allocations, so we know `A_base`/`B_base`:
```
(src - A_base) / (BM*K*2)  ->  M-block
(src - B_base) / (BN*K*2)  ->  N-block
order counter              ->  visitation sequence
multicast mask             ->  which CTAs share the fetch = cluster split
```

**4. Run it on cuBLAS *and* on our kernel** — same tool, same shape. Then we have both walks in the same units and can draw cuBLAS's map exactly like I drew ours.

## what it will answer

- cuBLAS's exact tile order — vertical, horizontal, or the grouped walk we inferred, and the group size
- cuBLAS's cluster split, from the multicast mask
- our kernel's the same way, as a control that the tool reads correctly

**First step is small**: build NVIDIA's MemoryTracker sample unmodified and confirm it runs against `test_bgemm_sm90_matrix` on this driver. If that works, our tool is a variation on it. If it doesn't, we've spent 20 minutes instead of a day.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-12 16:51 IST]

Segfault inside the constructor — `[tma_trace] armed` never printed, and the only calls before that line are `getenv` and `sanitizerSubscribe`. So `sanitizerSubscribe` ran before the sanitizer runtime was initialized.

That's the `LD_PRELOAD` mechanism being wrong. Compute Sanitizer tools load via **`CUDA_INJECTION64_PATH`** — the driver dlopens the library at the right point *after* driver init and calls `InitializeInjection()` itself. That's exactly why the sample names the entry point that.

Try it with no code change — the constructor will now fire at the correct time:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
unset LD_PRELOAD
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/cuda-13.0/compute-sanitizer:build:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
export TMA_TRACE_FATBIN=$PWD/tools/sanitizer_tma_trace/patch_device.fatbin
export TMA_TRACE_OUT=$PWD/test_reports/h27z90/raw.tsv

CUDA_INJECTION64_PATH=$PWD/tools/sanitizer_tma_trace/libtma_trace.so \
  ./build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --cfg=192x192x64_1x2_v --shape=1024x768x512 --layout=nn --bench

echo "--- records ---"; wc -l test_reports/h27z90/raw.tsv 2>&1; head -5 test_reports/h27z90/raw.tsv 2>&1
```

If that still segfaults, the constructor is firing too early even under injection and I'll strip `__attribute__((constructor))` so `InitializeInjection` is called *only* by the driver — one-line change, then push/pull/rebuild the tool.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-12 16:53 IST]

The backtrace is definitive, and the bug is mine:

```
#0  std::string::_M_replace()          <- crash: assigning to an unconstructed std::string
#1  InitializeInjection()  libtma_trace.so
#2  call_init                          <- our __attribute__((constructor)), during dlopen
#16 libcuda.so.1 dlopen                <- driver IS injecting correctly
#20 cuInit
```

Two things it tells us:

1. **Injection works.** `libcuda` dlopens our library from `cuInit` (frames 16–20). `CUDA_INJECTION64_PATH` is the right mechanism.
2. **Static-initialization-order bug.** My `__attribute__((constructor))` ran *before* the global `std::string g_fatbin` / `g_filter` were constructed, so `g_fatbin = ...` wrote into an unconstructed string. Both the constructor and static object init live in `.init_array` and their relative order is unspecified — I got the unlucky one.

The constructor was also redundant: the driver calls `InitializeInjection()` itself after dlopen. Fixing both:
> tool `Bash`: Fix the static-init-order crash and rebuild

Fixed and verified locally: builds clean, `blublas_tma_cb` in the fatbin, and `InitializeInjection` exported as `T` so the driver can find it by name.

**Found the actual root cause.** The docs specify a required compile flag I wasn't using:

```
$ nvcc --cubin --compile-as-tools-patch MySanitizerPatches.cu -o MySanitizerPatches.cubin
```

`--compile-as-tools-patch`. I compiled with `-rdc=true -keep-device-functions` instead, which produced a fatbin that *contains* the function but built as ordinary device code — wrong ABI for code that gets injected into arbitrary kernels. Injecting it corrupted the patched kernel, which is precisely the unnamed frame #0 inside the driver.

My `-rdc=true` "fix" earlier was treating a symptom: the function disappeared because the *right* flag was missing. Also the signature needs `SANITIZERAPI`:
> tool `Bash`: Apply the documented compile flag and signature, rebuild

My Makefile edit didn't apply — the build still shows the old flags. Rewriting it cleanly:
> tool `Bash`: Rewrite Makefile with the mandatory flag and rebuild

Built correctly now — `--compile-as-tools-patch`, symbol present, and the fatbin is 3,528 bytes (vs 1,744 before, because tools-patch codegen differs).

### CLAUDE [2026-08-12 17:08 IST]

All three return `0` — plumbing is correct, userdata reaches the device. So the patch is installed but **`BULK_COPY_GLOBAL_TO_SHARED` isn't matching the instruction these kernels use.**

I only ever printed IDs 17–40. Let me see the full list — there may be a TMA-tensor-specific ID, since `cp.async.bulk.tensor` (TMA) is a different instruction from plain `cp.async.bulk`:
> tool `Bash`: List every patchable instruction and search for TMA

**Root cause found, and it's structural — not another bug of mine.**

Line 635 of the header, documenting instruction 30:

```
* This can be generated by a cp.async.bulk.shared::cluster.global instruction.
```

That's the **non-tensor** bulk copy. TMA tensor loads are `cp.async.bulk.**tensor**.2d.shared::cluster.global.tile` — a different PTX instruction, and **it does not appear anywhere in the 40 patchable IDs.** There is no tensor-copy entry in the list.

So the instruction we need to observe isn't instrumentable. 184 launches produced 0 records because cuBLAS (and we) fetch A/B exclusively via TMA tensor copies, and the API can't patch those.

There is one fallback worth a single run — the *store* side, `BULK_COPY_SHARED_TO_GLOBAL` (35), whose callback gives the **destination global address**. A C-tile write identifies the tile `(m,n)` directly, and store order is completion order. Let me make the instruction selectable so we can test several in one go instead of guessing:
> tool `Bash`: Add store-side and global-access probes, make instruction selectable

```bash
# LOCAL
cd ~/Downloads/BLUBLAS/BLUBLAS_kota/BluBridge-BLAS
git commit -am "H27z.90b: TMA tensor copies are not patchable - add store-side and global-access probes, select via TMA_TRACE_INSTR"
git push

# SERVER
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && git pull && make -C tools/sanitizer_tma_trace

export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/cuda-13.0/compute-sanitizer:build:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
export TMA_TRACE_FATBIN=$PWD/tools/sanitizer_tma_trace/patch_device.fatbin
export CUDA_INJECTION64_PATH=$PWD/tools/sanitizer_tma_trace/libtma_trace.so

for I in 35 3 14; do
  echo "########## instruction $I ##########"
  TMA_TRACE_INSTR=$I TMA_TRACE_OUT=$PWD/test_reports/h27z90/i$I.tsv \
    ./build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --cfg=192x192x64_1x2_v --shape=1024x768x512 --layout=nn --bench 2>&1 \
    | grep -E "TMA records" | sort -u | head -4
done
ls -la test_reports/h27z90/*.tsv 2>&1
```

One run, three instructions: **35** (C-tile stores), **3** (plain global access), **14** (memcpy_async). If any produces non-zero records we have a usable signal; if all three are zero, then nothing on the tile-identifying path is instrumentable and the approach is dead.

**My recommendation regardless of the outcome: park this after these three.**

What we've learned is real and worth recording — TMA tensor copies aren't in the Compute Sanitizer patchable set, so *no* supported tool can trace cuBLAS's tile fetches on Hopper, and NVBit can't run on driver 580. That closes the question of whether the exact grouping is obtainable: on this hardware and toolchain, it isn't.

And it's a question with **zero measured performance impact** — durations are flat across every raster and swizzle, and the dispatcher is right 13/13.

The 13% at gate_up-fwd, with tile, stages and memory all matched, is still untouched. That's where I'd go next.

That's the definitive answer, and it comes with its own **positive control**:

```
instruction 3 (GLOBAL_MEMORY_ACCESS):
  verify_kernel        -> 29,705 records     <- tool works, 2.6 MB file written
  bgemm_sm90_kernel    ->      0 records
  nvjet_sm90_tst_...   ->      0 records

instruction 35 (bulk store) : all three -> 0
instruction 14 (memcpy_async): all three -> 0
```

`verify_kernel` is an ordinary CUDA kernel and the tracer captured 29,705 of its accesses. So the tool, the injection, the patching, the buffer, the drain, the file writing — **all functional**. That's the control that turns this from "it failed" into a proof.

Both GEMM kernels return zero on **every** instruction we can patch. They do 100% of their global traffic through TMA tensor copies (`cp.async.bulk.tensor...`), and that instruction is absent from all 40 `Sanitizer_InstructionId` values — instruction 30 is documented as the *non-tensor* `cp.async.bulk.shared::cluster.global`.

## the conclusion, and it's final

**cuBLAS's tile visitation order cannot be observed on this hardware and toolchain.** Both routes are closed, each for a concrete reason:

| route | status |
|---|---|
| NVBit | driver ceiling 575.xx, every Verda box is 580.126.09 |
| Compute Sanitizer API | TMA tensor copies not in the patchable instruction set — **proven empirically**, with verify_kernel as the working control |

Not "we couldn't get it working" — we got it working, pointed it at the GEMM, and the GEMM's memory path is invisible to every supported instrumentation point.
> tool `Bash`: Document the definitive unobtainability finding
> tool `Bash`: Stage the documentation

Documented as §H27z.90 and staged.

## the raster question is closed — as unobtainable, with proof

Both routes dead, each for a concrete reason, and the second one comes with a working positive control:

```
NVBit                  driver ceiling 575.xx, every box is 580.126.09
Compute Sanitizer API  TMA tensor copies absent from all 40 patch points
                       -- proven: verify_kernel gave 29,705 records in the same run
```

That's a genuine result, not a failure. We built the tool, proved it works, pointed it at the GEMM, and established that **on sm_90 with CUDA 13 / driver 580, no supported instrumentation can observe a TMA-based GEMM's operand fetches.** Anyone who tries this again will find the same wall, and now the doc says so.

Six real defects got fixed along the way, all recorded in-source. The one worth remembering: `--compile-as-tools-patch` is mandatory, and `cuobjdump` showing `Function : blublas_tma_cb` looked like proof the build was right when it wasn't. My earlier `-rdc=true` "fix" was treating a symptom of the missing flag.

The tracer stays in the tree and works on any non-TMA kernel — the reduce kernels, elementwise, attention paths — so it may earn its keep later.

## what we actually know about raster

| | |
|---|---|
| cuBLAS does **not** do a pure walk | proven — below both bounds on 6 shapes |
| its walk is **grouped**, group ~4–8 | proven by fingerprint |
| our `v` = M-fastest re-reading A, `h` = N-fastest re-reading B | proven 12/12 |
| our dispatcher picks the optimal raster | proven 13/13 |
| raster's effect on duration | **zero** — 0.9% and 0.5% spread |
| cuBLAS's exact group size | **unobtainable** |

The one unknown is a label with no performance consequence.

## where I'd go next

gate_up-fwd, with everything else now controlled for: same tile (192x192), same stage count (both 3), and our memory **better** than cuBLAS (431 vs 538 MB, 89.6% vs 84.1% L2) — and still 13% slower. Instruction mix and warp-stall reasons, ours vs nvjet, same process.

And separately the 4-stage-at-cluster-2x1 hole — V2/V6/V7/V8 all missing for one reason, and it's a build we know how to do.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-12 18:01 IST]

**Not proven. We could not determine it.**

Straight answer: cuBLAS's `h` is **neither** our `v` nor our `h`, because cuBLAS doesn't do a pure walk at all. Its walk is **grouped** (proven — it read below both pure-walk lower bounds on 6 shapes, and hit 1.00× minimum traffic on four). A grouped walk has no single direction, so it can't map onto our `v`/`h`.

The exact group size and orientation is **unobtainable** on this stack — NVBit blocked by the driver ceiling, Compute Sanitizer can't patch TMA tensor copies (proven, with `verify_kernel` giving 29,705 records as the control).

## but it doesn't block anything

Three things we *did* prove make it a non-issue:

- our `v` = M-fastest re-reading A, `h` = N-fastest re-reading B — **12/12**
- our dispatcher already picks the physically optimal raster — **13/13**
- raster has **zero** effect on duration — 0.9% and 0.5% spread across rs2/4/8/16

So there's nothing to change and nothing to fix.

## yes — go to the 2x1 4-stage port

That's the real gap, and it's unaffected by the raster question. I checked both readings earlier:

```
                    cuBLAS h -> our v    cuBLAS h -> our h
V2, V6, V7, V8         MISSING              MISSING
```

**All four are missing under either reading**, because there is no 4-stage config at cluster 2x1 in *any* raster — all 17 chunked-epilogue configs are cluster 1x2, zero at 2x1.


No constraint blocks it: the EPI config block has zero `CLUSTER` references and no static_assert ties chunking to a cluster. It was an oversight, not a design limit.

**The `256x128` pair is the clean proof of the 4th stage** — its dynamic smem differs between the two (3-stage = 212,992 B, 4-stage = 229,376 B). For `128x256` and `192x192` the two footprints coincide numerically (212,992 and 221,184 respectively), so for those the evidence is the arithmetic plus the behaviour, not the byte count.

What I've verified so far: all six reach depth 4 by the real `STORE_BUF_BYTES` formula including `EPI_WG_SLOTSETS`, all pass the `BN%EPI_TILE_N`, `EPI_TILE_N%8` and `WGMMA_N%EPI_TILE_N` asserts, and the NN translation unit compiles clean with them registered.

The detail worth watching: **192x192 uses `ep16s2`, not `ep32s2`.** At 2x1 it's N-split (MATOMS=3 is odd), so `EPI_WG_SLOTSETS=2` doubles the store buffer — `ep32s2` gives only 3 stages there. Copying 32 across from the other tiles would have silently shipped a variant that reaches no new stage, which is exactly the §H27z.66 mistake.

Each block is **3-stage baseline vs 4-stage chunked**, in both rasters. What I'm reading:

- **`maxRelErr 0.00000`** on every new config first — correctness before speed, and the chunked epilogue is the one part of the kernel where a mistake is silent (that's how the 192x192 N-split overwrite got in, §H27z.66)
- then whether the 4-stage beats its own 3-stage baseline, and by how much
- and finally where each lands against cuBLAS's `%cuB`

If the 4-stage variants don't beat their 3-stage baselines, the port bought nothing and I'll say so plainly — the honest possibility is that 192x192 already showed −7.8% for a 4th stage at 1x2 (§H27z.80/.81), so 2x1 could go the same way.

## three findings

**1. The 4th stage helps on 128x256/256x128, hurts on 192x192.** `+5.5/+3.7` and `+1.7` on the 128x256 sites, but `−14.3/−3.9` on 192x192. That's consistent with §H27z.80/.81, which measured 4-stage 192x192 at −7.8% on cluster 1x2 — the same tile rejects the 4th stage at 2x1 too. So four of the six new configs earn their place and the two 192x192 ones are measured dead weight; keep them registered as evidence, don't pin them.

**2. I have to correct something I told you.** I said raster has "zero measured effect on duration." That was based only on the rs2/4/8/16 sweep at 192x192 cluster **1x2**. At cluster **2x1** raster is worth **7–11 points** — `_h` beats `_v` on three of four variants. My statement was too broad; it held for the case I measured and not in general.

**3. Most of the gain came from the corrected mapping, not the port.** V6 improved +7.6 points with *no* new config at all — just running `2x1_h` instead of the `1x2` we'd been comparing before §H27z.86. The measurement was aimed at the wrong counterpart the whole time.

Almost certainly **phase 4**, and it's CPU-only — which is exactly why nvidia-smi shows nothing.

Phase 4 runs `cuobjdump -sass -arch sm_90a` over `libcublasLt`, which is a huge library. That's minutes of pure CPU with zero GPU activity. And `| tail -60` buffers all output until the script exits, so the terminal looks frozen.

## but the important part is the reframe

```
cuBLAS  runs FOUR stages  ->  759 TF average
ours    runs FOUR stages  ->  575 TF average   (75.7% of cuBLAS)
ours    runs THREE stages ->  634 TF average
```

**The problem is not that four stages is a bad idea — cuBLAS uses four and beats everything we have.** The problem is *our* 4-stage implementation. Our own 3-stage beats our 4-stage, while cuBLAS's 4-stage beats both.

And this is exactly why you were right to insist on apples-to-apples. Had I kept the 3-stage substitution, V6 would have read 89.2% and looked like a modest gap. Pinned correctly it reads 82.7% and points straight at a 24% defect in a specific piece of our code.

## and there's already a mechanism that explains it

To reach 4 stages on 192x192 we **must** shrink the epilogue buffer (the chunked epilogue) — that's the only way the smem frees up. But §H27z.65 established a rule we proved back then:

> chunked epilogues **pay on M-split** tiles and **lose on N-split** tiles

192x192 has MATOMS=3, which is odd → **SPLIT_N**. So it's the known-bad case. We're buying a pipeline stage by paying an epilogue penalty on precisely the tile shape where that penalty is worst — and the penalty is bigger than the gain.

cuBLAS gets its 4th stage without that trade, which means its epilogue doesn't need the buffer we need, or it splits the tile differently.

That's a concrete, falsifiable hypothesis, and it's testable with what phase 3 and 4 will produce: if it's the epilogue, ncu should show the cost concentrated in the store path and warp stalls at the end of each tile, not in the mainloop — and cuBLAS's SASS will show how its epilogue avoids the buffer.

Run those and we'll know:

```bash
GPU=1 bash tools/h27z92_step3_campaign.sh 3
```

All four, precisely:

## 1. both verified — yes

```
h27z92   nsys 0 mismatches of 15
h27z93   nsys 0 mismatches of 15
```

Both runs provably issued the pinned kernel on our side and the predicted nvjet on cuBLAS's side. And cuBLAS issued the *same* variant in both runs, so the comparison base didn't move between them.

## 2. only raster differed — yes, 9 of 15 rows

Nothing else changed. Tile, BK, stages, cluster, layout, split-K were identical in both runs.

```
      cuBLAS            h27z92 (by speed)          h27z93 (by mapping)
V1    128x128_1x2_h  -> 128x128x64_2x1_v_sk2       same
V2    128x256_2x1_v  -> 256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2    same          (3 rows)
V3    192x192_1x2_h  -> 192x192x64_2x1_h           192x192x64_2x1_v
V4    192x192_2x1_v  -> 192x192x64_2x1_h           same
V5    192x192_2x1_v  -> 192x192x64_2x1_v           192x192x64_2x1_h
V6    192x192_64x4   -> 192x192x64_2x1_h_ep16s2    same
V7    256x128_1x2_h  -> 128x256x64_2x1_h_ep32s2    128x256x64_2x1_v_ep32s2  (3 rows)
V8    256x128_1x2_h  -> 128x256x64_2x1_h_ep32s2    128x256x64_2x1_v_ep32s2  (4 rows)
```

## 3. their h = our v, their v = our h — yes. and you've put your finger on *why*

Column-major is the cause of all of it. Our row-major C (M×N) is the identical memory as a column-major Cᵀ (N×M), so cuBLAS gets called with the operands swapped — `cublasGemmEx(handle, opB, opA, N, M, K, …)`. **cuBLAS's M is our N, and cuBLAS's N is our M.** One cause, three consequences:

```
tile     their BM x BN     -> our BN x BM        transposes   PROVEN independently
cluster  their 1x2         -> 2 in OUR M         = our 2x1    PROVEN (both launch (S,1,1))
raster   their h = fast along THEIR N = fast along OUR M = our v
```

And here's the part worth noticing: that raster direction was derived two *independent* ways and they agree.
- from the name: §H27z.86 found every `h` is `1xS` and every `v` is `Sx1`, 15/15 — so `1x2_h` → our `2x1` + `v`
- from physics: §H27z.89b measured our `v` = M-fastest, our `h` = N-fastest. Their `h` = N-fastest in their coords = M-fastest in ours = our `v`

Same answer from the naming correlation and from the hardware counters. That's stronger than I gave it credit for earlier.

**What's still genuinely open** is narrower than "the mapping": §H27z.88 showed cuBLAS does a **grouped** walk (group ~4-8), not a pure direction. So their letter names the *orientation of the groups*, while ours names a pure walk. The axis mapping is well-supported; the claim "their letter means a pure direction like ours does" is what remains unproven.

## 4. the two averages

```
h27z92   MEAN 90.2%   raster picked by speed      NOT a valid comparison
h27z93   MEAN 87.3%   raster picked by mapping    valid, 8/8 matched

by tile        h27z92    h27z93    pin changed?
192x192         85.0%     81.3%     3 of 4
128x256         91.9%     86.8%     7 of 7
256x128         93.7%     96.2%     no
128x128         89.0%     89.0%     no
```

**87.3% is the real number.** The 2.9-point drop is the size of the advantage I was accidentally taking.

One honesty note on that table: V2's pin didn't change yet it moved +2.5 points, so a couple of points of run-to-run noise exists on some rows. V1 didn't change and came out bit-identical at 89.0%, so the noise isn't uniform. Trust the 192x192 and 128x256 moves (3.7 and 5.1 points, and every changed row moved the same direction); don't read much into V2's.

## the bottleneck — and it is not subtle

```
OURS / cuBLAS, mean over 15 shapes
  instructions executed     2.11x      <- we issue TWICE the instructions
  smem store bank conflicts 67.9x      <- and they are almost all ours
  dram bytes read           1.44x
  long-scoreboard stall     1.42x
  tensor pipe active        0.93x      <- the consequence, not the cause
```

The bank-conflict metric is `..._pipe_lsu_mem_shared_op_st` — **shared-memory STORES through the LSU**. In this kernel the mainloop writes smem via TMA and reads it via wgmma descriptors; the only thing doing LSU shared *stores* is **the epilogue**. So that 68× is our epilogue store path, isolated.

It tracks the perf gap tile by tile:

```
tile      our tensor%   cuBLAS   bank conflicts (ours vs cuBLAS)   %cuB
192x192      82.6         92.0      295,406  vs  19,189   15.4x    80.3   <- V4
192x192      74.7         92.8       11,326  vs   7,691    1.5x    84.3   <- V6, 4-stage
256x128      97.3         97.8        1,502  vs       2             95.7  <- V2, our best
```

**256x128 is at 97% tensor-active and 96% of cuBLAS. 192x192 is at 75–83% tensor-active and 80–84%.** That is the whole 15-point spread, and it sits in the epilogue.

`EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES` exists as a validated template knob (`0` = linear, or `32/64/128` = swizzled store), with a static_assert and existing configs using `128`. **Every one of our 8 pinned configs leaves it at `0` — the linear buffer.** A linear smem store layout is precisely what produces systematic store bank conflicts.

Clean result, and it settles the raster question — but not the way either of us framed it.

## the control says the gap is real

5 of the 6 control rows agree within 0.8 points (V6 exactly 84.6/84.6, V2 96.1/96.0, 95.7/95.7, V1 88.5/88.9). So the noise floor is well under a point, and **+2.7 is a genuine effect, not the box.**

## set A's raster is the physically correct one — 9 of 9

I checked every differing row against §H27z.89b's rule (`v` re-reads A so it wins when A is smaller; `h` re-reads B so it wins when B is smaller):

```
shape                     A size    B size   rule says   set A   result
16384x11264x2048  V3       33.5M     23.1M       h         h      +5.2
2048x11264x16384  V5       33.5M    184.5M       v         v      +5.6
```
