
Set A picks the operand-reuse-optimal raster on **every** shape, and wins on every shape where the two sets differ. The one tie is K=512, where there are too few k-iterations for tile order to matter — which is itself consistent with the rule.

## so the mapping assumption was wrong, and you were right to reject set B

This is the honest conclusion: **§H27z.86's raster name-mapping (`cuBLAS 1x2_h → our v`) is contradicted by measurement.** Following it put us on the physically wrong walk on 8 of 9 shapes, costing 5–8 points each.

That was the one field I flagged yesterday as resting on an unverified assumption, and it has now failed its first real test. §H27z.88 had already shown cuBLAS uses a *grouped* walk, not a pure direction — so their letter was never the same kind of object as ours, and mapping it onto ours by name was the mistake.

**Set A is the correct apples-to-apples choice**, and not because it's faster. cuBLAS is clearly running an efficient walk on these shapes; the way to match that is to run the efficient walk too, not to copy a label we can't decode. Matching behaviour beats matching nomenclature when the nomenclature is provably not comparable. Our dispatcher already picks this raster 13/13 on its own.

So the selection now stands as: **all 8 variants matched on tile, cluster, stages, layout and split-K, with raster chosen by the verified physical rule.** No field is chosen for being fast, and no field rests on an unverified naming assumption anymore.

**Set A baseline on this box: 90.8%.** That's what we optimise against.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-13 11:07 IST]

Field by field, `256x128_64x4_1x2_h_bz_coopA` → `128x256x64_2x1_h_ep32s2`:

```
cuBLAS field    means                        ours              same?
256x128         tile M x N                   128x256           YES - transposes (their M = our N)
64              BK, the K-block per step     the 64 in ...x64  YES - same field, we put it 3rd
x4              pipeline stages = 4          not in the name   YES underneath, see below
1x2             cluster                      2x1               YES - identical hardware cluster
h               raster                       h                 same letter
bz              beta = 0 (C not read back)   we run beta=0     same
coopA           their cooperative variant    n/a               closed in H12.5, not an axis we have
                                             ep32s2            OUR field, no cuBLAS counterpart
```

**1. their MxN = our NxM** — yes. Column-major vs row-major, operand swap. Proven.

**2. the 64** — that's **BK**, the K-block: each pipeline step loads 64 elements along K. We do carry it, it's the third number: `128x256x64`. Same field, different position.

**3. the 4 (pipeline depth) is not in our name, but it IS 4 underneath.** We don't name it because we don't *choose* it — it falls out of the shared-memory budget:

```
STAGE_BYTES = (128+256) * 64 * 2                     = 49,152 B per stage
STORE_BUF   = 1 slotset * 2 slots * 128 * 32 * 2     = 16,384 B for the epilogue
depth       = (231,424 - 16,384) / 49,152 = 4.37     -> 4 stages
```

**5. `ep32s2` = EPI_TILE_N 32, EPI_STAGES 2** — the chunked epilogue. Instead of parking the whole 128×256 output tile in shared memory before storing it, we store it in **32-column chunks**, with **2 buffers** so one chunk's TMA store overlaps the next chunk's writes.

That's what makes the 4th stage possible: a full tile buffer would eat far more than 16 KB, and every byte it saves goes back to the mainloop pipeline. It's our own field — cuBLAS's name has no equivalent because they solve the same problem differently.

**CUTLASS** (which cuBLAS's nvjet kernels are built on) stages a *sub-tile* of the output, multi-buffered — never the whole tile. And its automatic rule for the cooperative schedule, which is what we run:

```
tile_n   = gcd(min(32, CTA_N), CTA_N)   ->  32
StagesD  = min(EpiTiles, 2)             ->  2
```

That is **literally `ep32s2`**. Tile-N 32, 2 stages. We didn't pick those numbers — they're what CUTLASS derives, and we arrived at the same ones.

**DeepGEMM** reaches the same structure by a different derivation, which is why §H27z.61 treated it as confirmed rather than a guess.

So: same design, same parameters, our own naming. Not different from cuBLAS.

**But there is one divergence, and it's exactly the bottleneck.** Look at how DeepGEMM sizes its store block:

```
STORE_BLOCK_N = kSwizzleCDMode / sizeof(cd_dtype_t);   // the SWIZZLE ATOM width
```

They tie the store-buffer width to a **swizzle** mode. CUTLASS swizzles that buffer too. **We set `EPI_TILE_N=32` with `EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES=0` — a plain linear buffer, no swizzle.**

That is the whole story of the 68× bank conflicts: we copied the *structure* (sub-tile, double-buffered) and got the 4th stage from it, but we left out the *swizzle* that makes the stores conflict-free. Every warp lands on the same banks.

Which is why H27z.94 is the right first experiment on V8 — it adds exactly that missing piece, and keeps the unswizzled twin alongside so the measurement isolates the swizzle rather than confounding it with the chunk width.

Yes — same cluster. Simply:

**1. The physical thing launched is identical.** Both sides launch a **one-dimensional group of 2 CTAs**, `(2,1,1)`. Read straight from the launch records, 15 of 15 kernels, no exceptions. cuBLAS never launches a 2-D cluster at all.

**2. `1x2` vs `2x1` is only a label**, and each side writes it in its own coordinates. Their M is our N — the same swap that flips the tile from `256x128` to `128x256`. So their "1x2" reads as our "2x1". One cause, both effects.

**3. Inside the cluster, the 2 CTAs share one operand — and it's the same operand.**

```
cuBLAS 1x2  = 2 CTAs along THEIR N  -> they share THEIR A
their A  =  our B          (operand swap)
our 2x1     = 2 CTAs along OUR M    -> we share OUR B
```

So both have 2 CTAs multicasting the same matrix. Same behaviour, different name.

**The one honest gap:** we can't *directly read* cuBLAS's internal choice — the launch record shows `(2,1,1)` for both `1x2` and `2x1` on their side, and ours does the same, so the record can't separate them for either of us. What makes it safe is that the answer falls out of the operand swap we already proved for the tile, rather than being a separate assumption.

That's different from the raster, which had no such derivation and turned out wrong yesterday. The cluster does have one, and it's consistent.

```

SW64   span 4  shift 1   ->  (row >> 1) & 3  vs  row % 4    DIFFERENT
SW32   span 2  shift 2   ->  (row >> 2) & 1  vs  row % 2    DIFFERENT
```

So the claim *"probe_tma_swizzle.cu measured the two agreeing on all 512 elements"* covers **SW128 only** — 512 = 8 rows × 64 elements, the SW128 geometry.

And the config census makes this sharper:

```
SW128   5 configs existed before      I added 0
SW64    1 config existed before       I added 5
SW32    0 configs existed before      I added 2   <- never used by anything, ever
```

**Every config I added uses the two modes where the kernel formula and the probe disagree, and SW32 has never been instantiated before.**

My reading is that the *kernel's* version is the correct one — CUTLASS's `Swizzle<B,4,3>` XORs the granule bits with offset bits starting at bit 7 regardless of B, and with a 64 B row the low row bit sits at bit 6, giving `(row >> 1) & 3`. The probe's `r % SPAN` is only equivalent when the row is a full 128 B. But I'm not going to assert that as settled from reasoning alone.

**What makes it safe to run anyway:** the harness validates numerically. `run_one` only emits a result on `PASS`:

```bash
| awk -v c="$1" '$1==c && $4=="PASS"{print $7, $8; exit}'
```

A wrong swizzle corrupts the output tile, the test compares against a reference, and the row prints **FAIL** — we cannot silently record a bad number as a good one. So the run settles the question rather than risking a false result.

What to watch for:

```
if swz64 / swz32 rows show PASS   -> formula is right, read the timings
if they show FAIL                 -> kernel formula is wrong for narrow modes,
                                     and we have found a real latent bug in a
                                     path that shipped with 1 config already using it
```

That second outcome would matter beyond this experiment — `192x192x64_1x2_v_swz64r64` already uses SW64 and appears in §H27z.82's measurements.

## the answers

**Is it XOR swizzling only?** Yes, and that's the only kind that exists here. Hopper TMA supports exactly `NONE / 32B / 64B / 128B`, all XOR-based. CUTLASS's `Swizzle<B,M,S>` is a single XOR (`offset ^ shiftr(offset & yyy_msk, S)`), DeepGEMM's is `col ^= row % span`. There is no alternative pattern to choose or compromise on.

**Is ours implemented correctly?** Yes — proven, not assumed. `epi_swz_index` reproduces `cute::Swizzle<B,4,3>` and DeepGEMM's `get_swizzled_bank_group_idx` exactly on every (row, granule) pair for all three modes.

**Why DeepGEMM's `row % span` looked different from ours:** their `row` is the flat **128-byte-line** index (`bank_group_idx / 8`, since `kNumBankGroups = 128/16 = 8`), not the matrix row. Matrix row `r` starts at line `r*span/8`, and:

```
r*span/8  ==  r >> (3 - log2(span))      verified for span 2,4,8 over 256 rows
```

That identity **is** the `shift` in our formula. Same swizzle, expressed in different coordinates.

**The structure matches too, field for field:**

```
DeepGEMM  SMEM_CD_SIZE = BLOCK_M * kSwizzleCDMode    ours  BM * EPI_TILE_N * 2
DeepGEMM  kSwizzleCDMode/sizeof(T) == BLOCK_N        ours  C_BOX_N * 2 == EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES
CUTLASS   EpilogueTileAuto -> tile_n 32, StagesD 2   ours  ep32s2
```

## the one real defect found

**`examples/probe_tma_swizzle.cu` is wrong for SW32 and SW64.** It applies `r % SPAN` to the matrix row instead of the line index, so it only happens to be right for SW128 where the two coincide. That's the tool that was supposed to validate this — it would have reported a false mismatch on exactly the modes my configs use. It's a test file, not shipped code, so it changes nothing about the kernel, but it should be fixed before anyone trusts it again.

I was wrong earlier to suggest running it and reading FAIL as the answer — that was me offering to compromise instead of doing the analysis. The analysis is done now, from both reference implementations, and the kernel is correct.

Nothing to change. Ready to run:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && GPU=0 bash tools/h27z94_swizzle_ab.sh 1
```

Careful here — **these two static counts are not comparable**, and I want to flag that before drawing a conclusion:

```
                          ours      cuBLAS
static instructions       2,104     27,416     cuBLAS has 13x MORE
static HGMMA (wgmma)          4        368     cuBLAS has 92x MORE
dynamic (ncu, K=2048)    59,002     33,673     but WE execute 1.75x more
```

cuBLAS's mainloop is **massively unrolled** — 368 static wgmma instructions. Ours has **4**, a tight rolled loop. So static counts measure unrolling, not work. The dynamic number is the real one, and it says we execute 1.75× as many instructions to do the same math.

Both facts point the same direction: **our per-iteration overhead is high and cuBLAS amortises it away.** And there's a second structural difference in the mix:

```

uniform datapath    17.2%     37.2%     they push 2x more onto the scalar path
int/logic (vector)  20.7%     11.0%     we do that work on the vector path instead
```

Hopper's uniform datapath runs **in parallel** with the vector datapath, so address and index arithmetic placed there is close to free. cuBLAS puts 37% of its instructions there; we put 17%.

One correction to something I showed earlier that could mislead you. I flagged "ours has 4 static wgmma, cuBLAS has 368" as if ours were suspiciously low. It isn't — **4 is exactly right**: `BK=64` and wgmma is `k16`, so one k-step is `64/16 = 4` wgmma instructions. Our mainloop issues one k-step per iteration and rolls the loop, which is correct structure, not a defect. cuBLAS's 368 means they unroll many k-steps into straight-line code.

So the static difference is unrolling depth, nothing more. That's why I'm not drawing anything from it, and why the dynamic `smsp__inst_executed` from phase 2 is the number that matters.

> tool `Bash`: Check whether the barrier ID is compile-time or runtime

**Mechanism found, and the arithmetic proves it.**

```cpp
const int g = wg_id;                                    // runtime value, 0 or 1
asm volatile("bar.sync %0, %1;" :: "r"(bar), "r"(n));   // barrier ID in a REGISTER
```

`bar.sync` with a **register** operand — ptxas cannot prove which barrier IDs the kernel touches, so it conservatively reserves **all 16**. cuBLAS uses compile-time immediates (`bar.sync 0`, `bar.sync 1`, …) and reserves exactly 3.

The occupancy numbers confirm it exactly. An SM has 64 barriers:

```
ours     64 / 16 = 4    -> occupancy_limit_barriers = 4    matches measured
cuBLAS   64 /  3 = 21   -> occupancy_limit_barriers = 21   matches measured
```

## two separate problems, don't conflate them

**A. Barrier *reservation* — 16 vs 3.** Caused by the runtime barrier ID. Costs occupancy headroom. **Not currently binding**: both sides are limited to 1 block/SM by registers and shared memory (`occupancy_limit_registers = 1`, `occupancy_limit_shared_mem = 1` for both), so this isn't losing us time today. It's still wrong and it's nearly free to fix — `g` is only ever 0 or 1, so a two-way branch on compile-time immediates drops it from 16 to 2.

**B. Barrier *stalling* — 45% vs 24–32%.** This is the one costing time. It comes from how *often* we sync, not how many IDs we reserve: 2 `barrier_sync` per epilogue chunk × 8 chunks = 16 sync operations per output tile.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-13 14:25 IST]

Directly related — barrier stall is a *candidate cause* and tensor% is the *symptom*. But let me check whether the numbers actually support that, because they only partly do:
> tool `Bash`: Test whether barrier stall explains the tensor deficit

Good question — and the answer **partly undercuts my own hypothesis**, so let me be straight about it.

```
shape          K  tensor gap  barrier gap    %cuB
K512         512      -17.3        +22.5   76.7%
K2048       2048       -8.0        +15.7   92.8%
K11264     11264       -1.7        +13.4   96.7%
K50304     50304       -0.4        +12.8  100.1%
```

**At K=50304 we have a +12.8 barrier gap and essentially no tensor deficit — and we beat cuBLAS, 100.1%.** So high barrier stall is demonstrably compatible with full tensor utilisation.

The reason both can be true: this is a warp-specialised kernel. While one warpgroup sits at a barrier, the other issues wgmma. The tensor pipe stays fed. `barrier stall = 45%` means warps spend 45% of active time waiting — it does *not* mean the tensor cores idle 45% of the time.

So the honest relationship is:

```
barrier stall     CONSTANT ~45% at every K
tensor deficit    COLLAPSES: -17.3 -> -8.0 -> -1.7 -> -0.4
```

A constant cause cannot produce a collapsing effect by itself. What's actually going on: **barriers are a fixed per-tile cost, and fixed per-tile costs are invisible when K is large and fatal when K is small.** At K=50304 the mainloop is long enough to hide them; at K=512 there are only 8 k-iterations and nothing to hide behind.

That's the same shape as the instruction ratio — dead constant at 1.75× across a 100× range of K, yet only hurting at small K.

## what this changes about the target

**Barriers are not "the bottleneck" globally.** They're one component of a fixed per-tile overhead that only bites where K is small. Concretely:

```
fixing barriers should help    K=512 (76.7%) and K=2048 (92.8%)
it should do nothing for       K=11264 (96.7%) and K=50304 (100.1%)
```

That's still worth doing — K=512 is our single worst shape in the entire 15, and it's 1 of V8's 4. If it went from 76.7% to ~90%, V8's mean moves from 91.6% to about 95%.

But it also means the ceiling on this fix is bounded, and I shouldn't have implied barriers explain V8 as a whole. The two large-K shapes are already at or above parity and have nothing to gain.

**The sharper question is now: what exactly is the fixed per-tile cost at K=512?** Barriers are part of it. The 1.75× instructions are part of it. Whether either is the dominant part is not yet established — and K=512 is the one shape where it's measurable, because it's the only one where the cost isn't hidden.

> tool `Bash`: Compare BAR instructions in both kernels

Found it in the SASS, and it's unambiguous:

```
OURS    18x   BAR.SYNC.DEFER_BLOCKING R3, 0x80      <- barrier ID in a REGISTER
         3x   BAR.SYNC.DEFER_BLOCKING 0x0           <- immediate (the __syncthreads)

cuBLAS  46x   BAR.SYNC 0x0, 0x80                    <- ALWAYS an immediate
```

`R3` is the runtime `g = wg_id`. ptxas can't prove which barrier IDs are reachable, so it reserves all 16. cuBLAS only ever names barrier 0, so it reserves 3. That's the whole mechanism, and the occupancy arithmetic confirms it: 64 barriers per SM, 64/16 = 4 (ours), 64/3 = 21 (cuBLAS) — both match the measured `occupancy_limit_barriers` exactly.

## but here is the part you need before we spend a run on it

**Two things in that same output argue the fix won't move performance.**

**1. Barriers are not the binding occupancy limit.** Both kernels report `occupancy_limit_registers = 1` and `occupancy_limit_shared_mem = 1` — registers and shared memory already pin us to 1 block per SM. Going from 4 to 32 on the barrier limit changes nothing while 1 is the floor set by something else.

**2. cuBLAS executes MORE barrier instructions than us, statically — 46 versus 21 — and stalls LESS at them** (24–32% vs our 45%). So the count isn't what costs us. **The cost is how long we wait**, not how many barriers we declare or how many `BAR.SYNC` we issue.

Those are two genuinely different problems that I've been treating as one:

```
A  barrier RESERVATION   16 vs 3     cause: register operand
                                     cost:  occupancy headroom, NOT binding today
                                     fix:   compile-time immediate, ~5 lines
                                     expected perf gain: probably zero

B  barrier WAITING       45% vs 24-32%   cause: not yet established
                                         cost:  real, but hidden at large K
                                         fix:   unknown until we know why we wait longer
```

Fixing A is cheap, correct, and removes a real divergence from cuBLAS — worth doing on principle. But I'd be misleading you if I said it should speed anything up, because the resource it frees isn't the one we're short of.

B is where the time actually goes, and I don't yet know its cause. Waiting longer at a barrier means the *other* participants arrive late — so the question is what our warps are doing between barriers that cuBLAS's aren't.

My suggestion: do A anyway since it's five lines and provably correct, but treat it as a correctness/parity fix with an honest prediction of ~0%. Then spend the real effort on B, where I'd start by measuring what happens *between* our barriers rather than at them.

**We have a ~15 microsecond fixed overhead that cuBLAS doesn't.** That single number predicts all four shapes:

That's the whole story of V8. Not a percentage gap — **a constant 15 µs**, paid regardless of K. When the kernel runs 55 µs it's 27% of the time; when it runs 4300 µs it's 0.3% and we reach parity.

So:

The pattern is unmistakable — **`MEMBAR.ALL.CTA` immediately followed by `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S`, eight times**, once per epilogue chunk, plus a `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + MEMBAR.ALL.GPU + ERRBAR` triple in the prologue. Let me see the wider context to pin the source:

```
OURS, per epilogue chunk:              cuBLAS, per epilogue chunk:
  STS  [R16+0x30030], R37                F2FP.BF16.F32.PACK_AB
  STS  [R16+0x30230], R39                STSM.16.MT88.4 [R23+UR32], R24
  NOP                                    STSM.16.MT88.4 [R152+UR32], R28
  BAR.SYNC.DEFER_BLOCKING R3, 0x80       FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S
  BSSY B0, 0x1f20                        WARPGROUP.ARRIVE
  MEMBAR.ALL.CTA
  FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S
```

**We use plain `STS`. cuBLAS uses `STSM` — stmatrix.**

That one difference causes everything else. `STSM.16.MT88.4` is **warp-collective**: one instruction moves an 8×8 tile for the whole warp, and its ordering is handled internally. Plain `STS` is per-thread scattered stores, so before the TMA engine can read that shared memory you must:

1. `BAR.SYNC` — rendezvous all 128 threads of the warpgroup
2. `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA` — a full CTA-scope memory barrier to order those stores
3. only then `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S`

cuBLAS needs **only step 3**. We pay all three, **eight times per output tile**, once per chunk.

That closes the loop on every measurement:

```
plain STS instead of stmatrix
  -> BAR.SYNC + MEMBAR.ALL.CTA per chunk, 8 chunks per tile
  -> membar stall 5.9% at K=512, 0.0% for cuBLAS
  -> tensor 57.9% vs 75.2%
  -> 76.8% of cuBLAS
  -> and it amortises away as K grows, which is exactly what we measured
```

It also explains the barrier stall (45% vs 24–32%) and part of the 1.75× instruction count — 128 `STS` where cuBLAS issues a handful of `STSM`.

The prior "stmatrix is worth 0%" result was measured on a *linear* buffer, where you still need the barriers. **swizzle + stmatrix together has never been tested**, and it's exactly what cuBLAS does.

So the answer to your question — yes, there is a real problem, and this is it: **our epilogue stores with plain STS and pays a CTA barrier plus a full memory barrier per chunk; cuBLAS stores with stmatrix and pays neither.**

**STS** — "store to shared": one thread writes its own registers into shared memory, each thread independently.

**STMATRIX** — "store matrix": all 32 threads of a warp cooperate in one instruction to write an 8×8 tile into shared memory.

**The difference that matters:** STS is per-thread, so nothing guarantees the *whole* tile has landed — you must add `BAR.SYNC` (rendezvous the warpgroup) and `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA` (order the writes) before the TMA engine may read it. STMATRIX is warp-collective, so when the instruction retires the tile is complete and ordered by construction — only the cheap `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S` is needed. Same data moved, but one form needs two heavy synchronisations per chunk and the other needs none.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-13 14:52 IST]

Good questions — the details matter here.

**Is it only 8×8?** The tile granularity is fixed at `m8n8` on Hopper — that's hardware, you can't choose another shape. But you pick how *many* tiles per instruction: `.x1`, `.x2`, or `.x4`. Ours is `.x4`, so one instruction writes **four** 8×8 tiles = 256 elements.

**Registers per thread — and no, one register does not hold one value.** A register is 32 bits and bf16 is 16 bits, so **each register holds two bf16 values**. The arithmetic works out exactly:

```
one 8x8 bf16 tile   = 64 elements x 16 bits = 1024 bits
32 threads in a warp = 1024 / 32 = 32 bits per thread = ONE register per thread

.x4 -> 4 tiles = 4 registers per thread
     = 32 threads x 4 regs x 2 bf16 = 256 elements    matches 4 x 64
```

That's why our instruction has exactly four register operands:

```
stmatrix.sync.aligned.m8n8.x4.shared.b16 [%0],{%1,%2,%3,%4};
```

**Why 8×8 specifically, and why it's mandatory** — this is the part that makes it fast. `wgmma` leaves its results scattered across the warp's registers in a *fixed* per-thread pattern, and that pattern is built around 8×8 blocks. `stmatrix` consumes exactly that layout natively. So the accumulator comes out of the tensor core already in the shape stmatrix wants — no address arithmetic, no shuffling.

With plain `STS` you have to compute where each individual element belongs yourself, which is why our epilogue carries 128 `STS` plus all the `IMAD`/`LEA` address math, where cuBLAS issues a handful of `STSM`.

It also explains the swizzle prerequisite from earlier: stmatrix's write pattern is fixed by hardware, so the shared-memory layout has to match it — you can't bend the instruction to a linear buffer, you bend the buffer to the instruction. That's why `EPI_USE_STSM` is gated on `EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES != 0`.

Deep analysis. Three findings, and the first one is that **I was wrong again** — let me be precise about how.

## 1. every stmatrix config FAILED — and the source already said it would

```
16384x2048x512    swz64r64stsm    FAIL
16384x2048x512    swz64stsm       FAIL
...all four shapes, both configs
```

Line 3934 of the template, which I did not read before proposing this:

> *"Converting to STSM is REAL outstanding work, not a micro-tweak: the wgmma-fragment → stmatrix register/address mapping must be derived and CuTe-verified, not guessed."*

The stmatrix code compiles and runs but the register→address mapping was never finished. That comment sits 48 lines from the `barrier_sync` call I *did* read. I should have found it.

## 2. the SASS disproves my mechanism outright

This is the part that matters more than the failure. Per kernel (`ep32s2` matched 2 kernels, so halved):

```
                MEMBAR.CTA  MEMBAR.GPU  FENCE.VIEW   STS   STSM  BAR.SYNC
ep32s2               10          2          9        128     0      21
swz64r64stsm         10          2          9          0    16      21
cuBLAS                0          0        184          0   yes       -
```

**stmatrix replaced all 128 `STS` with 16 `STSM` — and the MEMBARs and BAR.SYNCs did not move at all.** 10, 2, 21 in both.

So my claim that "stmatrix removes the BAR.SYNC and MEMBAR" was **false**. Those come from our source calling `barrier_sync()` and `tma_store_fence()` unconditionally in the epilogue loop — they don't care which store instruction precedes them. Even a *working* stmatrix would not have removed them.

cuBLAS lacks them because of how it **structures** the epilogue, not because it uses STSM.

## 3. nothing beat the baseline, and atom staging actively hurts

```
128x256x64_2x1_h_ep32s2      91.5%    <- unchanged pin, still best
128x256x64_2x1_h_swz64       90.1%
128x256x64_2x1_h_swz64r64    87.7%    <- -8.5% at K=512
```

`EPI_ROWS=64` costs 8.5% at K=512 and 5.0% at K=2048. Worth knowing — that's the form the one "proven" stmatrix config uses.

## what the run did establish, precisely

The counts localise the remaining difference to one instruction pair:

```
ours     9x  MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S   (paired, one per epilogue chunk)
         1x  MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + 2x MEMBAR.ALL.GPU    (prologue, cluster fence)
cuBLAS 184x  FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S                    with NO MEMBAR at all
```

Our `tma_store_fence()` is `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta`, and on this toolchain that compiles to **MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S** — the 9 pairs match the 9 chunks exactly. cuBLAS gets the view fence *without* the CTA memory barrier.

So the open question is now narrow and concrete: **why does cuBLAS's async-proxy fence not carry a CTA memory barrier, and can ours drop it safely?** That's a correctness question about fence scope, not a tuning question, and I'm not going to guess at it after being wrong twice.

## also, a tool defect

Phase 2 printed `nan` for every stmatrix row and then computed `LARGEST EXCESS STALL: lg_score +nan`. The FAILed kernels produced no ncu rows and my analyzer averaged empty lists instead of reporting "no data". It should refuse to print a verdict from nothing — I'll fix that before it misleads someone.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-13 15:12 IST]

Your understanding is right, with one correction that narrows it usefully.

**We do know what causes them** — it's our own code, not a mystery:

```
barrier_sync(g, THREADS_PER_WARPGROUP)   x2 per chunk  ->  BAR.SYNC
tma_store_fence()                        x1 per chunk  ->  MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S
```

What was wrong was my claim that switching `STS`→`STSM` would remove them. It doesn't — they're emitted unconditionally, regardless of the store instruction.

**The correction that matters: BAR.SYNC is not the problem.**

```
                  ours   cuBLAS
BAR.SYNC            21       46     <- cuBLAS has MORE than us
MEMBAR.ALL.CTA      10        0     <- this is the difference
MEMBAR.ALL.GPU       2        0     <- and this
FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S   9      184
```

cuBLAS barriers **twice as often as we do** and stalls less. So chasing barrier count was wrong too. The only thing they never emit is **MEMBAR** — and that's exactly the stall term (`membar`) that tracks our deficit and reads 0.0 for them on all four shapes.

So the target is one thing: **our `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta` compiles to `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S`; cuBLAS gets `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S` alone.**

And "remove them" isn't quite the goal — a memory fence is there for correctness. The real question is **which fence cuBLAS uses that achieves the same ordering without the CTA memory barrier.** Let me check the reference implementations rather than guess:
> tool `Bash`: Find which async-proxy fence variants CUTLASS uses

CUTLASS uses the **same** fence as us — `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta`. So the difference isn't the PTX instruction. Let me settle it definitively by compiling the fence in isolation:
> tool `Bash`: Compile each fence variant in isolation and compare SASS

**Definitive, and it closes the door on my last idea:**

```
fence.proxy.async.shared::cta   (with clobber)  ->  MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S
fence.proxy.async.shared::cta   (no clobber)    ->  MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S
fence.proxy.async               (generic)       ->  MEMBAR.ALL.GPU + FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S   <- worse
```

**Every writable form of the async-proxy fence emits a MEMBAR on this toolchain.** The `"memory"` clobber makes no difference, and the unscoped form is worse (GPU-scope rather than CTA-scope). CUTLASS uses the identical PTX we do.

So cuBLAS's 184 bare `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S` with **zero MEMBAR cannot be produced from PTX at all.** Their nvjet kernels aren't compiled from PTX the way ours are — NVIDIA emits SASS through their own path and can issue the view fence without the memory barrier. That's not a technique we can copy; it's an instruction we don't have access to.

## so where that leaves it

We can't make each fence cheaper. **We can only issue fewer of them.**

We currently emit one `MEMBAR + FENCE` pair **per epilogue chunk**, and V8 has 8 chunks (`BN=256 / EPI_TILE_N=32`). Widening the chunk halves that:

```
                     chunks   MEMBAR+FENCE   BAR.SYNC   STORE_BUF   stages
ep32s2 (current)         8          9            21      16,384        4
ep64s2                   4          ~5           ~11     32,768        4    <- still matches cuBLAS 64x4
```

`EPI_TILE_N=64` is legal here (`WGMMA_N=256`, and `256 % 64 == 0`), needs no swizzle, needs no stmatrix, and touches no unfinished code — it's a single template argument on the config we already ship.

That's the only remaining lever I can see on this axis, and it's a modest one: it halves a cost we've measured at 6.1% of warp-active time at K=512, so the ceiling is maybe 2–3 points on the worst shape and nothing on the two large-K shapes.

Two things I want to be straight about before you decide:

- **I've been wrong twice on V8** (swizzle, then stmatrix), and both times the mechanism sounded right and the measurement killed it. This one has a smaller claim — fewer fences, not a different fence — but the same caveat applies.
- **The membar correlation is still only correlation.** It's the one stall term that tracks the deficit, which is suggestive, but we have never removed membars and measured the result. `ep64s2` would be the first experiment that actually does that, which makes it worth running even if the gain is small — it either confirms or kills the membar theory outright.

**Now I can see it.** Our mainloop, 96 instructions for 4 wgmma — and here's the repeating unit, once per wgmma:

```
VIADD        R6, R8, 0x20                    compute smem offset
LOP3.LUT     R6, R6, 0x3fc20, RZ, 0xc0       mask it
SHF.R.U32.HI R6, RZ, 0x4, R6                 shift right 4
LOP3.LUT     R6, R6, 0x10000, RZ, 0xfc       OR in the layout bits
R2UR         UR16, R6                        move VECTOR -> UNIFORM register
UMOV         UR19, 0x40000040
IMAD.MOV.U32 R7, RZ, RZ, 0x40000040
R2UR         UR17, R7                        move VECTOR -> UNIFORM register
HGMMA.64     x256x16.F32.BF16 R24, gdesc[UR16], R24
```

**We rebuild the wgmma matrix descriptor from scratch for every single wgmma** — and we build it on the *vector* datapath, then `R2UR` it across to the *uniform* datapath because `gdesc[]` reads from uniform registers. The same work also appears duplicated on the uniform side (`UIADD3`/`ULOP3.LUT`/`USHF`/`ULEA`, 28 instructions).

Roughly **70 of the 96 mainloop instructions are descriptor arithmetic**. Only 4 are actual math.

Let me confirm what cuBLAS does instead:
> tool `Bash`: Analyze cuBLAS per-wgmma instruction sequence

**Found the root cause, with proof from the instruction sequence.**

## cuBLAS, per wgmma — TWO instructions

```
HGMMA.64  x128x16.F32.BF16 R24, gdesc[UR16], R24
UIADD3    UR16, UR16, 0x2, URZ        increment descriptor
UIADD3    UR18, UR18, 0x2, URZ        increment descriptor
HGMMA.64  x128x16.F32.BF16 R24, gdesc[UR16], R24
UIADD3    UR16, UR16, 0x2, URZ
UIADD3    UR18, UR18, 0x2, URZ
HGMMA.64  ...
```

**Median gap between consecutive wgmma: 2.** Both are `UIADD3` on the uniform datapath — they just *add a constant* to the descriptor register and issue the next wgmma. At the stage boundary they do `UIADD3 UR16, UR16, 0x200` then `UIADD3 UR16, UR16, -0x6` — still plain adds, compensating for the wrap.

## ours, per wgmma — about TWENTY

```
VIADD        R6, R8, 0x20              recompute the smem offset
LOP3.LUT     R6, R6, 0x3fc20, RZ       mask
SHF.R.U32.HI R6, RZ, 0x4, R6           shift
LOP3.LUT     R6, R6, 0x10000, RZ       OR the layout bits back in
R2UR         UR16, R6                  cross VECTOR -> UNIFORM
UMOV         UR19, 0x40000040
IMAD.MOV.U32 R7, RZ, RZ, 0x40000040
R2UR         UR17, R7                  cross VECTOR -> UNIFORM
HGMMA.64     x256x16.F32.BF16 R24, gdesc[UR16], R24
   ...plus the duplicated uniform-path chain: UIADD3 / ULOP3.LUT / USHF / ULEA
```

**We rebuild the descriptor from scratch every single time**, on the vector datapath, then `R2UR` it across to the uniform datapath because `gdesc[]` reads from uniform registers. cuBLAS never leaves the uniform datapath.

```
per k-step      wgmma   overhead instrs   total
ours              4          ~92            96
cuBLAS            8           ~16            24
```

That is the **1.75× instruction count**, and it's in the **mainloop** — not the epilogue. Which is why all three of my epilogue hypotheses failed: I was looking in the wrong place entirely.

It also explains the `R2UR` count (8 per k-step) and the uniform-datapath share gap (ours 17.1% vs cuBLAS 37.2%) — cuBLAS keeps descriptors on the scalar path where the work is free; we compute on the vector path and pay to move it across.

## why this is consistent with the deficit collapsing at large K

A mainloop cost should scale *with* K, which looks like it contradicts the fixed-15 µs picture. It doesn't:

```
K=50304   tensor% 99.2   the tensor pipe is SATURATED -> extra instructions issue in its shadow, free
K=512     tensor% 57.9   the pipe is NOT saturated    -> instruction issue becomes the limit
```

The overhead is always there; it only *costs* when the tensor pipe has slack. That's exactly the measured pattern, and it also explains our flat 11.3% issue rate against cuBLAS's 22–28%.

## the fix, and why it's real this time

The wgmma descriptor is an smem address plus layout bits. Across consecutive k-steps the address advances by a **constant**, so the descriptor should be a live variable that gets `+= const` — which is literally what cuBLAS's `UIADD3 UR16, UR16, 0x2` is. Ours gets recomputed because the C++ derives it from the stage base each iteration and the compiler can't prove the delta is constant through the `stage % DEPTH` wrap.

Unlike the last three, this is not a counter correlation — it's the actual instruction stream, side by side, doing demonstrably different amounts of work for the same wgmma.

**The `& 0x3FFFF` mask is what defeats strength reduction.** In general `((a+d) & M) >> 4 ≠ ((a & M) >> 4) + (d >> 4)`, because the mask can wrap — so the compiler must recompute from scratch every time. It cannot know that shared-memory addresses never reach 0x40000.

## the change that follows, and why it's independent of the datapath question

`ks` is `#pragma unroll` and `AW_A`/`BM` are constexpr, so `koffA` is a **compile-time constant**. The descriptor difference between consecutive k-steps is therefore also a compile-time constant, and the addition is exact:

```
desc(A_smem + off) == desc(A_smem) + (off >> 4)
   valid because smem_base is __align__(1024), all offsets are 16-byte aligned,
   and addr < 0x40000 always (227 KB max smem), so the address field cannot carry into bit 16
```

So: build the descriptor **once per stage**, then `a_desc += DELTA` per k-step — literally cuBLAS's `UIADD3 UR16, UR16, 0x2`. That collapses ~20 instructions per wgmma to ~1, regardless of which datapath the base ends up on.

**Why our chain sits on the vector path.** The `R2UR` proves nvcc knows the value is warp-uniform — it just built it in vector registers first. Whether that's driven by `__cvta_generic_to_shared`, by register pressure, or by the `atom_row0` term, a toy kernel won't tell us, because the toy has none of the real kernel's pressure.

**The honest way to settle it is the change itself**: hoist the descriptor, then read the resulting SASS. If the increment lands in `UIADD3` on uniform registers, the question answered itself. If it lands in `VIADD` + `R2UR`, we've learned the datapath is a separate problem and we'll see exactly what it costs.

## and this is why the hoist is worth doing regardless

The two issues are **independent**:

```
issue A  we do the work 4x per k-step instead of 1x    <- the hoist fixes this
issue B  the work lands on the vector path             <- the hoist does not fix this
```

Even if B stays broken, A alone takes ~20 instructions per wgmma down toward ~1–2. If B also resolves, we match cuBLAS's `UIADD3`. The hoist removes work rather than relocating it, so it can't be made worthless by B.

## one vertical I have NOT explored, and should name

**Unrolling depth.** cuBLAS unrolls to 368 static wgmma; we have 4 (one k-step, rolled). Heavy unrolling is *how* they can keep a descriptor live in a register across many steps — the loop-carried dependency disappears. Our rolled loop forces the descriptor to be reconstructed at each iteration boundary.

So unrolling and the descriptor hoist may be **the same problem seen from two sides**, and the hoist may partly be the compiler's substitute for unrolling. That's worth knowing before we conclude anything from the result.

Everything else I can enumerate is closed: tile, cluster, stages, layout, split-K all match; bank conflicts, stmatrix and membar count are dead by manipulation; raster is settled by the operand-size rule; the ~15 µs fixed cost is characterised; wgmma width (ours n256 vs their n128) favours us, not them.

**My recommendation: implement the hoist, then read the SASS.** It's the only remaining lever that removes work, and its output answers the datapath and unrolling questions at the same time. Say go and I'll write it — carefully, since unlike the last three this touches the hot loop.

You're right, and that's the better order. The **diagnosis** is already done from SASS. What I haven't done is read cuBLAS's descriptor *lifecycle* — where `UR16` is born, how it's incremented, how it wraps. That tells me exactly what to write instead of guessing. Let me trace it:
> tool `Bash`: Trace the full lifecycle of cuBLAS's descriptor register

**Complete scheme, reverse-engineered.** Here's cuBLAS's descriptor lifecycle decoded:

```
PROLOGUE (once)
  UMOV    UR16, 0x2000040     addr field = 0x40, LBO field = 0x200 -- packed constant
  UIADD3  UR16, UR16, 0x400   add the base address (already >>4 encoded)

MAINLOOP (per k16 step)
  HGMMA ; UIADD3 UR16, UR16, 0x2      <- +2 units = +32 bytes = exactly one k16 step
  HGMMA ; UIADD3 UR16, UR16, 0x2
  HGMMA ; UIADD3 UR16, UR16, 0x2
  HGMMA ; UIADD3 UR16, UR16, 0x200    <- group boundary
          UIADD3 UR16, UR16, -0x6        compensate
  ...
          UIADD3 UR16, UR16, -0x200      come back
LOOP BACK
  UIADD3  UR16, UR16, -0x2406         one reset for the whole cycle
```

They pack **address + LBO into the low 32 bits (UR16)** and SBO + layout type into the high word, then only ever touch UR16. Every increment is a plain add to the address field — no mask, no shift, no rebuild, never leaves the uniform datapath.

**And our delta is identical to theirs.** For our geometry (`BK=64`, `SW128`, `AW_A=64`):

```
ks:        0    1    2    3
koffA:     0   16   32   48   elements
bytes:     0   32   64   96
encoded:   0    2    4    6   ->  delta = +2 per k-step, exactly cuBLAS's UIADD3 0x2
```

So this isn't a guess about what to write — it's a scheme read off their instruction stream, and our constants land on the same values.

To answer your question directly: **the SASS gave us the diagnosis and now the design.** What SASS *can't* tell us is whether nvcc will emit the increment we intend from the C++ we write — that depends on our whole kernel's register pressure, which only compiling shows. So the test isn't to discover the mechanism; it's to confirm the compiler cooperated. And phase 3 checks that directly by counting instructions per wgmma in the new SASS — if it's still ~20, the compiler ignored us and we'll see it immediately without needing the GPU.

## what's left, and one candidate we have never touched

The cost lives in **per-tile work**. Of that:


The last one fits the shape of the finding and nothing has probed it. Between consecutive tiles our pipeline has to **drain and refill** — 4 stages of TMA loads with no wgmma to overlap them. At K=2048 a tile is 32 k-iterations, so a 4-stage drain/refill is ~12% of the tile, paid *every* tile. cuBLAS's persistent scheduler may begin the next tile's loads while the current tile's epilogue is still running, so the drain never appears.

That is consistent with everything we've measured and with nothing we've tried:
- it's per-tile ✓ (just proven)
- it's invisible at large K ✓ (drain amortises over more k-iterations — matches the K=512→50304 collapse)
- it wouldn't be touched by conflicts, membars, or instruction count ✓ (all four dead)
- it explains why our issue rate is pinned at 11.3% regardless of what we remove ✓

That matters because the cluster is size 2, and cuBLAS's `gridDim.x = 2` **is** the cluster dimension — each cluster occupies one x-slice, with 66 clusters laid out along y. Ours flattens all 132 into x. The hardware assigns CTAs to SMs from grid coordinates, so those two produce **different CTA→SM mappings and different cluster placement**, even with identical CTA counts.

Let me verify the cluster dims and see how our tile mapping uses blockIdx:
> tool `Bash`: Compare grid and cluster geometry across all four shapes

```

cluster_dim    2x1      2x1        <- also identical
```

Both get 66 clusters of 2 CTAs. But **cuBLAS's `gridDim.x` equals `clusterDim.x` exactly**, so a cluster is one x-pair and the cluster index *is* `blockIdx.y` — free. Ours packs 66 clusters along x, so cluster index and rank must be **derived by division from `blockIdx.x`**.

```
ours            128    64    128    128    256
cuBLAS            3     0      0      0      0
```

**cuBLAS's epilogue contains no stores, no conversions, and no float math at all.** Ours contains all of it — 128 `STS`, 128 fp32→bf16 converts, 384 float ops for alpha/beta, 64 `LDG` reading C.

Their epilogue work isn't *cheaper* — **it isn't in the epilogue.** Their `F2FP`/`STSM` sit inside the mainloop region (which is why theirs is 680 instructions for 16 wgmma while ours is 96 for 4). cuBLAS **fuses the epilogue into the mainloop**, converting and storing each accumulator chunk as it completes, overlapped with the wgmma still running. We compute the whole tile, then stop, then run 1817 instructions of epilogue with nothing to hide behind.

That closes the loop on everything:

- **it's per-tile** ✓ the epilogue runs once per tile
- **the mainloop rates match to 0.4%** ✓ the math is the same; only where the store lives differs
- **it's ~15 µs / ~3400 cycles per tile** ✓ 1817 instructions with stalls lands in that range
- **and it explains all five dead hypotheses** — swizzle, membar count, stmatrix, instruction count and grid shape were all attempts to make a *serialised* epilogue cheaper. None of them attacked the serialisation itself.

It also explains the stall signature we could never account for: our warps show 47% barrier stall and 0% `mio_throttle` because during the epilogue they're synchronising instead of issuing memory work, while cuBLAS is `mio_throttle`d 14% because its memory pipes stay saturated throughout.

I want to be careful about one thing before calling this proven: this is a **static** region split, and "which side of the backward branch an instruction sits on" is not the same as "when it executes". You're right. Let me stop hypothesising and just read both store phases instruction by instruction, and account for every one.
> tool `Bash`: Dump both store phases instruction by instruction

Now I can see it, and it's concrete. Side by side:

**cuBLAS — a tight, regular pipeline, repeated:**
```
8x  F2FP.BF16.F32.PACK_AB          convert
2x  STSM.16.MT88.4                 store via stmatrix
    FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S
    WARPGROUP.ARRIVE / WAIT
@UP3 UTMASTG.3D                    TMA store to global
    UTMACMDFLUSH
    WARPGROUP.ARRIVE / WAIT
    UIADD3 UR32, UR32, 0x1000      one address update, uniform datapath
```

**No alpha. No beta. No bounds checks. No global address arithmetic.** The TMA descriptor handles addressing and out-of-bounds in hardware.

**Ours — a fast path, then a large second path:**
```
0x1620  8x F2FP + 8x STS                          the fast path, 16 instructions
0x1720  BRA 0x1dc0                                unconditional jump over what follows
0x1730  ISETP.GE.AND / ISETP.GE.OR  ...           per-element BOUNDS CHECKS
        @!P4 LDG.E.CONSTANT                       C read-back
        FMUL.FTZ x6                               alpha
        @!P4 PRMT / IMAD.U32 / FFMA.FTZ           beta
        IMAD.WIDE / LEA / LEA.HI.X                64-bit GLOBAL address computation
```

Two real differences, and they're different in kind:

**1. `8x STS` vs `2x STSM` per group — 4× more store instructions.** That's the stmatrix gap, and it's blocked by the unfinished fragment→stmatrix mapping, not by anything conceptual.

**2. A large secondary path** doing bounds checks, C read-back, alpha/beta, and 64-bit global addressing — none of which cuBLAS has, because their `_bz_` kernel is specialised and their TMA descriptor absorbs bounds and addressing.

## the thing I need to settle before saying anything more

That `BRA 0x1720` is **unconditional** — it jumps over the second path entirely. So that whole region may be **static bloat that never executes** at beta=0, in which case it costs us nothing at runtime and you're right that beta can't explain the overhead.

Or it's reached from a different branch and does execute.

**That's a dynamic question, and static SASS cannot answer it** — which is exactly the trap I keep falling into. But it's answerable: `smsp__inst_executed` already tells us how many instructions actually ran, and I can compute what the fast path alone *should* cost. If the measured count matches the fast path, the second path is dead code and we chase `STS`→`STSM`. If it's much higher, the second path executes and beta/bounds specialisation is the target.

That's arithmetic on data already on disk. Let me do that before proposing any test.

## so the bottleneck, stated precisely

**It is not instruction count anywhere.** In the mainloop we execute 1.71× and pay nothing, because the instructions hide behind wgmma. In the epilogue we execute 1.81× and pay 21×, because there is nothing to hide behind and the warps block.

The bottleneck is **the epilogue's stall behaviour** — our warps spend 3.38 cycles per instruction waiting, where cuBLAS's spend 0.29. That's consistent with the ncu stall profile all along (barrier 45–48%, membar 2–6%, `mio_throttle` 0.0% while cuBLAS is throttled 14%), and consistent with the epilogue being per-tile.

And it explains why "fewer syncs" failed: ep64s2 reduced the *number* of barriers but doubled the store buffer, cutting the overlap depth from 7 to 3 — it made each remaining sync block *longer*. The count was never the issue; **how long each one blocks is.**

That's the target: not fewer instructions, not fewer barriers — **overlap depth in the epilogue**, so the waits are already satisfied when reached. `EPI_STAGES` is currently 2. That's the one epilogue parameter we have never varied, and it's the one that directly controls how long a wait blocks.

```
230 rows in CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_KERNEL   = one row PER KERNEL LAUNCH
columns: start, end, gridX/Y/Z, blockX, registersPerThread, names
```

nsys is a **system tracer at kernel granularity** — it tells you *this kernel ran from t1 to t2*, not what executed inside it. There is no instruction order, no waiting time per instruction, no cycle-level detail. That data simply isn't collected.

Now the distribution is **mixed, not 100% epilogue** — and one instruction dominates:

```
0x64c0    7,914 samples   22.4%   EPILOGUE    <- single hottest
0x0d30    3,550           10.0%   MAINLOOP
0x1090    2,946            8.3%   MAINLOOP
0x0660    2,152            6.1%   PROLOGUE
0x6460    1,123            3.2%   EPILOGUE
0x06c0      776            2.2%   PROLOGUE
```

**One address holds 22.4% of every stall sample in the kernel.** Let me see what it is:
> tool `Bash`: Identify the hottest sampled instructions in the SASS

**FOUND IT.** The hottest instructions are all the **cluster barrier**:

```
0x64c0   22.4%   UCGABAR_WAIT       preceded by MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + MEMBAR.ALL.GPU + ERRBAR + CGAERRBAR
0x0660    6.1%   ERRBAR             same sequence
0x6460    3.2%   ERRBAR             same sequence
0x06c0    2.2%   UCGABAR_WAIT       same sequence
                 -------
                 33.9% of every stall sample in the kernel
```

That sequence is exactly our prologue code:

```cpp
if constexpr (CLUSTER_SIZE > 1) {
    fence_mbarrier_init_release_cluster();   // MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + MEMBAR.ALL.GPU
    cluster_arrive_relaxed();                 // UCGABAR_ARV
    cluster_wait();                           // UCGABAR_WAIT   <- 22.4% of all samples
}
```

And **cuBLAS emits zero `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA` and zero `MEMBAR.ALL.GPU`** — they don't do this at all.

Critically, it appears **twice**: once at `0x660` (before the mainloop) and again at `0x6440` (after it). Let me confirm whether the second one is inside the per-tile loop, because that would reconcile it with the per-tile finding:
> tool `Bash`: Find all cluster barrier call sites and the tile loop

**Confirmed — and this is the finding.**

```
3515-3517   prologue        once per CTA
3641        for (task_id...)   <- the PERSISTENT TILE LOOP (producer)
3662          cluster_sync()      <- INSIDE IT, once per tile
3881        for (task_id...)   <- the PERSISTENT TILE LOOP (consumer)
3890          cluster_sync()      <- INSIDE IT, once per tile
```

**We do a full cluster barrier on every tile, in both warpgroups.** That's `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + MEMBAR.ALL.GPU + ERRBAR + CGAERRBAR + UCGABAR_ARV + UCGABAR_WAIT` — a device-scope fence and a cross-CTA rendezvous — **per output tile**.

Everything now reconciles:

```
per tile                       YES -- it is inside the tile loop        matches the 8x tile sweep
~15 us / ~15 ns per tile       a cross-CTA barrier costs that order     matches both fits
mainloop unaffected            it sits outside the k-loop               matches the 0.4% slope match
cuBLAS has ZERO MEMBAR         they never do this                       matches the SASS census
34% of all stall samples       measured, not inferred                   the hardware chose it
warps blocked, pipes idle      explains barrier 47%, mio_throttle 0.0%
```

And it explains all six dead hypotheses in one line each: swizzle, stmatrix, membar count, instruction count, grid shape and epilogue fusion **all left `cluster_sync()` untouched**. I was optimising around a per-tile cross-CTA rendezvous the whole time.

It also explains why `ep64s2` made things *worse* rather than neutral — fewer chunks didn't remove the per-tile cluster barrier, but the bigger buffer cut the overlap that was partially hiding it.

**Don't run the `EPI_STAGES` sweep.** It tests overlap depth inside the epilogue, which isn't the cost.

The real question is now specific and answerable from the source: **why does each tile need a cluster-wide barrier at all?** The prologue one at 3515 is genuinely required — it protects mbarrier init against a peer CTA's remote arrive. The two inside the tile loop are a different matter, and they're what to examine.

Let me read what those two guard before proposing anything — that's a correctness question about the multicast pipeline, and getting it wrong would produce silent races rather than a slow kernel.

## the bottleneck

**A full cluster barrier on every output tile**, in both warpgroups:

```
MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + MEMBAR.ALL.GPU + ERRBAR + CGAERRBAR + UCGABAR_ARV + UCGABAR_WAIT
```

A device-scope fence plus a cross-CTA rendezvous, per tile. PC sampling puts **33.9% of all stall samples** on those four addresses, `UCGABAR_WAIT` alone at 22.4%. cuBLAS emits **zero** `MEMBAR` of either kind.

Everything reconciles: it's inside the tile loop (per-tile ✓), outside the k-loop (mainloop slope matches to 0.4% ✓), and it's a cross-CTA wait (explains barrier 47%, `mio_throttle` 0.0% ✓).

## but it is not an oversight — it is a correctness workaround

```
§H14.6  introduced it as the PROVEN root-cause fix for the NN A-multicast crash
§H14.7  removed it, claiming partitioned multicast is race-free by construction
§H27z.5 RESTORED it -- the claim addressed data symmetry, not the timing drift actually measured;
        an Xid 13 "CTA Not Present" persists and vanishes under compute-sanitizer
```

The race was never root-caused. Removing this blindly reintroduces a crash.

## and here is the specific opening

```
the documented crash    NN layout, A-multicast
V8                      nt layout, cluster 2x1 = B-multicast
```

**V8 is not the configuration the barrier was added for.** The workaround is applied universally; the race is documented for a different layout and a different multicast operand.

It's also already A/B-able — `-DBLUBLAS_SM90_PER_TILE_CLUSTER_SYNC=0`, both sites gated together (they must match or the cluster deadlocks).

## what I'd run, and the caveat that matters


**A single passing run proves nothing here.** The documented signature is a timing race that needs large-K *and* persistent together and disappears under instrumentation. So the measurement is only meaningful alongside the full correctness suite run repeatedly — and even then, "it passed" is weaker evidence than usual.

> tool `Bash`: Make EXTRA reach the library compile rule

Staged. Note `h27za3` (the EPI_STAGES sweep) isn't in this commit — that hypothesis is superseded, no point running it.

**1. PUSH — local**

```bash
cd ~/Downloads/BLUBLAS/BLUBLAS_kota/BluBridge-BLAS
git commit -m "H27za4: measure the per-tile cluster barrier - PC sampling puts 33.9% of all stall samples on UCGABAR_WAIT/ERRBAR inside the tile loop; also fix the Makefile so EXTRA reaches the library, without which the A/B would have compared a binary against itself"
git push
```

**2. BUILD — server, two builds, cpu only, slow**

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && git pull
bash tools/h27za4_v8_clustersync.sh build
```

That builds twice and then **verifies the two libraries actually differ** by counting `UCGABAR_WAIT` in each. If those counts match, the flag never reached the kernels and everything after is meaningless — check that line before continuing.

**3. RUN — server, GPU**

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && GPU=0 bash tools/h27za4_v8_clustersync.sh run
```

## how to read it

**Phase 1** gives the cost. If the barrier is the 15 µs, K=64 should move a lot (it's 39% of that kernel) and K=50304 should barely move.

**Phase 2 is the part that decides anything**, and I want to be blunt about it: this barrier exists because of an Xid 13 crash that was never root-caused, whose signature needs large-K *and* persistent together and which **disappears under instrumentation**. So:

- the correctness runs are deliberately on the **large-K** shape, **repeated**, and **un-instrumented**
- **"it passed" is weak evidence.** A timing race that only appears under specific conditions can pass five runs and fail the sixth
- a **failure** is strong evidence — it would prove the barrier is load-bearing for V8 too

The realistic good outcome isn't "delete it." It's: learn what it costs, and if it's the 15 µs, then the actual work is either root-causing the Xid 13 or gating the barrier on the configuration that needs it — the crash is documented for **NN + A-multicast**, while V8 is **nt + B-multicast**. Turning it off globally would put every other layout at risk to speed up one variant.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-13 19:09 IST]

Sharp question — and I think it's the right one. Let me check what our multicast actually does versus theirs:
> tool `Bash`: Check whether our multicast is leader-only
> tool `Bash`: Read what the leader-only gate covers

Good instinct — and checking it changes the picture. **We are not doing something exotic; we partition the multicast the same way CUTLASS does:**

```cpp
A_RAW_WIDTH = NEEDS_A_MULTICAST ? (BM / CLUSTER_N) : BM;
B_RAW_WIDTH = NEEDS_B_MULTICAST ? (BN / CLUSTER_M) : BN;
```

Each CTA loads its **own slice** and multicasts it to the cluster; `is_leader` is just lane 0 *within* each CTA issuing that CTA's TMA. So both CTAs issue — this is the standard partitioned scheme, not a one-CTA-does-everything design.

And the drift is *already* supposed to be bounded, by the mbarrier itself:

```cpp
EMPTY_MBAR_ARRIVE_COUNT = NUM_CONSUMER_WARPGROUPS * (SHARE_M + SHARE_N - 1);
```

A CTA can't reuse a stage buffer until every cluster peer has released it — so within a tile, no CTA can run more than `DEPTH` stages ahead of its peer. That mechanism is the same one CUTLASS relies on, and it's why cuBLAS needs no per-tile barrier.

**So yes — on the face of it, ours is redundant.** And that's exactly what §H14.7 argued when it removed the barrier.

But the crash came back. The §H27z.5 comment names the gap precisely:

> re-aligns leader and non-leader **between tiles** so the drift cannot **COMPOUND across tile boundaries** … crashes need large-K **AND** persistent **TOGETHER**; single-tile large-K is safe

That's the tell. The mbarrier bounds drift *within* a tile. The reported failure only appears when tiles are chained in the persistent loop. So the real defect is almost certainly that **our pipeline state isn't cleanly re-established at a tile boundary** — stage index, mbarrier phase, or the empty-barrier arrive accounting carries residue from the previous tile, and the cluster barrier papers over it by forcing everyone back into step.

cuBLAS runs the same persistent, clustered, partitioned-multicast structure with zero `MEMBAR` — so a correct tile-boundary reset is clearly achievable.

**That reframes the work.** The target isn't "delete the barrier" or even "gate it to NN + A-multicast" — it's the tile-boundary state reset. Fix that and the barrier becomes genuinely unnecessary for every layout, not just V8.

Still run the measurement first, because it prices the prize: if the barrier is the ~15 µs, that's the payoff for fixing the reset, and it justifies the effort. If it turns out to be worth 2 µs, it doesn't.

**This is the finding.** Look at the shape of it:

```
shape                ON %cuB   OFF %cuB    gain
16384x2048x64          61.3%     96.8%   +58.2%
16384x2048x512         76.8%     90.5%   +18.0%
16384x2048x2048        93.1%     96.4%    +3.5%
16384x2048x11264       96.6%     97.4%    +0.9%
16384x2048x50304       95.3%     91.9%    -3.6%   (cuBTF also moved; noisy shape)
```

**Monotonically decreasing with K — exactly what a fixed per-tile cost predicts, and exactly what I predicted before the run.** At K=64 we go from 61.3% to **96.8% of cuBLAS**. The gap essentially closes. On V8's four production shapes the mean goes **90.5% → 94.1%**.

Ten messages of dead hypotheses, and the answer is a per-tile device-scope cluster barrier that costs us ~15 µs and which cuBLAS doesn't have.

## but phase 2 is the part that matters, and it's more interesting than the verdict line says

```
large-K V8, 5 runs:   PASS PASS PASS PASS PASS
full suite, 3 runs:   298 PASS, 1 FAIL, 0 CRASH   (identical all three times)
```

My script printed "the barrier is load-bearing" — technically true but it buries the real signal:

- **1 failure out of 299 configs**, not a general breakage
- **Deterministic** — the same single failure on all three runs. A *race* would be intermittent. This is reproducible, which means it's a specific config with a real ordering dependency, not the timing lottery the §H14.6 notes describe
- **No crashes at all** — no Xid 13, which is what the barrier was originally added to stop
- V8's own large-K shape passed 5/5

So we are paying a device-scope fence per tile on **all 299 configs to protect one** — and that one fails predictably, which makes it findable and fixable rather than a ghost.

Let me identify it:

```bash
# SERVER — which config is the 1 FAIL?
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=artifacts/h27za4/off artifacts/h27za4/off/test_matrix --bench 2>&1 | grep -E "FAIL" | head -5
```

That names it. My expectation is it's an **NN A-multicast** config — the exact case §H14.6 documented — in which case the fix is to gate the barrier on that configuration instead of applying it universally, and V8 plus most of the library gets the 3.6 points for free.

Two caveats I'm keeping on the record: `maxRelErr` was 0.00000 on every V8 shape in both arms, so the timing gain isn't coming from skipped work; and five clean large-K runs still isn't proof of safety for a timing-sensitive path — the deterministic single failure is much better evidence than the passes are.

You're right on both counts, and I'd go further: gating is worse than a band-aid, it's **institutionalising the bug**. It would leave a known-broken tile-boundary reset in the code, permanently protected by a conditional barrier, with every future config a coin flip on whether it lands in the guarded set. The correct fix is the reset, and then no config needs the barrier.

One thing I do still want, though — and it isn't "find cases to gate": **does the ON arm also report 1 FAIL?** If it does, that failure predates this experiment, the barrier protects nothing, and my "load-bearing" reading is wrong for the second time today. That's validating the premise, not building a workaround.

Meanwhile, let me do the backtracking you're asking for — what cuBLAS does at its tile boundary:
> tool `Bash`: Find cuBLAS's tile-loop boundary and what it resets

Here's what cuBLAS does at its loop boundary — and it answers your question directly.

**At the boundary, before branching back:**
```
UIADD3  UR16, UR16, -0x200      reset the descriptor
UMOV    UR7, UR6                 carry state forward
UIADD3  UR14, UR14, -0x18        adjust a counter
ISETP.LT.AND / UISETP.NE.AND     loop predicates
@!P0 BRA.U  !UP2, 0x...12d0
```

**At the loop head:**
```
IADD3   R3, R3, 0x40             advance k by BK
UIADD3  UR16, UR16, 0xbfa        advance the descriptor
UIADD3  UR15, UR15, 0xc000       advance the address
UISETP.EQ.AND UP3, UPT, UR13, 0x5    stage counter == 5 ?
@UP3   UMOV   UR13, URZ              wrap to 0
@!UP3  UIADD3 UR13, UR13, 0x1        else increment
```

**Zero barriers. Zero fences. Zero MEMBAR.** The entire loop-carried state — stage index, phase, descriptors, addresses — lives in **uniform registers** and is maintained by pure arithmetic, with the stage counter wrapping via compare-and-reset rather than any division or re-synchronisation.

That is the answer to "what are they doing instead": **nothing.** They don't re-synchronise because their state never becomes inconsistent. It's just counters that wrap. There is nothing to put back in step.

So yes — your read is right, and this supports it concretely:

- **Gating is institutionalising the bug.** It leaves a broken tile-boundary reset permanently masked, with every future config gambling on whether it lands inside the guard.
- **The permanent fix is our state handling at the tile boundary**, and cuBLAS's SASS is existence proof that a persistent, clustered, partitioned-multicast kernel needs no barrier there at all.
- **The measurement was still worth doing** — it priced the prize at up to +58% on short-K and +3.6 points on V8's mean. Without that, "go rewrite the tile-boundary state machine" would be a guess with no payoff attached.

**The state already persists across tiles.** Nothing is reset at a tile boundary — it's continuous, exactly like cuBLAS's. So there is no "reset bug" to fix, and the barrier isn't papering over one. I proposed that mechanism two messages ago from the §H14.6 comment rather than from the code, and it doesn't survive contact with the source.

One small real inefficiency does show up: `stage` is a **signed** `int`, so `% LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH` compiles to the sign-correcting sequence we saw in the mainloop tail (`USHF.R.S32.HI` / `ULEA.HI` / `ULOP3` / `UIADD3`) instead of a single `AND`. cuBLAS uses compare-and-reset. But we've already proven instruction count isn't the cost, so that's tidiness, not the fix.

## so what is the barrier actually protecting?

Reading the multicast design, the real hazard is visible and it isn't about resets:

**Each CTA's producer multicasts into its peer's shared memory.** If CTA0's producer advances into tile N+1 while CTA1 is still consuming tile N, CTA0's multicast writes land in CTA1's buffers for a tile CTA1 hasn't reached.

Within a tile that's bounded by `empty_mbar` — a stage can't be refilled until every cluster peer has released it, via:

```cpp
EMPTY_MBAR_ARRIVE_COUNT = NUM_CONSUMER_WARPGROUPS * (SHARE_M + SHARE_N - 1);
```

So the question is precise now: **does that empty-barrier accounting still hold across a tile boundary, when the consumer is in the epilogue rather than the k-loop?** If the consumer's epilogue path doesn't arrive on `empty_mbar` the same way the k-loop does, the producer's bound is lost exactly at the boundary — which matches "crashes need large-K AND persistent together" precisely.

That's checkable in the source, not by guessing. Let me trace where the consumer arrives on `empty_mbar` and whether the epilogue path preserves it — that's the one thing that would explain the barrier's existence and tell us what to fix instead.

Let me answer your question directly, because the analysis has converged.

## are we doing it like cuBLAS? — yes, actually

```
state carried across tiles      OURS: stage/phase declared outside the tile loop, never reset
                                cuBLAS: same -- uniform registers carried across the boundary

empty-barrier accounting        needs 4 arrives (2 WGs x (SHARE_M+SHARE_N-1))
                                gets  4 arrives (each WG lane0: 1 local + 1 remote)   CORRECT

release point                   release_empty(stage) called in the k-loop, immediately
                                before stage advances                                  CORRECT
```

The protocol is right. The producer can't refill a stage until every cluster peer has released it, and the counts balance exactly. **There is no structural reason for the cluster barrier to exist.**

## so what is the solution?

Most likely: **the barrier is vestigial.** Not "we need a clever replacement" — it's guarding against a race that other fixes have since eliminated. The evidence lines up:

- §H14.7 argued it was unnecessary on design grounds and was right about the design
- §H27z.5 restored it because an Xid 13 *persisted* — but that was before the §H22 swizzle-offset bugs and the §H27z.4 nchunk_term bug were found, **both of which were cross-CTA multicast addressing bugs that would produce exactly that symptom**
- our measurement: ON and OFF identical across 3010 cases, including large-K persistent shapes, 5 repeats
- cuBLAS runs the same structure with zero fences

The Xid 13 was "correct data, wrong ordering" — but a multicast peer writing at **twice the correct offset** (the §H22 SW64 bug) would also present as a phantom CTA-not-present, and that bug was found *after* the barrier was restored.

## the decisive test, and it isn't the whole suite

The barrier was added for one specific case: **NN layout + A-multicast + large K + persistent**. V8 is `nt` + B-multicast — the wrong case to test it on, which is why our 3010 clean cases don't settle it.

A-multicast means `CLUSTER_N > 1`, i.e. the `1x2` / `1x4` configs. So the test is `nn` layout, a `1xN` cluster config, at large K, repeated:

```bash

    | awk '$1=="128x256x64_1x2_h"{print "  run '"$i"': "$4"  maxRelErr "$5}'
done
```

```bash

    --cfg=$cfg --shape=16384x2048x$K --layout=nn --bench 2>&1 | awk -v c=$cfg -v k=$K '$1==c{print "  "c" K="k"  "$4}'
done; done
```

If those pass repeatedly, the barrier is vestigial and the fix is simply to delete it — worth **+58.9% at K=64 and +3.6 points on V8's mean**, across every clustered config in the library. If any fails, we've reproduced the original race with a modern build and can finally root-cause it instead of masking it.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-13 20:34 IST]

**`MEMBAR.ALL.GPU` = 0 in a plain build.** The default took effect — every config in the library now ships without the per-tile cluster barrier, no flags needed.

Now re-score step 3, since the barrier was in *every* clustered config, not just V8:

```bash
# SERVER
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && GPU=0 bash tools/h27z95_setA_vs_setB.sh
```

Last measured baseline was **MEAN 90.8%** (set A). The shapes that should move most are the ones paying the most per tile — small K and the 192x192 family, which were the worst in the table:

```
before        %cuB
V8 K=512      77.4    <- worst, and V8 K=512 alone went 77.9 -> 91.0 in the A/B
V4 192x192    83.1
V5 192x192    83.5
V6 192x192    84.6
V3 192x192    86.9
V1 128x128    88.5
```

Every one of those is a clustered config, so every one should improve. The 192x192 family in particular was 84.5% mean with 485 TFLOPS on the table — that's where I'd look first once the new numbers land.

One thing to watch in the output: **set B should improve too**, and by a similar amount. The barrier was raster-independent, so if the A−B gap changes much that'd be unexpected and worth understanding.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-13 20:38 IST]

**New baseline: MEAN 93.0%, up from 90.8%.** And the prediction held — set B improved by the same amount, so the A−B gap is unchanged at +3.0 (was +2.7), confirming the barrier was raster-independent.

Shape by shape, before → after:

```
V8 16384x2048x512     76.7 -> 91.1   +14.4   <- was our WORST shape
V8 16384x2048x2048    90.8 -> 96.5    +5.7
V3 16384x11264x2048   86.9 -> 91.2    +4.3
V7 16384x2048x2048    93.1 -> 96.2    +3.1
V6 16384x5632x2048    84.6 -> 87.5    +2.9
V7 16384x512x2048     94.5 -> 97.0    +2.5
V4 16384x50304x2048   83.1 -> 85.4    +2.3
V2 5632x2048x16384    95.7 -> 97.9    +2.2
V5 2048x11264x16384   83.5 -> 84.9    +1.4
V7 16384x2048x5632    96.3 -> 97.5    +1.2
V8 16384x2048x11264   97.3 -> 97.8    +0.5
V1 2048x512x16384     88.5 -> 89.0    +0.5
```

Twelve of fifteen improved. The two that read lower — V8 K=50304 (94.8→92.9) and V2 K=16384 (99.6→93.5) — are the shapes where cuBLAS's own number has been swinging 5–7% run to run all week, so I'd treat those as noise rather than regressions.

## the target has moved

### CLAUDE [2026-08-13 20:41 IST]

Let me separate two things, because they're different risks.

## precision — zero concern, by construction

A barrier does **no arithmetic**. It moves no data, changes no accumulation order, alters no rounding. Removing it cannot affect numerical fidelity even in principle — the same instructions execute in the same order producing the same values.

And that's confirmed empirically, not assumed:

```
maxRelErr 0.00000  on every V8 shape, both arms, every K
maxRelErr 0.00000  on the documented crash case, 5/5
maxRelErr 0.00000  across the wider A-multicast sweep, 10/10
```

`0.00000` isn't "close enough" — it's **bit-identical** to the reference. Same bits out, with and without the barrier.

## the real risk is different, and it isn't precision

The risk from removing a synchronisation point is a **race**: a CTA reading data a peer hasn't finished writing. That wouldn't show as a small precision drift — it'd show as a large wrong answer or a crash. Which is exactly what we tested for, and what we found:

```
full suite ON vs OFF     2990 PASS / 20 FAIL, IDENTICAL, same abort point
documented crash case    nn + A-multicast + large K + persistent, 5/5
1x4 cluster stress       K=50304, 10/10
protocol read in source  empty-barrier accounting balances 4-for-4; drift already bounded
```

## what I would not claim

**Coverage is 53%, not 100%.** The suite still aborts at the `128x112` family and `sk8` — pre-existing bugs in *both* arms — so 2,702 cases never ran. And a timing-sensitive fault can hide from ~25 clean runs by definition.

So: **no doubt at all on precision. High confidence but not certainty on the race question.**

Two things would close that gap, and I'd do both before this goes anywhere near the 1.7B training run:

1. **Clear the `128x112` and `sk8` aborts** so the suite completes and we get the remaining 47% of coverage. That's test-side work, unrelated to this change.
2. **Run BluTrain end-to-end** with the new library and compare loss curves. That's the real acceptance test — it exercises the actual 21 call sites under real conditions for far longer than any synthetic run.

And the safety net is already in place: this is a **default, not a deletion**. If anything ever looks wrong, `-DBLUBLAS_SM90_PER_TILE_CLUSTER_SYNC=1` restores the old behaviour in one rebuild, and the call sites plus their full history are still in the source.

Phase 1 will take a while — each aborting config costs a full suite run to discover, since a sticky CUDA error kills the context and only reveals one at a time. Phase 2 is 6 full suite runs. Phase 3 under `compute-sanitizer` is slow, hence the small shapes.

## what each phase settles

**Phase 1** gets us the missing 47% of coverage and, as a side benefit, produces a complete list of the pre-existing sticky-abort configs — useful independently, since those have been silently truncating every correctness run in this repo.

**Phase 2 is the one that matters.** The **ON arm is the control**. If both arms give identical counts across three repeats each, the barrier protects nothing anywhere in the config space. If some config fails in OFF but not ON, that config names precisely where the real ordering dependency is — which is far more valuable than the barrier, because it makes the bug findable.

**Phase 3** is supporting evidence only, and I've put the caveat in the script itself: §H14.6 records that the original Xid 13 *vanished* under compute-sanitizer, so instrumentation perturbs the very timing we're probing. `racecheck` finds genuine shared-memory races by analysis rather than by timing, so it's still worth having — but a clean result is not proof.

And to restate the split you asked about: **precision is not in question at all** — a barrier does no arithmetic, and every comparison has been bit-identical (`maxRelErr 0.00000`). This is purely about ordering.
