**Work — 2026-08-13**

found the single largest bottleneck in the sm90 kernel by pc-sampling the instruction stream instead of guessing at it - a per-tile cluster barrier issuing a device-scope fence on every output tile that cuBLAS never issues - proved it was vestigial by reading the mbarrier protocol and by measurement, removed it, and took the 15-shape step-3 baseline from 90.8% to 93.0% of cuBLAS with bit-identical output, after six earlier hypotheses each died on measurement

---

## the six that failed, and what each actually changed

```
#  hypothesis           what i changed                  result
1  bank conflicts       swizzled epilogue buffer        conflicts 12,127 -> 173 (70x down, and
   §H27z.94             (EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES=64)          12x BELOW cuBLAS)   TIME UNCHANGED
2  stmatrix             EPI_USE_STSM=true               FAILED correctness - the fragment->
   §H27z.97                                             address mapping is unfinished; and the
                                                        SASS showed the barriers are emitted
                                                        unconditionally, so it would not have
                                                        helped even had it run
3  membar count         EPI_TILE_N 32 -> 64             MEMBARs -40%, membar stall 5.9 -> 4.9,
   §H27z.98             (halve the epilogue chunks)     but TIME 21.5% WORSE at K=512
4  instruction count    hoist the wgmma descriptor      dynamic instructions -14%
   §H27z.99             out of the k-loop               TIME UNCHANGED - killed the whole
                                                        category, not just the one idea
5  grid geometry        (132,1,1) -> (2,66,1) to        grid verified changed; duration,
   §H27za1              match cuBLAS exactly            tensor% and every stall IDENTICAL
6  epilogue fusion      nothing - tested the SASS       DISPROVED before any GPU run: both
   §H27za2              interleaving first              kernels are compute-then-store, 0 of 83
                                                        cuBLAS stores near a wgmma
   (a seventh, EPI_STAGES §H27za3, was built and then superseded before it burned GPU time)
```

Every one of those was me picking a region to attack. The pattern — "we differ from cuBLAS on counter X, change X, nothing happens" — went six for six.

## what actually found it

Two decompositions of data already on disk narrowed the search, then PC sampling closed it:

```
time  = a + b*K    ours a=16.6us b=0.08518   cuBLAS a=0.8us b=0.08555   SLOPES MATCH TO 0.4%
instr = a + b*K    ours a=8,642  b=24.09     cuBLAS a=4,782 b=14.11
```

The mainloop computes at cuBLAS's rate — the whole deficit is a fixed intercept. And in the epilogue we ran 1.81× the instructions but took **21×** the time: 3.38 cycles per instruction against cuBLAS's 0.29. It was stalling, not executing, which is exactly why every instruction-count and conflict-count fix did nothing.

PC sampling then named it outright — **33.9% of every stall sample in the kernel on one construct**:

```
0x64c0  22.4%  UCGABAR_WAIT      = cluster_sync() at template :3662 (producer) and :3890 (consumer),
0x0660   6.1%  ERRBAR              INSIDE the persistent tile loop. MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + MEMBAR.ALL.GPU
0x6460   3.2%  ERRBAR              + ERRBAR + CGAERRBAR + UCGABAR_ARV + UCGABAR_WAIT -- a device-
0x06c0   2.2%  UCGABAR_WAIT        scope fence per output tile, in BOTH warpgroups. cuBLAS: zero.
```

## performance, morning vs now

```
variant   shapes   morning    now     gain
V8             4     89.9%   94.6%   +4.7
V3             1     86.9%   91.2%   +4.3
V6             1     84.6%   87.5%   +2.9
V4             1     83.1%   85.4%   +2.3
V7             3     94.6%   96.9%   +2.3
V5             1     83.5%   84.9%   +1.4
V1             1     88.5%   89.0%   +0.5
V2             3     97.1%   95.8%   -1.3
ALL 15        15     90.8%   93.0%   +2.2
```

Seven of eight variants improved, twelve of fifteen shapes. Biggest single move: **V8 at K=512, 76.7% → 91.1% (+14.4)** — that had been the worst shape in the table. In the isolated A/B the same config at K=64 went **60.9% → 96.9%**.

**V2's −1.3 is one shape**, `2048x50304x16384`, reading 99.6% → 93.5%. cuBLAS's own number on it moved 799.8 → 819.2 TF between runs and has swung 5–7% all week. V2's other two shapes were flat and +2.2. I'd call it noise, but it should be re-measured before anyone quotes V2 as a regression.

## numerical fidelity

**Unchanged, and not at risk in principle.** A barrier performs no arithmetic — no data moved, no accumulation reordered, no rounding altered. Confirmed empirically at every step:

```
maxRelErr 0.00000   every V8 shape, barrier on and off, every K
maxRelErr 0.00000   all 15 step-3 shapes in the re-score
maxRelErr 0.00000   the documented crash case (nn + A-multicast + large K), 5/5
maxRelErr 0.00000   the wider A-multicast sweep 10/10, and 1x4 at K=50304 10/10
```

`0.00000` is bit-identical, not "close". The only risk from removing synchronisation is a race — a wrong answer or a crash, never a precision drift — and the full suite gave **identical** results with the barrier on and off (2990 PASS / 20 FAIL, same abort point).

## what is not finished

The suite still can't complete: **ten pre-existing configs kill the CUDA context**, none of them in our 8 pins and **none reachable from the dispatcher** (zero hits each), and all ten abort with the barrier on too. Coverage therefore isn't 100%, so the barrier removal ships as a *default* — `-DBLUBLAS_SM90_PER_TILE_CLUSTER_SYNC=1` restores it in one rebuild.

And the target has moved: the **192x192 family (V3–V6) is now the only group under 90%**, at 87.3% mean.

**experiment 1 - bank conflicts**

shared memory on the gpu is split into 32 banks and if many threads write into the same bank at the same time they get serialised one after another instead of going in parallel , the profiler showed our kernel had 12,127 of these conflicts while cublas had only 2,153 so i assumed our slow output-writing step was being choked by them , the fix for this is called swizzling which just means shuffling where each value is placed in shared memory so the writes spread across all banks evenly , i built swizzled versions of every pinned config and measured , the conflicts dropped from 12,127 to 173 which is 70 times fewer and actually 12 times better than cublas itself , but the runtime did not change at all , so it failed on performance but it did succeed at genuinely removing a real inefficiency and it proved conclusively that bank conflicts are not what separates us from cublas ,

**experiment 2 - stmatrix**

when the gpu finishes computing it has to move the results from registers into shared memory , we do this with a plain store instruction where each thread writes its own value one at a time , cublas uses a special instruction called stmatrix where all 32 threads of a warp cooperate to write an 8x8 block in a single instruction , i saw in cublas's machine code that they use stmatrix and we use 128 plain stores , so i assumed switching would remove both the stores and the synchronisation that plain stores force us to add , i built it and it failed correctness immediately , when i went back and read our own source properly there was a comment saying the register-to-address mapping for stmatrix was never finished and needed proper derivation , and worse , when i compared the machine code i found the synchronisation instructions are emitted no matter which store instruction is used so even a working stmatrix would not have removed them , this one failed on both counts and it also taught me to read the existing comments before assuming a code path is ready ,

**experiment 3 - memory barrier count**

a memory barrier is an instruction that forces the hardware to wait until all previous memory writes are visible before continuing , our output step issues one of these per chunk and we write the output in 8 chunks so we pay 8 barriers per tile , the profiler showed memory-barrier stalls were the only measurement that shrank as the problem got bigger which matched the shape of our slowdown exactly , so i assumed fewer barriers would help and i doubled the chunk width so there would be 4 chunks instead of 8 , the barriers did drop by 40 percent and the barrier stall did fall , but performance got 21 percent worse on the small-k shape , the reason is that doubling the chunk also doubled the buffer size which cut the overlap between writing one chunk and storing the previous one from 7 opportunities down to 3 , so i had accidentally changed two things at once , it failed on performance and it also taught me that this test was not clean enough to trust as a disproof ,

**experiment 4 - instruction count**

every wgmma matrix-multiply instruction needs a descriptor which is a 64-bit value telling the hardware where in shared memory the data sits , i read both machine codes side by side and found cublas rebuilds nothing , it just adds a constant to the descriptor between one multiply and the next so there are only 2 instructions between consecutive multiplies , we rebuild the whole descriptor from scratch every single time which takes about 20 instructions , overall we were executing 1.75 times as many instructions as cublas , so i rewrote it to build the descriptor once and add a fixed offset like cublas does , it worked exactly as intended and removed 14 percent of all executed instructions with bit-identical output , and the runtime did not move even slightly , this failed on performance but it was the most valuable failure of the day because it did not just kill one idea , it killed the entire theory that instruction count matters , our warps are stalled 88 percent of the time so the extra instructions were slotting into gaps we were not using anyway ,

**experiment 5 - grid geometry**

when a kernel launches you tell the gpu the shape of the grid of thread blocks , i noticed cublas launches a 2-dimensional grid of 2 by 66 while we launch a flat 1-dimensional grid of 132 , both give the same 132 blocks and the same cluster size so i had missed it earlier by only comparing the total , the shape matters because the hardware assigns blocks to physical units based on grid coordinates so the two layouts can place work differently , and cublas's shape also lets them read the cluster index straight out of a built-in variable where we have to compute it with a division , i added a mode that launches the identical 2 by 66 shape and confirmed with the profiler that the shape really changed , the runtime , the tensor core utilisation and every single stall measurement came out identical , complete failure with no side benefit , though i had rated this one unlikely before running it because our memory behaviour was already better than cublas's ,

**experiment 6 - epilogue fusion**

after all the multiplication is done the kernel still has to convert the results to bfloat16 and write them out and this final stage is called the epilogue , i noticed cublas's epilogue looked five times smaller than ours in the machine code and i thought they must be overlapping it with the multiplication so their output writing hides behind work that is still running while ours stops and does it separately , before spending gpu time i tested it by checking whether their store instructions actually sit in between their multiply instructions in the code , they do not , both kernels do all the multiplying first and then all the storing , zero of their 83 store instructions sit anywhere near a multiply , so this one was disproved before it cost a single run which is the only reason it is not on the list of wasted effort , and it also showed my earlier five-times-smaller comparison was measuring the wrong thing ,

**experiment 7 - per-tile cluster barrier , the one that worked**

after six failures i stopped guessing which part of the kernel to attack and used pc sampling instead which is a profiler mode that records exactly which instruction address the hardware is sitting on when it stalls , so the hardware picks the hot spot rather than me , it came back with 33.9 percent of every stall in the entire kernel landing on four instruction addresses and all four belonged to the same thing , a cluster barrier , a cluster is a group of thread blocks that share data and this barrier forces every block in the cluster to stop and wait for the others plus flush all memory across the whole gpu , and we were doing it once for every output tile in both worker groups while cublas never issues one at all , i then checked whether it was actually needed and it was not , our pipeline state already carries over correctly between tiles and the existing mbarrier accounting already stops any block from running ahead of its partner , it had been added long ago to work around a crash and two real addressing bugs found afterwards were the likely actual cause of that crash , i turned it off and measured , performance went up 58 percent on the shortest shape taking it from 60.9 to 96.9 percent of cublas , the overall average across all 15 shapes went from 90.8 to 93.0 percent , seven of the eight variants improved , the output stayed bit-identical everywhere and the full test suite gave exactly the same results with and without it , this one succeeded on performance and on correctness and it also removed genuinely dead code that was slowing down every clustered configuration in the library not just the one i was investigating ,

we did xor swizzlignonly right ?

### CLAUDE [2026-08-13 21:49 IST]

Yes — XOR swizzling only, and that's the only kind that exists on this hardware.

Hopper's TMA supports exactly four modes: `NONE`, `32B`, `64B`, `128B`, and all three non-zero ones are XOR-based. There is no alternative pattern to choose. We tested `SW64` on the 128x256/256x128 tiles and `SW32` on 192x192 (`SW128` isn't legal there because `WGMMA_N=96` isn't a multiple of 64).

And we verified our implementation is the *correct* XOR, not an approximation — it reproduces `cute::Swizzle<B,4,3>` from CUTLASS and DeepGEMM's `get_swizzled_bank_group_idx()` exactly, on every (row, granule) pair, for all three modes.

If you want paragraph 1 to say it precisely, this line covers it:

> the fix for this is called xor swizzling which just means shuffling where each value is placed in shared memory using an xor on the address so the writes spread across all banks evenly , and it is the only swizzle the hardware supports ,

One thing worth knowing for tomorrow: while checking this I found our **test file was testing a different swizzle formula than the kernel** — it used `row % span` where the kernel correctly uses `(row >> shift) & (span-1)`. Those only agree for `SW128`, so the file meant to validate `SW64` and `SW32` was validating neither. Fixed, but it means that test had been giving false assurance on the narrow modes.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-13 21:59 IST]

**Grid dimensions, ours vs cuBLAS** — read from ncu `launch__grid_dim_*`, identical on all four V8 shapes:

```
                    ours        cuBLAS
grid_dim_x          132            2
grid_dim_y            1           66
grid_dim_z            1            1
grid_size           132          132        <- same total, which is why I missed it
cluster_dim_x         2            2
cluster_dim_y         1            1
cluster_dim_z         1            1
cluster_size          2            2        <- same cluster
block_dim_x         384          384
waves_per_sm       1.00         1.00
```

So **ours is `(132, 1, 1)` and cuBLAS is `(2, 66, 1)`.**

Same 132 thread blocks, same 2-block cluster, same 384 threads per block — only the *shape* differs. I'd originally compared `launch__grid_size` (132 == 132) and concluded the launch config was identical, which is how it went unnoticed until I ranked all 99 metrics and it came out top.

Why it looked promising: cuBLAS's `gridDim.x` **equals** `clusterDim.x`, so one cluster is exactly one x-pair and the cluster index is just `blockIdx.y` — free. We pack 66 clusters along x, so we have to derive the cluster index and rank by dividing `blockIdx.x` by the cluster size. The hardware also assigns blocks to physical SMs from grid coordinates, so the two shapes can place work differently even at identical block counts.

Result when I matched their shape exactly (verified in the profiler as `(2,66)`): duration, tensor-core utilisation and every stall measurement came out **identical**. No effect at all.

pc sampling means

### CLAUDE [2026-08-13 22:04 IST]

**PC = program counter** — the register that holds the address of the instruction a warp is currently on.

**PC sampling** means the profiler wakes up every N cycles, looks at every warp, and writes down two things: which instruction address it's sitting on, and why it isn't issuing (waiting on memory, waiting at a barrier, and so on). Do that thousands of times and you get a histogram — **which exact instructions the hardware spends its time stuck on**.

That's what makes it different from everything else I'd been using. Normal ncu metrics are *totals*: "barrier stall is 47%", "you executed 59,001 instructions". True, but they don't say *where*. So for six experiments I was reading a total, guessing which part of the kernel was responsible, changing that part, and being wrong.

PC sampling removes the guess. It reports per address:

```
0x64c0  22.4%  UCGABAR_WAIT
0x0660   6.1%  ERRBAR
0x6460   3.2%  ERRBAR
0x06c0   2.2%  UCGABAR_WAIT
        ------
        33.9% of every stall sample in the kernel, on one construct
```

Then you map those addresses back onto the disassembled kernel and read what's actually there — which is how the cluster barrier turned up.

Two practical things that cost me time getting it working, worth remembering:

- `--section SourceCounters` collected nothing usable. Requesting the metrics **directly** worked: `--metrics smsp__pcsamp_sample_count,smsp__pcsamp_warps_issue_stalled_barrier,...`, and the export needs `--page source --print-source sass` — without `--print-source sass` it silently returns an empty file
- ncu reports **absolute** addresses like `0x79f75b7a7300` while the disassembler uses **relative** offsets from 0, so you must subtract the base. Before I did, every sample landed past the end of the kernel and the breakdown read a meaningless "100% epilogue"

Staged. Now — your read on this, before the commands.

**On being better at L2 hit and memory but not faster:** that's expected, and it's the same lesson as the bank conflicts. We cut those 70× (12,127 → 173, twelve times *below* cuBLAS) and the time did not move at all. Winning a counter that isn't the bottleneck buys exactly nothing. So "we beat them on L2" isn't a puzzle — it's evidence those counters aren't where the loss is.

**On tensor-core utilization:** plausible, but it would be a *symptom*, not a cause. The tensor pipe doesn't idle by choice — it idles because it's starved. So if tensor% is low, the real question is still "starved by what". The good news is the hypothesis is cheap to falsify: one ncu capture. If tensor% is at parity while duration isn't, it's dead on the spot. That's phase 2.

And note what the K-fit already told us: our **mainloop already computes at cuBLAS's rate, slope matched to 0.4%**. The tensor pipe in the steady state is fine. The deficit was a fixed per-tile intercept — we removed 16.6µs of it with the barrier, and what's left is whatever else sits in that intercept.

## The shape of the deficit has changed, and that matters

Fitting `time = a + b·K` on K=512/2048/11264 — residuals ±0.1µs, so the model is exact on those three:

The barrier removal took the intercept gap from **15.8µs down to 6.5µs** — that's the win, confirmed independently. What's left is a smaller fixed cost *plus* a slope gap that has grown from 0.4% to 1.3%, meaning the mainloop is now marginally implicated where before it matched exactly.

## Phase 2 — your tensor-utilization hypothesis is dead, and cleanly

```
K        tensor% ours   cuBLAS    gap
```

**The gap collapses with K, exactly like the deficit does.** At K=11264 and above we're at parity — 99.5% vs 99.6% tensor-pipe occupancy. A kernel with a structural tensor-utilization weakness cannot reach 99.5%. So low tensor% at K=512 is the *symptom* of per-tile overhead being large relative to a short mainloop, not a cause. Nothing to fix there directly.

## What the counters actually say

First, a caveat on the table you saw: the script matched column names by substring and grabbed ncu's `.avg` columns while labelling them `.sum`, and ncu scales `dur`/`dram` per row (µs vs ms, MB vs GB). Both sides shared the wrong column so **every ratio was still valid** — but I've fixed it to exact names. Corrected figures:

```
                        ours/cuBLAS     behaviour across K
tensor_i (tensor insts)     0.50        EXACTLY 2.00x on all four shapes
inst (total)                1.74        stable
  -> non-tensor insts       ~1.9x       1.86 / 1.91 / 1.93 / 1.94 — flat
bankconf                    7.47        FLAT in absolute terms (~1.94M every shape)
lgsb% (memory stalls)       1.53        stable
mem_thr%                    0.86        ours pinned ~60%, cuBLAS RISES 61->73%
sm_thr%                     0.95        near parity
```

Three things stand out:

**1. We issue exactly half the tensor instructions cuBLAS does — 2.00×, on every shape, to the power of two.** That's not noise, it's structural: our wgmma is twice as wide (BN=256 → `m64n256k16` against their `m64n128k16`). Fewer, fatter instructions. That's not a defect in itself, but a wider wgmma needs twice the accumulator registers, which squeezes everything else.

**2. Our memory throughput is pinned at ~60% of peak at every K while cuBLAS climbs to 73%.** This is the most stable difference in the whole table and the only one that doesn't collapse with K. And we simultaneously stall *more* on long scoreboard (1.53×) — stalling harder on memory while extracting less from it is the signature of too few loads in flight. It corroborates §H27z.96's independent finding that cuBLAS is memory-throttled and we are never.

**3. Bank conflicts are 7.5× cuBLAS and dead flat across K** (~1.94M regardless of shape) — so they're per-tile epilogue work, ~1,900 per tile. Worth noting, but §H27z.94 already proved removing them changes nothing.

## Phase 3 collected nothing — a flag name

```
==ERROR== unrecognised option '--sampling-interval'
```

CUDA 13's ncu renamed those to `--warp-sampling-*`. My retry passed the same bad flag, so both attempts died identically and the phase reported an empty source page as though the metrics were at fault. Fixed by dropping the flag (auto is the default) and asking ncu which pcsamp metrics it has rather than hardcoding names.

Also worth knowing for when it reruns: the region split reported **184 prologue / 96 mainloop / 1800 epilogue**. That "epilogue" is 86% of the kernel because the heuristic calls the inner k-loop the mainloop, so the persistent tile loop lands in "epilogue". That label means "not the k-loop" and nothing more — we read the per-address list, which is what found the barrier.

This is already deeply documented, and it changes the conclusion. Two settled facts from the source:

**The `MEMBAR` is not removable.** A probe (`fence_probe.cu`) showed *every* writable form of `fence.proxy.async` in PTX emits `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S`. CUTLASS uses identical PTX. cuBLAS's bare fence is not reachable from PTX — nvjet goes through NVIDIA's internal path.

**Why we need the pair at all:** we store with plain `STS` (per-thread), so the warpgroup must rendezvous (`BAR.SYNC`) and the stores must be ordered (`MEMBAR`) before the TMA engine reads that shared memory. cuBLAS uses `STSM`, which is warp-collective and internally ordered, so it needs only the fence.

```

the sync cost of our store chain alone:            5.63 us
```

**5.63µs of synchronization against a 6.39µs total deficit.** That's ~88% of everything we still lose, in one mechanism.

And it corrects the old membar theory: **`MEMBAR.ALL.CTA` costs only 0.16µs — 0.7%.** Removing it would buy nothing even if PTX allowed it. The cost is in `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S` (3.18µs) and `BAR.SYNC` (2.28µs). §H27z.98 was aiming at the cheap half of the pair.

Why cuBLAS doesn't pay it: `STSM` is warp-collective and internally ordered, so their chain is `F2FP → STSM → FENCE`. Ours is `F2FP → STS → BAR.SYNC → MEMBAR → FENCE`, because plain `STS` is per-thread and the warpgroup must rendezvous before the TMA engine may read that shared memory.

## Finding 1 — the "unfinished mapping" comment is stale

[template.cuh:4139](src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM90/Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh#L4139) says the fragment→address mapping "must be derived and CuTe-verified, not guessed." That was written before §H27z.76/.77. What actually exists now:

- verified by `probe_stmatrix.cu` at **0/256 mismatch**
- the address hoisted to cuBLAS's exact form — `(rr*9) ^ g`, no integer math in the loop (§H27z.77)

So it's not undone work. Per §H27za5 the real blocker is a **sticky illegal memory access** in `128x256x64_2x1_h_swz64stsm` — a bug to debug.

## Finding 2 — stmatrix alone cannot buy anything

```cpp
__syncwarp();
barrier_sync(g, Config::THREADS_PER_WARPGROUP);   // 4416 — UNCONDITIONAL
tma_store_fence();                                 // 4417 — UNCONDITIONAL
```

Neither is gated on `EPI_USE_STSM`. And the barrier isn't removable by stmatrix anyway: `stmatrix.sync.aligned` orders **one warp**, but one predicated thread issues the TMA for the whole **4-warp** warpgroup. cuBLAS confirms this — they still rendezvous (`WARPGROUP.ARRIVE/WAIT`), they just use a cheaper primitive.

## Finding 3 — the actual cause, and it isn't stmatrix

```cpp
if (lane_in_wg == 0) tma_store_wait<0>();   // 4497 — FULL drain, every chunk
```

We declare `EPI_STAGES=2` and the smem allocation already reserves **two slots** — but every chunk is fully drained before the next begins, so the second slot does nothing. The source says so itself:

> *"4b still ends every chunk with `tma_store_wait<0>`, so a slot is fully drained before it is reused... Relaxing that wait is 4c, and that is what makes the two slots real."*

**Step 4c was never done.** CUTLASS does exactly it — `tma_store_fn(epi_m_prev, epi_n_prev)`, storing the previous chunk while computing the current, with the comment *"We can delay issue of TMA store by one iteration to achieve better interleaving."*

And the PC sampling matches that diagnosis precisely:

```
sync stall  (BAR.SYNC + FENCE + MEMBAR)   5.63 us
epilogue real work (F2FP+FMUL+CS2R+STS)   2.93 us
```

**We spend nearly 2× longer waiting at sync points than doing the epilogue's actual work.** That is the signature of an un-pipelined loop — the barrier stalls because there is nothing to overlap it with.

The right first move is **not stmatrix**. It's completing the pipelining:

| | what | risk | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1a** | complete step 4c — relax `tma_store_wait<0>` so the 2 slots are real | **low** | no new mapping, no crash history, smem already allocated, CUTLASS-proven |
| 1b | fence before barrier (CUTLASS and cuBLAS both do; we're reversed) | low | 2-line change, probably small alone |
| 1c | stmatrix | **high** | debug a sticky illegal access; and its benefit is conditional on 1a existing anyway |

**1a is where the 5.63µs is reachable**, and we're already paying the shared memory for it and getting single-buffered behaviour.

One risk worth naming: §H27z.98 doubled the epilogue buffer and measured 21.5% worse, so smem pressure in this region is real. **1a adds no smem** — the slots are already allocated — so that failure mode doesn't apply here.

So where does 3.18µs of fence stall come from? Two candidate mechanisms, and they imply opposite fixes:

**(A) The fence is draining conflicted stores.** `STS` is fire-and-forget — it shows only 0.84µs — but the cost materializes at the fence, which must make those writes visible. **(B) The fence is just intrinsic latency × how often we execute it.** Per CTA: ~8 tiles × 8 chunks = 64 fences. At a few hundred cycles each that lands in the right range on its own, with conflicts irrelevant. If this is it, the only lever is **fewer fences**, i.e. fewer chunks.

## What each implementation actually does, per epilogue store

```
                    sync primitive              stores        buffer      drain
cuBLAS      WARPGROUP.ARRIVE/WAIT x2      2 x STSM        swizzled    (async)
CUTLASS     NamedBarrier::sync  x2        STSM            swizzled    delayed 1 iter
DeepGEMM    NamedBarrier::sync  x2        plain st_shared LINEAR      tma_store_wait<0>
ours        BAR.SYNC            x2.4      16 x STS        LINEAR      tma_store_wait<0>
```

DeepGEMM's SM90 epilogue is almost exactly ours:
```cpp
cute::tma_store_wait<0>();                              // full drain, same as us
cutlass::arch::NamedBarrier::sync(128, math_wg_idx);
... ptx::st_shared(smem_d_0 + i*4, ...)                 // plain stores, LINEAR indexing
cute::tma_store_fence();
cutlass::arch::NamedBarrier::sync(128, math_wg_idx);    // second barrier
```

**Two conclusions from that:**

1. `NamedBarrier::sync` compiles to `BAR.SYNC`. So **CUTLASS and DeepGEMM both emit BAR.SYNC per store, exactly like us.** Only cuBLAS uses `WARPGROUP.ARRIVE/WAIT`. That primitive is almost certainly unreachable from PTX — the same situation as the MEMBAR. Chasing it is likely a dead end, and now I have two independent implementations saying so rather than a guess.

2. DeepGEMM uses a **linear, unswizzled** buffer and doesn't stmatrix on SM90 at all. A heavily-tuned kernel choosing not to bother is real evidence that epilogue bank conflicts aren't where the time is — consistent with §H27z.94 measuring the swizzle as time-neutral.

## Which means mechanism (A) was wrong, but not dead — I mis-stated it

I said the fence might be "draining conflicted stores", and pointed at §H27z.94 as contradicting it. That test doesn't contradict what actually matters, because **swizzling changes the conflict pattern but not the store count** — still 16 `STS`. It never tested the thing that differs from cuBLAS.

The real difference is **16 `STS` vs 2 `STSM` per store**. The fence has to make *all* prior shared writes visible; ours has 8× more of them outstanding. That mechanism:

- explains why our fence costs more than theirs
- is untouched by §H27z.94 (swizzle doesn't reduce store count)
- is untouched by §H27z.98 (chunk width doesn't reduce stores per chunk-row)
- **has never been tested**, because stmatrix never ran

So stmatrix is back as the right target — for store count, not bank conflicts.

## But one thing is still unverified, and it's cheap

We do not know whether **cuBLAS stalls on its fences too.** If their 184 fences stall as hard as our 8, the fence is just the cost of a TMA epilogue, both sides pay it, and our 6.39µs is somewhere I haven't found. If their fences are cheap, store count is confirmed and stmatrix is justified.

I have never PC-sampled cuBLAS — today's phase 3 used `-k regex:"bgemm_sm90_kernel"` and excluded `nvjet`. Widening that regex is a one-character change, one run, no new code, and it's the apples-to-apples comparison this whole campaign is built on.

**My recommendation: run that before touching stmatrix.** It either justifies debugging a kernel with a context-killing crash history, or it saves us from doing that work on a wrong premise. Shall I wire it up?

Fix implemented and staged. Here's what it is:

## The bug, proven before any GPU time

```cpp
// WAS  -- (rr*9)^g  expands to  rr*64 + (rr^g)*8      hardcoded SPAN=8, SHIFT=0
stsm_lane_off[gl] = (((stsm_rr * 9) ^ (4*gl + stsm_am)) * 8);

// NOW  -- derived generally from epi_swz_index
stsm_lane_off[gl] = stsm_rr * WGrid::C_BOX_N
                  + (((stsm_rr >> Config::EPI_SWZ_SHIFT) ^ (4*gl + stsm_am)) * 8);
```

Plus the group index `stsm_lane_off[gj & 1]` → `[(grp_tc % C_BOX_N) / 32]`, since `& 1` only picks the in-chunk group when a chunk holds exactly two of them.

```
C_BOX_N=64 SPAN=8 SHIFT=0   old 0 mismatches    new 0     <- validated config, untouched
C_BOX_N=32 SPAN=4 SHIFT=1   old 168             new 0     <- V8; old max index 4344 of 4096
```

The out-of-bounds index is §H27za5's sticky illegal access. The wrong XOR is why the atom-staged twin returned wrong numbers instead of crashing. Two new `static_assert`s now pin the invariant that was silently violated.

## The beta path costs 0.01%

```
K=512, epilogue chunks       static sites   samples   % of kernel
LDG.E.CONSTANT (C read-back)          64          0       0.00%
FFMA.FTZ (beta*C + ...)              128          0       0.00%
ISETP.GE.OR (bounds guards)           64          0       0.00%
PRMT (bf16 unpack)                    64          0       0.00%
FSETP.NEU.FTZ.AND (beta != 0)          1          6       0.01%
-----------------------------------------------------------------
BETA PATH TOTAL                      321          6       0.01%

for comparison:  FENCE 5.28%   BAR.SYNC 3.72%   STS 1.40%
```

## First — those stall numbers are not what they look like

This is the trap the whole week turned on, so it's worth being precise:

**`barrier` 46.1 vs 23.6 — not overhead. Proven elastic, twice.**
- §H27z.99c: at K=50304 we sit at 93–98% of cuBLAS *while* barrier stall is 45%. High stall coexisting with near-parity means it isn't the cost.
- §H27z.98: we **halved** the barriers (`ep64s2`). The stall moved **−3.4 points** and the kernel got **12% slower**. If the stall were proportional to barriers it would have halved.

Warps park at whatever barrier exists. Remove barriers and they park longer at the ones left. **A stall percentage tells you where warps *wait*, not where time is *lost*.**

**`membar` 5.9 vs 0.0 — real, and worth 0.16µs.** Measured directly by PC sampling: `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA` is 0.7% of the fixed cost, the *cheap* half of the fence pair. And every writable form of `fence.proxy.async` in PTX emits one, so it isn't removable anyway.

**`mio_throttle` 0.0 vs 10–16% — this one is inverted, and it's the important one.** It means the memory/shared pipe is *saturated*. **cuBLAS has more of it and is faster.** They're pushing the memory pipes to the machine limit; we never do — 0.0%, not 0.1%, at every K and in every epilogue config. Ours isn't "less stalled", it's **under-fed**. That's the one counter that has survived every experiment and still has no explanation.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-14 16:30 IST]

Good question, and let me give you the full answer including a test that already exists in our data — because it changes whether this is worth GPU time.

## What `mio_throttle` actually is

**MIO = Memory Input/Output.** The full metric is `smsp__warp_issue_stalled_mio_throttle_per_warp_active.pct`, and NVIDIA defines it as:

> *Warp was stalled waiting for the **MIO instruction queue to be not full**. High in cases of extreme utilization of the MIO pipelines — shared memory instructions, special math functions, and dynamic branches.*

So it is **not** a memory-latency stall. It means: *you are issuing MIO instructions faster than that pipe can drain them, and the queue backed up.* It's a **saturation** signal. High `mio_throttle` means you're pushing a pipe to its limit.

That's why the sign is inverted from every other stall: cuBLAS has 10–16% and is faster. They're at the machine's limit on that pipe. We're at 0.0% — we never fill the queue.

## And there's a paradox in it worth seeing

```
per TMA store:   ours 16 x STS        cuBLAS 2 x STSM
```

`STS` and `STSM` **both go through MIO**. We issue *eight times more* MIO instructions per store than cuBLAS — and still never throttle. That's only possible if the limiter is **rate, not count**: our warps are stalled elsewhere and never issue fast enough to back the queue up. Issue rate confirms it — **ours 11.3%, cuBLAS 22–27.8%.**

So `mio_throttle = 0.0` isn't an independent problem. It's a *readout* of our issue rate.

## The test that already exists in our data

Same logic that killed the barrier theory — does the gap track the deficit?

```
K        our mio   cuBLAS mio    our %cuB
512        0.0        10.4         90.8
2048       0.0        14.4         96.3
11264      0.0        15.7         98.0
50304      0.0        15.9         ~97
```

**At K=11264 the mio gap is at its widest (0.0 vs 15.7) and we are at 98.0% of cuBLAS.** The gap is flat while the deficit collapses. By exactly the test we used on `barrier` and on `tensor%`, **`mio_throttle` cannot be worth much** — a difference that is fully present when we're at 98% is not what's costing us at 90%.

I'd be doing you a disservice to spend GPU time on it as a performance lever.

## But the question *behind* it is the right one

The commit/drain/release is **inside** the body. Unrolling by N gives N copies of it — **N drains, not one.** So unrolling alone cannot reduce the drain at all.

**Fix 1 — remove `#pragma unroll 1`.** One line, no correctness risk (the pragma only constrains the compiler), undocumented leftover from a failed spill experiment. Targets the +212.6µs of loop overhead. Cheap to test, and it's the kind of change that should never have needed a decision.

## Two corrections to what I told you

**cuBLAS does *not* unroll 10×.** Both k-loops contain exactly **12 HGMMA**. ## The actual mistake we're making

**We commit all 12 wgmma as one group and drain it to zero. cuBLAS splits the same 12 into three groups of 4, waits once, and crosses the back-edge with two groups still in flight.**

And there's a second detail in their sequence that matters: the `SYNCS.PHASECHK` (wait-for-full) sits **in the middle of their body**, between group 1 and group 2. Their loop is *skewed* — it drains work from the previous stage, releases it, then acquires the next stage and issues into it. Ours does acquire → issue → drain → release, strictly serialised, with nothing overlapping the back-edge.

That's why their warps park on `HGMMA` (2.00µs/k-iter) and ours park on `DEPBAR` (1.55µs/k-iter).

## Which means §H16.7 was directionally right and got the granularity wrong

§H16.7 tried `wait_group<1>` + deferred release and lost 10–12% to a stolen pipeline buffer. The SASS now shows cuBLAS doesn't defer across a *stage* — they subdivide the *commit* within the work they already hold, so 8 of the 12 wgmma stay outstanding without holding an extra smem buffer.

That's a materially different change from what §H16.7 tested, and it doesn't obviously cost a buffer.

```
ours     1 commit of 12 wgmma  ->  wgmma_wait_group<0>  ->  full drain     369,600 samples
cuBLAS   3 commits of 4        ->  ONE wait             ->  8 still in flight  29,727 samples
```
Plus their wait-for-full sits mid-body, so they cross the back-edge with work outstanding; we cross it empty.

**Fix, concretely:** split the single `wgmma_commit_group()` into one per group of 4, and use `wgmma_wait_group<2>`. All three groups read the **same stage the CTA already owns**, so unlike §H16.7 this does not defer a release across a stage boundary and shouldn't cost a pipeline buffer.

**The overhead is the wgmma drain: +307.5µs, plus +212.6µs of spin/branch around it.** One instruction — `WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE` at `0x1ed0` — is **53.8% of our entire k-loop**, 369,600 PC samples against cuBLAS's 29,727 on the same instruction doing the same job.

The `-428.5µs` on MATH is not a win — it's the same fact from the other side. Their warps sit *on* the wgmma because the tensor pipe is the limit. Ours sit *waiting for* it.

## Why it's there

We issue 12 wgmma and drain all 12 immediately, with nothing overlapping. cuBLAS drains with 8 already in flight from the previous iteration, so by the time their wait executes the work is done.

## Why we can't just copy it

Their overlap requires **holding the pipeline stage across the loop back-edge.** That costs one buffer. At our depth of 3 it leaves the producer 1 free instead of 2 — which §H16.7 already measured at −10–12%. Three adversarial reviews and the compiler independently confirmed there's no way to get the overlap without holding the stage: `release_empty` *is* the producer's write permission, issued on the line after the wait.

## What would remove it

**A fourth pipeline stage.** At depth 4, holding one across the back-edge still leaves 2 free — today's margin — and the drain becomes cheap the way theirs is.

```
192x192 stage = (192+192)*64*2 = 49,152 B
depth = (231,424 - STORE_BUF) / 49,152     <- the unchunked epilogue forces STORE_BUF high enough to cap it at 3
```

Chunking the epilogue shrinks `STORE_BUF` and buys the 4th stage, but chunking *alone* measured −4.42 on V3. So they have to be tested as a pair — the 4th stage paying for the chunking that enables it. That combination has never been measured, and it's the one path left.

No — sorry, that's my wording colliding. Two different things are both called "stage":

**Step 3** = the campaign milestone we're in (match then beat cuBLAS's 8 variants across the 15 shapes). We are still in it. There is no step 4.

**Pipeline stages** = how many shared-memory buffers the kernel keeps in flight inside the k-loop. That's `LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH`, and for 192x192 it's currently **3**.

The proposal is only the second one: **3 smem buffers → 4**, inside the kernel. Nothing about the campaign changes.

## What a pipeline stage is here

The kernel has a producer warpgroup loading tiles by TMA and two consumer warpgroups doing the wgmma. They pass data through N shared-memory buffers:

```
depth 3:   producer fills buffer 0, 1, 2 ... consumer drains 0, 1, 2 ...
           at any moment the consumer owns 1, the producer has 2 free to run ahead
```

Right now the consumer releases its buffer immediately after draining, so it only ever holds one. To get cuBLAS's overlap, the consumer must **hold its buffer one iteration longer** — which drops the producer from 2 free to 1, and that starvation is what §H16.7 measured at −10–12%.

```
depth 3, holding one longer:   producer gets 1 free   <- starves, measured loss
depth 4, holding one longer:   producer gets 2 free   <- same margin as today
```

So the 4th buffer isn't the optimisation. It's what makes the optimisation affordable.

## And it isn't free either

Shared memory is fixed at ~231 KB. A 192x192 stage costs 49,152 B. Four of them is 196,608 B, leaving only ~35 KB for the epilogue buffer — less than the unchunked epilogue currently uses. So buying the 4th stage requires **chunking the epilogue** to shrink that buffer, and chunking alone measured **−4.42** on V3.

That's the whole bet: chunking loses 4.42 by itself, but it buys a 4th stage, which makes the drain overlap legal, which is worth up to +307µs. Nobody has tested the three together — each was tried alone and each lost alone.

If the smem doesn't add up, then at 192x192 this is structural and the tile cannot match cuBLAS without changing tile shape. That would be a legitimate finding to write down, not a failure.

## Re-reading their SASS for *stage ownership* rather than wait depth

```
LDS / BAR.SYNC
ARRIVE, 4 HGMMA          <- reads the stage acquired LAST iteration
DEPBAR (wait until 0)    <- drains everything, same as us
SYNCS.ARRIVE             <- release that stage
SYNCS.PHASECHK           <- acquire the NEXT stage
ARRIVE, 4 HGMMA          <- 8 wgmma issued on the new stage...
ARRIVE, 4 HGMMA
[back-edge]              <- ...and the body ends here
```

Count what's held: they **release** the old stage *before* they **acquire** the new one. Never both. **Exactly one stage held at a time — identical to us.** No extra buffer anywhere.

The overlap comes from somewhere else entirely: **they split the twelve wgmma for a given stage across the back-edge.** Eight at the bottom of one body, four at the top of the next. Between the last issue and the drain sit the back-edge, an `LDS`, a `BAR.SYNC`, an `ARRIVE` and 4 more wgmma — and that is the work their drain overlaps with.

## So the correction

I said "the fix is a fourth stage." **It isn't.** Depth 4 doesn't fit and isn't needed. The fix is to rotate the **issue**, not the drain:

```
ours today     acquire s -> issue all 12 on s -> drain 12 -> release s -> back-edge
cuBLAS         ...issue 8 on s -> back-edge -> issue 4 more on s -> drain -> release s -> acquire s+1
```

Same one stage held, same `wait_group<0>`, same 12 wgmma. The only difference is that four of the twelve are issued *after* the back-edge, so the other eight have somewhere to retire.

That also explains why every attempt so far failed. §H16.7 moved the *release*. §H27zbA moved the *drain*. §H27zbB split the *commit*. **None of them moved the issue** — and the issue is the only thing that was ever in the wrong place.

## What it costs to build

It's a genuine software-pipelining restructure: the four wgmma at the top of iteration *k+1* read the stage acquired in iteration *k*, so the stage index, the descriptor bases and the accumulator targets all have to be carried across the back-edge. That's real work in the consumer loop — bigger than the knobs so far — but it needs no shared memory, no extra buffer, and it keeps `wait_group<0>` and the release ordering exactly as they are, which is what all three adversarial lenses required.

Two ways, both checkable in seconds and I checked neither before proposing it:

## The fix

```
for k:
    issue the CARRIED 4 wgmma on s_prev        <- head, from last iteration
    commit; wait_group<0>                      <- drains 12 for s_prev; 8 are already old
    release_empty(s_prev)
    mbarrier_wait(s_k)                         <- acquire, after release
    issue 8 wgmma on s_k                       <- tail, crosses the back-edge in flight
    s_prev = s_k
after the loop: issue the final 4, commit, wait<0>, release
```

It keeps `wait_group<0>`, the full drain, and release-before-acquire — every invariant the three adversarial reviews demanded. It needs no shared memory and no extra stage.

> tool `Bash`: Annotate cuBLAS's k-loop by pipeline role

Fully reverse-engineered. Their execution order, with accumulator registers revealing the structure:

```
addr   samples   role                  what
3400     1,428                         LDS
3420     1,337   rendezvous            BAR.SYNC
3450       227   fence                 WARPGROUP.ARRIVE
3460    35,868   MATH #1-4  -> R24     4 wgmma on accumulator group A, reading the OLD stage
3500    29,727   DRAIN                 waits: these 4 + the 8 from last pass = 12
3510       488   RELEASE               free the old stage
3520       192   ACQUIRE               wait for the new stage to be full
3540       263   fence
3580    20,164   MATH #5-8  -> R72     4 wgmma on group B, NEW stage
3630       239   fence
3670    72,899   MATH #9-12 -> R120    4 wgmma on group C, NEW stage
3760             back-edge             <- 8 wgmma leave the body in flight
```

**The accumulator registers are the key.** `R24 / R72 / R120` are three *independent* accumulator chains — our `acc[0] / acc[1] / acc[2]`, one per m64 atom. Because they're independent, **the order between them doesn't matter.**

That's what makes the skew legal. For a given stage, cuBLAS issues groups **B and C right after acquiring it**, and group **A one loop-pass later** — still before releasing that stage. The loop pass is not a k-iteration; it's shifted by one accumulator group.

## The fix, transcription-ready

```
int s_prev = -1;
for k in 0..k_iters:
    if s_prev >= 0:
        wgmma_fence()
        issue atom 0's K_STEPS wgmma on s_prev      <- the carried head
        wgmma_commit_group()
        wgmma_wait_group<0>()                       <- drains atom0(prev) + atoms1,2(prev)
        release_empty(s_prev)
    mbarrier_wait(s_k)                              <- acquire, after release
    wgmma_fence()
    issue atoms 1..MAX_ATOMS-1 on s_k               <- 8 wgmma, leave in flight
    wgmma_commit_group()
    s_prev = s_k;  advance stage/phase
after the loop:
    wgmma_fence(); issue atom 0 on s_prev; commit; wait_group<0>; release_empty(s_prev)
```

Every invariant the three adversarial reviews demanded is preserved: **full drain before release**, **release before acquire**, **one stage held**. No shared memory, no fourth stage, no wait-depth change.

**The one real cost:** `A_smem`, `B_smem` and the descriptor bases are computed from `stage`, so atom 0's descriptors for `s_prev` must survive the back-edge. That's the restructure — carrying a small amount of state, not redesigning the pipeline.

1. **Compile gate** (local, no GPU): does ptxas fire `C7517` again, and does the SASS actually end the body with 8 HGMMA outstanding? Measure the same two numbers — in-body gap and HGMMA-crossing-back-edge. If it's still `0`, ptxas defeated it and we stop, exactly as §H27zbA died.
2. **Correctness gate** (GPU): bit-exact `maxRelErr 0.00000` on V3/V4/V5. The skew reorders accumulation across independent chains, so this must be exact, not close.
3. **Measure**: V5 first (biggest slope gap), V3 as the second 192x192 shape, and V8 as a control — V8 is intercept-dominated so it should barely move. If V8 moves as much as V5, the mechanism isn't what we think.

That question just caught a real error in what I'd written. Here's the finalised mapping, from §H27z.87:

## The 3-letter suffix is **two independent fields**, not one

**Letters 1–2 = the operand transpose.** Proven single-variable (shape fixed at 4096³, only our layout varied — we pick the input, cuBLAS picks the kernel, so it's not circular):

```
our nn  ->  ..._coopA_NN T      nn -> NN
our nt  ->  ..._coopA_TN T      nt -> TN     <- swapped
our tn  ->  ..._coopA_NT N      tn -> NT     <- swapped
```
3/3, and `nn`/`nt` produced the *identical* kernel config with only the suffix moving. The swap is the operand swap — their A is our B.

**Letter 3 = a function of the TILE, not the layout.** Held layout at `nn`, varied only the shape, and the letter moved N→T anyway. Across the 164-shape archive **no tile ever carries both letters**:

```
'N' <- 112x128  128x192  128x256  144x128  168x128  176x128  192x192
'T' <-  64x64   128x64   128x128  192x128  256x128  320x128
```

So for mapping purposes **the third letter is noise** — that's why the rule is written `NN*`, `TN*`, `NT*` with a wildcard. It tells you which tile cuBLAS picked, not anything we control. (And note **192x192 always carries `N`** — which is why all four of our variants end in `...N`: NNN, NNN, NTN, TNN.)

This also dissolved H8.5's old caveat: that sweep had *fixed* op flags, so all 18 kernels were `TN` — constant, exactly matching the fixed `OP_T/OP_N`. It only looked layout-independent because the layout never varied.

## And it corrects the table I gave you 10 minutes ago

I'd used *"cluster label unchanged"* — which is claim **[A]**, the one §H27z.86 explicitly proves **wrong** (it was mine, and it was circular). The proven rule is:

```
cuBLAS 1x2_h  ==  our 2x1 raster v
cuBLAS 2x1_v  ==  our 2x1 raster h        <- both are cluster 2x1; only the raster letter flips
```

- raster has **zero measured effect on duration** — 0.9% and 0.5% spread across rs2/4/8/16

## 4 — The real find: shared memory

Identical on all four: **132 CTAs, 384 threads, 168 registers**. Grid *shape* differs (cuBLAS `(2,66,1)`, ours `(132,1,1)`) but both are 66 clusters of 2 — a labelling difference, not a mismatch. Occupancy is 1 CTA/SM either way.

| smem/CTA | ours | cuBLAS | we use + | % of the 233,472 B SM |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3-stage (V3/V4/V5) | 222,208 | 188,604 | **+33,604** | **95.2%** vs 80.8% |
| 4-stage (V6) | 222,208 | 213,204 | +9,004 | 95.2% vs 91.3% |

Our dynamic smem is **identical (221,184 B) across all four configs**, and the arithmetic says exactly why:

```
3 stages + full store   147,456 + 73,728 = 221,184   EXACT
4 stages + 24,576 store 196,608 + 24,576 = 221,184   EXACT  (V6's ep16s2)
```

That confirms the H17 model on silicon: **depth = (BUDGET − STORE_BUF) / STAGE, with BUDGET pinned at 221,184.** Stages are bought by shrinking the epilogue buffer, one for one.

And it **re-explains §H27zbC's depth-4 ceiling**: 4 stages unchunked needs `196,608 + 73,728 = 270,336` — the exact number recorded there as "exceeds SM90 budget". That ceiling comes from reserving a full `BM×BN` store buffer, **not from the hardware**. cuBLAS runs the same tile at the same 3 stages in 188,604 B and sits on 44,868 B of headroom where we have 11,264.

**I'm not claiming this is the bottleneck.** Occupancy is 1 CTA/SM either way, and cuBLAS *chose* 3 stages while holding 44 KB spare — so depth clearly isn't what they were short of. It's a measured structural difference with a named consequence, to be read against the census.

```
R2UR  UR27, R175                            move the other half

UIADD3 UR16, UR11, 0x2040, URZ              base + literal offset

USHF.R.U32.HI UR16, URZ, 0x4, UR16          >>4, the smem descriptor encoding
```

**cuBLAS increments a descriptor that already lives in a uniform register. We rebuild ours from a base pointer, from scratch, before every single wgmma.**

Counts per k-iteration — both loops isolated by the same region finder, span 154 vs 66, **12 HGMMA and 0 TMA on both**, so these are the k-loops and not the tile loops:

| pattern | ours | cuBLAS |
|---|---|---|
| `ULOP3.LUT` mask/or into descriptor | 24 | **0** |
| `USHF.R` >>4 descriptor encode | 12 | **0** |
| `UMOV 0x40000040` reload | 12 | **0** |
| `R2UR` reg→uniform move | 24 | **0** |
| `LOP3`/`SHF`/`VIADD`/`IMAD` non-uniform | 22 | **0** |
| `UIADD3` descriptor advance | 14 | 26 |
| **bookkeeping total** | **111 / 154 = 72.1%** | **28 / 66 = 42.4%** |
| **per HGMMA** | **9.2** | **2.3** |

cuBLAS has **literally zero** of the first five categories. Two details worth naming:

- **`UMOV UR25, 0x40000040` is reloaded 12 times per k-iteration** with an identical immediate. It's loop-invariant and re-materialised before every wgmma.
- **`R2UR` ×24** shuttles descriptor halves from regular into uniform registers. cuBLAS never does this — theirs are *born* uniform and stay there.

Yes — same disease, and **no, we never actually fixed it.** Both your instincts are right. Here's the record.

## Q1: V8 — we tried, and it was rejected

§H27z.99b ran DESC_HOIST on V8. Its own SASS table:

```
mainloop      per k-step  per wgmma  R2UR  VIADD  LOP3  SHF  UIADD3  ULOP3
ep32s2 (pin)      94        23.5       8     2      9    4      9      9
ep32s2_dh         80        20.0       8     0      6    1      6      6
cuBLAS            24         2.0       0     -      -    -      2      -
```

> **R2UR UNCHANGED at 8** — the hoist removes the arithmetic but cannot remove the vector→uniform **CROSSING**, because `gdesc[]` demands a uniform operand while our descriptor is built in vector registers. cuBLAS pays zero crossings.

So it was a **half fix**: arithmetic collapsed (VIADD 2→0, SHF 4→1, LOP3 9→6), crossings untouched. Net **−0.6 pts on V8**, not adopted. On V3 the same knob gave +0.65 and was marked ADOPT — and never turned on.

## Q2: the magic-number change is a different target, same disease

§H27z.83 in its own words:

> MUFU has no uniform-datapath form. One runtime divide therefore pins the tile index, and everything derived from it, to the **VECTOR datapath** where it competes with HGMMA for issue slots. **Our 113 `R2UR` instructions are the visible symptom: values computed on the vector path being shuttled back into uniform registers.**

So both are *"work stuck on the vector datapath that belongs on the uniform one"*, with `R2UR` as the shared symptom. §H27z.83 fixed **one source** — the tile decode, per-*tile*, MUFU 6→0. The **descriptor source, per-*wgmma*, was only half-fixed.** Today's V3 SASS confirms it: **24 `R2UR` per k-iteration, still there.**

## And I traced the actual origin today — this is new

```
2b7a6310  S2R R7, SR_TID.X                 <- threadIdx.x. S2R = VECTOR form.
2b7a6500  SHF.R.S32.HI R0, RZ, 0x1f, R7       SR_TID has no uniform form.
2b7a6520  LEA.HI R0, R0, R7, RZ, 0x7
2b7a6540  SHF.R.S32.HI R3, RZ, 0x7, R0     <- R3 = threadIdx.x >> 7 = WARPGROUP INDEX
   ...
          IMAD R178, R3, 0x3000, R178      <- warpgroup_idx * 12288 + base
          VIADD / LOP3 mask / SHF>>4 / LOP3
          R2UR UR26, R172                  <- THE CROSSING
```

`0x3000 = 12288 = 96 × 64 × 2` — exactly the per-consumer-warpgroup A-tile offset (192 rows split across 2 consumers). **The A-descriptor base is a function of `threadIdx.x`, so ptxas can never hold it in a uniform register, so every use costs a crossing.**

The contrast is clean: inside the k-loop we *do* read `S2UR UR9, SR_CgaCtaId` — the **uniform** form — so the CTA-id path is fine. It is specifically `SR_TID.X` poisoning the descriptor. cuBLAS reads no special register in its k-loop at all.

**That explains why DESC_HOIST couldn't help**: once a value is born vector-side, ptxas must re-cross it on every uniform use — it won't permanently promote a vector-derived value into a UR across a loop. Hoisting the *arithmetic* was never going to remove the crossing.

## So the fix is narrower than what I proposed an hour ago

Not "make descriptors increments" — **DESC_HOIST already does that** (`a_desc_base + (a_off_bytes >> 4)`, compile-time offset). The actual target is: **get `threadIdx.x` out of the descriptor chain.**

The concrete candidate: the consumer warpgroups already run separate paths, so branch on the warpgroup and use a **compile-time immediate** offset in each arm, rather than multiplying a tid-derived register. The base then stays uniform and the offset is an immediate.

I have **not** verified ptxas will cooperate. That's a compile-only check — zero GPU time, same method that killed drain-rotation in §H27zbA. Want me to build it and check whether `R2UR` drops in the SASS before we spend any GPU?

## What was redundant, and it's gone

`nchunk0 = g * WG_NCHUNKS` comes from `threadIdx`, so the B descriptor was **vector-born** and every use cost a crossing back to uniform. The mainloop is now specialised per consumer warpgroup (`run_mainloop(IC<0>{})` / `IC<1>{}`), so `nchunk0` folds to a literal and the descriptor is built entirely from `UR11` plus compile-time offsets — one branch, outside the k-loop, on a warpgroup-uniform value.

Gated on a new `_UNIFORM_B_DESC` (slot 27). `IC<-1>` reproduces today's code byte-for-byte.

**The local build reproduces the box exactly** — the pin compiles to 154 instructions / 24 `R2UR` / 12 `UMOV`-const, instruction-for-instruction what the H200 capture measured. So these counts aren't an approximation.

- **`R2UR` 24 → 1** — the crossing is gone
- **`DESC_HOIST` alone leaves it at 24** — independently reproducing §H27z.99b's V8 result on a different tile. Genuinely orthogonal knobs
- **Together: 154 → 93 instructions (−40%)**, better than additive
- **REG:168, STACK:0, LOCAL:0, SHARED:2048** — identical on all four arms, no spill

And it exposes the next redundancy: **12 `UMOV UR25, 0x40000040` survive in every arm** — the same immediate re-materialised once per wgmma. cuBLAS has zero.

## What I'm not claiming

This does **not** prove a time win. DESC_HOIST removed 14.9% of instructions for +0.65; on V8 it removed 14% for nothing. Instruction count has repeatedly failed to predict duration here. The justification is exactly yours — it's redundant work and cuBLAS does the same job in 2.3 bookkeeping instructions per wgmma against our 9.2. The timing gets measured, not assumed.

Correctness is also unproven until it's gated on silicon.

## So the two biggest lines in the ledger are the same root cause

```
DRAIN wait     34.77 vs  9.75   +25.02   <-- wgmma SERIALIZED (C7520)
control flow   34.78 vs 12.93   +21.85   <-- the spin branch
                                 ------
                                  +46.87  of the +9.80 net gap
```

The barrier spin branch **is** the divergent path that forces ptxas to serialize the wgmma. That's why our wgmma-math is 9.85 where theirs is 47.38 — theirs overlap, ours can't. And it's why the drain is 3.6× theirs.

**The sleep fix already removes it** — proven, not predicted: no `ticks≠0` config raises C7520 in the same compile.

## Answering your question directly: no, it's not one problem — here are all five

| # | what the warp is doing | ours | cuBLAS | excess | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **DRAIN wait** | 34.77 | 9.75 | **+25.02** | ⬅ same root cause as #2 |
| 2 | **control flow** (92.8% = spin branch) | 34.78 | 12.93 | **+21.85** | ⬅ fix built & verified |
| 3 | uniform addr math | 16.03 | 8.48 | +7.55 | ✅ tested → **neutral** |
| 4 | reg↔uniform moves | 3.74 | 0.14 | +3.59 | ✅ tested → **neutral** |
| 5 | **smem `STS`** | 2.92 | 0.39 | **+2.53** | ❗ untested (they use `stmatrix`) |
| — | **WGMMA math** | **9.85** | **47.38** | **−37.52** | they're compute-bound, we're not |

**But #1 and #2 turned out to be the same thing**, which I didn't know an hour ago. The compiler said so and we'd never read it:

> `(C7520) wgmma.mma_async instructions are SERIALIZED due to compiler-inserted WG.AR in divergent path`

— on **`192x192 c2x1 h` NN and `c2x1 v` TN**, V3's and V5's shipped pins. And the divergent path is the spin branch, with `WARPGROUP.ARRIVE` sitting three instructions inside it.

Proven three ways: only `ticks=0` configs are flagged (every `_slp` config is in the same compile and isn't); the SASS shows WG.AR inside the branch; and it is *not* `my_nchunks`.

**That's 46.87 units of gross excess from one construct**, and it explains the −37.52: their wgmma overlap, ours are serialized so they can't.

## Two things I got wrong, both caught before they shipped

**I diagnosed `my_nchunks` as the divergent path and "fixed" it. A/B on the real TU: control C7520=2, fixed C7520=2. No change. Reverted — the tree is byte-identical to HEAD.** What nearly let it through: a small 4-instantiation probe compile shows **zero** C75xx on *both* arms, which reads as "fixed" if you only run the fixed side. The diagnostic only appears when the real ~90-config TU is compiled with `-DNDEBUG -use_fast_math`. Reproduce the symptom before claiming a fix.

**And your instinct about registers was right in a way I'd missed:** the build uses `-Xptxas -O3` with **no `-v`**, so spills are never reported. `cuobjdump -res-usage` locally found **V6's shipped pin spills 48 B**, its rs twins 144 B, and `sw128` 64 B — none of it visible in any build log.

**The bank-conflict ratio (16.1×) and the short-scoreboard ratio (14.0×) match almost exactly** — short_scoreboard *is* the shared-memory stall, so these are the same phenomenon measured two ways.

Bank conflicts on `l1tex__...pipe_lsu_mem_shared` count **LSU** shared traffic — `STS`/`LDS`. wgmma reads smem directly, not through LSU, so those aren't in this number. **These 9.2M conflicts are our epilogue's `STS` writes.** cuBLAS uses `stmatrix` instead.

And in a persistent kernel with `EPI_STAGES`, tile N's epilogue overlaps tile N+1's mainloop — so those conflicts contend with the wgmma's own smem reads, which is a coherent path to a slower drain and a cooler tensor pipe.

Let me check whether we have a stmatrix config for this tile.
> tool `Bash`: Check whether a 192x192 stmatrix config exists

**192x192 has no stmatrix variant** — only 128x256 and 256x128 do. And there's a real blocker: `EPI_USE_STSM` requires `EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES != 0`, and the epilogue swizzle measured **−12.88 on this exact tile** (§H27zb4).

```
current pin          144       0         3

swz64+STSM            0      42         9        <-- every scalar store gone
```

Three things fall out:

2. **`swz64+STSM` eliminates scalar stores entirely: 144 → 0, replaced by 42 `STSM`.** Against cuBLAS's 18 we're still 2.3× the instruction count, but these are conflict-free matrix stores instead of scattered 32-bit ones.

3. **REG:168 STACK:0 on all nine** — no spill, no register growth.

That's the mechanism the ledger pointed at (bank conflicts 16.1×, short_scoreboard 14.0×), attacked with the instruction cuBLAS actually uses. And I've built the control so the swizzle's cost and stmatrix's benefit get scored separately rather than as one number.

**Three things settled:**

**1. §H27zb4's −12.88 is confirmed, not stale.** On the new pin it reproduces at **−14.03**. I hypothesised the verdict might be masked like `dh_ubd` was. It isn't — the chunking cost is real and unmasked. That hypothesis is dead.

**3. But it can't get back to the pin.** On 192x192 you cannot have stmatrix without chunking, and chunking costs ~1 point more than stmatrix saves. **REJECT.**

## And the falsifier I wrote before the run

> *if `swz64stsm` is no better than the pin despite bank conflicts going 9.2M → near-zero, then the conflicts were never on the critical path.*

Bank conflicts eliminated → **still 0.95 slower.** So the 16.1× bank conflicts and the 14.0× short_scoreboard were **not on the critical path.** That's the fourth thing on this shape that was a real, large, measurable excess and cost nothing to remove.

You're right, and that reframes it correctly. Let me name the exact mismatch.

**cuBLAS can keep 8 wgmma in flight cheaply because their descriptor comes from `UIADD3` increments — two live stages cost them two adds. Ours is rebuilt from a stage base, so two live stages cost 24 extra `R2UR` crossings.** Copying their structure imports a cost they don't pay.

So the question isn't "how do we do what they do" — it's **"how do we get drain overlap with only ONE cheap stage descriptor?"**

And there's an answer sitting in our own code: **`LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH` is 3, and the stage index is a runtime `% 3`.** If the k-loop is unrolled by 3, every stage index becomes a **compile-time literal** — 0, 1, 2 — and so does `head_stage`. Both descriptors then fold into compile-time offsets from the uniform base, and the two-live-stages problem disappears entirely.

That also explains something we observed and never used: **cuBLAS has five distinct k-loop bodies (spans 66/69/70/149/150). We have one.** They specialise; we don't. Not because specialising is their trick — because it's what makes *our* descriptor path work.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-18 16:12 IST]

Yes — and the cause is derivable from the traces we already have. Let me check one thing I've never measured: **the instruction spacing between consecutive HGMMA.**

The tensor pipe goes idle when nothing is queued. If our wgmma are issued further apart than cuBLAS's, the pipe drains *between* issues, not just at the DEPBAR.
> tool `Bash`: Measure HGMMA issue spacing on both sides

**Found it. This is the cause, and it's provable from the traces.**

```
                        before 1st HGMMA    in gaps    AFTER last HGMMA
OURS                         22.4%            3.5%          56.6%
cuBLAS                       16.5%           17.1%           1.6%
```

**56.6% of our k-loop sits after the last HGMMA. cuBLAS spends 1.6%.**

Our HGMMA are *already* tightly packed — gaps of 2, and the last four are back-to-back (gap 0). **Issue spacing is not the problem.** The entire difference is *where the loop ends*:

```
ours     [ issue 12 ] [ DEPBAR — drains to ZERO, 56.6% ] [ back-edge, pipe EMPTY ]
cuBLAS   [ issue 4 ] [ DEPBAR, counted mid-gap ] [ issue 8 ] [ back-edge, 8 IN FLIGHT ]
```

cuBLAS's 17.1% "in the gaps" is their DEPBAR sitting *inside* the HGMMA sequence. Ours is at the end. So their pipe never empties and **ours empties every single k-iteration** — that's the 88.3 vs 92.1 tensor%, and it's the whole slope gap.

**Carrying work across the back-edge is the only fix**, and for us it costs 48 `R2UR` because two live stages can't both stay uniform. Which is exactly the thing to fix on our side — make the stage a compile-time literal so both cost the same.
> tool `Bash`: Make the stage compile-time and check whether R2UR collapses

**`R2UR` 48 → 0.** The two-live-stages problem is solved — both descriptors are now compile-time offsets.

```
arm       instrs  HGMMA  R2UR  inflight
pin          211     37     1        0
skew2        279     38     0       25
```

Two caveats I have to state: the instruction counts are now **static and inflated** — the 3-way dispatch means the loop body contains three copies of the issue sequence but **only one executes per iteration**, which is also why the region-finder reports 37–38 HGMMA instead of 12. The real number is the *dynamic* count from ncu, not this.

And **this change touches `issue_atoms`, which every config uses** — so the gate has to cover the shipped pins, not just skew2.

## Yes — and they *are* all related. Here's the pattern

| what we changed | what it touched | result |
|---|---|---|
| `rs8` (tile order) | **where data lives** (L2) | **+3.27** ✅ |
| `dh_ubd` (descriptors) | **which register file** | **+0.77** ✅ |
| instruction count ×3 | *when* instructions issue | nothing |
| spin → NANOSLEEP | *how* we wait | counters identical |
| stmatrix | *which* store instruction | −0.95 |
| SKEW ×2 | *order* of issue | −0.78, −2.81 |

**Everything that worked changed where data goes. Everything that failed changed when instructions issue.**

And the counters say exactly why: `issue_active` **18.9% vs cuBLAS 13.5%**, `inst/cyc` 0.189 vs 0.135. **We have 40% more issue headroom than they do.** The issue pipe is nowhere near saturated, so instruction-level changes get absorbed by slack. Only data-placement changes move the clock.

## But then why did SKEW *lose* 2.8, if instructions are free?

Because its cost isn't instructions. **SKEW holds a stage across the back-edge, so the release happens later** — and §H16.7 measured exactly that at −10 to −12% ("deferring the release steals a pipeline buffer").

**Our producer is already 33% of the kernel. cuBLAS's is 12%.** SKEW makes the consumer smoother by making the producer wait longer — and ours is the one with no slack. cuBLAS can afford that trade; we can't.

## So the circle is:

```
consumer drains 12 wgmma to zero  ->  releases the stage late
   -> producer parks on EMPTY (24.6% of the kernel)
      -> stage refills late
         -> consumer's pipe is empty at the back-edge (22.4%)
            -> tensor% 88.3 vs 92.1
```

**With 3 stages there is no slack anywhere to absorb any of it.** cuBLAS also runs 3 — but their consumer releases fast (DEPBAR 9.77 vs our 34.23), so 3 is enough for them.

## Where we're actually going wrong — and it's one decision

```
smem, same tile, same 3 stages:   ours 222,208 B     cuBLAS 188,604 B
our 221,184 dynamic = 3 stages (147,456) + a FULL BM*BN store buffer (73,728)
```

**We reserve a whole 192×192 store buffer. cuBLAS reuses the mainloop stage memory for the epilogue** — the CUTLASS union trick, flagged in H17-RESULT and never acted on. That's why a 4th stage costs us 270,336 B (over the 233,472 B SM) and is impossible.

**That single allocation choice is why every scheduling fix has failed: there is no pipeline slack to absorb anything.** It's not that our mainloop is worse — it's that we have no room to hide latency, so every attempt to smooth one side starves the other.

Freeing ~33 KB via the union is the only lever that *adds* slack instead of redistributing it. It's also a real structural change to the epilogue, not a knob.

```
8 HGMMA issued after it = 8 in flight across the back-edge
```

**No mask, no shift, no `R2UR`, no rebuild, no second base.** The descriptor is initialised once outside the loop and walked with adds — including the wrap.

## So: is `dh`/`ubd`/`skew` "crap we invented"?

**No — `dh` and `ubd` are us catching up to what they get for free**, and the numbers say so: `dh_ubd` = **+0.77**, `rs8` (matching their measured grouped walk) = **+3.27**. Those aren't inventions, they're two thirds of the way to their descriptor.

**But we're not there.** Ours still costs 9.2 bookkeeping instructions per wgmma against their **2.3**, because `dh` hoists the descriptor *per stage* and then rebuilds it at each stage change. Theirs is never rebuilt at all — the `-0x400` at the back-edge walks it around the ring.

**And that's exactly why SKEW fails.** Their 8-in-flight needs no second descriptor, because there's only ever *one* register being advanced. Ours needs two live bases → 48 `R2UR` → +73 instructions → −2.8.

So you're right and I've been going at it backwards: **SKEW isn't a separate feature to add. It's free once the descriptor is a single incremented register.** I kept trying to bolt their *structure* onto our *addressing*, and paid for the mismatch every time.

The one thing to implement is what's on screen above: **one loop-carried descriptor register, advanced by constants, wrapped at the back-edge.** Then the 8-in-flight ordering costs nothing and the DEPBAR moves off 34.23.

That's a real change to the mainloop addressing — not a knob — and it's the last item. Given I've broken the build once today and had two analysis errors, I want to build it against the SASS check (does `R2UR` go to 0 *and* the k-loop drop toward 66) before any GPU time, exactly as we did for `ubd`.

Current committed state is clean and holds today's real wins: **V3 91.30 → 94.17, V4 91.08 → 94.41.** Want me to build the single-register descriptor now?

> tool `Bash`: Read the DescriptorIterator advance mechanism
> tool `Bash`: Read the descriptor advance body

**Found it. Definitive, and it's simpler than everything I built.**

```cpp
// CuTe DescriptorIterator::operator+
DescriptorIterator operator+(Index const& offset) const
{
    // Use 32bit calculation rather than 64 bit calculation as we only update part of desc
    GmmaDescriptor ret;
    ret.reg32_[0] = desc_.reg32_[0] + uint32_t(offset);   // ONE 32-bit add
    ret.reg32_[1] = desc_.reg32_[1];                      // upper half NEVER changes
    return { ret };
}
```

**CUTLASS holds one descriptor and advances it with a single add to the low word.** The upper 32 bits — leading-dim, stride, swizzle mode, layout type — are built once and never touched. That is *exactly* cuBLAS's `UIADD3 UR16, UR16, 0x2`.

**What we do instead:** call `make_gmma_desc_k_major(A_smem + off)`, which rebuilds *every* field including the upper 32 bits that never change — that's the `LOP3` mask, the `SHF`, the `OR`, per wgmma.

So:
- **neither reference specialises the stage** — CUTLASS uses a runtime `read_stage`, and it costs them nothing
- **the stage index was never the problem.** My `sp` dispatch, the unroll idea, SKEW's "two live stages" — all of it was solving a problem created by *our own descriptor construction*
- with a single walking descriptor, two live stages is just **two adds from one base**

And the arithmetic is already proven safe in our own tree — §H27z.99b: `desc(base+off) == desc(base) + (off>>4)` given 16-byte alignment and `base+off < 0x40000`. CuTe relies on the identical property (`start_address_` is 14 bits holding `addr>>4`; our max smem 232,448 < 262,144, so no carry into bit 16).

**The correct fix, matching both references:** hoist the descriptor base to *per-tile* scope and make the stage part of the added offset — instead of rebuilding the base per stage inside `issue_atoms`.

```
now:   a_desc_base = make_gmma_desc(smem_base + st*copy_size + atom_off)   // rebuild, per stage
       a_desc      = a_desc_base + (k_off >> 4)

right: a_desc_tile = make_gmma_desc(smem_base)                             // ONCE per tile
       a_desc      = a_desc_tile + ((st*copy_size + atom_off + k_off) >> 4)
```

That's one add, no rebuild, no crossing, no dispatch — and it removes the reason SKEW ever cost anything.


**The producer is not starved — it's idle waiting for a buffer back.** It only waits 6.37% the other way. I said earlier "our producer is 33% of the kernel, it has no slack." ## Does cuBLAS have `rs8` / `dh` / `ubd`?

**`rs8` — yes, effectively.** §H27z.88/.89 measured their memory fingerprint as *grouped rasterisation at group ~4–8*. They walk tiles in groups; we didn't. `rs8` is us copying their behaviour, and it's the +3.27.

**`dh` / `ubd` — no, and they don't need them.** They never rebuild a descriptor at all:
```

```
There's no "hoist" or "uniform" knob in their design because the descriptor is *born* uniform and never reconstructed. Our `dh`/`ubd`/`dw` are all us **catching up to what they get for free** — not features they have.

```cpp
// Use 32bit calculation rather than 64 bit calculation as we only update the part of desc
ret.reg32_[0] = desc_.reg32_[0] + uint32_t(offset);   // low word only
ret.reg32_[1] = desc_.reg32_[1];                      // high word copied, never added
```

**They add 32 bits. We add 64.** The address field lives entirely in the low word, so the carry can never reach the high word — which is why they can skip it and we shouldn't be computing it.

## Where we are

**Today's question was: why has SKEW never worked.** SKEW is the only structure that crosses the k-loop back-edge with wgmma still in flight — 8, which is cuBLAS's number — and it measured negative every single time.

**The cause is one statement.** A 20-arm SASS bisection, holding the loop body fixed and toggling only where `stage` is advanced:

```
peel does NOT advance                 96 instr   R2UR  2   IMAD  1
peel advances `phase` only            98 instr   R2UR  2   IMAD  1   <- phase is free
```

The peel advanced `stage` *and* so did the loop latch, so `stage` reached the loop header as a phi of two distinct computed definitions. ptxas then can't prove the descriptor chain warp-uniform, dumps all of it on the vector datapath, and pays 48 `R2UR` crossings per iteration handing descriptors back. **Not the modulo** — compare-select moved IMAD 33→31 and R2UR not at all.

Along the way three of my own earlier explanations died: two-live-stages, the 64-bit descriptor add, and the sentinel branch. §H27zd3 had already replaced the sentinel with a peel — **both cures cost the identical 48**, which is why it never came out ahead.

**Fixed:** advance moved to a single site (loop top, K−1×) plus one in the tail (1×) = K per tile, unchanged.

```
shipped SKEW           162     12    48       2    33         8
FIXED (dw+skew)        102     12     0      39     0         8
FIXED (dh_ubd+skew)    113     12     0      17     0         8
cuBLAS                  66     12     0      26     -         8
```

**Zero crossings, zero vector integer math — cuBLAS's profile — while keeping the 8-in-flight back-edge.**

2. **Non-skew is byte-identical to HEAD** — the shipped pin `rs8_dh_ubd` is the same 3,096 instructions; only `dw+SKEW` moved (3440→3272). `REG:168 STACK:0` throughout, no spills.
