### CLAUDE [2026-08-18 19:14 IST]

Good question, and it's the right thing to challenge. Let me not hand-wave it — those are `ptxas info`, not warnings, but there are two families and only one is harmless. Checking locally:
> tool `Bash`: Decode which ptxas GMMA diagnostics fire per config

No `C7518`/`C7520` — **the serializing ones don't fire at all.** Only `C7517` (wait injected) ×2 and `C7519` (arrive injected) ×4, and only on the skew arms; the pin fires nothing. So they *are* new. The question that matters is whether an injected wait landed **inside the k-loop**, because that would re-serialize it and kill the whole point:
> tool `Bash`: Check whether injected waits serialize the k-loop

Answered, and it's clean:

```
arm            k-loop DEPBAR   HGMMA   in flight   kernel-wide DEPBAR
pin (no skew)              1      12           0                    3
dh_ubd+SKEW                1      12           8                    7
dw+SKEW                    1      12           8                    7
```

**Nothing was injected into the k-loop.** It still has exactly **one** DEPBAR — same as the pin — and 8 wgmma still cross it in flight. If ptxas had injected a guard before the back-edge, `inflight` would read 0, and it doesn't.

The 4 extra DEPBARs are **outside** the loop, in the peel and the tail. That's expected: skew has more wgmma-group boundaries (peel commits once, loop commits twice, tail commits once), and ptxas guards the ones where the accumulator is read. Those run **once per tile**; the loop runs K−1 times per tile (K=32 on V3), so they're amortised ~32:1 and are not on the hot path.

So, honestly:

- **Not wrongly implemented.** No `C7518`/`C7520` — the *serializing* diagnostics — fire at all. Those are the ones that mean ptxas gave up and forced ordering.
- **Not free either.** 4 extra DEPBAR per tile is a real cost I'm not going to call zero. It's small and off the hot loop, and the measurement will include it.
- The old note in the docs said this was "expected and benign"; I re-derived it against the new code rather than trusting it, and it holds.

**`tensor%` is the gap itself, not a clue.** It measures what fraction of active cycles the tensor core is actually doing work: ours 89.1, cuBLAS 92.1. On mio_throttle — worth flagging before we park it, because it changes whether it's even worth doing later: **it isn't a knob you turn up.** It measures how backed-up the memory instruction queue is. Raising ours to cuBLAS's 15% wouldn't make us faster; it would just mean our memory pipe is more congested. Their higher number is most likely a *consequence* of finishing each iteration faster (more memory ops per unit time), not the cause of it. So "flush data more efficiently like cuBLAS" is a real goal, but `mio_throttle` is the wrong scoreboard for it. Parked, with that caveat recorded.

Now — tensor core usage. The first question has to be **where** the idle is, and there's a sharp fork:

- **per-k-iteration** → it's the mainloop, and SKEW left something on the table
- **per-tile** → it's the epilogue/prologue, and the mainloop is done

That fork is directly measurable by fitting `time = a + b·K`: the intercept is per-tile, the slope is per-k-iteration. On the **old** pin that fit gave slope = 103% of the gap, intercept ≈ 0 — pure mainloop. But SKEW changed the mainloop by 1.62 points, so that fit is stale and has to be redone before we decide anything.

## What the four phases decide

| phase | question | what it changes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | does 95.83 reproduce on this box | scales the ledger; a big move means the box changed |
| 2 | **producer waiting on EMPTY, or consumer waiting on FULL?** | opposite fixes — this picks one |
| 3 | does mio_throttle track %cuB across V3/V5/V7/V8? | kills or keeps the starvation story |
| 4 | **is the gap per-tile or per-k-iteration?** | mainloop vs epilogue — picks the next target |

Phases 2 and 4 are the ones that matter. If phase 4 says the gap moved into the **intercept**, the mainloop is finished and the epilogue is next. If it's still the **slope**, SKEW left something and we stay in the mainloop. Either way we stop guessing after this run.

P4 puts the mbarrier acquire between atom-0's commit and the drain:

```
acquire(stage)          <- the consumer's FULL-wait now overlaps atom-0's retirement
wait_group<0>           <- still a full drain, so no race
release(head)
issue atoms1,2(stage); commit
```

## What the measurement found

**The gap is the consumer draining its own wgmma — and the producer is slack, not cost.**

```
                    OURS      cuBLAS
PRODUCER region    34.11%     15.68%
  barrier wait     26.20%      6.55% + 3.75% sleep
CONSUMER region    63.47%     73.26%
  wgmma MATH       19.59%     45.79%
  DEPBAR drain     21.44%      9.42%
  barrier wait      5.52%      5.57%   <- identical to 0.05 points
```

The consumer's wait-for-data matches cuBLAS exactly, so the producer is keeping up completely — its 26% is idle-ahead. **`mio_throttle` is dead as a lead for the second time**: V5 runs 5.96 with tensor% 97.4 and still sits at 83% cuB; V7/V8 run ~0.00 and are our best shapes.

**Two of my own errors, both corrected:**

- The first role-split reported "no samples". The ncu CSV is two-level (kernel name, *then* the real header), and it matched `SYNCS.PHASECHK` when **the stall lands on the branch consuming the predicate**. Our barrier waiting was hiding in the "control flow" bucket the whole time — six `@!P1 BRA` sites totalling 28.3%. "Control flow" was never control flow.
- "Closing tensor idle → 99%" holds for V3 (1.0440 × 89.1/92.1 = 99.0%) but **is not a general law** — V5 is 1.2 tensor-points from cuBLAS and still 17 points behind.

## The fix built for it

Per pass we issue 12 wgmma: 8 at acquire, 4 (atom 0) one pass later. SKEW gave the 8 a full pass; the 4 still issue **immediately** before the drain covering them. `ACQ_FIRST` puts the stage acquire in between. SASS: **102 → 100 instrs, R2UR 0, IMAD 0, 8 in flight, DEPBAR still `0x0`, no spills.**

Rejected on correctness: `wait_group<1>` would leave atom 0 outstanding across the release — the producer could overwrite smem mid-read. ptxas emits `0x1` faithfully; my earlier note that it overrides it was wrong.

**Ceiling stated up front: bounded by the 5.52% FULL-wait, so expect a fraction of that — not the 12-point DEPBAR gap.** If it's flat, the drain is intrinsic wgmma latency and the next lever has to change the wgmma schedule itself.

Per our own rule, a box change voids all prior timings — so 95.79 on V3 is not a number I can trust on this machine until it's re-measured. Also worth noting there's already a `python` process holding 2074 MiB on that GPU, so it isn't idle.

Tree is clean at `1d899aa` and matches the box exactly — the phase-3 TFLOPS fix is in, all six skew arms registered, V3 pinned to `192x192x64_2x1_h_rs8_dw_skew`.

## Where we are

**V3 went 91.30 → 95.79 yesterday (+4.49), bit-exact.** Three things were adopted and one big thing was understood:

| change | gain | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `rs8` grouped rasterisation | +2.27 | tile order, L2 reuse (DRAM 2.11 → 0.864 GB) |
| `dh_ubd` efficient descriptor | +0.77 | descriptor datapath, R2UR 24 → 1 |
| **`skew` single-advance fix** | **+1.62** | 8 wgmma cross the back-edge, cuBLAS's structure |

The skew one was the day's real finding: the feature had measured negative every time for weeks because the peel advanced `stage` as well as the loop latch, which made ptxas abandon the uniform datapath for the whole descriptor chain (48 `R2UR` per iteration). One line moved → `R2UR 0, IMAD 0, 102 instrs, 8 in flight`.

**The barrier stall is now essentially closed:** 32.25 → 23.10 → 19.17 against cuBLAS's 18.42. And that's what makes today interesting — `tensor%` is still 89.1 vs 92.1 **with the barrier matched**, so the remaining idle is no longer warps waiting at barriers. The F/V refit says the gap is now **~75% per-k-iteration, ~25% per-tile** (the script printed 43% per-tile, but that was driven by a K=512 outlier; drop it and R² goes 0.84 → 0.99 with the intercept halving).

Rejected honestly: `ACQ_FIRST` (looked +0.48 at 7 reps, went +0.22 and overlapping at 15), `dw` alone, the 32-bit descriptor add, and `wait_group<1>` — that last one on **correctness**, it races the buffer release.

## Four things open

1. **Re-baseline** — new box, so every number above is unverified here
2. **V5 at 83.0%** — worst of the family by 12 points, same 192×192 kernel, and skew measured a clean zero on it

4. **The dispatcher cannot name `rs8_dw_skew`** — so BluTrain currently sees **none** of yesterday's gains

**Found it, and it's in our own harness — not the kernel, not the hardware.** The script that would have caught this was written and marked *"unrun, if it ever matters."* It matters now.

Three defects in `examples/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix.cu`, all of which scale with kernel duration — which is exactly why V3 (1.0 ms) is steady and V4 (4.5 ms) swings:

**1. V4 averages ~4 launches, V3 averages ~20.** `TARGET_MS = 20.0`, so `iters = 20/probe_ms`:

```
V3  16384x11264x2048 -> 7.56e11 flop -> ~1.0 ms -> iters ~ 20
V4  16384x50304x2048 -> 3.38e12 flop -> ~4.5 ms -> iters ~  4
```

Four samples measures the clock **ramp**, not steady state.

**2. Warmup is asymmetric.** Ours gets **5** warmup launches (line 826); cuBLAS gets **1** (line 685). At 4.5 ms that's 22.5 ms of conditioning for us against 4.5 ms for them.

**3. cuBLAS is always timed first** (line 708 vs line 840), so our kernel always inherits a GPU that just ran ~20 ms of saturated tensor work. Systematic, not random.

And the clincher is in the older note: when this was seen before, **both kernels swung ~7% and were anti-correlated** — we went up as they came down. Two unrelated kernels cannot do that on their own; only a shared machine state being handed back and forth produces it.

So to answer you directly: **not a race, not a silent bug in the kernel, and not really "hardware fluctuation" either.** `maxRelErr` is 0.00000 on every single rep including the 87% and the 101%, so the arithmetic is deterministic. It's our measurement method, and it biases every long-kernel `%cuB` number this campaign has produced.

|---|---|---|

Two things jump out:

So the machine *can* produce stable numbers; our kernel is the less repeatable of the two on that shape. That's a small but real signal about our kernel, separate from V4.

Locking helps **V3** a lot — both kernels then track each other almost perfectly and the ratio tightens to 1.5%. It barely touches **V4**. So clock/power is a real methodology improvement but it is *not* what makes V4 swing.

That makes sense in hindsight: 400 iterations of a 1 ms kernel is 400 ms of sustained full-power compute, which is the throttling failure mode the original `MIN_IT=3` comment warned about. **The right window depends on kernel duration** — too few iterations gives ramp noise, too many gives throttle noise. A single fixed `TARGET_MS` can't be right for both a 1 ms and a 4.5 ms kernel.

Worse, the same protocol gave V3 a 1.1% spread in one run and 4.4% in another. That's **between-rep** variation, and more iterations *within* a rep cannot fix it.

## What's actually broken in how we compare

Every script measures **config A nine times, then config B nine times** — sequential blocks. If the GPU drifts over the minutes between them, A and B are measured under different conditions, and the difference between their means picks that up as signal. That is exactly the shape of a spurious +1.62.

The fix is **paired, interleaved measurement with a null control**:

- measure A and B back-to-back *within* each rep and take the **per-rep difference**, which cancels drift
- rotate the arm order each rep to cancel ordering
- include the **same config twice under two labels** — if the protocol reports a difference between two identical configs, the protocol is broken and no result from it means anything

That null control is the piece we have never had, and it's what tells us the protocol's actual resolution — whether we can even detect a 1-point effect.

Good — let me not touch anything until this is proven. Three facts already, and one of them changes the framing:

**All three kernels use exactly 168 registers.** So this is *not* ordinary register pressure that a smaller footprint would relieve — the budget is identical and hard-capped. 384 threads × 168 = 64,512 of the SM's 65,536 registers, so 168 is the architectural ceiling for 3 warpgroups at 1 CTA/SM. **We cannot give it more registers.** Any fix must reduce what's live.

Now the question that decides whether this even matters:

**41 of 46 spill ops are inside a loop**, and the kernel is **14,624 instructions** against the non-chunked 192×192's ~3,096 — 4.7× bigger, with **864 `STS`**. The chunked epilogue is generating an enormous amount of code.

But static placement isn't the same as hot. The decisive question is whether any spill sits inside the **k-loop** specifically:
> tool `Bash`: Determine if any spill is inside the k-loop

Decisive:


**Only 1 of 46 spill ops is inside the k-loop. 45 are in the epilogue.** And the k-loop is essentially unchanged in size (154 → 159). So the spill is almost entirely epilogue-resident — which means the "48 B spill blocks V6" framing I gave you yesterday may be overstated. The k-loop runs 32× per tile; the epilogue runs once.

But the chunked epilogue **explodes the static code 6.3×** (2,304 → 14,624 instructions, 144 → 864 `STS`). That's the real anomaly, and whether it costs anything is a *dynamic* question static SASS can't answer.

Before designing GPU tests, one more thing has to be settled statically, because it determines whether removing chunking is even legal:
> tool `Bash`: Get SHARED memory and pipe depth for both configs

All three report `SHARED:2048` — that's only the *static* allocation; the kernel uses dynamic shared memory, so `cuobjdump` can't tell us what chunking actually buys. Let me get the real numbers straight from the template's own constants:
> tool `Bash`: Find the derived smem/depth constants
> tool `Bash`: Read the depth/smem derivation

`DERIVED_PIPE_DEPTH = (SMEM_DYNAMIC_BUDGET − STORE_BUF_BYTES) / STAGE_BYTES` — so chunking shrinks `STORE_BUF_BYTES` to buy pipe depth. That's exactly the trade. Let me print the real numbers:
> tool `Bash`: Locate the smem constants and enclosing struct
> tool `Bash`: Print the real smem/depth trade for V6

Now the trade is fully quantified — and this reframes the whole thing:

```

192x192_h (no chunk)   49152     73728       3    221184   11264
192x192_h_ep16s2       49152     24576       4    221184   11264
```

**Chunking cuts the store buffer 73,728 → 24,576 — exactly one stage — and buys `LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH` 3 → 4.** That is the entire reason `ep16s2` is V6's pin. The 48 B spill and the 6.3× code are what it *pays* for that depth.

So the real question isn't "fix the spill" — it's **"is depth 4 worth what it costs, and is there a cheaper way to buy it?"**

```
EPI_TILE_N=16 STAGES=2  <-PIN   12      24576
EPI_TILE_N=32 STAGES=1           6      24576   <- SAME smem, HALF the chunks
EPI_TILE_N=24 STAGES=1           8      18432   <- LESS smem
EPI_TILE_N=16 STAGES=1          12      12288
EPI_TILE_N=8  STAGES=1..3       24    6144-18432
```

**`32/1` buys the identical depth-4 for the identical shared memory with half as many chunks** — which should roughly halve that 6.3× code explosion, and may take the spill with it. The cost is no epilogue double-buffering.

## On CUTLASS — I checked before asserting, and it's not what I expected

I was about to tell you CUTLASS unions mainloop and epilogue smem. It doesn't:

```cpp
struct TensorStorage : cute::aligned_struct<128, _1> {
  EpilogueTensorStorage epilogue;      // both are plain members,
  MainloopTensorStorage mainloop;      // NOT a union
} tensors;
```

In `sm90_gemm_tma_warpspecialized_cooperative.hpp` they're co-resident, same as ours. So that's not a free win sitting in the reference implementation, and I'd have been wrong to claim it.

## What I think we should do

V6's static analysis stands on its own — it needed no GPU and it's solid: depth-4 + our knobs costs a 200 B spill and 15,840 instructions, depth-3 + our knobs is 2,808 instructions with zero spill. That's real and reproducible.

But **we cannot currently measure which is faster.** A 4.4-point floor cannot resolve the differences we're chasing, and running V6 A/Bs now would just generate more numbers we'd have to retract later.

I'd rather fix the instrument first. The floor has a specific, findable cause — two identical binaries should not differ by 1.43 ± 3 — and the candidates are narrow: `%cuB` re-measures cuBLAS every call so both numerator and denominator move; the harness may be re-picking a cuBLAS kernel per call; and 100 ms may be the wrong window for a 0.5–1 ms kernel.

The arithmetic confirms it: at 3 stages, `231424 − 3×49152 = 83,968` bytes remain, and a full 192×192 store buffer is 73,728. **It fits with room to spare — no chunking needed.** That's exactly our plain `192x192x64_2x1_h`. cuBLAS doesn't spill because they never tried to squeeze in a 4th stage.

```
nvjet_hsh_192x192_64x3_1x2_h_bz_coopB_NTN      <- 3 stages

nvjet_sm90_tst_192x192_64x4_1x2_h_bz_coopB_TNN <- 4 stages
```

**cuBLAS uses both 3-stage and 4-stage 192×192 kernels** and picks per shape. So "cuBLAS uses 3 stages" was wrong — they absolutely do run 4 stages on this tile.

Which means your question is the right one: **at 4 stages, how do they not spill?**

Here's the arithmetic that makes it sharp. A 192×192 fp32 accumulator across 2 consumer warpgroups:

```
192 x 192 = 36,864 accumulators / 256 threads = 144 registers per thread
168 register cap - 144 accumulators = 24 registers for EVERYTHING else
```

That's the real cause of the spill, not the epilogue. And there's a Hopper feature that exists precisely for it:
> tool `Bash`: Check setmaxnreg in our kernel and CUTLASS

**This is the root cause, and it's exactly what you said — cuBLAS/CUTLASS do it correctly and we don't.**

CUTLASS:

```cpp
static constexpr uint32_t LoadRegisterRequirement = !HeavyRegisterPressure ? 40 : 24;
static constexpr uint32_t MmaRegisterRequirement = !HeavyRegisterPressure ? 232 : 240;

cutlass::arch::warpgroup_reg_dealloc<LoadRegisterRequirement>();   // producer GIVES UP registers
cutlass::arch::warpgroup_reg_alloc <MmaRegisterRequirement>();     // consumers TAKE them
```

**The producer drops to 40 registers; the consumers take 232.** We run everyone at a flat **168**.

And that is precisely our spill:

```
192x192 accumulators / 256 consumer threads = 144 registers per thread
ours:    168 - 144 =  24 left for everything else  -> SPILLS
CUTLASS: 232 - 144 =  88 left                      -> no spill
```

Now look at V6's own config — the numbers are already there:

```cpp
Sm90WarpspecConfig<192, 192, 64, 2, 1, 0, true, true, 1, 0, 0, 0, 40, 232, ...>
                                                             ↑↑  ↑↑↑
                                        LoadRegisterRequirement  MmaRegisterRequirement
```

**40 and 232 — CUTLASS's exact values.** We wrote the split in, and it is not taking effect: every kernel comes out at 168.

The template says why, in two places that contradict each other:

```
line 3704:  gated on Config::USE_REGISTER_SPLIT (default OFF, ...)
```

The docs claim `§H27y.7 SOLVED` it — *"spill went 5124/6108 → 0/0 across all 169 kernels, C7507 and C7512 both gone, our SASS now contains the same SETMAXREG.TRY_ALLOC.CTAPOOL/.DEALLOC.CTAPOOL pair cuBLAS uses."* But V6 spills today at 168 registers. Let me check what's actually in the binary:

**The register split IS working** — my memory note saying it was removed is stale and wrong:

```
SETMAXREG.DEALLOC.CTAPOOL   0x28   = 40   (producer gives up)
SETMAXREG.TRY_ALLOC.CTAPOOL 0xe8   = 232  (consumers take)
```

Present in all five kernels, exactly CUTLASS's 40/232. `§H27y.7 SOLVED` is accurate. So we already do what CUTLASS does — and depth 4 **still** spills:

```
232 consumer registers − 144 accumulators = 88 free
depth 3, full-tile epilogue      -> 0 spill      (88 is enough)
depth 4, chunked epilogue        -> 46 spill     (12 chunks of bookkeeping is not)
depth 4, chunked + our knobs     -> 398 spill
```

So the chunked epilogue's own bookkeeping — 12 chunks, double-buffered, with indices, smem pointers and predicates live — is what breaks 88 registers. That's the real mechanism.

Now, your question: **how does cuBLAS run `192x192_64x4` without this?** We have their actual SASS captured. Let me read it:
> tool `Bash`: Reverse-engineer cuBLAS's epilogue from captured SASS

**Now we're getting somewhere. Four concrete differences, all in the epilogue:**

```
                     cuBLAS      ours
SETMAXREG          24 / 184    40 / 232      <- they take FEWER registers
epilogue STS             21         144      <- 7x more scalar smem stores
epilogue STSM            18           0      <- they use stmatrix, we use NONE
UTMASTG                  12           3
F2FP (fp32->bf16)        72         144      <- they convert with half the instructions
total instructions     1280        3272
```

**cuBLAS's consumer takes only 184 registers — *less* than our 232 — and still doesn't spill.** They don't need more registers; they need fewer, because their epilogue is fundamentally leaner: **18 `STSM` (stmatrix) instructions where we issue 144 `STS`**.

And `F2FP` 72 vs 144 says they pack two accumulators per conversion instruction where we do one.

Let me decode the exact instruction forms rather than infer:
> tool `Bash`: Decode exact epilogue instruction forms, cuBLAS vs ours

**Reverse-engineered. Here is exactly how cuBLAS writes its epilogue and how we do:**

```
cuBLAS                                    ours
 72x  F2FP.BF16.F32.PACK_AB R, R, R      144x  F2FP.BF16.F32.PACK_AB R, R, R   (same instruction)
 18x  STSM.16.M88.4 [R+UR], R              0x  ---
  3x  STS  (edge cases only)             144x  STS [R+IMM], R
 12x  UTMASTG.3D [UR], [UR]                3x  UTMASTG.3D [UR], [UR]
```

The conversion instruction is **identical** — both use `F2FP.BF16.F32.PACK_AB`. The difference is entirely in how the converted data reaches shared memory:

**cuBLAS: 18 `STSM.16.M88.4`. We: 144 `STS`.**

`STSM.16.M88.4` is **stmatrix** — one instruction moves four 8×8 16-bit matrices cooperatively across the warp, straight out of the registers in the layout wgmma already left them in. Check the arithmetic: 4 matrices × 64 elements = 256 elements per warp per instruction, × 18 instructions × 8 consumer warps = **36,864 = exactly 192×192**. One clean pass over the tile.

Our `STS [R+IMM], R` stores a register at a computed address. **Every one of those 144 stores needs its own address arithmetic held in registers** — and that is precisely what has no room left when the chunked epilogue is also holding 12 chunks of double-buffered state. It's why cuBLAS needs only 184 consumer registers while we ask for 232 and still spill.

So the answer to your question is: **cuBLAS doesn't spill because their epilogue costs almost no registers, not because they have more of them.**

And we already have the knob for this:
> tool `Bash`: Check the existing stmatrix knob

You're right, and let me answer the question directly instead of adding more threads.

## Are we comparing apples to apples? **No.**

cuBLAS's kernel for this tile is `nvjet_hsh_192x192_64x3_1x2_h_bz_coopB_NTN`. Here is every difference:

| | cuBLAS | ours | same? |
|---|---|---|---|
| tile | 192×192×64 | 192×192×64 | ✅ |
| raster | h | h | ✅ |
| stages | 3 (also has 64x4) | 3, or 4 with chunking | ⚠️ |
| **cluster** | **1×2** | **2×1** | ❌ |
| **coopB** | yes | not implemented | ❌ |
| **register split** | **24 / 184** | 40 / 232 | ❌ |
| **epilogue store** | **18× STSM** | 144× STS | ❌ |

So four real gaps. I've been reporting them one at a time as I found them, which made it look like I kept changing my story. That's on me — this is the full list.

## Why can't we just do what they do?

Honest status of each, no spin:

1. **1×2 cluster — we already have it.** `192x192x64_1x2_h` is built and registered. We simply pin the 2×1 version. This is a one-line pin change.
2. **Register split 24/184 — trivial.** They're template parameters. `40, 232` → `24, 184`.
3. **STSM epilogue — we have the knob, and it has a known bug.** `_EPI_USE_STSM` exists. It was pulled because `128x256x64_2x1_h_swz64stsm` produced wrong answers in 299 of 5766 cases, root-caused in the code comment to *"the stsm_lane_off hoist"*. So the feature is written but broken, and the bug is already located.
4. **coopB — genuinely not implemented.** This is a structural variant (cooperative tile shape), the one real piece of new work.

So three of the four are things we already built and simply aren't using, and the fourth is the only actual gap.

## Why we're still spilling

Not because we have fewer registers. **cuBLAS takes 184 and we take 232 — they need fewer.** Their epilogue writes the tile with 18 `stmatrix` instructions; ours needs 144 `STS`, each with its own address arithmetic held in registers. That address bookkeeping is what has no room left. Fix the epilogue store and the spill goes with it.

## What I propose, in order

```
1. pin the 1x2 cluster           -- already built, one line
2. set register split 24/184     -- template parameters
3. fix the stsm_lane_off bug     -- already root-caused in our own comment
4. coopB                          -- the only new work
```

Every one of these is verifiable in SASS with no GPU — spill count, `STSM` present, register split values — so the measurement problem doesn't block any of it.

## Answering your question: why does cuBLAS get depth 4 free and we don't

Both of us want 4 stages. The difference is what we each **pay** for it:

```
                              instructions   spill    tensor%
ours, depth4 (chunked)         169,816,061   48 B      78.5
ours, depth3                    87,416,800    0 B      88.9
cuBLAS, depth4                  54,673,658    0 B      92.7
```

cuBLAS reaches depth 4 by having an epilogue so cheap it barely needs shared memory or registers — **18 `STSM` instructions**. We reach depth 4 by chopping the epilogue into 12 double-buffered chunks, which costs **169.8M instructions and a 200 B spill once our knobs are on.**

So the answer is: **depth 4 isn't the problem — our way of buying it is.** Our chunked epilogue costs more than the 4th stage is worth, which is why depth 3 wins by 10 points. cuBLAS pays almost nothing for the same depth.

```
WGMMA math            7.22     48.22     -39.70
```

**cuBLAS spends 48% of its samples doing actual matrix math. We spend 7%.** Same pattern as V3 — our time goes to waiting (the "control flow" is the outlined barrier-spin branches) and draining, not computing.

## Two things I got wrong, corrected

2. **"cuBLAS uses 3 stages"** — no, they use 4. Depth 3 won only because *our* depth-4 implementation is expensive. Right action, wrong reasoning.

And the honest caveat, recorded in the pin: **this is the best available config, not the apples-to-apples match.** Matching cuBLAS means depth 4 *with a cheap epilogue*.

## Answering your question properly

You asked: we both implement stage 4, so how do they avoid the spill and we don't?

```
                    instructions    spill   tensor%
ours depth4         169,816,061     48 B     78.5
ours depth3          87,416,800      0       88.9
cuBLAS depth4        54,673,658      0       92.7
```

**cuBLAS gets four stages for 55M instructions. We pay 170M for the same four stages.** They don't need the smem freed by chunking, because their epilogue moves the tile with 18 `STSM` instructions instead of 144 `STS` — no per-element addresses to compute, nothing to hold in registers, no 12-chunk double-buffered bookkeeping. Their epilogue is nearly free, so the 4th stage costs them nothing.

Ours costs so much that dropping the 4th stage is worth **+10 points**.

That is a complete, evidence-backed answer to "why do they not spill and we do" — and it points at exactly one piece of work: **the STSM epilogue.** Fix that, and depth 4 becomes genuinely cheap for us too, which is the only path to matching cuBLAS rather than working around them.

## The cause, and it's one thing

Every 1000-instruction block of our epilogue is **~55% address arithmetic** (`IMAD` 4317, `LEA` 1179, `SHF` 870, `IADD3` 625, `VIADD` 488 = 7,479 total). Because we write the tile with **864 scalar `STS`**, each one needs its own address built per-thread on the vector datapath:

```
IMAD  R171, R185, 0xc0, R168     <- row*192 + col, per element
ISETP.GE.AND P3, ...             <- bounds check, per element
LEA   R188, P1, R171, UR16, 0x1  <- 64-bit address, per element
```

cuBLAS writes the same tile with **18 `STSM.16.M88.4`** — one instruction moves four 8×8 matrices for the whole warp, straight out of the wgmma accumulator layout. **No per-element address exists to compute.** Their entire epilogue address math is ~450 *uniform* ops.

So: **we pay 169.8M instructions and a 200 B spill because our epilogue computes 7,479 addresses that cuBLAS never computes at all.** The spill is downstream of that — those addresses have to live in registers, and at 232 registers with 144 taken by accumulators there is no room.

## The alternative to that cause

`STSM`. We already have `_EPI_USE_STSM`, and it's disabled because of a known bug. Let me read it:
> tool `Bash`: Read the known stmatrix bug

**The stmatrix bug was already fixed** — §H27za8: *"RE-REGISTERED after the stmatrix address bug was found and fixed... re-derived from `epi_swz_index`; enumerated over every (band,rr,am,gl): 0 mismatches at C_BOX_N 32 AND 64."*

So `STSM` works. It's just never been enabled for **192×192** — only for 128×256 and 256×128.

And there's a constraint that makes this fall out neatly:

```
static_assert(!_EPI_USE_STSM || _EPI_TILE_N % 32 == 0, ...)
static_assert(!_EPI_USE_STSM || _EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES != 0, ...)
```

`EPI_TILE_N` must be a **multiple of 32**. Our V6 pin uses 16 — which is why STSM could never have been on. And from the design-space sweep I ran earlier, of every legal depth-4 chunking there is exactly one that satisfies it:

```
EPI_TILE_N=32, EPI_STAGES=1   ->  6 chunks, STORE_BUF 24576, DEPTH 4, and 32 % 32 == 0
```

Let me build it and check in SASS, no GPU:
> tool `Bash`: Build 192x192 depth-4 with STSM and check spill

The compiler is telling me the exact constraint:

```
C_BOX_N*2 must equal EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES exactly (SW128 -> C_BOX_N 64, SW64 -> 32, SW32 -> 16).
A tile whose WGMMA_N is not a multiple of that width (e.g. 192x192, WGMMA_N=96)
must pick a narrower mode.

EPI_USE_STSM: C_BOX_N == EPI_SPAN*8, i.e. EPI_TILE_N*2 == EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES
```

So `C_BOX_N` is derived from `WGMMA_N`, not from `EPI_TILE_N`, and 192×192 has `WGMMA_N = 96`. Let me read how it's computed before guessing a value:
> tool `Bash`: Read how C_BOX_N and WGMMA_N are derived

Found it — the constraint is `C_BOX_N = EPI_TILE_N` when chunking, so `EPI_TILE_N × 2 == EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES`. My `SWZ=128` arm violates it (32×2=64≠128). That one's illegal; `SWZ=64` should be fine. Rebuilding without it:

```
V6 old pin + knobs (16/2)        15840      0   864       7198    192 B      371
32/1 + swizzle, no STSM          14168      0   432       6684      0 B        0
32/1 + swizzle + STSM             4224     42     0        789      0 B        0   <-- FIX
cuBLAS (whole kernel)             1264     18     3        ~450      0          0
```

**15,840 → 4,224 instructions. Address math 7,198 → 789, a 9× cut. Spill 192 B and 371 operations → zero.** And it keeps **depth 4**, so it matches cuBLAS's stage count instead of working around it.

Two things that tells us:
- **The 4th stage genuinely isn't worth it for us**, even with a clean epilogue. `EPI_STAGES=1` means no epilogue double-buffering, so the store can't overlap — that's likely what's left.
- **The knobs add nothing on this arm** (90.29 → 90.36) whereas they matter on depth 3.


**Depth 4 costs a flat ~5 points on all three shapes** — −5.06, −5.02, −4.81 — regardless of shape, with the controls reproducing to 0.03 and 0.14. This measurement is solid.

And the counters agree independently:

```
                barrier  shortsb   mio   issue%  tensor%    instructions
D4 + STSM        23.45    2.63    4.71    20.9    84.9      93,474,076
D3               22.23    1.37    7.41    20.5    88.9      87,411,018
cuBLAS           20.19    0.18   14.80    13.3    92.7      54,673,438
```

Depth 4 is worse on **tensor% (84.9 vs 88.9)** *and* **instruction count (93.5M vs 87.4M)**. Two independent signals, same direction.

## Why depth 4 loses — and it's a hard constraint, not a tuning miss

```
depth 4:  STORE_BUF = 24576, EPI_STAGES = 1  ->  6 chunk stores, NO double buffering
depth 3:  STORE_BUF = 73728                 ->  ONE full-tile store
```

Depth 4 leaves only 34,816 bytes for the epilogue. The store buffer costs `STAGES × 2 × BM × EPI_TILE_N × 2`, and STSM requires `EPI_TILE_N` to be a multiple of 32. So double-buffering at depth 4 needs `EPI_TILE_N ≤ 22` — **and 22 is not a multiple of 32.**

**Depth 4 + STSM + a double-buffered epilogue is arithmetically impossible on 192×192.** Depth 4 can only ever have a serialized single-buffered epilogue here, and that serialization is the ~5 points.

## What STSM did achieve

It was not wasted — it's the biggest structural fix we've made:

```
                      instrs   addr-math   spill      WGMMA share of samples
depth4 old (ep16s2)    15840      7198    192 B/371 ops        7.22%
depth4 + STSM           4224       789    0 / 0               19.25%
cuBLAS                  1264      ~450    0                   48.32%
```

**WGMMA share tripled, 7.22% → 19.25%.** Address math down 89%. Spill gone. It just can't overcome the serialized epilogue that depth 4 forces.

## Where the remaining gap now is

```
                  ours%   cuBLAS%   excess
control flow      35.92    10.17    +29.56   <- barrier-wait branches
DRAIN wait        21.29    10.57    +12.99
uniform addr math 13.61     7.94     +7.11
WGMMA math        19.25    48.32    -27.03
TOTAL            110.61   100.00    +10.61
```

The epilogue is no longer the problem — it's barrier waiting and the wgmma drain, same as V3.

**You were right to push, and I was wrong.** I only considered the BM-tall buffer and missed a third mode that exists in our own template:

```cpp
STORE_BUF_BYTES =
  EPI_ATOM_STAGED   ? (NUM_CONSUMER_WARPGROUPS * EPI_STAGES * EPI_SLOT_ROWS * EPI_TILE_N * 2)
: USE_CHUNKED_EPILOGUE ? (EPI_WG_SLOTSETS * EPI_STAGES * BM * EPI_TILE_N * 2)
                       : (BM * BN * 2);
```

**`EPI_ROWS=64` stages one m64 atom — 64 rows instead of all 192.** That's 3× smaller, and it changes the arithmetic completely:

```
budget at depth 4                                    34,816
BM-tall,   32 wide, 2 stages:  2*2*192*32*2 =        49,152   > budget  (what I checked)
ATOM(64),  32 wide, 2 stages:  2*2* 64*32*2 =        16,384   FITS
ATOM(64),  32 wide, 3 stages:  2*3* 64*32*2 =        24,576   FITS
ATOM(64),  32 wide, 4 stages:  2*4* 64*32*2 =        32,768   FITS
```

**Depth 4 + STSM + a double- (or even quadruple-) buffered epilogue is entirely possible.** I retract "arithmetically impossible."

And the cuBLAS evidence lines up: their highest shared-memory address is **0x344c8 = 214,216**, and 4 stages take 196,608 — leaving **17,608 bytes** of epilogue space. ## On your question — how cuBLAS beats us on barrier and drain

Decoded from their SASS, and it's two specific mechanisms:

**1. They sleep on a barrier miss; we spin.**

```
cuBLAS:  @!P0 NANOSLEEP.SYNCS 0xc350      <- 3.72% of their samples, 0xc350 = 50000 ticks
ours:    barrier SLEEP 0.00%              <- we never sleep
```

Their `barrier SLEEP` is 4.02% and ours is **0.00%**. Our wait is a tight spin — `TRYWAIT; @!P BRA self` — and `SYNCS` issues through the MIO pipe, so spinning burns MIO bandwidth and issue slots **on the same SM as the consumer warpgroups**. That is why our `mio_throttle` is 4.71 against their 14.80: they're using that bandwidth for memory, we're using it to poll.

This was tested before (§H27zc7, the `slp` arms) and measured **flat** — but that was on the old pin, when the 14,000-instruction epilogue was masking everything. §H27zd0's own rule applies: *a category is only actionable once whatever masks it is removed.* The epilogue tax is now gone, so this is worth re-testing rather than treating as settled.

**2. Their drain is half ours** — `DEPBAR` 10.57% vs 21.29% — which is what SKEW attacks, and SKEW is already on in these arms.

Let me wire both up and use the remaining GPU window:
> tool `Bash`: Add atom-staged and sleep arms, full build

```
opcode    static   samples   % of kernel

F2FP         336      409      0.66%

STSM          42      176      0.29%

--------------------------------------
DEPBAR         6    11871     19.23%   <- 6 instructions
BRA          212    19288     31.24%   <- 212 instructions
HGMMA         48    11255     18.23%
```

**218 instructions out of 4,216 — 5% of the code — consume 50.5% of the kernel.** Those are the stalls, and everything else is rounding error.

So three of my assumptions are dead:

| | assumption | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **D** | `FMUL` 672 redundant | **2.26%** — real but small; an `alpha==1` specialisation is worth ~2 pts at most |
| **E** | `LDG` 168 in a beta=0 epilogue | **0.00% — DEAD.** Predicated off, never executes, costs nothing |
| **F** | `F2FP` 336 vs 72 | **0.66% — DEAD** |

I was counting instructions that don't cost time. That's exactly the trap this project has hit three times before, and I walked into it again.

```
BRA      31.24%   <- warps stalled on the barrier predicate  (hypothesis C)
DEPBAR   19.23%   <- the wgmma drain
HGMMA    18.23%   <- our productive work.  cuBLAS: 48.32%
```

**Hypothesis C is now clearly the biggest single lever**, not a side idea. Those 212 `BRA` are the outlined barrier spin, and cuBLAS's equivalent is `NANOSLEEP` at 4.02% where we sit at 0.00%.

## And G — the measurement floor has a cheap fix

The 4.4-point floor comes from `%cuB` being a **ratio with two noisy terms** — we re-measure cuBLAS on every call. But ncu's per-launch duration for *our kernel alone* already showed **1.6% spread on V6, 2.9% on V3**. Measuring our own duration directly removes cuBLAS's variance and the harness loop entirely, which should put the floor well under 1 point.

```bash
v=[x for x in v if x>0]

"
```

One decisive structural fact, straight from our own source:

```cpp
line 268:  static constexpr int NUM_CONSUMER_WARPGROUPS = 2;   // cooperative: both on one tile
line 309:  static_assert(BM % NUM_CONSUMER_WARPGROUPS == 0, ...)

```

**We are cooperative by design** — both warpgroups split M on the *same* tile and march the same k-loop, so they hit the same barriers and drain in lockstep. There is no stagger knob.

But **ping-pong is register-infeasible on this tile**, so cuBLAS's asymmetry can't be that either: in ping-pong each warpgroup owns a *whole* tile, and 192×192 accumulators over 128 threads is **288 registers/thread against a 232 ceiling.** So I'm dropping the ping-pong reading of R3 — more likely their two clusters are a peeled iteration plus the steady-state loop (2 clusters × 12 wgmma = their 24 total), which has nothing to do with warpgroups.

## The honest bottom line on the 192×192 family

**Our best configuration is depth 3, and cuBLAS's is depth 4.** They can afford four stages because their epilogue costs 260 instructions and 9.65% of samples. Ours costs 4,224 instructions even with STSM — so our fourth stage costs more than it earns, every way we've built it (five variants tested).

That is the real structural difference, stated plainly: **not that we chose the wrong depth, but that our epilogue is 16× theirs and that forecloses the depth they use.**

Where we ended up today:

| V | this morning | now | config |
|---|---|---|---|
| **V6** | 84.80 | **95.34** | `192x192x64_2x1_h_rs8_dh_ubd_skew` |
| **V4** | 91.08 | **96.56** | same |
| **V3** | 91.30 | **95.79** | same |

And on depth 3 the remaining ~4.7 points are fully accounted for: `tensor% 92.7/88.9 = 1.0427` against a cycle ratio of `1.0490`. Nothing unexplained is left — only tensor idle, whose lever is the stage depth we can't currently afford.

Let me bank the confirmed wins, because all three pins still point at older configs:
> tool `Bash`: Repin V3 and V4 to the measured best config

Let me settle whether tensor% is a cause or a symptom, because the arithmetic matters here:
> tool `Bash`: Decompose tensor busy vs idle cycles

**Definitive — and it reframes your question exactly right.**

```
                  tensor BUSY    tensor IDLE    cycles
ours (depth3)         745,550         93,089    838,639
cuBLAS (depth4)       740,230         58,292    798,522
                   -----------    -----------
                   0.72% apart    +34,797 EXTRA
```

**Tensor-busy cycles are identical (0.72% apart) — as they must be, since the wgmma counts are bit-identical.** So `tensor%` is a **symptom, not a cause**: the same work in more total cycles mechanically lowers the percentage.

**cuBLAS does not use the tensor cores more efficiently. They use them exactly as much. They just have less dead time between uses.**

The entire gap is **34,797 extra idle cycles = 1,780 per tile** — and 87% of the total cycle gap. What predicts 1,780?

```
epilogue instructions:  ours ~2,808   cuBLAS 260   ->  difference 2,548
measured extra idle per tile:                           1,780
```

Same order of magnitude. **The epilogue is the tensor idle** — not through bank conflicts or address math (both dead), but simply because **no wgmma issues while it runs.**

So there are exactly two ways out, and only one is new:

1. **Shrink the epilogue further** — we've gone 13,836 → 2,808 instructions; cuBLAS is at 260. Still 10×.
2. **Overlap the epilogue with the next tile's mainloop.** The TMA store is asynchronous — once accumulators are staged into smem, the mainloop *could* restart immediately. If we currently block on the store completing before the next tile, that's dead time we're choosing to take.

Path 2 would hide the epilogue rather than shrink it, which is the bigger lever. Let me check what we actually do:
> tool `Bash`: Check if we block on the TMA store before the next tile

**Found it.** Two different store-wait policies in our code:

```cpp
line 4780:  if (lane_in_wg == 0) tma_store_wait<Config::EPI_STAGES - 1>();   // chunked: PIPELINED
line 5064:  if constexpr (!Config::USE_CHUNKED_EPILOGUE) tma_store_wait<0>(); // non-chunked: FULL DRAIN
line 5071:  if (lane_in_wg == 0) tma_store_wait<0>();
```

`tma_store_wait<0>` is `cp.async.bulk.wait_group.read 0` — **wait until every outstanding TMA store has completed.** And our best config, the depth-3 pin, is the **non-chunked** path, so it takes the full drain. The chunked path already leaves `EPI_STAGES-1` stores in flight, which is what CUTLASS does (our own comment at line 4766 says so).

Let me read the exact context before claiming it:
> tool `Bash`: Read the store-wait context on the non-chunked path

**Found the dead time, and the code says exactly why it exists:**

```cpp
tma_store_commit();
if constexpr (!Config::USE_CHUNKED_EPILOGUE) tma_store_wait<0>();   // <- our depth-3 pin
...
// "drain every outstanding store before this CTA moves to its next tile
//  and starts overwriting c_buf again."
if constexpr (Config::USE_CHUNKED_EPILOGUE) ... tma_store_wait<0>();
```

**Both paths fully drain the TMA store before starting the next tile**, and the stated reason is correct as far as it goes: the next tile will overwrite `c_buf`, so the store must finish first.

**But it waits far too early.** The next tile's *mainloop* never touches `c_buf` — it writes the A/B pipeline stages, which are a separate smem region (`SMEM = DEPTH×STAGE + STORE_BUF`). Only the next tile's *epilogue* touches `c_buf`.

So we stall the whole SM waiting for a store, when we could run **32 k-iterations of the next tile** first and only wait immediately before the next epilogue needs the buffer. That is dead time we are choosing to take, and no wgmma can issue during it — which is precisely the 1,780 idle cycles per tile.

That's the mechanism, it's the same pipelining CUTLASS does, and the fix is to move one wait:
> tool `Bash`: Locate the first c_buf write and confirm smem separation

**Confirmed safe:** `store_smem = smem_base + LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH * copy_size` — `c_buf` sits *after* all A/B pipeline stages, a completely separate region. The next tile's mainloop cannot touch it.

Let me read the epilogue entry and its sync structure before I move a barrier — getting this wrong means silent corruption or a hang, not a slowdown:
> tool `Bash`: Read epilogue entry and its barrier structure

Now I have what I need. The pattern is `lane 0 waits, then barrier_sync(g)` — and there's **already a `barrier_sync` at the top of the epilogue (line 4641)**, so the wait can sit immediately before it and be correctly covered. Implementing:
> tool `Bash`: Implement the late store wait and build

Built clean, all three layouts, 0 errors 0 warnings.

## To answer your question directly

**Tensor-core usage is the *symptom*, not the cause — and cuBLAS does not use the tensor cores more efficiently than us. They use them identically.**

```
                 tensor BUSY    tensor IDLE     cycles     wgmma issued
ours (depth3)        745,550         93,089     838,639      7,925,760
cuBLAS (depth4)      740,230         58,292     798,522      7,925,760
                  0.72% apart    +34,797
```

Bit-identical wgmma counts, and tensor-busy cycles **0.72% apart**. `tensor%` is lower for us purely because the same busy cycles are divided by more total cycles. **The entire deficit is 34,797 extra idle cycles — 87% of the 40,117-cycle gap — at 1,780 per tile.**

**And I found where those idle cycles come from.** Our own code, with the reason written next to it:

```cpp
// "drain every outstanding store before this CTA moves to its next tile
//  and starts overwriting c_buf again."
tma_store_wait<0>();
```

We fully drain the epilogue's TMA store **at the end of every tile**, and no wgmma can issue while it drains. The reasoning is sound but the placement is far too early: the next tile's **mainloop never touches `c_buf`** — `store_smem = smem_base + LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH * copy_size` puts it past every A/B stage. Only the next tile's *epilogue* needs that buffer.

So the wait now sits at the **top of the next epilogue**, with **32 k-iterations between commit and wait** to hide the latency. It reuses the `barrier_sync` already there, in the same lane-0-waits-then-sync pattern as the existing chunk-recycling wait, and the recycling `wait<EPI_STAGES-1>` is untouched — that guards slot reuse *within* a tile, a different guarantee.

```
cuBLAS                                 192x192_64x4                     DEPTH=4
```

So we reached **99.44 / 99.79 / 98.53 with a *shallower* pipeline than cuBLAS** — three stages against their four.

That needs stating plainly: **we are not apples-to-apples on stage count. We match their performance with a different structure.**

The reason is a hard smem constraint, not a choice:

```
full-tile epilogue buffer      = 192*192*2 = 73,728 B
4 stages                       = 4*49,152  = 196,608 B
196,608 + 73,728 = 270,336  >  231,424 budget   -> IMPOSSIBLE
```

**Depth 4 forces a chunked epilogue** (to fit the buffer in ~34 KB), and every chunked variant we built — five of them, including STSM and atom-staging — tops out at 92.16. The chunked epilogue costs about 7 points more than the fourth stage earns. Depth 3 with a full-tile buffer *and* the pipelined store wins outright.

And note `_lsw` did nothing for the depth-4 arm (92.16 → 92.11) because chunking was already pipelined — so the two fixes aren't additive there.

**What that leaves as a future lever:** cuBLAS runs depth 4 with a ~17.6 KB epilogue buffer, and we now know how to build a 16.4 KB one (atom-staged, STSM, zero spill). If the chunked epilogue can be made as cheap *per tile* as the full-tile one, depth 4 + `_lsw` should beat 99.4 rather than sit at 92. That's the only remaining path to actually matching their structure — but it isn't needed to match their speed, which we now do.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-19 16:06 IST]

I misspoke, and it's worth correcting precisely: **that constraint applies to *us*, not to cuBLAS — because cuBLAS never uses a full-tile epilogue buffer at all.**

Measured from their own SASS:

```
cuBLAS max smem address   0x344c8 = 214,216
4 stages                            196,608
                          ------------------
their epilogue buffer       ~        17,608 B      <- NOT 73,728
```

A full 192×192 buffer is 73,728 B and could never fit there. **They use a small, atom-staged epilogue — exactly the 16,384 B thing we built.** So nothing was impossible for them; I stated our constraint as if it were universal.

So what *are* we doing differently? It's not the buffer — we match that now. It's the **code**:

```
                   epilogue instrs   F2FP   FMUL   address math
cuBLAS                       260       72      0   ~380 UNIFORM (UIADD3/UIMAD/UMOV/ULDC)
ours (depth4+STSM)        ~3,500      336    672   ~740 VECTOR  (IMAD/SHF/LEA)
```

**`F2FP` 336 vs 72 is the tell.** With 144 accumulators per thread, 72 `F2FP.PACK_AB` (two accumulators each) covers the whole tile exactly once. We emit **4.7×** that — which means our conversion-and-store code is **duplicated per chunk**, fully unrolled across the 6 chunks, where cuBLAS emits it once and loops (their 72 `BRA` says loops).

That also retro-explains why `ea32s4` regressed: more epilogue stages meant more unrolled copies, not more overlap.

Let me check whether that's really what our code does:
> tool `Bash`: Check whether the epilogue chunk loop is unrolled

Let me correct myself again, because I just repeated the mistake I flagged this morning — **quoting static instruction counts as if they were time.**

Our epilogue's accumulator loops are fully unrolled and produce exactly the right count:

```
MAX_ATOMS(3) x WG_NCHUNKS x CREGS_CHUNK = 144 accumulators / 2 per F2FP.PACK_AB = 72
```

**72 — identical to cuBLAS.** So we don't convert more than they do. The 336 in the census is ~4.7 *copies* of the same code, because we emit specialised variants:

```cpp
line 4894:  if (beta == 0.0f) { ... }                                    // fast path
line 4946:  if (beta != 0.0f && global_row < M && global_col + 1 < N) {  // general path
```

Two beta paths × residue variants. And we already proved those copies **don't execute**: the `LDG` living in the beta≠0 copy took **0.00% of samples**, and all FP epilogue math together was 2.13%. So that difference is **code size, not time** — I shouldn't have presented it as the gap.

## So, straight answers

**"How does cuBLAS do depth 4?"** They use a ~17.6 KB atom-staged epilogue buffer, not a full-tile one. The 270,336 > 231,424 arithmetic was *our* constraint for a *full-tile* buffer, and I wrongly implied it bound them too. We can build their buffer — 16,384 B, already done and spill-free.

**"What are we doing differently?"** On the winning config: nothing about the buffer. We just chose the other side of a real trade:

```
depth 3 + full-tile buffer   ONE store commit + ONE barrier per tile   -> 99.44 / 99.79 / 98.53
depth 4 + chunked buffer     SIX store commits + SIX barriers per tile -> 92.16 best of 5 variants
```

Depth 4 buys one more stage of prefetch and pays **six times the epilogue synchronisation**. On these shapes the prefetch is worth less than the sync costs, so depth 3 wins by ~7 points. That's a measured trade, not a limitation — and `_lsw` can't rescue depth 4 because chunking was already pipelined (92.16 → 92.11, flat).

**And the honest bottom line:** we're at 99.4–99.8% of cuBLAS with a *simpler, shallower* pipeline than theirs. Matching their exact structure would require making 6 chunked stores as cheap as 1 full-tile store — which is real work for at most the 0.2–1.5 points we're still short, and only on V6. **V5 at 82.46 is 17 points behind and is where the actual remaining value is.**

### CLAUDE [2026-08-19 16:08 IST]

Good — but let me check the legal space first, because there's a constraint that may block it:
> tool `Bash`: Map the legal chunk-count space at depth 4

All four fit depth 4. But there's a hard constraint worth naming: **`EPI_TILE_N` must divide `WGMMA_N=96` *and*, for STSM, be a multiple of 32 with `EPI_TILE_N×2` a legal swizzle (32/64/128).** Only **32** satisfies all three — 64 doesn't divide 96, and 96 would need a 192-byte swizzle.

**So 6 chunks is forced if we want STSM.** Fewer chunks means giving up stmatrix. That makes it a clean two-way trade to measure:

```
2 chunks, no STSM   -> 3x fewer store commits/barriers, but scalar stores + address math
4 chunks, no STSM   -> middle
6 chunks, STSM      -> current best, 92.16
```

Building all three with `_lsw`:
> tool `Bash`: Add fewer-chunk depth-4 arms and build

Direct answer, from what's measured rather than guessed.

## What we do that is already identical to cuBLAS

```
wgmma issued        7,925,760  vs  7,925,760   bit-identical, verified on 3 shapes
tensor-busy cycles    745,550  vs    740,230   0.72% apart
F2FP needed per thread     72  vs         72   identical
register split       setmaxnreg both (40/232 vs 24/184)
tile / cluster / raster                        match
```

**So we are not doing extra math, extra conversions, or extra tensor work. None of it.**

## The one extra thing we were doing — found and fixed today

```cpp
tma_store_wait<0>();   // at the END of every tile
```

We waited for the epilogue's TMA store to fully drain **before starting the next tile**, when the next tile's mainloop never touches that buffer. **No wgmma could issue during that wait.** That was **34,797 idle cycles = 1,780 per tile = 87% of the entire gap.**

That is the answer to "what extra are we doing": *we were stalling the SM on a store we didn't need to wait for yet.* Moving that one wait took V3 to 99.44, V4 to 99.79, V6 to 98.53.

## What's still extra, and only at depth 4

At depth 4 the epilogue must be chunked (the buffer won't fit otherwise), so we do **6 store commits + 6 barriers per tile** where the depth-3 full-tile path does **1**.

But here's the thing that says this is *our* overhead and not inherent: **cuBLAS issues 12 TMA stores per tile** — they chunk more finely than we do — **and pay nothing for it**, because their entire epilogue is 260 instructions. So chunking itself isn't the cost. Our per-chunk barriers and bookkeeping are.

That's exactly what the arms I just built measure:

```
2 chunks, no STSM  (96/1)
4 chunks, no STSM  (48/2)
6 chunks, STSM     (32/3)  = 92.16 today
```

If fewer chunks climbs toward 99, the per-chunk **sync** is the overhead and depth 4 is reachable. If it falls, STSM matters more and depth 4 is capped where it is.

```
chunks  config                      %cuB     range
  1     depth3 full-tile + lsw     98.56  [97.9, 99.4]
  2     ea96s1  (no STSM)          96.37  [96.0, 96.9]   -2.19
  4     ea48s2  (no STSM)          94.54  [94.4, 94.8]   -1.83
  6     ea32s3  (STSM)             91.94  [91.5, 92.3]   -2.60
```

Every doubling of chunk count costs **~2 points**, ranges all separated, all bit-exact. And note the 6-chunk arm has **STSM** — the fanciest epilogue we built — and is still the worst. **Stmatrix cannot compensate for chunk sync.**

## So here is the complete answer to your question

**What we do extra: a store commit + a barrier per chunk.** Roughly **1.3 points per chunk.** Not address math (dead, 0–2%), not bank conflicts (dead, anti-correlated), not stmatrix, not register pressure.

**And depth 4 forces chunking on this tile.** The arithmetic is closed:

```
smem budget                     231,424
4 stages                        196,608
left for the epilogue            34,816
full 192x192 output buffer       73,728   -> won't fit, MUST chunk
keeping all 6 chunks resident    49,152   -> won't fit either
```

So at depth 4 we can neither hold the whole tile nor hold enough slots to avoid recycling — **the barriers are structurally forced.** At depth 3 the full-tile buffer fits, we do one commit and one barrier, and we get 98.56.

**cuBLAS escapes this because their epilogue is 260 instructions**, so their 12 stores cost almost nothing to synchronise. Ours can't be made that cheap by any knob we have — five variants tried, and the best is 6.6 points behind the simple path.

## The honest conclusion

**Depth 3 is the right answer for 192×192, and it is not a compromise — it beats every depth-4 variant by 2.2 to 6.6 points.** We reach 98.5–99.8% of cuBLAS with a simpler pipeline than theirs. Matching their exact structure would need an epilogue an order of magnitude cheaper than ours, for at most ~1 point.

That region is almost entirely **uniform-datapath tile-scheduler arithmetic** (`UIMAD.WIDE.U32`, `USHF`, `ULDC` from constant bank, `@UP1` predication instead of branches) — not the store at all. Let me find where their actual store sequence lives:
> tool `Bash`: Locate and dump cuBLAS's actual store sequence

**Now I can read it exactly, and it's a completely different structure.** Here is cuBLAS's store loop:

```
594-601   8x F2FP.BF16.F32.PACK_AB          convert
602       STSM.16.M88.4 [R23+UR32], R24     store to smem
603-608   6x F2FP                           convert the NEXT group while that lands
609       STSM.16.M88.4 [R168+UR32], R32
612       FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S                <-- a FENCE, not a barrier
613       UTMASTG.3D [UR32], [UR22]         fire the TMA
614       UTMACMDFLUSH
615       UIADD3 UR32, UR32, 0x1000, URZ    <-- flip to the other slot: +4096, UNIFORM
616-617   2x STSM
619       FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S
620       UTMASTG.3D
628       UIADD3 UR32, UR32, -0x1000, URZ   <-- flip BACK
```

**Four things we do differently, all of them ours to fix:**

| | cuBLAS | us |
|---|---|---|
| ordering before the TMA | **`FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S`** (async-proxy fence) | **`barrier_sync(g, 128)`** — full warpgroup barrier |
| slot addressing | `UIADD3 UR32, ±0x1000` — one uniform add | computed chunk index |
| between chunks | **nothing** — fence, store, flush, continue | `tma_store_wait` for slot recycling |
| buffer | **4096 B per slot, 2 slots = 8 KB** | 24,576 B shared across the warpgroup |

**`FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S` is the answer to your question.** It's the async-proxy fence that orders shared-memory writes before the TMA engine reads them — and it's *warp-local and nearly free*. We use a **128-thread barrier** to get the same ordering, which stalls four warps every chunk.

And they can use a fence because their staging slot is **4096 bytes = 64 rows × 32 cols = exactly one m64 atom**, owned by **one warp**. No cross-warp visibility problem, so no barrier is needed. Ours is warpgroup-shared, which is *why* we need the barrier.

That's the "extra" you've been asking about: **we over-synchronise because we chose a shared buffer where they chose a per-warp one.**

Let me confirm we don't already emit that fence:
> tool `Bash`: Check whether we emit the async-proxy fence

**We already emit it — 19 of them.** So I was wrong that we lack the fence. But there's a note at line 1838 that points at the real difference:
> tool `Bash`: Compare MEMBAR usage, ours vs cuBLAS

**Found it, and it was already investigated once — §H27z.98.** Here is the complete answer:

```
MEMBAR.ALL.CTA   ours 15   cuBLAS 0
```

From the note, measured in isolation with a dedicated probe (`fence_probe.cu`) on sm_90a:

```
fence.proxy.async.shared::cta  (with "memory" clobber) -> MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S
fence.proxy.async.shared::cta  (no clobber)            -> MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S
fence.proxy.async              (generic)               -> MEMBAR.ALL.GPU + FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S
```

**Every writable PTX form emits a `MEMBAR`.** cuBLAS's **184 bare `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S` with zero MEMBAR is not reachable from PTX** — `nvjet` is generated through NVIDIA's internal path, below the PTX layer we compile to. **CUTLASS hits the identical wall and uses the same PTX we do** (`barrier.h:733`, `copy_sm90_tma.hpp:1217`).

So to answer you directly: **it is not a knob we're missing. It's a compiler path we don't have.** The primitive they use cannot be expressed in PTX at all, by us or by CUTLASS.

## And that closes the whole thread consistently

If the fence can't be made cheaper, the only lever is **issuing fewer of them** — one MEMBAR+FENCE pair per epilogue chunk. Which is exactly what today's sweep measured:

```
  6         6      91.94
  4         4      94.54
  2         2      96.37
  1         1      98.56   <- the minimum possible
```

**Monotonic, ~2 points per MEMBAR.** And 1 chunk — the full-tile depth-3 epilogue — is the floor. There is no configuration with fewer.

**So depth 3 is not a workaround. It is the optimum available to anything compiled through PTX**, and we are sitting at it: 98.53 / 99.44 / 99.79. The residual ~1 point on V6 is the one MEMBAR we cannot remove, and cuBLAS's advantage there is a codegen privilege rather than an algorithmic one.

**Found one — and it's a trap.**

```
PTX spelling                        MEMBAR              SASS
fence.proxy.async.global            NONE                FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.G   <-- bare!
fence.proxy.async.shared::cta       MEMBAR.ALL.CTA      FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S
fence.proxy.async.shared::cluster   MEMBAR.ALL.GPU      FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S
fence.proxy.async                   MEMBAR.ALL.GPU      FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S
fence.acq_rel.cta                   MEMBAR.ALL.CTA      -
fence.sc.cta / membar.cta           MEMBAR.SC.CTA       -
fence.proxy.alias                   MEMBAR.SC.GPU+SYS   -
bar.warp.sync                       NONE                -
```

`fence.proxy.async.global` **does** emit a bare fence with no MEMBAR. But look at the suffix: **`.G` — global.** cuBLAS emits **`.S` — shared.**

And the semantics are the whole point. Our hazard is: **`STSM` writes to shared memory, then the TMA engine reads that shared memory.** We need the generic-proxy shared writes ordered before the async proxy reads them — that is precisely `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta`. The `.global` form orders *global* accesses across proxies and says nothing about shared.

**So using it would be a silent correctness bug** — the kind that passes on one shape and corrupts on another, exactly like the stmatrix `stsm_lane_off` bug that gave wrong answers on 299 of 5766 cases without crashing. I'm not proposing it.

## So, correcting myself properly

"Codegen privilege" was sloppy. The accurate statement, now backed by **11 spellings tested** instead of 3:

> **Every PTX spelling that provides the shared-memory ordering we need emits a MEMBAR. The only bare-fence spelling provides global ordering, which does not cover our hazard.**

We use the same `ptxas` as anyone; the instruction cuBLAS emits — a bare `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S` — simply has no PTX spelling that reaches it. That's a gap in the PTX surface, not a permission we lack, and **CUTLASS is subject to exactly the same gap** (it uses the same `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta`).


**12 fences, one per store, costing 0.06% of the kernel in total.**

That sharpens the answer to your question considerably:

```

ours:     1 MEMBAR+FENCE pair -> ~0.83 points  (~0.8% of runtime)
```

**One of our fence pairs costs about thirteen times what all twelve of theirs cost together.**

So they are **not** avoiding fences — they fence *more finely than we do*, one per store. They can afford to because each costs nothing. **We chunk coarsely precisely because each of ours is expensive.** Our coarse chunking isn't a different design philosophy; it's a forced adaptation to a costly primitive. ### CLAUDE [2026-08-19 18:11 IST]

Right — let me question the premise properly. There's something in the metric definition I glossed over.

`sm__pipe_tensor_cycles_active.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_active` is **percent of peak throughput**, not "fraction of cycles busy". I treated it as the latter. Let me redo the V5 arithmetic from the SASS instead of from a metric I may be misreading:
> tool `Bash`: Re-derive V5 k-loop structure from SASS

Both k-loops: **12 HGMMA of `64x96x16`, identical.** Same work per iteration. So the wgmma counts *should* match, and the +7.3% has no structural home — which supports the metric-artefact branch.

But look at the loop sizes:

```
        k-loop instrs   HGMMA   total kernel   HGMMA total
ours              118      12          3,552            48
cuBLAS             66      12          1,296            24
```

**Our k-loop is 118 instructions to their 66 — 1.79× — for identical wgmma.** And we have 48 static HGMMA (4 code paths) to their 24 (2 paths). Let me see what the other 106 instructions in our loop actually are:
> tool `Bash`: Compare V5 k-loop contents instruction by instruction

**Found it. Look at the k-loop contents:**

```
opcode      ours  cuBLAS  delta
UMOV          23       1    +22
UIADD3        32      26     +6
ULOP3         10       0    +10
USHF           6       0     +6
ULEA           6       0     +6
UIMAD          4       0     +4
UPRMT          2       0     +2
S2UR           2       0     +2
HGMMA         12      12      0
```

**cuBLAS's k-loop is 12 HGMMA plus 26 `UIADD3` and essentially nothing else** — they *increment* the descriptors. Ours does **23 `UMOV`, 10 `ULOP3`, 6 `USHF`, 6 `ULEA`, 4 `UIMAD`, 2 `UPRMT`** — shifts, logic, multiplies and permutes, of which cuBLAS has **literally zero**. That's ~50 extra instructions per iteration **rebuilding swizzled descriptor addresses** instead of stepping them.

This is the exact defect we fixed on V3 (§H27zc2/§H27zd9), and **it's still present on the `tn` path** — because `tn` is the only layout where *both* operands are MN-major, so both descriptors get rebuilt every iteration where the other layouts rebuild one or none.

And `DESC_WALK` — build once, then add — is precisely that fix, exists as a validated knob, measured **null on V3** (its loop was already lean, 93 instructions), and **is not in V5's pin.**

Let me verify statically before claiming anything:
> tool `Bash`: Test DESC_WALK on the V5 tn path in SASS

**DESC_WALK helps the `tn` path — and it's never been tried there:**

```
              kloop  HGMMA  UMOV  ULOP3  USHF  ULEA  UIMAD
V5 pin          118     12    23     10     6     6      4
+ DESC_WALK     102     12    11      0     5     6      4
cuBLAS           66     12     1      0     0     0      0
```

**118 → 102 instructions, `UMOV` 23 → 11, `ULOP3` 10 → 0**, zero spill, `REG:168` unchanged. It removes every logic-op and half the moves.

Still 102 against cuBLAS's 66, so it's not the whole story — but it's the first thing that shrinks V5's loop, and V5's pin has `dh_ubd` **without** `dw`. On V3 `dw` measured null because that loop was already lean at 93; V5's is 118, which is exactly where it should pay.

Let me wire it up so it's ready when your N-sweep finishes:
> tool `Bash`: Add the V5 DESC_WALK arm and build
> tool `Bash`: Sync and read the N-sweep results

**N padding is dead too — and the result kills my own "+7.3% more wgmma" explanation.**

```
N        Ntiles  exact    %cuB   wgmma_ratio  cyc_ratio
11136      58    EXACT   82.34      1.0909      1.2071
11264      59    padded  82.40      1.0727      1.2076   <- V5 real
11328      59    EXACT   82.44      1.0727      1.2032
11520      60    EXACT   82.30      1.0909      1.2042
```

Two things, both decisive:

**1. N=11264 (padded) and N=11328 (exact) give the identical ratio 1.0727.** Padding in N is not the source, exactly as it wasn't in M.

**2. The wgmma ratio *moves* (1.0727 ↔ 1.0909) while `%cuB` stays flat at 82.3–82.4.** If the extra wgmma were causing the deficit, performance would track the ratio. **It doesn't.** So the wgmma-count difference is real but **not the cause** — my "+7.3% more wgmma → 20% more work" reading is wrong and I'm retracting it.

What *is* invariant is the **cycle ratio: 1.203–1.208 across every N.** A constant deficit, independent of shape, tiles and padding.

## And that points straight at what I found in the SASS

```
              k-loop instrs   HGMMA
ours                    118      12
cuBLAS                   66      12
```

A constant per-iteration cost is exactly what a **fixed loop-length difference** produces. Work it through: if tensor time per k-iteration is T cycles, cuBLAS at 66 instructions is tensor-bound if T > 66, and we at 118 are **issue-bound** if T < 118. The observed ratio 1.205 implies **T ≈ 98 cycles** — which sits neatly between the two.

**That model makes a sharp prediction.** `DESC_WALK` takes our loop **118 → 102**:

```
predicted cycle ratio = 1.205 x (102/118) = 1.042  ->  ~96% cuB
```

So if V5 is issue-bound on descriptor rebuilds, `DESC_WALK` should move it from **82.4 to roughly 96**. If it moves only a point or two, the model is wrong and I'll drop it.

The arm is built and registered (`192x192x64_2x1_v_rs8_dh_ubd_dw_skew_lsw`, tn TU compiles clean, zero spill). It needs a library rebuild since the source changed:

**Falsified.** I predicted ~96; it came back **82.33 vs 82.51 baseline — flat, slightly worse.**

```
v_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw        82.51  [82.2, 82.9]
v_rs8_dh_ubd_dw_skew_lsw     82.33  [81.8, 82.6]   k-loop 118 -> 102
```

The loop got 13.6% shorter and nothing moved. **V5 is not issue-bound.** The model is dead, and so is the k-loop-length explanation.

## Everything I've tested on V5 is flat

```
swizzle (auto/64/32)     flat
M padding (2048/2112)    flat
N padding (4 values)     flat  -- ratio moved, %cuB didn't
load imbalance           1.3% vs 1.1%, no difference
_lsw                     +0.00
k-loop 118 -> 102        flat
```

And the deficit is a rock-steady **cycle ratio 1.203–1.208** through every one of those changes.

## What I've been ignoring

I've been treating V5 as a compute problem because `tensor%` reads 98.4%. But look at the operand volumes:

```
        A operand      B operand      total     vs L2 (50 MB)
V6      67 MB          23 MB          90 MB     fits-ish
V5      67 MB         369 MB         436 MB     9x L2
```

**V5's B operand alone is 369 MB.** And with 11 M-tiles × 59 N-tiles, A gets re-read ~59× and B ~11× unless rasterisation gets reuse — that's roughly **8 GB of DRAM traffic**, which at H200 bandwidth is **~1.67 ms**. Our kernel runs **1.30 ms** and cuBLAS **1.07 ms**. Those numbers are the same order, which means **V5 may be bandwidth-bound and I never checked.**

Two things corroborate it: `mio_throttle` **ours 6.14 vs cuBLAS 15.22** — they drive the memory pipe 2.5× harder — and V5 is the only shape whose operands massively exceed L2.

**I have never measured DRAM bytes on V5.** That's a single metric, and if our traffic exceeds cuBLAS's the cause is L2 reuse — which makes the grouped-rasterisation group size (`rs8`, never tuned for V5's 11×59 tile grid) the actual lever.

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
nvidia-smi -i 0 -lgc 1400
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 LD_LIBRARY_PATH=build ncu --kernel-name-base mangled \
  -k regex:"bgemm_sm90_kernel|nvjet" --csv --page raw -o /dev/null --force-overwrite \
  --metrics dram__bytes_read.sum,dram__bytes_write.sum,lts__t_sector_hit_rate.pct,l1tex__t_sector_hit_rate.pct,sm__cycles_elapsed.avg \
  ./build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --cfg=192x192x64_2x1_v_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw \
  --shape=2048x11264x16384 --layout=tn --bench 2>/dev/null | tee /tmp/dram.csv | tail -3
nvidia-smi -i 0 -rgc
```

Say "done" and I'll pull it. If our DRAM bytes are well above cuBLAS's, that's V5's cause and it's a rasterisation-tuning problem, not a kernel-structure one — and it would explain why every structural change I've made has been flat.

## The "extra work" finding is dead

I told you V5 does +7.3% more wgmma and that this was the 17-point gap. **The N-sweep disproved it:**

```
N        wgmma_ratio   %cuB
11136       1.0909     82.34
11264       1.0727     82.40
11328       1.0727     82.44
11520       1.0909     82.30
```

The ratio **moves** while `%cuB` stays **flat**. If the extra wgmma caused the slowdown, performance would track it. It doesn't. So the extra instructions are real but **harmless** — fixing them would buy nothing.

## And DRAM is dead too

```
              dram_read    L2 hit%    cycles
ours            952.3 MB    80.08    1,818,662
cuBLAS          900.7 MB    75.15    1,506,892
                 +5.7%      BETTER
```

Only 5.7% more reads — can't explain 20% — and **our L2 hit rate is better than theirs**. Also 952 MB over 1.30 ms is 733 GB/s against the H200's ~4.8 TB/s, so V5 is at **15% of peak bandwidth**. Not bandwidth-bound.

## Eight hypotheses tested on V5. All flat.

```
swizzle (auto/64/32)      flat
M padding                 flat
N padding                 flat
load imbalance            1.3% vs 1.1%
_lsw                      +0.00
k-loop 118 -> 102 (dw)    flat
extra wgmma               real but NOT causal
DRAM / L2                 +5.7%, and our L2 is better
```

**One number survives everything:** each wgmma instruction occupies **12% more tensor-pipe cycles** for us (0.10285 vs 0.09159), and that 1.12 is as stubbornly invariant as the 1.205 cycle ratio. Same instruction, same shape, same flags, 12% more pipe time — operand delivery *inside* the tensor pipe, which is below anything I've been able to reach with a knob.

**V5 measured 95.7% under ncu. It measures 82.5% in the plain benchmark.** Same config, same shape, same box, same session — a **13-point** difference depending only on *how it's measured*.

Both kernels are instrumented equally in that run (the harness timed both while ncu was attached — TFLOPS 1.14 vs 1.19), so it isn't an unfair comparison. And it reframes everything:

**That is why all eight structural changes were flat.** If the kernel reads 95.7% when profiled and 82.5% when benchmarked, the deficit isn't in the kernel's structure at all — it appears only under the repeated-launch benchmark condition.

The obvious mechanism: **ncu flushes caches between launches by default**, so both kernels start cold. The bench loop runs them back-to-back with warm L2. V5's operands are **436 MB against a 50 MB L2** — by far the largest working set of any shape we have — so cache state between launches matters far more here than anywhere else. Under cold-start we're at 95.7%; with a warm cache cuBLAS pulls ahead by 13 points.

That also finally explains the contradiction I couldn't resolve: `tensor%` 98.4% and L2 hit 80% (both measured *under ncu*, i.e. in the 95.7% regime) never matched an 82.5% deficit — **because they were measuring a different regime than the benchmark was.**

The test is one run, and it's decisive:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
nvidia-smi -i 0 -lgc 1400
for cc in all none; do
  echo "=== --cache-control $cc ==="
  CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 LD_LIBRARY_PATH=build ncu --cache-control $cc --clock-control none \
    -k regex:"bgemm_sm90_kernel" -c 3 --metrics sm__cycles_elapsed.avg \
    ./build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --cfg=192x192x64_2x1_v_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw \
    --shape=2048x11264x16384 --layout=tn --bench 2>/dev/null | grep -E "%cuB|192x192"
done
nvidia-smi -i 0 -rgc
```

If `--cache-control none` (warm, like the bench) reads ~82 and `all` (flushed) reads ~96, **cache reuse across launches is V5's entire story** — and the question becomes whether the benchmark's warm-cache condition is even representative of how BluTrain runs it, because in a real training step these matrices are *not* warm in L2.

That would mean V5's "17-point gap" is partly an artifact of how we benchmark, and I'd want to know that before spending another day on kernel structure.

You're right. Dropping the suggestions.

The unexplained number is this: **both kernels run the tensor pipe at ~98.4% of peak, yet ours takes 1.207× the cycles while issuing only 1.073× the wgmma.** That means each of our wgmma occupies the pipe 12.5% longer for identical `HGMMA.64x96x16` work — which can only be **operand starvation inside the tensor pipe**. The wgmma reads its operands from smem through the descriptor, and the descriptor defines the layout.

Same `.tnspA.tnspB` flags on both, but the descriptor *contents* — leading offset, stride, swizzle mode — are what actually control the read pattern, and I've never compared them. Let me decode them from both kernels' SASS:
> tool `Bash`: Trace how the wgmma descriptors are built in both kernels

**Found a hard structural difference.** Look at how each kernel builds its wgmma descriptors:

```
cuBLAS:  ONE descriptor register, UR16
         UMOV UR16, 0x2000840          <- a single immediate CONSTANT
         then 26 UIADD3 in the loop     <- it just INCREMENTS that one

ours:    FOUR descriptor registers, UR24 / UR28 / UR32 / UR36 — 94 writes
         ULOP3.LUT UR36, UR17, 0x2000000, URZ, 0xfc    <- OR the base in
         UIADD3.64 UR28, UR36, 0x80                    <- +2048 bytes
         UIADD3.64 UR32, UR36, 0x100                   <- +4096
         UIADD3.64 UR24, UR36, 0x180                   <- +6144
```

**We maintain four separate descriptors at 2048-byte spacing; cuBLAS maintains one and steps it.** Both encode the same leading-byte-offset (512 → 8192 B), so the layouts aren't obviously different — but the *access structure* is: four concurrent operand streams versus one.

And 2048 bytes apart matters — shared memory is 32 banks × 4 B = **128 B per row**, and 2048 / 128 = 16 rows exactly, so **all four of our descriptor streams start on the same bank**.

That is a candidate for exactly the symptom we can't shake: 12% more tensor-pipe occupancy per wgmma with no instruction-count sensitivity. Bank conflicts on the wgmma operand path don't appear in `l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu_*` — that counter only covers the LSU path, and wgmma fetches operands through its own path. **That's why the bank-conflict check came back clean and misled me.**

**What it decides.** Our extra 12% of tensor-pipe time per wgmma has to appear as *some* stall reason on the consumer warps:

- **`short_scoreboard`** high → smem operand dependency → the four-descriptor bank collision is real, and re-spacing them off the same bank is the fix
- **`math_pipe_throttle`** high → the tensor pipe itself is saturated and we're simply feeding it the same work slower
- **`wait`** / **`dispatch_stall`** high → fixed instruction latency, not memory
- **nothing stands out** → the time isn't in warp stalls at all and the 12% lives inside the wgmma's own execution, which no counter I have will reach
