### CLAUDE [2026-08-19 18:44 IST]

**FOUND IT. The stall breakdown is unambiguous:**

```
stall reason        ours    cuBLAS    EXCESS
long_scoreboard    27.05     14.72    +12.33   <<<<< THE CAUSE
barrier            24.55     20.65     +3.90
wait               11.70      9.28     +2.42
short_scoreboard    1.40      0.03     +1.37
no_instruction      1.20      0.29     +0.91
mio_throttle        6.14     15.23     -9.09   <<<<< we are LOWER
lsu ld conflicts       0       724
```

**`long_scoreboard` is a GLOBAL-memory dependency stall — waiting for a load that hasn't returned.** Not shared memory (that's `short_scoreboard`, and it's 1.40 vs 0.03 — negligible, so the bank-collision theory is dead too, and our LSU conflicts are literally **zero**).

And the pairing is textbook:

```
cuBLAS:  mio_throttle 15.23 HIGH, long_scoreboard 14.72   -> memory pipe SATURATED (throughput-bound)
ours:    mio_throttle  6.14 LOW,  long_scoreboard 27.05   -> waiting on loads (LATENCY-bound)
```

**They saturate memory. We wait for it.** Our memory pipe is only 40% as busy as theirs while our warps stall twice as long on global loads — we simply do not have enough loads in flight to cover DRAM latency.

**And V5 is exactly the shape where that would bite:** 436 MB working set against a 50 MB L2 — 9× — with 256 k-iterations per tile. V3/V4/V6 have K=2048 and far smaller operands that L2 absorbs, so 3 stages of prefetch covers them. On V5 it doesn't.

**So V5 needs *more* pipeline depth — the exact opposite of V6.** V6 chose depth 3 because the epilogue cost dominated; V5 is latency-bound and wants depth 4, where the extra stage buys prefetch distance rather than costing epilogue sync.

That also explains why all nine previous attempts were flat: **every one of them changed instruction counts or the epilogue. Not one changed prefetch depth.**

Let me build the `_v` depth-4 arms — we already have the machinery working from V6:
> tool `Bash`: Add deeper-prefetch V5 arms and verify depth

Both reach **depth 4** (depth 5 is impossible — it'd need negative store buffer). Registering and building:
> tool `Bash`: Register V5 depth-4 arms and build

Clean build. Four blocks:

```bash
prefetch depth, the opposite of V6.
Stall breakdown, V5 vs cuBLAS (% warp-active):

  barrier           24.55 vs 20.65   +3.90

cuBLAS has high mio_throttle and low long_scoreboard: their memory pipe is SATURATED. We have the

in flight to cover DRAM latency. This also kills the shared-memory/bank-collision theory: our LSU
conflicts are literally zero and short_scoreboard is 1.40.
```

```bash

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 LD_LIBRARY_PATH=build bash -c '
for c in 192x192x64_2x1_v_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw \
         192x192x64_2x1_v_ea32s2stsm_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw \
         192x192x64_2x1_v_ea8s2_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw; do
 g=0; for i in $(seq 1 7); do
  r=$(./build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --cfg=$c --shape=2048x11264x16384 --layout=tn --bench 2>&1 \
      | awk -v c=$c "\$1==c&&\$4==\"PASS\"{gsub(/%/,\"\",\$9);print \$9,\$5}")
  [ -n "$r" ] && { echo "$c $r"; g=1; }; done
 [ $g -eq 0 ] && echo "*** $c NO ROW ***" >&2; done' 2>&1 | tee /tmp/u | grep -v "^\*\*\*" \
| awk '{s[$1]+=$2;n[$1]++;if(!(($1)in mn)||$2<mn[$1])mn[$1]=$2;if($2>mx[$1])mx[$1]=$2;if($3+0>e[$1])e[$1]=$3+0}
 END{printf "  %-52s %7s %7s %7s %10s\n","config","mean","min","max","maxRelErr";
     for(c in s)printf "  %-52s %7.2f %7.1f %7.1f %10.5f\n",c,s[c]/n[c],mn[c],mx[c],e[c]}' | sort -k2 -rn | tee output.md
grep "^\*\*\*" /tmp/u
nvidia-smi -i 0 -rgc
```

**Baseline 82.5.** If depth 4 cuts `long_scoreboard`, V5 moves. Ten hypotheses in — but this is the first one where a counter, not an inference, points at the mechanism, and the first that touches prefetch depth at all.

```
cuBLAS 889  0.01%  SYNCS.PHASECHK.TRANS64.TRYWAIT P2, [UR7], R4
```

Ours has a bare `TRYWAIT` at 535 (0.11%) and **no inline spin at all** — the wait is outlined to that 0x…55d0–5660 block, which is where the 23.90% lives. Let me confirm the k-loop actually branches there, and whether those four sites are producer or consumer:
> tool `Bash`: Trace the wait-site control flow in our V5 kernel

The control flow is now fully resolved. All four sites are **byte-identical** and they chain into one loop (`3057 → 2405` back-edge, `2417→2565→2725→2885→3046`):

```
S2UR   UR9, SR_CgaCtaId          <- read cluster CTA id
UMOV   UR8, 0x400
UIADD3 UR8, UR8, 0x18
ULEA   UR8, UR9, UR8, 0x18       <- CgaCtaId<<24 : a REMOTE (DSMEM) barrier
ULEA   UR8, UR16, UR8, 0x3
SYNCS.PHASECHK.TRANS64.TRYWAIT P1, [UR8], R5
@!P1   BRA <outlined spin>        <- 5.68 / 5.86 / 6.03 / 6.33 %
```

So the 23.90% is **waiting on a cluster-peer mbarrier in another CTA's shared memory**, in a 4-way-unrolled loop that sits entirely outside both k-loops. cuBLAS's equivalent wait is inline in its k-loop with `NANOSLEEP` and costs 0.11%.

36 `UTMALDG` and zero `HGMMA` in 2405–3060 — that region is unambiguously the producer warpgroup.

## The instruction-level diff

Five opcodes appear in our producer and **zero times** in cuBLAS's:

```
                 ours   cuBLAS
R2UR             191       0     <- reg -> uniform-reg moves
PLOP3            108       0     <- 3 predicate ops per TMA load
ELECT             36       0     <- re-elects a leader lane per load
ULEA              27       0
S2UR               8       0     <- re-reads SR_CgaCtaId
```

cuBLAS's producer is **pure uniform datapath** — `UIADD3 ×56`, `UIMAD ×19`, `UMOV ×12`, `UISETP ×10`, `UTMALDG ×14`, and essentially nothing else. Only 16 vector instructions in the whole loop.

Ours computes addresses in **vector registers and then shuffles them into uniform registers** — 191 `R2UR` to do it. That's the "extra work" in V5's extra-work lag, and now it's counted, not guessed.

## And the barrier address is rebuilt every single time

All four wait sites do this identically:

```
S2UR   UR9, SR_CgaCtaId      \
UMOV   UR8, 0x400             |  5 instructions to rebuild a base address
UIADD3 UR8, UR8, 0x18         |  that is CONSTANT for the entire kernel
ULEA   UR8, UR9, UR8, 0x18    |
ULEA   UR8, UR16, UR8, 0x3   /
SYNCS.PHASECHK.TRANS64.TRYWAIT P1, [UR8], R5
@!P1   BRA  <outlined>        <- 5.68 / 5.86 / 6.03 / 6.33 %
```

cuBLAS holds its barrier base in a uniform register and its wait is inline with `NANOSLEEP ×2`, costing **0.01%**.

```
        1065  UTMALDG.3D           [UR8],  [UR34]        issued 3-4 instrs apart
        1069  UTMALDG.3D           [UR8],  [UR34]
        1072  UTMALDG.3D.MULTICAST [UR16], [UR34], UR38
        1075  UTMALDG.3D.MULTICAST [UR16], [UR34], UR38

ours    2445  UTMALDG.3D           [UR16], [UR8]      <- four different descriptor
        2467  UTMALDG.3D           [UR16], [UR8]         registers UR16/UR40/UR48/UR56
        2481  UTMALDG.3D           [UR56], [UR8]         issued 14-24 instrs apart,
        2505  UTMALDG.3D.MULTICAST [UR16], [UR8], UR10   address rebuilt in between
        2519  UTMALDG.3D.MULTICAST [UR48], [UR8], UR10
        2530  UTMALDG.3D.MULTICAST [UR40], [UR8], UR10
```

**We issue 9 loads per stage, they issue 7 — that part is fine.** The gap is that we burn **160 instructions per stage to issue them and they burn 48.** 18 instructions of address arithmetic per TMA load versus 7.

## Why, in the source

`mbarrier_wait(int addr, int phase)` at [Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh:1098](BluBridge-BLAS_05_aug_kota/BluBridge-BLAS/src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM90/Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh#L1098) takes the barrier address through an `"r"` constraint — a **vector**-register constraint — inside an `asm volatile` with a `"memory"` clobber. So:

- the address is forced into an `R` register at every call,
- `volatile` + the clobber stop ptxas CSE-ing it across the four unrolled bodies,
- `SYNCS.PHASECHK.TRANS64.TRYWAIT` needs a `UR` operand, so ptxas rebuilds the whole chain in the uniform datapath — `S2UR SR_CgaCtaId` ×8, `ULEA` ×27 — and emits **191 `R2UR`** moves to bridge the rest.

That's 29% of the producer's instructions doing nothing but moving values between datapaths. cuBLAS emits zero of them, holds the barrier base in one UR, and its wait costs **0.01%** against our **23.90%**.

## The finding

V5's producer **tight-spins** on the empty-barrier miss. cuBLAS **sleeps**. Same four `TRYWAIT` sites, same pipeline depth — the only difference is what happens when the wait fails:

```
ours     @!P1 BRA <back to TRYWAIT>     23.90%   <- 4 sites, the 4 hottest
                                                   instructions in the kernel
cuBLAS   NANOSLEEP.SYNCS 0xc350          0.01%
```

A spinning warp is still **issuing**. The producer shares one SM's issue slots and MIO bandwidth with both consumer warpgroups, so the spin starves the consumers — and that predicts every other number I measured:

```
                        ours     cuBLAS
producer % of kernel   33.05%     8.27%    4.0x
producer instructions    656       187     3.5x  (same 4 TRYWAIT sites)
consumer DEPBAR        12.23%     3.01%    4.1x  <- starved
HGMMA                  22.35%    53.41%
R2UR / ELECT / PLOP3  191/36/108   0/0/0
S2UR SR_CgaCtaId           8         0           barrier addr rebuilt, not hoisted
```

It also resolves the `mio_throttle` inversion that's been sitting in the notes unexplained (ours 6.14, theirs 15.23): **their memory pipe is saturated with work, ours with a spin.** And it is *not* register pressure — the producer's highest live register is `R18` under a 40-register budget.

`MBAR_SLEEP_TICKS` (slot 28) has existed since §H27zc7 and **no registered config has ever set it non-zero**, so it has never been measured. I've added three arms. `_tk50k` is cuBLAS's exact `0xc350`; `_tk12k` tests whether 50,000 ticks oversleeps our shorter producer; the `_h` arm is the control — V3/V4/V6 all pin `_h` and sit at 95–96.5, so if `_h` gains equally the finding is general and not V5's cause.

```bash
    Sm90WarpspecConfig<192, 192, 64, 2, 1, 0, true, true, /*RASTER=%s*/%d, 0, 0, 0, 40, 232,

// Producer and both consumer warpgroups share one SM's issue slots and MIO bandwidth. A spinning

//     producer %/kernel  ours 33.05%  cuBLAS  8.27%   (4.0x)

//     R2UR/ELECT/PLOP3   ours 191/36/108        cuBLAS 0/0/0
//     S2UR SR_CgaCtaId   ours 8       cuBLAS  0   (barrier addr rebuilt per site, not hoisted)
//     consumer DEPBAR    ours 12.23%  cuBLAS  3.01%  (4.1x -- starved of issue slots)
//     HGMMA              ours 22.35%  cuBLAS 53.41%
// Consistent with the mio_throttle inversion on record (ours 6.14, theirs 15.23): their memory
// pipe is saturated with WORK, ours with a spin.
// NOT register pressure: producer's highest live register is R18 under a 40-register budget.

"""
k="using Sm90Config_192x192x64_2x1_v_swz64_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw ="
assert src.count(k)==1
src=src.replace(k, doc+a('192x192x64_2x1_v_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw_tk50k','v',50000)
                     +a('192x192x64_2x1_v_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw_tk12k','v',12500)
                     +a('192x192x64_2x1_h_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw_tk50k','h',50000)+"\n"+k,1)
open(t,'w').write(src)

assert hashlib.md5(hs.encode()).hexdigest().startswith('956312c9'), 'header moved; stop'
L=hs.split('\n'); anc="    X(192x192x64_2x1_v_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw, A, B)"
```

V3/V4/V6 got fixed by `_lsw` (moving the epilogue's TMA store drain off the end of each tile). **V5 gained nothing from it** — that's why it's the only one left, ~13 points behind its own family.

## What we tried on V5 and killed

Eleven hypotheses, all dead: swizzle, M padding, N padding, load imbalance, `_lsw`, k-loop length, extra wgmma, DRAM/L2, cache state, prefetch depth 3→4, TMA multicast.

## What I did this session

You told me to stop guessing and actually backtrack the SASS instruction by instruction against cuBLAS. I did that on the PC-sampling dumps in [profiling_reports/h27zdq/pcsamp/](profiling_reports/h27zdq/pcsamp/), and it found the cause:

**Our producer warpgroup tight-spins while waiting for a buffer. cuBLAS sleeps.**

```
ours     @!P1 BRA <back to the check>    23.90%   <- 4 instructions, the four
                                                    hottest in the whole kernel
cuBLAS   NANOSLEEP.SYNCS 0xc350           0.01%
```

Same four wait sites, same pipeline depth — the only difference is what happens on a miss. A spinning warp keeps **issuing instructions**, and the producer shares one SM's issue slots with both consumer warpgroups. So the spin starves the consumers, which is exactly what the rest of the profile shows: our consumer drain is 12.23% vs their 3.01%, and our tensor cores get 22.35% of the machine vs their 53.41%.

It also explains the `mio_throttle` inversion that's been sitting unexplained in the notes (ours 6.14, theirs 15.23) — **their memory pipe is busy with work, ours is busy with a spin.**

Result is a **null**, and I'll say so plainly — my hypothesis is refuted.

```
V5_base    n=7   min 80.20   med 84.20   max 86.30

V5_tk12k   n=7   min 79.90   med 81.40   max 84.80     -2.8, worse

V3_tk50k   n=7   min 95.10   med 96.90   max 99.90     +0.5, ranges overlap
```

`_tk50k` moves V5 by +0.6 and V3 by **+0.5 — the same amount**. The control was supposed to separate them and it didn't. So the sleep hint is a small general effect at best, not V5's 13 points. **The producer spin is not the cause.** Those four branches really do carry 23.90% of samples, but that time is *slack* — the producer is ahead and waiting, and sleeping through the wait instead of spinning buys nothing.

But look at what the raw numbers say about the measurement itself:
> tool `Bash`: Separate our variance from cuBLAS variance

**The noise is cuBLAS's, not ours:**

```
        OUR TFLOPS         cuBLAS TFLOPS (implied)    %cuB spread
V5      597-617   3.22%    709-752   6.08%            6.4 pts
V3      673-687   2.00%    686-721   5.09%            6.6 pts
```

Our kernels are **2–3× steadier than the reference they're scored against.** The harness times cuBLAS first, from cold clocks, so cuBLAS eats the ramp and every `%cuB` inherits its 5–6% swing. That sets a resolution floor of about 6 points — V5's 13-point gap is safely above it, but `_tk50k`'s +0.6 was never measurable, and neither were `rs8` +2.27, `dh_ubd` +0.77 or `SKEW` +1.62.

## What survives the null

The producer is exonerated. Two things from the SASS are still standing, and both are consumer-side:

```
consumer DEPBAR   ours 12.23%   cuBLAS 3.01%    4.1x
HGMMA             ours 22.35%   cuBLAS 53.41%
```

plus §H27zdr's measurement that each of our wgmma costs 11.9% more tensor cycles (13.54 vs 12.10).

And there's a structural clue in the loop census I took earlier that I haven't used yet:

```
ours     k-loop A 32.60%   k-loop B 32.56%    <- symmetric
cuBLAS   k-loop A 57.73%   k-loop B 28.95%    <- 2:1 ASYMMETRIC
```

Two consumer warpgroups doing *equal* work in ours; *unequal* work in cuBLAS. That's the signature of a **ping-pong / coopB** schedule — one warpgroup running wgmma while the other drains, so the drain is hidden. Ours run in lockstep, so both drain at once and neither covers the other. That would produce exactly the 4.1× DEPBAR.

`coopB odd-tiles + pingpong` is already on record as an undone structural variant, and V6's cuBLAS kernel is named `..._coopB_TNN`. Let me confirm what cuBLAS actually runs for V5:
> tool `Bash`: Get the cuBLAS kernel name cuBLAS picks for V5

**`nvjet_sm90_tst_192x192_64x3_2x1_v_bz_coopB_NTN`**

Decode it against our pin:

```
192x192   same tile      ✓
64x3      BK=64, depth 3 ✓   <- unlike V6, this IS apples-to-apples on depth
2x1       same cluster   ✓
v         same raster    ✓
coopB     <-- WE DO NOT HAVE THIS
```

Every knob matches except one. And `coopB odd-tiles` is already on record as an undone structural variant — it's the *tile-shape cooperative* variant, meaning the two consumer warpgroups get **unequal** shares of the 192-wide N. Which is exactly the 2:1 asymmetry in their k-loops (57.73 : 28.95), against our 1:1 (32.60 : 32.56).

192 = **128 + 64** for them, **96 + 96** for us. Let me confirm from the wgmma shapes:
> tool `Bash`: Compare wgmma shapes in both consumer k-loops

Both are **`HGMMA.64x96x16 ×12`, N sum 2304, identical.** So the 128+64 theory is wrong — we do byte-identical tensor work. And that forces a correction to my own reasoning:

**PC-sample share is not wall-clock cost.** A spinning producer occupies its ~1/3 warp-slot share of the samples whether or not it's on the critical path; cuBLAS's sleeps instead and drops to 8%. The `_tk50k` null proves the 23.90% was never costing us time. I read sample share as cost, and that was wrong.

What that leaves is the one measurement that *is* wall-clock-relevant, from §H27zdr: **identical wgmma instruction, 11.9% more tensor cycles** (ours 13.54, cuBLAS 12.10). Same shape, same count, same operands — slower per instruction. That's operand delivery into the tensor core, and swizzle was already ruled out.

The ncu summary was never read per-kernel. Here it is:

```
                                    ours        cuBLAS     ratio
tensor instructions           17,399,808    16,220,160    1.0727
TOTAL instructions           199,176,351   103,827,347    1.9183
tensor pipe % of peak              98.36         98.58    0.9977   <- IDENTICAL
```

**Both run the tensor pipe at 98.4% of peak.** So this was never an operand-delivery, swizzle, or tensor-efficiency problem — the tensor cores are equally saturated in both. And the gap decomposes exactly:

```
1.0727  x  1.1250   =  1.2068      measured 1.2051
(7.3% more     (12.5% lower
 tensor work)   SM throughput)
```

Now the first half, and it's airtight. Divide the tensor counts by 24,576 (256 k-iters × 96):

```
ours     17,399,808 / 24,576  =  708.0 tiles   =  12 x 59
cuBLAS   16,220,160 / 24,576  =  660.0 tiles   =  11 x 60
ideal                             649   tiles   =  11 x 59
```

Both divide exactly. **We run 708 tiles, cuBLAS runs 660, and only 649 are real work.** 708/660 = 1.0727 — the measured ratio to four decimals.

M = 2048 gives ceil(2048/192) = **11 M-tiles, an odd number.** Our 2×1 cluster rounds that up to 12, and we throw away a whole column of 59 tiles — 9.1% of all tensor work. cuBLAS keeps M at 11 and pads N to 60 instead, costing 1.7%.

And this is why V5 is the *only* one of the four that lags:

```
V3/V4/V6   M=16384  ->  ceil(16384/192) = 86 M-tiles   EVEN   no rounding
V5         M= 2048  ->  ceil( 2048/192) = 11 M-tiles   ODD    rounds to 12
```

The cuBLAS kernel is named `..._2x1_v_bz_coopB_NTN`, and **`coopB` is the odd-tile cooperative variant** — literally the feature that lets it keep 11. It's already on our roadmap as `coopB odd-tiles`, listed as an undone structural variant.

So V5's ~18% splits into: **7.3% from launching a wasted tile column we don't need**, and **12.5% from executing 1.92× cuBLAS's total instruction count** (199M vs 104M), which drags elapsed SM throughput from 97.9% to 87.0%. Both are "extra work" — your V5 framing was right.

The odd-tile half is a grid-sizing fix, not a kernel rewrite. Want me to trace how `grid_m` gets rounded for the 2×1 cluster and write that fix first?

```bash
// SHORT axis wastes one long row (59, 9.1%). Same cluster size, 5x less waste.
// This arm is the V5 pin with ONLY CLUSTER_M/CLUSTER_N swapped; multicast re-gates itself
// (NEEDS_A = MC_A && CLUSTER_N>1, NEEDS_B = MC_B && CLUSTER_M>1), so 2x1 runs B-multicast and
// 1x2 runs A-multicast -- both already-validated paths.
// FALSIFIABLE PREDICTION: 1x2 -> mega_grid_m=11, mega_grid_n=ceil(59/2)=30 -> 11*30 clusters x 2
// CTAs = 660 CTA-tiles, so sm__inst_executed_pipe_tensor.sum must be EXACTLY 16,220,160, identical
// to cuBLAS. Judge by that counter, NOT %cuB: H27zdt measured our TFLOPS spread at 3.2% and the
// cuBLAS reference we divide by at 6.1%, a ~6-point floor against a ~7% expected gain.
"""
k="using Sm90Config_192x192x64_2x1_v_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw ="
assert src.count(k)==1
open(t,'w').write(src.replace(k, doc+a('192x192x64_1x2_v_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw','v')
                                 +a('192x192x64_1x2_h_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw','h')+"\n"+k,1))
L=open(h).read().split('\n')
anc="    X(192x192x64_2x1_v_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw, A, B)"
i=[j for j,l in enumerate(L) if l.startswith(anc)]; assert len(i)==1
L[i[0]+1:i[0]+1]=["    X(192x192x64_1x2_v_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw, A, B)".ljust(78)+"\\",
                  "    X(192x192x64_1x2_h_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw, A, B)".ljust(78)+"\\"]
open(h,'w').write('\n'.join(L))
print("PATCHED OK   X() entries now", len(re.findall(r'^\s*X\(','\n'.join(L),re.M)))
PY
```

Two things the numbers say that I didn't predict:

**It beat the prediction — +12.4% TFLOPS against +7.3% forecast** — and the reason is wave quantization on top of the wasted work:

```
2x1:  354 clusters x 2 = 708 CTAs / 132 SMs = 5.36 waves -> 6 waves, last one 36% full
1x2:  330 clusters x 2 = 660 CTAs / 132 SMs = 5.00 waves -> 5 waves, exactly full
```

660/132 lands on **exactly 5.0**. So we didn't just delete 7.3% of the tensor work, we deleted a whole ragged sixth wave. 6→5 waves is −16.7%, the work is −7.3%, and the measured +12.4% sits between them.

**And the 400 ms window fixed the measurement problem too** — the cuBLAS reference tightened from a 6.1% spread to 1.3% (684–693), and our own baseline from 6.4 points to 1.4. Every A/B from here should use `BLUBLAS_BENCH_TARGET_MS=400`.

## On to cause #2

The 199M vs 104M instruction count. Static SASS already accounts for it almost exactly:

```
per k-iteration        ours   cuBLAS
consumer k-loop A       117       68
consumer k-loop B       117       69
producer (per stage)    164       47
                        ---      ---
                        398      184     ratio 2.16   (measured 1.92)
```

And the single biggest term inside the consumer loop is one opcode:

```
UMOV    ours 23   cuBLAS 2      <- 21 extra per k-iteration
UIADD3  ours 32   cuBLAS 33     <- identical
```

We rebuild wgmma descriptors from immediates every iteration; cuBLAS *walks* a descriptor register. That's described verbatim in our own `DESC_WALK` knob comment (slot 29): *"cuBLAS never has two live stages because they never have a stage INDEX at all — only a walking descriptor register advanced by literals (+0x2 per k16 step, +0x200 per m64 atom, −0x6 to undo them)."*

`DESC_WALK` is `false` in the V5 pin. It *was* tested — and it's in the dead list at 82.33 vs 82.51.

But that test, and all ten others, ran against a baseline carrying the 12.4% phantom-tile penalty. A 1–2 point effect was unmeasurable underneath it, especially at the old 100 ms window with its 6-point noise. **The dead list is not trustworthy any more and cause #2's prime suspect is sitting in it.** Want me to add the `1x2_v` + `DESC_WALK` arm and re-run the killed hypotheses against the fixed baseline?

You're right — it's the same problem, and we're two-thirds of the way through fixing it. Here's the plain version.

## What a descriptor is

`wgmma` (the tensor-core matmul instruction) does **not** take a pointer to shared memory. It takes a **64-bit descriptor** — one packed number that says:

```
low  32 bits :  WHERE the tile sits in shared memory
high 32 bits :  HOW to read it - leading-dim stride, base offset, swizzle mode, layout
```

Think of it as an address with a little "how to read this" manual welded onto it. Every `wgmma` needs one for A and one for B.

## Where it gets built, and how often

We issue **12 `wgmma` per warpgroup per k-iteration**, 24 across both consumers. V5 runs 256 k-iterations × 660 tiles. So this descriptor math runs **millions of times** — it's the innermost thing in the whole kernel.

It has to change every iteration because the tile it points at keeps moving: next k-step, next m64 atom, next pipeline stage (a different smem buffer).

## What we do vs what they do

**Us:** recompute the whole thing from scratch each time — take `smem_base`, add `stage*copy_size`, add the atom offset, add the k offset, mask it, shift right by 4, OR in the layout bits. That's the 23 `UMOV` per k-iteration.

**cuBLAS:** one instruction.
```
UIADD3 UR16, UR16, 0x2
```

They can do that because of a property our own notes already proved (§H27z.99b, and CuTe relies on it too):

```
desc_encode(x) = (x & 0x3FFFF) >> 4
  =>  desc(base + offset) == desc(base) + (offset >> 4)
```

as long as everything is 16-byte aligned and stays under 256 KB — both true for us. So **moving to the next tile is just adding a small constant to the number.** The upper 32 bits — stride, swizzle, layout — never change at all. Built once at kernel start, never touched again.

That's the whole trick. A descriptor is just a number, and walking to the next tile is `+2`. We were treating it as "recompute the address, then re-encode it."

## Same problem — it's a 3-step fix and we've done 2

```
1. ubd  UNIFORM_B_DESC   DONE (this morning)
2. dh   DESC_HOIST       DONE
3. dw   DESC_WALK        NOT DONE   <- the 21 extra UMOV
```

`ubd` fixed the worst part: `nchunk0` depended on the warpgroup index `g`, so `g*12288` had to be computed at runtime, which shoved the value into a **vector** register (one per thread) and then had to cross it back to a **uniform** register with `R2UR` — 24 times per k-iteration. Specialising the mainloop per warpgroup made it a compile-time constant.

`dh` got the right *form* (`base + off>>4`) but still **rebuilds the base for every (stage, atom) pair** — that's why holding a second live stage costs a second rebuild.

`dw` is the last step: build the base **once per warpgroup**, fold stage/atom/chunk/k into the added offset. Then any number of live stages costs one add each — which is exactly cuBLAS's `UIADD3 +0x2`.

## And yes — it's in every variant

`dw` is off in all four pins. V3, V4, V6 all run `_dh_ubd_skew_lsw` with no `dw`. Every one of them still rebuilds the base per (stage, atom).

The morning's measurement on V3 (§H27zc1) was **111 address/descriptor bookkeeping instructions per k-iteration against cuBLAS's 28** — 72.1% of our k-loop versus 42.4% of theirs. `ubd`+`dh` cut into that; the current count is 105 non-wgmma against their 56. Still roughly 2×, and step 3 is the piece that closes it.

So the run I queued isn't a new guess — it's finishing a fix we already started, now that the phantom-tile penalty that was masking it is gone.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-19 20:12 IST]

Exactly right, and that's the sharpest way to put it. We deleted 19.5M instructions that were **off** the critical path — pure redundancy, no time attached. The remaining excess is 161.5M vs cuBLAS's 103.8M, still **57.7M**, and some fraction of *those* is what's costing us. Counting instructions can't tell us which; only position on the critical path can.

An instruction costs time here only if it delays something: a barrier release, the wgmma drain, or the gap between the last wgmma and the store. The descriptor math we removed sits in the consumer loop *while a wgmma is already in flight* — wgmma is async, so that math overlaps execution and is free. That's why the count fell and the clock didn't.

There's a more important consequence though. **Every number in my decomposition was measured on the broken 2×1 config:**

```
tensor instructions  17,399,808 vs 16,220,160     <- we now run 660 tiles, so these should be EQUAL
tensor % of peak          98.36 vs 98.58
sm throughput %           86.99 vs 97.86
cycles ratio                       1.2051
```

With the cluster fixed we do *identical* tensor work to cuBLAS — same 660 tiles, same 24 `HGMMA.64x96x16` per k-iteration. If both still ran the tensor pipe at 98% of peak we'd now be the same speed, and we're 6.8% off. So one of those numbers has moved, and which one moved tells us where the remaining time actually goes:

```
tensor instructions still higher  -> still doing extra work somewhere
tensor % of peak dropped          -> operand delivery, wgmma starved
throughput/elapsed gap remains    -> SM sitting idle, a pipelining stall
```

That's one run, and it replaces guessing with a measurement:

### CLAUDE [2026-08-19 20:14 IST]

Agreed — no more scattershot metrics. The targeted tool is PC sampling **with stall reasons**, on the fixed 1×2 kernel, diffed by address against cuBLAS. That points at the exact instruction, not a summary number.

The one thing blocking that has been a note in our own records saying this ncu only exposes `smsp__pcsamp_sample_count` — where samples land, not *why*. That's the difference between "warps are sitting here" (which misled us twice today: the producer spin and the instruction count) and "warps are **stalled** here waiting on X", which is the actual critical-path signal.

So before spending any GPU time, let's find out what this ncu can really give. This is a pure query — no kernel runs, instant:

```bash
echo "=== per-instruction PC-sampling stall metrics ==="
ncu --query-metrics 2>/dev/null | grep -i "pcsamp" | head -40
echo
echo "=== stall-reason metrics (aggregate) ==="
ncu --query-metrics 2>/dev/null | grep -i "warp_issue_stalled" | awk '{print $1}' | head -25
echo
echo "=== does this ncu have the sampling SECTIONS? ==="
ncu --list-sections 2>/dev/null | grep -iE "sampling|source|warp|stall"
echo
echo "=== ncu version ==="
ncu --version 2>/dev/null | head -3
```

What each outcome buys us:

- **`smsp__pcsamp_warps_issue_stalled_<reason>` variants exist** — best case. We get stall reason *per address*, run it on ours and cuBLAS, and the diff names the exact instructions where our warps are blocked rather than merely present. That is the direct answer to "where is the redundancy going".
- **Only `smsp__pcsamp_sample_count`, but a `WarpStateStats`/source section exists** — we drive it through `--section` instead of `--metrics`, which is how `ncu/v5.csv` got its stall columns in the first place.
- **Neither** — then the honest fallback is the SASS-level one: our `long_scoreboard` was 27.05% against cuBLAS's 14.72%, and `long_scoreboard` means waiting on global memory. In a warp-specialized kernel only the producer touches global, so that number pointing at 27% is a concrete thread to pull, and it's traceable statically in the SASS we already have locally.

Once we know which of the three we're in, I'll run the one measurement that fits and diff it by address.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-19 20:15 IST]

Both answers landed, and together they explain the paradox.

## The cluster fix is exactly right

```
                          ours          cuBLAS      ratio
tensor instructions  16,220,160      16,220,160    1.0000   <- IDENTICAL
cycles elapsed        1,530,965       1,517,122    1.0091   <- 0.91% slower
tensor % of peak          97.93           98.66    0.9926
throughput % of peak      96.32           97.19    0.9910
total instructions  181,089,308     103,828,293    1.7441
```

Tensor instructions now match cuBLAS **to the digit**. And in **cycles we are only 0.91% behind** — not 7%.

## So why does the clock say 7%?

Because **ncu locks the GPU clock** (`--clock-control base` is the default). Every number above is at a *fixed* frequency. The wall-clock benchmark runs at *free, boosting* clocks. Same cycles, different time, means one thing:

```
locked clock:   we are 0.91% slower   (cycles)
free clock:     we are ~7%  slower    (wall)
```

We execute **1.74× cuBLAS's instructions**. Those extra 77 million instructions do almost no *cycle* damage — they overlap the async wgmma, exactly as the `dw` null showed. But they still have to be fetched, decoded and issued, and that **burns power**, which pulls the sustained boost clock down. Cycles stay level; the clock they run at doesn't.

That reconciles everything from today: the producer spin costing nothing, `dw` deleting 19.5M instructions with no cycle gain, and the gap surviving anyway. Instruction count matters here — just through *power*, not through issue slots. And it explains why `dw` alone was too small: −10.8% instructions isn't enough to move a boost clock much.

## On PC-sampling stall reasons — that route is closed

`grep pcsamp` on `--query-metrics` returns **nothing**. Only the 19 aggregate `smsp__warp_issue_stalled_*` counters exist, plus `WarpStateStats` / `SourceCounters` sections. So per-instruction *stall reasons* aren't available on this ncu (2025.4.1) — we can get where samples land, never why, which is precisely the ambiguity that misled us twice today. Not worth more attempts.

## The one measurement that settles it

Derive the achieved clock for each kernel — cycles ÷ time — with clock control off:

```bash

B=build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix; S=2048x11264x16384
for k in bgemm_sm90_kernel nvjet; do
  ncu --metrics sm__cycles_elapsed.avg,gpu__time_duration.sum --csv --target-processes all \
      --clock-control none -k regex:$k -c 3 \
      $B --cfg=192x192x64_1x2_v_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw --shape="$S" --layout=tn --bench \
      > /tmp/c_$k.csv 2>&1
done
python3 - <<'PY'
import csv,collections
for k,lab in (('bgemm_sm90_kernel','ours'),('nvjet','cuBLAS')):
    rows=list(csv.reader(open('/tmp/c_%s.csv'%k)))
    h=next((r for r in rows if 'Metric Value' in r),None)
    if not h: print(lab,'NO HEADER'); continue
    mi,vi,ui=h.index('Metric Name'),h.index('Metric Value'),h.index('Metric Unit')
    d=collections.defaultdict(list)
    for r in rows:
        if len(r)==len(h) and r[0].isdigit():
            try: d[r[mi]].append((float(r[vi].replace(',','')),r[ui]))
            except ValueError: pass
    cyc=max(v for v,_ in d['sm__cycles_elapsed.avg'])
    t,u=max(d['gpu__time_duration.sum'])
    sec=t*{'nsecond':1e-9,'usecond':1e-6,'msecond':1e-3,'second':1}.get(u,1e-9)
    print("  %-7s cycles %12.0f   time %9.3f ms   achieved clock %6.0f MHz"%(lab,cyc,sec*1e3,cyc/sec/1e6))
PY
```

If ours comes back at a materially lower MHz than cuBLAS's, the remaining ~6% is power-driven and the lever is total instruction count — which makes `dw` worth keeping after all, as one contribution toward a target that needs several. If the clocks match, the power theory is dead and I'll say so.


And the remaining ~6.7 points is now **characterised, not mysterious**: roughly 2% extra cycles plus a few percent of clock throttling from executing 1.74× cuBLAS's instructions. That is not a structural defect in the kernel — the tensor work is now bit-identical to cuBLAS (16,220,160 both), the tensor pipe runs at 97.93% vs 98.66% of peak, and cycles are within 2%.

It also means there's no single knob left to find here. Closing the last few points needs broad instruction reduction across the whole kernel to lift the sustained clock — `dw`'s 19.5M is one real contribution toward that, just not one you can see on its own. That's a campaign, not a fix.

Now the attribution:
> tool `Bash`: Attribute the excess instructions by opcode

**There's the answer, exact and by opcode.** The excess is 90.5M warp-instructions, and it is overwhelmingly one thing:

```
opcode          ours       cuBLAS        excess   %gap
UMOV      35,058,540    3,229,402    31,829,138   35.2%
ULOP3     13,505,184        8,052    13,497,132   14.9%   <- 1677x
BRA       15,868,712    3,983,208    11,885,504   13.1%
ULEA       7,399,656            0     7,399,656    8.2%   <- cuBLAS ZERO
USHF       6,820,176       33,836     6,786,340    7.5%   <- 202x
UIMAD      7,131,960      445,368     6,686,592    7.4%
SYNCS      9,391,480    3,484,870     5,906,610    6.5%
```

**`UMOV + ULOP3 + ULEA + USHF + UIMAD` = 66.2 million = 73% of the entire excess.** Every one is uniform-datapath address arithmetic.

And the shape of it names the culprit precisely. Recall the descriptor encode:

```
desc_encode(x) = (x & 0x3FFFF) >> 4
                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^   ^^^^
                     ULOP3       USHF
```

`ULOP3` = the mask. `USHF` = the shift-by-4. cuBLAS executes **8,052 ULOP3 and 33,836 USHF in the entire kernel** — effectively zero. We execute 13.5M and 6.8M.

**cuBLAS never encodes a descriptor inside the loop. It only ever adds to one.** That's the `UIADD3 UR16, UR16, 0x2` we saw, and it's why their `ULEA` count is literally 0 while ours is 7.4M.

This is the same thing §H27zc1 recorded back in the morning — *"cuBLAS has literally ZERO of ULOP3-mask / USHF->>4 / UMOV-reload / R2UR"* — now measured as exact execution counts across the whole kernel rather than static counts in one loop.

One more thing worth flagging, because it kills a whole class of theory: **stall samples are ours 73,614 vs cuBLAS 83,628.** They stall *more* than we do. We are not stall-bound. We're doing more work.

So `dw` was aimed at the right target and only got 19.5M of the 66M. The question is where the other 47M sits:
> tool `Bash`: Locate where the descriptor arithmetic executes

**Fully localized.** The excess lives in one place:

```
region                     instr exec    % tot    of which DESC-math
consumer (HGMMA span)     143,831,160    73.7%      60,708,780   <-- here
producer (UTMALDG span)    31,465,104    16.1%       8,233,632
epilogue/tail              19,335,200     9.9%         842,556
prologue                      576,200     0.3%         130,548
```

**60.7M of the 66M descriptor arithmetic is inside the consumer k-loop.** And the top-executed instructions show the exact pattern, each running 673,200 times:

```
479   UMOV   UR12, UR4
480   WARPGROUP.ARRIVE
481   UIMAD  UR10, UR12, 0xc000, UR5
482   BSSY   B0, ...
483   UMOV   UR21, 0x40000040      <- descriptor UPPER word, a CONSTANT
484   UMOV   UR23, 0x80000020      <- descriptor UPPER word, a CONSTANT
485   UIADD3 UR11, UR10, 0x9000, URZ
```

`0x40000040` and `0x80000020` are the descriptor's **upper 32 bits** — leading-dim, stride, swizzle, layout. Those never change for the entire kernel. We reload them with `UMOV` **on every single k-iteration**.

The arithmetic closes exactly: ~23 `UMOV` per k-loop body × 673,200 executions × 2 consumer loops ≈ **31M**, against the measured 31.8M `UMOV` excess. cuBLAS executes 2.

Our own `DESC_WALK` doc states the rule we're breaking, verbatim: *"The upper 32 bits (leading-dim, stride, base-offset, layout type) are built once and never rebuilt."* `dw` builds the *base* once and got 19.5M of it — but the constant upper word is still being re-materialized, which is the other 47M.

So the chain is complete and every link is measured:

```
we rebuild the wgmma descriptor's constant upper word every k-iteration
   -> 66M excess uniform-datapath instructions, 60.7M of them in the consumer loop
   -> 1.74x cuBLAS's total instruction count
   -> more power drawn -> sustained clock 1557 vs 1582 MHz
   -> plus 1.9% more cycles
   -> 3.55% slower isolated, ~6.8% slower sustained
```

Not stalls — we stall *less* than cuBLAS (73,614 vs 83,628 samples). Just surplus work.

Let me find why those constants aren't held in registers:
> tool `Bash`: Find the wgmma descriptor construction code

The builder shows exactly why. `make_gmma_desc_k_major(addr)` assembles the **whole 64-bit descriptor on every call**:

```cpp
return desc_encode_sm90((uint64_t)addr)              // varies    -> ULOP3 + USHF
     | (desc_encode_sm90(K_LBO_BYTES) << 16ULL)      // CONSTANT  -> UMOV
     | (desc_encode_sm90(stride)      << 32ULL)      // CONSTANT  -> UMOV 0x40000040
     | (layout_type                   << 62ULL);     // CONSTANT  -> UMOV 0x80000020
```

Three of the four terms are compile-time constants, and we re-materialise and re-OR them **every single call**, 24 wgmma per k-iteration. That is precisely the `ULOP3 / USHF / UMOV` triple that dominates the excess, and precisely what cuBLAS replaced with one `UIADD3 +0x2`.

Let me see what `dw` actually covers, since it only reclaimed 19.5M of the 66M:
> tool `Bash`: Find all descriptor call sites and DESC_WALK coverage

Found the gap. `DESC_WALK` *is* implemented for both A and B (lines 4353, 4409) — but look at what it still has to compute:

```cpp
4414:  make_gmma_desc_mn_major<...>(B_smem + (ks * (16 * AW_B) + nchunk_term) * 2)
```

Even in walk form, the **offset itself** is derived from loop indices — a multiply (`UIMAD`), a mask (`ULOP3`), a shift (`USHF`). cuBLAS never computes an offset at all. Their descriptor is a **loop-carried accumulator advanced by literals**: `+0x2` per k16 step, `+0x200` per m64 atom, `-0x6` to unwind — which is exactly what our own slot-29 comment records from their SASS.

That's why `dw` reclaimed 19.5M of 60.7M: it removed the *base* rebuild but kept the *offset* arithmetic.

Let me read the exact expression so the fix is concrete rather than hand-waved:
> tool `Bash`: Read the DESC_WALK inner-loop expressions

Now I can see it precisely. Under `DESC_WALK` the inner expression is already right:

```cpp
const uint64_t a_desc = a_desc_stage + (uint64_t)(a_walk_off >> 4);
```

and `a_walk_off` is **fully compile-time** — `ks`, `nc`, `atom_idx` are `#pragma unroll` indices, `AW_*/BM/BN/WGMMA_N` are `constexpr`. So that line should already compile to cuBLAS's `UIADD3 desc, base, LITERAL`. Which is exactly why `dw` reclaimed 19.5M.

So the honest position: I know the mechanism and I know `dw` removes a third of it, but **the 60.7M figure was measured on the baseline, without `dw`.** I don't yet know what the remaining ~47M looks like or where it sits — and guessing from source is what got refuted twice today.

**Why ptxas rematerialises the barrier address.** Decoding the SASS: `(CgaCtaId << 24) + 0x418 + stage*8`. In a clustered launch `__cvta_generic_to_shared` returns the *DSMEM* form, where bits 24+ hold the CTA rank. So the address is `shared_window_base(rank) + 0x418 + stage*8`. The base is kernel-invariant — but ptxas is under UR pressure (46 distinct URs in the producer alone, ~63 available) and decides five cheap uniform instructions beat holding a live UR. It's a register-allocation heuristic, so "hoist it in source" won't work: it's *already* hoisted, at line 1906, and ptxas re-sinks it.

**The one thing ptxas cannot rematerialise is a loop-carried variable.** If a value is defined by a phi at the loop header and updated on the back edge, it *must* live in a register. That's not a hint — it's forced.

> tool `Bash`: Extract the SKEW loop body code

Structure is clear. Writing the unroll — align to the ring, then emit `D` literal bodies:
> tool `Bash`: Add the KLOOP_UNROLL knob and ring emitter

Now the main refactor — extract the body as a lambda and add the aligned/unrolled path alongside the original loop:
> tool `Bash`: Add the lambda and aligned-unrolled path, verify OFF path unchanged

OFF path byte-identical. Now the ON arm:
> tool `Bash`: Build and measure the unrolled arms

That's the documented trap and I walked into it. **`R2UR=48` per k-loop** — the exact number the file records:

> *"`stage` reaches the loop header as a phi of two DISTINCT computed definitions. ptxas then cannot prove the descriptor chain warp-uniform, drops all of it onto the vector datapath, and pays 48 R2UR crossings"*

My lambda writes `stage = S` from four different places (align, three literal bodies, residue), so the phi got *worse*, not better. The fix is that the unrolled bodies must never touch `stage` at all — the literals already carry the information:
> tool `Bash`: Remove stage writes from the unrolled bodies and remeasure

Unchanged — 159/165 with `R2UR=48`. So `stage` wasn't the trigger. Let me look at what's actually crossing datapaths rather than guess a third time:
> tool `Bash`: Inspect the vector-path instructions in the unrolled body

That's the **align/residue** loop, not a main body — `VIADD R8,R8,0x1` with `IMAD R172,R176,0xc000` is the runtime-stage path. My loop detector picks innermost loops, and the main unrolled loop spans all three bodies, so it reports `HGMMA=36`, not 12. I measured the wrong loop. Looking for the real one:
> tool `Bash`: Find the real main unrolled loop with HGMMA=36

**It works.** My detector was reporting the align/residue loops. The real main loop:

```
HGMMA=36   190 instrs [711..900]   R2UR=1  UMOV=18  UIADD3=56  IMAD=6
                                   -> 63 instructions per body
```

```
baseline          117 per body
dw                101
dw + UNROLL        63     <- cuBLAS is 68
```

**63 against cuBLAS's 68 — we're now smaller than their k-loop**, with `R2UR=1` and `IMAD=6`, i.e. the descriptor chain stayed on the uniform datapath. The literals folded exactly as intended. Confirming it's genuinely three clean bodies:
> tool `Bash`: Verify the unrolled main loop has no runtime stage math

Confirmed — this is exactly cuBLAS's pattern now:

```
719  UMOV UR28, UR8
720  UMOV UR29, 0x40000040        <- descriptor upper word, once per body
722  UIADD3.64 UR20, UR28, 0x1800 <- LITERAL (stage 2 folded: 2*0xc00)
726  HGMMA
727  UIADD3.64 UR20, UR28, 0x1880 <- +0x80 literal
729  HGMMA
730  UIADD3.64 UR20, UR28, 0x1900
732  HGMMA
733  UIADD3.64 UR20, UR28, 0x1980
735  HGMMA
```

Zero hits for `0xc000` (the `stage*copy_size` multiply) and zero for `0x55555556` (the mod-3) anywhere in the main loop. Both are gone. The only survivors are the two `SR_CgaCtaId` barrier rebuilds — that's item ②, still open.

**Expected executed-instruction saving:** `(101−63) × 673,200 × 2 = 51M`, taking us 175M → ~124M against cuBLAS's 105M. A −29% cut, which is the first change big enough to plausibly move the clock (`dw`'s −10.5% didn't).

Caveats I want on the record before you run it: static size grew 3384 → 4096 (+21%, three body copies) so I-cache is an unknown, and the align/residue loops are bloated at ~160 instructions — but they execute ~4 of 256 iterations, so ~1.6%.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-19 21:13 IST]

**Both readings in, and together they close this avenue.**

```
                    instructions      x cuBLAS      %cuB min/med/max     TFLOPS med
baseline           181,038,325         1.7437      92.10 / 92.80 / 94.10    639.09
dw                 161,495,666         1.5554      91.40 / 93.00 / 93.80    640.74
dw + unroll        150,494,640         1.4495      92.10 / 93.50 / 94.40    643.78
cuBLAS             103,826,000
```

The unroll is **bit-exact and really does cut instructions** — 161.5M → 150.5M. But two things are true and I'll state both plainly.

**My arithmetic was wrong.** I predicted ~124M from `38 × 673,200 × 2 = 51M`; the actual saving was 11.0M. The main unrolled loop clearly isn't carrying as large a share of executions as the per-body count implied, so that estimate was too aggressive.

**And the wall clock is another null.** 93.50 median against 92.80, ranges 92.10–94.40 versus 92.10–94.10 — almost total overlap. +0.7 is inside the noise band.

That's now three consecutive cuts on the same lever:

```
dw            -20.5M    ->  null
dw + unroll   -11.0M    ->  null (+0.7, overlapping)
total         -30.5M  (-16.9% of the kernel's instructions)
             wall clock: 92.80 -> 93.50
```

**Instruction count is not what's costing V5 the remaining points.** The power/clock theory predicted a real but small effect, and a 17% cut failing to move anything measurable is strong evidence against it being the lever. I'd rather call that now than keep grinding a mechanism the data has refuted three times.

## Where V5 actually ended up

```
start of today   82.20 %cuB
1x2 cluster      92.80        +10.6, ranges separated, the real fix
+ dw + unroll    93.50        +0.7, within noise
```

Against the family: V3 95.79, V4 96.56, V6 95.14, **V5 93.50**. No longer the outlier — it was one wasted tile column all along.

On what to pin: `1x2_v_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw` is already in `pins.sh` and is the honest choice, since `dw`/`unroll` add real complexity for a gain we cannot measure. The unroll is validated bit-exact on all three residue classes and sits in the tree behind a default-off knob, so it costs nothing to leave available.

What the remaining ~6.5 points *is*: the 1.9% extra cycles measured earlier, plus clock, and neither traces to instruction count. That's a fresh investigation, not a continuation of this one.

Two things still owed from today: §H27zdu (the cluster fix) and §H27zdv/§H27zdy (these negative results — worth writing down precisely so nobody re-runs them) into `analyzations_h200.md`, and the EOD with the items you flagged. Say the word and I'll write either.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-20 11:29 IST]

No — `2x1_v` is *supposed* to stay at 84%. That's the broken arm, kept only as the control.

`2x1` means the cluster spans 2 CTAs along **M**. V5's M is 2048, which is 11 tile rows — an odd number — so the cluster rounds it up to 12 and runs a whole phantom column of 59 tiles. **That waste is inherent to clustering the odd axis.** There's no knob that fixes it while staying 2x1 on this shape; the only fix is to cluster the other axis, which is what `1x2` is. So `2x1` at 84% and `1x2` at 94.5% is exactly the expected result — if `2x1` had *also* jumped to 95%, it would mean our explanation was wrong and something else caused the gain.

**And the fix reproduced on new hardware:**

```
                old box (dark-leaf)      new box (deep-ball, GPU 1)
2x1_v            82.20                    84.20
1x2_v            92.80                    94.50
gap             +10.60                   +10.30      <- reproduced
ranges          separated                separated   (85.20 < 92.50)
```

This box is slightly faster in absolute terms — cuBLAS medians ~697.9 here vs ~687 before, ours 659 vs 639 — so absolute TFLOPS from yesterday aren't quotable, but every %cuB is, and the finding holds independently of hardware. `maxRelErr` 0.00000 throughout.

So V5 now sits at **94.50%** on this box, and the family stands:

```
V3  99.44    V4  99.79    V6  98.53 (stage 3) / 96.37 (stage 4, apples-to-apples)
V5  94.50    <- was 82.20 yesterday morning
```

Yesterday's other three arms (`dw`, `dwunr`, the unroll) are all in the tree and registered, so they can be re-measured here whenever you want — but they were nulls on the old box and the instruction-count lever is closed, so I wouldn't spend GPU time re-confirming them.

What's actually open for V5: ~5.5 points, and we know it is **not** instruction count (three cuts, −17%, no movement) and **not** stalls (we stall less than cuBLAS). The untested idea is the one in that older `e949a2c` commit — prefetch depth, backed by `long_scoreboard 27.05 vs 14.72`, and it's the only V5 hypothesis ever backed by a stall counter rather than an inference. It predates the tile-column fix, so it deserves a run against the corrected baseline. Want me to set that up?

**PHASE A — all 15 shapes at their pinned configs.** Sources `pins.sh` so the pins can't drift:

```bash

export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 BLUBLAS_BENCH_TARGET_MS=400

[ -x "$B" ] || { echo "build first"; exit 1; }
: > $O
for v in "${PIN_ORDER[@]}"; do
  IFS='|' read -r shape lay cfg <<< "${PIN[$v]}"
  for r in $(seq 1 $REPS); do
    $B --cfg="$cfg" --shape="$shape" --layout="$lay" --bench 2>&1 \
      | awk -v v="$v" -v s="$shape" -v l="$lay" -v c="$cfg" '$1==c{print v,s,l,$4,$5,$7,$8,$9}'
  done
done | tee -a $O
echo "" >> $O
echo "===== SUMMARY  variant / shape / lay / n / %cuB min-med-max / ours med / cuBLAS med / status =====" >> $O
awk '{k=$1"|"$2"|"$3; c[k]++; p[k"#"c[k]]=$8+0; f[k"#"c[k]]=$6+0; b[k"#"c[k]]=$7+0;
      if($4!="PASS")st[k]=$4; if($5>e[k])e[k]=$5}

   for(i=1;i<n;i++)for(j=i+1;j<=n;j++){if(x[j]<x[i]){t=x[i];x[i]=x[j];x[j]=t}
     if(y[j]<y[i]){t=y[i];y[i]=y[j];y[j]=t} if(z[j]<z[i]){t=z[i];z[i]=z[j];z[j]=t}}
   split(k,a,"|");
   printf "%-4s %-18s %-3s n=%d  %6.2f /%6.2f /%6.2f   ours %7.2f  cuB %7.2f  %s err=%s\n",
     a[1],a[2],a[3],n,x[1],x[int((n+1)/2)],x[n],y[int((n+1)/2)],z[int((n+1)/2)],
```

That's 105 timed invocations at a 400 ms window — budget roughly 30–60 minutes, longer for the 50304-N shapes. I kept REPS=7 deliberately rather than trimming it: changing the rep count between comparisons is what made yesterday's early numbers unquotable, and I'd rather these be directly comparable to V5's.

**PHASE B — which cuBLAS kernel each shape actually gets.** This is what decides apples-to-apples, and we've never captured it for V1, V2, V7 or V8:

```bash

      $B --cfg="$cfg" --shape="$shape" --layout="$lay" --bench > /tmp/k_$v.csv 2>&1
  python3 - "$v" "$shape" "$lay" "$cfg" <<'PY'
import csv,sys

PY
done
```

## Phase 2 — this is the finding: **not one of the 15 shapes is a full apples-to-apples match**

```
V     ours                          cuBLAS                                   differs on
V1    128x128 2x1 v  sk2            128x128  64x6 1x2 h  splitK   NTT        cluster, raster, stages
V2*   256x128 2x1 h                 128x256  64x4 2x1 v  coopA    NTN        TILE, raster
V3    192x192 2x1 h                 192x192  64x3 1x2 h  coopB    NNN        cluster
V4    192x192 2x1 h                 192x192  64x3 2x1 v  coopB    NNN        raster
V5    192x192 1x2 v                 192x192  64x3 2x1 v  coopB    NTN        cluster
V6    192x192 2x1 h                 192x192  64x4 2x1 v  coopB    TNN        stages, raster
V7*   128x256 2x1 h                 256x128  64x4 1x2 h  coopA    NNT        TILE, cluster
V8*   128x256 2x1 h                 256x128  64x4 1x2 h  coopA    TNT        TILE, cluster
```

Three things jump out. **The tile itself differs on 10 of 15 shapes** — V2×3, V7×3, V8×4 — and in opposite directions: we pin 256x128 where cuBLAS picks 128x256, and 128x256 where it picks 256x128. **cuBLAS varies its cluster per shape** (1x2 on V1/V3/V7/V8, 2x1 on V2/V4/V5/V6) while we are fixed at 2x1 everywhere except V5. And **cuBLAS uses coopA or coopB on every single shape** — we have neither.

That reframes the campaign: "%cuB" on 10 of 15 shapes has never been a parity comparison at all, it's us-with-one-tile against cuBLAS-with-another.

I've got the workflow checking the load-bearing parts — whether cuBLAS's tile string really reads M×N the same way ours does (V2c at N=50304 and V7 at M=16384 have opposite aspect ratios and should settle it), whether we already have registered configs with the matching tiles, and whether the spreads here are tight enough to trust these medians (V8's 90.40–97.00 is 6.6 points, so that one certainly isn't). I'll report when it lands.

```
coopA/coopB      closed H12.5
```

So the %cuB numbers **are** genuine parity numbers on tile and layout, and the one open GROUP-1 gap is **stage count** — which the rollback note already names: *"4 stages on 256x128/128x256 is blocked by our full-tile epilogue buffer (13 sites), and split-K exists only on 64x64 not 128x128 (2 sites)."*

That's the thread worth pulling, because it connects to work already done: **V6's parked stage-4 arm (`ea96s1`, atom-staged STSM epilogue) reached 96.37 and is exactly the technique that unblocks the full-tile epilogue buffer.** It's proven on one tile; the blocker it solves is what stops depth 4 on 13 of the 21 call sites.

Also worth keeping in view from the rollback record: pinning cuBLAS's own variants at all 21 sites measured **86.1% → 73.2%** — every site slower, no exceptions. So matching more fields is a *diagnostic* to find defects, not a route to more speed.

The coverage result itself stands and is new: all 15 shapes measured, median **95.0%**, worst V1 at 87.40, and V3/V4/V6 at 96.90/97.10/95.50 rather than the 99s I quoted from the old 20 ms window.

## V5 — one lead left, and it's cheap to settle

V5 is now **fully matched** (tile ✓ layout ✓ stages 3=3 ✓) and sits at 93.80, against its two matched peers V3 96.90 and V4 97.10. Same tile, same stage count, same everything — **3 points behind**. That's the cleanest signal on the board.

What's closed: instruction count (three cuts, −17%, zero clock movement), the producer spin (slack), and stalls generally — we stall *less* than cuBLAS.

What's open is the hypothesis in that `e949a2c` commit, and it's the only V5 idea ever backed by a stall counter instead of an inference:

```
long_scoreboard   27.05 vs 14.72   +12.33   global-memory dependency
mio_throttle       6.14 vs 15.23    -9.09   their memory pipe saturated, ours 40% as busy
short_scoreboard   1.40 vs  0.03            shared memory: negligible
lsu ld conflicts      0 vs    724
```

Not enough loads in flight to cover DRAM latency — and it's V5-only because its working set is **436 MB against a 50 MB L2 (9×)** with 256 k-iters per tile, where V3/V4/V6 have K=2048 and L2 largely absorbs the operands.

Two caveats that make this worth exactly one measurement rather than a campaign: those counters were taken on the **broken 2x1 baseline** with 708 tiles and a ragged 6th wave, so some of that latency signature may have been the phantom column; and depth-4 on V5 *was* tried yesterday, giving 82.36 / 81.94 / 70.84 against 82.46 — flat to much worse, but again on the broken baseline. One ncu stall capture on the fixed 1x2 config tells us whether `long_scoreboard` is still +12 or whether the cluster fix already absorbed it.

## Then the ordering I'd argue for

**The 4-stage epilogue-buffer blocker, not V2 or V1 in isolation.** It's one blocker covering **V2 + V7 + V8 = 10 of 15 shapes**, and the technique that unblocks it is already proven — V6's `ea96s1` atom-staged STSM epilogue, which is what let depth 4 fit at all and reached 96.37. Fixing it once moves two-thirds of the model's shapes.

**V1 last, and separately.** It's the worst shape at 87.40 but it's one shape, and its gap is structural in a different way: cuBLAS runs 64x6 + split-K on 128x128, while our split-K exists only on 64x64. That's new code, not a config change.

So: one ncu run on V5 to close or confirm the latency lead, then the epilogue buffer for the 10 shapes, then V1. Want me to write the V5 stall capture into `tools/` and push it?

### CLAUDE [2026-08-20 12:13 IST]

Good question, and the answer flips from what I implied — because the depth-4 blocker is probably **not** a performance win.

Here's the evidence against doing it first. On V6, where we *did* unblock depth 4 with the STSM atom-staged epilogue, it came out **behind** depth 3:

```
V6 stage 3   98.53      <- what we ship
V6 stage 4   96.37      <- the apples-to-apples match, 2.2 points SLOWER
```

And the reason is documented and structural: `%cuB tracks MEMBAR count at ~0.83 pts each (1→98.56, 3→96.37, 6→94.54, 9→91.94)`. Depth 4 forces chunking, chunking needs ≥3 MEMBARs against depth 3's 1, so depth 4 starts ~1.7 points behind — and that's blocked on the PTX bare-fence gap, not on our epilogue code. It lines up with the other measurement on record: pinning cuBLAS's own variants at all 21 sites went **86.1% → 73.2%**, every site slower.

So porting depth 4 to V2/V7/V8 buys us a *correct apples-to-apples comparison on 10 shapes* — which is a diagnostic that exposes where our depth-4 implementation loses — but the expected immediate effect on %cuB is negative. That's real value for finding defects, and it's the wrong thing to do first if we're chasing points.

## The order I'd argue for

**1. V5 — one ncu run.** Not a campaign. It's fully matched (tile ✓ layout ✓ stages 3=3 ✓) and 3 points behind its matched twins V3/V4, so anything found there is a pure implementation defect. The single open hypothesis needs one stall capture on the fixed 1x2 config to see whether `long_scoreboard +12.33` survived the cluster fix.

**2. V2 — never investigated at all.** Three shapes, and the weakest of the covered families:

```
V2   94.50    V2b  94.50    V2c  91.00
```

V2c at 91.00 is the second-worst shape on the board. Zero prior work, zero prior hypotheses — and V5's +10 came from exactly that situation: a structural bug in untouched code that no correctness test could see. I already checked the obvious one, and none of V1/V2/V7/V8 has an odd clustered-axis tile count, so it isn't the same bug — but nobody has looked at anything else there.

**3. The depth-4 blocker** for V2+V7+V8, as an apples-to-apples diagnostic with eyes open that it may score lower.

**4. V1 last.** Worst shape at 87.40, but one shape, and it needs new code — cuBLAS runs 64x6 + split-K on 128x128 while our split-K exists only on 64x64.

So: V5's one run, then V2 with fresh eyes, then the blocker, then V1. Want me to write the V5 stall capture into `tools/` and push it?

### CLAUDE [2026-08-20 12:39 IST]

Decisive on all three counts. Let me check one disambiguation before I call it:
> tool `Bash`: Check for per-K absolute TFLOPS and DRAM data
> tool `Bash`: Extract per-K DRAM and cache metrics

All three questions answered, and the third one turned up something new.

## 1. The latency hypothesis is **refuted**

```
K       working set   long_scoreboard   L2 hit%
512        13 MB          29.36          94.13
2048       52 MB          29.62          87.08
4096      104 MB          30.08          84.41
8192      208 MB          29.67          83.54
16384     416 MB          28.15          80.29
```

`long_scoreboard` is **flat across a 32× change in working set** — and it's still 29.36 at K=512 where 94% of accesses hit L2 and there's almost no DRAM traffic. "Not enough loads in flight to cover DRAM latency" cannot produce a stall that's identical when there is barely any DRAM latency to cover. The L2 hit rate moved properly (94→80), so the experiment worked; the stall just doesn't follow it.

The signature itself did survive the cluster fix — `+13.68` now vs `+12.33` before — so it's real and belongs to the kernel, not to the phantom column. It just isn't what e949a2c said it was.

## 2. Depth 4 is confirmed dead, this time on a correct baseline

```
baseline depth 3     92.60  (91.50-94.30)
ea32s2stsm depth 4   93.20  (92.50-93.90)   +0.6, ranges overlap
ea8s2 depth 4        85.30  (84.30-87.20)   -7.3
```

## 3. The real finding — **V5's deficit is a function of K, and it's DRAM re-reads**

Same config, same M, same N, only K changes:

```
K=512   96.90     K=2048  96.70     K=4096  93.50     K=8192  93.40     K=16384  93.20
```

**At K=2048 — V3 and V4's K — V5's config scores 96.70**, right alongside V3's 96.90 and V4's 97.10. The 3-point gap isn't about `tn`, or the cluster, or the config. It appears as a cliff between K=2048 and K=4096 and then flattens.

And the DRAM counters say why. Ideal traffic is `(2048 + 11264) × K × 2` bytes if every byte is read once:

```
K        ideal      measured     re-read ratio    mio_throttle
512      13.0 MB     13.2 MB        1.01              9.41
2048     52.0 MB     86.5 MB        1.66              6.26
4096    104.0 MB    228.6 MB        2.20              5.47
8192    208.0 MB    460.3 MB        2.21              5.15
16384   416.0 MB    943.3 MB        2.27              5.23
```

**We move 2.27× the necessary bytes at K=16384**, and the ratio steps up exactly where %cuB falls off. `mio_throttle` tracks it inversely — 9.41 down to 5.23 — while cuBLAS holds 15.28. That reframes the original observation: their memory pipe isn't saturated because they're latency-bound, it's busy because they're using it efficiently; ours is idle *and* wasteful.

So it's not a latency problem, it's a **locality** problem — and the knob that controls L2 tile-walk locality is the raster swizzle, which V5 pins at `rs8`. The earlier "raster has zero duration effect" result was measured on shapes whose working set fits in L2, where there is nothing for it to fix.

**One measurement is missing before I'd act on this: cuBLAS's own DRAM read volume on this shape.** If they also move ~2.2× then the re-reads are inherent to the tiling and the gap is elsewhere; if they move 1.3× then we've found it. That's one ncu capture, and it should go in the same run as an `rs2/rs4/rs8/rs16` sweep on V5's real shape. Want me to write it?

We don't — I checked, and both old V5 captures have **zero** dram/L2 columns: they collected stall, tensor and throughput metrics but never memory-traffic ones. So the cuBLAS comparison genuinely needs one capture. But that's cheap, and it rides along with the fix attempt.

And your main point is right: **2.27× is waste on its own terms.** We move 943 MB where 416 MB would do. Whether cuBLAS also wastes it doesn't change that removing it makes us faster — cuBLAS's number just tells us how much is reachable.

One caution before I write it, because it may bound what's achievable. At K=16384 each 192-wide panel is `192 × 16384 × 2 = 6.3 MB`, and the 11 M-panels alone are **69 MB against a 50 MB L2**. So no tile-walk order can hold even one full column of A — there may be a hard floor well above 1.0×. That's exactly why the re-read ratio jumps at K=4096 (where panels cross ~1.6 MB and the working set outgrows L2) and then sits flat at ~2.2.

That makes the raster swizzle the right first thing to try — it's the knob that sets how many tiles share a cached panel, it costs nothing to test, and `rs8` was chosen on shapes where L2 held everything and the choice was free.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-20 14:01 IST]

Let me lay it out plainly.

## Where V5 stands

```
yesterday morning    82.2%   of cuBLAS
after the tile fix   93.6%
with rs1 (today)     95.5%
cuBLAS               100%
```

**The gap is not cleared. About 4.5 points are left.**

## What we tested today and what died

**Theory 1 — "V5 is waiting on slow memory."** Dead. We changed K so the data went from 13 MB to 416 MB — a 32× change — and the waiting-on-memory counter never moved (29.4 → 28.2). It was even the same when everything fit in cache. So it was never waiting on memory.

**Theory 2 — "V5 needs deeper prefetch (4 stages)."** Dead, now properly tested on the fixed kernel. +0.6, inside the noise. The other 4-stage variant was 7 points worse.

**Theory 3 — and this one was real.** We were **reading the same data from memory over and over**.

## What `rs1` actually is, in plain terms

The GPU splits the output into 660 small tiles and works through them. **`rs` is how many tiles it groups together as it walks.** Our setting was 8 — do 8 tiles as a block, then move on.

That grouping decides what stays in cache. With a group of 8, the chunk of data needed is too big to keep, so it gets thrown out and fetched from memory again. With a group of 1, the working set stays small and the cache holds it.

Measured, same job, only the walk order changed:

```
group 8  (now)   reads   953 MB from memory     scores 93.6%
group 1  (rs1)   reads   672 MB from memory     scores 95.5%
the job actually needs  416 MB
```

**Same maths, same answer, 281 MB less memory traffic.** That's pure waste we were doing and now don't have to.

And it's not one lucky number — all five settings line up in order, 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 getting steadily worse on both traffic and speed. That's why I trust it.

## Should we do it?

**Yes.** It's a one-line pin change, it measured better on both the counter and the clock, and the ranges don't overlap (rs1's worst run beat rs8's best run). Nothing to lose.

One honest note on why we're still 4.5 short: **we now move 25% fewer bytes than cuBLAS does** (672 MB vs their 901 MB) and we're *still* slower. So the memory traffic was a real cost we've now removed, but it isn't the last one. Where the remaining 4.5 points go is genuinely not known yet.

The bigger prize is that eight of the fifteen shapes have the same large-K setup where this setting matters — V1, V2, V2b, V2c, V5, V7b, V8c, V8d — and all of them are on `rs8` today. If it carries across, that's a couple of points on over half the model for a one-line change each.

So: pin V5 to `rs1`, then test the other seven. Want me to do both in one go?


**The right supergroup really is a function of K.** At K=2048 removing the grouping is catastrophic — V4 goes from 2426 MB to 9276 MB, nearly 4× the traffic and −6.8 points. At K=16384 it's the reverse. Same knob, opposite sign, exactly as the panel arithmetic predicted (0.79 MB panels group well, 6.3 MB panels thrash).

**On V5 specifically, be aware the evidence softened.** Two independent runs both favour `rs1` — +1.9 in H27zg and +0.9 here — but at REPS=9 the ranges now *overlap* (rs1 min 93.80 vs rs8 max 94.70), where yesterday's run had them separated. What doesn't wobble is the DRAM figure: **676.5 vs 932.5 MB, −27.5%**, deterministic and reproduced across both runs. Consistent direction twice plus a hard counter is enough for me to pin it, but it's a ~1-point change, not a 10-point one.

V6 is a genuine tie (95.70 vs 95.20, DRAM within 4%) — makes sense, its N=5632 is small enough that the working set never gets big either way.

## The lead this opened up

Look at V4's `rs8` row: **2425.8 MB, 9.31× ideal**, and V3's **430.2 MB, 3.98× ideal**. Those are our two best-scoring shapes and they're still moving 4–9× the necessary bytes. If grouping harder helps at small K, then `rs8` may not be far enough — `rs16` is available (the knob caps at group 16), panels there are only 0.79 MB, so a group of 16 costs ~25 MB and still fits the 50 MB L2.

V4 is the largest shape in the model. Going after its 9.31× is a bigger prize than V5's remaining points.

So I'd do: **pin V5 → `rs1`** (settled), keep `rs8` on V3/V4/V6, and immediately test **`rs16` on V3 and V4**. Want both in one push?

### CLAUDE [2026-08-20 14:39 IST]

**Clean close — `rs8` is already the optimum, and the two curves are textbook U-shapes.**

```
V3  group   2      4      8 ✓     16
    DRAM  1008.2  601.1  454.0   687.2  MB
    %cuB   92.60  94.60  96.30   93.80

V4  group   2      4      8 ✓     16
    DRAM  5511.3 4028.7 3033.0  3995.6  MB
    %cuB   93.90  95.90  97.60   96.20
```

Both metrics, both shapes, minimum bytes and maximum score all landing on **group 8**. `rs16` is worse on both. The knob is fully explored at K=2048 and the pins stay as they are.

## And the two experiments together give a closed-form rule

```
K=2048   panel = 192*2048*2  = 0.79 MB   optimum group  8   ->  8 x 0.79 = 6.3 MB
K=16384  panel = 192*16384*2 = 6.29 MB   optimum group  1   ->  1 x 6.29 = 6.3 MB
```

**The optimum group size × panel size is the same constant, ~6.3 MB.** Which reduces to:

```
optimal group  ≈  16384 / K
```

K=2048 → 8 ✓, K=16384 → 1 ✓, and it predicts V6 (K=2048) → 8, which is what H27zh measured. That's a real law, not a fitted curve — it says the walk should keep about 6.3 MB of operand panel live regardless of shape, and today the group is hardcoded per config instead of derived. That belongs in the dispatcher.

**One honesty correction.** I said the DRAM counter was deterministic — it isn't, quite. V4's `rs8` read **2425.8 MB** in H27zh and **3033.0 MB** here, same config, same shape, 25% apart. V3's moved 430.2 → 454.0 (5%). So cache state carries between runs and the byte figures have real variance too. The *shape* of the curves is consistent across both runs and that's what the conclusion rests on, but individual byte numbers shouldn't be quoted to three digits.

## Where V5 and the campaign stand

```
V5   82.20 (yesterday morning)  ->  93.60 (cluster fix)  ->  95.00-95.50 (rs1, now pinned)
V3   96.30      V4   97.60      V6   95.70
```

V5's raster work is done — `rs1` pinned, ~1 point and −27.5% traffic. The remaining ~4.5 points on V5 are still unexplained, and we now know they're **not** instruction count, **not** stalls, **not** depth, and **not** memory traffic, since at `rs1` we move 25% fewer bytes than cuBLAS and are still behind.

> *"WGMMA_SKEW needs >= 2 m64 atoms per warpgroup: it carries atom 0 to the next pass and issues the rest on acquire, so MAX_ATOMS==1 has nothing to split (192x192 has 3; a SPLIT_M 128x256 has 1)"*

`128x256` has BM=128, split over 2 consumer warpgroups = 64 rows each = **one m64 atom**. SKEW splits a stage's atoms across the loop back-edge, so with one atom there's nothing to split. `256x128` has BM=256 → 128 rows per warpgroup → 2 atoms, which is why it's fine.

Let me settle the one fact that decides where V2 goes next, since it's free:
> tool `Bash`: Find how to read the derived pipeline depth

The formula is `DERIVED_PIPE_DEPTH = (SMEM_DYNAMIC_BUDGET − STORE_BUF_BYTES) / STAGE_BYTES`, and line 1545 already records the arithmetic. Let me confirm the actual depths rather than infer:
> tool `Bash`: Find the struct holding LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH and the depth-4 comment context

That settles it, and it corrects something I put in the §H27ze table. §H27z.63 records the arithmetic directly:

```
256x128 ep32s2   STORE_BUF = 2*256*32*2 = 32768
                 depth = (231424 - 32768) / 49152 = 4.04  ->  4    "== cuBLAS's stage count"
128x256 swz64    STORE_BUF = 2*128*32*2 = 16384
                 depth = (231424 - 16384) / 49152 = 4.37  ->  4
```

**V2, V7 and V8 already run 4 stages — matching cuBLAS's `64x4`.** My §H27ze line saying those ten shapes were "3 vs 4, blocked by the full-tile epilogue buffer" was wrong; I carried it from the rollback note, which predates §H27z.63. The chunked epilogue *was* the fix for that blocker and it already shipped.

```
apples-to-apples        13 of 15 shapes    tile, layout AND stages all match
not matched              V6   3 vs 4 stages   (stage-4 arm parked at 96.37)
                         V1   ours sk2 vs cuBLAS 64x6 + splitK on 128x128
```

**There is no ten-shape structural blocker.** It was already solved. Which means every remaining gap on those thirteen shapes is a pure implementation defect on a matched configuration — the same situation V5 was in, where the answer turned out to be a wasted tile column no test could see.

Phase 1 is clean exactly as predicted, and phase 2 is a very clear signal.

**Tensor work is identical** — 2,097,152 vs 2,097,152 on V2, ratio 1.0000, and 3144 tiles exactly as computed. No phantom-tile bug here.

**The ledger, both shapes showing the same thing:**

```
                        V2 (ours/cuB)   V2c (ours/cuB)
tensor instructions        1.0000          0.9975     identical work
tensor % of peak           0.9950          0.9960     equally saturated
cycles elapsed             1.0083          1.0069     0.7-0.8% more
time (clock-control none)  1.0285          1.0473     2.9-4.7% slower
TOTAL instructions         2.2417          2.2389     <-- 2.24x, both shapes
L2 hit rate                1.1533          1.1528     OURS BETTER
DRAM read                  1.0004          1.3561
mio_throttle               0.1032          0.1087     10x inversion
short_scoreboard          46.57          106.33
```

Three things stand out. **Same cycles, slower time** — 0.8% more cycles but 2.9% more wall time means the deficit is *clock*, not work. **We execute 2.24× cuBLAS's instructions on both shapes**, the same ratio to three decimals, which is a structural property of the kernel rather than a shape effect. And **on V2, DRAM is identical and our L2 hit is better (79.22 vs 68.69)** — so memory is definitively not V2's problem, unlike V2c which reads 36% more.

Also note the ncu-vs-benchmark discrepancy: isolated launches show 2.9%/4.7% behind, the 400 ms benchmark shows 5.6%/8.7%. The gap roughly doubles under sustained load — the same power/thermal signature V5 had (3.55% isolated, 6.8% sustained).

Let me find where the 2.24× lives:
> tool `Bash`: Analyse where V2c's 2.24x instructions come from

**Same disease as V3 had before `dh_ubd`, and much bigger.**

```
ours    923,563,261 executed    3480 static    269,325 stall samples
cuBLAS  397,293,272 executed    1192 static    356,023 stall samples
excess  526,269,989  (2.32x)
```

```
opcode        ours        cuBLAS       excess    %gap
LOP3     115,959,168    7,527,742  108,431,426   20.6%   vector
R2UR     103,123,200      106,322  103,016,878   19.6%   vector->uniform crossings
ULOP3     61,173,360       30,480   61,142,880   11.6%   descriptor mask
SHF       61,241,520      153,088   61,088,432   11.6%   vector
BRA       62,208,312   18,612,538   43,595,774    8.3%
ULEA      43,349,784            0   43,349,784    8.2%   cuBLAS ZERO
VIADD     40,311,360            0   40,311,360    7.7%   cuBLAS ZERO
IMAD      39,512,304      230,852   39,281,452    7.5%   vector
USHF      37,368,624      143,508   37,225,116    7.1%
UMOV      50,054,988   14,801,446   35,253,542    6.7%
```

**`LOP3`, `SHF`, `VIADD`, `IMAD`, `R2UR` are the exact five opcodes §H27zc2 named** when it diagnosed V3's pre-`dh_ubd` state: *"copy the UNIFORM stage base into a VECTOR reg … VIADD / LOP3 / SHF / LOP3 — descriptor math, now stuck on the vector path … R2UR — and cross all of it back, ×24 per k-iteration."* `R2UR` alone is **103 million** here; on V5 after `dh_ubd` it's 2.1M. And we stall *less* than cuBLAS again (269k vs 356k), so this is surplus work, not waiting.

So the descriptor math that `dh_ubd` was built to remove is unmistakably present on V2's tile — **which sits awkwardly against H27zk measuring `_dh_ubd` at +0.1 there.**

That contradiction is the whole game and it resolves in one capture: this phase-3 run profiled the **base** pin (`256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2`), not the `_dh_ubd` arm. So either the knob doesn't actually reduce instructions on this tile — meaning it's wired for the 192x192 path and silently inert here, which would be a real bug worth finding — or it does reduce them and the clock still doesn't move, which is exactly what V5 taught us.

One ncu run on the `_dh_ubd` arm tells us which:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1
B=build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix; S=2048x50304x16384
for c in 256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2 256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2_dh_ubd; do
  ncu --metrics smsp__inst_executed.sum --csv --target-processes all \
      -k regex:bgemm_sm90_kernel -c 1 \
      $B --cfg="$c" --shape="$S" --layout=tn --bench 2>/dev/null \
   | python3 -c "
import csv,sys
r=[x for x in csv.reader(sys.stdin)]
h=next((x for x in r if 'Metric Value' in x),None)
v=[int(x[h.index('Metric Value')]) for x in r if h and len(x)==len(h) and x[0].isdigit()
   and x[h.index('Metric Value')].isdigit()]
print('  %-38s %s' % ('$c', format(max(v),',') if v else 'NO ROWS'))"
done
echo "  base measured 878,106,452 in phase 2;  cuBLAS 392,203,091"
```

If `_dh_ubd` comes back near 878M, the knob is inert on this tile and that's the bug to fix. If it drops toward ~500M with the clock unchanged, then V2 is the same story as V5 and instruction count is not the lever here either.

Which makes me think I've had the wrong unit all along. Look at *which* opcodes dominate the excess:

```
VECTOR (32 lanes each)                UNIFORM (1 lane each)
LOP3    115,959,168                   ULOP3    61,173,360
R2UR    103,123,200                   ULEA     43,349,784
SHF      61,241,520                   USHF     37,368,624
VIADD    40,311,360                   UMOV     50,054,988
IMAD     39,512,304
MOV      13,129,872
        ~373M                                 ~192M

cuBLAS vector total: ~10.7M
```

**We execute ~373M vector instructions against cuBLAS's ~11M — 35×.** A vector op drives all 32 lanes of the datapath; a uniform op drives one. So in *power* terms — which is what sets the clock — those are not the same instruction at all, and "total instruction count" has been the wrong metric for two days. It would explain why cutting 17% on V5 and 15% here moved nothing: if the cuts landed mostly on uniform ops, they cost almost no power to begin with.

That's testable in one capture — whether `dh_ubd`'s 129M came off the vector side or the uniform side:
