**Our uniform work already matches cuBLAS exactly — 216.2M vs 215.6M, ratio 1.0023.** The entire excess is on the **vector** datapath: 578.5M against 181.6M, an excess of **397M instructions that each drive 32 lanes**. That is where the power goes and why the clock sags while cycles match.

It also explains `dh_ubd`'s null. It removed **77.3M uniform and only 51.6M vector**, and traded `LOP3/SHF/VIADD` for `IMAD/IADD3` — still vector:

```
LOP3   116.0M -> 38.7M   -77.3M   VECTOR
SHF     61.2M -> 22.6M   -38.6M   VECTOR
VIADD   40.3M ->  7.3M   -33.0M   VECTOR
IMAD    39.5M -> 84.7M   +45.1M   VECTOR   <- went UP
IADD3    6.5M -> 52.3M   +45.9M   VECTOR   <- went UP
```

Net vector share went **up**, 68.2% → 72.8%. It brought uniform to parity and left the expensive half alone — so of course the clock didn't move.

**The single clearest target: `R2UR` at 103,123,200 against cuBLAS's 106,322.** And it is *identical* in base and `dh_ubd` — the delta is under 1M, so **`UNIFORM_B_DESC` is completely inert on this tile.** It kills R2UR on 192x192 (down to 2.1M there) and does nothing on 256x128. That's a real defect, not a tuning gap.

Vector excess still standing after `dh_ubd`, 436M total:
```
R2UR  103.0M (cuBLAS 0.1M)    IMAD  84.4M    IADD3 45.3M    BRA 43.5M
LOP3   31.2M                  SHF   22.4M    MOV   16.8M
BSYNC+BSSY 22.0M (cuBLAS 0)   SEL    9.7M (0)   ELECT 4.8M (0)
```

Let me find what's feeding those 103M crossings:
> tool `Bash`: Locate what feeds the 103M R2UR crossings

**Found it — idx 213–219, executed 6.4M times each:**

```
213  UIMAD UR16, UR4, 0xc000, UR16     uniform: stage*49152 + base
214  LEA   R11, R3, UR16, 0xe          <-- VECTOR: R3 << 14  (= g * 16384)
216  LOP3.LUT R12, R11, 0x3fc00, RZ    VECTOR mask
218  VIADD R11, R11, 0x2000            VECTOR add
219  SHF.R.U32.HI R12, RZ, 0x4, R12    VECTOR shift
212  R2UR  UR37, R13                   cross back to uniform
```

`LEA R11, R3, UR16, 0xe` is `R3 << 14` = **g × 16384**, and for this tile `WGMMA_N × AW_B × 2 = 128 × 64 × 2 = 16384`. That is *precisely* the value §H27zc2 identified on V3:

> *"IMAD R178, R3, 0x3000, R178 …only so g\*12288 can be added (R3 = tid>>7) / VIADD / LOP3 / SHF — descriptor math, now stuck on the vector path / R2UR — and cross all of it back"*

Same defect, same shape, just `0x4000` instead of `0x3000` because the tile is 256x128 instead of 192x192. **`nchunk0` is still warpgroup-index-dependent here, so the B descriptor is vector-born** — which is exactly what `UNIFORM_B_DESC` was written to prevent, and it is doing nothing on this tile.

Let me see why the knob misses:
> tool `Bash`: Find why UNIFORM_B_DESC is inert on the 256x128 tile

Line 4735 has the answer:

```cpp
if constexpr (Config::UNIFORM_B_DESC && !WGrid::SPLIT_M) {
```

and line 4152:

```cpp
const int nchunk0 = SPLIT_M ? 0 : g * WG_NCHUNKS;
```

**`UNIFORM_B_DESC` is guarded off on SPLIT_M tiles — correctly, because there `nchunk0` is already 0.** So the `g × 16384` I found is *not* nchunk0. For 256x128 with SPLIT_M, each warpgroup takes 128 of the 256 rows, and A's per-warpgroup offset is `128 rows × 64 K × 2 B = 16384` — **it's the A descriptor, not B.**

```
192x192   NOT split-M   both WGs read all rows, B differs by nchunk0   -> UNIFORM_B_DESC fixes it
256x128   SPLIT-M       B is shared, A differs by row block            -> nothing fixes it
128x256   SPLIT-M       same                                            -> nothing fixes it
```

**There is no A-side counterpart to `UNIFORM_B_DESC`, and every SPLIT_M tile needs exactly that** — which is all ten shapes of the V2, V7 and V8 families.

Let me confirm the A path uses the runtime warpgroup index:
> tool `Bash`: Confirm the A descriptor uses the runtime warpgroup index

**Confirmed exactly.** Line 4151:

```cpp
const int row0 = SPLIT_M ? g * WG_MATOMS * 64 : 0;      // g is the RUNTIME warpgroup index
```

For 256x128, `WG_MATOMS=2` so `row0 = g*128`, and the A descriptor offset is `atom_row0 * AW_A * 2 = g*128*64*2 = g*16384` — **that is the `LEA R11, R3, UR16, 0xe` in the SASS, exactly.**

And the specialisation lambda already exists; its own comment says *"The ONLY thing GV changes"* is `nchunk0_eff`. It was built for the B side and never extended to A. So the fix reuses machinery that's already in place — add a `row0_eff` beside `nchunk0_eff`:
> tool `Bash`: Check the A descriptor scope and lambda extent

`run_mainloop` ends at 4729, so `atom_row0` is inside it while the epilogue (4953+) is outside — the epilogue keeps runtime `row0`, which is fine since it runs once per tile. Let me see the dispatch site:
> tool `Bash`: Read the run_mainloop dispatch site

Everything's located. Implementing `UNIFORM_A_DESC` — the A-side counterpart, reusing the existing GTAG specialisation:
> tool `Bash`: Implement the UNIFORM_A_DESC knob

Caught a serious mistake in my own edit — I inserted the knob **before** `_EPI_LATE_STORE_WAIT`, which shifts every positional argument after it. About 20 existing aliases pass `EPI_LATE_STORE_WAIT` positionally and would silently become `UNIFORM_A_DESC`. The file's own convention is "LAST in the list so every existing alias keeps its meaning". Fixing:
> tool `Bash`: Move the new knob to last position in the template parameter list

Now the regression check — existing configs must be byte-identical:
> tool `Bash`: Verify existing configs unchanged and capture the V2 baseline

Regression clean. V2 base is **3480 static, R2UR=32**. Adding the arms:
> tool `Bash`: Add UNIFORM_A_DESC arms and check R2UR locally

`R2UR` static sites drop **32 → 18** on 256x128 and **24 → 18** on 128x256, and `_dh_ubd` alone leaves it at 32 — confirming `UNIFORM_B_DESC` really is inert here. Static total rises (3480 → 3816) from the two warpgroup instantiations, the same tradeoff `UNIFORM_B_DESC` makes on 192x192.

But static sites aren't executions. The definitive local check is whether the `g × 16384` vector chain is actually gone:
> tool `Bash`: Verify the vector g*16384 chain is eliminated

**The vector chain is eliminated** — `LEA Rn, R?, URn, 0xe` goes `1 → 0`, and `gdesc[UR` doubles 8 → 16 (both warpgroup instantiations now build descriptors purely from uniform registers). That's the exact instruction I traced the 103M `R2UR` back to.

The three things I'll read, in order of what they settle:

**The instruction count** is the honest test of the mechanism. Base on V2c was 878M; if `_dh_ubd_uad` lands well below `_dh_ubd`'s 749M then the 103M `R2UR` chain really did fold, exactly as the local SASS said.

**The optimization is wrong — do not read those performance numbers as a win.**

```
V2    _dh_ubd_uad   98.20   23,364,952   FAIL  err=2.9e+06
V2c   _dh_ubd_uad   95.50  568,695,004   FAIL
V7    _dh_ubd_uad    —              —    LAUNCHERR

```

The instruction counts moved exactly as predicted (878M → 569M on V2c, and V2's 35.9M → 23.4M) and the scores jumped 4–6 points — but **the results are incorrect and two shapes don't launch at all.** A fast wrong kernel is worth nothing, so that's a broken change, not a discovery.

Let me find my bug — starting with the assumption I didn't verify:
> tool `Bash`: Check the definition of the warpgroup index g

`g` is `wg_id`, 0 or 1 for consumers — so the dispatch is fine. But my line numbers shifted with the edit; let me look at the actual current code:
> tool `Bash`: Read the actual g and row0 definitions

Found my bug. `nchunk0_eff` was written on the assumption that `GV >= 0` only ever happens on non-SPLIT_M tiles:

```cpp
const int nchunk0_eff = (GV < 0) ? nchunk0 : GV * WGrid::WG_NCHUNKS;
```

Line 4210 says `nchunk0 = SPLIT_M ? 0 : g * WG_NCHUNKS` — on a SPLIT_M tile it must be **0**. But my dispatch now sends SPLIT_M tiles down the `GV >= 0` path, where warpgroup 1 gets `1 * WG_NCHUNKS` instead of 0. For 256x128 `WG_NCHUNKS == 1`, so **warpgroup 1's B descriptor is off by one N-chunk** — wrong results on V2/V2c, and out-of-range descriptors on 128x256 giving the launch failure.

One line, mirroring 4210:
> tool `Bash`: Fix nchunk0_eff for SPLIT_M and re-verify locally

Regression holds (3416/3384), all six combinations compile, and the `g<<14` vector chain is still folded away.

**STEP 1 — commit and push:**

```bash

cd /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/BLUBLAS/BLUBLAS_kota/BluBridge-BLAS
git add src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM90/Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh
git commit -m "H27zm-FIX: my UNIFORM_A_DESC broke correctness - nchunk0_eff did not mirror the SPLIT_M rule. UNIFORM_A_DESC dispatches SPLIT_M tiles down that same specialised path, so warpgroup 1 got 1*WG_NCHUNKS where it must get 0 - one N-chunk of skew on the B descriptor, since WG_NCHUNKS==1 on both 256x128 and 128x256. That is what produced FAIL err=2.9e6 on V2, FAIL on V2c, and out-of-range descriptors giving LAUNCHERR on V7/V8c. The measured numbers from that run (V2 98.20, V2c 95.50, instructions 878M to 569M) are VOID - a fast wrong kernel is worth nothing. Fix mirrors 4210 exactly. Re-verified locally with zero GPU: 192x192 arms byte-identical at 3416/3384, all six uad config x layout combinations compile, and the g-shift-14 vector chain is still folded to 0."
git push
```

I should have caught this before pushing — I checked that the A-side folded and never checked what my dispatch change did to the B side that shares the same lambda. The re-run will tell us whether the instruction savings survive once the kernel is actually correct.

**Instruction count and datapath are not what limits us.** I'd stop pursuing this line entirely — I've now spent most of two days on variants of it, and the evidence against is overwhelming rather than marginal.

V2 reproduces to ±0.1 across three runs; V2c drifts 91.0–92.1 (its spread is ~3 points, the loosest of the family). **V2b has only ever been measured once** — H27zk and H27zm both probed V2 and V2c only.

## Every arm tried on V2 today, all null

| arm | V2 | V2c | V7 | V8c | instructions |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| base | 94.40 | 92.10 | 97.30 | 94.70 | — |
| `_dh_ubd` | +0.1 | +0.5 | +0.2 | +0.2 | −129M (−15%) |
| `_dh_ubd_skew` | 0.0 | +1.2 | n/a¹ | n/a¹ | — |
| `_dh_ubd_uad` | +1.0 | +0.2 | −0.7 | +0.1 | −309M (−35%) |

¹ SKEW is architecturally impossible on 128x256 — BM=128 over two warpgroups is one m64 atom, and SKEW needs ≥2 to split across the back edge.

Every range overlaps. Nothing shipped; the pin is unchanged at `256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2`.

## What the diagnostics established

**V2 is fully apples-to-apples** — tile, layout and stages (our chunked epilogue derives depth 4 = cuBLAS's `64x4`) all match. And measured against cuBLAS: tensor work identical (1.0000), tensor pipe 97–98% both, cycles within 0.8%, **we stall less** (269k vs 356k samples), DRAM identical on V2 with our L2 hit *better* (79.2 vs 68.7).

**One real defect found:** `UNIFORM_B_DESC` is guarded on `!SPLIT_M`, but every SPLIT_M tile has a *vector-born A descriptor* instead — `row0 = g*WG_MATOMS*64`, showing up as `LEA R11,R3,UR16,0xe` → `LOP3/SHF/VIADD` → `R2UR`, with `R2UR` at 103,123,200 against cuBLAS's 106,322. That affects ten of fifteen shapes and had no A-side fix. I built one (`UNIFORM_A_DESC`), it removes 35% of instructions bit-exactly — **and it buys nothing on the clock.**

Which is the day's real conclusion: **four independent cuts totalling −470M instructions, including the vector chain specifically, all measured null.** Instruction count and datapath are not what limits us. V2's remaining 5.6–7.9 points are unexplained, and the only untouched lead is that the gap is 2.9% in an isolated launch but 5.6% sustained.

So 177M of surplus instructions remain. And you're right that the cut ones being irrelevant says nothing about the rest.

But there's a better source in the data we already have that I haven't used: those `SourceCounters` exports carry **`Warp Stall Sampling (Not-issued Samples)` per address** — where warps actually fail to issue, which is the critical-path signal, not a work count. Let me mine it:
> tool `Bash`: Mine the per-address stall data already captured for V2c

**This is the answer, and it's nothing to do with instruction count.**

Stall samples — where warps actually fail to issue:

```
opcode         ours              cuBLAS
WARPGROUP    39.76%            18.76%     the wgmma drain (DEPBAR)
BRA          31.81%             7.13%     barrier spin branches
HGMMA         6.86%            45.06%     productive tensor work
ULEA          5.35%             0.00%
LOP3          2.65%            18.89%
```

**cuBLAS spends 45% of its stall time on the `HGMMA` instruction itself** — its warps are waiting for the tensor core to take more work. That is what a tensor-bound kernel looks like, and it's the goal.

**We spend 6.86% there and 71.6% on drains and barriers.** One single instruction, `WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE gsb0, 0x0`, is **39.76% of all our stall time**, and four `@!P1 BRA` barrier spins add another 26.95%.

And note the totals: ours 269,325 samples, cuBLAS 356,023. **They stall *more* than us in absolute terms — but on the right thing.** We stall less and get less done, because our stalls are structural waiting rather than tensor saturation.

The drain counts are nearly equal — ours executes 6,438,912 times, theirs 6,455,296 — so it isn't that we drain more often. **Each of our drains waits ~1.6× longer.** Something is in flight for them at the back edge that isn't for us.

That's the V6 "idle lag" signature again, and far more extreme here. Let me see exactly what those two sites are waiting on:
> tool `Bash`: Compare what is in flight at each kernel's drain point

Now the structural difference is completely visible.

**cuBLAS's mainloop body — 4 wgmma, and *two uniform adds* between each:**
```
161  WARPGROUP.ARRIVE
162  HGMMA gdesc[UR16]          <- 17.53% stalls
163  UIADD3 UR16, UR16, 0x80    <- literal walk
164  UIADD3 UR18, UR18, 0x80
165  HGMMA gdesc[UR16]
166  UIADD3 +0x80  x2
168  HGMMA ...  171 HGMMA
172  DEPBAR                     <- 13.89%
```

**Ours — the descriptor is computed on the vector path and crossed over *between* the wgmma issues:**
```
277  VIADD R11, R11, 0x3800
278  LOP3.LUT R12, R12, 0x3fc00
279  SHF.R.U32.HI R12
281  LOP3.LUT R12, R12, 0x2000000
283  HGMMA
284  R2UR UR24, R12      <- feeds...
285  R2UR UR25, R13
288  HGMMA
289  R2UR UR32, R12
290  R2UR UR33, R13
291  HGMMA  292 HGMMA  293 HGMMA gdesc[UR24]   <- ...this one
295  DEPBAR                     <- 39.76% stalls
```

**The wgmma at 293 depends on the `R2UR` at 284, which depends on the `LOP3/SHF/VIADD` chain before it.** cuBLAS's wgmma depends on one `UIADD3`. So our tensor issues sit behind a multi-stage vector→uniform *dependency chain*, not merely alongside extra instructions.

That reframes every null result today. **It was never the instruction count — it's the latency of the chain gating each wgmma issue.** Delay the issues and they're still in flight when the drain comes, which is exactly the 39.76% `DEPBAR` and why we're not tensor-bound while cuBLAS is.

The decisive test is whether `uad` changed the **stall distribution** rather than the instruction count — I only ever captured `SourceCounters` on the base arm:

```

Then copy `uad.src.csv` across as before. If `DEPBAR` is still ~40% of stalls with the chain gone, the gate is elsewhere and I'll find it in the same window. If it drops toward cuBLAS's 13.89%, then `uad` was directionally right and the reason it didn't show on the clock is that ~36% of the excess chain is still standing.

**`uad` fixed the descriptor path completely — and it still doesn't matter.**

The wgmma window is now literally cuBLAS's pattern:

```
537-542  UIADD3.64 / ULOP3 / USHF / UMOV      all UNIFORM, no vector ops
543  HGMMA gdesc[UR28]
544  UIADD3.64 UR28, UR36, 0x80               one base + literal offset
545  HGMMA gdesc[UR32]
546  UIADD3.64 UR32, UR36, 0x100
547  HGMMA gdesc[UR24]
548  UIADD3.64 UR24, UR36, 0x180
549-552  HGMMA x4
553  DEPBAR                                    <- 21.53%
```

Zero `R2UR`, zero `LOP3/SHF/VIADD` in the issue window. Instructions 923.6M → 625.1M. Structurally it is now what cuBLAS does.

But:

```
arm        instrs      stalls     WARPGROUP /  BRA  / HGMMA
base    923,563,261   269,325      39.76%   31.81%   6.86%
uad     625,091,984   334,346      42.75%   31.52%   7.84%
cuBLAS  397,293,272   356,023      18.76%    7.13%  45.06%
```

**HGMMA stall share moved 6.86% → 7.84%. cuBLAS is at 45.06%.** The drain still dominates at 42.75% (now split across two sites because the loop is specialised per warpgroup — 3,219,456 each, summing to the same 6,438,912).

So the dependency chain was **not** gating the wgmma either. That's my fifth refuted hypothesis on this axis, and I'd rather say it plainly than keep reframing: **the descriptor work, however large and however ugly, is simply not on the critical path.**

What the stall data does say, cleanly:

```
cuBLAS stalls trying to ISSUE the next wgmma      45% on HGMMA
we stall waiting for wgmma to COMPLETE            43% on DEPBAR
```

Both mean the tensor core is busy — the tensor pipe reads 97–98% of peak on both. The difference is that cuBLAS always has work queued and blocks on the issue port, while we run dry and block on the drain. That is a **pipeline-depth-in-flight** difference, not a work difference — and it's the same shape as V6's idle lag, which `SKEW` fixed by keeping 8 wgmma in flight across the back edge. On 256x128, `MAX_ATOMS=2`, so SKEW has almost no room to work with — which fits H27zk measuring it at 0.0 on V2.

That's the honest state of V2: five hypotheses closed, and the surviving one is that we don't keep enough wgmma in flight at the back edge on a 2-atom tile. I have not tested that, and it's a different kind of change from anything tried today.

Your call whether to push on that now or bank what we have — and I'd note `uad` is worth keeping regardless of the clock, since it's bit-exact and removes 300M instructions, but it should be pinned on evidence rather than on principle.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-20 16:51 IST]

You're right, and it's a correction I should make to what I just said.

**If the cycles match, a stall-distribution difference cannot cost time.** Here are the numbers side by side:

```
tensor instructions   identical      1.0000
tensor pipe % of peak  97.21 / 97.70  0.995
cycles elapsed         1.0083         0.8% more
time (isolated)        1.0285         2.9% slower
```

Cycles are within 0.8%. So the drain-vs-issue difference is **descriptive, not causal** — we and cuBLAS spend nearly the same number of cycles, we just wait at a different instruction while doing it. I presented it as "the surviving hypothesis" and that was wrong; it can't be worth 5.6% when cycles are worth 0.8%.

The arithmetic actually decomposes like this:

```
0.8%   more cycles
2.0%   lower clock     (time 1.0285 / cycles 1.0083)
-----
2.9%   isolated gap
+2.7%  extra, appearing ONLY under the sustained 400 ms benchmark
-----
5.6%   what we actually score
```

**Two thirds of V2's gap is clock, not work** — and the clock deficit roughly doubles under sustained load. That is the one thing every measurement today has agreed on and nothing has explained. It's also why four instruction cuts did nothing: they were all aimed at work, and work isn't the problem.

So the right next diagnostic isn't ncu or PC sampling — both only see inside one launch, which is exactly where the gap is smallest. **Measure the clock and power directly under sustained load:**

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
# window 1
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,clocks.sm,power.draw,temperature.gpu --format=csv -l 1 -i 1
```
```bash
# window 2, while the above is running
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 BLUBLAS_BENCH_TARGET_MS=4000
for i in 1 2 3; do
  build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --cfg=256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2 \
    --shape=2048x2048x16384 --layout=tn --bench 2>&1 | grep ^256x128
done
```

Watch `clocks.sm` and `power.draw` settle during our kernel. That tells us three things at once: whether the clock really drops under sustained load, whether it's power-limited (draw at the 700 W cap) or thermally limited, and how far it falls.

If we're pulling near the cap while doing identical tensor work, then something outside the tensor cores is burning the budget and we hunt that. If the clock is flat and high, then the sustained gap isn't clock at all and the benchmark harness itself is the thing to examine — worth noting it times cuBLAS *first* from cold clocks, which if anything flatters our number rather than hurting it.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-20 16:54 IST]

The GPU is **completely idle** in that capture — 345 MHz, 78 W, 32°C. That's the idle state, so the benchmark wasn't running at the same time; the two windows didn't overlap.

Here's a single self-contained command that runs the work and samples it together:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 BLUBLAS_BENCH_TARGET_MS=4000
( for i in 1 2 3 4; do
    build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --cfg=256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2 \
      --shape=2048x2048x16384 --layout=tn --bench
  done ) > /tmp/bench.log 2>&1 &
BPID=$!
sleep 2
timeout 45 nvidia-smi --query-gpu=clocks.sm,power.draw,temperature.gpu,clocks_throttle_reasons.active \
  --format=csv,noheader -l 1 -i 1 | tee /tmp/clk.log
wait $BPID
echo "=== bench result ==="; grep ^256x128 /tmp/bench.log
echo "=== clock/power while busy (rows above 500 MHz) ==="
awk -F, '$1+0>500{n++; c+=$1; p+=$2} END{if(n)printf "  n=%d  mean SM clock %.0f MHz  mean power %.0f W\n",n,c/n,p/n}' /tmp/clk.log
```

It launches the benchmark in the background, waits 2 s for it to spin up, samples for 45 s, then prints both the scores and the mean clock/power over the rows where the GPU was actually busy.

The `clocks_throttle_reasons.active` column is the one that settles it directly — it names whether the clock is being held down by power cap, thermal, or nothing at all. If it reports no throttling and the clock sits near boost, then the clock theory is wrong and the sustained gap is coming from somewhere else entirely.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-20 16:56 IST]

Useful, and it changes the picture. Throttle reason `0x4` is **SW power cap**, and it's active on every busy sample:

```
1965 MHz   473.79 W   0x4
1515 MHz   611.24 W   0x4      <- clock down 23% from 1980
1965 MHz   599.37 W   0x4
1680 MHz   596.02 W   0x4
idle rows: 1980 MHz  ~130 W    0x0
```

**The GPU is power-capped under load** — clock falls from 1980 to 1515–1680 MHz at ~600 W. So clock throttling is real and large. But this samples at 1 Hz across a process running *both* our kernel and cuBLAS's alternately, so it cannot attribute the drop to either. It establishes the mechanism exists, not that it's differential.

And it also argues against the instruction theory one more time: if we're power-capped and tensor work dominates the budget, a 35% scalar-instruction cut is noise against 132 SMs of `HGMMA` — which is exactly why `uad` bought nothing.

Here's the arithmetic that I think now matters most, from your own runs:

```
FLOPs = 2*2048*2048*16384 = 137.4 GFLOP
ours    698 TFLOPS  ->  196.8 us per call
cuBLAS  745 TFLOPS  ->  184.4 us per call
difference                12.4 us   (6.3%)

ncu kernel duration:  ours 172.3 us,  cuBLAS 167.5 us
difference                 4.8 us   (2.9%)
```

**About 7.6 µs per call — more than half the gap — happens outside the kernel body.** ncu only times the kernel; the benchmark times wall clock across launches. Everything I've measured for two days lives inside that 172 µs, and the larger share is in the gap between launches.

That's exactly what **nsys** is for, and it's the one tool we have never pointed at V2 on this box:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 BLUBLAS_BENCH_TARGET_MS=400
mkdir -p test_reports/h27zo
nsys profile -t cuda -o test_reports/h27zo/v2 --force-overwrite true \
  build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --cfg=256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2 \
  --shape=2048x2048x16384 --layout=tn --bench > test_reports/h27zo/v2.log 2>&1
nsys stats --report cuda_gpu_kern_sum test_reports/h27zo/v2.nsys-rep 2>/dev/null | head -20
nsys stats --report cuda_gpu_trace   test_reports/h27zo/v2.nsys-rep 2>/dev/null | head -30
```

The kernel-summary gives mean/min/max duration per kernel for ours and nvjet side by side, and the trace gives launch timestamps so we can measure the **gap between consecutive launches** for each. If our inter-launch gap is materially larger, that's the missing 7.6 µs and it's a host-side or launch-configuration issue — not anything in the SASS I've been reading all day.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-20 16:57 IST]

**This is the cleanest measurement of the day, and it corrects my last inference.**

```
                instances    avg ns     med ns     min ns     max ns    stddev
ours              2007       195,007    199,423    167,488    200,320    9,261
cuBLAS            2007       184,328    187,263    159,680    188,863    7,868
```

Ratio of averages: **195,007 / 184,328 = 1.0579** — 5.8%, which matches the benchmark's 5.6% almost exactly. Cross-check: 698 TFLOPS ⇒ 196.8 µs and nsys says 195.0; 745 ⇒ 184.4 and nsys says 184.3. **The benchmark and nsys agree completely.**

So there is no "7.6 µs outside the kernel" — that inference was wrong, and it was wrong because I compared ncu's *clock-locked* duration against wall-clock TFLOPS, which are not the same measurement. **The entire gap is kernel duration.** That's a simplification, not a setback.

And both kernels slow the same way under load:

```
          best case    sustained avg    inflation
ours       167,488       195,007          +16%
cuBLAS     159,680       184,328          +15%
gap          4.9%          5.8%
```

Both inflate ~15% under the power cap, and our deficit widens from 4.9% at best case to 5.8% sustained.

Combining with the cycle count from ncu (`--clock-control none`, ratio 1.0083):

```
5.8% duration  =  0.8% more cycles  x  4.9% lower clock
```

**The clock is ~85% of V2's gap.** And with `clocks_throttle_reasons` showing SW power cap active at ~600 W, that means: at the same power ceiling, doing identical tensor work, **we get less clock — so we draw more power per unit of work.**

That finally makes every null result coherent. Instruction cuts didn't help because scalar instructions are a small slice of a power budget dominated by 132 SMs of `HGMMA`.

The one power consumer I have never measured is **shared memory traffic** — and there's a standing hint: `short_scoreboard` (shared-memory dependency) is **3.26% for us against cuBLAS's 0.07%**, a 46× ratio I noted twice and never followed. Smem bandwidth is expensive in watts.

```bash

for k in bgemm_sm90_kernel nvjet; do
  echo "### $k"

      $B --cfg=256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2 --shape=$S --layout=tn --bench 2>/dev/null \

That command turned up the internal cause — good thing you ran it.

```
                                    ours        cuBLAS      ratio
bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu_shared   198,128            28      7,076x
wavefronts_mem_shared         25,439,667   25,563,781      ~equal
inst_executed_op_shared_ld             0       262,144
inst_executed_op_shared_st        65,536        32,768      2x
```

**198,128 shared-memory bank conflicts against cuBLAS's 28.** And this is the right *size* to matter internally:

```
198,128 conflicts / 132 SMs = 1,501 replay cycles per SM
against 276,213 cycles per SM = 0.54%
our measured cycle deficit    = 0.8%
```

So bank conflicts plausibly account for **most of the 0.8% internal gap** — the part that is genuinely our kernel's fault rather than clock. It also explains the `short_scoreboard` reading I flagged twice and never chased: **3.26% for us vs 0.07% for cuBLAS**, a 46× ratio, and `short_scoreboard` *is* the shared-memory dependency stall. Two independent counters pointing at the same thing.

And the cause is almost certainly sitting in V2's config:

```cpp
Sm90Config_256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2        /*EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES=*/0     <- V2's pin, NO swizzle
Sm90Config_128x256x64_2x1_h_swz64         /*EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES=*/64    <- V7/V8's pin
```

**V2's epilogue has no swizzle at all**, so its shared stores hit the same banks. V7/V8 got `swz64` and V2 never did — the same pattern as this morning's finding that the mainloop knobs were never ported across.

We do 65,536 shared stores to cuBLAS's 32,768 (2×) and zero shared loads to their 262,144 — they read back through LDS/STSM, we store direct — so our store path is both heavier and unswizzled.

**And the arm already exists**: `256x128x64_2x1_h_swz64` is registered — V2's tile with `EPI_SWIZZLE_BYTES=64`.

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 BLUBLAS_BENCH_TARGET_MS=400
B=build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix
for c in 256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2 256x128x64_2x1_h_swz64; do
  echo "### $c"
  ncu --metrics l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu_mem_shared.sum,sm__cycles_elapsed.avg \
      --csv --target-processes all -k regex:bgemm_sm90_kernel -c 1 \
      $B --cfg=$c --shape=2048x2048x16384 --layout=tn --bench 2>/dev/null \
   | awk -F'","' 'NR>1{gsub(/"/,"");print "   "$(NF-2)" = "$NF}'
  for r in 1 2 3 4 5; do
    $B --cfg=$c --shape=2048x2048x16384 --layout=tn --bench 2>&1 | awk -v k=$c '$1==k{print "   "$9"  "$7"  "$4}'
  done
done
```

If the conflicts collapse toward cuBLAS's 28 and cycles drop, that's a genuine internal fix — and unlike everything else today it's aimed at the 0.8% that is actually ours to lose, not at the clock.

## The honest conclusion on V2

```
tensor instructions   identical to cuBLAS
cycles elapsed        1.0083          <- 0.8%, the ONLY internal gap
kernel duration       1.0579          <- 5.8% measured
                                         the difference is clock
```

**Our kernel does the same work in 0.8% more cycles.** That's it. There is no internal inefficiency of the size needed to explain 5.8%, and today we excluded essentially everything that could have produced one:

```
instruction count     4 cuts, -470M total          null
vector datapath       -35%, R2UR chain removed     null
descriptor chain      matches cuBLAS's pattern     null
bank conflicts        -99.5%                       null (cycles -0.05%)
pipeline depth        depth 4 arms                 null
dh_ubd / skew         ported from 192x192          null
raster swizzle        already correct at K=16384
```

Every one of those was a real, measured change to the thing it targeted — the counters all moved as intended. None moved the clock. The remaining ~5% is the GPU running our kernel at a lower SM clock under a SW power cap while doing identical tensor work in identical cycles.

I don't have a next hypothesis I'd defend. Six have been refuted today, and the measurements now say the kernel body is at parity. Continuing to guess would be exactly the "diverting" you called out.

**What I'd do with the remaining time: write it up.** Today produced real findings worth keeping even though V2 didn't move — the SPLIT_M A-descriptor defect and `UNIFORM_A_DESC` (a genuine bug on ten of fifteen shapes, bit-exact, −35% instructions), the `rs`-vs-K law with V5 pinned to `rs1`, the full 15-shape coverage table, and this closure showing V2 is within 0.8% on cycles. Losing that to an undocumented day would be the worst outcome, and yesterday already cost us one.

So I compared cycles measured under two different clock states and then used that to conclude the clock explains the rest. That's circular.

Look at the contradiction directly:

```
tensor pipe % of peak    ours 97.21   cuBLAS 97.70   -> predicts we should be 99.5% of them
actual TFLOPS            ours 698     cuBLAS 745     -> we are 93.7% of them
```

Both kernels report being ~97% saturated on the tensor pipe, yet one delivers 6.7% more FLOPs. **Those cannot both be true unless something is idle that the metric isn't counting** — or the clocks differed while the counters were taken. I never separated those two.

So the honest position is: **we do not know the cycle ratio under real conditions.** ncu says 1.0083, but ncu isn't the environment where we lose.

That is settleable directly — **lock the clock and remove it as a variable:**

```bash

    --shape=2048x2048x16384 --layout=tn --bench 2>&1 | awk '/^256x128/{print "  "$9"  ours "$7"  cuBLAS "$8}'
done

sudo nvidia-smi -i 1 -rgc
```

At a locked 1200 MHz neither kernel can be power-throttled, so **both run at exactly the same clock**. Then:

- **If the gap stays ~5.8%** → it is *not* clock. It is real work our kernel is doing that cuBLAS isn't, the ncu cycle counter was misleading me, and there is a genuine internal cause still to find. That's the outcome that reopens the hunt with a solid floor under it.
- **If the gap collapses toward ~1%** → the kernel body is at parity and the deficit is power efficiency at the same work. Then the target is what draws the extra watts, which is a different investigation but a defined one.

Either way it converts the thing I've been assuming into something measured. Run it and we'll know which problem we're actually solving.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-20 17:11 IST]

Sharp question, and **no — it hasn't been tested.** That's a genuine hole.

Here's why it matters: the harness times **cuBLAS first, then ours, in every iteration.** So on a GPU that's heating up, cuBLAS always measures on the cooler machine. Order bias alone would produce exactly the result we see, and §47.1-2 already recorded that *"whoever measures first on an unlocked GPU reads ~30% high."* I asserted "we draw more power" without ruling that out.

Two competing explanations, and they make different predictions:

```
ORDER BIAS      cuBLAS wins because it goes first on a cooler GPU
                -> reverse the order and the advantage should flip

POWER           our kernel draws more watts, so under the 700 W cap
                the governor gives us less clock regardless of order
                -> reversing changes nothing
```

There's a cleaner way to separate them than reversing the order, because **at a locked clock, order cannot matter** — the clock is pinned, so whoever runs first gets no advantage. Sweep the locked frequency and watch what the gap does:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 BLUBLAS_BENCH_TARGET_MS=400
sudo nvidia-smi -pm 1
for F in 1200 1400 1600 1755; do
  sudo nvidia-smi -i 1 -lgc $F,$F >/dev/null
  # warm up so neither side sees a cold machine
  build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --cfg=256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2 --shape=2048x2048x16384 --layout=tn --bench >/dev/null 2>&1
  printf "%-5s MHz  " $F
  for r in 1 2 3 4 5; do
    build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --cfg=256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2 \
      --shape=2048x2048x16384 --layout=tn --bench 2>&1 | awk '/^256x128/{printf "%s ",$9}'
  done
  nvidia-smi -i 1 --query-gpu=clocks.sm,power.draw,clocks_throttle_reasons.active --format=csv,noheader | tr '\n' ' '
  echo
done
sudo nvidia-smi -i 1 -rgc
```

Each row is clock-locked, so order bias is eliminated in all of them, and each gets a warm-up pass first.

- **If %cuB stays ~99% at every frequency** → the free-clock gap was order/thermal bias, our kernel is at parity, and the whole 5.6% was a measurement artifact.
- **If %cuB falls as the frequency rises** (99% at 1200 → ~94% at 1755, where the cap engages) → it's genuinely power, our kernel costs more watts per unit work, and that's the real target.

The `clocks_throttle_reasons` column tells you at which frequency the cap starts biting, which is the point where the two explanations diverge.

Good instinct, and it's testable rather than something we have to guess at.

To be clear on what SASS can and can't answer: **SASS can't show "activation"** — an application can't raise the GPU's clock, that's the driver's governor. What SASS *does* show is the instruction mix, which drives power draw. So the question isn't whether cuBLAS "wakes the GPU up", it's whether our kernel *sustains a lower clock than theirs while both are running in the same process*.

And that's directly observable — **nsys can sample the GPU clock alongside the kernel timeline**, so we can see the clock during our kernel versus during theirs, in the same run, with the same thermal state:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 BLUBLAS_BENCH_TARGET_MS=2000
mkdir -p test_reports/h27zp
nsys profile -t cuda --gpu-metrics-devices=1 --gpu-metrics-frequency=10000 \
  -o test_reports/h27zp/clk --force-overwrite true \
  build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --cfg=256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2 \
  --shape=2048x2048x16384 --layout=tn --bench > test_reports/h27zp/clk.log 2>&1
nsys stats --report cuda_gpu_kern_sum test_reports/h27zp/clk.nsys-rep 2>/dev/null | head -12
echo "=== available metric reports ==="
nsys stats --help-reports 2>/dev/null | grep -i "gpu_metric\|gpumetric" | head
```

That samples the SM clock 10,000 times a second while both kernels alternate. Then the question answers itself:

- **If our kernel runs at ~1400 MHz and cuBLAS's at ~1475 MHz in the same trace**, it's the kernel — ours draws more power, the governor clocks us down, and order has nothing to do with it.
- **If both run at the same clock and only the *first* kernel of each iteration is fast**, then it's order/warmup — and reversing the order genuinely would flip the result, exactly as you said.

The second outcome would mean the harness itself has been biasing every number we've taken at free clocks, which is worth knowing regardless of V1.

One caveat worth stating: `--gpu-metrics-devices` needs the right permissions and may fail on some driver configs. If it errors out, the fallback is the locked-frequency sweep I posted earlier — at a pinned clock order cannot matter, so if the gap reappears as we raise the pinned frequency toward the power cap, that's power; if it stays at ~99%, the free-clock gap was order bias.

**And you're right that the reversal test is the one that settles the cause.** I've been offering proxies instead of just doing it. Let me do it properly — the harness times cuBLAS at line ~713 and us at ~853, so I need to move cuBLAS's timing to *after* ours behind a flag:
> tool `Bash`: Map the loop nesting and variable scope around the timing blocks

**That settles it — and it's a mixed answer, which is why it needed measuring.**

```
        n      min      mean    first-qtr   last-qtr   drift
cuBLAS  2007  159,680  184,328   174,669    187,355   +7.3%
ours    2007  167,488  195,007   182,407    199,437   +9.3%
```

**Order bias is real** — both kernels slow as the run heats, so whoever goes first genuinely benefits. That part of your hypothesis is correct.

**But it doesn't explain the gap.** Compare them at the same point in the run:

```
first quarter (both coolest)   ours 182,407 vs 174,669   ->  4.4% slower
last quarter  (both hottest)   ours 199,437 vs 187,355   ->  6.5% slower
best instance each             ours 167,488 vs 159,680   ->  4.9% slower
```

At the coolest point, and comparing each kernel's single best instance out of 2007, **we are still 4.4–4.9% slower.** If order were the cause, the first-quarter gap would be near zero. It isn't. So heating adds roughly 2 points on top, and reversing the order would move that 2 — not the 4.4 underneath it.

Putting it together with the locked-clock run:

```
same clock (1200 MHz locked)   we are 98.9-99.9%   -> work is at parity
free clocks, equally warm      we are 4.4% slower  -> not work, not order
```

**So yes — they are doing something, and now it's named: cuBLAS's kernel draws less power for identical tensor work, so the governor gives it a higher clock.** Not a warm-up trick, not ordering. Power efficiency at equal work.

And there's a practical consequence I should flag: **nsys is a far better instrument than the benchmark.** It gave 2007 instances per kernel, so its mean is tight to a fraction of a percent, where nine `%cuB` reps carry a ±1.5-point wobble. Every "null" today was judged against that wobble — a 35% instruction cut might plausibly buy ~1% of clock, which the benchmark literally cannot see but nsys can.

That's the next thing worth doing, and it's cheap: **re-measure base vs `uad` under nsys and compare mean kernel duration over ~2000 instances each.** If `uad` lowers our mean duration at free clocks, then instruction count *does* buy clock, we've had a real win sitting unmeasured all day, and it points straight at what to keep cutting.

**One nsys run per shape** — but each run captures every kernel instance inside the 400 ms timed loop, so the sample per shape is large:

```
V2  (~180 us kernel)   ~2000 instances
V4  (~4 ms kernel)     ~100 instances
```

So the *mean* within a run is tight — that's the point of using nsys over the harness's single number.

But you're right to ask, because that's **not** the same as reps. One run doesn't sample **run-to-run** variation — different thermal start, different allocations. With the clock locked that variation should be much smaller than at free clocks, but "should be" isn't measured.

The script appends with a separator each time it runs, so the simplest fix is just to run it three times:

```bash

```

That gives three independent locked runs across all 15 shapes, and if a shape's `%cuB(min)` agrees to within a few tenths across all three, the parity claim is solid. It roughly triples the time to 60–90 minutes though.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-20 17:22 IST]

Two good questions.

**How this differs from the 3 reps.** Those were 3 harness invocations, each reporting *one* aggregate `%cuB` — 3 data points per shape. nsys records **every individual kernel launch**: ~2000 instances on V2, ~100 on V4. So the mean is built from thousands of timings, not three, and its standard error is roughly 45× smaller.

But your objection is still valid — one nsys run doesn't sample **run-to-run** variation (thermal start, allocation). So the proper form is both: **3 nsys runs**, each containing thousands of instances. Within-run precision from the instances, between-run confidence from the repeats. That's what makes it a validation rather than a spot check.

**On 1400 — no, that's not the top, and it was never meant to be.** 1400 was the value recorded for a *B300*; this H200 idles at 345 and boosts to **1980 MHz**. We locked at 1200 because the requirement is "low enough that the power cap never engages", not "as high as possible" — at free clocks we saw the cap (`0x4`) biting at 1515–1965 MHz and ~600 W.

But there's a real caveat I should raise rather than let it slide: **parity at 1200 MHz does not automatically mean parity at 1800 MHz.** Lowering the SM clock doesn't slow DRAM, so a memory-heavy kernel looks relatively better at low clock. If our kernel is more compute-limited than cuBLAS's, 1200 MHz could be flattering us and the parity could partly be an artifact of the low clock.

So the validation should be **3 runs × more than one frequency**:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
nvidia-smi -i 1 --query-supported-clocks=gr --format=csv,noheader | head -3
nvidia-smi -i 1 --query-supported-clocks=gr --format=csv,noheader | tail -3

for F in 1200 1500 1755; do
  for i in 1 2 3; do
    GPU=1 FREQ=$F bash tools/h27zq_locked_nsys.sh V1 V5 V2c V4
  done
done 2>&1 | grep -E "^  V|locked at"
```

Four shapes — V1 (the claimed outlier) and three that read 99% — at three frequencies, three runs each. That's 36 measurements, each with hundreds-to-thousands of instances, and it answers both questions at once: does parity reproduce run to run, and does it hold as the clock rises toward where real work happens. Roughly 45–60 minutes.

Watch the `locked at` line in each block — if the requested frequency isn't actually held at 1755 (the cap engaging), that row is invalid and we drop it and use the highest frequency that stays pinned.

what sthat 1200 thing ? frequeny? liekwhat sthe unts ? 1200 what /

### CLAUDE [2026-08-20 18:36 IST]

**1200 MHz** — megahertz. It's the SM clock: how fast the GPU's compute cores tick.

On this H200:

```
345 MHz    idle
1200 MHz   what we lock it to for measuring
1755 MHz   we tried this, the power cap overrode it
1980 MHz   maximum boost
```

Normally the GPU picks this number itself, second by second, based on temperature and power draw. That's the whole problem — it was giving cuBLAS ~1474 MHz and us ~1401 MHz, so cuBLAS looked faster partly just because it was being *run* faster.

`nvidia-smi -lgc 1200,1200` forces min and max both to 1200, so it can't move. Then both kernels tick at exactly the same rate and any difference left is real work.

**Why 1200 specifically:** it has to be low enough that the GPU never hits its **700 watt** limit. Above that limit the card cuts the clock to protect itself, and then the lock stops holding — which is exactly what happened at 1755, where the cap pulled it down mid-run and quietly ruined that measurement.

Absolute speeds drop when locked — at 1200 MHz we get ~598 TFLOPS instead of ~698 — but that doesn't matter, because **both** kernels are equally slowed. We're comparing the ratio, not the raw number.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-20 18:42 IST]

All good questions, and one of them exposes something I glossed over.

**"If we're equal at 1200, we should be equal at 1300, 1400, 1500 too — right?"** That's the key one, and **not necessarily.** Lowering the SM clock does *not* slow DRAM. So at 1200 MHz the memory system is relatively *faster* compared to compute than it is at 1755. If our kernel is more compute-bound and cuBLAS's more memory-bound, low clock flatters us and the 99% could be partly an artifact. The 1755 numbers hinted exactly that — 94.7% on V2c instead of 99.2% — though that run was contaminated because the cap overrode the lock.

**"Why does cuBLAS get 1474 and we get 1402?"** Because the GPU is at its **700 W** limit and the governor gives each kernel whatever clock keeps it under that. Ours draws more watts per unit of work, so it gets less clock. It's not our mistake in the sense of a bug — it's a property of what our kernel does per cycle.

**"Are they doing something special to draw power?"** No — nobody can request a clock from inside a kernel. The only lever is *drawing less power*, which the governor rewards automatically.

**"Is it the execution order?"** Partly, and I owe you a straight answer: the nsys per-instance data showed both kernels slow as the run heats (cuBLAS +7.3%, ours +9.3%), so order *does* matter — but at the coolest quarter we were still 4.4% behind, and best-instance to best-instance 4.9%. So order accounts for ~2 points of the ~6.5, not the base. **The full reversal test still hasn't been run**, and it's the honest way to nail that last piece.

Your instinct is right: measure across the ladder, and check the lock actually holds. That's the run:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 BLUBLAS_BENCH_TARGET_MS=400
mkdir -p test_reports/h27zt; OUT=test_reports/h27zt/SUMMARY.md
trap 'sudo nvidia-smi -i 1 -rgc >/dev/null 2>&1' EXIT INT TERM
sudo nvidia-smi -pm 1 >/dev/null 2>&1
{
echo "# H27zt frequency ladder, V2 2048x2048x16384 tn   $(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)"
printf "  %-6s %-30s %-22s %s\n" "lock" "%cuB x5" "clock DURING run" "verdict"
for F in 1200 1300 1400 1474 1500 1600 1700 1755; do
  sudo nvidia-smi -i 1 -lgc $F,$F >/dev/null
  ( timeout 40 nvidia-smi -i 1 --query-gpu=clocks.sm --format=csv,noheader -lms 200 > /tmp/clk_$F.txt ) &
  SP=$!
  printf "  %-6s " "$F"
  for r in 1 2 3 4 5; do
    build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix --cfg=256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2 \
      --shape=2048x2048x16384 --layout=tn --bench 2>&1 \
      | awk '/^256x128/{printf "%s ",$9}'
  done
  kill $SP 2>/dev/null; wait $SP 2>/dev/null
  awk -v f=$F '{gsub(/ MHz/,"");if($1+0>500){n++;s+=$1;if($1+0<mn||!mn)mn=$1}}
    END{if(n)printf " mean %4.0f min %4.0f    %s\n",s/n,mn,(mn+0>=f-15?"LOCK HELD":"CAP OVERRODE - INVALID")}' /tmp/clk_$F.txt
done
} 2>&1 | tee $OUT
sudo nvidia-smi -i 1 -rgc >/dev/null
echo "SAVED: $OUT"
```

It samples the clock every 200 ms *while the benchmark runs* and prints the minimum actually sustained, so a lock that silently stops holding is flagged `CAP OVERRODE - INVALID` instead of quietly poisoning the number — the exact failure that wasted the 1755 run.

I included **1474** specifically, since that's what cuBLAS sustains. If we hold 99% at 1474 with the lock intact, then the kernel is genuinely equal at cuBLAS's own operating point and the entire remaining gap is that they can *reach* 1474 while we can't. If parity instead decays as frequency rises even while the lock holds, there's a real frequency-dependent difference and the 1200 result was flattering us.

`V8` was one of the six I'd skipped. So there's no contradiction — both readings hold.

```
V8   16384x2048x512      K=512      94.8%
V8b  16384x2048x2048     K=2048     98.0%
V8c  16384x2048x11264    K=11264    99.5%
V8d  16384x2048x50304    K=50304    99.1%
```

**Parity tracks K.** Small K is where we lose, and it recovers as K grows. Same story on the other side of the set:

```
V1   2048x512x16384      N=512      90.3%    small N
V7c  16384x512x2048      N=512      98.5%    small N but small K too
```

So both real deficits are shapes with **one small dimension** — V1 with N=512, V8 with K=512 — and every fat shape is at parity. That makes sense mechanically: with a small dimension there are few tiles or few k-iterations, so the per-tile prologue and epilogue stop being amortised and start dominating. It's the regime where fixed overheads matter, which is exactly where a hand-tuned library pulls ahead.

That also sharpens tomorrow's target considerably. It isn't "V1 and V8 are two unrelated problems" — it's **one problem: we lose on skinny shapes**, and V1 (N=512) and V8 (K=512) are the two worst instances of it, with V8b at 98.0 as a milder case of the same thing.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-20 18:48 IST]

**This is exactly the test you asked for, and it answers it cleanly.**

```
lock    %cuB (median)   actual clock mean/min    verdict
1200        99.3            1200 / 1200          LOCK HELD
1300        99.8            1305 / 1305          LOCK HELD
1400        99.7            1410 / 1410          LOCK HELD
1474        98.1            1481 / 1455          cap overrode
1500        97.7            1493 / 1440          cap overrode
1600        96.0            1573 / 1425          cap overrode
1700        95.5            1653 / 1440          cap overrode
1755        95.4            1677 / 1425          cap overrode
```

**Your prediction was right.** At 1200 we're 99.3%, at 1300 99.8%, at 1400 99.7% — **flat across every frequency where the clock genuinely holds.** So the parity isn't a low-clock artifact, and the concern I raised about the memory/compute balance shifting was unfounded. Good that we checked it rather than assumed.

And it pins down the threshold precisely: **the power cap starts biting between 1400 and 1474 MHz.** Above that the lock stops being honoured — at 1755 the GPU only sustains a minimum of 1425 despite being told 1755 — and parity decays monotonically: 98.1 → 97.7 → 96.0 → 95.5 → 95.4.

That's the whole story in one table:

```
below the cap    we and cuBLAS are equal          99.3-99.8%
above the cap    we lose progressively            down to 95.4%
```

When both kernels get pulled down to ~1425 MHz, whoever draws more watts per unit of work loses more effective clock — and that's us. Note the earlier free-clock measurement had cuBLAS sustaining 1474 and us 1401; that sits exactly in the region this table shows the cap taking over.

Three things now settled that were guesses this morning:

**Our kernel is genuinely equal to cuBLAS on V2** — not a 1200 MHz fluke, verified at three independent locked frequencies.

**The production gap is entirely the power cap**, and it's worth ~4.5 points on this shape.

**Valid measurement band is 1200–1400 MHz** on this H200. Anything at or above 1474 is contaminated and should be discarded — including the h27zr run I mistakenly took at 1755.

Which means the two real kernel targets stand as V1 (90.3%) and V8 (94.8%), both measured inside the valid band, and the power question is a separate track worth 1.3–8.2 points depending on shape.

### USER [2026-08-20 18:49 IST]

contasminated means ? like cap verride means ?waht ? explainin simple english

### CLAUDE [2026-08-20 18:49 IST]

Simple version.

**Cap override** — we *ask* the GPU to hold a fixed speed, but the GPU has a hard 700 watt limit. At high speed doing heavy maths it would burn more than 700 W, so it ignores our request and drops the speed to protect itself. Our lock loses; the power limit wins.

You can see it in the numbers — this is what the script was checking:

```
we asked 1400   ->  it actually held 1410      lock won
we asked 1755   ->  it only managed 1425       cap won, 330 MHz below what we asked
```

**Contaminated** — the measurement is spoiled and can't be trusted.

The whole point of locking the clock was to force both kernels to run at the *same* speed, so any difference left is purely "whose code is better". But once the cap takes over, the GPU is back to choosing the speed itself — and it gives cuBLAS more than us, because our kernel draws more power. So the number we get is mixing two things again:

```
what we wanted to measure:   is our code as good as theirs?
what we actually measured:   is our code as good as theirs, AND who got given more speed?
```

That's why the 95.4% at 1755 is worthless for judging the kernel, while the 99.7% at 1400 is real — at 1400 the clock genuinely stayed put for both.

So the rule going forward: **only 1200–1400 MHz on this GPU.** Above that the lock silently stops working, and a broken measurement looks exactly like a good one unless you check the actual clock during the run — which is the mistake that made the earlier 1755 run useless.

This runs at **free clocks** — that's the condition we actually care about — and samples the SM clock 10,000×/s while both kernels alternate. The last block just discovers the table layout so I can write the correlation query.

Once we have that, the query joins each clock sample to whichever kernel was executing at that timestamp, and we get exactly what you're asking: **mean SM clock while our kernel ran vs mean SM clock while cuBLAS's ran, in the same process, same thermal state.**

import sqlite3, os, bisect
for case in ('free','cap1755'):
    db='test_reports/h27zu/%s.sqlite'%case
    print("="*70); print("CASE:", case)
    if not os.path.exists(db): print("  no sqlite"); continue
    c=sqlite3.connect(db)
    tabs=[r[0] for r in c.execute("select name from sqlite_master where type='table'")]
    mt=[t for t in tabs if 'METRIC' in t.upper()]
    print("  metric tables:", mt)
    # find the SM-clock metric id by name
    name_tab=[t for t in tabs if 'TARGET_INFO' in t.upper() and 'METRIC' in t.upper()]
    ids={}
    for t in name_tab:
        cols=[d[1] for d in c.execute("pragma table_info(%s)"%t)]
        try:
            for r in c.execute("select * from %s"%t):
                row=dict(zip(cols,r))
                nm=str(row.get('metricName') or row.get('name') or '')
                if 'clock' in nm.lower() or 'SM' in nm:
                    ids[row.get('metricId', row.get('id'))]=nm
        except Exception: pass
    print("  clock-ish metrics:", ids)
    # kernel intervals
    ks=list(c.execute("""select k.start,k.end,s.value from CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_KERNEL k
                         join StringIds s on s.id=k.shortName order by k.start"""))
    iv=[(a,b,'cuBLAS' if 'nvjet' in n else ('ours' if 'bgemm_sm90_kernel' in n else None)) for a,b,n in ks]
    iv=[x for x in iv if x[2]]
    starts=[x[0] for x in iv]
    for t in mt:
        cols=[d[1] for d in c.execute("pragma table_info(%s)"%t)]
        if 'timestamp' not in [x.lower() for x in cols]: continue
        print("  using", t, cols[:6])
        agg={}
        for mid,nm in (ids.items() or [(None,None)]):
            try:
                q="select timestamp, value from %s where metricId=? "%t
                rows=list(c.execute(q,(mid,)))
            except Exception:
                continue
            if not rows: continue
            for ts,val in rows:
                i=bisect.bisect_right(starts,ts)-1
                if i>=0 and iv[i][0]<=ts<=iv[i][1]:
                    agg.setdefault((nm,iv[i][2]),[]).append(val)
            for (nm,k),v in sorted(agg.items()):
                print("    %-28s %-7s n=%-6d mean %.0f"%(nm,k,len(v),sum(v)/len(v)))
        break
PY
```

Two profiles — one at **free clocks** (the production condition, where cuBLAS supposedly holds ~1474 and we ~1401) and one **locked at 1755** where we know the cap overrides. Then it joins every clock sample to the kernel that was executing at that instant.

That gives the number you've been asking for: **cuBLAS's actual sustained clock versus ours, side by side, in the same run and the same thermal state.** If they really do sit ~70 MHz higher while doing identical tensor work, that's it proven directly, and the follow-on question becomes what makes their kernel cheaper in watts.

import sqlite3, bisect

```
V2  free   95.2%   ours 1393 MHz   cuBLAS 1456 MHz   -4.4%

At a held lock both kernels get **identical** clocks (1405 vs 1404) and we score **99.8%**. Let the governor choose and cuBLAS takes 4.4% more clock and we score **95.2%**. The arithmetic closes exactly: `99.8 × (1 − 0.044) = 95.4 ≈ 95.2`. **The entire production gap on V2 is the clock, measured per kernel rather than inferred.**

DRAM Read/Write Bandwidth [Throughput %]
Compute Warps in Flight
Unallocated Warps in Active SMs
```

Those are exactly the quantities that determine power draw. Adding them costs nothing — same capture:

**This is the answer.** Everything matches except one thing:

```
                    ours    cuBLAS

SMs Active          95.5    95.4      identical

**Identical tensor work, identical memory traffic, identical occupancy — and we issue instructions at 2.24× cuBLAS's rate.**

And that number is independently corroborated: ncu measured `smsp__inst_executed.sum` at 35,946,060 vs 16,035,216 on this exact shape — **ratio 2.2417**. Two completely different instruments, same 2.24×. It's also stable across free and locked clocks (24.5/11.0 and 24.7/11.0), so it's structural, not thermal.

So the full causal chain is now closed, every link measured:

```
we issue 2.24x the instructions per cycle
  -> the fetch/decode/issue pipeline burns more watts at identical tensor work
  -> under the 700 W cap the governor gives us less clock: 1389 vs 1457 MHz
  -> 4.7% slower in production
  -> but at a held clock we are 99.8% -- the work itself is equal
```

**And this reopens the instruction-count question, which I closed too early today.** I cut 470M instructions across four experiments and called them all null — but every one was judged by `%cuB` at free clocks, which carries a ±1.5-point wobble. The right instrument was `SM Issue`, and I didn't have it.

The prediction is now sharp and testable: `uad` cut V2's instructions 35.9M → 23.4M (−35%). If issue rate follows, it should fall from 24.7% toward **~16%**, against cuBLAS's 11.0% — and the sustained clock should rise with it.

Actually that needs the config swapped, which the script takes from `pins.sh`. Quickest is a direct one-off:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 BLUBLAS_BENCH_TARGET_MS=1000
sudo nvidia-smi -i 1 -rgc >/dev/null 2>&1
for c in 256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2 256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2_dh_ubd_uad; do
  nsys profile -t cuda --gpu-metrics-devices=1 --gpu-metrics-frequency=10000 \
    -o /tmp/iss_$c --force-overwrite true build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix \
    --cfg=$c --shape=2048x2048x16384 --layout=tn --bench > /tmp/iss_$c.log 2>&1
  nsys export --type sqlite --force-overwrite true -o /tmp/iss_$c.sqlite /tmp/iss_$c.nsys-rep >/dev/null 2>&1
  echo "### $c   $(grep -o '[0-9.]*%' /tmp/iss_$c.log | tail -1)"
  python3 - "$c" <<'PY'
import sqlite3,sys,bisect
c=sys.argv[1]; db='/tmp/iss_%s.sqlite'%c
d=sqlite3.connect(db)
mets={(t,m):n for t,m,n in d.execute("select typeId,metricId,metricName from TARGET_INFO_GPU_METRICS")}
ks=list(d.execute("""select k.start,k.end,s.value from CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_KERNEL k
                     join StringIds s on s.id=k.shortName order by k.start"""))
iv=[(a,b,'cuBLAS' if 'nvjet' in n else ('ours' if 'bgemm_sm90_kernel' in n else None)) for a,b,n in ks]
iv=[x for x in iv if x[2]]; st=[x[0] for x in iv]
for want in ('SM Issue','Tensor Active','GPC Clock'):
    key=next((k for k,n in mets.items() if want.lower() in n.lower()),None)
    if not key: continue
    agg={'ours':[],'cuBLAS':[]}
    for ts,val in d.execute("select timestamp,value from GPU_METRICS where typeId=? and metricId=?",key):
        i=bisect.bisect_right(st,ts)-1
        if i>=0 and iv[i][0]<=ts<=iv[i][1]: agg[iv[i][2]].append(val)
    if agg['ours'] and agg['cuBLAS']:
        o=sum(agg['ours'])/len(agg['ours']); b=sum(agg['cuBLAS'])/len(agg['cuBLAS'])
        if o>1e6: o,b=o/1e6,b/1e6
        print("   %-16s ours %8.1f   cuBLAS %8.1f"%(want,o,b))
PY
done
```

If `uad` drops SM Issue and lifts our clock, then **every "null" today was a measurement failure, not a real null** — and reducing instructions becomes the concrete lever for closing the production gap on all 13 parity shapes.

## Where V1 lags, and why

It is **not** work, memory, or occupancy — those are identical:

| | ours | cuBLAS | |
|---|---|---|---|
| HGMMA issued | 524,288 | 524,288 | 1.0000 |
| DRAM bytes read | 83,917,824 | 83,912,192 | 1.0001 |
| waves/SM | 0.97 | 0.97 | 1.0000 |
| **cycles** | **83,423** | **75,625** | **1.1031** |
| tensor pipe active | 82.28% | 90.99% | 0.9043 |

The whole 10.3% is the tensor unit sitting **idle**. And one instruction owns it — 30.35% of every not-issued stall sample in our kernel, 100% of them `stall_barrier`:

```
idx249  HGMMA ... , gsb0                 <- commit the group
idx250  WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE gsb0, 0x0    <- 866 samples, 30.35%.  drain to ZERO
idx251  BRA  (back-edge)
```

In plain terms: **we fire 4 tensor instructions, then stop dead and wait for all 4 to finish, then spend ~62 scalar instructions rebuilding descriptors with the tensor unit doing nothing — 128 times per CTA.** cuBLAS keeps **8** in flight across its back-edge, so its drain overlaps real work: it drains once per 8 HGMMA, we drain once per 4.

## Why it hasn't been fixed — and what's actually new

Every obvious fix is on an explicit "**DEAD FORMS, so none is proposed a fifth time**" list, and I'm not re-proposing any of them. But look at what they all share:

```
wait_group<1> + release deferred across a stage   §H16.7    -10 to -12%   <- measured AT DEPTH 3
any wait_group<N>, N>0, at depth 3                §H27zbB   RACE          <- says "at depth 3"
drain rotation WGMMA_ROTATE 1/2                   §H27zbA   compile kill (C7517)
descriptor rewrite alone (dw / dh / ubd / uad)    §H27zdb   93.79 vs 94.21 pin, null-to-negative
```

And §H27zbA's own conclusion: *"the fix is not a wait or a commit at all — **it is a FOURTH STAGE**. With depth 4, holding one stage across the back-edge still leaves 2 free for the producer."* That was parked because 192×192 stages are 49,152 B and the budget only affords 3.

**V1's tile is 128×128. Its stages are 32,768 B and it already runs at depth 6.** The precondition the docs named as *the* blocker is already satisfied, for free, on exactly the shape still lagging — and it was never tested there, because all the drain work was done on the 192×192 tile at depth 3. Holding one stage costs V5 a third of its pipeline; it costs V1 a sixth.

Two things I'm also correcting, so they don't mislead later:

- I dropped the instruction-count argument (we run 25.9 instructions per HGMMA, cuBLAS 9.0). §H27zdb closed that thread permanently — instruction count went **up 14% and got faster**. Three prior efforts already burned on it.
- `WGMMA_SKEW` — the one mechanism proven to move this exact counter (V3 barrier 32.25 → 23.10, +1.62) — is **statically illegal** on V1: `static_assert(!SKEW || MAX_ATOMS >= 2)`, and 128×128 gives each warpgroup exactly 1 m64 atom. Same for V8's 128×256. That's why the SKEW win never reached these two.

One caveat on the ledger: it profiles the GEMM kernel only, so the split-K reduce is excluded on both sides.

Next step is to build **`wait_group<1>` + release deferred by one stage as a new default-false knob** and gate it on V1's pin at depth 6 — §H16.7's exact mechanism, with the only objection ever measured against it (the buffer cost) removed by the depth. Falsifier is clean: if V1 doesn't move at depth 6, the held-buffer trade is not the cost here and the mainloop thread closes for V1 too. Want me to write it?

Li256ELi128ELi64ELi2ELi1E ... Li0ELi4E ... ELb1ELb0E
     256   128   64    2 1        RS=0 SPLIT_K=4      SKEW=true

All four skew arms, both `Sm90Layout0` (NN) and `Sm90Layout2` (TN). So the configs compiled fine.

But look at the last line: it linked **`build/libmyblas.so`** — the *library*. It never rebuilt the **test binary**, which is where the registry lives:
> tool `Bash`: Find the test build target

Found it — and it's **my error in the BUILD block I gave you.**

```make
all: lib          <- plain `make` builds ONLY the library
tests: lib        <- separate target; this is what rebuilds build/test_bgemm_sm90_matrix
```

The library got the new kernels (you can see them in ptxas), but the **test binary was never rebuilt**, so its embedded config registry is stale — `--cfg=256x128x64_2x1_v_sk4` matched nothing and printed nothing. Exactly the symptom.

Worth noting the `tests` recipe ends in `| grep -v "warning:" || true`, so a test compile error is swallowed and the build still reports success. Let me get you a command that doesn't hide that:
> tool `Bash`: Get LIBNAME and link flags for targeted test build

`LIBNAME := myblas`. Let me harden the gate script first so this can never silently waste a GPU run again — it should refuse to start if an arm isn't in the binary:
> tool `Bash`: Add stale-binary guard to gate script

## The structural prediction was exact. My causal claim was wrong.

**Phase 3 — hit precisely:**
```
pin          4.00 HGMMA per drain
256x128 sk4  8.00          <- exactly cuBLAS's 7.94
```
So the SASS reading in §H27zo was right: two m64 atoms per warpgroup does put 8 wgmma between drains.

**Phase 2 — the falsifier I wrote into the script *before* the run:**
```
tensor pipe active   81.94 -> 86.93   +4.99   PREDICTED, happened
stall_barrier        27.35 -> 33.51   +6.16   PREDICTED TO FALL. IT ROSE.
```

**I'm recording that as a failed prediction, not reinterpreting it.** My story was that the drain is expensive because nothing overlaps it. That's wrong. **Halving the drain count doubles what each drain waits for** — DEPBAR's share of samples went *up* (30.76% → 35.45%) with half as many DEPBARs. Fewer, longer drains. Total barrier time didn't fall.

So the 5.44% cycle gain is real but it is **not** the drain being relieved. What moved alongside it was instructions (−29.4%), short-scoreboard and wait. Which of those is causal, this run does not establish.

## Two other results worth keeping

**SKEW is not V1's lever.** Given `WG_MATOMS=2`, `_skew` measured **89.61 vs 89.99 without**, and added 2.08M instructions. §H27zdb's V3 +1.62 doesn't transfer. So the SKEW lockout on BM=128 was never what was costing V1 — that whole line of reasoning is closed.

**The kernel got 5.44% faster and end-to-end got worse** (90.37 → 89.99). The ncu ledger profiles `bgemm_sm90_kernel` only; sk4's reduce over four fp32 partial sets isn't in it, and I never captured `dram__bytes_write` — my omission. §H27zn had already measured that curve on the pin's own tile (sk2 90.1, sk4 80.7, sk8 66.7).

## Where that leaves V1

**V1 stays at 90.37% on cuBLAS's own tile.** Nothing adopted — every arm's range overlaps the pin's.

And the probe is **confounded**: it changed tile, atoms-per-warpgroup, split factor *and* depth (6→3) at once. The 5.44% can't be attributed to atoms-per-warpgroup. There's no cheaper isolation — the only single-variable test is 128×128 at sk2 with `NUM_CONSUMER_WARPGROUPS=1`, which *is* the refactor. So it's **supported, not proven**, and I'd want your call on it rather than starting the biggest change in the campaign on a mixed result.

Good morning. Two operational things about this box first, then the full picture.

## This box is different, and that matters

```
old:  deep-ball-purrs-fin-03   GPU 1
new:  quick-home-speaks-fin-03  GPU 0    <- single H200, index 0, 143771MiB, idle 81W/700W

So V1's 90.37% needs re-confirming here before I trust any comparison against it. And every script I wrote defaults to `GPU=1`; on this box it must be `GPU=0`.

**Second, and more urgent:** yesterday's `test_reports/*/SUMMARY.md` were **never committed**, and the box that held them is gone. I checked — `git ls-files test_reports/` has 38 files, none of them from yesterday. What survived:

- ✅ **§H27zn / §H27zo / §H27zo-RESULT** — I wrote the numbers into `analyzations_h200.md`, so V1's diagnosis is safe

- ❌ **§H27zs (all-15-shapes locked table) and §H27zt (frequency ladder) have ZERO mentions in the docs** — they exist *only* in the two screenshots you sent yesterday

Those two are the most load-bearing results we have (they're what proved 13 of 15 shapes are already at parity), and right now they live in an image. I want to transcribe them into the doc before anything else.

## Where the project actually stands

**Goal:** BluBLAS matching then beating cuBLAS on SM90 for the 1.7B BluTrain model. Step 3 = our 8 kernel variants against cuBLAS's 8, across the 15 distinct shapes at 21 call sites.

**The scoreboard, at locked clock:** 13 of 15 shapes sit at **98.0–100.0%** of cuBLAS. At free clocks the median was only 95.0% — that difference is the power governor, not the kernels. Only two genuine gaps remain:

| | shape | locked %cuB | diagnosis |
|---|---|---|---|
| **V1** | 2048x512x16384 tn | **90.37** | single-wave, mainloop-bound — fully diagnosed |
| **V8** | 16384x2048x512 nt | **94.8** | K=512 → 8 k-iters, prologue/intercept-bound — untouched |

Both are skinny-dimension shapes, and they're **two different diseases** — the V1 fix almost certainly won't touch V8.

**Solved earlier:** V5 82.20 → 92.80 (phantom tile column, +10.6), V6 84.53 → 95.14 (+10.61), V3/V4/V6 pinned on `rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw`, and the measurement methodology itself (locked clocks + the cap-override trap).

## V1, where yesterday ended

Apples-to-apples is **fully confirmed** — cuBLAS runs `nvjet_sm90_tst_128x128_64x6_1x2_h_bz_splitK_NTT`: same 128×128 tile, same BK 64, same 6 stages (ours derives 6), same split-K, same layout. Identical tensor work (524,288 HGMMA), identical DRAM, identical 0.97 waves. We just take **10.3% more cycles** with the tensor pipe at 82.28% against their 90.99%.

I read their SASS and found the cause: **they give both m64 atoms to one consumer warpgroup** (8 wgmma per drain, 4 left in flight across the back-edge, release lagged one stage). We hardcode `NUM_CONSUMER_WARPGROUPS = 2`, so each warpgroup owns one atom — 4 per drain, nothing in flight.

The probe reached `WG_MATOMS=2` and the **structural prediction was exact: 4.00 → 8.00 per drain**, tensor pipe +4.99 points, kernel cycles −5.44%. But **the falsifier I pre-registered failed** — barrier stall *rose* 27.35 → 33.51 instead of falling, because halving the drain count doubles what each drain waits for. So the gain is real but not from where I claimed. Also settled: **SKEW is not V1's lever** (89.61 with vs 89.99 without).

Verdict on record: the `NUM_CONSUMER_WARPGROUPS=1` refactor is **supported, not proven** — the probe changed tile, atoms/warpgroup, split factor and depth all at once.

Found the hole. Line 59 reads the clock **once, at idle, before any kernel runs** — that's exactly the weak check that let the silent cap override through before. Let me take the sampler from the ladder script that produced your `LOCK HELD / CAP OVERRODE` column:

That's the right mechanism — background-sample `clocks.sm` at 200 ms while the benchmark runs, then compare against what was requested. Porting it into the gate so **every measured row carries the clock that actually ran**:
> tool `Bash`: Add during-run clock sampling to every gate row

Yes — and I just closed a real hole in it.

**What was already right:**
```bash
sudo nvidia-smi -pm 1                          # persistence mode
sudo nvidia-smi -i $GPU -lgc 1200,1200         # lock SM clock
trap '... nvidia-smi -rgc' EXIT INT TERM       # always restore, even on Ctrl-C
ncu ... --clock-control none                   # stop ncu overriding our lock with its own
```

**What was wrong:** the script read `clocks.sm` **once, at idle, before any kernel ran**. That is precisely the check that failed us before — you ask for 1755, the pre-run read looks fine, and the card silently runs 1425 under load. A locked clock is not a held clock.

Every row now samples `clocks.sm` at 200 ms **during its own benchmark** and prints what actually ran:

```
cfg                                mean  min  max  maxRelErr  clkAvg clkMin lock      verdict
128x128x64_2x1_v_sk2              90.37 ...                     1200   1200 HELD      (pin)
128x128x64_2x1_v_sk2_dh_dw_uad    ...                           1200   1200 HELD      ...
```

and a row whose clock slipped is marked `INVALID (clock OVERRODE)` in the verdict column, so it can't quietly be compared against a held row.

**One caveat you should know:** the valid band **1200–1400** was established on `deep-ball-purrs-fin-03`. The cap threshold is a property of the individual card and its cooling, so it is **not guaranteed on this box**. 1200 is the bottom of the old band so it should hold — and now if it doesn't, the run tells us instead of hiding it.

You're right — the model failed, not the data. The data is good; my lens was wrong. Let me go back to the samples with a stricter lens: **stall samples localise TIME, so partition the consumer mainloop by *phase* and compare the shape, not the totals.**
> tool `Bash`: Partition each consumer mainloop by phase

**This is it. It's structural, and it's measurable.** Partitioning each consumer body by *where the stall happens relative to the HGMMAs*:

```
                                        instrs   stalls   dominant reason
OURS
  1 acquire + descriptor setup (pre-1st)   31     33.9%   long_sb 51%, wait 27%, short_sb 21%
  2 issue window (HGMMA..HGMMA)            33      6.0%   wait 98%
  3 drain / back-edge (post-last HGMMA)     2     60.1%   barrier 99%

cuBLAS
  1 acquire + setup (pre-1st)               6      7.3%   wait 69%
  2 issue window (HGMMA..HGMMA)            28     92.7%   barrier 75%
  3 post-last HGMMA                         6      0.0%   -- NOTHING
```

**cuBLAS's DEPBAR lives *inside* the issue window** — four HGMMAs before it, four after. Whenever it stalls, the tensor pipe still has queued work. Its post-last-HGMMA phase has **literally zero samples**.

**Our DEPBAR sits after the last HGMMA**, so when it stalls the tensor queue is empty. Then we cross the back-edge into 31 instructions of acquire + descriptor build before the *first* HGMMA can issue — also with an empty queue.

**94.0% of our mainloop stall time (33.9 + 60.1) happens with nothing queued on the tensor pipe. For cuBLAS it's 7.3%.**

That is exactly the closed budget's missing mechanism — it explains *why* idle is 15,958 vs 6,814, and it explains why instruction count failed: 31 instructions before the first HGMMA is what costs, not the 66 total.

The fix is to **straddle the wait with HGMMA issue**. `WGMMA_ROTATE` was built for precisely this ("where the drain sits, not how deep it waits") and was killed on *compile* grounds — ptxas C7517 injecting extra waits, DEPBAR 2→4 — but **that census was run on 192×192 only**. Let me check it on V1's tile, locally, no GPU:

**Clean negative, and cheaply:** the `WGMMA_ROTATE` compile kill **reproduces on 128×128** — `DEPBAR 1 → 3` plus the C7517 injected-wait warning on both modes 1 and 2. Not tile-specific. That knob stays dead; I won't propose it.

But the finding stands, and it gives me a **testable design target: minimise the instruction distance from loop-top to the first HGMMA.** And I can test that right now against the six configs we just measured, with no GPU — if phase-1 length predicts the measured %cuB, the lens is right.

That's now **two static metrics that failed to predict the measured outcome** (instruction count, pre-HGMMA distance). That is itself informative: the difference is **dynamic, not static** — which is exactly why PC sampling found it and the static counts didn't.

**cuBLAS puts 39 instructions and four HGMMA issues between the commit and the wait. We put one instruction and zero.** When their DEPBAR stalls (891 samples, 64.4% — it's their biggest stall too), four freshly-issued wgmma are already queued behind it. When ours stalls, nothing is.

And the consequence is measurable on both sides of the pipeline:

```
                        cuBLAS                         OURS
acquire (TRYWAIT)    idx190,   0 samples          idx196+197, 287 samples (long_sb)
                     no spin loop at all          @!P0 BRA <self>  -- inline spin
release              idx189,   0 samples          end of body, after a full drain
producer             NANOSLEEP, 43.3% = slack     spins on EMPTY barriers, 23.6%
```

**The causal chain, all measured:** we commit and drain back-to-back → the buffer is released at the very end of the body → the producer can't run ahead and spins on empty barriers → the consumer's acquire then finds data not ready (287 samples) → the tensor pipe idles. cuBLAS releases one whole iteration earlier in effect, so its producer has slack and its acquire *never stalls*.

This independently reproduces §H27zb9's reading, which was right. And §H27zbA identified the fix — move the drain to the top of the next iteration — but ptxas blocks it. I re-verified that block on this tile today (`DEPBAR 1 → 3`, C7517). So the question is now narrow and answerable locally:
> tool `Bash`: Locate injected DEPBARs under WGMMA_ROTATE

Now I can see exactly why the known fix is blocked — and it's a **compiler behaviour, not a design flaw**:

```
WGMMA_ROTATE=0 (today)              WGMMA_ROTATE=1
  0c40 TRYWAIT  (acquire)             0c20 DEPBAR gsb0,0x0   <- ROTATION WORKED, drain is now at the TOP
  0c90 WARPGROUP.ARRIVE               0db0 TRYWAIT (acquire)
  0d90 HGMMA #1..#3                   0df0 WARPGROUP.ARRIVE
  0e90 HGMMA #4, gsb0   COMMIT        0f80 HGMMA #1..#3
  0ea0 DEPBAR gsb0,0x0  <- 1 instr    10f0 HGMMA #4, gsb0   COMMIT
       after the commit               1190 DEPBAR gsb0,0x0   <- ptxas INJECTED
                                      1320 DEPBAR gsb0,0x0   <- ptxas INJECTED
```

**The rotation does exactly what we want** — it moves the drain to the top of the loop, ahead of the acquire, which is cuBLAS's shape. Then ptxas puts two drains back right after the commit (C7517: *"warpgroup.wait is injected to allow use of registers defined by GMMA"*), restoring the old behaviour plus overhead. So §H27zbA's "compile-only kill" was recorded correctly, but the reason is narrower than "this doesn't work" — **something in our loop tail reads the accumulator registers between the commit and the rotated drain, and ptxas has to make that safe.** cuBLAS's only reader between its commit and its drain is another HGMMA, and wgmma→wgmma accumulator ordering is free.

That is a bounded, local, zero-GPU question: *which statement in our loop tail triggers the injection.*
