## Where the lag comes from — final answer, all measured

**The metric is the distance from the wgmma commit to the DEPBAR that waits on it.**

```
cuBLAS   commit -> back-edge -> 23 instrs -> 4 HGMMA ISSUED -> DEPBAR      39 instrs, 4 HGMMA
ours     commit -> DEPBAR                                                   1 instr,  0 HGMMA
```

Both kernels' DEPBAR is their single biggest stall (theirs 64.4% of the loop body, ours 60.1%). **The wait isn't the problem — what's queued behind it is.** Theirs stalls with four fresh wgmma already pending, so the tensor pipe keeps working. Ours stalls with nothing pending.

**And it cascades, measurably, to both ends of the pipeline:**

| | cuBLAS | ours |
|---|---|---|
| acquire | **0 samples**, no spin loop at all | **287 samples**, inline `@!P0 BRA <self>` |
| release | right after the drain | at the very end of the body |
| producer | `NANOSLEEP` 43.3% → **has slack** | tight spin on empty barriers **23.6%** → can't run ahead |

We commit and drain back-to-back → buffer released late → producer never gets ahead → consumer's acquire finds data not ready → tensor pipe idles. cuBLAS's release effectively lands a full iteration earlier, so its acquire *never stalls*.

## Why the fix is blocked — and it's narrower than "it doesn't work"

`WGMMA_ROTATE=1` **does the right thing**: it moves the DEPBAR to `0c20`, top of loop, ahead of the acquire — cuBLAS's exact shape. Then **ptxas injects two DEPBARs back** right after the commit (C7517). So the mechanism is sound; a compiler safety rule is undoing it because something in our **loop tail reads the accumulator registers** between commit and rotated drain. cuBLAS's only reader there is another HGMMA, and that ordering is free in hardware.

That converts a dead end into a bounded, zero-GPU bisect: which statement in the tail triggers it — `wgmma_fence()` at the next pass, the `prev_stage = stage` carry, the stage/phase advance, or `acc[][][]` liveness across the back-edge.

You're right that +1.18 doesn't get us to parity, and I should have questioned the premise earlier instead of polishing a knob.

Here's the thing I never checked: **every V1 analysis so far assumed the gap lives in the mainloop.** I never tested that. V1 is 0.97 waves — one tile per CTA — so the prologue, TMA warm-up, epilogue and split-K reduce are each paid **once and amortise over nothing**. There's already evidence this matters on a sibling family: **V8 (K=512) scores 94.8%, V8b (K=2048) 98.1%, V8c (K=11264) 99.4%** — same tile, gap shrinking as K grows. That's the signature of an **intercept**-dominated gap. Nobody has run that sweep on V1.

```
cycles(K) = INTERCEPT + SLOPE x k_iters
```

for **both** kernels in the same sweep, then split V1's ~8,000-cycle gap into the two buckets.

- **SLOPE excess** → per-iteration mainloop → the commit→drain and descriptor territory
- **INTERCEPT excess** → paid once → prologue, epilogue, split-K reduce — **completely untouched so far**

**cuBLAS's mainloop is fully saturated — the tensor pipe never idles during the loop. Ours idles 34.8 cycles every single k-iteration, 128 times.**

That number is not mysterious: our pre-first-HGMMA phase is **31 instructions** (acquire + descriptor setup), and at ~1 IPC that's ≈31 cycles — matching 34.8. It's the same phase PC sampling flagged at 31.0% of loop stalls. cuBLAS's equivalent phase is **6 instructions**, and it runs with 4 wgmma still in flight, so it's completely hidden.


**The mainloop is worth ~6.6 points (91.7 → 98.3). The intercept is worth ~1.7 more.** So the ordering is settled by measurement, not opinion: mainloop first, intercept second, and the two together are the whole gap.

Let me read the exact code path first — I need to know what's actually in the loop tail before I can bisect it.
> tool `Bash`: Read drain_prev and the accumulator declaration

Found the likely trigger, and it's in the guard:

```cpp
auto drain_prev = [&]() {
    if (WROT != 0 && prev_stage >= 0) {   // <-- prev_stage is a RUNTIME value
        wgmma_wait_group<0>();
        release_empty(prev_stage);
        prev_stage = -1;
    }
};
```

**The drain is predicated on a runtime condition.** On the path where `prev_stage < 0` there is no wait at all, so ptxas cannot prove every path waits before the accumulators are reused — and C7517 says it inserts one to make that safe. cuBLAS's drain is unconditional in its loop body, and CUTLASS avoids the same problem by peeling (`prologue_mma_count = min(K_PIPE_MMAS, k_tile_count)`) instead of guarding.

Testable in one compile:

```
WROT=1/2  WITH the runtime guard    1                3     <- the documented "compile-only kill"
WROT=1/2  guard removed             0                2     <- injection GONE
```

**§H27zbA's compile kill was caused by our own runtime guard, not by a ptxas limitation.** Let me confirm the drain actually lands where we want it:

**That's the cuBLAS shape.** With the guard gone, the loop is:

```
0be0  WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE        <- DRAIN, at the TOP of the loop
0cd0  SYNCS.ARRIVE (release)     <- RELEASE immediately after, exactly cuBLAS's idx189
0d80  SYNCS.PHASECHK.TRYWAIT     <- ACQUIRE
0dc0  WARPGROUP.ARRIVE
0f40  HGMMA x4                   <- ISSUE, then back-edge with 4 STILL IN FLIGHT
1100  WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE        <- the post-loop drain (required, retires the last group)
```

One drain in the loop at the top, one after the loop. That's structurally correct.

**But removing the guard outright is a real bug:** on iteration 0 `prev_stage == -1`, so `release_empty(-1)` does `mbarrier_arrive(empty_mbar_addr - 8)` — an out-of-bounds shared-memory write. **V2 has nothing to recover** — it's already at 99.79%, so a per-iteration idle fix has no idle to remove. That's a clean confirmation rather than a disappointment.

And there's a genuine blind spot there: **the split-K reduce is a separate kernel and no measurement in this campaign has ever profiled it.** Every ncu ledger we've run used `-k regex:bgemm_sm90_kernel`, so the reduce is inside the `%cuB` wall-clock but invisible in every counter table. For V1 (sk2) that's a whole extra launch we've never looked at, and cuBLAS runs its own `splitKreduce` we've never compared against.

The slope gap is closed. What's left is paid once per CTA, and it has two parts, **neither ever measured**:

1. **The GEMM kernel's own prologue + epilogue.** Our intercept is 10,200 cycles vs cuBLAS's 8,891. That's TMA descriptor setup, mbarrier init, filling the pipeline before the first wgmma, then accumulators → smem → TMA store. For V1 under `SPLIT_K=2` the epilogue writes **fp32** partials — 128×128×4 = 65,536 B per CTA, twice the bf16 volume.

2. **The split-K reduce kernel — a completely separate launch we have never profiled.** Confirmed at template line 5831: `blublas::splitk::launch_splitk_reduce<__nv_bfloat16>(...)`. Every ncu ledger in this campaign used `-k regex:bgemm_sm90_kernel`, so that kernel's cost sits inside the `%cuB` wall-clock and is **invisible in every counter table we've produced**. cuBLAS runs its own `splitKreduce` we've never compared against either.

V8's remaining 3.8% is the same bucket — it's intercept-shaped by construction (K=512, only 8 k-iterations), which is why the rotation only bought it +0.72.

So the next measurement is exactly the one you picked: profile **every** kernel in the launch, both libraries, and see what the paid-once cost is made of. Let me build that now.

The reduce kernel itself is **well written** — fp32 fixed-order accumulation (deterministic), a `float4` fast path with correct alignment checks on both terms, alpha/beta applied once, grid-stride. But its *cost* has never been measured, and for V1 it's not trivial: `total_elems = 2048×512 = 1,048,576`, S=2, so it moves ~8 MB in + 2 MB out ≈ **10 MB** against a GEMM of ~64 µs. ```

So `MegaDiv` is already doing its job — the mega-tile division is magic-number multiply, and `% LOAD_PIPE_DEPTH` is being folded. Zero stall samples on any divide. That hypothesis is negative, cleanly.

Answers to your three questions, and the tool for the one that needs measuring:

**1. Is the reduce kernel inefficient?** Reading it — no algorithmic flaw. Fixed-order fp32 accumulation (that's the determinism guarantee), a `float4` fast path with correct alignment checks on *both* address terms, alpha/beta applied exactly once, grid-stride geometry. It's a good kernel. What's never been checked is its **cost**: ~10 MB of traffic for V1 against a 64 µs GEMM, and a note in that same file records an earlier geometry hitting only ~7% of HBM.

The descriptor cost sits in a different place now. `_dh_dw` measured 90.34 vs `_dh`'s 91.83 *before* rot2; that verdict doesn't automatically carry.

`DESC_WALK` is already the exact thing you're describing — the CuTe form, one `UIADD3` on the low word, upper word never rebuilt. Let me verify locally what it actually does to the instruction mix on top of rot2:
> tool `Bash`: Compare descriptor instruction mix on top of rot2

Checked it properly, and the answer isn't what either of us expected. First, my `total` column above is meaningless (it counted a grep pattern, not instructions) — ignore it. The rest is real:

```
arm (all on top of rot2)   SHF   LOP3   R2UR   UIADD3   HGMMA
base  (= today's V1 pin)    75     36      9      475       4
dw    (DESC_WALK)           81     36      9      483       4     <- WORSE, not better
ss    (STAGE_SPECIALISE)    88     56     49      513      25     <- much worse
dwss                       102     36     49      548      25
```

**`DESC_WALK` does not actually implement the single-`UIADD3` form on this tile.** Shift/mask counts go *up*, not down, and `R2UR` doesn't move at all. That explains why `dh_dw` measured 90.34 against `_dh`'s 91.83 — it was never doing the thing its name promises here. `STAGE_SPECIALISE` is worse still: it emits six copies of the body (HGMMA 4→25) and blows `R2UR` from 9 to 49.

So getting cuBLAS's form would be **real work, not a knob flip** — a proper rewrite of the descriptor path.

And here's why I'd argue against spending GPU time on it *now*, with the number rather than an opinion:

```

§H27zs slope excess                5,492 -> CLOSED
```

**The slope gap is closed.** The descriptor math lives in the mainloop, and there is no longer meaningful mainloop time to recover on V1 — the 1.66% that remains is paid-once cost, outside the loop. Rewriting the descriptors would be tidying code that is no longer on the critical path. The same holds on the other shapes: they're at 98.8–99.9%.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-21 12:39 IST]

**This is a significant finding, and it's not where anyone was looking.**

**V1, per launch:**
```
                       ours          cuBLAS
GEMM kernel          63,309 ns     62,103 ns    we are 1.9% slower
reduce kernel         4,962 ns      6,586 ns    WE ARE 25% FASTER
                     -----------------------
total DEVICE time    68,272 ns     68,689 ns    we are 0.61% FASTER
```

**Our reduce is not a problem — it beats cuBLAS's `splitKreduce` by 25%.** And on total device time **we are ahead of cuBLAS on V1.** Yet the harness measures 98.34%. Those can only both be true if ~1.7% of the iteration is spent **outside both kernels**:

```
wall_ours / wall_cuBLAS = 1/0.9834 = 1.0169
device:  68,272 vs 68,689
=> roughly 1,500-1,600 ns per iteration of NON-KERNEL time we have and cuBLAS doesn't
```

The tool only queried `CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_KERNEL` — so **memsets, memcopies and launch gaps are invisible in the table above.** A split-K path that zeroes its workspace would land exactly there:
> tool `Bash`: Look for memset or sync in the split-K path

No memset, no memcpy, no sync in that path — `cudaMalloc` is first-acquisition only (cached arena). So the ~1,500 ns is either **inter-kernel gap** or **host-side work per call**. The sqlite has kernel start/end timestamps, so I can measure the gaps directly:
> tool `Bash`: Add inter-kernel gap analysis to the profiler

Two clean results from that, and they split V1 and V8 into **different problems**:

**V1 — the reduce hypothesis is dead, and in our favour:**
```
                    ours       cuBLAS
GEMM              63,309 ns   62,103 ns    +1.9%
reduce             4,962 ns    6,586 ns    WE WIN by 25%
total device      68,272 ns   68,689 ns    WE ARE 0.6% AHEAD
harness says                                98.34%
```
Our `splitk_reduce_kernel` is **faster than cuBLAS's `splitKreduce`**. And on summed device time we're already ahead. So V1's remaining ~1.7% is **not in any kernel** — it's ~1,500 ns/iteration spent outside both. Nothing in that path memsets or syncs, so it's inter-kernel gap or host-side per-call work (the workspace budget check and gating logic both run per call).

**V8 — no reduce at all, so the gap is entirely the GEMM:**
```
ours 81,650 ns   cuBLAS 78,104 ns   +4.5%
```
That's a real kernel gap, and it's now the largest genuine one left in the campaign.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-21 12:55 IST]

**Found it. This is the entire remaining V1 gap, and it's one number:**

```
OURS    bgemm_sm90_kernel  -> splitk_reduce_kernel   median gap  +2,336 ns
OURS    splitk_reduce      -> bgemm (next iter)      median gap  +1,600 ns
cuBLAS  nvjet              -> splitKreduce_kernel    median gap    -192 ns   <-- NEGATIVE
```

A **negative** median gap across 1,371 samples isn't noise — it means cuBLAS's reduce kernel **starts before its GEMM has finished**. On Hopper that's **Programmatic Dependent Launch**: the follow-on kernel's CTAs launch early, do their address setup while the producer drains, and only block at `cudaGridDependencySynchronize()` when they actually need the data.

**We serialize; they overlap.** The arithmetic closes:

```
gemm -> reduce      ours 2,336   cuBLAS  -192   we lose 2,528 ns
reduce -> next gemm ours 1,600   cuBLAS ~1,912  we gain   312 ns
                                          net   we lose ~2,216 ns
measured non-device excess (independent)        ~1,900 ns
our total gap/iter 3,936 ns  vs  the 3.62 us computed from TFLOPS
```

Two independent derivations landing within ~15% of each other. So:

- V1's **kernels already beat cuBLAS** — 67.9 µs device vs their 68.8
- our **reduce is 25% faster** than `splitKreduce`
- we lose the whole thing on **one un-overlapped kernel transition**

## What to do about it

`cudaLaunchAttributeProgrammaticStreamSerialization` on the reduce launch, `cudaTriggerProgrammaticLaunchCompletion()` at the end of the GEMM's epilogue, `cudaGridDependencySynchronize()` in the reduce before its first workspace load. That's the mechanism producing cuBLAS's −192 ns, it's a Hopper feature we already target (`sm_90a`), and it's confined to the split-K path — no change to the GEMM mainloop we just spent the day fixing.

Worth ~2.2 µs on 71.9, so roughly **+2.5 points on V1**, which would put it at or slightly past parity given we're already ahead on device time.

Two caveats before I build it: PDL only helps when the consumer has real setup work to do before touching producer data (ours does — grid-stride index math and the alignment checks), and the correctness contract is that no load may cross the sync. Both are checkable locally.

Want me to implement it? It's contained: the launcher's reduce launch, plus the two intrinsics. I'd gate it behind a default-off knob and SASS-diff the `off` path to prove nothing shipped changes, same as the rotation.

> tool `Bash`: Locate kernel, producer TMA load, and beta read
> tool `Bash`: Read the SM90 kernel entry

Kernel body opens at 3931. Let me find where the mainloop ends so the trigger lands after the wgmma work, not before it:
> tool `Bash`: Find the mainloop-to-epilogue boundary
> tool `Bash`: Read just past the mainloop close

Trigger point is line 4999 — right after `run_mainloop` and before the epilogue, exactly A9's position. Let me see the host launch block, then patch everything at once:
> tool `Bash`: Read the SM90 host launch block
> tool `Bash`: Port A7 PDL to the SM90 template

Now the two checks that matter — `PDL=false` must be byte-identical, and `PDL=true` must emit the cuBLAS instructions:
> tool `Bash`: Verify PDL off is byte-identical and on emits ACQBULK/PREEXIT

**Both checks pass.** The only difference in the `PDL=false` build is the **mangled symbol name** (one extra `Lb0E` for the new template parameter) — the instruction stream is untouched. Let me prove that rigorously rather than eyeball it:
> tool `Bash`: Strict instruction-only diff and PDL instruction placement

Placement is exactly cuBLAS's shape:

```
0x0150  ACQBULK                       <- entry wait
0x1000..0x1190  HGMMA x4, gsb0        <- mainloop
0x1390  PREEXIT                       <- trigger, AFTER the last wgmma
```

And `PDL=false` is **2,880 instructions identical** — nothing shipped changes.

But there's a piece I'd miss and it's the one that matters for V1: **the GEMM firing `PREEXIT` is only the producer half. The reduce has to opt in as the consumer**, or the gemm→reduce gap stays exactly as it is:
> tool `Bash`: Read the reduce kernel launch

The reduce launches with `<<<>>>`, which can't carry the attribute. It needs `cudaLaunchKernelEx` plus a wait before its first workspace read:
> tool `Bash`: Add PDL consumer half to the split-K reduce
> tool `Bash`: Wire USE_PDL through and register the V1 PDL arm

Everything compiles clean. **A7 PDL is ported to SM90, both halves:**

```
GEMM (producer + consumer)
  entry     prefetch_tensormap(A,B,C) then griddep_wait()   -> ACQBULK at 0x0150
  after last wgmma  griddep_launch_dependents()             -> PREEXIT  at 0x1390
  host      cudaLaunchAttributeProgrammaticStreamSerialization + blublas_NO_PDL

split-K reduce (the dependent that matters for V1)
  entry     griddep_wait() before its only read of ws
  host      converted <<<>>> -> cudaLaunchKernelEx so it can carry the attribute

PDL=false : 2,880 instructions, INSTRUCTION-IDENTICAL to pre-patch
```

Only A7 — I deliberately did **not** port A8's narrowed wait or A9's machinery, since both measured neutral on B300 ("PDL exhausted"). The one thing taken from A9 is the trigger *position*, which is free.

That's more than the ~3 points I predicted, and I want to say why before we bank it. PDL doesn't only close the 2,336 ns gemm→reduce gap — it also hides the 1,600 ns reduce→next-gemm launch latency. Total measured dead time was 3,936 ns/iteration ≈ 5.5% of 71.9 µs, which matches +6.5 over rot2.

**Two things to verify before this becomes the pin, and one caveat:**

**1 — Isolate PDL's own contribution.** That run compared against the *old* pin, so it bundles rot2 + PDL. Direct A/B:
```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas

```

**2 — The chain test, which is the real correctness gate.** `examples/test_pdl_chain.cu` already exists from B300 and it's arch-independent:
```bash
make tests TEST_SOURCES=examples/test_pdl_chain.cu 2>&1 | tail -4
GPU=0 ./build/test_pdl_chain
```
This matters because the benchmark loop is a **soft case for PDL**: every iteration writes the same `dC` from the same inputs, so the entry wait is satisfied trivially. The chain test feeds GEMM1's output into GEMM2's input, which is what BluTrain actually does layer-to-layer. `maxRelErr 0.00000` in the loop does **not** prove the contract holds there.

**The caveat I'd attach to the 104.84%:** cuBLAS's `nvjet` fires `launch_dependents` (producer half) but we don't know whether it opts in as a *consumer*. If it doesn't, we're now extracting overlap in a back-to-back loop that cuBLAS isn't — real for BluTrain's workload, but it means "104.84%" is a loop-throughput number, not a claim that our kernel is 4.8% better in isolation. On isolated device time we were 0.6% ahead; that's the honest single-shot figure.

Both checks are quick. Then I'd update the pin and document — and V1 goes from the campaign's worst shape to its first one past parity.

What it does: runs the chain once with `blublas_NO_PDL=1` to get a strictly-serialized reference, then re-execs a child with PDL live and compares **bit-exactly** over 200 chained runs. It re-execs because both launchers cache the env lookup in a function-local `static`, so the flag can't be flipped inside one process — worth knowing if you ever use that kill-switch mid-run.

## Where V1 went today

```
start                             90.4%
+ dh    descriptor hoist          91.7    +1.18   paired instrument, 21/21 reps positive
+ rot2  drain position            98.54   +7.85   ranges separated
+ PDL   launch overlap           104.79   +6.25   ranges separated, chain-gated
                                          -----
                                          +14.4
```

Plus **V8 95.51 → 96.23**, and six clean negatives across the V7/V8 family that stopped the rotation being applied where it doesn't pay.

## What actually got us there

Honestly: **three of my hypotheses were wrong and retracted** — instruction count, drain *count*, and static pre-HGMMA distance. Each refutation narrowed the search. What worked was the closed cycle budget (tensor-busy equal to 0.44% across kernels, so the gap *is* idle) → the slope/intercept fit (80.8% per-iteration) → PC sampling localising it to the commit→drain distance → a local SASS bisect showing the "ptxas kill" was **our own runtime guard**, not the compiler.

And the last piece was yours: PDL was already solved on B300 and I was about to re-derive it from scratch. Checking the other arch's log first would have saved the whole derivation — `feedback_diff_against_proven_code_first` exists for exactly that, and I'd only been applying it across modules, not across arches.

**Three process problems worth fixing**, all of which cost time today:
- `make tests` reported success after a ptxas **fatal** and produced no binary — third time its `|| true` hid a real failure
- the B300 chain gate isn't arch-portable (`.cta_group::2`), so SM90 needed its own
- both launchers cache `getenv("blublas_NO_PDL")` in a function-local static, so the kill-switch can't be flipped mid-process

**Open for whenever you want it:** V8 at 96.23 is now the worst shape and its gap is intercept-shaped; PDL hasn't been tried on any shape but V1; and six shapes (V2b, V2c, V3–V6) still carry old-box numbers that need re-measuring here.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-21 13:44 IST]

Exactly right, and it's simpler than a port — **the port happened once, in the template.** Per shape it's just which alias the pin names:

```
PIN[V1]=...128x128x64_2x1_v_sk2_dh_rot2_pdl     <- benefits, so the pin names the _pdl twin
PIN[V7]=...128x256x64_2x1_h_swz64               <- doesn't, so the pin stays as-is (PDL defaults false)
```

No code is added or removed per variant. `_PDL` defaults to `false`, so every config that exists today is already PDL-off and **instruction-identical** — I verified that (2,880 instructions, no diff). Enabling it is one template argument; the `_pdl` alias just gives it a name the pin can point at.

Plus `blublas_NO_PDL=1` as a runtime override that kills it even on a `_pdl` config — useful for A/B or if something downstream misbehaves.

**One design point worth raising before we adopt per shape, though:** PDL is a property of the **pair of consecutive launches**, not of one kernel.

- the **producer** half (`PREEXIT`) is an unconditional hint — harmless, fires for whatever comes next
- the **consumer** half (the launch attribute + `griddep_wait`) is what actually opts in

So in a benchmark loop, shape X follows itself — both halves are X's, and the measurement is clean. But in **BluTrain**, layer N is shape X and layer N+1 is shape Y. If X is PDL-on and Y is PDL-off, Y never opts in and **no overlap happens at that boundary**, regardless of what X measured in isolation.

That means a per-shape adopt/reject decided in the benchmark may not transfer to the model. Two ways to handle it, and I'd want your call once we see the sweep:

1. **Per-shape** (what the sweep measures) — safe, but leaves overlap on the table at mixed boundaries
2. **Default-on everywhere**, matching SM103, and only turn it off where a shape measurably regresses — this is what actually helps back-to-back layer GEMMs, and it's what cuBLAS does

The sweep gives us the per-shape numbers either way; it just changes whether we read a small negative as "reject" or as "acceptable cost for a real-workload win". Worth deciding with the data in front of us rather than now.

**Nothing regresses beyond the noise floor.** Five real gains, ten neutral, zero real losses. All `maxRelErr 0.00000`, all clocks HELD. Median 99.87%, worst 98.11%, five shapes at or above 100%.

## My recommendation: default-on — and the data now makes it, not the argument

I raised the per-shape-vs-default-on question before we had numbers. The sweep settles it: the only reason to reject default-on was "it might regress where there's no gap to recover," and **that regression doesn't exist above the measurement floor.** Combined with the pair-boundary problem — mixed shapes follow each other in BluTrain, so partial adoption silently loses the overlap — per-shape adoption costs real throughput and buys nothing measurable.

**But not by flipping the template default.** That would change all 400+ registered configs and lose the byte-identical property. Cleaner: **point the pins at the `_pdl` aliases.** Only the 8 pinned configs change; everything else stays untouched and provably identical.

Two caveats I want on the record before this ships:

1. **The chain test only ran on the 128×128 config.** It does generalise — the `griddep_wait()` is at kernel entry, in shared template code, identical for every tile, and an entry wait trivially dominates every later read. So the contract isn't tile-dependent. But I'd rather say that than let it be assumed.
2. **`beta != 0` is untested.** Every measurement here is `beta = 0`. The epilogue's `C_in` read is the second global read of prior-grid data, and our entry wait covers it structurally — but addmm paths have never been run with PDL on. That's a gate to add before BluTrain integration.

Want me to update the pins, document the sweep, and add a `beta != 0` case to the chain test?

Good questions — let me check the beta claim in the code rather than assume:
> tool `Bash`: Check whether beta=0 skips the C_in read
> tool `Bash`: Read the documented beta short-circuit
> tool `Bash`: Find the beta guard in the epilogue

Checked it — **you're right to ask, and the answer is no extra work.** Line 5465:

```cpp
if (beta != 0.0f && global_row < M && global_col + 1 < N) {
```

`beta != 0.0f` is **first** in a short-circuiting `&&`, so at `beta = 0` there's no `C_in` load, no multiply, no add — just a uniformly-false predicate. The code even documents it at line 5399: *"NOT a correctness bug and NOT DRAM traffic: `beta != 0.0f` is FIRST in..."*. So running at `beta = 0` was correct and cost nothing.

**But that's exactly why it's a gap for PDL.** The `C_in` read is the *second* global read of prior-grid-written data — and at `beta = 0` it never executes. So every PDL measurement today skipped the one path that could expose a missing wait. It's not that beta=0 was wrong; it's that it left one branch unexercised.

Our entry wait covers it structurally (it's before everything), so I expect it to pass. But "expect" isn't a gate, and `addmm` is a real BluTrain path.

## Per-shape vs default-on

**Default-on**, and the sweep decides it rather than the argument:

```
worst regression        -0.21   (V3)
resolution floor         0.56
=> NOTHING regresses beyond what we can measure
13/15 positive, 5 real gains, mean +0.93
```

The only reason to prefer per-shape was "it might cost where there's no gap." That cost doesn't exist above the floor. Meanwhile per-shape has a real, structural cost:

**PDL is a property of the pair, not the kernel.** BluTrain runs layer N (shape X) → layer N+1 (shape Y). If X is PDL-on and Y is PDL-off, Y never opts in as consumer and **that boundary gets zero overlap** — regardless of what either measured alone. With 15 shapes interleaving, partial adoption fragments the chain everywhere. That's why SM103 and cuBLAS are both default-on.

**How to turn it off — you have both levers, which is what makes default-on safe:**

```
compile-time   pin the non-_pdl alias        per shape, needs a rebuild
runtime        blublas_NO_PDL=1              global, no rebuild, same var as SM103
```

The env var is the real safety net for BluTrain: if anything misbehaves in the model, one variable reverts every kernel to strict serialization and you can A/B it in place.

**One implementation note:** I'd adopt by pointing the **pins** at the `_pdl` aliases, *not* by flipping the template default. Flipping the default changes all 400+ registered configs and loses the byte-identical property we've been protecting all day. Pointing the pins changes only the 8 that ship.

So the plan:
1. Add a `beta != 0` case to the SM90 chain test — the last untested PDL path
2. If it passes, point all pins at `_pdl`
3. Document the sweep

Shall I do that? And you're right that BluTrain is the real test — but I'd rather close the `beta` gate here, where a failure is a one-line diff, than find it inside a training run.

That's not urgent for benchmarking — we pin explicitly — but it *is* what BluTrain actually calls, so it's the gap between "100.02% pinned" and "100.02% in the model."

### CLAUDE [2026-08-21 14:29 IST]

**Decisive, and it settles your question about the descriptor/modulo classes on V8:**

```
ours    cycles = 32,939 + 8247.13 x k_iters    R2 = 1.0000
cuBLAS  cycles = 25,673 + 8246.52 x k_iters    R2 = 1.0000

SLOPE excess     0.61 cycles/iter  ->     5 cycles  =  0.1% of the gap
INTERCEPT excess                      7,266 cycles  = 99.9% of the gap
```

**Our mainloop is identical to cuBLAS's — the slopes match to 0.01%** (8247.13 vs 8246.52), R²=1.0000 on both, and cuBLAS stayed on the *same* kernel across all four K values, so unlike V1's sweep this fit is uncontaminated.

So: **the descriptor rebuild, the shift/mask, the modulo — all of it is worth 5 cycles out of 7,271 on V8.** They're real inefficiencies, and on this shape they are worth nothing. Chasing them here would be the mistake I nearly made twice today.

**V8's entire gap is 7,266 cycles of paid-once cost, and the intercept is 33% of its total runtime** (32,939 of 98,476 at K=512).

One number in the ledger that looks alarming but isn't:
```
sm__inst_executed_pipe_tensor.sum    ours 262,144    cuBLAS 524,288    ratio 0.5000
```
Exactly half — because our 128×256 tile derives `WGMMA_N = BN = 256`, so we issue `HGMMA.64x256x16` where cuBLAS issues `64x128x16`. Half the instructions, double the work each. Same FLOPs, not a deficit.

What *is* suggestive: our kernel is **3,098 SASS lines to cuBLAS's 1,194** — 2.6× the code, and the gap is entirely in the code that runs once.

## Where V8 stands, and what it means for the inefficiency classes you asked about

**The mainloop is finished on V8.** Slopes match cuBLAS to 0.01%, R²=1.0000, same kernel across the whole sweep. The descriptor rebuild, the shift/mask, the modulo — every one of those lives in the mainloop, and the mainloop contributes **5 cycles of a 7,271-cycle gap**. They are real inefficiencies and they are worth nothing here.

That's now true on both real gaps: V1's slope closed with `rot2`, V8's was never open. **All remaining distance on this campaign is paid-once cost.**

For V8 that's **32,939 cycles of intercept — a third of its runtime** — against cuBLAS's 25,673. And our kernel is 3,098 SASS lines to their 1,194. The census will say which once-running region holds it: TMA descriptor setup, mbarrier init, the pipeline fill before the first wgmma, or the epilogue's accumulator→smem→TMA store path.

My prior, stated before the data: **the epilogue.** V8 writes a 128×256 bf16 tile per CTA through a chunked, swizzled store buffer, and at 8 k-iterations there's nothing to amortise it against. But V1's producer spin loops were also invisible until this exact census, so I'd rather read it than guess.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-21 14:31 IST]

**V8's intercept is located, and it's the per-tile code.** The exec counts decode cleanly — `k_iters = 8`, and `65,536 / 8,192 = 8`, so:

```
exec 8,192  = once per TILE per warp   (1024 tiles x 8 warps)  -> prologue + epilogue
exec 65,536 = 8,192 x 8 k_iters                                -> mainloop
```

```
                            addrs   instrs/tile/warp   %instr   %TIME
OURS  mainloop  (65,536)      83                        43.6%   49.2%
OURS  PER-TILE  ( 8,192)     632          632           41.5%   19.5%   <- the intercept
OURS  producer spin (7,664)   36                         2.2%   24.3%   <- @!P1 941, a spin BRA

cuBLAS mainloop (50,208)      40                        31.2%   38.6%
cuBLAS PER-TILE ( 8,192)     230          230           29.3%   27.0%
```

**Our per-tile prologue+epilogue is 632 instructions to cuBLAS's 230 — 2.75×, on the exact code the slope fit says is 99.9% of the gap.** That's the intercept, and it's now localised rather than inferred.

Two targets, both new:

**1 — the per-tile path, 632 vs 230 instructions.** Top stall sites in that region are `DEPBAR 182, @P1 134, BSSY 113`. `BSSY` is divergent-branch bookkeeping — 113 samples of it in code that runs once per tile means the epilogue is branching a lot. Our kernel is 3,096 SASS addresses to cuBLAS's 1,192 overall, and this region is where the excess lives.

**2 — the producer spin loop: 24.3% of our time on 2.2% of instructions**, `@!P1` 941 samples. That is the *same signature* as V1's four producer spin loops (3.9% instrs / 23.6% time) — a `TRYWAIT` + self-branch waiting on empty barriers. V1's turned out to be a symptom of the consumer releasing late, not a cause. Here the consumer's mainloop is already at cuBLAS parity, so it may be a genuine producer-side cost this time.

I'd want to separate those two before touching either — and the honest way is the same one that worked today: partition the per-tile region into prologue vs epilogue and see which half holds it, then check whether the producer spin shrinks when the epilogue does.

Want me to build that split, or would you rather bank today's work first? We're at **mean 100.02%** with V8 the only shape below 98.1, and V8's remaining 1.9 points are now a well-defined target rather than an open question.

3. **What does cuBLAS spend its 230 per-tile instructions on**, and which of our 632 have no counterpart.

Then we have causes, and the fixes follow from which of the three it is.

`ep64` **halves** the fences. **stmatrix + swizzle deletes them** — that's how cuBLAS gets to zero MEMBAR.
> tool `Bash`: Check for existing stmatrix configs on V8's tile

Both exist and are registered — and §H27z.97 says the combination **has never been measured on any tile**. Before spending GPU time, the decisive question is local: **does stmatrix actually remove the MEMBAR?**
> tool `Bash`: Test locally whether stmatrix removes the MEMBAR

**Decisive, and it kills the bigger lever — for free, no GPU:**

```
config                  MEMBAR  BAR.SYNC  FENCE   STS   STSM  BSSY
pin  (ep32+swz64)          8       19       9     128     0     21
ep64 (+swz128)             4       11       5     128     0     70
stsm (swz64+stmatrix)      8       19       9       0    16     19
str64                      8       19       9       0    16     19
```

**stmatrix does NOT remove the MEMBAR.** It swaps 128 `STS` for 16 `STSM` and leaves the synchronisation completely unchanged — 8 MEMBAR, 19 BAR.SYNC, 9 FENCE, identical to the pin. §H27z.97's premise, *"only TOGETHER do they delete the BAR.SYNC and the MEMBAR"*, is **refuted by compilation**. That experiment doesn't need running.

**`ep64` does exactly what §H27z.98 designed: MEMBAR 8→4, BAR.SYNC 19→11, FENCE 9→5.**

But it isn't free, and this is new: **`BSSY` goes 21 → 70.** Divergent regions more than triple, and `BSSY` was 14.2% of the epilogue. So `ep64` is a genuine trade — half the fences, triple the branching — and which side wins is not predictable from here.

Region composition proves the cost is the per-chunk sync bundle (BRA 21.3 + BSSY 14.2 + FENCE 5.9 + BAR.SYNC 5.3 = 46.7%), not barrier_sync alone (5.3%) - my first two guesses were wrong and are retracted. Confirms H27z.98, which had already diagnosed the membar and built ep64s2. NEW NEGATIVE, free by compilation: stmatrix does NOT remove the MEMBAR (still 8/19/9, only STS 128 -> STSM 16), so H27z.97's delete-the-membar premise is refuted without a GPU run. ep64 halves MEMBAR 8->4, BAR.SYNC 19->11, FENCE 9->5, but takes BSSY 21->70."
```bash
git push
```

§H27z.98's prediction is on record — *"~2-3 points at K=512"* — and V8's gap is 1.9. So if the fence halving dominates the BSSY increase, this closes V8. If the branching dominates, it regresses and the epilogue's cost is structural: the fence count is set by chunk count, chunk count is capped at 64 wide by the swizzle, and we'd be at the floor of what this epilogue design can do.

Either way it's the last cheap lever on V8, and it's measured rather than guessed this time.

```bash
  SH=$sh LAY=$lay PIN=128x256x64_2x1_h_ep64swz128_rot2_pdl \
  ARMS="128x256x64_2x1_h_ep64swz128_pdl" GPU=0 bash tools/h27zo_v1_gate.sh 1

```

Prediction on record: **the rot0 twin beats the rot2 version on all six** (recovering the 0.05–0.40 that `rot2` costs there), and V8 keeps `rot2` since it's the one shape where it pays.

Both shapes that were real gaps this morning are past or near parity, and the campaign is **above 100% on average**.

The three levers that did it — `rot2`, PDL, `ep64` — were **all already half-solved in the logs**: `WGMMA_ROTATE` was built and misdiagnosed as a ptxas kill, PDL was fully implemented and gated on B300, and `ep64s2` was designed with the exact arithmetic in §H27z.98. I re-derived each one the hard way, and several of my own hypotheses got refuted in the process (instruction count, drain count, static distance, barrier_sync, bounds checks, stmatrix). That's the clearest lesson of the day: **read `analyzations_*.md` and the other arch before deriving anything.**

Two things still open when you want them: **V6 at 98.81** is now the worst shape and has never been diagnosed, and the **dispatcher is stale** — its table predates today entirely, so BluTrain wouldn't currently select any of these pins.

## What produced it

Three levers, all found by measurement rather than by trying things:

```
rot2   drain position       V1 +7.85, V8 +0.72, negative on six others -> applied selectively
PDL    launch overlap       all 15, mean +0.93, worst regression -0.21 vs a 0.56 floor
ep64   halve epilogue fences  whole 128x256 family, +0.06..+0.84, gain tracks K exactly
```

The `ep64` result is the one I'd point at as the cleanest: its gain across seven shapes collapses with K in lockstep with the membar share §H27z.98 had measured independently — 0.84 at K=512 (5.9% membar), ~0.2–0.4 at K=2048 (2.3%), ~0.1 above that. That's the mechanism confirming itself, not a fit.

- **V6 at 98.81** is now the worst shape and has never been diagnosed. Same 192×192 pin as V3/V4, which sit at 99.2/99.9 — so it's shape-specific, not tile-specific.

- The V8d `rot0` row was invalidated by the Ctrl-C killing the clock lock; nothing depends on it.

Everything is pushed and documented through §H27zzb-RESULT, retractions included.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-21 15:34 IST]

V6 is a **different disease again**, and there's a number here that hasn't appeared all day:

```
dram__bytes_read.sum   ours 272,685,824   cuBLAS 243,664,896   ratio 1.1191
```

**We read 11.9% more DRAM — 29 MB extra.** V1 and V8 were both `1.0001`. And it shows everywhere downstream:

```
long_scoreboard    ours 34.06   cuBLAS 20.08   1.70x     (waiting on memory)
mio_throttle       ours  6.81   cuBLAS 14.81   0.46x
L2 hit rate       85.68%       86.20%          same      -> we REQUEST more, not cache worse
```

And the region census says where that lands:

```
OURS    producer spin (exec 82,032)   23.8% of time    @!P1 7,584
        producer spin (exec 82,560)   12.5% of time    @!P1 3,547
                                      ----- 36.3% total
cuBLAS  producer wait (exec 104,841)   5.8% of time    @!P0 1,661
```

**Our producer spins 36.3% of the time; cuBLAS's waits 5.8%.** That's consistent with fetching 29 MB more — the producer is genuinely starved on memory, not on buffer release.

Slope fit is clean (same cuBLAS kernel all four K, R²=1.0000): **61% intercept, 39% slope** — mixed, unlike V1 or V8.

Now, one quantitative candidate worth checking before anything else. V6 is a `2x1` cluster, so **B should be multicast** — fetched once and broadcast to both CTAs. If that isn't firing, B gets fetched twice:

```
B = 5632 x 2048 x 2 = 23.1 MB      excess measured = 29.0 MB
```

Same order. Let me check whether B-multicast is actually active for this config on `nt`:
> tool `Bash`: Check whether B-multicast is active on V6

`D=0111` — `NEEDS_B_MULTICAST = 1`, so it's **configured on**. But configured isn't emitted. Let me check the SASS actually issues cluster-scope loads:
> tool `Bash`: Check whether V6 emits multicast TMA loads

Multicast is **firing** — `7 UTMALDG.4D.MULTICAST` alongside 7 plain ones (B multicast across the 2×1 cluster, A not, since `CLUSTER_N=1`). Hypothesis refuted; that's not the 29 MB.

But the capture already contains the metric that attributes over-fetch directly — the SourceCounters CSV carries **`L2 Theoretical Sectors Global Excessive`** per address, which is exactly "sectors requested beyond ideal":
> tool `Bash`: Add per-address L2 sector attribution

The L2 sector columns are **present in the header but empty** — `--section SourceCounters` doesn't populate them; they need the memory-workload section. So that route needs a new capture, and I'm not going to guess at Hopper's TMA counter names.

Here's the honest state of V6:

**Proven:**
```
61% intercept / 39% slope     (R2=1.0000, same cuBLAS kernel across all four K)
DRAM read      +11.9%         272.7 MB vs 243.7 MB -- 29 MB extra
L2 hit rate     equal         85.68 vs 86.20  -> we REQUEST more, we don't cache worse
long_scoreboard 1.70x         34.06 vs 20.08  -- waiting on memory
producer spin   36.3%         vs cuBLAS's 5.8%
tensor work     identical     7,925,760 both
```

**Refuted:** B-multicast is not the cause — the SASS emits `7 UTMALDG.4D.MULTICAST` alongside 7 plain loads, exactly as designed for a 2×1 cluster.

**Unknown:** which operand the 29 MB is, and why.

The decisive test doesn't need exotic counters — **scale M and N independently and watch how the excess moves.** A's traffic scales with the N-tile count, B's with the M-tile count:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
for s in "16384x5632x2048|baseline" "8192x5632x2048|M halved" "16384x2816x2048|N halved"; do
  IFS='|' read -r sh tag <<< "$s"; echo "===== $tag  $sh ====="
  SH=$sh LAY=nt PIN=192x192x64_2x1_h_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw_pdl GPU=0 FREQ=1200 \
    bash tools/h27zn_v1.sh 2
done
```

Phase 2 only — just the ledger, ~1 minute each. Then:

- **excess scales with M** → it's **B** being re-fetched per M-tile → an L2 residency / traversal-order problem on B
- **excess scales with N** → it's **A** being re-fetched per N-tile
- **excess stays ~29 MB flat** → it's a fixed over-fetch, most likely the residue (192 divides neither 16384 nor 5632)

That last one is worth flagging: V6 pads to 86×192 = 16,512 rows and 30×192 = 5,760 columns, so ~1–2% of the fetch is provably wasted. That's not 11.9%, but it's a floor we can't remove without changing the tile.

I'd rather run those three ledgers than keep hypothesising — I've been wrong six times today doing the latter, and this costs three minutes.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-21 15:40 IST]

**The experiment is confounded — my design error.** Look at the tensor work on the halved shapes:

```
                    ours tensor    cuBLAS tensor   ratio
baseline             7,925,760      7,925,760      1.0000
M halved             4,055,040      2,883,584      1.4062
N halved             3,962,880      2,883,584      1.3743
```

Ours halves correctly (3,962,880 = exactly half). **cuBLAS drops to 0.364× when the FLOPs drop to 0.5× — it switched to a kernel with a different wgmma shape.** Cross-comparison on those two rows is invalid, and it's my fault: phase 2 doesn't print the cuBLAS kernel name the way the slope tool does.

**But our own scaling is valid, and it says something real:**

```
                  our DRAM     vs baseline    our L2 hit    cuBLAS L2 hit
baseline          271.1 MB        1.000         85.30%         85.17%
M halved          131.1 MB        0.484         86.36%         84.81%
N halved          177.4 MB        0.654         81.41%         89.56%
```

**Halving M cuts our DRAM by 52%. Halving N cuts it by only 35% — and our L2 hit rate *drops* to 81.41% while cuBLAS's *rises* to 89.56%.** Our memory behaviour is N-sensitive and degrades as N shrinks; theirs improves.

And that lines up across the three shapes sharing this exact pin:

```
V4   N=50304   99.94
V3   N=11264   99.23
V6   N= 5632   98.81   <- smallest N, worst score
```

**Score tracks N.** Same tile, same cluster, same pin, same K — only N differs, and it orders them exactly.

That points at traversal order / L2 locality, which is the `RASTER_SWIZZLE` knob. §H27zi closed that knob with *"rs8 IS the optimum at K=2048, and there is a LAW"* — but the supergroup law is stated as a function of **K only**, and it was measured on **V3**. If the optimum also depends on N, V6 at half V3's N may want a different group.
> tool `Bash`: Check for existing rs variants and re-read the supergroup law

The law is stated precisely, and it's **N-independent**:

```
group x panel ~= 6.3 MB      panel = BM x K x 2  (a tile-row of one operand)
K= 2048   panel 0.79 MB   ->  group  8
K=16384   panel 6.29 MB   ->  group  1
```

V6 is K=2048 → group 8 → `rs8`, which is exactly what its pin uses. **By the law, our raster swizzle is already correct.**

But the law was derived on **V5, V3 and V4** — and it has no N term, while the thing I just measured is that our L2 degrades specifically as **N** shrinks (81.41% at N=2816 vs 85.30% at N=5632, while cuBLAS goes the other way). V6 has the smallest N of the three shapes sharing this pin, and it's the worst of the three.

So this isn't "let me try raster again" — it's **testing a stated law on a shape outside the set it was derived from**. That's cheap and legitimate: all five configs already exist and are registered, so it needs **no build**.

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
SH=16384x5632x2048 LAY=nt PIN=192x192x64_2x1_h_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw \
ARMS="192x192x64_2x1_h_rs1_dh_ubd_skew_lsw 192x192x64_2x1_h_rs2_dh_ubd_skew_lsw 192x192x64_2x1_h_rs4_dh_ubd_skew_lsw 192x192x64_2x1_h_rs16_dh_ubd_skew_lsw" \
GPU=0 bash tools/h27zo_v1_gate.sh 1
```

Run without PDL on both sides so `rs` is the only variable — PDL measured +0.05 on V6, well inside the floor, so it isn't hiding anything.

**Two outcomes, both useful:**
- **rs8 wins** → the law holds at small N, the knob really is closed, and V6's 29 MB is something else. I'd then go after the `long_scoreboard 1.70x` directly rather than the traversal order.
- **another rs wins** → the law needs an N term, and that would matter beyond V6, since it's the rule the whole 192×192 family is pinned on.

I'll also say plainly: my M/N scaling experiment was **confounded** — cuBLAS switched kernels on both halved shapes and phase 2 doesn't print its kernel name. I should add that to the ledger the way the slope tool has it, so the next person doesn't read those two rows as a valid comparison.

And that has a direct DRAM consequence:

```
cluster 2x1 (ours)  -> clusters M -> B is multicast   B = 5632 x 2048 x 2 =  23.1 MB
cluster 1x2         -> clusters N -> A is multicast   A = 16384 x 2048 x 2 = 67.1 MB
```

**We are multicasting the small operand. A is 2.9x bigger than B.** Multicast halves the fetch of whichever operand it covers — so clustering the other axis should save roughly 2.9× more traffic. import csv,sys,re
```bash
for f in sys.argv[1:]:
    rows=list(csv.reader(open(f))); hdr=rows[1]; body=rows[2:]
    iS,iI=hdr.index("Source"),hdr.index("Instructions Executed")
    ni=[i for i,h in enumerate(hdr) if h.endswith("(Not Issued)")]
    def ex(x):

    def sm(x): return sum(int(x[i].replace(",","")) for i in ni if x[i].replace(",","").isdigit())

        s=x[iS].strip()
        if re.search(r'UTMALDG|UTMASTG|LDGSTS|\bLDG\b|\bSTG\b',s):
            tot+=ex(x)

PY
```

That prints every TMA load and store in both kernels with how many times each ran. Three things it settles at once, none of which I can guess:

### CLAUDE [2026-08-21 16:09 IST]

Now it's clear, and it **corrects something I said earlier.**

```
                            OURS                    cuBLAS
TMA loads, plain          82,560                  82,560
TMA loads, MULTICAST      82,560                  82,560
                         -------                 -------
TOTAL LOADS              165,120                 165,120     IDENTICAL

loads per tile-iteration       2                       2     (A + B)
bytes per load        192x64x2 = 24,576       same tile, same box
TMA stores                15,480                 247,680     16x more, on THEIR side
```

**Our load path is structurally identical to cuBLAS's** — same instruction count, same 50/50 multicast split, same box size. We are **not** issuing more fetches or bigger fetches. So the 29 MB cannot be the load path.

Which means it has to be **L2 reuse — the order tiles are visited.**

And that forces me to retract something: I claimed *"L2 hit rate is equal, so we request more rather than cache worse."* **That was wrong.** `lts__t_sector_hit_rate` counts **all** sectors including writes, and our store instruction counts differ from cuBLAS's by **16×** (15,480 vs 247,680 — they store in many small pieces, we store in few large ones). That store traffic dilutes the metric, so "equal hit rate" tells us nothing about the read hit rate. My whole "we request more, not cache worse" line was built on a confounded number.

So the chain is now:

```
loads identical            -> not fetching more
stores don't affect reads  -> not the epilogue
=> the 29 MB is READ REUSE, i.e. traversal order
```

That's the raster direction — `h` walks N-fastest, `v` walks M-fastest, changing which operand is reused between consecutive tiles. cuBLAS uses `2x1_v`; we use `2x1_h`. We swept the supergroup **size** (rs1…rs16, all null) but never the **direction**.

I proposed that run before as a guess and you were right to push back. It now has a proof behind it: the loads are provably identical, so ordering is the only variable left that can move read traffic.

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
SH=16384x5632x2048 LAY=nt PIN=192x192x64_2x1_h_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw \
ARMS="192x192x64_2x1_v_rs8_dh_ubd_skew_lsw" \
GPU=0 bash tools/h27zo_v1_gate.sh 1 2
```

Config exists, no build. **Phase 2 is the test, not phase 1:** `dram__bytes_read` must fall from 272.6 MB toward cuBLAS's 243.7. If it doesn't move, traversal order is eliminated too and the only thing left is a read-specific L2 capture to find where the misses actually are.

**Confirmed, on V6, from their own SASS:**

```

MEMBAR      static  1, exec  20,640    static  0, exec       0    <- ZERO

```

**cuBLAS executes 12× more fences and 15× more barriers than us — and wins.** Because each of theirs is a *bare* `FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S` costing ~nothing, while ours drags a `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA` behind it.

So the answer to your question is: **we are not doing the same thing, and we can't.** Not because we chose badly — because we're already at the *minimum* of the only curve available to us:

```
our curve (measured, §H27zdp):   1 MEMBAR -> 98.56   3 -> 96.37   6 -> 94.54   9 -> 91.94
we are at 1. That is the floor.  Chunking finer (which is how you get depth 4) moves us RIGHT.
cuBLAS is at 12 chunks with 0 MEMBARs -- not on our curve at all.
```

They chunk **fine** because it's free for them. We chunk **coarse** because each chunk costs us 0.83 points. Same destination, different price per step. Depth 4 isn't refusing us — we can't afford the tickets.

And STSM is not the difference: I compiled it, we still emit 8 MEMBARs with STSM. **The MEMBAR comes from the PTX fence intrinsic, not the store instruction.** That's now verified from both sides.

**So there is exactly one blocker, and it's named:** PTX has no bare async-proxy fence. Every writable spelling emits `MEMBAR`; §H27zdo enumerated 11.

**And exactly one route around it, which your instinct pointed at:** don't stage C through shared memory. No smem staging → no generic-to-async proxy hazard → **no fence at all**, and no store buffer competing for the stages. We just proved that path works — the split-K epilogue runs it today:

```
V1 under SPLIT_K=2:   UTMASTG 0    STS 0    STSM 0    STG 102
```

Zero TMA stores, zero shared stores. It writes straight to global. That's the existence proof, and freeing its dead buffer just bought V1 a 7th stage.

Extending it to `SPLIT_K=1` gives V6 **depth 4 and zero MEMBARs simultaneously** — both blockers, one change, using validated code. Now we can name it exactly, because the per-chunk cost isn't one instruction — it's a **bundle**, and only part of it is the MEMBAR:

```
our per-chunk cost (measured on V8's epilogue, §H27zzb):
   BRA  21.3%  +  BSSY 14.2%  +  FENCE 5.9%  +  BAR.SYNC 5.3%   =  46.7%
   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ branch reconvergence -- 35.5%, the LARGEST part
```

And look at how cuBLAS's epilogue is built versus ours:

```
             static UTMASTG   static STSM   chunks   shape of the code
cuBLAS            12              18          12     FULLY UNROLLED, straight-line
ours               3               0           1     a LOOP, with BSSY/BRA reconvergence
```

**cuBLAS has one static store instruction per chunk — twelve chunks, twelve stores, no loop.** Ours is a rolled loop with divergent regions. So their marginal cost per chunk is a barrier plus a bare fence. Ours is a barrier, a MEMBAR, a fence, **and** a branch-reconvergence pair.

So there are **two** reasons we can't chunk like them, not one:

1. **The MEMBAR** — ptxas lowers `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta` to `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S`. cuBLAS does `BAR.SYNC` first (32 per tile — 15× more than us), which already makes the writes CTA-visible, then emits a *bare* fence. Same semantics, and **our MEMBAR is very likely redundant after our own BAR.SYNC** — ptxas just can't prove it and emits it anyway. That's a compiler conservatism, and it's the part we're genuinely blocked on.

2. **The rolled, branchy chunk loop** — that's **ours**, not the compiler's, and it's the *bigger* share of the bundle (35.5% vs the fence's 5.9%). cuBLAS pays zero for it because their epilogue is straight-line.

Point 2 has never been tried and isn't blocked by anything. If unrolling the chunk loop removes the `BSSY`/`BRA` cost, the per-chunk price drops toward cuBLAS's, and fine chunking — and therefore **depth 4** — becomes affordable even while we still pay the MEMBAR.

That reframes the 0.83-points-per-chunk law: it was measured on our *current* branchy loop, so it's a property of our implementation, not a law of nature. I'd been treating it as a hard constraint.

Both are worth doing, and I can point at the exact cause of the branching. Let me check the chunk loop:

**Found the exact line.** 5314:

```cpp
const int my_c_nchunks = (g == 0) ? WGrid::C_NCHUNK0 : WGrid::C_NCHUNK1;   // RUNTIME, line 5235
...
if (Config::USE_CHUNKED_EPILOGUE && epi_ch >= my_c_nchunks) continue;      // line 5314
```

The chunk loop runs to the **compile-time max** and then **runtime-skips** the extra iterations with a `continue` on a runtime predicate. **That `continue` is the `BSSY`/`BRA` — one divergent region per chunk.** cuBLAS has none because their chunk count is a constant and their epilogue is straight-line.

And for V6's tile it's pure waste: 192×192 is an N-split with `NCHUNKS = 192/96 = 2`, so `C_NCHUNK0 = C_NCHUNK1 = 1`. **Both arms of that ternary give the same value** — the branch can never diverge, but it's written as a runtime ternary on `g`, so the compiler emits the test anyway.

So the fix is small and safe:

```cpp
constexpr bool SYM = (WGrid::C_NCHUNK0 == WGrid::C_NCHUNK1);
const int my_c_nchunks = SYM ? WGrid::C_NCHUNK0                       // compile-time
                             : ((g == 0) ? WGrid::C_NCHUNK0 : WGrid::C_NCHUNK1);
```

With `SYM` true the bound folds to a constant, `epi_ch >= my_c_nchunks` folds away, the loop unrolls, and the `BSSY`/`BRA` go — the 35.5% share, which is **six times** the fence's 5.9%. That's the larger half of the per-chunk cost and it isn't blocked by ptxas at all.

I did not fix it. It went 98.81 → 98.88, inside its own 0.31 floor. What I *did* do is close out every hypothesis with a measurement:


V6's remaining 1.1 points is the **MEMBAR**, and that one is genuinely blocked: `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta` always lowers to `MEMBAR.ALL.CTA + FENCE.VIEW.ASYNC.S`, 11 spellings enumerated, and stmatrix doesn't change it. cuBLAS emits 12 bare fences and zero MEMBARs because nvjet bypasses PTX — **verified on V6's own SASS today**, not taken from a note.

The one route around it is the **bufferless epilogue**: no smem staging → no proxy fence *and* no store buffer → depth 4 and zero MEMBARs together. The split-K path already runs exactly that (`UTMASTG 0, STS 0, STG 102`), which is both the existence proof and where today's free V1 stage came from.

|---|---|---|---|---|

What differs on V6 is the other two axes: cuBLAS runs it at **depth 4** where the other three get depth 3 (V6 is the only one), and its cluster is `2x1_v`, which maps to our `1x2_h` — not the `2x1_h` we pin.

The difference is stark. cuBLAS's hot branches are preceded by **address math**, not by a barrier poll — there is no `TRYWAIT` spin in their top sites at all. And the ledger says cuBLAS has `barrier SLEEP` 4.02% where we have 0.00%. Let me identify the exact wait instruction each side uses:

cuBLAS's mbarrier wait loop **backs off with `NANOSLEEP`**. Ours re-polls immediately — a tight spin with no backoff, which is why the samples pile onto the `@!P0 BRA` back-edge (27.9% across four sites) instead of onto a sleep instruction. **Now we have concrete differences.** This is the answer to "what are we doing differently":

| | ours | cuBLAS | diff |
|---|---|---|---|
| IMAD | 376 | 18 | **+358** |
| STS | 144 | 3 | +141 (they use `STSM` 18) |
| SHF | 119 | 10 | +109 |
| ISETP | 127 | 29 | +98 |
| ULOP3 | 85 | 6 | +79 |
| **FMUL** | **288** | **0** | **+288** |
| **LDG** | **72** | **1** | **+71** |
| F2FP | 144 | 72 | +72 |
| PRMT / LEA / PLOP3 / ULEA | 274 | 8 | +266 |

Two of these are not "address math is hard" — they're **things that should not be there at all**:

- **FMUL 288, cuBLAS has literally zero.** That's `alpha * acc` as a separate multiply.
- **LDG 72 in an epilogue running beta=0.** Global *loads* to read C when C isn't being read.

cuBLAS has 0 and 1 because it **specializes on alpha==1 / beta==0**. Ours are runtime values, so the compiler must emit the read-C path and the multiply on every call — plus all the address math feeding those 72 loads. Let me confirm that's what our code does:
> tool `Bash`: Inspect alpha/beta handling in the epilogue

Line 5593 has a **runtime** `if (beta == 0.0f)` split — so both arms are compiled in, which is why `LDG 72` exists statically. My memory note says those LDGs are 0.00% of samples, i.e. never executed at beta=0. So LDG is code size, not time.

But **FMUL 288 is different — it executes.** `acc * alpha` runs on every element regardless, and cuBLAS emits *zero*, meaning they specialize `alpha==1` at compile time. Phase 2 measured `FMUL` at **+0.27** in cuBLAS-time units — against a **0.09 floor** and a **1.07 gap**, that's 3× resolvable and a quarter of the gap.

And this sharpens §H27zdt's rule usefully: samples on a *spin branch* are waiting and free; samples on `FMUL`/`IMAD`/`ULEA` are issue slots actually consumed. Let me check what the harness passes:

OFF path byte-identical. Now the ON path — does it actually reach cuBLAS's counts:

No effect — identical counts. So the pin doesn't compile through the path I patched. There must be more than one epilogue variant. Let me find every place alpha is applied:

There's a second site at 5674 — the plain-`STS` path, which is what the pin actually uses (STS 144, STSM 0). Let me see it:

**That's a major structural win.** The specialization does exactly what cuBLAS does:

| | ours off | ours **on** | cuBLAS |
|---|---|---|---|
| FMUL | 288 | **0** | 0 |
| LDG | 72 | **0** | 1 |
| PRMT | 72 | **0** | 1 |
| **F2FP** | 144 | **72** | **72** |
| ISETP | 128 | 44 | 29 |
| **total** | **2824** | **1696** | **1265** |

Total instructions **2824 → 1696, a 40% cut** — our size ratio to cuBLAS goes from 2.2× to 1.34×, and `F2FP` now matches them *exactly*. The beta arm was carrying a duplicate set of conversions. Unlike BRA and WARPGROUP, these are epilogue **work** instructions that genuinely execute. Registering and gating it:
> tool `Bash`: Register a1b0 and build its gate with a null control

Gate works but the header is stale from the sed. Let me fix it and verify the arg wiring:
> tool `Bash`: Fix the gate header and verify wiring

Wiring is correct. This is the concrete "what are we doing differently" answer, acted on:

**We multiply by alpha when alpha is 1, and we compile a read-C path when beta is 0. cuBLAS does neither** — it builds a separate kernel for the unit-alpha case. That's why `FMUL` is 288 vs their 0, and why `F2FP` is 144 vs their 72 (the dead beta arm carries a duplicate conversion set).

Specializing it locally, verified before any GPU time:

```
A1B0=false   FMUL 288  LDG 72  PRMT 72  ISETP 128  F2FP 144  total 2824
A1B0=true    FMUL   0  LDG  0  PRMT  0  ISETP  44  F2FP  72  total 1696
cuBLAS       FMUL   0  LDG  1  PRMT  1  ISETP  29  F2FP  72  total 1265
```

**40% fewer instructions**, `F2FP` exactly matching cuBLAS, size ratio to them 2.23× → 1.34×. `EPI_A1B0=false` re-verified byte-identical at 2808, so nothing shipping moved.

Worth noting how the second site was found: patching only the stmatrix arm changed *nothing*, which is what exposed that the pin compiles a different plain-`STS` path. If I'd trusted the first edit I'd have shipped a no-op.

And why this one may convert where BRA didn't: §H27zdt's rule is that sample share isn't cost **for waiting instructions** — a spinning producer accrues samples while idle. `FMUL`/`F2FP`/`PRMT` are epilogue work; a warp executing them is consuming an issue slot. Build failed, and the local check that passed was inadequate — **my `reg.cu` only includes the header, which doesn't instantiate the kernels.** The real instantiation happens in `Bgemm_sm90_{nn,nt,tn}_variants.cu`. That's the same trap that caught `ep128swz128`, and I walked into it again.

`ea64s1` (`EPI_TILE_N=64`) is structurally invalid on 192x192: `C_BOX_N` must divide each warpgroup's N width, and NN uses an asymmetric N-split. Let me build a probe that actually instantiates, and find which values are legal:

All fail including 192, so the probe itself is broken. Let me see the actual error:

My macro names collide with the layout enum — `-DTN=96` rewrites `Sm90Layout::TN` in the header. Renaming them:

Now I have the truth: **`EPI_TILE_N=96` is legal on all three layouts; 64 and 192 are not.** Removing `ea64s1`:

All four configs now instantiate cleanly on NN/NT/TN. Two mistakes were mine and both are worth naming:

**My local check didn't actually instantiate anything.** `reg.cu` just `#include`s the header — templates aren't instantiated until something calls them, which happens in `Bgemm_sm90_{nn,nt,tn}_variants.cu`. The check above is the correct one: explicitly instantiate `launch_bgemm_sm90<Config, layout>` for each config × each layout.

**My first fixed probe was silently sabotaged** — `-DTN=96` rewrote `Sm90Layout::TN` in the header, so *every* value including 192 reported FAIL. Had I trusted that, I'd have concluded atom-staging was impossible. Renamed the macros; legal `EPI_TILE_N` on 192x192 is **32 and 96 only**.

`ea64s1` is gone (it needed `C_BOX_N` to divide each warpgroup's N width, and NN uses an asymmetric split). `ea96s1` survives and is the one that matters — depth 4 at 2 chunks.

If all three agree, the measurement is sound and the gap is real; if `swap` or `preheat` moves `%cuB` by more than 0.5, then no `%cuB` measured under the default order is trustworthy at free/high clocks — which would retroactively affect a lot of numbers.

Frequencies are **queried from the card**, not assumed: `free` plus 1200/1300/1400/**1474**/1500/1600/1700/1755 plus up to four more the card reports above those. Clock is sampled *during* each run at 100 ms, and any row whose sustained clock falls below the request is tagged `CAP-OVERRODE` — not a datum, since §H27zt put the 700 W cap edge between 1400 and 1474 on this H200.

Phase 2 then runs nsys at `free` and `1200` on V1/V3/V6/V8 to confirm cuBLAS and we issue the *same* kernels at both — so a clock difference can't be confused with a different kernel being selected.

Two things I'd flag before you go. The matrix uses `tools/pins.sh` as-is, which is the validated best-known set — it does **not** include today's `dw` (+0.26 on V6), since `dw` has only been measured on V6 and sweeping it across all 15 is a separate run. And the V6 warp-local fix (`maxRelErr 28473` → slot-recycling drain) is still unrun; that gate is independent and can go whenever.

Answering each:

**STORE_BUF** — I left a dash out of laziness, and it was misleading. cuBLAS is *not* zero and does *not* skip the store buffer: 0x400 per warp × 8 warps × 2 slots = **16,384 B, exactly what warp-local computes.** We matched them there.

**slot/warp** — `0x400` *is* 1024. Same number written in two bases. My presentation error, not a difference.

**BAR.SYNC** — cuBLAS has **2**, not 0. The "0" was a different claim: zero barriers *between an STSM and the UTMASTG that consumes it*. So warp-local at 3 is **one** barrier away from them, not three.

**Tensor work** — identical, and I never claimed otherwise: dynamic `inst_executed_pipe_tensor` is **7,925,760 on both sides, ratio exactly 1.0000**. Static HGMMA 48 vs 24 is unrolling, not work.

**STS vs STSM — you're right and this is a real gap.** They write smem with **18 stmatrix**; warp-local uses **72 plain STS** for the same bytes. Four instructions where one would do. I wrote plain stores when I built it, which was the lazy choice.

**1928 vs 1265** — real, 663 extra instructions, and STS→STSM is only ~50 of them. The rest needs decomposing.

No — I mis-stated that. Let me quote the actual measurement:
> tool `Bash`: Read the actual STSM vs STS measurement

No — I got that wrong. The actual measurement, §H27z.76:

> *probe_stsm_banks.cu measured STSM on a LINEAR layout at 192 conflicts / 3.217 ms against STS's 192 and 3.230 ms*

So on a linear buffer they're a **tie** — STSM is marginally *faster*, 3.217 vs 3.230, same 192 conflicts. STSM is never worse. The correct statement is that **stmatrix alone buys nothing**; it needs the swizzle, and only then is it worth 1.93×. My "slower than STS" was wrong and I should have quoted the number instead of paraphrasing.

One caveat that stops 1.93× being as big as it sounds: that's 1.93× *on the store path*, and the store path is ~1.4% of the kernel. So the honest expectation is a small net gain, not a large one.

But re-reading that section turned up something that matters more — **a conflict with my own geometry:**

> *cuBLAS stages 8 rows per warp (§H27z.73, decoded from its SASS — warp stride 0x400 = 8 rows × 128 B)*

§H27z.73 decoded their 1024 B slot as **8 rows × 128 B**. I built warp-local as **16 rows × 32 cols**. Both are 1024 B, so both "match" the slot size I put in the table — but they're different *shapes*, and I never noticed because I only checked the byte count.

That likely matters for exactly the reason we're discussing: 128 B rows line up with the swizzle and bank granularity, while my 64 B rows put two rows per 128 B bank row — which is how you get conflicts, and conflicts are precisely what makes stmatrix worthless. So cuBLAS may use 8×128 *because* it's the shape that makes STSM pay.

My 16×32 is still self-consistent (I write it and describe it the same way), so correctness shouldn't depend on this. But if the shape is wrong, STSM on top of it will underdeliver the same way the linear probe did.

Two things to settle, and the first is free: re-derive their box shape from the SASS I already have — the two `STSM` in their burst were at row bases `R23` and `R168`, and whether that offset is +8 rows or +32 columns decides it. Then confirm warp-local is correct on GPU 3 before changing geometry underneath it.

Want me to re-decode the box shape now, or get the correctness run in first?

```cpp
if (lane == 0) tma_store_wait<0>();   // only lane 0 waits
```

Lane 0 drains, the other 31 don't wait for it, so they start overwriting the warp's slot while its stores are still in flight. ### CLAUDE [2026-08-22 12:17 IST]

You're right — I found it by reading the code, and it's my bug:

```cpp
for (aa) for (nc) for (cb) {
    slot = base + (cb & 1) * SLOT;                    // ping-pong keyed on cb
    if (cb >= EPI_WL_STAGES) { wait; }                // recycle guard keyed on cb
```

**`cb` resets to 0 on every new atom.** Trace it: `aa=0,cb=2` writes slot 0 and issues its store. Then `aa=1,cb=0` computes slot 0 again — and the guard `cb >= 2` is false, so **it doesn't wait** and overwrites bytes the copy engine is still reading. With 3 atoms × 3 column-boxes there are 3 unguarded reuses per tile, and the damage accumulates with tile count. That's exactly the observed shape: 1 tile survives, error grows with tiles.

The ping-pong needs a running sequence across the whole nest, not a per-atom index:
> tool `Bash`: Fix the slot ping-pong to use a running sequence counter

The bug was mine and I should have found it by reading rather than by five rounds of probing. `slot = base + (cb & 1) * SLOT` with the recycle guard also keyed on `cb` — and `cb` restarts at 0 for every atom. So `aa=1,cb=0` reuses the slot `aa=0,cb=2` is still storing from, with the guard reading false. Three unguarded reuses per tile, which is precisely why one tile survived and the error scaled with tile count.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-22 12:52 IST]

Clean, unambiguous, and negative: **warp-local is −2.59.** Ranges fully separated (99.10–99.20 vs 96.50–96.70), null control 0.00, `maxRelErr 0.00000`. Depth 4 is present and correct, and it costs us.

The interesting part is what that rules out. Warp-local runs **1936 instructions vs the pin's 2832** — *fewer* — and has the extra stage, and is still slower. So the loss isn't instruction count (already closed three ways) and isn't depth. It's the store structure itself:

| | pin | warp-local | cuBLAS |
|---|---|---|---|
| TMA stores per tile | 3 | **72** (8 warps × 3 atoms × 3 boxes) | — |
| bytes per store | 12,288 | 1,024 | 1,024 |
| STS / STSM | 144 / 0 | **72 / 0** | 3 / **18** |
| BAR.SYNC | 4 | 4 | 2 |

We went from 3 large TMA commands to 72 small ones. cuBLAS uses the same 1024 B granularity and doesn't pay for it — but they feed it with **18 stmatrix**, not 72 plain stores, and with half our barriers.

Also worth correcting an expectation I set: depth being worth 17.65/stage **downward** doesn't mean 3→4 returns anything like that. Removing a stage starves the pipeline; adding one to an already-fed pipeline is diminishing returns. I should have said the slope is asymmetric rather than implying depth 4 was worth ~17.

So there's one identified lever left — STSM plus the swizzle it requires, which is the actual cuBLAS shape. Honest estimate: stmatrix measured 1.93× **on the store path**, and that path is a small share of the kernel, so it plausibly recovers the 2.59 but I would not bet on it clearing it by much.

Given that, your call on where the day goes:

**(a)** One more focused pass on warp-local — STSM + swizzle + drop the two extra barriers, which is genuinely "like cuBLAS" and the last untried thing in the epilogue.

**(b)** Park warp-local at correct-but-slower (it's committed, default-off, gated, harmless), keep V6 at the **99.19** the `dw` pin gives, and move to the clock-frequency matrix → dispatcher → BluTrain as you planned this morning.

**V6 right now, both measured today on GPU 3, locked 1200, 400 ms, 7 reps, null control 0.00:**

| | depth | %cuB | range | maxRelErr |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **stage 3** — `dw` pin (shipping) | 3 | **99.19** | 99.10–99.20 | 0.00000 |
| **stage 4** — warp-local | 4 | **96.60** | 96.50–96.70 | 0.00000 |

**Stage 3 is ahead by 2.59, and that's our shipping config.** cuBLAS runs this shape at stage 4 (`192x192_64x4`), so we're still not matching them structurally — we're just faster our way than their way, as we've implemented it.

Every route to stage 4 we've tried, all as deltas against the stage-3 pin:

| route to depth 4 | delta | why it cost |
|---|---|---|
| `ep16s2` — chunking ×12 | −21.0 | 12 chunk handoffs |
| `dstg` — bufferless STG | −17.06 | loses TMA + stmatrix |
| `ea32s3` — chunking ×6 | −6.24 | 6 chunk handoffs |
| `ea96s1` — chunking ×2 | −3.11 | 2 chunk handoffs |
| **warp-local** | **−2.59** | 72 small TMA stores fed by plain STS |

So warp-local is the **best stage-4 route so far** — it beats the next best by 0.5 and it's the only one that gives nothing up (keeps TMA, keeps the full buffer, no chunking). It's just not yet better than stage 3.

One caveat on comparing those rows: the first four were measured on earlier boxes against the same stage-3 pin, so the deltas are comparable but not the absolute numbers.

What it costs and what's left: warp-local uses **72 plain STS** where cuBLAS uses **18 stmatrix**, and **4 BAR.SYNC** where they use 2. That's the whole remaining difference in the store path — instruction count isn't it (warp-local is 1936 vs the pin's 2832 and still slower).

**Every lane shows exactly ±64 bytes** — the two `STSM` sit side by side in a 128-byte row. So:

Deliberately two steps, not one. Last time I went straight to timing on a kernel that turned out to be wrong and we burned half a day. The swizzle changes *where every byte lands in shared memory* and changes the TMA descriptor to match — if those two disagree by even one granule, output is silently wrong. `wl_validate` covers 42 cases including residues, batch, all three layouts and the real shape ×3, so a mismatch shows immediately rather than after a timing run.

What this step is and isn't: it's the **prerequisite**, not the payoff. Swizzling alone just removes bank conflicts from the 72 plain STS — worth something, possibly little. The payoff is stmatrix on top, which is only legal once the layout is swizzled, and which replaces 72 STS with ~18 STSM. I'm doing them separately so that if something breaks we know which one did it.

One thing I want to be careful about and will check in the SASS after correctness passes: I derived SW64 from our 32-column box, while cuBLAS uses 128 B rows by packing two logical rows per smem row. Those aren't the same layout — mine is the simpler one our existing machinery already validates. If the swizzle passes correctness but buys nothing, that packing difference is the next thing to look at rather than assuming stmatrix will rescue it.

One honest caution before I build it. The accumulator fragment doesn't hand a lane 8 consecutive columns; `wgmma_frag_rowcol` gives each lane 2 rows spread across many columns, while `stmatrix.m8n8.x4` wants each lane to supply one row of an 8×8 matrix. The existing validated block solves that with a specific `rg[4]` packing plus `stsm_lane_off[]`, and adapting it to the warp-local box is intricate register-mapping work — the kind where a subtle error costs hours, exactly what you warned about. Read together those two describe **different bottlenecks, not different amounts of the same one**. `mio_throttle` is the memory pipe refusing more work; `long_scoreboard` is waiting for loads to come back. cuBLAS is **saturating** the memory pipe — throttled 14.77% — while we're **starving** on it, waiting 31.99%. That's an exploitable asymmetry rather than just a deficit. We have ~9 points of memory-pipe headroom they don't, which means room to keep more loads in flight — and it's consistent with the depth result: depth 3→2 cost 17.65 because the pipe starved, and we're still on the starved side of that curve even at depth 4.

The `nan`s persist, so those six metrics aren't being collected at all — my prefix fix addressed the wrong cause. I'll stop burning runs on the plumbing; the stall data is intact and it's the part that matters.

These are **different bottlenecks, not different amounts of one.** cuBLAS is *bandwidth*-bound — throttled 14.76% because the memory pipe won't take more. We're *latency*-bound — waiting 31.97% for loads to return, with 9 points of pipe headroom they don't have.

That's the asymmetry you asked about, and it's genuinely in our favour. It also explains the depth slope: 3→2 cost 17.65 because the pipe starved, and even at depth 4 we're still on the starved side of that curve.

But I checked the obvious exploit and it's closed: depth 5 needs 5 × 49,152 = 245,760 B of stage buffer against a 231,424 B budget — **impossible for 192×192 at BK=64 regardless of how small we make the store buffer.** So "just prefetch deeper" isn't available on this tile.

Also worth noting the swizzle+stmatrix did move the load side slightly: `long_scoreboard` 33.53 → 31.97 and `mio_throttle` 7.57 → 5.70 versus the stage-3 pin.

3. **Did ncu complain?** Its log would say if a metric was rejected — I've been discarding that output.

One of those three will name it. The distinction matters because it's the difference between "I asked wrongly" and "this GPU/driver won't give it".

And the metric I most want back is `l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu_mem_shared` — the swizzle gained +2.06 and I've been explaining that as "removed bank conflicts" without ever measuring conflicts on our kernel.
