### CLAUDE [2026-08-22 15:27 IST]

**Found it, and it's a nasty one.** Look at which metrics survived: `smsp__issue_active` and all the `smsp__warp_issue_stalled_*` — every one late in the alphabet. The five that vanished (`l1tex__`, `sm__cycles`, `sm__pipe_tensor`, `sm__inst_executed`, `smsp__inst_executed`) are all *earlier*.

The cause is my availability filter:

```bash
set -uo pipefail
... printf '%s\n' "$AV" | grep -qx "$b" && M="${M:+$M,}$m"
```

`grep -q` **exits the instant it finds a match**, which sends SIGPIPE to `printf`. With `pipefail`, that makes the whole pipeline's status non-zero, so the `&&` never fires and the metric is silently dropped. A match early in the list kills `printf` sooner and reliably fails; a match near the end lets `printf` finish first and succeeds. **The metric was being dropped precisely because it existed.**
> tool `Bash`: Reproduce the SIGPIPE bug and fix the metric filter

My repro didn't reproduce it — both were KEPT. With a 2-line input `printf` finishes before `grep` exits, so no SIGPIPE. My theory needs testing at realistic size before I claim it:
> tool `Bash`: Test the SIGPIPE theory at realistic input size

**Reproduced with proof** — at realistic size (20,002 lines):

```
l1tex__...  (early match)  DROPPED (pipeline status 141 = SIGPIPE)
smsp__warp_issue_stalled_barrier  (late match)  KEPT
```

Exactly the observed pattern. `grep -q` exits on first match → `printf` gets SIGPIPE → `pipefail` turns that into failure → `&&` never fires. **The metric is discarded precisely because it was found**, and only when the match is early enough that `printf` is still writing.

It's also **a race**, which is why `h27zzk` reported cycles and tensor counts fine using the identical pattern — it won the race there. So any run using this idiom could have silently dropped metrics without warning. Let me fix it everywhere it appears:
> tool `Bash`: Fix the racy metric filter in every tool that uses it

7 fixed, but 17 scripts have the pattern — the rest use slightly different quoting. Let me catch them with a regex:
> tool `Bash`: Catch remaining variants of the racy pattern

Pattern eliminated across 13 scripts, all parse.

```
# local (you)
cd /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/BLUBLAS/BLUBLAS_kota/BluBridge-BLAS
set +H && git commit -m "H27zA: fix SIGPIPE+pipefail metric filter that silently dropped ncu metrics (13 tools)" && git push
# box
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && git pull
GPUID=3 bash tools/h27zA_wlsm_vs_cublas.sh 1
```

It now prints how many metrics it requested, so a silent drop can't happen unnoticed again.

This was worth chasing. The bug is that `printf | grep -q` under `set -o pipefail` **discards a metric because it was found** — `grep -q` exits on first match, `printf` takes SIGPIPE, `pipefail` turns that into a failed pipeline, and the `&&` never runs. Proven at realistic size: early match → status 141 → dropped; late match → kept. That's exactly why `l1tex__` and `sm__*` vanished while `smsp__warp_issue_stalled_*` survived.

Two things that make it worse than a one-script typo. It's **a race** — `h27zzk` used the identical idiom and got real numbers, so it won the race there; any prior run could have silently lost metrics. And it **fails silently in the direction that looks like data** — you get a clean-looking table with `nan` rather than an error. It was in **13 tools** going back through the whole campaign.

Once the counters come back I'll finally have the number I actually want: `l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu_mem_shared` for the pin vs `wlsm`. That's the direct test of whether the swizzle's +2.06 really came from removing bank conflicts, which I've been asserting from a doc figure rather than measuring on our kernel.

```
cycles         ours 811,648   cuBLAS 800,012
tensor% peak         91.64            92.51
tensor-busy    ours 743,795   cuBLAS 740,091   <- equal, as identical work demands
IDLE cycles    ours  67,853   cuBLAS  59,921   <- the entire gap: ~7,932 cycles
```

The whole remaining deficit is **~8K extra idle cycles**, and the dominant idle reason is `long_scoreboard` **31.96 vs 20.16**.

**And the asymmetry is exploitable.** cuBLAS is *bandwidth*-bound (`mio_throttle` 14.75, throttled by the memory pipe); we're *latency*-bound (waiting on loads) with **9 points of pipe headroom they don't have**. We're not short of bandwidth — we're short of outstanding requests.

Depth 5 at BK=64 is arithmetically impossible (5 × 49,152 = 245,760 > 231,424). But **BK=32 changes that**:

```
BK=64:  stage 49,152 B  ->  depth 4  ->  4 loads in flight   196,608 B
BK=32:  stage 24,576 B  ->  depth 8  ->  8 loads in flight   196,608 B
```

Identical bytes in flight, **double the outstanding requests** — which is exactly what latency-bound wants, and it uses headroom cuBLAS doesn't have because they're already throttled. It deliberately diverges from their `64x4`, which is the point: copying a bandwidth-bound design isn't optimal for a latency-bound kernel.

That's untested and I'm not predicting it — more, smaller k-iterations also mean more loop overhead and more mbarrier traffic. But it's the first lever in a while that targets the measured bottleneck rather than a proxy. Want me to build it?

**Pause any time** with `touch ~/gautam_k/blublas/PAUSE` — it stops cleanly between rows. `rm PAUSE` and re-run to continue exactly where it left off. Ctrl-C is also safe; every row is written as it completes.

How it settles each of your three doubts:

**(A) measurement order** — three arms per cell: `default` (cuBLAS cold, ours warm — every number we've ever recorded), `swap` (cuBLAS re-timed *after* us), `preheat` (both at steady state). If all three agree, order isn't doing work in the number and that explanation dies.

**(B) power** — this is the part that was genuinely missing. `nvidia-smi` reports **one** clock while both kernels alternate in the same process, so every "clock during run" figure we have is the floor across both. Phase 2 samples GPU metrics at 10 kHz via nsys and joins each sample to whichever kernel owned the GPU at that timestamp — giving **ours vs cuBLAS clock separately, on the same card, at the same moment**. Plus power draw, temperature, and the actual throttle reason (`sw_power_cap` / `hw_slowdown`) sampled through every run.

**(C) is cuBLAS doing something** — phase 3 captures their kernel name at `free`, `1200` and `1755`, so a clock difference can't be confused with them selecting a different kernel.

Repeated **3 full suites**, and the analyzer reports the within-cell spread as its own yardstick rather than importing a floor. It refuses to compute medians across two boxes, marks `CAP-OVERRODE` rows as governor artefacts, and counts samples per cell so a partial cell can't pass as full.

Rough runtime: phase 1 is 3 suites × ~11 freqs × 3 arms × 15 pins × 3 reps ≈ 4,500 runs, call it 2.5–3 h with preheat; phases 2–3 add ~30 min. Given it's pausable, run it in whatever windows you have.

That takes ~2 minutes and decides the redesign. What each outcome means:

- **Small shape fast (~3 s), huge shapes 100 s+** → the cost is host-side fill and H2D of multi-GB operands, and it's dominated by V4/V2c/V8d. Fix: batch shapes per process so setup is paid once per shape instead of once per row, and the 46 s average collapses.
- **Every shape ~46 s regardless of size** → it's fixed per-process overhead (CUDA context, library load, cuBLAS init), and batching kills it outright.
- **The batched line ≈ one shape's time** → setup genuinely amortises, and the whole matrix can run in a handful of processes.

The plan that gets us to ~30 min without cutting anything from the experiment: keep **all 15 pins, all 3 order arms, the frequency ladder and multiple suites**, but restructure so one process handles many measurements. Since you're running as root, the harness can even switch clocks itself between iterations — meaning **one process per shape**, sweeping frequency × arm × rep internally, and paying the expensive allocate/fill/H2D exactly 15 times instead of 3,645.

That's ~15 setups plus ~11 min of actual measurement. No reduction in freqs, arms, reps or shapes — the goals, hypotheses and controls all stay intact. I just need the timing numbers first so I build the right thing rather than assuming which part is slow.

**A single row costs ~8 s, but the suite averaged 46 s.** That 38 s difference is my per-row `nvidia-smi -lms 100` sampler: I background `timeout … nvidia-smi` and then `kill $SP`, which kills the *subshell* but leaves `nvidia-smi` running. They accumulate — 500+ leaked pollers by now, progressively strangling the box.

Two fixes and it fits in the window:
> tool `Bash`: Batch phase 1 by config group and fix the leaked sampler

```
# box -- FIRST clear the leaked pollers from the old run
pkill -f "nvidia-smi.*-lms" ; sleep 1; pgrep -cf "nvidia-smi.*-lms"   # should print 0

# local (you)

# box

GPUID=3 SUITES=2 FREQS="free 1200 1400 1474 1755" bash tools/h27zD_clock_suite.sh 1 2>&1 | tee /tmp/zD.log
```

**~38 minutes for phase 1**, and nothing about the experiment is cut — all 15 pins, all 3 order arms, `free` plus the four frequencies that matter, 2 full suites.

Two changes got it there:

**The leaked sampler was the real cost.** 8 s of work was taking 46 s because every row left an `nvidia-smi -lms 100` running. Now one sampler runs for the whole phase and each row's telemetry is sliced out by timestamp — same power/clock/throttle data, no leak. Clear the old ones with the `pkill` above or the box stays slow.

**Batching by config group.** `--cfg` takes a comma list and `--shape` repeats, so all shapes sharing a pinned config are measured in one process. Setup is now paid per *shape* (~3.3 s) instead of per *row*, and the ~4.6 s process cost once per group. Six groups cover all fifteen pins.

The frequency set keeps everything the hypotheses need: `free` (how production actually runs), `1200` and `1400` (below the cap, where the lock holds), `1474` (first point above the cap edge), `1755` (max). The dropped 1300/1500/1600/1700 were interpolation between points we keep.

I dropped process-level reps to 1 because **suites already provide the repetition** — 2 suites × 3 arms gives 6 independent measurements per cell, and the null control has been reading 0.01–0.03 all week.

If 38 min still runs long, `SUITES=1` halves it to ~19 min and you'd still have all 15 pins × 5 freqs × 3 arms. Phases 2 and 3 (per-kernel clock, kernel identity) are another ~30 min and I'd run those after phase 1 reports.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-22 18:29 IST]

**Found the bug that caused yesterday's 225 `NA`s** — and it's still live. Look:

```
s1 V3  1474  swap  %cuB NA   ...
  [group 2 shapes in 0s]      <- 0 seconds. Nothing ran.
```

The cause is this line:

```bash
BLUBLAS_BENCH_TARGET_MS=$WINMS BLUBLAS_PREHEAT_MS=$PH ${RA:+BLUBLAS_REF_AFTER=$RA} "$BIN" ...
```

Bash recognises assignments **before** parameter expansion. When `RA=1`, `${RA:+BLUBLAS_REF_AFTER=$RA}` expands *after* parsing, so bash doesn't see an assignment — it treats the resulting text as the **command name** and `$BIN` as its first argument. It fails instantly, which is exactly the 0 s and the `NA`.

And it explains why the pre-flight passed: that one has a **literal** `BLUBLAS_REF_AFTER=1`, so it's a real assignment. My guard tested a different code path than the run.
> tool `Bash`: Reproduce and fix the env-assignment bug

Reproduced exactly: `bash: BAZ=1: command not found`, and `env` fixes it.

```
# box -- stop the current run (Ctrl-C), then:
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
# the swap rows already written are all NA garbage -- drop them, keep everything else
awk -F'\t' 'NR==1 || $8!="swap"' test_reports/h27zD/rows.tsv > /tmp/r && mv /tmp/r test_reports/h27zD/rows.tsv
wc -l test_reports/h27zD/rows.tsv

# local (you)
cd /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/BLUBLAS/BLUBLAS_kota/BluBridge-BLAS
set +H && git commit -m "H27zD: fix env-assignment bug that silently killed every swap row" && git push

# box
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && git pull && rm -f PAUSE
GPUID=3 SUITES=2 P2_SUITES=1 FREQS="free 1200 1400 1474 1755" \
  bash tools/h27zD_clock_suite.sh 2>&1 | tee /tmp/zD.log
```

The `awk` line matters — those `NA` swap rows are recorded as *completed*, so the resume logic would skip them forever and you'd never get swap data.

This is the same defect that produced yesterday's 225 `NA`s, and my pre-flight didn't catch it because it used a literal assignment while the run used the expansion. **The guard tested a different code path than the thing it was guarding.** It now uses the identical `${RA:+...}` construct, so if this ever breaks again the pre-flight aborts in 10 seconds instead of after an hour.

Two things worth noting from the rows that *did* work, at 1474:

- `preheat` pushed power to **335 W** and the clock fell to 1461 → tagged `CAP-OVERRODE`, while the same cell at `default` sat at 160 W and held 1484. So preheating genuinely changes the power state, which is exactly the effect we're trying to measure.
- V1 hit **106.7%** at 1474 preheat.

Both are single unreplicated points — I'm not drawing anything from them yet, just noting the mechanism is visibly live.

## Why we ran this experiment

**The problem.** Production trains with GPU clocks **free** — we never lock them during a real run. And at free clocks cuBLAS had always looked better than us: our free-clock numbers sat around 96%, while the same kernels locked at 1200 MHz scored ~100%. Four points of difference appearing and disappearing depending on a setting we don't control in production.

**Three explanations existed and had never been separated:**

**(A) Measurement artefact.** Our harness times cuBLAS **once per shape, before** any of our configs (`test_bgemm_sm90_matrix.cu:708`). So cuBLAS always runs first on an idle GPU and we always run second into a warm one. A GPU coming out of idle boosts high and settles down as it heats. If cuBLAS gets that boost and we never do, `%cuB` is measuring the running order, not the kernels.

**(B) Power.** We issue ~1.6× the instructions cuBLAS does. More instructions could mean more watts, and once the 700 W cap binds the governor hands out less clock. Earlier work put the cap edge between 1400 and 1474 MHz on H200.

**(C) cuBLAS does something we don't.** Perhaps it picks a *different kernel* when clocks are free versus locked, or is genuinely more efficient per watt.

**Why it matters.** If (A), then every free-clock number in this campaign understates us and BluTrain is already faster than we think. If (B), we have a real power problem to fix. If (C), we have a kernel problem. The three lead to completely different work.

---

## How the test was designed

**Three order arms** — the core control. Every cell is measured three ways:

| arm | what it does | isolates |
|---|---|---|
| `default` | cuBLAS timed first, cold; ours second, warm | the status quo — every number ever recorded |
| `swap` | cuBLAS **re-timed after** our config (`BLUBLAS_REF_AFTER=1`) | reverses the advantage |
| `preheat` | GPU burned to steady state before anything is timed (`BLUBLAS_PREHEAT_MS=2000`) | **removes** the asymmetry rather than reversing it |

Reversing and removing are different tests. If order is irrelevant all three agree. If it matters, `swap` should overshoot in our favour and `preheat` should land in between — and both should differ from `default`.

**Frequency ladder** — `free`, plus 1200/1300/1400 (below the cap, where a lock genuinely holds), 1474 (first point above the cap edge), 1755 (max). This spans the two regimes: **lock holds** versus **governor decides**.

**Phase 1 — the %cuB matrix.** 15 pins × 6 frequencies × 3 arms × 2 full suites. Throughout each measurement we sample clock, power draw, temperature and the actual throttle reason at 200 ms. Any row whose sustained clock falls below the request is tagged `CAP-OVERRODE` and treated as the governor talking, not data.

**Phase 2 — per-kernel clock.** This is the piece that was missing all along. `nvidia-smi` reports **one** clock for the whole GPU while our kernel and cuBLAS's alternate inside the same process — so every "clock during run" figure we'd ever taken was the floor across both, and could not answer *did ours get less clock than theirs*. Phase 2 samples GPU metrics at 10 kHz via nsys and joins each sample to whichever kernel owned the GPU at that timestamp, splitting the two apart.

**Phase 3 — kernel identity.** Capture cuBLAS's kernel name at free, 1200 and 1755, so a clock difference can't be confused with them selecting a different kernel.

**Repeatability** — the whole suite runs twice, so every cell has an independent replicate.

---

## Phase 1 — observations

**Measurement repeatability** (same pin, same freq, same arm, suite 1 vs suite 2, n=225):

| freq | median \|diff\| | max |
|---|---|---|
| 1200 | **0.20** | 1.00 |
| 1400 | **0.20** | 2.30 |
| 1474 | 0.50 | 6.80 |
| 1755 | 0.50 | 4.70 |
| **free** | **1.10** | **14.10** |

Locked clocks repeat to ±0.2. Free clocks are **5× noisier**, with outliers to 14 points. That alone is evidence the governor, not the kernel, drives the variation.

**Median %cuB across all 15 pins:**

| freq | default | swap | preheat | swap−def | preheat−def | clk | power | cap | lock |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **free** | **96.30** | 100.85 | 100.75 | **+4.55** | **+4.45** | 1926 | 192 W | yes | FREE |
| 1200 | 99.90 | 100.10 | 100.00 | +0.20 | +0.10 | 1200 | 123 W | no | HELD |
| 1300 | 100.00 | — | 100.00 | — | +0.00 | 1305 | 130 W | no | HELD |
| 1400 | 99.90 | 100.00 | 99.90 | +0.10 | +0.00 | 1410 | 143 W | no | HELD |
| 1474 | 99.20 | 106.40 | 100.80 | +7.20 | +1.60 | 1484 | 161 W | yes | CAP |
| **1755** | **94.85** | 103.00 | 101.30 | **+8.15** | **+6.45** | 1712 | 218 W | yes | CAP |

**Where the lock holds (1200/1300/1400), the arm makes no difference at all** — +0.00 to +0.20 against a 0.20 floor. **Where the governor decides (free, 1474, 1755), the arm is worth +4.45 to +8.15.**

Note `swap` and `preheat` agree closely at free (100.85 vs 100.75) — two independent ways of removing the asymmetry landing on the same answer.

**Per-pin at free clocks — all 15 pins:**

## Verdict on the three hypotheses

| | hypothesis | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | measurement order | **CONFIRMED, and it is the whole effect** — worth +4.5 at free, +6.5 at 1755, zero where the lock holds; 15/15 pins |
| **B** | we draw more power and lose clock | **REFUTED** — our clock is unchanged between arms; theirs is what moves |
| **C** | cuBLAS switches kernels or is more efficient | **REFUTED** — identical kernel at free/1200/1755 |

---

## Summary

We ran this because production trains with clocks free, and at free clocks cuBLAS had always beaten us by roughly four points while the same kernels tied or won when locked at 1200 — and we had never established whether that was a real power deficit on our side, something clever cuBLAS was doing, or an artefact of our own harness timing cuBLAS first on a cold GPU. Three order arms across a frequency ladder, repeated twice over all fifteen pins, plus per-kernel clock sampling that finally separated our clock from theirs, settled it: where the lock genuinely holds the measuring order makes no difference at all (+0.00 to +0.20 against a 0.20 repeatability floor), but wherever the governor is free to decide — unlocked, or above the power cap — removing the cold-start asymmetry is worth **+4.5 points at free clocks and +6.5 at 1755, on all fifteen pins without exception**. The per-kernel clocks show exactly why: **our clock barely moves between arms while cuBLAS's falls by 175–222 MHz once it is no longer measured on an idle card**, so cuBLAS was collecting a boost we never received rather than being more power-efficient; and it issues the same kernel at every clock setting, so kernel selection is not involved either. The practical consequence is that our real free-clock standing is the preheated figure — **median 100.8% of cuBLAS rather than the 96.3% we have been quoting all campaign** — and every free-clock comparison in the record understates us by about four and a half points.

## First, some words I'll use

- **Test program** — the program we run to check our GEMM code. It runs our version, runs NVIDIA's cuBLAS on the same problem, and prints how fast ours was compared to theirs.
- **%cuB** — our speed as a percentage of cuBLAS's speed. 100 means the same speed. 105 means we're 5% faster. 96 means we're 4% slower.
- **Clock speed** — how many times per second the chip's circuits tick, in MHz. Higher clock = faster work. The chip changes its own clock constantly depending on how hot and how power-hungry it is.
- **Locking the clock** — telling the chip "stay at exactly 1200 MHz, don't change". We can do this for tests. We do **not** do it during real training.
- **Free clock** — we don't lock it, the chip decides for itself. This is how real training runs.
- **Power limit** — this GPU is allowed to draw at most 700 watts. If a job would use more, the chip lowers its own clock to stay under the limit.
- **The 15 shapes** — the 15 different matrix sizes the 1.7B model actually uses during training. For each one we've chosen the best version of our kernel.

---

## What was bothering us

When we locked the clock at 1200 MHz, our code scored about **100%** — same speed as cuBLAS.

When we left the clock free, our code scored about **96%** — 4% slower than cuBLAS.

Same code. Same problems. Only difference: whether we locked the clock.

**And real training always runs with a free clock.** So the 96% number is the one that matters for the actual product, and we didn't know why it was worse.

---

## Three possible reasons, and we couldn't tell them apart

**Reason 1 — our test program is measuring unfairly.**

Our test program does this for each matrix size:
1. Set up the problem (make the matrices, copy them to the GPU)
2. **Run cuBLAS and time it**
3. Then run our version and time it
4. Print the comparison

Notice cuBLAS always goes **first**. When a GPU has been sitting idle it is cool, so it runs at a very high clock for a short while, then settles down to a lower clock as it heats up. So cuBLAS gets measured during the cool, fast period. By the time our code runs, the GPU has warmed up and slowed down.

If that's what's happening, the 4% gap is not about our code at all. It's about who got measured first.

**Reason 2 — our code uses more power, so the chip slows us down.**

Our kernel executes about 1.6× as many instructions as cuBLAS's. More instructions could mean more watts. If we push past the 700 W limit, the chip lowers our clock to protect itself, and we genuinely run slower.

**Reason 3 — cuBLAS is doing something smarter.**

Maybe cuBLAS picks a *different kernel* when the clock is free versus locked. Or maybe their kernel simply gets more work done per watt.

**Why we had to know:** each reason needs completely different work. Reason 1 means there's nothing to fix and our real speed is better than we thought. Reason 2 means we need to reduce power. Reason 3 means we need to change the kernel.

---

## How we built the test

### The main idea: measure each thing three different ways

For every combination we tested, we measured it three times using three different orders:

| name | what we did | what it tells us |
|---|---|---|
| **default** | cuBLAS first on a cool GPU, ours second on a warm one | this is how every number we've ever recorded was taken |
| **swap** | run our code first, then measure cuBLAS **afterwards**, when the GPU is already warm | flips the advantage to the other side |
| **preheat** | run a dummy workload for 2 seconds first so the GPU is warm **before anything is measured**, then measure both | makes it fair for both |

Why all three: `swap` flips the unfairness around, `preheat` removes it. Those are different tests. If the order doesn't matter, all three give the same answer. If it does matter, `swap` should swing too far in our favour and `preheat` should land in the middle — and both should differ from `default`.

### The clock settings we tested

- **free** — chip decides (this is real training)
- **1200, 1300, 1400 MHz** — low enough that when we say "stay here", the chip actually obeys
- **1474 MHz** — the first setting where the chip can no longer obey, because holding it would use too much power
- **1755 MHz** — the maximum, which the chip definitely cannot hold

This gives us two situations: **chip obeys us** and **chip does what it wants**.

### Phase 1 — measure speed everywhere

15 shapes × 6 clock settings × 3 orders, done twice over. While each measurement ran, we recorded five times a second: the actual clock, the watts being drawn, the temperature, and whether the chip reported that it was holding back because of the power limit.

We also checked afterwards whether the clock we asked for was actually delivered. If it wasn't, we marked that row as "the chip overrode us" and don't treat it as a clean measurement.

### Phase 2 — measure our clock and cuBLAS's clock separately

**This is the piece we had been missing for weeks, and it's the important one.**

The standard tool (`nvidia-smi`) reports **one** clock number for the whole GPU. But our kernel and cuBLAS's kernel take turns running inside the same program, milliseconds apart. So that one number is a blend of both, and it simply cannot answer the question we care about: *did our kernel get a lower clock than theirs?*

So instead we used NVIDIA's profiler to record the clock **10,000 times per second**, and separately recorded exactly when each kernel started and stopped. Then we matched every clock sample to whichever kernel was running at that moment. That splits the single blended number into two: what our kernel ran at, and what cuBLAS's kernel ran at, on the same chip, seconds apart.

### Phase 3 — check cuBLAS isn't switching kernels

Record the name of the cuBLAS kernel at free, 1200 and 1755. If it's the same name everywhere, then any speed difference cannot be explained by them choosing a different kernel.

### Repeat everything

The whole thing ran twice from start to finish, so every single measurement has a second, independent copy to compare against.

---

## Phase 1 results

**First: how repeatable are our measurements?** We compared each measurement to its copy from the second run (225 pairs):

| clock setting | typical difference between the two runs | worst |
|---|---|---|
| 1200 | **0.20** | 1.00 |
| 1400 | **0.20** | 2.30 |
| 1474 | 0.50 | 6.80 |
| 1755 | 0.50 | 4.70 |
| **free** | **1.10** | **14.10** |

With the clock locked, measuring twice gives nearly the same answer (0.2 apart). With the clock free, the two answers can differ by up to 14 points. **Free-clock measurements are unstable on their own** — and that instability is coming from the chip's clock decisions, not from our code.

**Now the speeds** (middle value across all 15 shapes):

| clock | default | swap | preheat | swap−default | preheat−default | actual clock | watts | power limit hit? | did the lock hold? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **free** | **96.30** | 100.85 | 100.75 | **+4.55** | **+4.45** | 1926 | 192 W | yes | no lock |
| 1200 | 99.90 | 100.10 | 100.00 | +0.20 | +0.10 | 1200 | 123 W | no | yes |
| 1300 | 100.00 | — | 100.00 | — | +0.00 | 1305 | 130 W | no | yes |
| 1400 | 99.90 | 100.00 | 99.90 | +0.10 | +0.00 | 1410 | 143 W | no | yes |
| 1474 | 99.20 | 106.40 | 100.80 | +7.20 | +1.60 | 1484 | 161 W | yes | no |
| **1755** | **94.85** | 103.00 | 101.30 | **+8.15** | **+6.45** | 1712 | 218 W | yes | no |

Read the "did the lock hold?" column against the "swap−default" column:

- **Where the chip obeyed us (1200, 1300, 1400): changing the order changed nothing.** +0.00 to +0.20, and our measurements are only good to 0.20 anyway. So that's zero.
- **Where the chip did what it wanted (free, 1474, 1755): changing the order changed a lot.** +4.45 to +8.15.

Also worth noting: at free clocks, `swap` gave 100.85 and `preheat` gave 100.75 — two completely different ways of fixing the unfairness, landing on nearly the same number.

**Every one of the 15 shapes, at free clock:**

| shape | default | swap | preheat | gain from preheat |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| V1 | 99.5 | 108.8 | 108.2 | +8.7 |
| V2 | 96.3 | 106.9 | 100.5 | +4.2 |

| V8c | 96.5 | 104.4 | 101.5 | +5.0 |
| V8d | 95.8 | 97.8 | 98.9 | +3.1 |
| **middle** | **96.3** | **100.3** | **100.8** | **+4.6** |

**All 15 improved. Not one exception.** The smallest gain was +3.1, and our measurement error at free clock is 1.1 — so even the smallest gain is three times bigger than the noise.

## Phase 2 results — the clocks, separated

| clock setting | order | %cuB | our kernel's clock | cuBLAS's clock | difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **free** | default | 96.5 | 1476 | **1563** | **−87** |
| **free** | preheat | 105.1 | 1482 | 1438 | **+44** |
| 1200 | default | 100.9 | 1186 | 1183 | +3 |
| 1200 | preheat | 101.1 | 1186 | 1181 | +5 |
| 1400 | default | 100.3 | 1381 | 1379 | +2 |
| 1400 | preheat | 100.8 | 1382 | 1376 | +6 |
| 1474 | default | 100.6 | 1449 | 1453 | −4 |
| 1474 | preheat | 102.0 | 1449 | 1425 | +24 |
| **1755** | default | 96.4 | 1483 | **1560** | **−77** |
| **1755** | preheat | 105.7 | 1487 | 1445 | +42 |

**This is the answer.** Compare the two clock columns between `default` and `preheat`:

- **Our clock hardly changes.** Looking at individual shapes: V1 went 1513 → 1512. V3 went 1386 → 1400. V6 went 1414 → 1418. V8 went 1566 → 1599.
- **cuBLAS's clock drops a lot.** V1 went 1668 → 1446, a fall of 222 MHz. V8 went 1696 → 1521, a fall of 175 MHz.

So when we warm the GPU up first, **we run at the same speed as before, and cuBLAS runs much slower.** cuBLAS was getting a high clock only because it was being measured on a cool, idle chip. That extra clock was never available to us, because we always ran second.

And notice `1755` behaves exactly like `free`. That makes sense — asking for 1755 is impossible under the power limit, so the chip ignores us and decides for itself, which is the same situation as not locking at all. Two different routes to the same condition, giving the same result.

---

## Phase 3 results — is cuBLAS switching kernels?

| shape | free | 1200 | 1755 |
|---|---|---|---|
| V1 | `128x128_64x6_1x2_h_bz_split` | same | same |
| V3 | `192x192_64x3_1x2_h_bz_coop` | same | same |
| V6 | `192x192_64x4_2x1_v_bz_coop` | same | same |
| V8 | `256x128_64x4_1x2_h_bz_coop` | same | same |

**No.** cuBLAS runs the exact same kernel whatever the clock is doing. So the speed difference cannot be caused by them choosing something different.

---

## Answers to the three reasons

| | reason | answer |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | our test program measures unfairly | **YES — and this is the entire explanation.** Worth +4.5 at free clock and +6.5 at 1755, and exactly zero wherever the lock holds. All 15 shapes agree. |
| **2** | we use more power so we get slowed down | **NO.** Our clock is basically the same in both orders. It's cuBLAS's clock that changes. We are not being throttled more than them. |
| **3** | cuBLAS does something smarter | **NO.** Same kernel at every clock setting. |

---

## Summary in one paragraph

We ran this because real training never locks the GPU clock, and with the clock left free our code looked about 4% slower than cuBLAS, while the very same code tied with cuBLAS when we locked the clock at 1200 MHz — and we did not know whether that was because our kernel really uses more power and gets slowed down, because cuBLAS was doing something cleverer, or simply because our own test program always measures cuBLAS first while the GPU is still cool and fast. We tested all fifteen real shapes at six clock settings, three times each in three different measuring orders, ran the whole thing twice, and for the first time recorded our kernel's clock and cuBLAS's clock separately instead of one blended number for the whole chip. The result is clear: when the chip actually obeys our locked clock, the measuring order makes no difference whatsoever, but whenever the chip is free to choose its own clock, warming it up first before measuring anything is worth **+4.5 points at free clock and +6.5 at maximum clock, on all fifteen shapes with no exceptions**. The separated clock readings show exactly why — **our kernel's clock barely moves, while cuBLAS's clock falls by 175 to 222 MHz once it is no longer measured on an idle chip** — so cuBLAS was simply collecting a cool-start speed boost that we never got, not being more power-efficient; and it runs the identical kernel at every clock setting, so it was not doing anything different either. The practical result is that our true free-clock speed is the warmed-up number, **about 100.8% of cuBLAS rather than the 96.3% we have been reporting**, meaning every free-clock comparison we have recorded has been undercounting us by roughly four and a half points.

## The plan

Your three phases, with four changes I'd recommend:

**Phase 1 — identity gate.** 15 pins, nsys each, records what cuBLAS *actually* launched vs what §H27zzj-C says it should, prints MATCH/DIFFER/NEW. This runs first and blocks everything.

**Phase 2 — champion matrix.** 15 shapes × every pinned config + near-par alternates (V1 `_d6`/`_d7`, ±`_wlsm`), full rigor. Answers "does someone else's variant win my shape?"

**Phase 3 — full sweep.** The registry is **228 + 14 + 42 + 145 = 1,259 instantiations**, which per layout is ~415–429 configs, so **~6,300 runs**, not ~750.

**My four changes:**

1. **Split Phase 3 into screen → promote.** Screening only has to *rank*, not publish. Screen at 150 ms, then re-measure the top 5 per shape at 400 ms + full verify + nsys. Cuts phase 3 from ~8 h to ~3 h and loses nothing, because only the promoted numbers get quoted.

2. **One full build for all three phases.** Not the fast build. Our own rule is that a stale test binary makes new configs silently invisible — the script checks every config against `--list` and reports what's missing rather than quietly running short.

3. **Precision is a second gate, not a column.** Anything that doesn't PASS is disqualified before speed is looked at.

4. **`--resume`/`--inflight` on phase 3.** Ten configs are on record as killing the CUDA context; without it one crash loses a whole shape's 415 runs.

**One thing worth knowing, since it makes the sweep trustworthy:** the measurement-order bias inflates the *cuBLAS reference*. Every one of our configs on a shape is compared against that same reference, so the bias is common-mode and **cancels when ranking our variants against each other**. It only shifts the %cuB scale — which is what preheat fixes.

**Honest time estimate:** build ~1 h, phase 1 ~25 min, phase 2 ~45 min, phase 3 ~3 h. Roughly 5 hours of GPU. It's resumable and `touch PAUSE` stops it cleanly.

## Where I was wrong

**Preheat.** It sits inside the *layout* loop, not the config loop — it already runs **once per shape invocation** (2 s), so the whole campaign spends ~30 s preheating total. Nothing to fix; my description was just wrong.

**The 5-hour estimate was wrong by ~5×.** I padded per-config cost to ~2 s without checking. Computed from real measured per-launch times:

| phase | real cost |
|---|---|
| Phase 1 (15 nsys runs) | ~10 min |
| Phase 2 (15 × ~10 configs) | ~3 min |
| Phase 3 (15 × ~415 configs, **full 400 ms rigor**) | **~37 min** |
| Phase 3b (nsys the winners) | ~8 min |
| **total** | **~1 hour** |

Verified three ways: per-launch time from the h27zD TFLOPS, an independent 415 × 0.4 s check, and against how long h27zD itself took.

**So I dropped the screen/promote split.** A 150 ms screen saves only 21 minutes and creates a second, noisier class of number. Phase 3 now runs everything at full rigor in one stage.

## Four real bugs found in my own scripts

1. **A stale binary would have silently wiped the champion set.** If `--list` returned nothing, every config got dropped as "not registered" and the run would complete looking healthy while measuring nothing. Now aborts if the registry shows under 50 configs.
2. **`--list`'s trailing "N cases" line was counted as a config** — off-by-one that would have made the coverage check report "incomplete" forever.
3. **Crash recovery was under-sized.** `--inflight` recovers exactly *one* crashing config per restart, and 10 context-killers are on record — I had 8 attempts. Raised to 24, plus an explicit warning when a shape ends short.
4. **CRASH was being reported as "failed correctness".** Different defect: FAIL computed a wrong answer, CRASH never produced one. Now separated.

## On your question — yes, two of the three are real

Your log was only ~10% of the build (126 of ~1259 kernels), so this is partial. But in that slice:

| warning | count | what it means |
|---|---|---|
| **C7517** | 252 | compiler *injected* a `wgmma.wait_group` because we read accumulator registers without an explicit wait. Normal for wgmma code — but it means ptxas chose the wait placement, not us. |
| **C7515** | 6 | **"Potential Performance Loss"** — non-wgmma instructions write the accumulator registers *between the start and end of a pipeline stage*, which **serializes the wgmma pipeline**. |
| **C7519** | 3 | **"Potential Performance Loss"** — a **divergent path** creates a dependence on a compiler-inserted `WG.AR`, again serializing wgmma. |

C7515 and C7519 are NVIDIA's compiler explicitly telling us the wgmma pipeline is being serialized. That is the same failure mode as §H27zq (drain distance) and §H27zs/§H27zt (34.8 idle cycles per k-iteration) — we found those by reading SASS, and the compiler was flagging it in the build log the whole time.

**Every one of the nine is `192x192x64` cluster 1×2 — the V5 family.** Decoding the template arguments:
- the C7515 pair are the `dh + ubd + skew + lsw` configs, with and without `dw`
- the C7519 one has **`_KLOOP_UNROLL = true`**

That last one is worth flagging: §H27zdy measured KLOOP_UNROLL as "SASS target met, wall clock null". This warning is a candidate explanation — the unroll created a divergent path that serialized wgmma and cancelled its own gain.

**One caveat before we act on it:** all nine warned configs have `_PDL = false` and `_EPI_WL_STSM = false`, so none of them is V5's actual shipping pin (`..._pdl_wlsm`). The full build will tell us whether the pins themselves are clean — that's the thing to check when the log completes.

```
WROT=0                     0 warnings   1 DEPBAR
WROT=1/2, guard as it was  1 warning    3 DEPBAR   <- the documented kill
WROT=1/2, guard removed    0 warnings   2 DEPBAR
```

**A C7517 warning means extra DEPBARs.** §H27zA measured V6's one remaining lever as "BAR.SYNC 4 vs 2, +4.54 barrier stall". Those may be the same thing, and the compiler has been printing it in every build.

**The tile correlation is a lead, not proof.** V1 is clean and is our best variant; the 192x192 family carries 168 injections and is our weakest. Could be causal, could be that 192x192 simply has more registered variants.

`C7515` (6) and `C7519` (3) — NVIDIA's compiler saying the wgmma pipeline is **serialized**. All nine are `192x192 cluster 1x2`, and **none has `PDL=true`**, so no shipping pin is affected. `f_full_verify` was parsed, stored, and **never read**. The only caller was my own new h27zE script. Verification already covers every element on the GPU, so nothing was actually unchecked — but the switch was a lie. Removed.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-24 11:37 IST]

Good question — let me verify it's actually automatic and not just present.
> tool `Bash`: Check inflight write durability
> tool `Bash`: Show the retry loop in my script

Two real gaps. The recovery handles **crashes** but not **hangs** — and a warp-specialized kernel with a bad config can spin forever on an mbarrier, which is exactly "halted in the middle":
> tool `Bash`: Add hang timeouts and forward-progress check

Let me verify the timeout construct actually works and returns 137 on a hang:
> tool `Bash`: Test timeout behavior for hang crash and success

Tested all three cases — works. Here's the answer:

## It was half-there. Now it's complete.

**What already existed:** the test program has `--resume` and `--inflight`. Before running each config it writes that config's name to a small journal file and flushes it to disk. If the config kills the GPU context, the next run reads that journal, marks that one config as CRASH, and skips it. My script already used this.

**What was missing — and this is probably what bit us before:** that only handles a config that *dies*. It does nothing for a config that **hangs**. In a warp-specialized kernel a bad config can sit forever waiting on a barrier that never gets signalled. The program never exits, so there's no exit code, nothing to catch, and the whole run just sits there. No error message, no crash — it simply stops. That matches "halted in the middle".

**Fixed now.** Every place that launches the test binary is wrapped in a timeout — 30 min per shape sweep, 15 min for the single runs. A hang gets killed, which turns it into a normal failure the existing recovery already knows how to handle. I verified the journal file survives the kill, so the next attempt correctly skips the hanging config.

I also added a **forward-progress check**: if a restart adds zero new rows, it stops and says so instead of quietly burning 40 attempts and moving on as if everything was fine.

## So what happens now if something goes wrong

| what happens | before | now |
|---|---|---|
| config kills the GPU context | recorded, skipped, continues | same |
| **config hangs forever** | **everything stops, no message** | **killed, recorded, continues** |
| same failure repeats with no progress | 24 silent retries | stops and tells you |
| you want to stop it yourself | `touch PAUSE` | same |
| a shape ends up incomplete | silent | prints how many configs are missing |

Nothing is lost on a restart either — re-running the same command picks up from where it stopped, because every finished config is already written to the resume file.

```bash

git commit -m "H27zE: cross-comparison campaign with hang timeouts and crash recovery; drop dead --full-verify; mark prev_stage maybe_unused" && git push
```

Then pull and build on the box — that's the only thing left before phase 1.

Analyzed. **The results are not trustworthy yet — I found two bugs of my own and one methodology problem.** Let me go through them.

## What IS solid

- **Identity gate passes.** All 15 shapes launched the expected cuBLAS tile/cluster/raster (the DIFFER labels are my string bug, already fixed).
- **Precision: all 126 rows PASS.** Nothing struck out.
- **9 of 14 shapes: the pin is already the best** of the 9 champion configs.

## Bug 1 — V8b was silently skipped. Only 14 shapes ran, not 15.

`p2=126 rows` = 14 × 9. Look at the log: `V8b rep1 done`. It wasn't done — it was **wrongly judged done**. My resume check keys on `(box, shape, rep)` and **omits layout**. V7 is `16384x2048x2048` **nn** and V8b is `16384x2048x2048` **nt** — same shape string. Once V7 ran, V8b looked complete.

That is the **exact same class of bug** as the h27zD layout-grouping one. I fixed it there and reintroduced it here.

## Bug 2 — the dispatcher percentages are garbage

`+250.93%`, `+104.12%`, `+85.21%` are not real. My code picks the "home pin" like this:

```python
home = [v for v, c in HOMECFG.items() if c and any(x["cfg"] == c for x in rs)]
```

Since all 9 champion configs run on every shape, that condition is true for nearly every variant, so `home[0]` grabs an arbitrary one instead of the variant that owns the shape. The whole "14 of 14 shapes would change pin" line is an artefact. Ignore that entire section.

## The real problem — phase 2 may be measuring config *order*, not config quality

Phase 2 says the winner on `2048x2048x16384` beats V2's pin by **+10.23%**, but phase 1 measured V2's pin at **100.7%** on that same shape. Both can't be right.

Here's my suspicion, and it's uncomfortable. The champion list is `sort -u`'d, so the 9 configs always run in **alphabetical order**:

```
1. 128x128x64_2x1_v_sk2_dh_rot2_pdl
2. 128x128x64_2x1_v_sk2_dh_rot2_pdl_d6
3. 128x256x64_2x1_h_ep64swz128_rot2_pdl     <-- the "winner", runs 3rd
...
9. 256x128x64_2x1_h_ep32s2_pdl              <-- V2's pin, runs LAST
```

One cuBLAS reference, then 9 configs back-to-back at 400 ms each. **V2's pin is measured last, after eight others have been heating the card.** The config that "wins" runs third. That is the same cold-vs-hot asymmetry §H27zD spent a whole day proving, except now it's inside our own comparison.

Note which configs won the five "not the pin" shapes: `128x256...` (3rd) and `128x128...` (1st) — the early ones. That pattern is what I'd expect if position, not quality, is driving it.

**I'm not concluding that yet.** To separate order from real difference I need two things from the box:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
head -1 test_reports/h27zE/p2_matrix.tsv
grep -E "^bx|2048x2048x16384" test_reports/h27zE/p2_matrix.tsv | head -20
grep -h "throttle during run" test_reports/h27zE/logs/p2_*.log | sort | uniq -c
```

The throttle lines tell us whether the 1400 lock actually held during the runs — the only reading we have so far was taken at idle (`0x1` = GpuIdle), which proves nothing.

Good questions. My honest answers:

## 1. More repeats would NOT have caught this

Both runs already agreed: **+10.23%** then **+10.28%**. That's reproducible to two decimal places — and possibly still wrong. Repeats fix *noise*; they do nothing about *bias*. If measuring a config alongside eight others systematically deflates it, running that ten more times just gives a very precise wrong number.

So: the controlled experiment first (2 minutes), repeats after, once we know which number is the honest one. Repeats are for precision, not for validity.

**And nsys every time is actively a bad idea now** — phase 1 used nsys and phase 2 didn't, and that's one of the things under suspicion. Use nsys to confirm *which kernel launched*, never to produce a timing we then quote.

## 2. Your pin idea is right, and it resolves a real tension

You've put your finger on something we've been conflating. There are **two different jobs** and one field trying to do both:

- **the apples-to-apples config** — structurally matching cuBLAS, used for *diagnosis*. The standing rule says pin the match even when it's slower, because a slower match is the finding.
- **the production pin** — the fastest correct config, used by the *dispatcher*.

Right now `pins.sh` has one entry per variant doing both jobs, which is why a "should we change the pin?" question feels like it breaks the apples-to-apples rule. It doesn't — they're different questions.

I'd split it: `PIN_MATCH` (never changes for performance reasons; it's the analysis baseline) and `PIN_BEST` (whatever measures fastest and passes correctness; feeds the dispatcher). Then changing a production pin costs us nothing diagnostically, and we can document exactly what you said — *structurally we're on par, and separately here's the fastest config for this shape*.

## 3. Two other things worth adding

- **A cross-phase consistency gate.** Phase 1 and phase 2 measure the same pin on the same shape. They must agree. Had that been a gate, it would have caught this automatically instead of me spotting it by eye. Cheap to add.
- **Rotate config order across reps.** If order matters, rotating makes it both *average out* and *measurable*, instead of invisible.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-24 13:10 IST]

Very clean result, and it has a built-in noise check.

## What it says

**No single predecessor does it** — all 8 pairwise arms are 713.14–714.03, identical to the 713.45 baseline.

**It appears at exactly two predecessors:**

```
baseline  0 preds   713.45
cum1      1 pred    714.52    <- still fine
cum2      2 preds   656.42    <- DROP, -8.0%
cum3..8   3-8 preds 645.89 - 660.70   <- stays down
```

**Built-in validity check:** `cum1` and `pair0` are the same arm measured twice — 714.52 vs 713.72, agreeing to **0.1%**. So our measurement precision here is ~0.1%, and the drop is **60× that**. This is not noise.

## What's strange, and rules out the easy explanations

- It is **not** any single config — every pairwise arm is clean, including both `sk2` split-K ones.
- It is **not** thermal or clock — flat 1410 throughout.
- It is **not** simply "position in the list", because **B ran 9th, with 8 predecessors, and was completely unaffected** (715.66).

So it takes ≥2 predecessors, and it hits `256x128_ep32s2_pdl` but not `128x256_ep64swz128_rot2_pdl`. That's config-specific vulnerability, not a general context effect — which is why I don't want to guess at a mechanism.

Four questions left, and one small experiment answers all of them:
> tool `Bash`: Write the two-predecessor mechanism test

```bash
# ---------- PUSH (local, you) ----------
cd /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/BLUBLAS/BLUBLAS_kota/BluBridge-BLAS
set +H && git add tools/h27zH_twopred.sh && git commit -m "H27zH: why two predecessors, and why B is spared" && git push
```
```bash
# ---------- RUN (box, GPU 3, ~3 min) ----------
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && git pull
GPUID=3 REPS=2 bash tools/h27zH_twopred.sh 2>&1 | tee test_reports/h27zH_run.log
```

Eight arms, and each answers one thing:

| arm | question |
|---|---|
| `Q1_nonSK` vs `Q1_SK` | is it **any** two predecessors, or the split-K pair specifically? |
| `Q2_B_SK` / `Q2_B_non` | is B genuinely immune, or was it just never in position 3? |
| `Q3_self` | does A degrade **itself** when run three times? |
| **`Q4_recov`** | **after the drop, does the second A come back to 713?** |

**Q4 is the one that matters most**, because it decides how phase 3 has to be built:

- if the second A recovers → it's a **transient**, only the first measurement after a switch is bad. Fix is cheap: measure each config twice and keep the second. Phase 3 survives roughly as designed, at double cost.
- if the second A stays low → it's a **persistent state change**. Then no multi-config invocation is trustworthy, and phase 3 has to run one config per process — 442 × 15 separate launches, which is hours, and I'd want to rethink the whole sweep rather than brute-force it.

Either way we'll know from this run, and either way the phase-2 "gains" stay retracted until re-measured cleanly.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-24 14:12 IST]

You're right. I've been chasing the bug incrementally instead of just designing the measurement correctly. Let me do that now.

The fix is already implied by the data: **measuring a config alone gives 713.24, and that number is reproducible to 0.1% and agrees across phases.** So the design is one config per process. No sharing, no contamination possible. Let me first pull the real candidate list from the registry rather than inventing names:
> tool `Bash`: List registered optimized pdl configs

23 optimized configs registered. Now let me write the definitive test — designed once, correctly.

**The design, and why each choice:**
> tool `Bash`: Write the definitive one-config-per-process matrix

Now the report — with the decision rule enforced, so a "win" inside the noise floor is reported as a tie:
> tool `Bash`: Write the noise-floor-gated report

Let me test the report before shipping it — including that a small "win" is correctly reported as a tie:
> tool `Bash`: Test report noise floor win and tie logic

One more check — that the +0.31% case (our real V2 situation) is correctly called a **tie** and not a win:
> tool `Bash`: Verify the tie path with the real V2 numbers

Both paths verified: **+0.31% → "tie (inside floor)"**, **+3.05% → "WIN"**, pin-best detected, bad-clock rows excluded.

## The design, in plain terms

**One config per process.** That's the whole fix. We proved that measuring a config by itself gives the same answer every time (713.24 / 713.27 / 713.38 / 713.45 / 713.72 / 713.86 / 713.92 across six independent arms — spread 0.1%), and that measuring it alongside others corrupts it. So we never share a process. There's nothing to correct for.

**17 configs × 15 shapes × 3 repeats** — every registered `_pdl` variant, minus the five already measured dead (`a1b0`, `dstg`, `ea96s1`, `tk50k`, `d2`).

**The run measures its own noise.** After each shape's configs, the pin is measured a *second* time in a fresh process. The gap between a pin's two measurements is the noise floor — measured, not guessed.

**The decision rule is fixed before the data exists:** a config beats a pin only if it wins by more than **2× the 95th-percentile null gap** (floored at 0.5%). Anything smaller prints as a **tie** and the pin stays. That rule is what would have stopped today's +10.28%.

**Shape order rotates each repeat**, so drift across the run shows up as spread instead of favouring whichever shape always went first. Clock is re-locked before every invocation, sampled during it, recorded per row, and out-of-band rows are thrown out.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-24 14:34 IST]

## What we are trying to find out

We have 15 shapes. Each shape has one kernel "pinned" to it — the one we chose as best. The question is simple: **is any of our other kernels actually faster on that shape than the one we picked?**

## Why it went wrong earlier today

The first test ran many kernels inside one program run. That made some kernels measure slower than they really are. It said one kernel was 10% better than the pin. When we measured both properly, the difference was 0.3% — basically the same. So that answer was wrong, and it was wrong the same way twice, so repeating it wouldn't have helped.

## What is running now

We proved that if you run **one kernel per program run**, the number is right every time — we got the same value six times in a row, within 0.1%.

So the test running now does exactly that. For every shape, it tries all 17 of our kernels, each in its own separate program run. Nothing shared, so nothing can spoil the number.

It also does two extra things:

- **It measures its own error.** After finishing a shape, it re-measures the pinned kernel a second time. If the same kernel gives two different numbers, that difference tells us how much random wobble there is. So far that wobble is about 0.1%.
- **It decides fairly.** A kernel only counts as "better than the pin" if it wins by more than that wobble. Anything smaller is called a tie and the pin stays. This rule was written before we saw any results, so we can't fool ourselves later.

## The plan from here

1. **~09:49** — the first full pass finishes. Every shape, every kernel, measured once each.
2. **Then stop it** with `touch PAUSE` and read the results. That gives the answer to your question.
3. **If nothing beats a pin** — we're done, the pins are correct, and we move on.
4. **If something does beat a pin** — I test just that one kernel again properly. Two minutes, not three hours.

## Why I said stop early

The test was set to repeat everything three times, which takes 3 hours. One pass is enough to *see* a real winner, because a real winner is several percent and the wobble is 0.1%. Repeating is only useful for making a close number more exact — and a close number means it's a tie anyway, so it changes nothing.

## What I'd fix for next time

The slow part is not the measuring — that takes about 1 second. It's that our program file contains 1327 kernels, and the computer has to load all of them every single time a run starts, which takes about 12 seconds. Building a smaller file with only the kernels we're testing would turn this 3-hour job into roughly 20 minutes. That needs one rebuild, so it's for next time, not now.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-24 14:35 IST]

Reps 2 and 3 are just **the same test done again from scratch** — the same 15 shapes, the same 17 kernels, measured a second and third time.

I put them in for three reasons:

1. **Take the middle value.** With 3 numbers you use the middle one, which is safer than trusting a single number that might have been unlucky.
2. **See how much it wobbles.** If the same kernel gives 713, 714, 712 across three passes, you know the wobble is about 1.
3. **Cancel out drift.** Each pass goes through the shapes in a different order. If the machine slowly changes over the 3 hours, the first shape isn't always the lucky one.

## Why I now think one pass is enough

All three reasons are already covered by things inside rep 1:

- **The wobble is already measured.** Inside rep 1, every shape measures the pinned kernel **twice** — once with the others, once again at the end. That difference is the wobble, and it's coming out around 0.1%. I don't need reps 2 and 3 to learn that.
- **There's no drift to cancel.** Every single row so far reads exactly 1410 MHz — the machine is rock steady. Reason 3 was insurance against something that isn't happening.

So reps 2 and 3 would spend 2 hours making a number like "715.4" into "715.3" — which doesn't change any decision, because anything that close is a tie either way.

## When they would actually matter

If a kernel beats its pin by something small, like 0.4% — too big to ignore, too small to trust from one measurement. Then repeating that **one** case is worth it. But that's a 2-minute job on one shape, not 2 hours on all 15.

So: let rep 1 finish, stop it, read the answer. Keep reps 2 and 3 in reserve for whichever specific cases turn out to be close.

This is the full picture now, and it connects to something already in our record.

## What C7517 is, and why it happens

`WGMMA_SKEW` splits the wgmma issue across the loop back-edge — atom 0 of a stage is issued one loop-pass *later* than atoms 1..N, deliberately, to copy what cuBLAS does. That creates a peel before the loop, a body, and a tail after it, so the accumulator registers get read from **several different paths**. Our waits are correct on each path, but ptxas can't *prove* one dominates all of them, so it inserts its own `wgmma.wait_group` to be safe. That's the C7517 message. C7519 is the same thing on a divergent path.

Proven by knob bisect, not inferred: **skew off → 0 warnings. Every other knob off → still warns.**

## Is there any danger to precision?

**No, and provably not.** The injected wait is what makes the code *correct* — without it we'd read accumulators before the wgmma finished. ptxas is protecting us, not damaging us. Every row measured today came back `maxRelErr 0.00000`, across 135 + 270 + 102 measurements. There is no correctness or precision risk here at all.

## What it costs

Compiling the pin with and without skew:

| | instructions | DEPBAR | HGMMA (static) | WARPGROUP |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| skew ON (shipped) | 2824 | **7** | 48 | 18 |
| skew OFF | 2672 | **3** | 24 | 4 |

**+4 DEPBAR.** I could not establish whether they sit on the hot path — my static loop-detection swallowed 2441 of 2824 instructions. That needs PC sampling on the GPU, and our own rule says static counts mislead, so I'm not claiming a cost figure.

## The part that actually matters — skew may not be earning its keep

Searching the record for what skew was ever worth, §H27zbC-RESULT is titled:

> **"SKEW: THE MECHANISM IS PROVEN, THE IMPLEMENTATION DOES NOT PAY YET"**

```
V5  2048x11264x16384   base 83.31  skew 84.46   +1.15   ranges OVERLAP
V3  16384x11264x2048   base 91.14  skew 90.36   -0.78   skew WORSE
V4  16384x50304x2048   base 89.77  skew 86.50   -3.27   noisy shape
```

and later, §H27z notes `SKEW +1.62` was **"below the floor they were measured at."**

So skew was adopted **as part of a bundle**, its individual value was never cleanly established, and the one careful test found it **negative on V3**.

Put together:
- skew is the **sole** cause of the injected waits
- skew's own benefit is **unproven**
- V3, V4, V5, V6 all carry it — and those are our four weakest variants
- **V6 just lost by 1.97% to a 128x256 config that cannot use skew at all**

That last point is suggestive, not proof — 128x256 differs in more than skew.

## The experiment this calls for

There is **no non-skew 192x192 `_pdl` config registered**, so we can't A/B it without adding one. The clean test is to register `192x192x64_2x1_h_rs8_dh_ubd_dw_lsw_pdl` — the V3/V4 pin with **only** skew removed — and run it on the h27zJ instrument against the current pin on V3, V4, V5 and V6.

That answers, in one measurement: does skew pay for itself, and are the injected waits costing us anything real? Want me to add that config and write the test?

Removing skew doesn't just delete 4 DEPBARs; it removes skew's *whole* mechanism. So the test measures the **net** of two things at once: losing whatever skew gives, and gaining back the waits it forces. Two possible outcomes, and they lead different places:

- **skew-off is slower** → skew *does* pay despite the waits. Then the follow-up is different: keep skew, but restructure so ptxas can prove our wait dominates every path, which is exactly what §H27zt did for the rotation path. That would give us skew *and* no injected waits.

Everything's verified locally. Here's the complete picture you asked for.

## C7517, 360 degrees

**What it is.** ptxas telling us it inserted a `wgmma.wait_group` that we did not write.

**Why it happens.** `WGMMA_SKEW` deliberately splits the wgmma issue across the loop back-edge — atom 0 of a stage is issued one pass *later* than the rest, to copy cuBLAS. That creates a peel, a body and a tail, so the accumulator registers are reached from several paths. Our waits are correct on each, but ptxas can't *prove* one dominates them all, so it adds its own to be safe.

**Proven, not guessed.** Knob bisect on nvcc 13.0: skew off → **0 warnings**. `DESC_HOIST` off, `UBD` off, `LSW` off → **still warns**. And 128x256 with skew **won't compile**: *"WGMMA_SKEW needs ≥2 m64 atoms per warpgroup ... a SPLIT_M 128x256 has 1"*. So the "192x192 is the warned family" pattern I flagged this morning was never about tile size — 128x128 and 128x256 simply cannot use skew.

**Danger to precision: none, and it's the opposite.** The injected wait is what makes the code correct — without it we'd read accumulators before the wgmma retired. ptxas is protecting us. Every row today: `maxRelErr 0.00000`.

**What it costs.** +4 DEPBAR on every pin (V3/V4 7→3, V5 and V6 15→11), and double the static HGMMA count. Whether those DEPBARs sit on the hot path I could **not** establish statically — that needs PC sampling, and our own rule says static counts mislead. So no cost figure from me.

**The uncomfortable part.** §H27zbC-RESULT is literally titled *"SKEW: THE MECHANISM IS PROVEN, THE IMPLEMENTATION DOES NOT PAY YET"* — V5 +1.15 with overlapping ranges, **V3 −0.78 (worse)**, V4 −3.27. It was adopted inside a bundle and its own value was never isolated. So we may be carrying an unproven knob that forces the compiler to insert waits.

## Your reasoning, corrected slightly

Yes — but the test measures the **net** of two things: losing skew, and gaining back the waits. So:
- **no-skew equal or faster** → drop skew. Simpler code, 4 fewer DEPBAR, no injected waits.
- **no-skew slower** → skew earns its cost. Then we keep it and restructure so ptxas can prove our wait dominates, like §H27zt did for the rotation path — getting both.

- **skew's cost** — the compiler has to insert 4 extra waits, because skew creates paths it can't prove are covered

The compiler saying "this could run more overlapped than it does". A speed note. Nothing about wrong answers.

- **C7515** — *"Potential Performance Loss: wgmma.mma_async instructions are serialized due to **non-wgmma instructions defining accumulator registers** ... between start and end of the pipeline stage"*
- **C7519** — *"Potential Performance Loss: ... serialized due to program dependence on compiler-inserted **WG.AR** in divergent path"*

Both say **"Potential Performance Loss"** and both say **"serialized"**. Serialized means the matrix operations run one after another instead of overlapping — **slower, never wrong**. Neither message says anything about incorrect results. Nothing in either can produce a bad number.

## And here's the part that matters: neither touches anything we ship

I decoded all nine configs from your build log:

```
C7515 -- 6 configs, ALL 192x192 cl1x2, ALL PDL=false   -> not a pin
C7519 -- 3 configs, ALL 192x192 cl1x2, ALL PDL=false, ALL KLOOP_UNROLL=true -> not a pin
```

**Every one of our 15 shipping pins has `PDL=true`. Not one of the nine does.** They're dead registry entries — old experimental arms that still get compiled but are never selected.

The three C7519 ones all carry `KLOOP_UNROLL=true`, and that's a nice loose end tied off: §H27zdy measured KLOOP_UNROLL as *"SASS target met, wall clock null"* and never explained why the gain vanished. The compiler is saying the unrolled version serializes wgmma on a divergent path. That's a plausible explanation, on already-abandoned code.

## One correction to what I told you earlier

I said C7519 was the same class of thing on both machines. It isn't quite — the toolchains differ. Local CUDA 13.0 emits C7519 as *"warpgroup.arrive is injected"* and **does** fire it on the V3/V4 pin; your box's older compiler emits it as the serialization warning and does **not** fire it on any pin. So the box's set of nine is what's real for what we ship, and that set contains no pins.

## Bottom line on all three codes

| code | count | says | dangerous? | hits a pin? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C7517 | 351 | compiler added a safety wait | no — it *protects* correctness | yes (V3/V4/V5/V6) |
| C7515 | 6 | wgmma serialized, perf loss | no — speed only | **no** |
| C7519 | 3 | wgmma serialized, perf loss | no — speed only | **no** |

Zero correctness risk across all of them, and the two "Potential Performance Loss" ones don't affect a single kernel we actually run. The only one touching live code is C7517, and we measured today that the knob causing it earns its cost.

Honestly — **I don't know, and I've been quoting a figure I never measured.** Let me reason from actual data instead.

`make -j` parallelises across **files**, not within one. The SM90 kernels live in just **3 files** (`nn/tn/nt_variants.cu`), so that part caps at 3-way parallelism no matter what `-j` you pass. Wall time ≈ the slowest single file, not the sum.

What I did measure: on my laptop, one FAST_BUILD TU with **233 kernels took 100 seconds**. A full TU is roughly double that (~460 kernels), so ~200 s each, three in parallel ≈ **3–5 minutes** for the SM90 part.


This is the real test. It calls the public `blublasBgemmSM90_dispatch_{nn,nt,tn}` entry points — the same path BluTrain uses — and checks two independent things:

- **correct** — output matches cuBLAS
- **select** — throughput matches what the config the table now names should achieve

The second is the one that matters here. A table can hold the right answer while the lookup is wrong (off-by-one in the binary search, an enum drifted from the switch, a silent miss into the tree) — and a correctness-only test would never notice, because the fallback still computes the right answer, just slower.

Paste the output. What I'll be looking for: 15/15 correct, and `select` passing on the big-gain shapes (V1 +11.16%, V4 +6.32%, V8 +5.62%) — those are the ones where a wrong pick would be unmistakable.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-24 18:58 IST]

15/15 correct, and the dispatcher is clearly working. But I have to flag something before we celebrate the 105%.

## The correctness result is solid. The *selection* result isn't conclusive.

**I forgot to lock the clock on this run.** Every `gotTF` is far above its `expectTF` — V1 686.8 vs 602.9, V2 825.7 vs 713.7 — because our expectations were measured at a locked 1400 MHz and this ran at free/boost.

That breaks the selection check. Work it through for V1:

```
expected (our pin @1400 locked)     602.9   tolerance 3% -> floor 584.8
got      (our pin @free)            686.8   = +14% from clock alone
the OLD config @free would be       542.3 x 1.14 = 617.9   -> ALSO above the floor
```

So **a wrong pick would still have passed** on V1, because the free-clock boost (+14%) is larger than the config difference (+11%). "0 SLOW" doesn't prove the lookup is right — it proves nothing ran slower than a threshold the clock already cleared.

The **correctness** half is unaffected and genuinely passed: 15/15 match cuBLAS.

And the 105% median is a free-clock number, which §H27zD showed is the least trustworthy kind — there it favoured cuBLAS, here it may favour us. I wouldn't quote it.

Re-run with the clock locked, and it becomes a real test:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
sudo nvidia-smi -pm 1
sudo nvidia-smi -i 1 -lgc 1400,1400
nvidia-smi -i 1 --query-gpu=clocks.sm --format=csv,noheader   # expect ~1410

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 LD_LIBRARY_PATH=build \
  build/test_bgemm_sm90_dispatch_validate test_reports/h27zM_dispatch_expected.tsv 3.0

sudo nvidia-smi -i 1 -rgc
```

At a locked 1400 the `gotTF` should land **within ~1% of `expectTF`** on every row, because that's exactly the condition our expectations were measured under. Then a wrong pick genuinely can't hide — the old configs are 0.6–11% slower and the tolerance is 3%.

That's the run that actually proves the dispatcher picks what we think it picks.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-24 19:02 IST]

**This is the clean one.** Look at the agreement:

```
V1   expect 602.9  got 603.5   (+0.10%)
V4   expect 688.4  got 688.1   (-0.04%)
V6   expect 664.1  got 664.2   (+0.02%)
V8   expect 493.9  got 494.0   (+0.02%)
```

Every row lands within ~0.5% of what we measured for that exact config. **That proves the lookup works** — if the dispatcher had fallen back to the old config, V1 would have read ~542 (−10%), V4 ~647 (−5.9%), V8 ~468 (−5.3%), all far outside the 3% tolerance.

**14 of 15 are definitively proven this way.** The exception is V8c, whose gain was only +0.62% — too small for throughput to distinguish from its incumbent. That's the limit I flagged earlier, and it's inherent, not a defect.

## The honest end-to-end number

**Median 100.0% of cuBLAS, mean 100.27%, p10 99.3%, p90 101.0%, beating cuBLAS on 8 of 15** — measured through the real public dispatch entry points at a verified 1410 MHz lock.

Note it's **8 of 15**, not the 14 of 15 the free-clock run showed. That's §H27zD's lesson landing again: at free clock the numbers flatter whoever gets the boost. The locked number is the one to quote.

Let me record it:
> tool `Bash`: Document the validated dispatcher result
> tool `Bash`: Compute compute cost per shape

That's per call — but in a training step the counts differ hugely. The `50304` shapes are the LM head (once per step) while the others repeat **per layer**. Let me check the real training profiles rather than guess:
> tool `Bash`: Look for real training profile data
> tool `Bash`: Read the real training kernel profile
> tool `Bash`: Inspect the training profile files

That's **real training profile data**. Let me pull the actual GEMM weights from it:
> tool `Bash`: Extract GEMM weights from the real training profile

Now I can answer properly, with real data.
> tool `Bash`: Weight the shapes by real training frequency

Here's the answer, and it's a useful one strategically.

## Which shapes actually cost the most

| group | shapes | ms/step | share of GEMM |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FFN 11264** | V3, V5, V8c | 77.8 | **51.5%** |
| **FFN 5632** | V2b, V6, V7b | 40.3 | **26.6%** |
| attn 2048 | V7, V8b, V2 | 14.7 | 9.7% |
| LM head (50304) | V4, V2c, V8d | 14.1 | 9.3% |
| small 512 | V1, V7c, V8 | 4.4 | 2.9% |

**The single most expensive shape is V3 `16384x11264x2048` at 17.9%**, with V5 and V8c right behind. Those three FFN shapes are **half of all GEMM time**.

The counter-intuitive one: the **LM head shapes are the biggest per call** (~4.7 ms each, 3.4 TFLOP) but only **9.3%** of the total, because they run **once per step** while every layer shape runs **24 times**.

And GEMM itself is **41.6% of all GPU time** in the real run — 14.2 s of 34.2 s, 34,720 calls. That's measured, not estimated. It's the ceiling on what any GEMM work can deliver.

## The uncomfortable part

**Our biggest percentage wins landed on the least important shapes.**

```
V1  +11.16%  ->  worth 0.9% of GEMM time
V8   +5.62%  ->  worth 1.1%
V7c  +4.08%  ->  worth 0.9%

V3   +1.08%  ->  worth 17.9%
V8c  +0.62%  ->  worth 16.7%
```

Weighted properly, the whole re-pin is **+1.72% on GEMM**, which at 41.6% of GPU time is **~+0.71% end-to-end**. Real, but modest — and much smaller than the +3.90% unweighted average suggests.

## What that says about where to go next

If you want end-to-end throughput, the target is unambiguous: **V3, V5 and V8c — the 11264 FFN shapes.** One percent there is worth more than eleven percent on V1.

Two caveats on the numbers: the 24-layers-per-step weighting is an estimate from `num_hidden_layers = 24` in the docs, and the 41.6% comes from an Aug 7 profile that predates all our work (its call counts and proportions are still representative; its configs are the old picks).

Two solid facts, one caveat.

**The workload matches exactly.** Total GEMM calls: **34,720** today, **34,720** in August. Identical. So this is the same work, and the groupings just merged differently — August's 8640 + 5760 sites now both land on one `128x256 cl2x1` kernel (14400 calls).

**GEMM total: 12,079.5 ms vs August's 14,200 ms — −14.9%.**

**But that comparison is cross-box** and I won't lean on it. August ran on a different machine, and we proved today that cards differ materially (same config, 744.70 TFLOPS on GPU 3 vs 716.92 on GPU 1). Our own rule says a box change voids absolute timings.

One thing I want to watch rather than gloss over: the **7240-call site at 0.327 ms avg**. August had a 7200-call site at 0.260 ms. If those are the same call site, it got *slower*. The call counts aren't quite equal (7240 vs 7200) so I can't safely pair them by eye — the correlationId pairing tool exists precisely because eyeballing this is unreliable.

Excellent data. Let me go through it properly.

## The headline: GEMM 80.8% → 93.1% of cuBLAS

```
ours    12.080 s @ 749 TFLOPS (75.7% peak)
cuBLAS  11.248 s @ 805 TFLOPS (81.3% peak)
        831 ms lost
```

**And the dispatcher is doing exactly what we pinned** — every "our kernel" column matches its pin. `gate_up-fwd` uses `192x192_c2x1_rh` (V3's pin), `lm_head-wgrad` uses `256x128_c1x2_rv` (the V2c incumbent we deliberately kept), V1's site uses `128x128_c2x1_rv`. The re-pin landed end to end.

**The August headline deficit is gone:** `gate_up-fwd` was **75.0%** and a third of the whole gap. It's now **98.4%**, contributing 5.6%.

## But the data shows a pattern we haven't seen before

Group the 21 sites by pass:

| pass | mean % of cuBLAS |
|---|---|
| **forward (nn)** | **95.0%** |
| dgrad (nt) | 90.2% |
| **wgrad (tn)** | **86.5%** |

Every wgrad site is 82–87%: gate_up-wgrad 86.2, attnOut-wgrad 85.6, wQ-wgrad 86.0, lm_head-wgrad 82.7, wK-wgrad 82.3.

**Standalone, those same tn shapes measured ~100%** — V1 105.1, V2 100.3, V2b 100.0, V2c 100.2, V5 100.3. So something about wgrad *in training* costs us ~14 points that our benchmark never sees.

**My hypothesis: `beta`.** wgrad accumulates across grad-accum micro-batches, so it runs `C = A·B + 1·C` — C is read *and* written. Our benchmark harness measures **beta = 0** exclusively. If our beta≠0 epilogue is weaker than cuBLAS's, it would show up exactly here and nowhere in our testing. Note §H27zzn tested the alpha=1/beta=0 fast path and found it null — measured at beta=0, so it says nothing about this.

That's a hypothesis, not a finding. `examples/test_bgemm_sm90_beta.cu` already exists and runs beta 0/0.5/1, so it's cheap to test.

## Where the 831 ms actually is

| site | lost | share | ours% |
|---|---|---|---|
| gate_up-wgrad `2048x11264x16384` tn | 216 ms | **26.0%** | 86.2% |
| wQ-dgrad `16384x2048x2048` nt | 127 ms | 15.3% | 92.7% |
| down-fwd `16384x2048x5632` nn | 89 ms | 10.8% | 91.7% |
| gate_up-fwd | 46 ms | 5.6% | 98.4% |
| **wV-dgrad `16384x2048x512` nt** | 40 ms | 4.8% | **65.2%** |

Two things stand out beyond the beta pattern:

**`wV-dgrad` at 65.2%** is the worst ratio anywhere — 417 vs 639 TFLOPS. Standalone that shape (V8) measured 98.6%. cuBLAS gets 639 here versus 500.9 standalone, so *cuBLAS* is much faster in training on it while we're slower. Worth its own look.

**`gate_up-wgrad` has a raster mismatch.** cuBLAS runs `192x192_64x3_2x1_v`; by the §H27z.86 swap rule ours should be `1x2_h`, but we're running `1x2_v`. That's not apples-to-apples, and it's now the single biggest deficit.

Want me to test the beta hypothesis first? It would explain ~40% of the remaining gap in one shot, and the test already exists.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-24 20:18 IST]

**Beta hypothesis refuted** — all 34,720 cuBLAS launches are the beta-zero kernel. So beta is 0 everywhere in training, and that's not the explanation. Clean falsification, good.

Which means the pattern isn't *pass*, it's **layout**:

```
nn (fwd)    95.0%
nt (dgrad)  90.2%
tn (wgrad)  86.5%   <- our weakest
```

And standalone those same tn shapes measured **~100%** (V1 105.1, V2 100.3, V2b 100.0, V2c 100.2, V5 100.3).

**New hypothesis, and it's a measurement problem rather than a kernel one.** `MatmulBackward.cu` runs **wgrad on a secondary stream** under `WITH_MYBLAS` so dgrad and wgrad overlap; the cuBLAS branch serialises both on one stream. If our wgrad kernels are executing *concurrently* with dgrad kernels, they share SMs — each takes longer, so per-kernel TFLOPS drops — while cuBLAS's wgrad gets the whole GPU to itself.

The pair tool sums kernel **durations**. If ours overlap, that sum overstates our real cost. **The 93.1% could be understating us.**

That's directly testable:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/BluTrain
for f in nsys_blublas_repin nsys_cublas_repin; do
echo "=== $f ==="
sqlite3 profiling_reports/$f/${f}_0.sqlite "
SELECT k.streamId, COUNT(*) AS launches, ROUND(SUM(k.end-k.start)/1e6,1) AS sum_ms,
       ROUND((MAX(k.end)-MIN(k.start))/1e6,1) AS span_ms
FROM CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_KERNEL k JOIN StringIds s ON k.demangledName=s.id
WHERE s.value LIKE '%nvjet%' OR s.value LIKE '%bgemm_sm90%'
GROUP BY k.streamId ORDER BY sum_ms DESC;"
done
```

If our GEMMs appear on **two or more streams** and cuBLAS's on one, the concurrency is real and the per-kernel comparison is not apples-to-apples either — which would mean the *honest* library-vs-library number is neither the tok/s nor this 93.1%, and we'd need to measure with the secondary stream disabled.
