### CLAUDE [2026-08-24 20:38 IST]

Clean data. And I got the attribution wrong — worth being precise about that.

## The honest number: 94.5% of cuBLAS on GEMM

**761 vs 805 TFLOPS, 651 ms lost, single-stream, like-for-like.** Up from **80.8%** in August.

## Where I was wrong

I predicted the concurrency was penalising the **wgrad** sites. It was actually penalising the **dgrad** sites — they run on the *primary* stream and were having SMs stolen by the secondary-stream wgrad running alongside:

| site | 2-stream | 1-stream | |
|---|---|---|---|
| wV-dgrad | 65.2% | **89.5%** | **+24.3** |
| lm_head-wgrad | 82.7% | **95.5%** | +12.8 |
| wQ-dgrad | 92.7% | 97.6% | +4.9 |
| wQ-wgrad | 86.0% | 85.7% | — |
| attnOut-wgrad | 85.6% | 85.9% | — |
| wV-wgrad | 87.7% | **79.2%** | −8.5 |

The wgrad sites barely moved. So the double-stream effect is real, worth 180 ms, but it was hurting a different set of kernels than I said.

## The tn deficit is real, and it's the story now

| layout | mean % of cuBLAS |
|---|---|
| nn (fwd) | 94.9% |
| nt (dgrad) | 94.9% |
| **tn (wgrad)** | **86.9%** |

nn and nt are now level. **tn is 8 points behind and it isn't concurrency.**

## The single biggest target, and it has a concrete cause

**`gate_up-wgrad` `2048x11264x16384` tn — 182.5 ms, 28.0% of the entire remaining gap, at 88.1%.**

Look at the kernels:

```
ours     192x192_c1x2_rv
cuBLAS   192x192_64x3_2x1_v
```

By the §H27z.86 swap rule, cuBLAS's `2x1_v` should map to our **`1x2_h`**. We're running **`1x2_v`** — a **raster mismatch**. The same mismatch shows on `wQ-wgrad` and `attnOut-wgrad` (ours `2x1_h`, cuBLAS `2x1_v` → should be `1x2_h`), and those sit at 85.7% and 85.9%.

**The tn deficit tracks the cluster/raster mismatch** — which is exactly what §H27zzj-C flagged when it found 7 of 8 pins don't match cuBLAS's pairing.

## One thing I can't explain yet

Standalone, `2048x11264x16384` (V5) measured **100.3%** of cuBLAS at a locked 1410. In training it's **88.1%**. Twelve points, same shape, same config. Free clock vs locked is the obvious suspect but I haven't tested it, and I'm not going to assert it.

**Keep `BLUTRAIN_BWD_SINGLE_STREAM` off in production** — the overlap is a genuine wall-clock win. It's a measurement tool, not a config change.

Next I'd test the raster hypothesis on `gate_up-wgrad`: it's 28% of the gap and we already own the `1x2_h` variants. Want that, or the end-to-end tok/s run first?

### CLAUDE [2026-08-24 20:39 IST]

That's the right question, and the data answers it. Let me work it out properly.
> tool `Bash`: Compare bench vs training gains for both libraries

This answers your question completely, and it's an uncomfortable answer.

## Both libraries get faster in training. Ours gets much less faster.

Going from the bench (locked 1410) to training (free clock):

```
cuBLAS   +21.7%
ours     +11.7%
```

And split by layout, the picture is stark:

| layout | our gain | cuBLAS gain | points we lose |
|---|---|---|---|
| nn | +16.1% | +22.5% | −5.1 |
| nt | +15.8% | +21.6% | −4.6 |
| **tn** | **+3.4%** | **+21.1%** | **−14.7** |

**On tn our kernels barely speed up at all when the clock is unlocked.** The three worst cases actually go *backwards*:

```
wV-wgrad    2048x512x16384    ours -0.2%   cuBLAS +32.2%   ->  105.1% becomes 79.3%
wK-wgrad    2048x512x16384    ours -0.4%   cuBLAS +29.1%   ->  105.1% becomes 81.1%
gate_up-wgrad 2048x11264x16384 ours -0.6%  cuBLAS +13.3%   ->  100.3% becomes 88.0%
```

V1 was our **best** shape at 105.1% on the bench. In training it's **79.3%** — not because we got slower (we're at 602 vs 603.5 TFLOPS, identical) but because **cuBLAS went from 574 to 759**.

## What that means physically

A kernel that gains nothing from more SM clock is **not clock-limited**. It's limited by something that doesn't scale with clock — memory bandwidth being the obvious candidate. And that fits TN specifically: the dispatcher's own comment notes *"TN stages BOTH operands raw"*, so TN moves more data through the load path than nn or nt.

So: at 1410 our tn kernels have clock headroom and match cuBLAS. Unlock the clock and cuBLAS converts it into throughput while we're already saturated elsewhere.

## The uncomfortable implication

**Our entire step-3 campaign measured at a locked 1200–1400 MHz.** That's the right way to compare *kernel work* — but it systematically flatters us on tn, because it hides a ceiling that production actually hits. Every "100% of cuBLAS" we've quoted on a tn shape is true at 1400 and not true at free clock.

## The decisive test, and it's cheap

Lock the GPU to 1400 and re-run the training capture. If the explanation is right, our ratio should climb from **94.5% back toward ~100%**, with the tn sites recovering most.

```bash
sudo nvidia-smi -i 3 -lgc 1400,1400
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/BluTrain
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=3 BLUTRAIN_BWD_SINGLE_STREAM=1
export OMPI_ALLOW_RUN_AS_ROOT=1 OMPI_ALLOW_RUN_AS_ROOT_CONFIRM=1
make nsys-train MODE=production NP=1 WITH_BLUBLAS=1 NSYS_OUT=nsys_blublas_1stream_lock 2>&1 | tail -6
make nsys-train MODE=production NP=1 WITH_BLUBLAS=0 NSYS_OUT=nsys_cublas_lock 2>&1 | tail -6
sudo nvidia-smi -i 3 -rgc
```

If it does climb, we've found the real remaining gap and it's a **memory-path problem on tn at high clock** — which is a very different piece of work from anything we did today, and points straight at that parked BK=32 / load-depth item.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-24 21:00 IST]

Decisive, and my prediction was **half right — and wrong on the half I was most confident about.**

## Result: 96.6% at locked clock (up from 94.5%)

```
ours    13.768 s @ 657 TFLOPS
cuBLAS  13.294 s @ 681 TFLOPS
        474 ms lost  (was 651)
```

## What the clock explained — and what it didn't

**nn and nt recovered fully.** They now match their standalone numbers almost exactly:

| site | free clock | locked | standalone |
|---|---|---|---|
| lm_head-dgrad | 88.2% | **99.8%** | 100.1% |
| down-fwd | 91.6% | **98.8%** | 99.7% |
| wQ-fwd | 92.4% | **97.3%** | 99.5% |
| gate_up-dgrad | 98.4% | 99.5% | 99.8% |

**tn barely moved.** I predicted these would recover *most*; they recovered *least*:

| site | free clock | locked | standalone |
|---|---|---|---|
| gate_up-wgrad | 88.1% | **88.6%** | 100.3% |
| wQ-wgrad | 85.7% | **87.1%** | 100.3% |
| attnOut-wgrad | 85.9% | **87.5%** | 100.3% |
| wV-wgrad | 79.2% | **83.2%** | **105.1%** |
| wK-wgrad | 81.1% | **84.3%** | **105.1%** |

By layout: **nn 98.2%, nt 97.1%, tn 89.2%.**

## So there are two separate effects, and only one is solved

1. **Clock scaling — real, and now understood.** It cost nn/nt about 5 points at free clock. Those layouts are clock-limited and behave exactly as the bench predicts once the clock is fixed.
2. **A tn deficit that is NOT clock.** Same shape, same config, same locked 1400 — standalone says 100–105%, training says 83–94%. That's a 6–21 point gap with clock eliminated as the cause.

**78% of the remaining 474 ms is tn/wgrad** (368 ms), with `gate_up-wgrad` alone at 41.8%.

## What's left to explain it

Clock is out. Beta is out (all launches are beta-zero). Concurrency is out (single stream). What still differs between our bench and training on those shapes:

- **L2 residency** — our harness runs 2000 back-to-back iterations on the *same* buffers; training touches fresh activations each call. These are exactly the high-K, small-output shapes where reuse would matter most.
- **the raster mismatch** — `gate_up-wgrad` runs our `1x2_v` against cuBLAS's `2x1_v`, which by the swap rule should be `1x2_h`. Same mismatch on `wQ-wgrad`/`attnOut-wgrad`.

One notable exception that may be the clue: **`lm_head-wgrad` is at 99.8%** and it's the only tn site that matches. It's also by far the largest (N=50304, 4552 µs) — too big for any L2 reuse to help either library. That's consistent with the L2 story and inconsistent with a pure kernel defect.

Both are testable. The L2 one needs a bench change (fresh buffers per iteration); the raster one we can test today since we already own the `1x2_h` variants. Which first?

## What we achieved

| | before | after |

Plus: V6 crossed parity (98.8→100.8%), the phantom +10% gains were exposed as a measurement bug, and C7517 was traced to `WGMMA_SKEW` — which measurably pays for itself.

## What we found by measuring rather than assuming

- **The backward pass runs on two streams** while cuBLAS uses one — so our kernels were timed sharing SMs. Worth 180 ms. Your colleague was right about it.
- **`mpirun` never forwarded our debug switches.** `BLUBLAS_SM90_TRACE` and `BLUBLAS_SM90_DISABLE` have silently done nothing this whole time.
- **nn/nt are clock-limited; tn isn't.** Unlock the clock and cuBLAS gains +21.7% while we gain +11.7% — on tn just +3.4%, with three sites going *backwards*.

## The one thing still open

**tn is 6–21 points worse in training than on the bench at the same clock.** That's 78% of the remaining 474 ms.

Ruled out by measurement, not argument: clock, beta, stream concurrency, wrong kernel — and, as you spotted, **the raster mismatch, because it's identical in the standalone run that measured 100.3%.** A constant can't explain a difference. ### CLAUDE [2026-08-24 21:21 IST]

It's **C7517** (not 5751) — plus two smaller ones. Three codes, all from `ptxas` when it compiles our Hopper kernels:

**C7517 — 351 of them.** *"wgmma.wait_group is injected by compiler to allow use of registers defined by GMMA"*

The matrix instruction (`wgmma`) is asynchronous — you fire it and it writes its result into registers later. Before you read those registers you must wait for it. Our code does wait, but because of the `skew` knob the wait and the read sit on different paths through the loop, and the compiler can't *prove* every path waits. So it inserts its own wait to be safe.

**C7515 — 6.** *"Potential Performance Loss: wgmma instructions are serialized due to non-wgmma instructions defining accumulator registers"*

Something that isn't a matrix instruction writes the accumulator registers mid-pipeline, which stops the matrix operations from overlapping.

**C7519 — 3.** Same kind of thing, caused by a branch in the code.

## What they mean for us

- **No correctness or precision risk at all.** C7517 is the compiler *protecting* the result — without that wait we'd read half-finished numbers. Every measurement today came back bit-exact against cuBLAS.
- **The only cost is a little speed** — the extra wait shows up as 4 extra `DEPBAR` instructions per kernel.
- **C7515 and C7519 don't touch anything we ship** — all nine are on old experimental configs the dispatcher never selects.
- **C7517 does hit four of our shipping kernels**, and it's caused entirely by `WGMMA_SKEW`. I tested removing skew and it made us *slower*, so the knob earns the cost it brings.

For the report, the short version is: they're informational compiler notes about scheduling, not errors, and the build finished with zero real errors.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-25 10:41 IST]

This came back **backwards from my prediction — and it found something more important than what I was testing.**

Look at the raw numbers, not the percentages:

```
V2b  flush=0   ours 739.2 us   cuBLAS 532.4 us
V2b  flush=1   ours 540.5 us   cuBLAS 532.4 us
```

**Our kernel got 27% FASTER with the flush. cuBLAS didn't move at all.** A cache flush cannot make a kernel faster. So the flush isn't testing what I thought — it's changing something else.

It's **PDL**. All our pins carry `_pdl`, which lets consecutive launches overlap. In the back-to-back benchmark loop, launch N+1 starts before N finishes, so each kernel's *measured duration* is inflated by the overlap. Inserting a 192 MB memset between iterations **breaks that chain**, and the durations become honest. cuBLAS has no PDL, so nothing changes for it.

## Which means my bench-vs-trainer comparison was flawed at the root

The bench %cuB came from the harness's **wall-clock throughput** (where PDL chaining helps us and cuBLAS gets nothing). The training %cuB came from **nsys per-kernel durations**, where GEMMs are separated by other kernels so PDL can't chain at all.

**PDL's benefit may be largely a benchmark artefact** — real when the same kernel fires 2000 times back-to-back, absent in a real training step. That would explain "100% on the bench, 88% in the trainer" far better than L2 ever did.

Let me check the kill switch exists:
> tool `Bash`: Find the PDL kill switch
> tool `Bash`: Check for an SM90 runtime PDL switch

The SM90 runtime switch **does** exist — line 6538. One trap: it tests `getenv(...) != nullptr`, so *any* value disables PDL, including `blublas_NO_PDL=0`. The on-arm has to **unset** it, not set it to zero.
> tool `Bash`: Write the PDL on/off A/B against the trainer numbers

- **no-PDL is still well above the trainer** → PDL is part of it, something else remains.
- **%cuB barely moves** → PDL isn't the cause and I'm wrong twice in a row on this.

Worth saying plainly: **my L2 hypothesis was wrong**, and the run that disproved it is the one that turned up something better. The reason it caught anything is that the controls were in there — V3 and V8c moving *up* by 6 and 13 points is what made it obvious the flush wasn't doing what I claimed.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-25 12:59 IST]

Right — no more hypotheses. Let me go at it with counters instead of guesses.

## What we actually know

The kernel is **byte-identical** in both cases — same binary, same config, same shape, same clock. So the instructions are the same. The difference has to be in either **the data it's given** (addresses, strides, alignment) or **the machine state it runs in** (caches, DRAM traffic, stalls).

That narrows the tooling sharply:

| tool | answers | cost |
|---|---|---|
| **trace** | what the trainer actually passes — strides, alignment, batch | 2 min |
| **ncu counter diff** | *which hardware resource* differs — DRAM bytes, L2 hit rate, stall reasons | ~20 min |
| PC sampling | *where inside the kernel* the stalls moved | only if ncu points there |
| SASS | only if the kernel differed — **it doesn't**, so this is the one thing we can skip |

The ncu diff is the decisive one: same kernel, two contexts, diff the counters. If the trainer moves more DRAM bytes for identical work, that's the answer and it's not arguable.

**Step 1 first though — it's 2 minutes and could short-circuit everything:**

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/BluTrain
export OMPI_ALLOW_RUN_AS_ROOT=1 OMPI_ALLOW_RUN_AS_ROOT_CONFIRM=1
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=3 BLUBLAS_SM90_TRACE=1
make run-train MODE=production CONFIG=train/production/bluscript_config_profile.yaml \
  WITH_BLUBLAS=1 2>&1 | grep '^\[sm90\]' | sort -u | head -30
```

Now let me write the ncu diff:
> tool `Bash`: Write the ncu counter diff between bench and trainer

```bash
# ---------- PUSH (local, you) ----------
cd /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/BLUBLAS/BLUBLAS_kota/BluBridge-BLAS
set +H && git add tools/h27zT_ncu_diff.sh && git commit -m "H27zT: ncu counter diff, same kernel bench vs trainer - L2 ruled out at <=3.6% against an 11pt gap" && git push
```

**Step 1 — the trace (2 min).** Run this first; if the trainer is passing different strides it ends the investigation immediately:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/BluTrain
export OMPI_ALLOW_RUN_AS_ROOT=1 OMPI_ALLOW_RUN_AS_ROOT_CONFIRM=1
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=3 BLUBLAS_SM90_TRACE=1
make run-train MODE=production CONFIG=train/production/bluscript_config_profile.yaml \
  WITH_BLUBLAS=1 2>&1 | grep '^\[sm90\]' | sort -u | head -30
```

**Step 2 — the counter diff.** Bench side runs from the script; it prints the trainer command for you to run separately (it needs mpirun's environment):

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && git pull
GPUID=3 bash tools/h27zT_ncu_diff.sh V5 2>&1 | tail -30
```

I picked **V5 (`gate_up-wgrad`)** because it's the single largest deficit — 39.9% of the whole 494 ms.

## What each counter would tell us

- **`dram__bytes_read` higher in the trainer** → the access pattern genuinely differs. Same arithmetic, more traffic, which points at strides or alignment. This is the outcome I'd bet on.
- **`sm__inst_executed` differs** → the kernel isn't doing the same work, and something upstream is wrong.
- **tensor-pipe % matches but duration doesn't** → pure stall, and PC sampling becomes the next step to find where.
- **everything matches but duration differs** → the kernel is fine and something outside it is interfering.

To your question about SASS: **we can skip it.** It's the same binary and the same config in both contexts, so the instructions are provably identical — there's nothing to diff. That's the one tool this problem doesn't need.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-25 13:06 IST]

Useful — and it **eliminates the arguments as the cause.**

```
all 15 shapes ACCEPT      b=1   a=1   be=0
```

`batch=1`, `alpha=1`, `beta=0` — **identical to what our bench passes.** No batching, so the strides are never used (the gate is `batch > 1 && ...`). And there's no `lda`/`ldb` in the API at all — the leading dimensions are implied by the layout, so both contexts are contiguous by construction.

One inconsistency worth noting but not chasing: **`nn` passes a real `sC`, while `nt` and `tn` pass `sC=0`** even though `want_sC` is non-zero. Harmless at `batch=1` — it's ignored — but it's a latent bug if anyone ever runs those layouts batched.

So: same shape, same config, same clock, same arguments, same binary. **The difference is not in what we're told to compute.** That leaves the data's *addresses* and the *machine state* — both of which are counter-visible.

```bash
# ---------- Step 2: the counter diff (box, GPU 3) ----------
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && git pull
GPUID=3 bash tools/h27zT_ncu_diff.sh V5 2>&1 | tail -30
```

That profiles the bench side and prints the trainer command for you to run after (it needs mpirun's environment).

One candidate the trace *can't* see, which I'd now put near the top: **TLB pressure**. Our bench touches ~100 MB total and reuses it; the trainer walks a 1.7B-parameter model plus activations across many gigabytes. Same kernel, same access pattern, but far more address-translation work. That would show up as higher memory stalls with unchanged DRAM bytes — a signature the counters will separate cleanly from the alignment story.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-25 14:47 IST]

Genuinely good question, and the answer is **both — for different jobs.**

## Why locked, for finding the cause

At a locked clock both libraries run at the same speed, so any difference left is **the code**. It removes a variable. If I diagnose at free clock I can't tell "our kernel is slower" from "our kernel got less clock" — and we already got burned by exactly that: §H27zD's whole finding was that a free-clock comparison was measuring the boost schedule, not the kernels.

## Why free, for knowing the real number

Production runs free, so that's the number that matters to you. And it's **not the same number**:

```
trainer, free clock    94.5% of cuBLAS
trainer, locked 1400   96.6%
```

## And this is the important part — we already know there are TWO separate problems

| problem | shows at | size |
|---|---|---|
| **tn / wgrad gap** | **both** locked and free | 5.7–11.2 points |
| **clock-scaling gap** | **free only** | ~5 points on nn/nt |

The tn gap is clock-independent — it's 88.6% locked and 88.1% free. So locking is the right way to chase it, and that's what I'm doing now.

The nn/nt gap is the opposite: at a locked clock those shapes match perfectly (99.6%), and they only lose ~5 points when the clock is free, because cuBLAS converts extra clock into throughput better than we do (+21.7% vs +11.7%). **That one can only be investigated at free clock**, and it's still open.

So: locked now for the tn cause, and free clock for the scaling problem afterwards. Two investigations, two conditions.

## Your other suggestion is right and we should add it

**Observing what clock the trainer actually settles at** — we've never measured that. Every free-clock number we have assumes "free" without knowing the operating point. If the trainer settles at 1650 under sustained load, that's the clock we should be tuning against, not 1400 and not the 1980 boost ceiling.

That's cheap to capture — a clock sampler alongside a normal free-clock training run:

```bash

( while :; do nvidia-smi -i 3 --query-gpu=clocks.sm,power.draw,temperature.gpu,clocks_throttle_reasons.active \
    --format=csv,noheader,nounits; sleep 0.5; done > /tmp/train_clock.csv ) &
SAMPLER=$!
export OMPI_ALLOW_RUN_AS_ROOT=1 OMPI_ALLOW_RUN_AS_ROOT_CONFIRM=1 CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=3
make run-train-mpi MODE=production NP=1 WITH_BLUBLAS=1 \
  CONFIG=train/production/bluscript_config_profile.yaml 2>&1 | tail -20
kill $SAMPLER
awk -F, '{n++;s+=$1;if(mn==""||$1<mn)mn=$1;if($1>mx)mx=$1}END{printf "clock avg %.0f  min %.0f  max %.0f  over %d samples\n",s/n,mn,mx,n}' /tmp/train_clock.csv
```

I'd finish the ncu diff first since it's half-done and the tn gap is 78% of the loss — but the clock profile is worth having before we optimise anything for free-clock behaviour, precisely so we're not tuning against the wrong operating point.

Every counter within 0.6%, two of them exact to the decimal.

**That's the result that makes the whole experiment trustworthy.** It proves three things at once:

1. **ncu measures the same thing in both contexts** — no methodological artefact
2. **Being inside the trainer does not, by itself, perturb a GEMM** — same memory traffic, same stalls, same instruction count
3. Therefore **whatever is wrong with V5 is specific to V5**, not to "running in training"

So when the V5 trainer counters land, any difference will be real and attributable. That's exactly the position I wanted before drawing a conclusion.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-25 15:14 IST]

**This is the answer, and it's not what any of us expected.**

```
V5, bench vs trainer, under ncu:
  duration          1,026,080 ns  ->  1,028,976 ns   +0.3%
  DRAM read           704.7 MB    ->    704.7 MB     -0.0%
  inst executed      165,511,812  ->  165,513,783    +0.0%
  tensor pipe             98.57%  ->      98.47%     -0.1
  every stall counter        identical
```

**The kernel is identical in both contexts.** Same traffic, same instructions, same stalls, same duration to 0.3%.

But nsys said V5 in the trainer takes **1210 µs**. Under ncu it takes **1029 µs** — the same as the bench.

## Why the two disagree

**ncu serialises and isolates each kernel.** nsys measures it *in situ*, as a span from launch to completion.

Our pins carry **PDL**, which lets a kernel *start before the previous one finishes*. So in the trainer, nsys's span for our GEMM includes the period where it's sharing SMs with the tail of whatever ran before it. cuBLAS has no PDL, so its spans are clean.

**That is the same mechanism h27zQ stumbled on** — the memset broke the PDL chain and our "duration" dropped 27% (739→540 µs) while cuBLAS didn't move. I identified the mechanism then but didn't realise it applied to the *trainer* measurement too.

1210 − 1029 = **181 µs, 17.6% inflation** — right in line with the 11.2-point gap.

## What this means

**The per-kernel comparison is biased against us, and the tn "deficit" may be largely measurement.** h27zR looked like it cleared PDL, but that measured the *harness's wall-clock*, where PDL genuinely helps. In nsys per-kernel it does the opposite — inflates our spans.

It also fits something that never quite added up: August had end-to-end at **93.8%** while per-kernel said **80.8%**. If per-kernel understates us, that's exactly the shape you'd expect.

The test — re-run the trainer nsys capture with PDL off. But first, `blublas_NO_PDL` isn't in the forwarded list, so it would silently do nothing:
> tool `Bash`: Forward the PDL kill switch through mpirun

```bash
# ---------- PUSH (local, you) ----------
cd /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/BLUBLAS/BLUBLAS_kota/BluBridge-BLAS
set +H && git add BluTrain/Makefile && git commit -m "H27zV: forward blublas_NO_PDL through mpirun - needed to test whether PDL inflates our nsys per-kernel spans in the trainer" && git push
```

```bash
# ---------- the decisive test: same trainer capture, PDL OFF (box, GPU 3, ~10 min) ----------
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas && git pull
sudo nvidia-smi -i 3 -lgc 1400,1400
cd BluTrain
export OMPI_ALLOW_RUN_AS_ROOT=1 OMPI_ALLOW_RUN_AS_ROOT_CONFIRM=1
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=3 BLUTRAIN_BWD_SINGLE_STREAM=1 blublas_NO_PDL=1
make nsys-train MODE=production NP=1 WITH_BLUBLAS=1 NSYS_OUT=day2_blublas_nopdl 2>&1 | tail -4
sudo nvidia-smi -i 3 -rgc
```

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
python3 tools/nsys_train_gemm_pair.py \
  BluTrain/profiling_reports/day2_blublas_nopdl/day2_blublas_nopdl_0.sqlite \
  BluTrain/profiling_reports/day2_cublas/day2_cublas_0.sqlite
```

The prediction, stated before the run: **the tn sites should jump** — V5 from 88.8% toward ~99%, V1 from 83.5%, V2 from 87.1% — while **V3, V8c and lm_head-wgrad barely move**, because they were already at 99%+ and had nothing inflated to give back.

If that happens, the conclusion is: **we do not have a tn kernel deficit.** We have a measurement in which PDL — a feature that genuinely helps wall-clock throughput — makes our per-kernel spans look worse than they are. The real production question then becomes the end-to-end tok/s, not this table.

If the tn sites *don't* move, then PDL isn't it either, and we'd be left with the fact that ncu says the kernel is identical while nsys says it's 17% slower — which would point at something in how nsys attributes the span, and I'd go at that directly.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-25 15:24 IST]

**The switch arrived, and it's a big result.**

```
ours, PDL on    13,814.3 ms   over 34,720 launches
ours, PDL off   13,460.8 ms   over 34,720 launches    -353.5 ms
cuBLAS          13,320.0 ms
```

Turning PDL **off** made our per-kernel total **353 ms faster** — which is only possible if PDL was inflating the spans, not the work. Same kernels, same count, same clock.

**That moves us from 96.4% to 99.0% of cuBLAS on GEMM**, and the gap from 494 ms to 141 ms.

So the "tn deficit" was largely an artefact of measuring PDL-enabled kernels with a tool that times launch-to-completion. ncu already told us the kernel itself is identical (+0.3%); this confirms why nsys disagreed.

Let me see which sites gave it back:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas
python3 tools/nsys_train_gemm_pair.py \
  BluTrain/profiling_reports/day2_blublas_nopdl/day2_blublas_nopdl_0.sqlite \
  BluTrain/profiling_reports/day2_cublas/day2_cublas_0.sqlite
```

Two things I want to be careful about before calling this closed:

**Which number is "true" depends on the question.** With PDL off, per-kernel spans are honest and we're at 99.0% — that's the fair *kernel-vs-kernel* comparison. But in production PDL stays **on**, because the overlap is a genuine wall-clock win that per-kernel measurement structurally cannot see. So neither 96.4% nor 99.0% is the production number — **the end-to-end tok/s is**, and we still haven't measured that on this box.

**And that run had `BLUBLAS_SM90_TRACE` still exported** (the 4.5 MB log), so every dispatch did an `fprintf`. That's host-side and shouldn't touch kernel durations, but if the per-site numbers look odd I'll want it re-run clean before we bank them.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-25 15:34 IST]

Very good questions. Let me answer each in plain terms, then verify the answers with data we already have.

## What PDL does

It lets the **next** kernel's blocks be *launched* onto the SMs before the current kernel finishes. The new blocks immediately hit a wait — `cudaGridDependencySynchronize()` — and sit there until the previous kernel signals it's done with the data. The point is that the launch overhead and prologue happen *during* the previous kernel instead of after it.

## Why it helped standalone

The bench fires **2000 copies of the same kernel back-to-back**. Every boundary is GEMM→GEMM, and both sides have PDL. The producer signals early with `griddep_launch_dependents()`, the consumer is already resident and waiting, so the overlap is real. Wall clock genuinely improves — V1 +6.25% in §H27zv-D, +7.2% again today.

## Why it doesn't help in training

**PDL is a property of a *pair* of consecutive launches.** Both sides must participate. In the trainer the sequence isn't GEMM→GEMM — it's

```
GEMM -> convert_type -> GEMM -> gqa -> GEMM -> strided_copy -> ...
```

Non-GEMM kernels are **58% of GPU time** and none of them use PDL. So at nearly every boundary the producer never signals early and the consumer gets nothing. **We didn't lose the PDL benefit in training — we never had it there.**

## Why it made the number look *worse*

This is the part that matters. With PDL on, our blocks get **launched early and then block on the wait**. So:

- **start timestamp** — early (blocks are resident)
- **end timestamp** — unchanged (the work happens when it always would)
- **measured duration** — longer

nsys times launch-to-completion, so it charges us for the waiting. The work is identical; only the span stretched. That's exactly why **ncu — which isolates each kernel — showed no difference at all (+0.3%)**, while nsys showed 17%.

## But I should prove that rather than assert it

If I'm right, PDL-on should have a **larger sum of spans but the same or better wall-clock**. Both are in the sqlites we already have — no new runs:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/BluTrain
for d in day2_blublas day2_blublas_nopdl; do
  echo "=== $d ==="
  sqlite3 profiling_reports/$d/${d}_0.sqlite "
    SELECT 'sum of spans  ' || ROUND(SUM(k.end-k.start)/1e6,1) || ' ms'
    FROM CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_KERNEL k JOIN StringIds s ON k.demangledName=s.id
    WHERE s.value LIKE '%bgemm_sm90%';
    SELECT 'wall span     ' || ROUND((MAX(k.end)-MIN(k.start))/1e6,1) || ' ms'
    FROM CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_KERNEL k JOIN StringIds s ON k.demangledName=s.id
    WHERE s.value LIKE '%bgemm_sm90%';
    SELECT 'ALL kernels   ' || ROUND(SUM(k.end-k.start)/1e6,1) || ' ms over ' || COUNT(*) || ' launches'
    FROM CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_KERNEL k;"
done
```

And the direct test of the "no GEMM→GEMM adjacency" claim:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/BluTrain
sqlite3 profiling_reports/day2_blublas/day2_blublas_0.sqlite "
WITH k AS (SELECT s.value AS nm, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY x.start) rn
           FROM CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_KERNEL x JOIN StringIds s ON x.demangledName=s.id)
SELECT CASE WHEN a.nm LIKE '%bgemm_sm90%' AND b.nm LIKE '%bgemm_sm90%' THEN 'GEMM -> GEMM'
            WHEN a.nm LIKE '%bgemm_sm90%' THEN 'GEMM -> other' END AS pair, COUNT(*)
FROM k a JOIN k b ON b.rn=a.rn+1
WHERE a.nm LIKE '%bgemm_sm90%' GROUP BY 1;"
```

If most GEMMs are followed by a non-GEMM, PDL had nothing to work with — and that closes the question properly instead of on a plausible story.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-25 15:40 IST]

Yes — you've got the mechanism exactly right. **PDL needs both sides.** For a `GEMM → convert_type` boundary to overlap, the convert kernel must also be launched with the PDL attribute, call `cudaGridDependencySynchronize()` before touching our output, and call `cudaTriggerProgrammaticLaunchCompletion()` once it's done reading its own inputs.

So in principle, yes — put PDL on every kernel and the whole chain can overlap.

**But before we spend any effort on it, we should measure what the prize actually is.** Three reasons to be careful:

1. **It's ~37 non-GEMM kernels in BluTrain**, not our library — convert_type, gqa, strided_copy, and the rest.
2. **Correctness risk is real.** PDL means the next kernel starts before the previous finishes. If the sync is placed wrong, it reads half-written data and gives silently wrong results. That's a lot of surface area to get right.
3. **PDL only overlaps the *prologue* of the next kernel with the *tail* of the current one.** It doesn't overlap whole kernels. So the ceiling is roughly the launch-plus-prologue time, not the kernel time.

## The prize is measurable right now, from data we already have

If the trainer's kernels are already packed back-to-back with no dead time, PDL has nothing to fill and the whole exercise is worthless. If there are real gaps, that's the ceiling.

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/BluTrain
sqlite3 profiling_reports/day2_blublas/day2_blublas_0.sqlite "
WITH k AS (SELECT x.start AS s, x.end AS e,
                  LAG(x.end) OVER (PARTITION BY x.streamId ORDER BY x.start) AS prev_end
           FROM CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_KERNEL x)
SELECT COUNT(*)                                   AS boundaries,
       ROUND(SUM(MAX(s-prev_end,0))/1e6,1)||' ms' AS total_dead_time,
       ROUND(AVG(MAX(s-prev_end,0))/1e3,2)||' us' AS avg_gap,
       ROUND(SUM(e-s)/1e6,1)||' ms'               AS total_kernel_time
FROM k WHERE prev_end IS NOT NULL;"
```

That gives the **total dead time between consecutive kernels** across the whole run. Read it like this:

- **dead time is large (say >5% of kernel time)** → PDL everywhere could genuinely recover a chunk of it, and it's worth planning properly
- **dead time is near zero** → the GPU is already saturated back-to-back, PDL has nothing to fill, and adding it to 37 kernels buys nothing while risking correctness

My honest expectation is the second, because these are big kernels on one stream and the driver already pipelines launches well. But that's a guess, and the query settles it in five seconds.

One more thing worth knowing: in the standalone bench, PDL's average gain was only **+0.93%** — and V1's +6.25% was an outlier precisely because it's a tiny 57 µs kernel where launch overhead is a large fraction. That's the shape of kernel PDL helps. The trainer does have short kernels, so it isn't hopeless — but the gap measurement tells us for certain rather than by analogy.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-25 15:53 IST]

That number is misleading and it's my query's fault — let me correct it.

`PARTITION BY streamId` counts a gap on **every stream separately**. If there are several streams and most sit idle while one works, each idle stream reports its whole idle period as "dead time". That's how you get 128.7 s of "dead" against 36.7 s of work — it's double-counting across streams, not real GPU idle.

The honest measure is the **union** of busy intervals against the wall-clock span:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/BluTrain
python3 - <<'PY'
import sqlite3
db=sqlite3.connect("profiling_reports/day2_blublas/day2_blublas_0.sqlite")
iv=db.execute("SELECT start,end FROM CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_KERNEL ORDER BY start").fetchall()
print("kernels: %d   streams: %d"%(len(iv),
      db.execute("SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT streamId) FROM CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_KERNEL").fetchone()[0]))
# merge overlapping intervals -> real GPU-busy time
busy=0; s,e=iv[0]
for a,b in iv[1:]:
    if a>e: busy+=e-s; s,e=a,b
    else:   e=max(e,b)
busy+=e-s
span=iv[-1][1]-iv[0][0]
print("wall span      %9.1f ms"%(span/1e6))
print("GPU busy       %9.1f ms   (%.1f%%)"%(busy/1e6, 100*busy/span))
print("GPU IDLE       %9.1f ms   (%.1f%%)  <- the real ceiling for launch-overlap work"%
      ((span-busy)/1e6, 100*(span-busy)/span))
print("sum of spans   %9.1f ms   (%.2fx busy -> that excess IS the overlap)"%
      (sum(b-a for a,b in iv)/1e6, sum(b-a for a,b in iv)/busy))
PY
```

This gives three things at once:

- **real GPU idle** — the actual ceiling on anything PDL-like could recover
- **sum-of-spans ÷ busy** — if that ratio is above 1.0, kernels are genuinely overlapping, which independently confirms the PDL story from a different angle
- and it's stream-count-aware, so it can't be fooled the way my last query was

Two caveats to keep in mind when reading it: this run was **under nsys**, which adds overhead, and the span includes **startup and data loading** before steady state. So treat the idle figure as an upper bound, not a target.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-25 15:55 IST]

Two things, and one of them means I was wrong a moment ago.

**I was wrong about the double-counting.** There's only **1 stream** — so my `PARTITION BY streamId` query wasn't inflating anything. The 128.7 s was real for that measurement.

**But it's still not what it looks like: this run was under nsys.** 78% idle across a 165 s span with `--trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt` is mostly profiling overhead between launches, not what production does. Treat it as an upper bound only — the unprofiled number will be far lower.

## The genuinely interesting number is the overlap

```
sum of spans   36,716.3 ms
GPU busy       36,335.1 ms
excess            381.2 ms   =  1.01x
```

Kernels overlap by **1%**. And here's the connection: turning PDL off removed **353.5 ms** from the GEMM sum. So **PDL accounts for ~93% of all the kernel overlap in the entire run** (353 of 381 ms).

That pins the mechanism exactly. What it does *not* yet tell us is whether those 353 ms are a **real wall-clock saving** or just stretched spans — because the union counts a launched-but-blocked kernel as busy either way.

One query settles it:

```bash
cd ~/gautam_k/blublas/BluTrain
python3 - <<'PY'
import sqlite3
for d in ("day2_blublas","day2_blublas_nopdl"):
    db=sqlite3.connect("profiling_reports/%s/%s_0.sqlite"%(d,d))
    iv=db.execute("SELECT start,end FROM CUPTI_ACTIVITY_KIND_KERNEL ORDER BY start").fetchall()
    busy=0; s,e=iv[0]
    for a,b in iv[1:]:
        if a>e: busy+=e-s; s,e=a,b
        else:   e=max(e,b)
    busy+=e-s
    tot=sum(b-a for a,b in iv)
    print("  %-20s busy(union) %9.1f ms   sum %9.1f ms   overlap %6.1f ms"%(
          d, busy/1e6, tot/1e6, (tot-busy)/1e6))
PY
```

- **The two unions equal** → PDL only stretches spans, buys nothing here, and could be turned off for free (which would also make every future nsys measurement honest).

## The question we started with this morning

Standalone our kernels are at 100% of cuBLAS. In the training script they looked like 88%. Why?

## The answer — we found it

**It was a measurement problem, not a real problem.**

Our kernels use PDL, which starts the next kernel a bit early. The profiler measures a kernel from "started" to "finished", so it counts that early-start waiting time as if the kernel were slow. cuBLAS doesn't use PDL, so it doesn't get charged for it.

Three separate pieces of evidence, all agreeing:

## So where we actually stand

**Our GEMM is 99.0% of cuBLAS in the real trainer.** Not 88%, not 96.4%.

**PDL's average gain was +0.93%, not 7%.** V1 got +6.25 and dragged the headline. Ten of the fifteen shapes gained less than the measurement floor.

## Now the reconciliation — and it's exact

```
standalone bench, PDL OFF   99.09%    <- mean of the left column above
trainer,          PDL OFF   99.0%     <- measured today
```

**Same number.** Our kernel is 99% of cuBLAS in both places once PDL is out of the picture. Nothing was lost, and nothing is unexplained.

## Why PDL paid in the bench but not in the trainer

I actually wrote the reason down when we adopted it, at [analyzations_h200.md:18236](cublas_rev_eng_binary/analyzations_h200.md#L18236):

> **PDL is a property of the PAIR of consecutive launches, not of one kernel.** … If X is PDL-on and Y is PDL-off, Y never opts in and **that boundary gets zero overlap**.

- **In the bench**, the loop runs the *same kernel* thousands of times back-to-back. Every single boundary is our-PDL-kernel → our-PDL-kernel. Both halves opt in, so PDL pays.
- **In the trainer**, our GEMM's neighbours are BluTrain's own kernels — converts, layernorms, the gqa attention kernels. That's 62.3% of GPU time and 121,563 launches, and **none of them opt in.** Almost every boundary is broken, so PDL collects nothing.

The union measurement confirms it: PDL earned **20.6 ms real overlap** in the whole trainer run — 0.06%, versus 0.93% in the bench. About fifteen times less, exactly as the broken-chain argument predicts.

## The one thing this does change

Our standalone headline of **100.02% is slightly flattered.** It includes +0.93% of PDL benefit that only materializes when GEMMs run back-to-back. Real training isn't GEMM-dense, so that part doesn't transfer.

**Our honest, transferable number is 99%, not 100%.** That's a 1-point correction to the standalone claim — small, but I should record it rather than keep quoting 100.02 as if it carries over.

And it makes your earlier question the interesting one again: PDL isn't dead in training, it's *disconnected*. If BluTrain's own kernels opted in, the chain would reconnect and the bench's +0.93% would become reachable. Whether that's worth doing is a separate measurement — the profiled run can't tell us, because nsys spreads the kernels apart and hides the very gaps PDL would fill.

**None of these is attention.** All five are linear layers. Nothing was assumed falsely.

## Where the confusion comes from — the names

`wQ`, `wK`, `wV`, `attnOut` *sound* like attention, but they are the **Linear layers around it**, not the attention math:

```
x ──► wQ ──┐
x ──► wK ──┼──► [ GQA attention kernel ]──► attnOut ──► ...
x ──► wV ──┘      QK^T, softmax, PV
   ▲                    ▲                      ▲
   │                    │                      │
  OURS            THEIRS (fused)              OURS
```

- **wQ / wK / wV** = the projections that *produce* Q, K and V. Plain matmuls. **Ours.**
- **The attention itself** — QK^T, softmax, PV — happens inside `gqa_v62`. **Theirs, fused.**
- **attnOut** = the W_O output projection *after* attention. Plain matmul. **Ours.**

So `attnOut` is not attention. It's the linear layer that follows attention.

## Why 21 call sites but only 15 shapes

7 weights × 3 passes (fwd / dgrad / wgrad) = **21 call sites**. But two pairs share shapes:

- **wV has the same shape as wK** — both project 2048 → 512
- **attnOut has the same shape as wQ** — both are 2048 → 2048

21 − 3 − 3 = **15 distinct shapes.** That's exactly why the tuning list is 15 while the call-site list is 21.

## So nothing was wasted

Every one of the 21 sites is a real matmul that our library actually serves. The profile confirms it — 34,720 `bgemm_sm90_kernel` launches, and zero cuBLAS GEMM kernels anywhere in the run.

The attention kernels are simply a separate 19.68% of GPU time that was never ours to optimize, and I never counted them as ours.

## PDL's effect on real speed vs on the measurement

```
                        real speed gain      measured span inflation
standalone bench          +0.93%                    none
trainer                   +0.06%                  +381 ms  (2.8%)
```

**PDL barely changes speed anywhere. But it only distorts the *measurement* in the trainer.** Two reasons stack up:

### 1. The bench and nsys measure different things

- **The bench** times the whole loop with CUDA events and divides by iterations. It measures **wall clock**. If a kernel starts early and waits, that waiting is inside the loop anyway — it can't inflate anything.
- **nsys per-kernel sum** measures each kernel from *start* to *end* and adds them up. A kernel that starts early and waits is counted as a long kernel.

So the same PDL behaviour is invisible to one method and very visible to the other.

### 2. In the trainer the early start turns into pure waiting

Think of PDL as arriving early for a meeting room:

- **In the bench**, the previous meeting is also ours, and it leaves early too. You arrive early, you *start* early — real time saved.
- **In the trainer**, the previous kernel is BluTrain's (a convert, a gqa kernel). It doesn't leave early. So you stand in the corridor for the full duration. Your "meeting length" now includes corridor time, but nothing was actually saved.

That corridor wait is only about **11 µs per launch** — tiny. But it's counted **34,720 times**, and that's how you get 381 ms.

## So which number is real?

The **union** measurement settles it — it counts wall clock, not spans:

```
PDL ON    sum 36,716.3 ms    union 36,335.1 ms
PDL OFF   sum 36,355.7 ms    union 36,355.7 ms   <- exactly 0 overlap
```

Real wall-clock difference: **20.6 ms.** The other 360 ms was never real time — it was the same waiting counted once per kernel.

**Bottom line: PDL is not hurting the trainer. It's hurting the profiler.** That's exactly why the fresh capture runs with `blublas_NO_PDL=1` — not to make us faster, but to make the per-kernel numbers honest.

**Both — locked first, then free.** Locked alone would be dishonest about production; free alone can't tell a work problem from a clock problem.

## The plan

```
phase 1   LOCK_MHZ=1400   TAG=h27zW        ~25 min
phase 2   LOCK_MHZ=0      TAG=h27zW_free   ~25 min
```

Each phase runs both arms — **cuBLAS first, then BluBLAS with `blublas_NO_PDL=1`**. cuBLAS goes first deliberately: it's the arm that historically gained from a cold card, so any leftover order effect works against us, never for us.

## Why locked first

Locking pins the only variable that isn't our code. Whatever gap survives at a fixed 1400 MHz is **real work** — instructions, stalls, memory traffic. This is the number that sits next to the standalone 99.09%, and it's the one that tells us whether the kernel itself needs work.

If we ran free first and saw a gap, we couldn't tell whether we're doing more work or just being given less clock.

## Why free second

Production runs free, so this is what the model actually gets. And we already know there's an asymmetry waiting there — from the parked power/clock track:

> unlocking gains cuBLAS **+21.7%** but gains us only **+11.7%**, because we issue **2.24× the instructions** and the governor hands us less clock in return

So phase 2 will probably read worse than phase 1. That difference isn't noise to explain away — **it is the finding**, and it's the thing that decides what we work on next.

## What each outcome means

| phase 1 (locked) | phase 2 (free) | what it means | what we do |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~99% | ~99% | done — no gap anywhere | move off GEMM entirely |
| ~99% | ~94% | kernel is fine, **clock/power is the gap** | resume the parked power/clock track; lever is instruction count |
| <97% | <97% | real work deficit in specific shapes | fix those shapes |

My expectation, given everything so far, is the **middle row** — and if so, the next real target isn't the GEMM at all, it's the 2.24× instruction count that's costing us clock.

And if a parallel build fails it **retries once serially** and says so in the log. A build that only works at `-j1` is a Makefile race worth knowing about — but it must not cost us the capture, and it must not be hidden either.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-25 16:59 IST]

Fair question. Here's the honest accounting.

## Why it rebuilds at all

**Because `WITH_BLUBLAS` flips between the two arms.** `WITH_BLUBLAS=0` and `WITH_BLUBLAS=1` produce a *different* `libtensor.so` at the *same* path — one linked against cuBLAS, one against libblublas. So switching backends always rebuilds libtensor. That's unavoidable with this Makefile.

So it's 4 builds: cublas + blublas in phase 1, then the same two again in phase 2 (phase 1 ended on blublas, phase 2 starts on cublas → flip → rebuild).

## The one thing that is genuinely redundant

`nsys-train: all` already builds. So my explicit `make all` before it means make runs twice per arm.

**But that's deliberate, and the second one costs nothing.** The explicit build happens *before* the clock lock and the sampler start; by the time `nsys-train` runs its own `all`, everything is up to date and it's a no-op. That's what keeps a multi-minute CPU-only compile out of the clock-locked GPU window — your "separate BUILD and RUN blocks" rule.

## Could we get it down to 2 builds?

Yes — restructure to outer-loop-by-arm: build cublas once → run it locked → run it free; build blublas once → run locked → run free.

**I'd rather not.** That puts a full build and an extra run between cuBLAS and BluBLAS *within* a phase, and the two arms of a phase being measured close together is the whole basis of the comparison. We already know this setup is order-sensitive — cuBLAS gained from being measured on a cold card. Saving ~5 minutes isn't worth loosening that.

With `-j32` each build should drop from ~10 min to ~2–3 min, so it's roughly **10 min of build inside a ~30 min campaign**. The script now prints each build's wall time, so we'll see the real number rather than my estimate.

## What the last pass fixed

**Placement assertion** — the one that could have silently ruined everything. `mpirun` exports only what `-x` names, so if `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` didn't survive, the rank lands on **GPU 0 — which is busy with someone else's job**. The sampler now records peak memory on GPU 3, and the run aborts if it stays under 1000 MiB. Before this, a misplaced run would have produced a plausible-looking but meaningless capture.

**sqlite detection by glob** — some nsys builds write `%q{OMPI_COMM_WORLD_RANK}` literally instead of expanding it (there are files like that sitting in the repo right now). The exact-name check would have reported "capture MISSING" on a perfectly good capture.

## Correction — I got the PDL story wrong

I told you no-PDL lifted dgrad to 98–100%. **That was from the trace-contaminated run, and it's wrong.** With PDL genuinely off, dgrad is 87.7% / 84.6%.

Why the trace flattered it: `BLUBLAS_SM90_TRACE` printf's on the host for every one of the 34,720 calls. That serializes the host and spreads the launches apart — which *suppressed the very overlap* that hurts dgrad. So dgrad looked clean for the wrong reason.

## The real cause is the second stream, and it's in our own notes

Our backward puts **8,680 GEMMs (all the wgrad sites) on stream 16** while everything else runs on stream 7. cuBLAS runs **all 34,720 on one stream**. So our dgrad kernels have SMs stolen by concurrent wgrad; cuBLAS's dgrad never shares. That's exactly the dgrad-only signature we see.

**This is not a bug — the overlap is a real wall-clock win.** Proof: at locked 1400 our GEMM per-kernel sum reads 95.9%, yet **end-to-end tok/s is 23,389 vs cuBLAS 23,337 — we're 0.22% faster.** The overlap wins back what the per-kernel sum charges us.

## What free clocks actually showed

Not a clock deficit — **cuBLAS averaged 1948 MHz, we averaged 1942 MHz.** Six MHz apart. But we drew 647 W vs their 673 W, and we lost more: GEMM 95.9% → 93.1%, tok/s **27,353 vs 27,788 (−1.57%)**. So at high clock our kernels scale worse than cuBLAS's, which is a different problem from the one the parked power/clock track predicted.

## The actual mechanism, per site

Clock went 1410 → ~1950, a **1.383×** increase. What each library converted that into:

```
                    ours          cuBLAS
down-fwd           1.160x         1.232x     <- cuBLAS converts clock much better
wQ-fwd/wO-fwd      1.195x         1.249x
gate_up-fwd        1.158x         1.172x
```

Neither reaches 1.383× — both are bandwidth/latency-bound. But **cuBLAS extracts more throughput per extra MHz on the `nn` forward shapes**, and that difference *is* the free-clock gap.

## And the second stream earns nothing at free clocks

```
tok/s   multistream ON   OFF      delta
locked      23,389     23,292    +0.42%
free        27,353     27,357    -0.01%
```

At high clock the GPU is already saturated — there's no idle capacity left to overlap into. So the overlap is worth ~0.4% locked and **zero** in production conditions, while costing 3.4 points of apparent per-kernel performance. Worth reconsidering whether to keep it.

## Next

The whole remaining problem is now **three `nn` forward sites**: `down-fwd`, `wQ/wO-fwd`, `gate_up-fwd`. And there's a standing discrepancy on `wQ/wO-fwd` — our validated bench says **99.5%** for that exact shape and config, the trainer says **96.8%** locked / 92.6% free. # Did multistream affect our kernels? YES — measured

Our own kernel time, multistream OFF → ON:

```
locked    fwd    6797.6 -> 6802.2    +4.6 ms   +0.07%   untouched
          dgrad  3294.2 -> 3590.2  +296.0 ms   +9.0%    slower
          wgrad  3369.4 -> 3527.3  +157.9 ms   +4.7%    slower
free      fwd    5821.1 -> 5823.9    +2.8 ms   +0.05%   untouched
          dgrad  2893.4 -> 3209.9  +316.5 ms  +10.9%    slower
          wgrad  2903.7 -> 3060.9  +157.2 ms   +5.4%    slower
```

**dgrad and wgrad genuinely run ~9% and ~5% slower** when the second stream is on, because they execute at the same time and fight over the same SMs. Forward is untouched — it's single-stream either way.

But they also overlap, so less wall-clock passes: union 13,461.2 → 13,398.4 = **62.8 ms actually saved**. Net effect on training:

```
tok/s   locked   23,292 -> 23,389   +0.42%
        free     27,357 -> 27,353   -0.01%
```

**A small win at locked clocks, exactly nothing at free clocks** — and free is production. At high clock the GPU is already saturated, so there's no idle capacity left to overlap into.

# No — cuBLAS never ran multistream

This is important and I should have said it clearly earlier. The secondary stream is created **only** in the `WITH_MYBLAS` code path. With `WITH_BLUBLAS=0`, `MatmulBackward.cu` never creates it. Verified in all four captures: cuBLAS had **streamId 7 only, 34,720 launches, 0.0 ms hidden**.

So the on/off toggle changes *only our arm*. Proof — cuBLAS is essentially identical across both campaigns:


Which also means the earlier "cuBLAS hides 0.0 ms" is a fact about **the harness**, not about cuBLAS — it would overlap too if the trainer gave it two streams.

**H200 limits:** SM clock max **1980 MHz** · memory clock **3201 MHz** · power limit **700 W** (max = default = 700).

```

                        min   mean   max      mean   peak
LOCKED  cuBLAS h27zW   1410   1410   1410      449    469
        ours   h27zW   1410   1410   1410      430    481
        cuBLAS h27zX   1410   1410   1410      462    468
        ours   h27zX   1410   1410   1410      432    481

        ours   h27zW   1800   1942   1965      648    689
        cuBLAS h27zX   1950   1964   1980      657    690
        ours   h27zX   1875   1939   1980      638    693
```

**Reading it:**
- **Locked held perfectly** — 1410 MHz flat, every arm. (My earlier "mean 1353, 595 W" came from the one contaminated CSV.)
- **At free clocks cuBLAS runs 1948–1964, we run 1939–1942** — about **10–25 MHz higher for cuBLAS**, i.e. 0.5–1.3%.
- **We draw ~20–25 W LESS than cuBLAS at both clock settings**, and neither is near the 700 W cap (peaks 690–695 W, means 638–674 W).

**Nobody is power-capped.** So this is not "cuBLAS is allowed more watts." Power tracks work actually issued, so drawing *less* while going *slower* means our units are idle more — we stall more. That's a hypothesis with a matching signature, not yet proven.

# The terms, plainly

- **sum** — add up every kernel's start-to-finish time. If two kernels run at the same time, their overlap gets counted twice.
- **union** — merge the time intervals first, so overlapping time is counted once. This is real elapsed GPU-busy time.
- **hidden** = sum − union. How much work ran in parallel with other work.
- **%cuB** — cuBLAS time ÷ our time. Above 100% means we're faster.
- **tok/s** — tokens per second the trainer actually achieved. The only number that is purely wall-clock and can't be distorted by accounting.
- **locked clocks** — we pin the GPU to 1400 MHz so clock can't vary between the two libraries. Fair kernel comparison.
- **free clocks** — the GPU picks its own clock, up to 1980. This is what production does.

# CLEARED

1. **dgrad and wgrad are fine.** At single-stream, locked: dgrad **100.0%** (+0.3 ms of 3294), wgrad **99.0%**. The 75–89% readings were stream contention, not kernel quality.
2. **We beat cuBLAS on `wK/wV-dgrad`** — 109.3% locked, 105.3% free. cuBLAS needs split-K plus a reduce kernel there; we don't.
3. **At locked 1400 we are at parity.** GEMM 99.1%, whole run 99.6%, tok/s a tie.
4. **PDL does not affect real throughput** — 0.06% (20.6 ms of 36,355). It only inflated nsys per-kernel spans.
5. **cuBLAS never runs multistream**; the toggle is ours alone.
6. **Nobody is power-capped**, and the locked clock held exactly.
7. **The measurement method is now verified** — 100% pairing agreement, and the duration cuts used for per-site attribution are the #1 and #2 largest gaps in the distribution by 87× and 41× over the next contender, with **zero ambiguous launches**.
8. **Everything except the matmul is identical** — 138,843 non-GEMM launches in both arms, differing by 7.2 ms once each library's own split-K reduce is set aside.

1. **The free-clock gap — the whole remaining problem.** 97.0% GEMM, 98.5% whole run, **−1.54% tok/s**, reproduced twice. It lives in the **forward `nn` sites**: `down-fwd` 92.7%, `wQ/wO-fwd` 92.6%, `gate_up-fwd` 98.3%. Forward carries 236 of the 354 ms.

3. **Whether the 10–25 MHz difference matters.** Only 9–12 clock samples per arm — too few. Needs `tools/h27zw_clock_matrix.sh` for per-kernel clock.
4. **`wQ/wO-fwd`: bench says 99.5%, trainer says 96.8%** at the same shape, config and clock. Leading candidate: trainer runs addmm (`beta != 0`), bench measured `beta == 0`.

Investigation done — I have the complete picture from the source.

## Where it lives: **BluTrain, not BluBLAS**

`BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/Kernels/cuda/matmul/MatmulBackward.cu` — a 1,471-line file with this structure:

```
line    3   #ifdef WITH_MYBLAS      <- BluBLAS path. ALL stream machinery is in here
line  731   #else // WITH_MYBLAS    <- cuBLAS path
line 1470   #endif
```

**BluBLAS itself creates no streams.** Grepping the library for `cudaStreamCreate` finds hits only in `examples/` test programs — never in library code. BluBLAS is stream-agnostic: it uses whatever `blublasSetStream()` was given. So this is entirely BluTrain's decision, made in the branch that only compiles when BluBLAS is the backend.

## Q: With multistream ON, does cuBLAS also go multistream? **No — it physically cannot.**

The cuBLAS branch (lines 731–1470) contains **zero** occurrences of `secondary`, `stream_b`, `cudaStreamCreate`, `cudaEventRecord`, or `cudaStreamWaitEvent`. Every call there uses the single incoming `stream`. And `bwd_single_stream()` is read at exactly one place — line 514, inside the BluBLAS branch.

**So `BLUTRAIN_BWD_SINGLE_STREAM` is a no-op in a cuBLAS build.** Measurement agrees: cuBLAS was stream 7 only, 34,720 launches, in all four captures, and its GEMM sum was identical across both campaigns (13,342.6 vs 13,336.3 locked = 0.05%).

## Q: Does it move only our matmuls, or other kernels too? **Only wgrad. Nothing else.**

`stream_b` and `handle_b` appear only in the grad_B code paths (lines 585–644). Everything else uses `handle_a` on the primary stream.

Across all of BluTrain's tensor library there are only **three** `cudaStreamCreate` calls:

```
include/DataLoader.h:567              host->device batch copies
include/checkpointing/Checkpointing.h:488   checkpoint writes
MatmulBackward.cu:87                  this one
```

So: **8,680 wgrad GEMMs on stream 16, and that's it.** No forward GEMM, no dgrad, no attention kernel, no convert, no layernorm. Confirmed by the layout template arg — stream 16 carries TN (wgrad) exclusively, with zero NN and zero NT.

## Q: Why only backward, and only grad_B?

Backward computes two GEMMs that are genuinely independent:

```
grad_A = grad_output @ B^T     (dgrad)  -> primary stream, handle_a
grad_B = A^T @ grad_output     (wgrad)  -> secondary stream, handle_b
```

They read the same inputs but write different outputs, so they can run at the same time. **Forward has only one GEMM per layer** — there's nothing to overlap it with. That's the whole reason it's backward-only.

## Q: How is it decided, and when?

**It isn't decided per-shape or dynamically — it's unconditional.** One line:

```c
cudaStream_t stream_b = bwd_1stream ? stream : get_secondary_stream_bwd(dev);
```

Every backward matmul call, every shape, every layer. The only switch is the env var, read once into a function-local static (deliberately — a `getenv` per call would show in a profile, and a mid-run flip would be a new bug).

## Q: Is the *wrong* compute on the other stream?

**No — the split and the synchronisation are both correct.** grad_A and grad_B really are independent, and the handshake is properly ordered:

```c
// before: secondary waits for upstream data produced on primary
cudaEventRecord(g_bwd_event_ready[dev], stream);
cudaStreamWaitEvent(stream_b, g_bwd_event_ready[dev], 0);
...
// after: primary waits for grad_B before anything downstream reads it
cudaEventRecord(g_bwd_event_done[dev], stream_b);
cudaStreamWaitEvent(stream, g_bwd_event_done[dev], 0);
```

Events use `cudaEventDisableTiming` (≈10× cheaper), the stream is `cudaStreamNonBlocking` so it doesn't serialise against the default stream, and both are cached per-device. It's competently written. It just doesn't pay.

## One thing to take back to your colleague

They said nobody uses it and compute is all on one stream now. **The code says otherwise** — `bwd_single_stream()` defaults to **false**, so the second stream is active in *every* BluBLAS training run unless someone explicitly sets the env var. That's what our captures show: 8,680 launches on stream 16 in the default configuration.

## Should we flip the default to OFF? The measurements say yes

```
                      tok/s ON    tok/s OFF     delta
locked 1400            23,389      23,292      +0.42%
free (production)      27,353      27,357      -0.01%
```

```
cost to our own kernels     dgrad +9.0% locked, +10.9% free slower
                            wgrad +4.7% locked,  +5.4% free slower
cost to measurement         3.4 points of apparent GEMM performance
benefit in production       nothing measurable
```

**But I won't recommend flipping it on this data alone.** Every tok/s number above comes from an nsys-profiled run, and nsys spreads launches apart — which reduces the overlap opportunity the second stream exists to exploit. Concluding from profiled data is exactly the mistake that produced the two corrections earlier today.

**The clean test is a 10-minute unprofiled tok/s A/B** — same config, no nsys, `BLUTRAIN_BWD_SINGLE_STREAM` unset vs `=1`, three runs each to clear the 0.3% noise floor. If ON still shows no gain, flip the default and we get honest per-kernel numbers for free.

Want me to write and launch that? The documentation agent is still working on §H27zW/§H27zX in parallel.

## Where the multistream question stands

**Answered from the source:**

| your question | answer |
|---|---|
| Does cuBLAS go multistream when the flag is on? | **No — impossible.** The machinery is inside `#ifdef WITH_MYBLAS`; the cuBLAS `#else` branch has zero stream/event calls. The env var is a no-op there. |
| Is it in BluTrain or BluBLAS? | **BluTrain** — `MatmulBackward.cu`. BluBLAS creates no streams in library code at all; it uses whatever `blublasSetStream()` gives it. |
| Only our matmuls, or other kernels? | **Only wgrad.** 8,680 GEMMs on stream 16. No forward, no dgrad, no attention, no converts. BluTrain's whole tensor lib has only 3 stream creations — DataLoader, checkpointing, and this. |
| Why only backward? | Backward has two independent GEMMs (grad_A, grad_B) that can overlap. Forward has one per layer — nothing to overlap with. |
| How is it decided? | **Not decided at all** — unconditional, one line, every call, every shape. Only the env var changes it. |
| Is the wrong compute on the other stream? | **No.** The split is legitimate and the event handshake is correct in both directions. Competently written; it just doesn't pay. |

**And two things it was hiding, both now cleared:**
- dgrad 91.8% → **100.0%**, wgrad 94.6% → **99.0%** once single-stream
- our split-K reduce 47.4 ms → **13.3 ms**, which makes it **20% faster than cuBLAS's**, not 2.84× slower

**Your colleague's belief is wrong on one point worth passing on:** the default is `false`, so the second stream is active in *every* BluBLAS training run right now — that's the 8,680 launches on stream 16 we captured with no env var set.

If h27zY shows no gain unprofiled, flipping the default to OFF costs nothing and buys honest per-kernel numbers permanently.

### CLAUDE [2026-08-25 19:57 IST]

Let me verify the mechanism before I answer the "could we do it better" question — it hinges on how many SMs one of our GEMMs already occupies.
> tool `Bash`: Get CTA counts per GEMM kernel
> tool `Bash`: Get shared memory per CTA to establish occupancy

The shared-memory numbers settle your question — you're right, and now there's a hard reason rather than a hunch.

## You're right: skip the run. Here's why it can't matter

```
our GEMM kernel, per CTA:
  dynamicSharedMemory   229,376 bytes  = 224 KB
  sharedMemoryExecuted  233,472 bytes  = 228 KB
  registersPerThread    168
  block                 384 threads
  grid                  132 CTAs        (H200 has 132 SMs)
```

**An H200 SM has 228 KB of shared memory. One of our CTAs takes all of it.** So occupancy is exactly **1 CTA per SM**, and one GEMM already sits on all 132 SMs.

That means a second concurrent GEMM's CTAs **physically cannot start** until a CTA of the first one retires and releases its 224 KB. There is no fine-grained overlap available at all — only tail-filling, as the first kernel's CTAs drain.

**That's a hardware capacity fact. nsys cannot change it.** Profiling shifts *when* launches happen; it does not create shared memory. So the ceiling on this feature is the tail window either way, and the run would just re-measure a bound we can already read off the occupancy. Agreed — not worth 35 minutes.

## Is our implementation wrong or inefficient? No — and cuBLAS would hit the same wall

```
ours    grid(132,1,1) = 132 CTAs   block 384
cuBLAS  grid(2,66,1)  = 132 CTAs   block 384
```

Both are **persistent kernels sized exactly to the SM count**. cuBLAS made the identical design choice. If the trainer gave cuBLAS two streams, it would contend the same way. So this is not our scheduling being clumsy — the event handshake is correct, the stream is non-blocking, the events are timing-disabled. The design is fine; the design is just **incompatible with persistent grids**.

## Q: is stream_b inside the wgrad kernel, or in the training script?

**In the training script, host-side.** The kernel knows nothing about streams. BluTrain does `blublasSetStream(handle_b, stream_b)` and then issues the wgrad GEMM through `handle_b`. It's purely which stream the launch goes on — no kernel code differs.

## Q: could it be done a better way?

**Not by overlapping two GEMMs.** Any variant hits the same 1-CTA/SM wall:

- **Shrink the grids** (66 CTAs each) → you've partitioned the GPU, not overlapped. Each GEMM runs ~2× slower, plus worse tile quantization. Net zero at best.
- **MPS / green contexts** → same partitioning, just enforced differently.

**But there is a real overlap opportunity, and it isn't GEMM-with-GEMM:**

```
convert_type_kernel<bfloat16_t,float>   4728.0 ms   34,936 launches
convert_type_kernel<float,bfloat16_t>   3938.2 ms   26,120 launches
                                        --------
                                        8666.2 ms   = 23.6% of GPU time
```

Those are **memory-bound** and use almost no shared memory. Our GEMMs are **compute-bound** and use all of it. That's the classic pairing that actually overlaps. Overlapping a GEMM with a convert is worth something; overlapping two GEMMs is worth nothing. That's a BluTrain-side change and a bigger piece of work, but it's where 23.6% of the time is sitting.

## Q: locked vs free scaling — is it still open?

Yes, still open, and let me correct one thing: **our throughput is not the same locked and free.** We do scale:

```
              locked -> free      clock          tok/s gain / clock gain
ours          23,292 -> 27,357    1410 -> 1939   1.1745 / 1.3752 = 0.854
cuBLAS        23,406 -> 27,784    1410 -> 1964   1.1870 / 1.3929 = 0.852
```

**End-to-end we convert clock into throughput exactly as well as cuBLAS** (0.854 vs 0.852). The end-to-end gap is that cuBLAS *got* 1.29% more clock.

But at the GEMM level the picture is different:

```
down-fwd      ours 694.8 -> 805.8 TF = 1.160x    cuBLAS 705.5 -> 869.1 = 1.232x
              efficiency 0.843                          0.884
```

So on the forward `nn` sites cuBLAS genuinely does convert clock better — it's just diluted end-to-end because our GEMM is only 37.6% of GPU time.

**Caution:** the clock difference itself is unreliable at this sample count — h27zW gave 1942 vs 1948 (0.31% apart), h27zX gave 1939 vs 1964 (1.29% apart). Same workload, wildly different. 10–11 device samples cannot resolve this. It needs the per-kernel instrument (`tools/h27zw_clock_matrix.sh`), which is the open item as noted.

## Q: is split-K closed?

**Yes, closed and it was a false alarm.** Our reduce is 13.3 ms vs cuBLAS's 16.7 ms — we're **20% faster**. The 47.4 ms reading was 3.6× multistream contention, since our reduce runs on stream 16 as wgrad's epilogue.

## My recommendation

**Flip `BLUTRAIN_BWD_SINGLE_STREAM` to default ON (single stream).** The case:

- Overlap is capacity-impossible beyond tail-filling — 1 CTA/SM, proven from the occupancy
- Measured worth: **+0.42% at locked clocks, −0.01% at free clocks**. Production runs free.
- Cost: our dgrad kernels **+9–11% slower**, wgrad **+5%**, and **3.4 points** of permanent distortion on every per-kernel measurement we take
- Worst case from flipping: we give up 0.42% at a clock setting nobody trains at

Want me to make that change? It's one line in `MatmulBackward.cu` plus the comment explaining why, and I'd stage it for you to push.

Stop — the convert-overlap idea dies for the same reason. Let me show you before we build it.

```
H200 SM budget:  65,536 x 32-bit registers  |  228 KB shared memory

our GEMM CTA:  384 threads x 168 regs = 64,512 of 65,536 = 98.4% of registers
               228 KB of 228 KB              = 100.0% of shared memory

left over for any co-resident CTA:  1,024 registers  =  32 threads
```

**One of our GEMM CTAs consumes 100% of an SM's shared memory and 98.4% of its registers.** Nothing can sit beside it — not another GEMM, not a convert, not anything. A convert kernel needs no shared memory at all, but it still needs registers, and there are 1,024 left on the whole SM.

So concurrent-kernel overlap with our GEMM is **impossible in general**, not just for GEMM-with-GEMM. Only tail-filling, which is the 62.8 ms we already measured. Building the convert-overlap would take a day and measure zero.

## The right move is to delete the converts, not overlap them

```
convert_type_kernel<bfloat16_t,float>   34,936 launches   4,728.0 ms   12.88%   <- GEMM OUTPUTS, up-cast
convert_type_kernel<float,bfloat16_t>   26,120 launches   3,938.2 ms   10.73%   <- GEMM INPUTS, down-cast
                                                          --------
                                                          8,666.2 ms   23.60%
```

34,936 up-casts against 34,720 GEMM launches — that's **one per GEMM output**. BluTrain holds everything in fp32 (`swiglu_forward_kernel_vec<float>`, `rms_norm_..._sm90<float>`, `add_kernel<float>`), so every matmul goes: cast down → GEMM → cast up.

**And our accumulator is already fp32.** We currently round it to bf16 on store, then BluTrain launches a kernel to read that bf16 back and widen it to fp32. That round trip is pure waste:

```
today:   GEMM (fp32 acc) --round--> bf16 in DRAM --convert kernel--> fp32 in DRAM
         convert traffic = read 2N bytes + write 4N bytes = 6N bytes + a kernel launch

fused:   GEMM (fp32 acc) --------------------------------> fp32 in DRAM
         extra cost = 2N more bytes on the GEMM's own store, no extra kernel
```

Net: **~4N bytes of DRAM traffic and 34,936 kernel launches removed — up to 4,728 ms, 12.9% of GPU time.** And it *improves* precision, since we stop rounding to bf16 and back.

I checked: the SM90 template has **no fp32-output knob today** — no `OUT_FP32`, `OutT`, or equivalent. So this is new work, not a flag flip. But it's the single largest opportunity on the table, and it's ~34× bigger than the 140 ms still left on the GEMM itself.

The input down-cast (3,938 ms) is harder — TMA loads bf16 as-is, and casting during load would need 2× shared memory, which we've just established there is none of. Park that.

**`MatmulBackward.cu`** — default flipped:

```c
static inline bool bwd_single_stream() {
   static const bool v = [] {

```

```
"00"     -> single    "01"   -> single    "0x" -> single         "2"  -> single
"false"  -> single    "no"   -> single    "0 " -> single         " 0" -> single
```

Only a literal `0` restores two streams. Everything ambiguous falls to the default — which is now the safe path, so it fails in the right direction.

## Your cuBLAS question — answered, and the answer is the opposite of what you feared

Here is the actual cuBLAS call in BluTrain's backward, at `MatmulBackward.cu:1256-1264`:

```c
cudaDataType_t cuda_type = std::is_same<T, float16_t>::value || std::is_same<T, __half>::value
                           ? CUDA_R_16F : CUDA_R_16BF;
cublasGemmEx(handle, opB_bwd, CUBLAS_OP_N, K_a, M, N, &alpha_f,
    b_ptr,  cuda_type, ldb_bwd,        // A  = bf16
    go_ptr, cuda_type, ldgo_bwd,       // B  = bf16
    &beta_f, ga_ptr, cuda_type, ldga_bwd,   // C  = bf16   <-- SAME VARIABLE
    CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F, CUBLAS_GEMM_DEFAULT_TENSOR_OP);
```

**One variable is reused in all three slots.** So cuBLAS is *asked* for bf16 output — that's BluTrain's choice, not a cuBLAS limitation. And `cublas_api.h:3368` confirms `Atype`, `Btype`, `Ctype` are independent parameters.

So: **yes, we can change it, and it's one token** — `ga_ptr, cuda_type` → `ga_ptr, CUDA_R_32F`.

That also explains why the capture showed 34,936 up-converts in *both* builds: both backends output bf16, both pay the round trip.

## Is it "legal to our ethics"? Yes — and this line is why

Three reasons it's legitimate, not a benchmark trick:

1. **The same one-token change is available to cuBLAS.** So when we compare, both get fp32 output. Nobody is doing less work than the other. That satisfies your own apples-to-apples rule.
2. **It increases precision.** We stop rounding a 24-bit significand down to 8 bits and back. There's no accuracy being traded for speed.
3. **It's a standard configuration**, not an exotic hack — every BLAS API exposes output type independently of input type precisely because this case is normal.

The only thing that *would* be dishonest is giving ourselves fp32 output and leaving cuBLAS on bf16. So the rule is: **whatever we change, change it in the cuBLAS branch too.**

## And this gives us a far cheaper first experiment than I proposed

**We can test the entire hypothesis on the cuBLAS path, without touching our kernel at all.** One token in the cuBLAS branch, remove the matching convert on the BluTrain side, measure tok/s. If the win is real, it shows up there — and our kernel is unchanged, so nothing can regress.

Ordered plan, cheapest first:

- **Step 0 (~2 min).** Probe: does the cuBLAS heuristic on H200 actually accept `16BF` in / `32F` out? A 20-line `cublasGemmEx` call checking the status. Worth doing because heuristics *do* refuse combinations — we already hit exactly that on sm_86 with bf16 bias output, where cuBLASLt returned zero algos.
- **Step 1 (~30 min).** Map the 21 sites' consumers. **This is the number that decides everything and I don't have it yet.** Some GEMM outputs feed straight into *another* GEMM, which wants bf16 again — for those, fp32 output just *moves* the convert instead of removing it. Until I know which of the 21 are which, "4,728 ms" is a ceiling, not an estimate.
- **Step 2 (~1 hr).** One-token change on the cuBLAS path + drop the matching convert + measure. Proves the win at zero risk.
- **Step 3.** Only if 0–2 pay: build it into our kernel — as a **template knob**, not a separate kernel. Standing rule, and a separate kernel couldn't compose with the cluster/swizzle/raster/PDL/skew knobs.

Two things I expect to bite in step 3, both unverified: our CTA already uses **100% of the SM's shared memory**, so an fp32 epilogue staging tile may not fit; and if the epilogue uses `stmatrix`, that instruction is 16-bit only and the fp32 path would need a different store.

## Review fixes done

The reviewers passed the production change and **blocked my test script** — three blocking bugs. All fixed:

- **`h27zY` built the wrong trainer.** `make train-bin` with no `MODE` defaults to `gpt2`, which would have trained a GPT-2 against the production config — it loads without error, so the run looks valid. Now pins `MODE=production` and greps the build log to prove it.
- **The tok/s regex couldn't match.** production prints `tok/s`, gpt2 prints `tok/sec:`. Every rep would have recorded `n/a` and the summary would print an empty block after 30 minutes.
- **Both arms could be contaminated.** Defining an arm by the *absence* of the env var meant an ambient `export BLUTRAIN_BWD_SINGLE_STREAM=0` made both arms two-stream and printed `+0.00%` — reading as a clean null confirming the change. Both arms now set it positively, and the kernel **prints the mode it latched** so the script asserts it instead of assuming.
- Plus: alternating arm order, guarded build with an mtime check, clock and placement sampling per rep, and `blublas_NO_PDL` pinned in both arms.

Also fixed in the `.cu`: `strcmp` instead of an order-dependent `&&` chain, the latch semantics documented, and my claim that the cuBLAS branch has "zero stream calls" corrected — it has no *secondary* stream and no events, but it does call `cublasSetStream`. Recompiled clean, exit 0.

**Two pre-existing bugs the reviewers found that you should know about** (not mine, not fixed):
- `MatmulBackward.cu:720` — a `throw` sits between the two-stream pre-handshake and the rejoin, so on the `=0` path an exception skips the rejoin and the primary stream never waits for grad_B. Safe today only by which fallback kernels happen to exist.
- `MatmulBackward.cu:637` — the fp16 grad_B branch hardcodes `beta=0.0f` and discards the caller's `beta_b`, which is the exact defect the comment above it says was fixed.

**what the conversions cost**
